items.title: REFERRAL TO THE COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE (COW) MEETING ON FEBRUARY 25, 2026, FOR A DISCUSSION RELATING TO THE ANNUAL PERFORMANCE EVALUATION FOR CITY MANAGER ERIC T. CARPENTER.
items.action: Item Referred. Item separated from the Consent Agenda by Commissioner Fernandez. The Item was referred by Acclamation to the Committee of the Whole Meeting of February 25, 2026. Vote: 7-0. Marla Alpizar to handle.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Item Referred. Item separated from the Consent Agenda by Commissioner Fernandez.
The Item was referred by Acclamation to the Committee of the Whole Meeting of February 25,
2026. Vote: 7-0. Marla Alpizar to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Commissioner Fernandez explained that he separated the Item due to concerns about timing. He
stated that the City Manager’s employment contract requires the City Commission to conduct an
annual performance evaluation within 45 days before or after the anniversary date, which he noted
falls on July 24. According to the contract, the earliest suitable time for the evaluation would be
early June. He expressed concern that the Item appeared on the agenda several months earlier
than necessary and asked why the evaluation is being proposed now rather than in line with the
contractual schedule.
City Manager Carpenter explained that the evaluation would ordinarily have been scheduled as part
of the Committee of the Whole calendar in 2025, but that it had been inadvertently omitted from the
October 2025 agenda. It was further stated that the Item was being brought forward now to address
that omission.
Commissioner Fernandez acknowledged the explanation but reiterated that he would prefer to
conduct the evaluation in June, in line with the contract, to give the City Manager more time to
make progress on several key goals the City Commission had publicly identified. He specifically
mentioned permitting, which he noted has been an ongoing concern raised by multiple
Commissioners.
Mayor Meiner inquired about the reason for including it on the agenda now.
Commissioner Fernandez said he prefers to stick closely to the contract’s schedule to avoid
performing an evaluation in the middle of the cycle or when the City is busy with operational issues
like Spring Break and permitting. He stressed that his goal is to give enough time for progress on
those priorities before doing a formal evaluation.
City Manager Carpenter explained that the Item has been placed on the agenda now, even though
historically evaluations occur within 45 days of the anniversary date, because last year that timeline
was missed.
Mayor Meiner stated that although he does not feel strongly about it, he would like to provide
feedback. He believes it is beneficial for the City Commission to convene in a room together to
discuss the evaluation, particularly given Sunshine Law constraints that limit informal discussion
outside of a noticed meeting. He suggested that, because of the delay, the City Commission could
conduct an evaluation now to address the missed cycle from the prior year and then conduct
another evaluation later in the year in accordance with the contract. The Mayor stated that he did
not see an issue with that approach.
Commissioner Fernandez clarified that he is not contemplating any financial considerations, such
as bonuses, at this time and emphasized that the discussion will be limited to performance
feedback. He expressed openness to holding a discussion on February 25 and noted that
evaluations of this nature are typically led by the Mayor. He also stated that he preferred such Items
to be sponsored through the Mayor’s office rather than being self-initiated.
City Manager Carpenter clarified that Human Resources had placed the Item on the agenda and
that historically, evaluations had been brought forward in different ways, including sponsorship by
the Mayor.
Mayor Meiner indicated that he has assumed sponsorship because he has been asked to select a
date for the Item.
Commissioner Fernandez said he would follow the Mayor’s lead on this. Usually, the Commission
defers to the Mayor in such matters. He will follow the Mayor’s guidance if he believes now is the
right time.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas stated that she is a new member of the City Commission and does not
feel fully equipped to provide a comprehensive evaluation and would appreciate additional time.
She acknowledged, however, the competing desire to give feedback before the City Commission’s
focus shifts heavily toward Spring Break activities. She indicated she is torn but suggested that a
discussion in March or April might be appropriate.
The Mayor noted that an April timeframe would match the anniversary dates of other Charter
Officers. However, it was also noted that City Manager Carpenter had previously declined to
participate in that cycle because it did not fall within the contractual 45-day window around his
anniversary date.
City Manager Carpenter stated that an April date would align with the other Charter Officers. He
was asked last year if he wanted to be included, and he politely declined because it was not within
the 45 days of his anniversary date.
Commissioner Fernandez asked to have a discussion on February 25 to address the missed
evaluation from the prior year, while also committing to conducting a second evaluation later in the
year in strict compliance with the contract’s timing requirements. He explained that this approach
would help the Commission catch up and stay contractually compliant going forward.
The Item was referred to the Committee of the Whole by a 7-0 vote.

items.title: REFERRAL TO THE FINANCE AND ECONOMIC RESILIENCY COMMITTEE TO DISCUSS THE FEASIBILITY, FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS, AND EXPECTED OUTCOMES REGARDING THE POTENTIAL ESTABLISHMENT OF A MOUNTED (HORSE) POLICE PATROL.
items.action: The Item was dually referred to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee and the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by Commissioner Fernandez. The Item was dually referred by acclamation to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee and the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee. Jason Greene and Mark Taxis to place on the respective Committee Agendas Pending List. Chief Wayne Jones to handle.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: The Item was dually referred to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee
and the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee. The Item was separated
from the Consent Agenda by Commissioner Fernandez. The Item was dually referred by
acclamation to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee and the Public Safety and
Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee. Jason Greene and Mark Taxis to place on the
respective Committee Agendas Pending List. Chief Wayne Jones to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Commissioner Fernandez introduced the Item regarding the feasibility of establishing a mounted
horse patrol within the Police Department. When the City considers creating or analyzing law
enforcement operations, it is important to clearly outline potential patrol functions, operational
effectiveness, and public safety considerations. A mounted patrol could impact policing strategy,
deployment, community engagement, and overall effectiveness, so it warrants careful and thorough
review. Out of respect for the process and the subject matter, the Item should also be referred to
the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee. He noted that he was surprised to
see a public safety-related Item referred solely to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee,
as matters involving policing and law enforcement are typically first reviewed by the Public Safety
and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee.
Mayor Meiner agreed with Commissioner Fernandez and believes a dual referral makes sense to
the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee and the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality
of Life Committee.
The Item was dually referred to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee and the Public
Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee by acclamation.

VOTES:

Pursuant to Ordinance 2015-3954, Sec. 2-12(3), Addendum Agenda Item RDA 1 was approved by
Mayor Meiner for inclusion on the agenda.
Commissioner Bhatt introduced Item C4 U, an addendum referral to the Public Safety and
Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee. The purpose of the referral is to discuss and develop the
details of a 12-month Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing Pilot Program in North Beach, with a
total cost not to exceed $100,000. The Item also requests that the Administration create guidelines
and application criteria for the program.
The motion to approve the referral was made by Commissioner Bhatt and seconded by
Commissioner Alex Fernandez. The vote was unanimous in favor.
Commissioners Magazine noted that the program aims to incentivize redevelopment of affordable
housing rather than new construction.
Commissioner Bhatt apologized to attendees for the wait and thanked them for their patience and
involvement. She noted that the Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) expressed strong
support for the Item and highlighted that 10% of CRA revenues must be legally allocated to
affordable housing. The pilot program is designed to promote infill housing and redevelopment
without demolition.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, CONSENTING TO THE APPOINTMENT OF JOHN REBAR AS THE DIRECTOR OF THE NEWLY STRUCTURED DEPARTMENT OF PARKS, FACILITIES, FLEET, AND BEACHES OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH.
items.action: Resolution 2026-34065 was adopted. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by Commissioner Fernandez. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 7-0. Marla Alpizar to handle.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34065 was adopted. The Item was separated from the Consent
Agenda by Commissioner Fernandez. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the
Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 7-0. Marla Alpizar to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Commissioner Fernandez thanked the Mayor and explained that he deliberately separated the Item
to raise procedural concerns. He wants to address the Item directly and noted that the City
Manager had previously explained that it involved a restructuring of City departments.
City Manager Carpenter confirmed that this was correct. He explained that, in this instance, the City
had combined the Facilities and Fleet functions and created a consolidated Department of Parks,
Facilities, Fleet, and Beach Operations.
Commissioner Fernandez emphasized that departments are created by the City Commission
through Ordinance. He explained that once departments are established by Ordinance, the City
Commission then adopts a budget and appoints department directors accordingly. He noted that
the City Commission has not amended the City’s organizational chart, nor has it adopted an
Ordinance to eliminate the Fleet Department or the Facilities Department or to formally consolidate
those functions into a single department. Before approving such a restructuring, he wants to
understand the cost savings and any unintended consequences, especially regarding the Parks
Department. He explained that, while the City routinely receives complaints about many
departments, the Parks Department is one of the few that consistently receives positive feedback
from the public. He described the Parks Department as operating effectively and delivering high-
quality services, stating that he does not want to jeopardize that success. He reiterated that it is
within the authority and jurisdiction of the City Commission to create, consolidate, or eliminate
departments by Ordinance, while the appointment of directors remains within the City Manager’s
prerogative. He expressed concern that, as the City closely analyzes cost savings and efficiencies,
the City Commission needs assurances that consolidating multiple functions under a single director
would not negatively impact service delivery, especially for parks operations. Having one director
oversee such a large portfolio effectively creates a role comparable to an Assistant City Manager,
even if not titled as such. He stated that he wants clarity on the budget implications, whether there
would be actual savings, and whether the expanded scope would compromise the high level of
service currently provided by the Parks Department, which he described as “second to none.”
City Manager Carpenter acknowledged Commissioner Fernandez’s concerns and stated that his
goal is to introduce a clean-up Ordinance within the next few months to formally address the
restructuring. He explained that the consolidation aims to improve the City’s organizational structure
and operational efficiency in the short term. He mentioned that he had contacted the
Commissioners beforehand to discuss the change and agreed that the Parks Department has been
very successful, attributing much of that success to the leadership of the Department Director John
Rebar. He added that expanding the director’s responsibilities would demonstrate his ability to
manage a broader scope and additional operational demands.
Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the Resolution, seconded by Commissioner
Fernandez. Vote: 7-0.
items.motion: Suarez made a motion to adopt the Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34079 was adopted. The Item was separated from the Consent
Agenda by Commissioner Suarez. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the Resolution,
seconded by Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas. Vote: 7-0. Jose Gonzalez to handle.
DIRECTION:
• Prepare an LTC, detailing:
1. Total number of current trolley vehicles.
2. Number of vehicles currently wrapped with advertising.
Jose Gonzalez to handle.
• Transportation team to develop creative revenue strategies
1. Explore advertising opportunities on trolleys.
2. Consider innovative funding ideas to support transportation services.
Jose Gonzalez to handle.
• Explore ways to offset costs without cutting resident services
1. Review expenses and identify areas for internal savings.
Jose Gonzalez to handle.
Per Commissioner Suarez’s request, Jose Gonzalez, Transportation and Mobility Director,
explained that this is a Resolution approving an increase to the hourly rate of the trolley service
during the transition period. This is the time under the new trolley contract when they are still using
the current trolley vehicles until the new vehicles are delivered and put into service. This Item
accounts for higher costs in terms of maintenance, insurance, repairs, and inflation over the past six
years, during which there has been no rate increase. In response to Commissioner Suarez, he
noted that inflation has been calculated at about 25%. This Item, based on months-long
negotiations with the vendor, settled on a 15% increase to the current hourly rates, which they
consider fair and reasonable. The CPI has been approximately 25% since 2020. This rate would
apply to the current vehicles, and that contract is a decade old. In continued responses,
Commissioner Suarez announced that for this fiscal year, the net fiscal impact is $950,000, and for
a full 12-month period, it is $1.4 million. This increase would be implemented immediately upon
approval and would only be in effect during the transition period. Once the new vehicles are in
service, this rate would no longer apply, and a new rate of $124.19 per hour would be instituted. If
this Item is approved, the rate for the current vehicles would be $87.42 per hour for high-floor
trolleys and $100.69 for low-floor trolleys. Subsequently, these rates would remain in effect until the
transition period ends. After it expires and the new vehicles are in service, the $124.19 hourly rate
will take effect.
Commissioner Suarez warned his colleagues that at the last meeting, they approved the rollback
rate. If this results in an extra $1.4 million coming out of their budget, that money will need to be
taken from elsewhere. He emphasized that whenever more funds are required, and they want to
stay committed to the rollback rate, those funds must come from other areas. A million dollars is a
significant amount, and he wanted to make sure everyone is aware of that.
Commissioner Magazine noted that since the budget meeting eight months ago, they have been
preparing for a large gap in Transportation Funding. They discussed creative ways to raise revenue
and talked about advertising. This is anecdotal, but he has been paying increasing attention to the
number of buses and trolleys in the City that are completely unwrapped and unadvertised. The fact
that the rates are not being utilized, even during events like the College Football National
Championship, Art Basel, which recurs annually, and a revamped Spring Break, is concerning. With
the upcoming World Cup, G20 in a year, and other major events, he is having a hard time believing
the current efforts are enough. Businesses want to advertise on delivery robots, yet the City cannot
find better advertising options for trolleys. He appreciates Commissioner Suarez's comments and
acknowledges there may be many options, but solutions will need to come from somewhere. They
have been sounding the alarm about transportation contracts for a year. He challenges staff to do
two things: first, if trolleys are stored overnight in off-site yards, they can obtain an LTC by midweek
next week, detailing how many trolleys they have and how many are currently wrapped with
advertising. Second, he wants the Transportation team to develop more creative ways to raise
funds to maintain a robust transportation system. Jose Gonzalez will handle this.
Jose Gonzalez, Transportation and Mobility Director, mentioned that they are reviewing the entire
operating budget to identify opportunities to cut, reduce, streamline, or eliminate services when
necessary. These discussions are part of the City’s budget process.
Commissioner Magazine requested an internal review. When they cut a billion-dollar budget, it
should not start with residents or community services. Instead, they should evaluate how to become
more efficient and save money internally before making cuts that affect the community.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas has a discussion Item, R9 AJ, about generating revenue through
creative proposals, including naming rights. After the discussion, she suggested exploring ways to
offset some of the costs to avoid cutting too much into residents' services. She requested to see the
numbers for trolley service utilization.
Commissioner Suarez motioned to adopt the Resolution, seconded by Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas.
Vote: 7-0.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34106 was adopted. Office of the City Clerk, Hernan Cardeno, and
Jason Greene to handle. Clerk’s Note: This Item was approved as part of the Consent Agenda.
Mayor Steven Meiner acknowledged the presence of Miami-Dade County Tax Collector Dariel
Fernandez, stating that the City was honored to have Mr. Fernandez in attendance. Mayor Meiner
noted giving Mr. Fernandez a shout-out during the State of the City address the previous evening
and thanked him for his partnership and updates.
Dariel Fernandez addressed the Commission, thanking them for the opportunity to speak and
introducing himself as the County Tax Collector. Mr. Fernandez expressed support for Item C7 AW,
sponsored by Commissioner Alex Fernandez, and explained that the Resolution would create
greater coordination related to compliance with Federal Cuban sanctions and reinforce the
importance of proper authorization for businesses operating under Federal sanctions programs. Mr.
Fernandez stated that for more than 65 years, the Cuban communist and socialist dictatorship has
oppressed the people of Cuba, exported repression, and continued operating with financial support
and special agreements from other nations. He emphasized that no community understands this
reality better than Miami-Dade and highlighted the importance of sanctions, enforcement, and
accountability measures. Mr. Fernandez thanked Commissioner Fernandez and the City
Commission for considering the Item, affirmed his office’s readiness to support lawful compliance
and serve the public with professionalism, and said, “God bless Miami-Dade County. God bless
Miami Beach. And God bless the United States of America.” Mr. Fernandez then continued with an
announcement, stating that in three weeks, on March 5, the Miami-Dade County Tax Collector’s
Office would open a new office in Miami Beach for the first time. He invited all attendees to the
opening and explained that the Office would allow residents to avoid traveling to Downtown Miami
for services. Services would include applying for local business tax receipts, renewing car
registrations, renewing IDs, obtaining new driver’s licenses, purchasing fishing and hunting
licenses, paying property taxes, and receiving assistance with property tax questions. Mr.
Fernandez stated that the Office would feature 13 to 14 service windows and expressed excitement
about serving the people of Miami Beach. He thanked the City Manager, Commissioner Alex
Fernandez, Mayor Meiner, and the entire Commission for their support.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez spoke in support of the Resolution, emphasizing that the initiative
reinforces compliance with existing laws at the Federal, State, and County levels governing
transactions and business activities involving Cuba and other sanctioned foreign governments.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that the Resolution does not create foreign policy but ensures the
enforcement of existing laws. He explained that when businesses are identified as illegally
engaging with Cuba, the City should act to shut down their operations and make clear that such
activities have no place in the community. Commissioner Fernandez stressed the importance of
supporting democracy and opposing regimes that have destroyed families, killed people, and
imprisoned opponents. He thanked Mr. Fernandez for bringing the initiative forward and
commended the Commission for prioritizing people first.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine expressed appreciation for Mr. Fernandez’s commitment to Miami
Beach and Miami-Dade County, noting his active presence throughout the community.
Commissioner Magazine requested to be added as a co-sponsor of the Resolution and shared a
personal story about his daughter’s mother, who grew up under a communist regime in Poland and
witnessed her father being kidnapped and never returning. Commissioner Magazine stated that the
Resolution is meaningful to families who have experienced oppression and thanked Commissioner
Fernandez for his leadership.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez thanked the Commission for also approving a related Resolution on
consent, expressing hope for a peaceful transition to democracy in Venezuela. (See Item C7 AF.)
He noted that Venezuela recently captured and arrested another dictator who repressed rights and
executed people, drawing parallels to Cuba. Commissioner Fernandez thanked the Commission for
standing in unity with the Venezuelan community and emphasized that what unites these efforts is
opposition to oppression.
Mayor Meiner stated that he is looking forward to the upcoming opening of the Tax Collector’s
Office on March 5.
Clerk’s Note: This Item was approved as part of the Consent Agenda.
Handouts and Reference Materials:
1. Email from Dariel Fernandez, Miami-Dade County Tax Collector, Date: February 3, 2026, RE:
Letter of Support for Item C7 AW Regarding Oversight of Commerce With Cuba.

Land Use and Sustainability Committee. Thomas Mooney to place on the Committee Agenda
and to handle.
Commissioner Suarez wants to reconsider and discuss what they are really aiming to achieve. The
current situation on Washington Avenue is clearly heading downward. They have attempted
landscaping, lighting, and tree wrapping, which help but do not address the core issue. Today, there
are still vacant stores, foreclosures, homelessness, nuisance businesses, and too many adult-
oriented businesses and small shops. In about a one-mile stretch, there are over 35 vacant or
neglected storefronts; this is not a thriving corridor. The harsh truth is that no one visits Washington
Avenue as residents; that should concern everyone involved. The last significant update to the
City's comprehensive zoning and urban planning for this corridor was in 1989, when he was five
years old. Cities do not remain unchanged for decades; they either improve or decline. At the same
time, we must acknowledge a larger issue. Great cities worldwide embrace mixed-use urban
planning. People live above shops, streets are lively day and night, and neighborhoods are
designed for living, working, and playing, not just for cars or tourists. Miami Beach has fallen behind
in providing housing for residents, young professionals, families, seniors, and the essential
workforce. Nearly 90% of City staff do not live in Miami Beach, with many commuting over an hour
each way; not by choice, but because that is where affordable housing is located. When cities fail to
build accessible housing, people are pushed further out, commutes grow longer, traffic worsens,
and development pressure pushes outward. That is why growth tends to occur near the Everglades,
not because it makes sense, but because housing closer to jobs has been blocked. It is also why
the State passed the Live Local Act. When cities do not provide enough housing, the State
intervenes by overriding local zoning authority, which may increase housing in some areas but
sacrifices local control and environmental protections. Urban scholar Richard Florida summed it up
well: the true crisis in American cities is the forgotten middle, people earning too much for
affordable housing but not enough to afford decent housing. His proposals include improving safety
through activity, reducing long commutes, and building housing where infrastructure already exists.
The question is simple: Is Washington Avenue a corridor they are proud of today? If not, are they
willing to lead? This presents an opportunity to reimagine Washington Avenue as one of Miami
Beach’s greatest streets, a place where people live, walk, work, and belong. A street built for
residents, not just visitors. That is the vision behind this presentation. Click here to view. Discussion
held.
Thomas Mooney, Planning Director, explained that when Commissioner Suarez approached him
two years ago, he was at a National Planning Conference in Minneapolis and had a lengthy
conversation about Washington Avenue. One of the key topics promoted nationally in urban
planning is mixed-use development, especially in City areas, introducing residential spaces that can
be used without cars by utilizing transit. He mentioned to Commissioner Suarez that Washington
Avenue has never been approached comprehensively regarding incentivizing residential
development, despite a small residential bonus of 0.5 being in place since 1989. However, no one
has taken serious steps to build residential units. In fact, in 2015, when a task force focused on
Washington Avenue, staff recommended providing incentives for residential development as well.
The task force initially disagreed because they wanted to prioritize hotels, believing Washington
Avenue was better suited for commercial use. Their argument then was that adding residential units
would bring more people 24/7 who could use the spaces morning, noon, and night, and the only
way to achieve that is through an infusion of residential development. Discussion held.
Commissioner Suarez stated that staff recommended, at the time, offering more incentives for
residential development. However, the task force decided not to pursue that and instead incentivize
more hotel development, which Planning Director Mooney agreed with. Commissioner Suarez
believes it is important to play this video from that period to provide historical context. Click here to
view.
Commissioner Suarez said this is a bad idea that has failed badly. Washington Avenue, until
recently, when the three new Commissioners and the Mayor were elected, was full of gunfire almost
every High Impact weekend, and they had to wash blood off the streets. It was chaos. Even now,
they have done everything to beautify Washington Avenue. The streets are clean, trees are
decorated with beautiful lights, and landscaping is perfect, but many storefronts are vacant. There is
a lot of homelessness, and unfortunately, businesses deal with homeless people buying and selling
stolen bikes. Residents rarely visit Washington Avenue. Planning Director Mooney’s staff
recommended more residential development, but he was overruled in favor of more transient use,
and now the corridor is a failure because of that decision.
Thomas Mooney, Planning Director, mentioned that he suggested to Commissioner Suarez that
there should be a more tangible incentive for residential development. This incentive should go
beyond just an FAR increase in height and be more substantive yet strategic. Not simply a
straightforward FAR increase like in Town Center (TCC), where developers can do anything they
want with it, but something with guardrails that ensures those taking advantage of the incentive
would build non-transient residential units that better serve the area. Washington Avenue is a
defined commercial corridor with established transit options, including bus lines and potential micro-
mobility or trolley networks. While it lacks a dedicated regional transit system on fixed rail or
dedicated lanes, Planning Director Mooney believes there are enough people willing to use transit
who would not need a car. Therefore, the incentive could be structured around reducing car
dependency to prevent further strain on already-constrained roadways. This incentive targets
inherently urban dwellers, specifically those without vehicles or with just one or two vehicles who
rarely drive daily. It is designed for residents who rely on transit or micromobility. The incentives are
based on this concept. Additionally, the proposal suggests an FAR up to 4.0, with a maximum
height of 100 feet, including bonuses. This height constraint aligns with the characteristics of a large
commercial corridor. Massing studies included with the proposal illustrate different design options.
A rigorous Historic Preservation Board (HPB) approval process will oversee each application,
allowing the board to maintain control and ensure taller buildings incorporate articulation. This
approach aims to increase the number of full-time residents along Washington Avenue who do not
rely on cars, instead using transit or micromobility, ultimately fostering daytime, nighttime, and
neighborhood activity. The proposal’s specifics specify that the FAR increase applies only to non-
transient residential uses above the first level. It does not apply to hotel uses or other uses. The
plan includes a minimum micromobility component on the first floor to provide residents with access
to micromobility options. To qualify for the height bonus, projects must incorporate a larger-area
network-type micromobility infrastructure. The minimum lot size for eligible projects is 13,000
square feet to prevent small lots from being used to develop a few luxury units and then claiming
the FAR increase, even if they are non-transient. The goal is to promote lot aggregation, which can
be challenging given Washington Avenue’s established and developed properties, owned by
multiple entities. The proposal also requires that any nonconforming uses, such as illegal nightclubs
or nuisances no longer permitted, be discontinued as part of the incentive. This ensures that the
first floor remains dedicated to neighborhood uses that improve the character of the area.
The current maximum residential height is 50 feet. The proposal permits 75 feet for residential, with
an extra 25 feet bonus (up to 100 feet) if the project is car-free and meets micromobility
requirements.
The reason for this is that they did not want to see the height being used for only one or two levels
of parking structure; they preferred that space to be used for the actual residential units. If they are
not taking advantage of the height bonus, they could provide up to 20% of the required parking
allowed under parking district #1. If they want the extra height, it should be reserved only for
residential units. The project would need to exceed the micromobility requirements and participate
in a public micromobility network. This has a sunset clause, which is important because one of the
goals of this City Commission is to incentivize this, so including a timeframe prevents property
owners from abusing the system. It also serves as a safety valve: if, after three or four years, the
City Commission is not satisfied or if people take advantage of this, the Commission can let it
sunset. Regarding Commissioner Suarez’s comments, he clarified that if someone inquires about
Live Local projects on Washington Avenue, they could achieve up to a 6.375 FAR, provide parking
on-site, and the maximum height would range between 300 feet and 500 feet, depending on the
location. If the parcel is within a mile of Alton Gateway, they can go up to 500 feet. All other
properties would be within a mile of the Miami Beach Convention Center Hotel site and would be
limited to 300 feet. Under State preemption, they would have no control over that, and there would
be no public hearing; applicants could simply submit an application that would be approved
administratively.
Commissioner Suarez wants to discuss transparently where Paul Cejas has a private application if
this comprehensive zoning plan does not go through. He wants to hear from his representative why
they need the 75 extra feet in height for developing the property. It is not an equity firm that owns
this property; it is Ambassador Cejas, who has owned it for 30 years. He bought it when no one
else wanted to invest in Miami Beach. He took a risk and believed in the City. When he talked to the
stakeholders, he listened, and he would like them to explain why they need the height.
Cecilia Torres-Toledo of Akerman LLP, representing Ambassador Paul Cejas along with Neisen
Kasdin, stated that they have been working with Ambassador Cejas for nearly two and a half years
to redevelop the corner of 16th and Washington Avenue. He has examined the property and
redeveloped it multiple times. Past approvals for similar projects have been granted, but it simply
does not pencil out economically. To redevelop that corner, a high-end luxury product would be
necessary, which is not what the City desires or what Ambassador Cejas wants at this point. With
the by-right FAR and height available for this parcel, they can achieve a reasonable density. The
CD-3 zone has the highest density in the City, allowing for 150 dwelling units per acre, but they lack
sufficient FAR or height to reach that limit. Thanks to incentives in this legislation and their private
application, should this project not move forward, they could utilize a 3.25 FAR and a 150-foot
height limit to develop 210 units. This would be 210 apartments in the heart of Lincoln Road and
Washington Avenue, a much-needed addition to the residential housing stock. The project has
already been presented to the Planning Board, which approved a CUP for it. They also presented to
HPB and are working on addressing some design comments before returning. They have a
concrete project ready to proceed, with 210 units, a vital housing addition to what is effectively
Miami Beach’s downtown. They have received letters of support from the Washington Avenue BID
and the Lincoln Road BID and are eager to move forward. However, without additional FAR or
height, they cannot realize the project.
Commissioner Suarez added that part of the legislation was removed partly because former
Commissioner Rosen Gonzalez made a point about it. He wants to set a 1,200 square foot cap on
unit size. They removed the maximum, and he wants to see how his colleagues feel about this.
When talking about government housing, it is usually based on AMI. As he said, there is a forgotten
middle where people do not make enough to qualify for government housing but not enough for
market-rate housing. Some tools legislators could use are defining what they want as a City:
whether they want to pave the way for more 2,000 or 3000 square foot units, or if they prefer a
standard unit size. Developments like the Floridian, the Cosmopolitan, the Courts, the Waverly, and
the Flamingo hotels suggest that such projects are no longer being built. Instead, there is either
government housing based on AMI or ultra-luxury units exceeding 3,000 square feet. This situation
allows developers to claim they will not make a lot of money but will earn good profits, creating an
environment in which they can work rather than setting rules. He wants to think long-term and sees
Washington Avenue as different from what it is today, looking ahead 30 years. Although he does
not own property there and has no skin in the game, he believes this is good legislation for the
City's future. The neighborhood has struggled, and the old idea that hotels on Washington Avenue
would revive it has failed. He wants to propose ideas that are proven, true, and supported by City
staff and urban planner scholars worldwide. He hopes to gain support from the City Commission
and to make a good-faith effort to revitalize a corridor that has struggled over the past few decades.
Thomas Mooney, Planning Director, clarified that they initially set the maximum unit size, but it was
somehow removed. The Administration believes this is a very good idea, and the Planning Board
also recommended a maximum unit size of 1,300 square feet.
Commissioner Fernandez agrees that Washington Avenue needs to be revitalized. His concern is
that even with a sunset date, this legislation would immediately reward bad property owners. From
the video shown, they saw businesses and empty storefronts that were well-maintained, or
businesses that do not represent the caliber and quality of businesses they would want to have
here. In his opinion, these owners would be instantly rewarded with valuable upzoning once this
passes, regardless of their management style. The market value would be created at Second
Reading when this legislation passes, and the entitlement would become usable at that point. The
land value development would happen soon after. As Planning Director Mooney confirmed, the
requirement states that a building permit must be obtained; without it, the upzoning is lost. Once a
building permit is issued, that entitlement is secured. Over his 30 years in the City, the Planning
Director knows this is a common practice; people do this regularly, so the market value, the
entitlement, and the land value are being set now, with the sunset provision in a few years.
However, this does not undo the immediate grant of development rights given today, meaning
owners who have neglected properties that have negatively impacted the City and contributed to
the decline of this corridor would still receive the valuable upzoning benefits. Benefits that good
property owners would also get, without needing to show any performance, investment, or public
benefit. He supports redevelopment and increasing the number of residents. He advocates for
revitalizing Washington Avenue. He supports incentives but believes the key is in how they are
granted. He worries that this blanket upzoning, at a scale that is too large, may be too much for
their infrastructure right now. The impact analysis on the agenda makes this clear; this legislation is
not a modest change. It proposes increasing the FAR to 100% (from 2.0 to 4.0) and maintaining a
density of 175 units per acre across the entire area. It is not tied to specific projects. It is a blanket
policy across the corridor.
Thomas Mooney, Planning Director, stated that when the impact analysis was conducted for the
large area, they considered the entire area and assumed that every parcel would be developed and
built out. The likelihood of this happening is low, but if every eligible parcel were built out, there
would be a potential increase of 2,462 residential units. In response to Commissioner Fernandez,
Planning Director Mooney explained that the analysis shows a potential increase of 861,700 gallons

Commissioner Fernandez noted that they must assume that if they grant benefits to people, those

ACTION: Ordinance 2026-4793 was adopted. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record.
The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on
Second Reading; seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Roll Call: 7-0. Thomas Mooney to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Commissioner Fernandez thanked the Mayor and introduced the Item, explaining that it proposed
creating a temporary pilot program aimed at encouraging the reactivation of vacant storefronts
within key commercial corridors of the City. In conversations with residents throughout the
community, many expressed nostalgia for an earlier era of Miami Beach, one characterized by live
music, cafés, dinner venues, brunch spots, and intimate entertainment experiences. Residents
often mentioned beloved former establishments like Van Dyke’s and expressed a desire to see
similar venues return. Currently, under the City’s zoning code and regulations, many of those
historically popular concepts would not be permitted today. This highlights the need for corrective
measures. The goal of this Ordinance is to revive vitality and joy in struggling commercial corridors,
enabling residents, families, and visitors to enjoy dining and live entertainment in a responsible and
regulated way. The proposal would establish a temporary program lasting through December 31,
during which eligible businesses could apply for administrative approval to offer indoor live
entertainment in designated areas such as Lincoln Road, Collins Avenue, Alton Road, Washington
Avenue, 71st Street, and 41st Street. This process would bypass the Conditional Use Permit (CUP)
process. The Ordinance specifies a clear expiration date and states that, if unintended
consequences occur, the City Commission can simply allow the program to sunset. Conversely, if
the program is successful, the City Commission may choose to extend it.
Thomas Mooney, Planning Department Director, confirmed that Commissioner Fernandez had
accurately summarized the proposal and added that the Ordinance establishes a temporary
regulatory framework through the end of the year, which the City Commission can extend if
necessary. The program would permit restaurants and alcoholic beverage establishments with
indoor entertainment only to skip Conditional Use approval, as long as they meet certain eligibility
criteria and safeguards. It would only apply to businesses within an existing building that received a
Certificate of Occupancy (CO) on or before January 1, 2025, to prevent bypassing the process. No
outdoor, rooftop, or adult entertainment will be allowed. The maximum occupancy will be 750
persons, targeting small to mid-sized venues rather than large clubs. Currently, a restaurant without
entertainment that exceeds certain occupancy limits needs a CUP. Under this pilot program,
qualifying venues could operate indoor entertainment administratively, as long as occupancy stays
within the 750-person limit.
Commissioner Magazine expressed strong support for the proposal and asked to be added as a co-
sponsor, while also seeking clarification on Planning Board feedback.
Planning Director Mooney explained the eligibility requirements, highlighting that the program is
only for restaurants and supper clubs, not standalone nightclubs. Outdoor and rooftop
entertainment are excluded because they are more likely to cause nuisances for nearby residential
and commercial areas. All rooftop and open-air entertainment currently needs a CUP under the City
Code, regardless of size or purpose.
Commissioner Fernandez inquired about safeguards if an establishment misuses the administrative
approval.
Nick Kallergis, Chief Deputy City Attorney, confirmed that the City already has enforcement
authority under existing Code provisions, which allow revocation of approvals if an establishment
becomes a nuisance or repeatedly violates City, State, or Federal law. Violations may include
habitual noise Ordinance breaches, misrepresentation, illegal activity, or other significant violations.
In such cases, administrative approval could be revoked, and the business would need to pursue a
CUP if it wants to continue offering entertainment. The adoption of the Ordinance would not limit the
City’s enforcement authority, and administrative approvals could be revoked if necessary.
Planning Director Mooney further clarified that any CUP obtained during the pilot period will not
sunset with the Ordinance and will remain valid unless revoked under existing procedures.
Discussion continued regarding occupancy limits.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that she supports the Item but wants to understand the mechanism in
place if an establishment turns out to be a bad actor.
Planning Director Mooney replied that if an establishment begins to receive violations, it could
potentially be subject to sections of the City Code that, if broken habitually, could cause the
establishment to lose its Business Tax Receipt.
Commissioner Bhatt further inquired about who is overseeing this.
Planning Director Mooney stated that code enforcement in Miami Beach is driven by complaints.
The Code Enforcement Department needs to be notified of a problem for them to respond.
Commissioner Fernandez explained that since this pilot program has an expiration date, the goal is
to encourage property owners to fill storefronts while the program lasts. This relaxes the restriction
for Conditional Use. If the program fails, the City Commission will simply decide not to pursue it next
year.
David Wallack mentioned that having 750 people at an establishment indicates a significant
capacity and advised caution.
Commissioner Fernandez said he appreciates Mr. Wallack’s opinion and mentioned that 750
people is a considerable number. He also wants to find out whether Mango’s is an indoor or outdoor
venue.
Planning Director Mooney responded that Mango’s is an indoor venue.
Commissioner Fernandez inquired if this Ordinance would apply to nightclubs or restaurants.
Planning Director Mooney responded that the occupancy limit applies only to indoor spaces and
that the Ordinance does not permit nightclubs or open-air venues.
Deputy City Attorney Kallergis reaffirmed that the Ordinance was intentionally designed to exclude
high-impact nightlife venues and instead promote restaurant-based live entertainment in purely
commercial corridors, away from residential neighborhoods like Sunset Harbor, West Avenue, and
South of Fifth.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas stated that she supports the Ordinance. She addressed Mr. Wallack’s
concern and mentioned that the Ordinance states “up to 750 people.” That is a high number to
reach, and she does not think we need to worry about it at this point.
Mitch Novick said that open-air entertainment is a nuisance, especially along the 10th block of
Ocean Drive. When people drive by blasting loud music, that is what heightens the carnival-like
atmosphere.
Troy Wright said they will encourage Washington Avenue businesses to join this program.
Commissioner Fernandez reiterated that the goal is to use this legislation to fill vacant spaces. The
City cannot depend on the positive activation of special events. The free market is the best way to
fill events. We need property owners to cooperate.
Mr. Wright agreed that they will reach out to the Washington Avenue property owners as much as
possible. It will not be easy, but they are committed to doing their part to help make this legislation a
success.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that Miami Beach has an unoccupied space in North Beach at La
Poubelle, which has since become the most successful business in North Beach. It is an enclosed
live cabaret establishment where shows sell out quickly, featuring only local entertainment. This is
exactly the kind of initiative they are seeking. We want to promote live music in the City while
maintaining order, as we have grown as a City and will continue to evolve. She expressed concerns
about rising commercial rents and the displacement of long-standing local businesses. Although the
City is working to lower regulatory barriers, the success of corridor revitalization ultimately depends
on property owners’ willingness to cooperate with fair leasing practices.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas responded to Mr. Novick’s comments, stating that no outdoor or adult
entertainment is allowed, and no part of it shall be located on top of the building.
Commissioner Fernandez asked whether pop-up establishments could benefit from this Ordinance.
Deputy City Attorney Kallergis responded that nothing prevents a pop-up from using this Ordinance.
Sara de los Reyes, Sunset Harbour Neighborhood Association, stated that she supports the idea
that no entertainment should be allowed in neighborhoods where it is prohibited, and emphasized
the importance of enforcing noise regulations.
Amy Mehu, representing the 41st Street BID, expressed gratitude for the Ordinance and highlighted
its potential to support both vacant spaces and existing businesses.
Johann Moore, a resident, urged strict enforcement of indoor noise limits and supports the
program’s goal to activate vacant storefronts responsibly.
Commissioner Fernandez spoke to the audience and business representatives, reminding them
that this Ordinance is a temporary incentive and emphasizing that its continuation depends on
visible results.
Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading; seconded by
Commissioner Suarez. Roll Call: 7-0.

ACTION: Ordinance 2026-4794 was adopted. The Item heard in conjunction with Item R5 F. The
title of the Ordinance was read into the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner
Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading; seconded by Commissioner
Dominguez. Roll Call: 7-0. Thomas Mooney to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Clerk’s Note: Items R5 E and R5 F were discussed together.
Commissioner Magazine noted that the City has not always done enough to promote positive
developments throughout Miami Beach. He believes the area is on track to become the “American
Riviera” within a few years, highlighting that the City has some of the most valuable real estate in
the world, including major beachfront properties along Collins Avenue. Several high-profile
redevelopment projects are in progress or moving forward, such as renovations at the Shore Club,
new ownership at the Delano, ongoing work at the SLS, and the opening of new luxury assets like
the Faena. The broader luxury market is gaining momentum with renowned brands like Aman,
Bulgari, and Casa Cipriani. This corridor is set to become one of the most desirable in the world. It
is fitting to recognize and celebrate this investment and growth. Once completed, this corridor will
be a key jewel in the local economy.
The public hearing was opened.
Mable Patel, a representative from the OKO Group, thanked Commissioner Magazine and the rest
of the City Commission. The Aman Hotel site is actively under construction, with plans to open the
hotel by the end of 2027 and the residences expected to open in summer 2027. He added that the
project is progressing steadily, and the eighth floor of the residences was recently poured.
Mitch Novick praised the development team for the visible progress on the site. He then asked a
question about the language in the Item, expressing concern about whether the request included an
additional “bonus,” referencing prior approvals and asking for clarification on what was being
authorized.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that this is not a bonus increase in the building's total volume or
square footage. The request concerns repurposing interior space for usability, and it does not
expand the building’s overall envelope.
Thomas Mooney, the Planning Department Director, concurred with Commissioner Fernandez’s
explanation.
Daniel Ciraldo expressed concern about zoning authority and voter oversight. The City Charter
previously allowed for referenda on certain zoning issues, but he believes that this authority has
been affected by State action in 2023, referencing HB 41. Zoning decisions are increasingly made
by the City Commission rather than by voters. The City should work to restore referendum rights,
and residents should have greater direct influence over zoning decisions.
Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading; seconded by
Commissioner Dominguez. Roll Call: 7-0. Thomas Mooney to handle.

ACTION: Ordinance 2026-4796 was adopted. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record.
The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Dominguez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on
Second Reading; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Roll Call: 7-0. John Norris to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Commissioner Dominguez introduced the Item and explained that staff had found gaps in the
current Code that allowed Temporary Use Permits to be renewed indefinitely, effectively bypassing
the requirement to bring properties into full Code compliance. The purpose of the Ordinance is to
close those gaps. She asked John Norris to provide further details.
John Norris, Public Works Director, explained that the issue involved repeated renewals of
Temporary Use Permits while properties were ostensibly in the process of being brought up to
Code. He stated that, in practice, some applicants were receiving Temporary Use renewals
repeatedly without resolving underlying compliance issues. The proposed Ordinance would end that
practice by limiting the number of allowable Temporary Use renewals. Specifically, the Ordinance
would allow up to three Temporary Use renewals. The first renewal fee would be $162, and
subsequent renewals would increase to $2,090. He stated that this structure was designed to give
applicants enough time to fix deficiencies and obtain a permanent certificate, while also providing a
financial incentive to resolve issues quickly instead of relying on repeated temporary approvals.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that this is good policy.
No one in the audience or on Zoom asked to speak on the Item.
Commissioner Dominguez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading; seconded
by Commissioner Fernandez. Roll Call: 7-0.

items.title: AN ORDINANCE OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, AMENDING CHAPTER 70 OF THE CODE OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, ENTITLED “MISCELLANEOUS OFFENSES,” BY AMENDING ARTICLE II, ENTITLED “PUBLIC PLACES,” BY AMENDING DIVISION 2, ENTITLED “BICYCLING, SKATEBOARDING, ROLLER SKATING, IN-LINE SKATING, MOTORIZED MEANS OF TRANSPORTATION, ELECTRIC BICYCLING, MOPEDS, MOTORCYCLES, MOTORIZED BICYCLES, AND MOTORIZED SCOOTERS,” BY CREATING SECTION 70-73, TO BE ENTITLED “SAFE OPERATION OF PERSONAL DELIVERY DEVICES AND MOBILE CARRIERS,” TO IMPOSE ADDITIONAL LOCAL SAFETY REQUIREMENTS CONSISTENT WITH STATE LAW; AND PROVIDING FOR REPEALER, SEVERABILITY, CODIFICATION, AND AN EFFECTIVE DATE.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Ordinance 2026-4797 was adopted as amended. The title of the Ordinance was read
into the record. The Public Hearing was held. A motion was made by Commissioner Suarez to
adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading with changes; seconded by Commissioner Bhatt. Roll
Call: 7-0. Hernan Cardeno, John Rebar, and Chief Wayne Jones to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
AMENDMENT:
Speed Limit Adjustment - Changed from a uniform 8 mph to: 6 mph on sidewalks and 10 mph
on crosswalks.
Commissioner Bhatt explained that the City is preempted by the State, and it is ironic because the
State passed the Home Rule, yet they are preempted. She is doing what she believes is right for
the community. Delivery robots are not causing problems in many cases, but they are in some. The
City has narrow sidewalks that were designed 100 years ago, when bicycles, delivery robots,
strollers, and ADA mobility devices were not considered. Now, they are forced to accept these on
their streets, making the best of an unfortunate situation. An Item was passed via Consent Agenda,
C7 AR, to conduct a survey of the sidewalks to better understand if they pose actual hazards in
certain areas, and this will be addressed later. At that time, she will return with photographs of
standoffs, tipped-over machines, people trying to figure out which way to go, near misses in traffic,
and actual collisions. Meanwhile, they will try to make this as safe as possible for pedestrians, who
should take precedence over corporate profit. With that, she turned it over to the Office of the City
Attorney.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Rob Rosenwald reiterated that they are governed by State law regarding
how they can regulate delivery robots, but they are permitted to operate on sidewalks and
crosswalks. There are State-imposed rules on their operation, and the City incorporated these into
the Ordinance as required by State law. The scope of their regulation primarily concerns safety
regulations within the context of allowing these robots on sidewalks and streets. The original
version, which retains many of the same provisions, required a permit system, safety devices to
enhance visibility, speed regulation, and other measures. During Second Reading, after
Commissioner Rosen Gonzalez completed her term and Commissioner Bhatt took over as sponsor,
additional regulations allowed under the Statute were added. These include prohibiting the display
of commercial advertising, setting the maximum speed at 8 mph, changing the allowed stationary
time on the sidewalk to 30 minutes, and adding a new regulation that no robot may operate on any
of the City’s Beachwalk or Baywalk. There is a six-month grace period for operators to come into
compliance.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, clarified that the Baywalk and Beachwalk are separate Ordinances
to be heard individually. Additionally, he mentioned that the speed limit may be increased to 8 mph,
up from 6 mph.
Commissioner Bhatt thanked Commissioner Magazine for bringing up the Item on the Beachwalk in
case it gets delayed somewhere. As it is in the language, with his permission, they can include it
together within the 6-mph speed limit, and this was accepted. Discussion held.
Commissioner Dominguez noted that they received an email from Serve Robotics, and she has
questions about it. The first concern was that the per-device speed was not reasonably related to
the City’s stated regulatory objectives. The Ordinance bases its regulatory authority on public
safety, predictability, visibility, and monitoring, all of which are imposed on the operator level, not on
individual devices. The fee structure should have a rational relationship to the government interest;
the per-robot charge functions as a revenue mechanism rather than a safety-based regulatory tool.
So, why is it applied to a robot rather than an organization?
Chief Deputy City Attorney Rob Rosenwald explained that it is a policy decision the City
Commission can make; either scheme would be legally defensible. A per robot scheme is rationally
related to their ability to regulate and keep safe, however many they send. If they have ten robots,
they need less enforcement; with more robots, they need to do more at a higher cost. They can
charge much more than $100 per robot or charge by the organization; there are many rational
bases for reimbursing the City for maintaining safety. This is the scheme he included in the
Ordinance, which he believes is the most rational. It is a policy decision for the Commission. In
continued remarks, Commissioner Dominguez added that the City can regulate the robots’ safety,
and the legislation proposes a slightly lower speed limit. The original First Reading version was six
mph, but after speaking with Serve Robotics, it was raised at their request to assist and per their
suggestion.
Commissioner Bhatt noted that it was easier to cross the street than walk on the sidewalks and to
avoid accidents. She is not in favor of raising the speed limit and does not want to go to ten mph
anywhere. This is a commercial enterprise, and she has no concern that they will make a lot of
money, which is great, but they also have to cover the costs of doing business. A per-unit cost of
operation is a viable way to manage this, as the Office of the City Attorney pointed out; more units
mean more issues. Back in the day, when there were taxis, each taxi had a medallion, and that is
just how things worked. Discussion held.
Commissioner Suarez knows that some intersections are not functioning properly and that there
may not be enough time to cross certain roads, and he does not want to see an accident caused by
a delivery robot going too slowly.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Rosenwald explained that the City Commission can set different speed
limits. The current regulation states a uniform speed limit of 8 mph everywhere. When
communicating with Commissioner Suarez, he explained that as long as they have a rational basis
for their decision, it is legally defensible. Anyone can sue the City for anything, and they often get
sued over unrealistic claims, but the City does not have any actual liability just because they
regulate something. It is similar to if they got hit by a taxicab or other delivery vehicle. The
discussion continued.
Commissioner Dominguez added that a bicycle or scooter can go at any speed, and these robots
are more regulated with cameras; they stop for pedestrians, and she suggested hearing from the
operator.
Commissioner Bhatt agrees that it is very frustrating that they do not have a current mechanism to
regulate e-devices and bicycle speed. They are finally seeing some movement in Tallahassee and
are working with County Commissioner Lopez. Hopefully, soon this will become something they can
manage better because they can talk to Julio Blanco, a Police Officer who was injured by an e-biker
and broke his elbow. She has friends who are doctors, and if they could share photographs without
violating HIPAA, it would shock their hair. It is dangerous, and it has not yet been addressed at the
State or Federal level, which must happen. However, this does not mean they should accept any
approach that creates yet another obstacle for pedestrians walking on the sidewalks. She would be
happy to amend this to 10 mph for crossing the crosswalks to get them out of the traffic lanes, and
6 mph on sidewalks to prevent accidents with people minding their own business, walking where
they are supposed to.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, announced the Public Hearing.
Yariel Diaz from Serve Robotics, via Zoom, appreciates the City's work on this Item. They share the
same goals of keeping sidewalks safe, accessible, and comfortable for everyone while allowing new
technology to operate responsibly. At Serve, they work with delivery partners Uber Eats and
DoorDash to provide robot delivery for small restaurants within Miami Beach. To date, they have
delivered for over 161 restaurants in the City. They have some suggestions. They operate with
either 20 or 30 robots and have heard arguments about the enforcement costs for the City, which is
why, in the initial Item, they suggested a per-organization fee much larger than what a robot fee for
20 robots would be. This would avoid the need to switch back and forth between charges for
operators versus robots. Regarding the eight-mile count, the amendment made by Commissioner
Bhatt is acceptable to them. They appreciate the Commissioners' consideration of the crosswalk
speed, which is honestly one of their biggest concerns because lowering the crosswalk speed may
limit the robots' ability to safely cross busy intersections, especially since they are not timed the
same. Another concern is advertising. A total ban on advertising raises fairness and First
Amendment concerns, and there may be more targeted and content-neutral ways to address this.
Cities like Chicago have implemented review periods for advertising to ensure there are no obscene
or pornographic items as part of the review process, as opposed to a flat-out ban. They believe that
small adjustments will help the Ordinance better achieve its goals. They support the Ordinance;
most of it is common sense, and they thank the City Commission for continuing to work on
improving the community.
Carl Hansen, via Zoom, supports the suggested ten and six mph speed limits. This provides a good
balance between lower sidewalk speeds and the necessary crosswalk crossing speed. Their main
concern is about the advertising prohibition, which was not part of the initial discussion. He arrived
at the end of the meeting, but they fully support the City exploring and discussing regulations for
advertising on personal delivery robots. They believe this topic deserves more time and request that
it be pulled for a separate discussion so they can meet and evaluate the benefits, similar to other
devices. Operating these devices in public is costly, and advertising helps keep prices low for local
businesses. If new fees are imposed on operating them, it will hinder their ability to subsidize
delivery costs through advertising, which could negatively impact merchants and customers. Their
goal is to reduce cars on the street, ease parking impact, and do so safely. It is wise to have
adequate space, and they look forward to collaborating with the City on this. They hope there will be
time to develop an advertising policy that makes sense for everyone.
Johann Moore, via Zoom, shared a few observations. He insisted that he saw one of the robots
cross an intersection on the crosswalk while the light was red. Another concern from the community
is that corner curb cuts are too steep and angled. He has seen a robot stop far enough back from
the intersection so it could see the crosswalk light, but in that position, it blocked the sidewalk.
Anyone with a wheelchair, he warns the City, could file an ADA complaint lawsuit. He has
mentioned this before. Please keep that in mind. An elderly person, someone using a cane,
someone with a shopping cart, or someone with a baby carriage, finds it difficult. He wonders if the
Commission can consider how to address this. He would prefer all crosswalk lights be automatic
again, as during the pandemic, or make it more difficult for delivery robot developers to add features
like a garage door opener that would enable the robot to request to cross. He submitted a metric for
comparing accident rates of delivery bikes, whether motorized or not, and suspects that robots
might be safer, but the speed limit is crucial.
Bruce, whose last name is not given, via Zoom, is a pedestrian who typically walks a mile in 20
minutes, which is about three mph, and he has never had a problem crossing the street. Older
people walk slower, so hearing ten mph for robots when pedestrians only go about three mph is just
crazy.
Mathew Gultanoff, via Zoom, thanked the sponsors for the Item because speed regulation is a
sound policy, and he is supportive. The sidewalks are relatively wide, from eight to under three feet
in some places, and Miami Beach is an urban area. Crossing the street, he walked down Alton
Road, and a robot had a message asking him to please push the button for the robot. He did not
see it, but his daughter pushed it, and the robot said Thank You, which highlights the issue of
accessibility. The City has the ability to regulate speed for bicycles, e-bikes, and micromobility on
pathways such as the Beachwalk, and it is best practice and one of the tools available to keep
everyone safe on the pathways. It is a policy that should be considered now for safe access.
Wayne Roberts, via Zoom, has no issue with the technology, except that society should make it
harder for these companies to take over jobs like Uber drivers and delivery services. Ultimately, this
could lead to an increase in homelessness because jobs requiring certain levels of education, and
for immigrants, might disappear. He feels sad for society, but technology will move forward with or
without them, and they cannot build a wall against it.
Kevin Kruger, a member of the public, stated that it is a sidewalk and bicycles and others are not
permitted; they use them, but he is a people person and prefers to see pedestrians rather than
robots. Technology is great, but it has taken away jobs and shifted power to corporations and the
State. Public safety is an elected official’s top priority, followed by job creation. However, they are
losing jobs that could benefit those needing flexible delivery roles or entry-level positions, which
now go to nameless, robotic faces. As a pedestrian, he finds this situation annoying and
overwhelming. He would like to see them do the right thing for the beautiful beach town.
The public hearing concluded, and Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance as
amended.
Mayor Meiner clarified that they are preempted by the State, so they are trying to work within the
framework they have. Discussion continued.
A motion was made by Commissioner Suarez to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading as
amended to ten mph on crosswalks and six mph on sidewalks; seconded by Commissioner Bhatt.
Roll Call: 7-0.
