ACTION: Ordinance 2026-4798 was adopted. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record.
The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Bhatt made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on
Second Reading; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Roll Call: 7-0. Office of the City
Attorney and Chief Wayne Jones to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Mayor Meiner thanked his co-sponsors, Commissioners Bhatt and Magazine, and noted that this
addresses municipal offenses. If there is a hate crime involved, as read by the City Clerk, then there
is a minimum of a 30-day jail sentence, consistent with State law.
Commissioner Bhatt moved the Item, seconded by Mayor Meiner.
The public hearing was held.
Johann Moore, via Zoom, is only bothered by the lack of mention of what political stance or
ideology. No one should be attacked publicly or privately because they are Zionist, anarchist, or
socialist. This is a well-meaning point despite its possible association with the sponsor.
Wanda Jaiman asked for clarification on what they are voting on.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, clarified that this hate crime Ordinance is adopted with the same
language as the State law. It provides for a minimum sentence of 30 days in jail unless a judge
determines that it is not in the best interest of the community, especially when a crime is motivated
by hate based on the specified characteristics in the legislation, including race, political affiliation,
religion, and others. During continued questions from Ms. Jaiman, he deferred to Deputy City
Attorney Mark Fishman.
Deputy City Attorney Mark Fishman responded to Ms. Jaiman that calling someone unkind words
like “crippled old lady” would not automatically be a crime or criminal offense, so there would be no
criminal charge. Without a criminal charge, a hate crime charge cannot be filed because no crime
has been committed.
City Attorney Dopico stated that if a crime is committed that is separate from name-calling, such as
physically assaulting someone, and the perpetrator makes disparaging comments about the victim's
race, or threatens to harm the victim because of their race, then this Ordinance would apply.
Wanda Jaiman wants to clarify this issue because it is very sensitive. They are facing difficult times
in Miami Beach, marked by divisions for many reasons, and she aims to understand what the
Ordinance actually covers. If someone calls another person a Muslim or her a Catholic, would that
violate the Ordinance? Would it be considered a hate crime if someone describes a person as a
terrorist-Muslim or Jew? She wants to know what the Commission is voting on because it is
supposed to be fair for every religion, race, woman, disabled person, and everyone else.
Mayor Meiner explained that it is considered equal, but it must be a crime committed under the
Statute.
Deputy City Attorney Fishman explained what must happen if a crime is committed and the Court
finds that it was motivated by hate. If the crime was motivated by hate, then this Ordinance applies,
similar to the State statute. The issue is that the City has its own municipal offenses unique to
Miami Beach, and it previously did not have a penalty for crimes motivated by hate. They are now
implementing something that already exists in the State statutes, but Miami Beach could not
enforce it before due to a lack of authority. Now, they have clarified the statute so that if a crime is
deemed a hate crime by the Court, a mandatory jail sentence will be imposed. There are several
categories that encompass everyone.
Commissioner Magazine added that it relates to what Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas said about Miami
Beach going through tough times. He often feels like there are two different worlds: the real world
and the social media world. Tuning into social media can be toxic, and he has tried to tune it out as
much as possible without missing anything important related to his job. However, when he is simply
picking up his daughter from school, he sees a beautiful community of parents of all races, sexual
orientations, and backgrounds who respect and love each other. When he goes to the supermarket,
he talks to friends and strangers. What makes Miami Beach unique is that very few people who live
here are originally from or choose to stay here long-term. There is so much toxicity online, often
intentionally created to be that way. If residents allow it, they keep feeding into it, and it can change
the way they think about and perceive this beautiful place. But if they take their faces out of their
phones, they realize they are here because they want to impact positive change and make their
City better. They live in an incredible place, and while there is still work to do, he disagrees with the
idea that there is so much hatred and division. There are two worlds: social media and real life, and
he encourages people to distinguish what is real from what is fabricated. He also thanked Ms.
Jaiman, noting she always has an open door for him.
Mayor Meiner praised Commissioner Magazine for his comments and said he agrees with his
sentiments.
Wanda Jaiman attempted to contact the Commissioners, but some refused to answer her, and
others deliberately blocked her. She recognizes the semantic violations and wants to do her best.
She loves Miami Beach and respects every single one of them. On social media, this is the only
way they can express themselves because they do not feel heard, and it is frustrating that they do
not like what is happening, and no one listens to them. Some residents believe elected officials
have forgotten about them, feeling they do not matter. However, elected officials are on the dais
because the residents voted them in. She is seeking peace. This situation is even affecting her
deeply. She has to stand up for what she knows is wrong, and it begins with the dais engaging with
residents. The real issue is the lack of engagement.
Mayor Meiner echoed Commissioner Magazine’s sentiments, noting he is frequently told multiple
times a day that residents are grateful to live in the City. There are always ways to improve, which
motivates residents and officials alike to work toward that goal. Residents often say there is no
better place to live, feeling safe and comfortable, and some groups across the spectrum tell him
they see the City as a safe haven for everyone and plan to keep it that way. That is why the City’s
ratings in various categories, measured by national groups, are always at the top, something that
does not happen by accident. The City’s safety net primarily depends on its incredible residents
who do not tolerate hatred. Although no City is immune to issues, the diversity of opinions is a
strength, and he saw this morning how the seven officials reflect the residents’ values of tolerance.
They will never accept hate in the City; they made that clear today in a big way. He thanked
residents, businesses, and the Commission. While they may disagree on policies, they unite in their
commitment to maintaining a safe, accepting, and welcoming City.
Commissioner Fernandez loves serving as a City Commissioner and the opportunity it provides to
represent a diverse community. He enjoys representing the wide range of people that make up
Miami Beach's vibrant melting pot, whether it is the Jewish, Episcopalian, Black, LGBTQ, women in
the Women’s Commission, Hispanic groups, or other communities. That sense of representing and
advocating for diversity is what he truly values about Miami Beach. He speaks up when different
groups are targeted. Sometimes, people wish to see that passion reflected across all groups. This
Commission has shown equal passion in protecting everyone and expects the same commitment to
fight against antisemitism, racism, discrimination against Hispanics, and prejudice toward the
LGBTQ community, doing so vocally and with equal fervor for all. He believes this is why many
community members feel safe here: they know their elected leaders will stand up for them, fight for
their safety, and speak out with the same passion, no matter their background.
Mayor Meiner agreed because this legislation precisely does what it states: it guarantees that if
anyone from these diverse backgrounds mentioned here is targeted and a crime is committed
against them because of their beliefs, lifestyle, or other listed reasons, it will be prosecuted to the
fullest extent of the law.
A motion was made by Commissioner Bhatt to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading, seconded
by Mayor Meiner.
Commissioner Fernandez and Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas requested to be listed as Co-sponsors.

ACTION: Ordinance adopted on First Reading as amended. See related Discussion Item R9 O.
The Title of the Ordinance was read into the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner
Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading as amended; seconded by
Commissioner Suarez. Roll Call: 7-0. The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for
February 25, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice. Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda,
if received. Office of the City Attorney and John Norris to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
AMENDMENTS:
1. Include 9–16 Unit Multifamily Buildings in Residential Waste Program
o Changed the threshold so that apartment and condominium buildings with 9 to 16 units are
automatically included in the City’s residential garbage collection program instead of being
required to negotiate private waste contracts.
2. Opt-Out Provision
o Allow these buildings to opt out of the residential program if they prefer to maintain private
waste contracts.
o Default is automatic inclusion, with opt-out as an option.
3. Future Flexibility
o Discussed and agreed to explore allowing buildings that initially opt out to opt in later, with
details to be finalized between First and Second Reading.
4. Annual Application Proposal
o Proposed an amendment (to be refined before Second Reading) for an annual application
process for eligible buildings to participate in the residential program.
Commissioner Fernandez explained that residents in buildings with nine to 16 units face a difficult
and costly situation, as they are generally too small to negotiate favorable contracts with private
waste haulers. Buildings with fewer than nine units, up to eight units, are included in the City’s
residential garbage collection program. Once a building exceeds nine units, it must negotiate its
own contract, which often results in higher costs for services. This Ordinance would include those
nine-to-16-unit apartment and condominium buildings in the residential waste collection program.
As a result, many of these buildings could see significant savings, some exceeding $1,000 per
month, that can be passed on to their residents living in small buildings.
John Norris, Public Works Director, confirmed that, based on their analysis, most customers would
see a significant decrease in monthly solid waste costs. In response to Commissioner Fernandez,
he stated there is no issue for residents to opt into the program annually. The only concern is the
legality, especially when negotiating the Waste Connection residential contract. Since solid waste
contracts involve a fixed number of units, updated annually from the tax roll, that would be his only
concern. Administratively, they can handle that.
Commissioner Fernandez suggested that, between First and Second Reading, they find a way for
these nine-to-16-unit apartment buildings to opt out if they wish to have individual contracts. If they
do not hear from them, then these buildings are considered part of their residential programs. Often,
these are self-managed associations without professional management or brokers; most are Mom
and Pop landlords who are unsophisticated, or buildings passed down through generations. They
can help make this easier and potentially save costs, which would then be passed on to tenants.
Regarding the return of surplus dividends, there was discussion about how to assist tenants and
those who are homesteaded. The City could develop a structure to operate services that identify not
just a one-time dividend check but ongoing, recurring savings each month. They hope condominium
associations will pass these savings to condominium owners through their fees, or landlords could
pass the savings directly to tenants. He then moved his Item.
Commissioner Dominguez proposed a similar amendment between First and Second Reading to
ensure that all multi-family residents with nine to 16 units could apply annually for waste collection
by the single-family waste contractor.
Commissioner Fernandez added that some buildings are self-managed, and people with other jobs
automatically become part of the residential program that will save them money if they do not opt
out.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, asked whether the idea is that multifamily residential units
between nine and 16 would need to opt in or out.
Commissioner Fernandez’s intention is for them to opt out. He will defer to the City Attorney, but he
wants the default to be that they help tenants and condominium owners save money by
automatically including buildings in the residential waste agreement. If the buildings choose not to
do that, then they opt out.
Public Works Director John Norris asked if, when they initially opt out, it can be up to them to
contact the City if they want to opt in later.
Commissioner Fernandez agreed with that and is happy to work with the Administration and hold a
Sunshine meeting with Commissioner Dominguez to discuss further details. He thanked Public
Director John Norris for putting together the list; it was very impressive how much money they will
be able to save residents.
Commissioner Fernandez moved the Item, seconded by Commissioner Suarez.
The Public Hearing opened.
Johann Moore, via Zoom, emphasized the importance of this legislation for Flamingo Park
Neighborhood. His building has eight units, six of which are small, and that means that an average
lot that has two floors and is a contributing building in his neighborhood will be covered, and that
applies to the great majority of contributing buildings in the historic district.
Daniel Ciraldo, via Zoom, stated that he had raised his hand and sent emails when his name was
mentioned on a prior Item (R5 B and R5 C) but did not receive a response. Any investigation should
be allowed to proceed before making any allegations. It was very concerning to see Commissioners
making accusations about him and MDPL without any evidence. They will address that in another
forum, but he thanked the City Commission for allowing him to speak.
Mitchell Bierman, on behalf of Waste Connections, noted that Item R9 O is relevant to the
discussion, and Mayor Meiner called the Item.
Mitch Novick asked the Commission how this would impact his nine-unit building in the Flamingo
Park Neighborhood.
In response to Mitch Novick, Public Works Director John Norris stated that he would be affected
positively and explained that they will review individual buildings to see current payments and
compare them to what they would pay under the residential plan. They have conducted an exercise
by sampling buildings across the City and showing the potential savings based on that sample.
Waste Connectors or the City would need to meet with him to figure that out.
Commissioner Fernandez mentioned that if, for any reason, Mitch Novick finds himself in a situation
where he doesn't see savings or if placing him in a residential program impacts a larger contract he
might have with other properties, they might consider giving him the option to opt out so he can
negotiate his own terms. There could be landlords like Mr. Novick who own a small building or two,
and this flexibility would benefit him. If he prefers to stay with what the City is offering as part of the
residential program and enjoy the savings, or if it is better for him, he can choose to opt out.
Monica Entin, on behalf of James Cavanaugh, thanked the City Commission for the amendment
and explained that representing a single building owner is one thing, but when they have an owner
with multiple buildings across the City, each owned by separate entities, the City may not be aware
of that. They look it up and see one entity probably controlling several properties and offering a
lower price for one building. However, when this individual owns multiple buildings with different
contracts, it could negatively impact them if they cannot negotiate all buildings simultaneously. They
appreciate the opportunity for owners to opt in or out, depending on what the City Attorney deems
best for the City. As long as owners can make their own choices regarding their buildings, they are
thankful it.
The discussion continued, and in response to Commissioners Suarez and Fernandez’s comments,
Public Works Director Norris noted that this legislation only covers nine to 16 units.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, clarified that the Ordinance can be changed to allow anything over
one unit to opt out. Currently, two to eight units are automatically included in the single waste hauler
contract, so it is up to the City Commission.
Commissioner Fernandez suggested holding a Sunshine meeting to discuss that with the City
Attorney or the Public Works Director to see how it would work. He does not know if the residential
waste agreement currently requires them to keep units one through eight as part of that contract,
and he is unsure whether they can make that decision now.
Commissioner Suarez suggested working on that between First and Second Reading and agreed to
hold a Sunshine meeting.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, closed the Public Hearing.
Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to approve the Ordinance on First Reading as amended;
seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Roll Call taken: 7-0. Second Reading Public Hearing is
scheduled for February 26, 2025.

ACTION: Resolution 2026-34115 was adopted. The Title of the Resolution was read into the
record. A motion was made by Commissioner Magazine to adopt the Resolution; seconded by
Commissioner Bhatt. Vote: 7-0. David Gomez to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Commissioner Bhatt introduced the Item regarding the replacement of the previously removed
rainbow crosswalk. The proposal involves replacing the rainbow crosswalk that was removed
following directives from the State government. Several artists, architects, and landscape architects
involved in the original installation had offered their professional services to the City free of charge
to develop a thoughtful and understated design to honor the original crosswalk. The proposed
installation will extend slightly into Lummus Park without increasing the amount of sidewalk paving.
Instead, it will replace existing pavement with decorative pavers, with grass planted between them
to maintain permeability and limit additional hardscape. The new design will not simply recreate a
traditional painted crosswalk but will incorporate the shape and essence of the original rainbow
configuration in a more integrated and permanent way. The corners of the installation will feature
the actual salvaged pavers, carefully palletized when the original crosswalk was removed. The City
retained many of these pavers, eliminating the need to create new materials. Additional pavers are
also available for use. The financial impact on the City will be minimal, mainly covering staff time for
permits and installation. The matter generated strong emotional reactions within the community.
She recalled being present on the evening the pavers were removed and saw many residents and
visitors who appeared visibly emotional and distressed. Some visitors reportedly expressed that the
removal diminished their perception of Miami Beach as an inclusive destination. While the rainbow
crosswalk holds special significance for the LGBTQ community, it also serves as a symbol for the
entire Miami Beach community. The original installation paid tribute to Leonard Horowitz’s vibrant
color palette, who was pivotal in revitalizing the Art Deco district. Restoring the crosswalk is
important both symbolically and culturally. It is essential that the installation be completed before
April Pride Month to reaffirm the City’s commitment to inclusivity and support for all communities
calling Miami Beach home.
Commissioner Fernandez thanked the sponsor and co-sponsor for introducing the Resolution.
Preserving the legacy of the rainbow crosswalk and reinstalling it using salvaged pavers is about
visibility, dignity, and respect. He recognized the emotional impact its removal had on the
community and stated that restoring it will send a clear message to residents and visitors about the
City’s values. This Resolution is particularly meaningful because it has been sponsored and
supported by straight allies on the City Commission. While it would have been easy for him, as an
openly gay man, to sponsor the Item himself, the message is even more powerful when allies step
forward in solidarity. He expressed appreciation on behalf of the LGBTQ community and reaffirmed
his full support for the Resolution.
Commissioner Magazine stated that the Item reinforces Miami Beach’s longstanding identity as one
of the most inclusive communities in South Florida and in the United States. He asked to be added
as a co-sponsor and will move the Item.
Commissioners Dominguez and Fernandez also requested to co-sponsor the Item.
A motion was made by Commissioner Magazine to adopt the Resolution; seconded by
Commissioner Bhatt. Vote: 7-0.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34117 was adopted as amended. A motion was made by
Commissioner Fernandez to adopt the Resolution as amended; seconded by Commissioner Bhatt.
Vote: 7-0. Office of the City Manager and Chief of Police Wayne Jones to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
AMENDMENTS:
Beach Closing Flexibility
• Beach will not automatically close at 6:00 p.m.
• The City Manager may extend beach hours based on real-time conditions.
• Additional beach access points may be opened to reduce congestion.
Parking Garages and Lots in the Art Deco Cultural District
• Garages and lots between 5th and 15th Street will remain open, not automatically closed.
• City Manager authorized to apply High-Impact Parking Rates up to $100, starting at $40 and
adjusting as needed.
• Clarification added that Lincoln Road garages may also be opened under this flexibility.
On-Street Parking
• On-street parking on Washington Avenue will be restored.
• Enforcement increased to prevent tailgating, open containers, loud music, or illegal activity.
• City Manager has discretion to manage Ocean Drive and Collins Avenue similarly based on
real-time conditions.
Barricades
• All barricades removed from Ocean Drive, Collins Avenue, and Washington Avenue.
• Barricades allowed only in designated hot spots (e.g., 9th Street on Collins, and 7th Street
block of Washington) at the City Manager’s discretion.
Sidewalk Cafés
• Sidewalk cafés will remain open by policy.
• City Manager and Police Chief may temporarily close them if conditions deteriorate.
License Plate Readers (LPR) and Lane Reductions
• LPR lane-reduction start time may be pushed later (after dinner hours) to reduce impacts to
restaurants and visitors. (Permanent LPR system continues operating regardless of lane
reductions.)
Neighborhood Protections
• Enhanced parking enforcement, including Alpha Bravo–style deployment, in:
o Flamingo Park
o South of Fifth
Authority of the City Manager
• City Manager receives operational flexibility to respond in real time regarding:
o Beach closures
o Garage operations and parking rates
o Street parking restrictions
o Sidewalk café closures
o LPR / lane-reduction timing
o Emergency curfews if needed
o Flexibility granted with the expectation of clear boundaries, responsive decision-making, and
coordination with the Police Chief.
Mayor Meiner explained that they have much to be proud of regarding the measures taken.
Working collectively with the City Administration and Police Department, alongside State law
enforcement, County partners, and neighboring city Police departments, they have reasons to be
proud. However, they also look for potential improvements. Interestingly, the narrative often
suggests that businesses opposed all these measures. He believes that some local businesses
may oppose certain measures, but overall, he has heard mostly positive feedback. The City’s resort
tax numbers, hotel occupancy rates, and room rates are at record levels, showing that they have
done a lot to protect residents and businesses. Two years ago, before these measures, they faced
streets with murderers and unacceptable chaos, stampedes, danger to lives, and the measures
taken saved lives. That is a fact, and that is their purpose: to save lives and maintain an open,
welcoming City. Families now stroll down Ocean Drive with strollers, people rollerblade, enjoy the
City, dine outside, something that was not common during past Spring Breaks. Today is a good
time to consider potential steps for further improvement, but overall, he is inclined to keep the
successful measures, with a few exceptions.
City Manager Carpenter noted that the Administration has heard the City Commission loud and
clear: they do not want to backslide on safety, but they want to pivot slightly from their recent
approach to make it more balanced. They have a Comprehensive Plan, and he has challenged all
departments to identify their directional focus for March 2026. It is important to highlight that
Resolution 2025-33783, sponsored by Mayor Meiner and Commissioner Fernandez, was adopted
to allocate resources to 16 specific items related to Spring Break 2026: 1) adopt and execute a
heightened law enforcement staffing plan, including Alpha Bravo staffing from Thursday through
Sunday on the second and third weekends in March. They will have enhanced staffing throughout
March, especially on the second and third weekends, the 12th through the 15th and the 20th
through the 22nd, due to challenges historically linked to St. Patrick’s Day; they plan to deploy
Alpha Bravo staffing of the Police Department alongside outside agencies, with significant Police
presence on the ground, since this has been a recurring request. 2) They will rigorously enforce the
open container law. 3) Public beaches will close at 6:00 p.m. on the first, second, and third
weekends. They request flexibility because of high-quality events planned for the beach off
Lummus Park, including Wodapalooza and the Adidas Athlete Program. 4) Sidewalk café
operations on Ocean Drive may be suspended if necessary, though he believes it will not be
needed; decisions will be made based on real-time conditions. 5) The City’s Noise Ordinance will
be enforced year-round. 6) Code, Parking Enforcement, and Fire staffing will be increased
throughout March. 7) The possibility of a secure perimeter on Ocean Drive or parts of it will be
further explored; secured zones may be established at beach activations. 8) Midnight curfews will
be considered if deemed necessary by the City Manager; this would be a last resort, used only if
things go significantly wrong, as an optional tool. 9) A comprehensive marketing and
communications campaign is underway, and they plan to present it to the Commission. 10) They
will work with Uber, Lyft, and other ride-share apps to communicate restrictions, including
establishing pickup and drop-off points to prevent traffic issues. 11) All City-owned and operated
parking lots and garages in the Art Deco Cultural District (between 5th and 15th Streets) will close
from 5:00 p.m. Thursday to 6:00 a.m. Monday during the second and third weekends of March. 12)
Due to beach activations, flexibility is requested regarding garage closures; high-impact measures
allowing to increase parking rates up to $100 will stay in place if necessary. 13) On-street parking
restrictions on Ocean Drive, Collins Avenue, and Washington Avenue are being considered, with
the ability to make real-time decisions about blocking parking only if certain locations pose
problems. 14) They will collaborate with the County to explore closing the Venetian Causeway,
although the County has not yet agreed to closures. 15) Creating special event zones as part of the
Comprehensive Plan is being considered. 16) All alternative transportation modes will be explored
to reduce traffic congestion, aided by the new trolley contract and water taxi services. He is happy
to provide further details. Yesterday’s Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee
Sunshine meeting was productive. He welcomes feedback from the Commission, with department
directors present to answer specific questions.
Commissioner Fernandez emphasized the need for a calibrated and flexible Spring Break
operational plan that prioritizes public safety. The plan should protect the tools and strategies
developed over the past year and apply them precisely based on real-time City conditions. It is
important to note that the City Manager's comments are not about undoing the successful Spring
Break strategy of previous years. That strategy has proven effective as a safety framework. The
challenge is to implement it intelligently and proportionally, without harming businesses or residents’
quality of life, while maintaining the City’s welcoming character. Regarding sidewalk cafés, he
supports keeping them open unless conditions change. These are permitted businesses that utilize
sidewalk space, and visitors from across the country want to sit outside and enjoy the weather,
especially in March. Automatically shutting them down would send the wrong message and unfairly
penalize business owners doing nothing wrong. He supports allowing the City Manager, in
partnership with the Chief of Police, the discretion to shut them down if conditions worsen. He also
advocates keeping the barricades on Ocean Drive, Collins Avenue, and Washington Avenue, but
supports removing or scaling them back where possible, as they create an uninviting, aggressive
visual. Yesterday, they discussed that some hot spots, like the 900 block of Collins Avenue or the
700 block of Washington Avenue, may warrant keeping barricades based on data and history, but
they should not be imposed by default along all areas. The goal is to avoid normalizing a lockdown
when a managed open approach can be safe. On parking and garages, last year they closed
garages with a $100 rate, and he supports maintaining that, especially with the upcoming activities
and health events in the City. These visitors are good tourists who respect and support the local
economy. He favors keeping garages open and adjusting parking rates flexibly, allowing the City
Manager to respond to market conditions, raising or lowering rates as needed. He also believes
opening garages helps reduce illegal parking in residential zones, as on-street parking becomes
available. Regarding beach closing times and access, he sees no reason to close the beach at 6:00
p.m., especially with upcoming events that might require later hours. Instead, he supports giving the
City Manager and Police Chief flexibility on closing times. Access points to the beach have been
limited to two locations, which residents have expressed concerns about due to congestion and
crowding. Increasing access points and extending open hours could mitigate these issues, and he
supports that. Regarding traffic control, the community supports DUI checkpoints and LPR readers
at entry points. He suggests delaying the LPR operations from 9:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m. to avoid
traffic delays for those heading into the City for dinner. These tools are valuable, but they also have
unintended consequences, and the community’s feedback is important. Overall, the approach is to
keep these measures available if needed, not to implement them as default policies from the start.
They will be used in emergencies or as needed. He thanked the City Manager for attending
yesterday’s meeting and participating in the discussion.
Commissioner Bhatt thanked Commissioner Fernandez in his new role for convening the Public
Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee sunshine meeting yesterday to have this
conversation, something she has had on the agenda for months but was not reached. They talked
about it for hours and hashed out much of the nuance, which has been her desire for months when
she put it on the agenda. She is glad the meeting occurred, and for those who missed it, she
encourages them to go back and watch, as good ideas were exchanged.
In response to Commissioner Bhatt’s question, the City Manager confirmed that the sidewalk cafés
will be open during the day by default.
Commissioner Bhatt noted that Lady Gaga is performing a one-night-only concert on Friday the
13th as a replacement for last year’s canceled event. The Administration should plan proactively;
even if only a fraction of attendees come to the Beach, it is important to determine the show’s end
time and ensure the MacArthur Causeway remains clear. She does not want their Police Officers to
become less vigilant, but perhaps they can delay License Plate Readers (LPRs) and DUI
checkpoints until after the concert lets out. She deferred to the Police and safety experts on how to
manage that. The beach access policies, including closing times and how people access beaches,
need rethinking; having only two access points is counterproductive. She understands that this
offers more control, but there are other management options. It also makes the beach experience
less enjoyable because visitors are crowded into limited spaces instead of spreading out along the
beach. The weather is beautiful, but some prefer to visit the beach later in the day when the sun is
not so intense, and visitors and residents should have that option. She supports having measures in
place to address potential issues, but also emphasizes that, after two years of disruptions, they had
to break the circuit and re-educate the public on acceptable behavior in Miami Beach. They want
people to return and treat the City with care, respect, and the affection it deserves. Do not do things
here that you would not do at home. Residents have spent their lives building businesses here, and
they welcome both visitors crossing the Causeway and those from around the world, encouraging
consideration for others and responsible conduct.
Mayor Meiner agrees with some ideas to ease certain restrictions. One of the biggest issues for him
is the barricades, but he is concerned about granting too much flexibility, as he believes that was
part of the problem in the past. The City Commission previously set strict restrictions that the City
Manager and Police Chief enforced effectively. It becomes difficult when there is a constantly
changing situation and unclear guidelines, so he supports easing restrictions if necessary, but they
should be clearly defined, whether it involves barricades or parking. He has heard from businesses
about a possible voucher program, where businesses could use a QR code for verification with a
set number of vouchers.
William MacDonald, Parking Director, explained the challenge with the new system, which will be
fully operational within the garages before Spring Break. It will be able to do everything they do
now, with added benefits. Whether using the App for on-street parking and parking lots or managing
garages that can issue vouchers, the system has those capabilities. The challenge lies in reaching
out to every business and determining who gets what. They have spoken with Lissette Garcia
Arrogante, Tourism and Culture Director, and held a meeting with the Anchor institutions about this
issue, specifically, what they could do to ensure that attendees at the event have parking options.
The system can handle that; it just depends on who receives what and when. That is the difficult
part, but the technological capabilities will be in place.
Mayor Meiner inquired about the causeways because he spent a lot of last Spring Break on the
MacArthur and Julia Tuttle Causeways. At one point, he observed Officers confiscating illegal
weapons from a vehicle, which was highlighted in social media posts the Police shared about
removing serious ammunition from the roads during DUI checks and drug seizures. The issue is
serious, but interestingly, he recalled that some years ago, they waited up to four hours; the longest
wait he experienced last year was 45 minutes. He believes that, through collaboration with
policymakers, the Police have improved their response and handled their duties more effectively
without causing extreme delays. It is all about balancing safety efforts, because those guns, which
could have been used in Miami Beach, are a real concern. Although the full extent of potential
weapon use remains unknown, we do know that some of these weapons have been involved in
gang-related shootings within the City, and efforts continue to prevent such incidents.
Commissioner Dominguez understands the Mayor’s concerns, but before 2024, there was COVID-
19 and then post-COVID, which were completely different. Since then, the activations have
improved dramatically. She feels comfortable making some changes and pivoting. One of her
colleagues mentioned that March has beautiful weather, but many City businesses rely on it to get
through the tough months of August and September. She supports the later DUI checkpoint and
closing one lane, which absolutely needs to be done, so people coming to dine at restaurants can
do so without waiting or missing their reservations. Sidewalk cafés should remain open, with no
barricades except in the hotspots mentioned, such as 7th Street, 9th Street, Collins Avenue, and
Washington Avenue. They have exciting programming coming up, and people will be looking for
parking. The barricade's appearance is not good, so removing it is a positive step. Keeping the
garages and lots open on Lincoln Road is important since last year, the businesses suffered
greatly, and this year, on top of everything, they also face construction challenges. They need all
the help they can get. The City Manager noted that the City has worked with the County on the
bridges and asked if the Coast Guard is also involved.
Eric Carpenter, the City Manager, clarified that the Coast Guard controls the bridges' operation; the
County is the entity they have contacted in the past to explore the possibility of closing the
causeways to residents only. During those discussions, the County has been resistant.
Commissioner Dominguez saw the marketing campaign on social media last night; she thought it
was fun and is excited about it. She praised the Communications team and GMCVB for completing
it.
Commissioner Magazine appreciates Commissioner Fernandez’s leadership in Public Safety and
Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee. The Committee had a productive collaborative discussion.
When discussing changing or maintaining measures, it is important to consider where they were,

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, DIRECTING THE ADMINISTRATION TO PREPARE A BUDGET AMENDMENT TO APPROPRIATE IN FISCAL YEAR 2026 AN ADDITIONAL $111,000 TO THE CITY’S PREKINDERGARTEN SCHOLARSHIP PROGRAM (THE “PROGRAM”) FOR THE 2026-27 SCHOOL YEAR TO ALLOW EACH OF THE 37 WAITLISTED FAMILIES RECEIVE UP TO $3,000 IN SCHOLARSHIP FUNDS; FURTHER, DIRECTING THE ADMINISTRATION TO INCREASE THE NUMBER OF AVAILABLE PREKINDERGARTEN SCHOLARSHIPS IN THE PROGRAM FROM 192 TO 230 FOR FUTURE SCHOOL YEARS, EFFECTIVE IN FISCAL YEAR 2027, REPRESENTING AN ADDITIONAL INCREASE IN THE BUDGET IN THE AMOUNT OF $111,000 TO MEET THE DEMONSTRATED DEMAND AND INTEREST FROM THE CITY’S RESIDENTS, WITH THE TOTAL FUNDING IN FY 2027 AND FUTURE YEARS BEING $690,000 TO PROVIDE 230 SCHOLARSHIPS OF UP TO $3,000 EACH; AND FURTHER, WAIVING, BY 5/7TH VOTE, THE REQUIREMENT IN SECTION 2-14(D)(1)A OF THE CITY CODE TO REFER ANY AGENDA ITEMS IN EXCESS OF $75,000 TO THE FINANCE AND ECONOMIC RESILIENCY COMMITTEE.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34118 was adopted. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to
adopt the Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Bhatt. Vote: 7-0. Dr. Leslie Rosenfeld and
Tameka Otto Stewart to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Mayor Meiner stated that this is a straightforward Item and explained that it concerns the City’s Pre-
K Scholarship Program, which provides financial assistance to families with Pre-K students
attending non-public schools. He clarified that the program is open to any eligible private Pre-K
provider and is not limited to a specific type of school. He noted that applicants come from a broad
cross-section of Miami Beach residents. To his knowledge, Miami Beach is the only City in Florida
to offer this type of scholarship in addition to what is provided by the State. The City’s scholarship
provides up to $3,000 per eligible student. Last year, the City successfully closed the funding gap to
ensure that all eligible applicants received awards. However, during the current budget cycle, a
shortfall has not been fully addressed. As a result, while 192 students have been awarded the
$3,000 scholarship, an additional 37 eligible applicants remain on a waitlist. Approval of this Item
before the City Commission would close a funding gap of approximately $111,000, allowing all
eligible applicants to receive funding. This program is well-received, highly impactful, and aligned
with the City’s broader goals of supporting families and early childhood education. He thanked his
colleagues for their strong support and requested a motion.
Commissioner Fernandez asked how we can spread the word so residents know such a program
exists.
Dr. Leslie Rosenfeld, Chief Education and Performance Officer, addressed the Commission and
said that the program is currently in its fourth year. She reported that the City has 29 Pre-K provider
partners and works actively to raise community awareness. Outreach efforts include coordinating
with existing provider partners, collaborating with the Early Learning Coalition and the State, and
delivering consistent community-wide messages to inform residents and prospective residents
about the opportunity. The program supports the City’s goal of encouraging families to stay in Miami
Beach and attracting new residents, especially those looking for strong educational options. She
noted that the program has been very well received by the Miami Beach community.
Commissioner Fernandez mentioned that Saint Patrick’s School offers a Pre-K program, but it is not
listed as a participating provider. Is there a reason for this?
Dr. Rosenfeld stated that Saint Patrick’s is not currently a program partner, but clarified that the
application process to become a partner is open year-round. The City encourages all eligible Pre-K
providers to apply and collaborate with the program.
Commissioner Fernandez expressed interest in ensuring that Saint Patrick’s School and its families
are fully informed and able to participate. He noted the size and importance of the school within the
Miami Beach community and emphasized that students there should have access to the same
opportunities as students at other schools, including those outside the City limits that already
benefit from the program.
Dr. Rosenfeld replied that City staffers have met with Father Cid and the school’s leadership in the
past and that Saint Patrick’s is invited to participate each year, both directly and through families
who apply for and receive scholarships. She reiterated that Saint Patrick’s, like all eligible providers,
is welcome to partner with the City.
Commissioner Fernandez asked once again if there is a reason why Saint Patrick’s School is not
participating.
Dr. Rosenfeld explained that schools decide independently whether to participate. Over time,
different providers have mentioned various reasons, such as staffing shortages, existing programs
already in place, or a desire not to engage in the City’s reimbursement process. She pointed out
that some families have successfully encouraged schools to join, helping the program grow to 29
partners.
Commissioner Fernandez recommended a more proactive outreach strategy, suggesting that the
City collaborate directly with Saint Patrick’s to guide them through the process and ensure they fully
understand the program. He highlighted that many families would benefit and urged the City to
make every effort to provide equitable access.
Mayor Meiner thanked Commissioner Fernandez for encouraging Saint Patrick’s participation. He
recalled a similar situation with other schools and agreed that proactive involvement could be
beneficial.
Dr. Rosenfeld stated that staff will continue outreach efforts and expressed optimism that Saint
Patrick’s could potentially become the 30th participating provider.
All members of the City Commission asked to be listed as co-sponsors.
Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Resolution; seconded by Commissioner
Bhatt. Vote: 7-0.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, APPROVING THE MATERIAL TERMS OF A SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH AND SUNTEX MARINA INVESTORS, LLC (SUNTEX) PURSUANT TO THE OFFICE OF THE INSPECTOR GENERAL (OIG) AUDIT DATED APRIL 17, 2025 AND AUTHORIZING THE CITY MANAGER TO NEGOTIATE AND FINALIZE A SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT CONSISTENT WITH THE MATERIAL TERMS REFLECTED IN THIS RESOLUTION AND IN A FORM ACCEPTABLE TO THE CITY ATTORNEY; AND FURTHER, AUTHORIZING THE CITY MANAGER AND CITY CLERK TO EXECUTE THE SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT; AND FURTHER, AUTHORIZING THE CITY MANAGER TO TAKE THE NECESSARY STEPS FOR THE IMPLEMENTATION THEREOF, INCLUDING THE NEGOTIATION OF AN AMENDMENT NO. 5 TO THE MARINA LEASE AGREEMENT DATED JUNE 24, 1983 CONSISTENT WITH THE TERMS OF THE SETTLEMENT; AND FURTHER, AUTHORIZING THE CITY MANAGER AND CITY CLERK TO EXECUTE AMENDMENT NO. 5 TO THE LEASE AGREEMENT IN A FORM ACCEPTABLE TO THE CITY ATTORNEY.
items.action: Resolution 2026-34119 was adopted as amended. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the Resolution as amended, seconded by Mayor Meiner. Vote: Ozzy Dominguez and Mark Taxis to handle.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34119 was adopted as amended. Commissioner Suarez made a
motion to adopt the Resolution as amended, seconded by Mayor Meiner. Vote: Ozzy Dominguez
and Mark Taxis to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
AMENDMENTS:
Return for Updated Agreement
Bring back to the City Commission with an updated Settlement Agreement. Require that the Lease
Amendment and Parking Agreement Amendment return to the City Commission for approval.
Resident Priority for Marina Slips
Codify a policy ensuring Miami Beach residents have first priority for available slips before offering
them to outside charters or non-residents, regardless of boat size.
Mayor Meiner introduced the Item and gave a shout-out to the Police Department and Code
Enforcement for the many steps taken to address the chaos. He also acknowledged South of Fifth
Neighborhood Association (SOFNA), which was active in reaching out to the City Commission and
taking legislative steps, along with enforcement tools. Overall, it was a good job all around.
Ozzy Dominguez, Director of the Asset Management Division, noted that R7 Y is reviewing the
Office of Inspector General (OIG) audit of the Marina. Items identified in the audit were responded
to by Suntex Marina. Over the past few months, City staff has had opportunities to meet and
discuss these items with Suntex. They have reached a settlement agreement and want to present it
today for review, discussion, and approval. Some issues in the OIG report have already been
settled, including the Business Tax Receipts (BTRs) that were not in place; now the Marina slip
owners have their BTRs. Also, there was a sales tax discrepancy that was overbilled to Suntex
Marina on behalf of the City, and a credit has been issued. The settlement with Suntex Marina
includes the Marina providing the City with 1,000 square feet of office space on its upland property,
usable by Police, Code, or Ocean Rescue, valued at $ 50,000 per year, with a 3% escalation
annually for the duration of the current Marina agreement. Additionally, the City will receive one
boat slip for Ocean Rescue, and the Marina will provide two additional 45-foot boat slips, valued at
$ 84,000 per year, plus escalation during the agreement. Currently, the Marina agreement allows
the City to earn 0. 0.2 cents per gallon on fuel; this rate has been increased to 0. 0.6 cents,
estimating annual revenue of $ 56, 000 in the first year. The agreement will also clarify the definition
of gross receipts regarding the upland property operating expense reinvestment, as identified in the
OIG report. Currently, expenses are out-of-pocket costs incurred by the landlord and billed back to
upland tenants; the existing agreement does not specify that these are not revenue or profit for the
Marina but are reimbursements for out-of-pocket expenses. This will be clearly defined in the new
agreement. The verbiage regarding parking revenue will also be revised so that 35% of gross
revenue, less any bad debts, will be remitted to the City. Lastly, Suntex Marina has agreed to
contribute $ 240,000 to the City for the marine patrol dock improvement project at Maurice Gibbs
Park. This contribution has a total value over the lease term of $9 million, with a present value of
about $ 4.6 million.
Commissioner Suarez explained that many residents have approached him over the years,
complaining about the difficulty of getting a slip at the Miami Beach Marina, with waits of up to 2
years. He believes there should be a policy allowing Miami Beach residents to get priority
regardless of the boat size requested, since it is their Marina. Is that something the Inspector
General can incorporate into this deal?
Ozzy Dominguez, Asset Management Division Director, addressed Commissioner Suarez and said
he believes residents have the first dibs on the slips. He needs to check on that again today. He
specified that there is language in the agreement allowing them to work into it. It is a policy that the
Marina currently upholds, and he will double-check that and incorporate it into the agreement.
Discussion continued.
Inspector General Joseph Centorino stated that the OIG does not participate in negotiations, as that
is the responsibility of the City Administration. They have the information and report and are
involved in the negotiations. They reviewed the settlement, spoke to the relevant parties, and during
this process, he kept in touch with people in the Administration. He concluded that the City engaged
in good-faith negotiations and secured significant concessions from the Marina, which are both
substantial and valuable. Unfortunately, due to a lack of oversight during the Marina's operations,
the City was placed in a tough position regarding negotiations. He hopes this issue will be
addressed moving forward. He was impressed that the Administration achieved an increase in the
gasoline rate, which is part of the contract and cannot be changed by the City. The Administration
successfully negotiated an increase from two cents to six cents, which he considered significant.
Overall, from what they observed, the negotiation was successful, and the Administration handled it
well.
Ozzy Dominguez, Asset Management Division Director, replied to Commissioner Suarez that they
have not yet finished the draft agreement; they are willing to present it, receive direction or
approval, and then move forward.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, clarified that the Resolution, as drafted, approves the terms of the
agreement and does not require returning to the Commission for approval of the Settlement
Agreement. He also suggested amending the lease if they want that included. Discussion was held.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that Suntex has 30 charters, and with this amendment, which he
thinks is great, it is a public Marina. It should be the priority and first use for residents and taxpayers
who own the public Marina, before it is used by members outside our community. It is horrible when
residents who want to boat have to go to Miami or other areas. The property should be reserved for
City residents. As Commissioner Suarez has mentioned, once a commercial dock becomes
available because someone left, the priority should be a City resident before opening it to another
charter.
Michael Grieco, on behalf of Suntex, knows that historically, when a charter gives up its slip, they
convert it to private. Currently, about 50% of the private slips at the Marina are Miami Beach
residents, and Suntex has a policy that gives first refusal to City residents before listing the slips
publicly. There is a significant waiting list, and this minor amendment would simply codify a policy
they already follow. Discussion held.
Commissioner Suarez moved the Item as amended for it to come back to the City Commission with
an updated agreement, seconded by Mayor Meiner. Vote: 7-0.

Commissioner Suarez voiced opposition to Amanda Knapp’s appointment as Chair of the Human
Rights Committee, emphasizing that the objection is not based on ideology but on concerns
about her temperament and professionalism. Commissioner Suarez cited personal experience,
mentioning that Ms. Knapp publicly referred to him in a derogatory manner, displaying hostility
and disrespect that are not suitable for a leadership role centered on dialogue and inclusion. He
also cited reports from City Manager Eric Carpenter and others describing Ms. Knapp’s
interactions with staff as combative and abrasive, including instances in which she berated City
employees to tears during meetings. Commissioner Suarez stressed that the Chair must be
capable of de-escalating conflicts and promoting constructive collaboration, urging colleagues to
reconsider and vote against Ms. Knapp’s confirmation to protect the Committee's credibility and
staff well-being. He read an email into the record indicating that Ms. Knapp had spoken
disrespectfully to a staff member in front of Committee members, which led the staff member to
report the incident to her supervisor. The supervisor described the staff member as visibly upset,
in tears, and frustrated over the interaction. Additionally, Commissioner Suarez displayed a video
(Click here to see the video) in which Knapp made derogatory comments about him. He also
quoted a remark by Commissioner Fernandez, in which Commissioner Fernandez stated that he
would not support individuals who use their platforms to promote hate and division, as he made
his appointments.
Commissioner Fernandez stated he would not support the appointment of Ms. Knapp. He also
said he would not have supported Ines Flax’s appointment to the Affordable Housing Advisory
Committee for similar reasons. Commissioner Fernandez shared a post from Ms. Flax’s
Facebook page in which she made hateful political comments that promote division in the
community. He believes that boards and committees are meant to bring people together, even if
they come from different parties, and that divisiveness cannot be tolerated.
Commissioner Suarez stated that once he was informed of the post, he withdrew Ms. Flax’s
nomination. He also asked Commissioner Bhatt to withdraw her nomination of Ms. Knapp.
Commissioner Bhatt agreed that there should be a middle ground. However, she believes that
Commissioner Suarez himself has sometimes been an agent of division.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he has never made derogatory comments about any of his
colleagues. If he ever appointed someone who spoke about a colleague in a disrespectful way,
he would have removed them immediately, just as he did with Ms. Flax.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that there should not be a double standard between elected officials
and appointees to committees. Although she was present when the derogatory remarks were
made, she did not hear them. Her comments to people that day were, “You are a citizen of this
country. You are permitted to use your voice to express your dissatisfaction with the
government.” The point Commissioner Bhatt was trying to make was that as we work to improve
our communities, we should also treat our colleagues with respect. Commissioner Bhatt
withdrew her nomination of Ms. Knapp. While she praised Ms. Knapp’s work, she does not
believe that her rhetoric or upsetting staff is appropriate.

Commissioner Suarez opposed the appointment of Laura Veitia to the North Beach CRA Advisory
Committee. He emphasized that the concern is not personal or about integrity but about maintaining
public trust and preventing conflicts of interest. Commissioner Suarez pointed out that the CRA
manages redevelopment policies and public funds, including housing programs, and that appointing
the co-owner of a property management company presents an inherent conflict since CRA
decisions on housing and density directly affect property management opportunities. He stressed
that this issue cannot be addressed through occasional recusals and raised additional concerns
about family business ties and past dealings with major developers, which could reinforce the
perception of a small group influencing redevelopment decisions. Commissioner Suarez warned
that, even without any wrongdoing, public confidence could be damaged and urged choosing
someone whose private business interests are explicitly separate from North Beach development.
He concluded he cannot support this appointment and recommended considering other boards,
such as the Human Rights Committee, for service instead.
Commissioner Fernandez asked the City Attorney whether the North Beach CRA Advisory
Committee has decision-making authority or if it is purely advisory, and whether this appointment
differs from instances when real estate developers are appointed to boards.
City Attorney Ricardo J. Dopico confirmed that it is an advisory committee and stated that
responses to ethics questions are always based on facts.
Commissioner Fernandez stressed that the North Beach CRA Advisory Committee only serves in
an advisory role and does not have decision-making power. He clarified that the CRA Board, which
is the governing body, ultimately approves all actions, including the budget, which is then subject to
approval by the County. Although the advisory board can make recommendations through motions,
these are not binding, and the CRA Board has previously rejected such suggestions. Commissioner
Fernandez recognized Commissioner Suarez’s concerns but pointed out that the appointee is a
longtime resident and stakeholder who deserves respect, and he expressed discomfort with publicly
calling out individuals in this way.
Commissioner Dominguez mentioned that they are also a very philanthropic family. They are long-
time residents and contribute to many initiatives in the North Beach Fountain area. Commissioner
Dominguez inquired whether there are any bylaws related to conflict of interest or if it was just an
opinion.
City Attorney Dopico responded that we could ask Ms. Veitia to seek an opinion from the
Commission on Ethics.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that other North Beach business owners are on the Committee,
and it would not be fair to make one member go through a different process.
Commissioner Suarez reiterated concerns about conflicts of interest, explaining that the issue
arises from the nature of the appointee’s business in property management. He noted that the
North Beach CRA allocates 10% of its budget to affordable housing, and decisions related to
housing could intersect with property management interests. He emphasized the importance of
maintaining public trust by minimizing potential conflicts, regardless of whether the role is advisory
or non-advisory, and stated that greater separation from private business interests enhances
credibility.
City Attorney Dopico mentioned that if Ms. Veitia ever wished to do business with the City, she
would need to seek an opinion from the Commission on Ethics. This applies to any kind of
business, not just property management.

OCEAN FRONT AUDITORIUM, LOCATED AT 1001 OCEAN DRIVE, MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA
33139; AND (II) AUTHORIZING THE CITY MANAGER TO EXECUTE A LETTER AGREEMENT
WITH MDPL, IN A FORM APPROVED BY THE CITY ATTORNEY'S OFFICE, MEMORIALIZING
SAID EXTENSION.
City Manager Carpenter stated that, after the Item was posted, the City was contacted by the Office
of the Inspector General (OIG), which advised that an investigation related to MDPL was still
ongoing. The Inspector General expects to issue a report, or at least a draft report, within
approximately 30 days. The purpose of including this information on the record is to make sure that
no one votes without understanding that unresolved issues might still exist and could influence the
City Commission’s decision-making.
Mayor Meiner acknowledged the City Manager’s comments and stated that this Item has received
significant public attention. The Mayor noted that the City Commission had received a large number
of emails about this matter, and emphasized the importance of not ignoring it entirely. The Mayor
indicated that the City Commission would make a decision after hearing from the relevant parties.
Commissioner Suarez stated that, now that the matter is being discussed, he would like to revisit
previous concerns raised at the committee regarding MDPL’s internal practices, especially the
collection of lobbying-related fees from developers and any bylaw changes meant to prevent what
he described as egregious and abusive behavior associated with past leadership. He wants the
Inspector General to speak on the issue, noting that the Inspector General personally contacted him
and advised against taking final action before the investigative report is issued. He also asked for
responses from MDPL’s leadership, mentioning that the City Commission has received a flood of
emails supporting a three-year extension. Additionally, he questioned why a “call to action”
message was sent to the MDPL membership while an OIG report is pending. Doing so puts the City
Commission in a difficult position. He requested clarity from MDPL’s representatives to ensure the
matter could move forward more smoothly once formally considered, either later that day or after
the report is released.
Inspector General Centorino addressed the City Commission and asked if there was a specific
question he should answer.
Commissioner Suarez asked whether it would be appropriate to vote on the Item today and the
reason why.
Inspector General Centorino responded that the OIG does not take a position on the Item itself. His
Office has been conducting a lengthy investigation since last summer, and it is nearing completion.
Without going into specifics, he mentioned that the investigation involves serious issues related to
how operations were conducted and that the upcoming report will identify and explain these
problems. Regardless of the outcome, there will likely be a need for restructuring and changes in
how the organization functions moving forward. He advised that, from a governance perspective,
the City Commission would benefit from having as much information as possible before making a
long-term decision. The investigation and audit cover numerous financial issues, and the report will
help inform the City Commission’s next steps.
Commissioner Suarez asked the Chair of MDPL about why a call-to-action message was sent to
members considering the pending OIG investigation. This kind of outreach applies public pressure
to vote quickly, even though the City Commission is trying to wait for information that might raise
concerns and influence decisions.
Roger Goldblatt, Chair of MDPL, stated that the organization has received many requests from
members asking how they can help and that the organization has previously conducted similar
outreach on major issues. He described the message as meant to show support and inform
members on how to contact public officials. MDPL members are worried that the building and lease
are at risk and want to assist.
Commissioner Suarez inquired whether MDPL had notified its members about being under an
ongoing Inspector General investigation.
Mr. Goldblatt replied that he does not believe they had.
Commissioner Suarez emphasized that failing to disclose the ongoing investigation is problematic
and mentioned that, in his view, the report timeline has been lengthened because new information
keeps coming to light. He would have preferred MDPL to act in good faith by informing its members
that the City Commission is waiting for the Inspector General’s report before taking any action.
Mr. Goldblatt stated that MDPL believed it was within its rights to contact members and that it had
not acted improperly. MDPL has new leadership, including a new Executive Director and a new
Chair, and argued that the organization is being penalized for the past conduct of individuals no
longer involved. The records were left in disarray, and the current leadership is doing its best to
respond to requests for information.
Commissioner Suarez said that, from his view, MDPL seems to be pressuring the City Commission
to act before all facts are available. He does not like feeling pressured to vote while the OIG advises
caution and the City Commission is pushing for transparency and accountability.
Meg Lousteau, the new Executive Director of the Miami Design Preservation League, introduced
herself and stated that her first day in the role was November 17, 2025. She explained that MDPL
sent the email to members because the vote was scheduled today, and they wanted to show the
City Commission the level of community support for the organization and its work. She understands
the seriousness of the concerns and has taken feedback from the Inspector General’s Office to
heart. She advised that MDPL is in discussions with a CPA to conduct a governance, internal
controls, and operational review. She recognized that things had not been done properly in the past
and that she and Mr. Goldblatt are committed to meaningful reforms. She has not been in the role
long enough to build longstanding trust but offered to meet with Commissioners individually to
discuss operations and answer questions.
Commissioner Dominguez expressed strong support for MDPL and acknowledged its decades of
contributions to the City, describing the organization as a key part of the Art Deco identity that made
Miami Beach famous. She also took a call from the Inspector General and understands the
guidance to mean the City Commission should delay a long-term agreement until the report is
released, so that any necessary contractual adjustments or safeguards can be included.
Commissioner Bhatt expressed concern about penalizing an organization that is crucial to Miami
Beach for the misconduct of a former Executive Director. MDPL is significant not only to Ocean
Drive but also to citywide historic preservation, including MiMo architecture and other historic
neighborhoods. Its location acts as a visible public center for education and outreach, and moving it
would undermine its mission. She advocates for stronger accountability through contract terms such
as KPIs, metrics, and regular reporting, and she voiced frustration that the OIG’s notice arrived so
late in the process, causing what she sees as unnecessary last-minute drama. MDPL’s members
should be informed about the pending report, but it is also common for elected officials to advise
residents on how to engage when an important Item is on the agenda.
Commissioner Magazine commended Mr. Goldblatt for fostering a more collaborative tone, which
has shifted his perception of MDPL compared to previous years. He also received the same volume
of constituent emails and acknowledged the outreach effort. He asked Mr. Centorino whether the
investigation targets an individual, multiple individuals, or the organization as a whole.
Inspector General Centorino replied that the question is difficult to answer. He explained that
individuals had engaged in certain conduct, but he also identified structural issues within the
organization that contributed to those outcomes. He emphasized that the OIG is not targeting the
organization itself, but rather examining serious problems that need correction. The investigation
started before the current leadership was in place, and earlier cooperation issues had delayed
progress, although he stated he has received positive reports regarding the cooperation of current
staff.
Commissioner Suarez stated that the City Commission needs the OIG information before
committing to a long-term agreement and argued that moving forward too quickly could weaken the
City’s negotiating leverage. He expressed particular concern about fundraising practices, especially
accepting donations from developers, and emphasized that he wants to ensure reforms are genuine
and enforceable before finalizing any multi-year agreement.
Ozzie Dominguez, Asset Manager, clarified that the lease expired in December and was already
extended through June 30, 2026.
Commissioner Magazine suggested a short-term plan: extend the current lease to give time to
review the Inspector General’s report, collaborate with MDPL on reforms, and then negotiate a
long-term agreement with safeguards. He proposed extending the lease through September 2026,
noting that August is usually a quieter time and that the City Commission should not be negotiating
“with a gun to its head.”
Vice Mayor Mateo-Salinas stated that she supports delaying a long-term decision until the report is
available. She also wants to meet with the new MDPL leadership to understand what bylaw
changes and reforms have already been made and expressed support for the organization while
recognizing the seriousness of previous issues.
Commissioner Fernandez inquired with the City Attorney whether such agreements include a
termination clause.
The City Attorney confirmed that the City usually includes a termination-for-convenience clause.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that if the City retains the right to terminate and the contract can
include clear requirements for transparency and reform, such as a stronger separation between
fundraising and advocacy, he would be comfortable moving forward while allowing the new
leadership time to make changes. He suggested giving MDPL until the end of the year to show
progress.
Commissioner Suarez reiterated his preference to wait for the OIG report before directing staff to
negotiate a long-term agreement. Extending the lease on a shorter basis would avoid signaling that
the City is disregarding the Inspector General’s advice.
Mr. Goldblatt stated that MDPL revised its bylaws about six months earlier and provided them to
Commissioners and the OIG. The donation policy was also updated, including limits on developer
donations and procedures for returning funds when conflicts of interest arise.
Commissioner Suarez said he believes developer donations should not be accepted at all and
voiced concerns about potential conflicts of interest.
Ms. Lousteau reiterated that MDPL would comply with, respond to, and learn from the Inspector
General report, viewing it as an opportunity for necessary reforms. MDPL is planning for Art Deco
Weekend’s 50th anniversary, expected during MLK Weekend in 2027. She expressed a desire for
MDPL to stay in the current building and continue serving the community there.
Commissioner Fernandez highlighted the need for a “firewall” between development-related
fundraising and advocacy, emphasizing that advocacy must stay independent to preserve
credibility.
Commissioner Suarez asked whether MDPL would consider being subject to Sunshine Law-type
transparency requirements, such as noticed meetings and minutes, given that the organization
operates in a City-owned facility and receives significant subsidy.
Ms. Lousteau replied that she would need to consult counsel because MDPL is a private nonprofit,
and she expressed concerns that imposing Sunshine requirements could complicate advocacy
efforts that might sometimes diverge from City positions. She agreed, however, that this could be
discussed over the coming year.
City Clerk Granado clarified that the motion being considered is to extend the lease until December
31, 2026. This extension allows time for the Inspector General report to be issued and for reforms
to be addressed before finalizing a longer-term agreement.
Commissioner Magazine made a motion to adopt the after-the-fact-Resolution to extend the lease
to December 31, 2026, seconded by Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas. Vote: 7-0.
