ACTION: Discussion held.
Action Items Summary
1. Implement Mid-Review Communication Process
o Timeline: Within 30 days
o Quarterly reports on permits resolved through this process
o Reference: Motion 1
2. Reduce Permits with Four or More Review Cycles
o Goal: Cut by 50% within six months
o Progress update after three months
o Reference: Motion 2
3. Launch Text Notification System for Inspections
o Scheduled to go live in early March
o Alerts include initial scheduling and “two stops away” notice
4. Explore Automated Email Verification for Permit Contacts
o CIO to review feasibility and report back
5. Continue Development of AI Integration
o RFQ closes March 6, 2026
o AI to detect incomplete documentation and improve accuracy
6. Explore Expanding Business Concierge and Walk-Through Services
o Launch one-stop shop on first floor of City Hall
o Evaluate specialized restaurant permitting program
7. Maintain Reviewer and Inspector Consistency
o Ensure resubmissions return to the same reviewer
o Limit re-inspections to previously identified issues
8. Public Relations Strategy
o Explore hiring a PR firm to repair reputation and communicate improvements
Mayor Meiner thanked his colleagues for attending and emphasized the importance of
improving the permitting process to make Miami Beach a premier City for business. He
acknowledged recent improvements and expressed appreciation to City Manager Eric
Carpenter, Assistant City Manager Maria Hernandez, and Building Director Vince Seijas for their
efforts. Mayor Meiner highlighted the economic impact of issuing permits, noting that it creates
jobs, investment, housing, and tax revenue. He referenced recent business trends, including
companies relocating to Miami Beach, and stressed the need to streamline processes to attract
investment and maintain competitiveness. He described recent initiatives such as Building
Department walkthroughs and the Business Ready program, which is transitioning from
quarterly to monthly sessions to assist businesses with permits and licenses. Mayor Meiner also
shared observations from a recent event at FIU, where other local leaders identified permitting
reform as a top priority. He concluded by reiterating that improving the permitting process is
among the City’s highest priorities, alongside public safety, and that the City must seize the
current opportunity to position Miami Beach as a global destination for business.
City Manager Eric Carpenter acknowledged the Commission’s direction and stated that the City
has been working on permitting improvements for two years. He noted that significant
groundwork has been completed and expressed confidence in the team’s ability to implement
further changes. City Manager Carpenter credited Maria Hernandez for leading efforts to
improve the Building Department and the broader permitting process and invited her to present
an update.
Assistant City Manager Maria Hernandez provided a presentation summarizing the permitting
process and recent improvements. Click here to view. She explained that six internal
departments are involved in permitting, excluding external agencies such as the Department of
Health and the Department of Environmental Protection. Assistant City Manager Hernandez
shared volume data, noting that in fiscal year 2025, the City issued approximately 12,200
permits, processed 2,300 submittals per month, conducted 5,600 inspections, and handled
4,200 monthly calls. She highlighted major milestones, including reducing the number of permit
types from 250 to 150, launching Phase Two and Phase Three walkthroughs for residential and
business permits, implementing the City Services Concierge (Decision Engine), and retraining
approximately 200 employees with assistance from consultant Bob Moran. Assistant City
Manager Hernandez also described outreach efforts, including brochures and social media
campaigns to educate the public on permits, violations, and business tips. Assistant City
Manager Hernandez reviewed legislative actions initiated by the Commission in 2024 and 2025,
including items from the Permit Process Improvement Committee and initiatives sponsored by
individual commissioners. She noted additional proposed legislation for 2026 related to Land
Development Regulations. Assistant City Manager Hernandez reported improvements in permit
intake processing, reducing the average turnaround from 2.5 days to less than one day. She
presented historical data on review cycles, showing progress since 2018 and post-COVID
adjustments. Assistant City Manager Hernandez explained that 68% of permits are now
completed in two review cycles or fewer, and 84% in three cycles or fewer. She acknowledged
that permits requiring four or more cycles remain a challenge, with some cases reaching 20 or
more cycles, and stated that eliminating excessive review cycles is a priority.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine asked Assistant City Manager Hernandez how long each
review cycle typically lasts.
Assistant City Manager Hernandez explained that average turnaround times across
departments are generally less than 10 business days, aided by the walkthrough process
involving multiple departments. She noted that the City targets a ten-day turnaround for all
permit types, with most departments averaging under six days. Assistant City Manager
Hernandez clarified that the review cycle includes time with both the City and the customer. On
average, permits remain with the City for five business days and with the customer for ten
business days, resulting in a fifteen-day cycle. She provided an example from 2025, when new
residential construction permits averaged eleven days with the City and twenty-seven days with
the customer per cycle, totaling thirty-eight business days for one cycle. Assuming three cycles,
the process could take approximately 114 business days, or nearly six months, for a single-
family home permit. Commercial alteration permits follow a similar pattern but typically require
less time. Assistant City Manager Hernandez added that over-the-counter permits are
processed quickly, citing 3,300 issued permits and 408 walkthrough permits since July of the
previous year, with expectations to reach approximately 1,000 in 2026.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt requested to view the full slide and observed that while the City
can control its portion of review time, customer delays remain outside its control. Commissioner
Bhatt asked why customers often take three to four weeks to respond.
Assistant City Manager Hernandez identified incomplete and incorrect submittals as a major
issue, explaining that such errors automatically trigger additional reviews. She stated that the
City plans to analyze these issues and develop strategies to ensure complete and accurate
submissions. Assistant City Manager Hernandez noted that staff often acts as a quality
assurance consultant for applicants, which consumes time and resources. She proposed
creating a database indicator for incomplete submissions and exploring incentives for accurate
submissions while discouraging repeated errors. Assistant City Manager Hernandez suggested
that artificial intelligence could assist in improving submission accuracy.
Commissioner Bhatt expressed concern that assisting applicants with incomplete submissions
reduces efficiency for those who submit correctly. Commissioner Bhatt emphasized the
importance of identifying pain points and improving the website interface to minimize errors.
Assistant City Manager Hernandez agreed, noting that time spent on incomplete submissions
delays reviews and creates a backlog.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez asked whether the City has data on the nature of incomplete or
incorrect submittals.
Assistant City Manager Hernandez responded that while anecdotal information exists, formal
data is lacking. She indicated that the Planning Department could provide insights and
committed to collecting detailed data in the future.
Commissioner Fernandez observed that minor technical issues, such as stamp requirements,
often cause significant delays without affecting safety or structural integrity. He recommended
analyzing whether errors stem from design professionals or technical requirements.
Assistant City Manager Hernandez agreed and reiterated the importance of data-driven
solutions. Assistant City Manager Hernandez then introduced the City Services Concierge, also
known as the Decision Engine, a software platform designed to guide users through processes
such as bill payment, permit applications, business assistance, and public records requests.
She explained that the tool helps applicants access accurate information and navigate
requirements efficiently. Assistant City Manager Hernandez noted that the Economic
Development Department spearheads the City Business Concierge program, which provides
guidance, access to grants, and incentives for businesses. She highlighted recent outreach
efforts, including the launch of the “Miami Beach Means Business” campaign and the production
of promotional videos.
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas asked whether applicants are notified by telephone or email
when submissions are incomplete.
Assistant City Manager Hernandez deferred to Building Director Vince Seijas for clarification.
Building Director Vince Seijas explained that the system automatically sends email notifications
to all contacts associated with the permit record, including contractors and design professionals.
He noted that past issues with incorrect contact information have been addressed. Building
Director Seijas stated that applicants remain in a stopped status until corrections are made and
documents re-uploaded. He confirmed that telephone calls are typically made during later
review cycles to expedite resolution.
Assistant City Manager Hernandez resumed the presentation and described the Decision
Engine’s functionality, including its ability to provide tailored guidance for specific applications
such as condominium projects. She reiterated that the platform aims to streamline processes
and improve customer experience. Assistant City Manager Hernandez concluded by introducing
a promotional video featuring a local business owner. Click here to view the video.
Video description:
Natalia Morales, from MYKA Greek Frozen Yogurt, appeared in the video and described her
experience opening a business in Miami Beach. Ms. Morales highlighted the City’s support
during the permitting process and emphasized the benefits of operating in a diverse and vibrant
community.
Assistant City Manager Hernandez continued the presentation, noting that the City has
produced additional short videos featuring businesses on 41st Street and in North Beach, and
plans to expand the campaign to include CEOs who have relocated their companies to Miami
Beach. She explained that certificates of use (CUs) and business tax receipts (BTRs) are a
critical issue and that the City is revising the process to initiate these requirements earlier.
Previously, businesses often discovered these obligations only after obtaining a certificate of
occupancy, which caused delays. The new approach will begin the process sooner to avoid last-
minute complications.
Assistant City Manager Hernandez outlined next steps and recommendations, including
conducting additional workflow analyses to identify opportunities to reduce unnecessary reviews
for certain permit types. She stated that consultant Bob Moran will assist with this targeted
initiative. Assistant City Manager Hernandez also referenced planned changes to land
development regulations and lot split procedures, which Planning Director Thomas Mooney will
address. She reiterated the goal of incentivizing applicants to submit complete and accurate
packages to minimize review cycles. Additional initiatives include launching a Building
Assistance and Business Concierge on the first floor of City Hall to provide a one-stop shop for
residents, businesses, and condominium representatives; implementing artificial intelligence
software to detect incomplete documentation; introducing 24-hour digital permits for expedited
electronic reviews; and reinstating Design Professionals Day for one-on-one consultations.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine asked what level of personalized assistance applicants receive
and shared an example of a business owner who waited 21 days for a review, only to have the
application fail due to a missing letter of intent. Commissioner Magazine questioned why staff
do not proactively contact applicants to resolve minor issues instead of requiring a full
resubmission and additional waiting periods.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez suggested allowing applicants a 24-hour grace period to correct
deficiencies before failing an application, emphasizing that proactive communication could
prevent unnecessary delays.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine reiterated concerns about a lack of personalized service and
urged staff to adopt a customer-focused approach rather than a process-driven mentality. He
stressed that minor issues should be resolved through direct communication rather than
prolonging the review process.
Assistant City Manager Hernandez responded that the proposed Business Concierge program
is intended to assist applicants in navigating the process, but acknowledged that the current
system relies heavily on formal procedures.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine pressed further, asking whether planning staff currently
contacts applicants during the review process to resolve minor issues.
Planning Director Thomas Mooney stated that staff typically respond when applicants reach out
with questions, but proactive calls during reviews are not standard practice. He noted that initial
comments are typically sent by email.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez emphasized that proactive outreach should become the
standard rather than the exception, arguing that communication is essential to serving residents
effectively. He suggested that providing applicants with a short grace period to correct minor
issues would prevent delays and reduce the need for multiple review cycles.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine agreed, stating that the City should prioritize solutions over
clearing queues and adopt a service-oriented approach.
Planning Director Thomas Mooney acknowledged the recommendation and indicated that the
City could explore implementing proactive outreach for certain application types, particularly
those involving minor corrections.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez concluded that establishing a grace period as a standard
practice would help filter out minor issues that can be resolved quickly, while more complex
technical matters would still require additional time.
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas expressed agreement with the points raised by
Commissioner Joseph Magazine and Commissioner Alex Fernandez regarding proactive
communication. She suggested that staff notify applicants before failing an application, allowing
a window of 48 hours or more to correct deficiencies. Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas noted that
early feedback could reduce overall processing time by preventing repeated review cycles. She
asked whether staffing limitations prevent more frequent outreach.
Planning Director Thomas Mooney acknowledged staffing challenges, citing vacancies, training
needs, and temporary absences. He stated that these factors make it difficult to maintain
proactive outreach, but agreed that the Department could begin implementing more direct
communication.
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas asked how this change could be implemented across all
departments involved in permitting.
Planning Director Thomas Mooney responded that he would work with senior planners to
convey the message and explore options for improving outreach.
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas then asked City Manager Eric Carpenter about the current
walk-through process.
City Manager Eric Carpenter explained that walk-throughs occur three days per week on the
second floor of the Building Department, where representatives from all permitting-related
departments assist applicants in person. He stated that the process has been successful and
noted that it began as a one-day-per-week initiative before expanding. City Manager Carpenter
indicated that further expansion would depend on demand and staffing capacity, as walk-
throughs require staff to step away from regular review duties. He emphasized that the City’s
goal is to issue permits efficiently and suggested exploring incentives to achieve one- or two-
cycle reviews.
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas questioned why walk-throughs are not offered five days per
week and asked whether staff could review plans during periods without in-person applicants.
City Manager Eric Carpenter reiterated that expansion is possible if volume warrants it, but
noted that walk-throughs are resource-intensive.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez asked how many hours staff dedicate to walk-throughs during
each session.
Assistant City Manager Maria Hernandez responded that walk-throughs operate from 8:00 a.m.
to 12:00 p.m., with the last ticket issued at 11:00 a.m. She explained that the process involves
moving applicants through multiple stations, which can be loud and distracting, but allows for
immediate resolution of issues. Assistant City Manager Hernandez noted that walk-throughs are
limited to smaller projects, such as window or roof permits, and do not include large-scale
developments. She highlighted the proposed 24-hour permit option as an alternative for
applicants unable to attend in person, offering expedited electronic review. Assistant City
Manager Hernandez stated that the Decision Engine tool also helps applicants prepare
complete submissions by providing checklists.
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas confirmed that walk-throughs accommodate both residential

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34134 adopted. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by
Commissioner Suarez. A motion was made by Commissioner Dominguez to adopt the Resolution,
seconded by Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas. Vote: 7-0. Lissette Garcia Arrogante to handle.
Commissioner Suarez believes it is unfair for others to accuse him of being hateful simply because
he is pulling an Item on the Consent Agenda for discussion. He emphasizes that he is not against
Pride and has attended every Pride festival even before his election. He is the only Commissioner
with an openly gay Aide. When they bring an Item on the Consent Agenda, it is expected to pass
unanimously, and this particular Item includes $250,000 in recurring funds since the 2000s.
Considering that the City has agreed to cut its budget by 5% for FY2027, and acknowledging that the
State is also targeting Pride festivals through other means, it is important to discuss both topics, which
is why he pulled the Item. He finds it disheartening that there appears to be a call to action to the gay
community, claiming he is hateful for discussing this. He stresses the need for more conversation
about what the City represents, how they will achieve their goals, how to fund these initiatives, and
how to withstand pressures from the State attempting to shut down this program. An adult discussion
about reducing the budget while still supporting cultural programs and organizations is necessary.
Since the City staff is asked to cut 5% of the budget, a difficult task, any funding decisions, whether
for Gay Pride, the Jewish Film Festival, or other events, should be subject to honest discussion. He
affirms he is not anti-gay or anti-arts, despite attempts to portray him otherwise. He calls for a serious
discussion on how to continue funding $300,000 in taxpayer money annually, especially amid
expected pressure from the Administration to lower the budget. Additionally, they recently learned
that the State is trying to eliminate Pride events through other means, and any elected official
sponsoring such events could face removal from office. He believes this issue warrants public
discussion and wants to dispel rumors that he is hateful for bringing it up on the Consent Agenda. It
is personally offensive to him, as he has always supported the LGBTQ community. He suggests
discussing whether this funding should be permanent, whether grant applicants should begin sharing
cost savings for taxpayers, or whether funding should be included in the annual budget to avoid
recurring debate. He also raises concerns about how to proceed if the State makes Pride illegal,
questioning how they will support these organizations moving forward without risking their political
careers. He welcomes input from colleagues and acknowledges that Commissioner Fernandez’s aide
circulated a call to action to SAVE and LGBTQ members. However, he finds it unfair that he has been
targeted and accused of being hateful toward the community, which he refutes. He emphasizes the
need for an honest discussion about fiscal responsibility and the implications of the State potentially
banning Pride parades in Florida, which is why he decided to separate the Item.
Commissioner Fernandez clarified that when his Aide reached out to the LGBTQ community,
Commissioner Suarez’s name was not mentioned in the email. In fact, they asked people to keep
their remarks respectful, professional, and focused on the issue of the sponsorship. He does not
believe anyone addressed Commissioner Suarez as being hateful and confirmed this with the City
Clerk. They are here to protect everyone's dignity, and he does not tolerate attacks on his colleagues.
The message from his Office to the volunteer committee did not mention Commissioner Suarez by
name and specifically asked individuals to speak in a professional tone. He wanted to ensure there
were no misunderstandings or mischaracterizations of the facts. Commissioner Fernandez added
that there was nothing disrespectful; the email from his Office to the committee members, who care
about this issue, did not mention Commissioner Suarez’s name. As he noted, the message
encourages people to be respectful and professional. That is very important. Ultimately, Pride
represents people's ability to live freely and openly; it signifies their dignity and also carries a
significant economic impact for Miami Beach. Over 150,000 attendees come to the City from across
the country and around the world, including Argentina, Spain, and Canada. Based on a study, he saw
that about 75% of them are out-of-town visitors who stay in hotels, support City restaurants, and
strengthen the local economy. Pride can always happen. The State cannot prevent Pride from
happening; they may be able to restrict their funding in the future, but Pride is very much aware of
the ongoing conversations in Tallahassee. What happens in the future remains to be seen, and they
need to address that. They also need to review their sponsorships, which have been affected because
corporate sponsors fear retaliation, just as the LGBTQ community is feeling. The retaliation the
community faces is the same as that experienced by their corporate allies, who have helped sustain
this event over the years. He does not know whether they will be able to continue this long-standing
tradition in the City without the City's support. Currently, the loss of State support allows them to keep
this tradition alive. If that support changes in the coming years, they are aware of those discussions
and will pivot as needed to keep the parade going. Maybe in the future it will not be a weeklong
festival; it might take other forms depending on what the State does, but they cannot let the constant
fear of State actions hinder them from doing what is right today. Pride exists today not because of
him or his LGBTQ colleagues or former colleagues, but because of the City Commission and the
straight allies of this dais who, over the years, have made Pride happen and sustained it with funding.
No personal comments were directed toward Commissioner Suarez, and no one mentioned his name
publicly today. Everyone was encouraged to address the issue with respect and professionalism. He
stated that this is deeply personal; people are facing hate. He could face removal from Office for
supporting his community, and that is hateful. This is not the only community facing such backlash,
but he does not believe anyone here suggests hate is coming from this dais, as he emphasized that
their strength is due to their straight allies. He does not want this false narrative and message to be
manipulated or twisted because that is not what is happening.
Commissioner Suarez believes that he and Commissioner Fernandez share similar views on many
cultural organizations, aiming to enhance their financial stability. He thinks they need to have a
genuine discussion about diversifying their financial support for cultural anchors. He notes that this
support cannot always come from the City government because funding is being cut by the State and
County, and he does not want Miami Beach taxpayers to bear the burden of every program. Moving
forward, they should be honest about who qualifies for grant funding. They already discussed this
before lunch, which is why he separated the Item. They are not that far apart, and encouraging
nonprofits and organizations to diversify their funding for City events is beneficial; it strengthens both
the organizations and the City, and there is nothing wrong with having that discussion. There will
come a time when funding may no longer come from the State; perhaps another recession is on the
horizon, and serious budget cuts will be necessary if property tax values fall, especially considering
that the State of Florida is already contemplating tax cuts and potential elimination of property taxes.
During such times, they will need to have tough conversations about how to fund everything.
Nonetheless, he wanted to start the dialogue about the ongoing funding of organizations that receive
City tax dollars.
Commissioner Fernandez suggested referring an Item to the Finance and Economic Resiliency
Committee because it applies selectively to one organization but could be used across the board,
similar to the Resolution on the agenda that was not called. This Resolution urges entities to pursue
diversity and funding, especially in light of conversations at the dais. It is their responsibility to inform
stakeholders about discussions on the dais, considering their own fiscal constraints or potential
changes in State laws that could require belt-tightening. Providing a heads-up allows organizations
to plan and find alternative funding sources. This is reasonable, but what he is proposing warrants a
separate agenda Item. While laws are what they are, they should not cherry-pick which ones to apply
different criteria to. He recommended establishing a uniform grant review policy and considering the
Administration's recommendations for the future. Meanwhile, they should support Pride. It is not only
a cultural event promoting community inclusivity, especially for groups that have not always been
welcomed or tolerated, but also benefits the City’s economic development. It attracts tourism and
supports local businesses in April, which historically has been a strong month for commerce.
Recently, however, businesses struggled in March due to policies that affected their economic impact.
Pride positively impacts hotel stays, venue activities, and increased restaurant reservations, all of
which have a ripple effect on the City’s economy. Supporting Pride is the right thing to do, aligns with
the City’s identity, and reflects taxpayers’ values, supporting all groups they have traditionally backed.
If concerns about future funding exist, a comprehensive policy approach would be more effective than
piecemeal decisions through individual grants.
Commissioner Suarez is not trying to be piecemeal, which is why he pulled many Items from the
Consent Agenda related to finances and City funding, some of which have nothing to do with cultural
organizations and nonprofits. He aims to be a fiscal hawk on the Commission and is not targeting any
one group, entity, or group of entities. He plans to do what he was elected to do and be a good
steward of their finances.
Commissioner Dominguez echoed Commissioner Fernandez’s remarks. The LGBTQ committee has
faced attacks for many years, and the hate directed at them is unjustified and unfair. Even during her
campaign and others, they were targeted with misinformation about the trans community, which was
hateful and unnecessary. She remains and will always be an ally. The gay community has significantly
contributed to shaping Miami Beach into what it is today. The Pride Festival is a beautiful event; it
does not result in stampedes or shootings. It is about love, fun, economic impact, and celebrating a
wonderful occasion. She moved the approval of the Item, if it has not already been moved or
seconded, if it has. It is a vital Item for the City and for her.
Commissioner Magazine fully supports the Item and has requested to be added as a co-sponsor.
This is an incredible and inspiring event for him to get fit next year. Commissioner Suarez is an equal-
opportunity critic; his comments are not specific or targeted. A few months ago, Commissioner
Magazine proposed an Item related to an economic development incentive for a company that
promotes beautiful women, which Commissioner Suarez also opposed. Since Commissioner Suarez
took his seat, he has been very conservative regarding the City’s fiscal finances. He and
Commissioner Suarez have been friends for many years; politics can be turbulent, and while they
may not know what is in each other's hearts, they have had honest discussions. Though they
sometimes disagree, his colleague Commissioner Suarez has never expressed anything hateful.
Commissioner Magazine is very supportive of this and thanked Commissioner Fernandez.
Commissioner Fernandez explained that the concerns of the community demonstrate that this is a
community that rightfully has many reasons to feel a heightened sense of sensitivity. It is a community
that has been targeted repeatedly; they face more and more policies each year that aim to silence
them, their visibility, and the expression and identification of the LGBTQ community. Constant policies
and bills are being introduced, including recent discussions about HIV medication funding, which
appears to be an attempt to force HIV-positive individuals to leave the state. He thanked Mayor
Meiner for co-sponsoring that legislation with him. The residents have every reason to feel a
heightened sense of sensitivity because they feel like they have a target on their backs.
Commissioner Suarez might not feel it as intensely, but it is very real. In recent years, Commissioner
Fernandez reported that he had experienced hateful speeches directed at him that he had never
encountered before. As society seems to be making progress and advancing, they sometimes
regress. This is similar to the Jewish community, which feels heightened sensitivity and a sense of
being targeted, even in conservative political circles that traditionally supported them. Now, some
segments are expressing openly nationalist and anti-Semitic rhetoric. Many community members are
feeling this way right now, and the most important role for elected officials is to foster community, not
just buildings and parks, but a genuine community of people who support each other. Whether
residents belong to the LGBTQ+, Jewish, Spanish, Black, or white communities, they should continue
to look out for one another, as they have historically, because that is what makes the City beautiful
and unique. It is inspiring when members of the public call in saying they have attended Pride events
even before moving to Miami Beach. They are a vibrant, diverse community. Commissioner Suarez’s
points about fiscal responsibility are well taken, but he believes it is best to work together to develop
legislation that addresses issues holistically, rather than individually. When policies are addressed
one by one, segments of the community sometimes feel targeted, even if that is not the intention.
Overall, the focus should be on the overall management of grants and policies, rather than isolated
reactions. Discussion held.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas is also 100% supportive of Pride and the funding proposed. South Beach
was built by gay people; it would not be South Beach without the LGBTQ community, and she thanked
them for that. She recounted walking home on Washington Avenue when she saw a group of guys
on the west side of a dark street, and she felt fear, but then she realized it was Nathan’s Bar, an
LGBTQ+ lounge, and people were outside, so she felt safe; she thanked them for keeping her safe,
too. As a woman, she did not know what she was going to walk into until she realized that it was a
gay bar, so now she is lucky enough to be up here to protect them, their events, and their funding.
During her campaign, she had a conversation where one day she spoke with someone from the
Orthodox community, who asked her to just keep them safe, they feel comfortable in their home, they
can wear kippahs, traditional uniforms, and wear, please keep them safe, and that means a lot to her.
Thirty minutes later, she spoke with a gay man asking her to keep them safe, they feel comfortable
here, they can hold hands and wear rainbow flags, and she agreed. It struck her how those
conversations mirrored these two communities that are so different, but this is their home, and they
both deserve to feel safe, no matter who they represent or love. She is happy to support Pride and
will second the motion or make the motion to adopt.
Commissioner Bhatt echoed words, mentioning she is also a proud straight human being, and she
loves Pride. She came with her daughter two years ago and was dazzled by how joyful it is, and God
knows they could use some joy in their lives, when people walk around, whether gay or any other
community with an enormous target on their back for just existing, it is insane to her that they would
hasten in the State’s efforts to undermine protecting residents and visitors who come here to enjoy
this event. The City Commission shares the concerns of economic resiliency going forward, they do
not know what the future holds in terms of property tax cuts, tax rollback, and so on, but when an
event is as well established with as much global impact as Miami Beach Pride is, people coming in
from not only around the State but from around the world to spend the best week of the year why
would they do anything in Miami Beach to hasten in a change that may not even happen. Some may
recall that her background is in branding and marketing, and that she entered the industry shortly
after Absolute Vodka launched. Absolute Vodka is a slightly better than mediocre vodka from
Sweden, it is fine, but in 1981 in the heart of the AIDS epidemic they took a gamble and bought the
back page ad box on advocate magazines, they invested by taking a leap of faith on the gay
community at the height of the crisis because they know that the gay community, LGBTQ leads the
way in economic impact and in terms of transformation, but it is economically demonstrated over
decades and they have not wavered in that position since 1981 and almost 50 years later this slightly
better than mediocre vodka remains between the number two or within the top five vodkas in the
country. This is an investment in the City’s economic well-being. She understands the concerns; it is
a large grant. They give very large grants to many other events that come to Miami Beach, which are
incredibly impactful. The events coming for Spring Break are a worthwhile expenditure of the funds

ACTION: Resolution 2026-34146 was adopted. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt
the Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Dominguez. Vote: 7-0. Office of the City Clerk and
Christina Baguer to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Pursuant to Ordinance 2015-3954, Sec. 2-12(3), Addendum Agenda Item C7 AB was approved by
Mayor Meiner for inclusion on the agenda.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that it is alarming to see the Legislature becoming the Zoning Board
of the City of Miami Beach. The powers of our Historic Preservation Board are so important, and
when someone sees they are not getting their way, they should not be able to get assistance from
the State Legislature to circumvent the taxpayers of this community, who deserve to have a right to
be heard, and deserve applications for historic properties to be met with objective criteria.
Mayor Meiner agreed with Commissioner Fernandez’s statement.
Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Resolution; seconded by Commissioner
Dominguez. Vote: 7-0.
Clerk’s Note:
10:16:53 a.m.
Susanna Santoro, via Zoom, thanked Commissioner Fernandez and the Commission for advancing
Item C7 AB opposing HB-399. This is important not only from a historic preservation standpoint but
also from a broader perspective of fairness, infrastructure, concurrency, fiscal responsibility, and
critical life safety. Miami Beach is a barrier island with limited recreation routes, traffic congestion,
and documented emergency access challenges. Preserving meaningful local review of development
intensity is crucial for public safety and ensuring equitable governance. This guarantees that all
property owners are subject to consistent evidentiary standards affecting traffic, emergency
response, water, sewer, stormwater systems, and that properties are properly evaluated before
approvals are granted. Such measures are essential to protect residents and visitors, and, in the long
term, to ensure the community's financial stability. (Ms. Santoro spoke on Item C7 AB during the
public comment period for Item R7 U)
items.motion: Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Dominguez.

items.title: AN ORDINANCE OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, AMENDING CHAPTER 70 OF THE CITY CODE, ENTITLED “MISCELLANEOUS OFFENSES,” BY AMENDING ARTICLE II, ENTITLED “PUBLIC PLACES,” BY AMENDING DIVISION 3, ENTITLED “ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES,” BY AMENDING SECTION 70-87, ENTITLED “CONSUMPTION, SERVICE, SALE AND POSSESSION OF OPEN CONTAINERS OF ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES ON OR IN PUBLIC PLACES; WARNING SIGNS REQUIRED,” BY AMENDING AND SETTING FORTH EXCEPTIONS TO THE PROHIBITION ON CONSUMING, SERVING, SELLING, OR POSSESSING AN OPEN CONTAINER OF AN ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGE ON OR IN ANY PUBLIC PLACE; AND BY AMENDING AND CLARIFYING THE RESPONSIBILITIES OF ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGE ESTABLISHMENTS, AND PERSONS OR ENTITIES AUTHORIZED BY THE CITY TO SELL ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES ON OR IN ANY PUBLIC PLACE, REGARDING THE PROHIBITION ON ALLOWING ANY PERSON TO TAKE AN ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGE FROM THE LICENSED PREMISES OR AUTHORIZED AREA; AND PROVIDING FOR REPEALER, SEVERABILITY, CODIFICATION, AND AN EFFECTIVE DATE.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Ordinance 2026-4802 was adopted. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record.
The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on
Second Reading; seconded by Commissioner Magazine. Roll Call: 6-0. Absent: Commissioner
Fernandez. John Rebar to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Absent
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Commissioner Magazine stated that this has been discussed over the last few months. Miami Beach
is a different City than it was a few years ago, and we are still evolving into a different kind of City,
becoming more civil, resident-friendly, and upscale in our tourism. We are expanding amenities that
will not be abused or misused. This will resemble places like the Italian Amalfi Coast or the French
Riviera, where people can enjoy beverages within designated areas of the beach. We are working
within a more budget-conscious framework, and this is a pilot program that we can adjust if anything
goes wrong.
Commissioner Suarez stated that when he brought this up, he had concerns about the large number
of illegal vendors selling products out of backpacks along the beach. More often than not, these illegal
vendors are selling drugs on a regular basis. It is unrealistic to police this kind of activity across seven
miles of beach. He believes this pilot program could help free up Police resources. He asked the
Police Chief or a representative from the Police Department to inform the City Commission whether
enforcing the illegal sale of alcohol and drugs from backpacks on the beach is difficult.
Marlen Rivero, Police Division Major, said that enforcement is difficult. Last year, when this topic
arose, they were able to make arrests. In 2025, there were about 34 arrests of illegal vendors. For
every arrest made, many more go uninvestigated.
Commissioner Suarez said he wants to see how much difference this makes and if it stops illegal
vendors from selling junk on the beach. This pilot program is only for beer and wine. These illegal
vendors could be selling spiked drinks from their backpacks to target certain visitors.
Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading; seconded by
Commissioner Magazine. Roll Call: 6-0. Absent: Commissioner Fernandez.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into
the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the
Ordinance on First Reading; seconded by Commissioner Bhatt. Roll Call: 7-0. The Second Reading
Public Hearing is scheduled for March 18, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice. Lilia Cardillo to
place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Tameka Otto Stewart and Office of the City
Clerk to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Commissioner Magazine explained that the City has tremendous resources, many of which involve
its boards and committees. Since the Commission has united around being more disciplined in
spending, something demonstrated through various discussions and efforts, he was surprised to see,
during the first two budget cycles, that they spent so much time discussing incremental spending that
is driven by the Commission year over year. While it is important to note that every dollar added to
the government budget is not unique to Miami Beach, it becomes difficult to eliminate those costs.
There was no focus on the overall cumulative spending that led up to that point. In a billion-dollar
budget, they looked at an incremental $30 to $40 million of spending driven by the Commission over
the past year, with only $4.5 million available to cover it. They had to figure out how to fit $30 million
into a $4 million shortfall, which sparked lively conversations. However, to truly make a difference in
their agenda, they cannot do so through new spending alone; they need to analyze how they arrived
here. The Budget Advisory Committee (BAC) is an excellent resource to undertake that task, and like
them, they would only analyze proposed new spending. He really wants to remove restrictions and
empower them because they have limited resources. These are well-qualified individuals willing to
serve the City, and they could delve into the details of how they reached a billion-dollar budget and
recommend efficiencies to the City Commission, which could then propose them as part of the budget
cycle.
Commissioner Bhatt likes the idea but is concerned because this is a volunteer position, and they are
giving them a large scope. For the work to be valuable, it needs to be very detailed, and people must
really understand what they are examining. So, how does he plan to support their efforts by providing
the background and resources they need? What is the work product he can reasonably expect from
them?
Commissioner Magazine explained that during the recent budget cycle, they directed the Finance
Department to start producing a line-by-line budget. They did not have much detail initially. They have
graphs showing the percentage breakdown of spending sources, but they did not get a very detailed
view until they ordered the City Manager to return with cost-saving proposals. At that point, they
received a line-by-line budget. CFO Greene is currently preparing this. At the State level, they have
an accounting system that tracks where every dollar goes. The Committee members meet regularly,
and giving them access to this more detailed budget will help them identify and address potential
inefficiencies. Until now, they did not have this level of detail.
Budget Director Tameka Otto Stewart added that they undertake this process every year internally
and do not normally present the full details because it consists of hundreds of pages of documents.
Budget Director Otto Stewart added that the Finance Department begins this process in-house each
year and that it involves hundreds of pages of documents. She explained that for the departments
the Budget Advisory Committee requested to review this year, the Committee received the full
line-item package last month and has access to review it and provide feedback.
Commissioner Bhatt understands that they tasked the Administration with creating a detailed line-by-
line item budget; she supported this with Commissioner Magazine. Her question was about the
Committee as a group of volunteers: what is their work product? They will review the budget as
departments roll it out, but she asks what exactly they are supposed to do. How will they gather
historical information and understand how things work? What are they expected to produce to offer
recommendations, and how does the process all fit together? It is a big ask for volunteers, and she
wants to make sure they do not set the scope so broadly that the outcome becomes unhelpful.
Commissioner Magazine added that they can collaborate to formalize the final output and provided
examples. This is an advisory role, but in his view, the detailed budget should be accessible to the
90,000 residents and anyone else interested. It should be publicly available data where people can
see exactly where every dollar goes. This would be a more structured process, still evaluating
incremental spending, but it might help identify some inefficiencies within the billion-dollar budget.
CFO Jason Greene explained that the BAC does not consider the incremental budget increase.
Instead, they establish their own agenda at the start of the year and select from all City Departments.
They then review the budgets department by department.
Budget Director Otto Stewart further explained that the Committee selects which departments to
review and that, because they meet only once per month, they chose the larger departments such as
Police, Fire, Parks, and Public Works, as well as the Mayor and Commission Office. She stated that
this year they are going further into detailed line-item information, as requested, and that the
departments will appear before the Committee to present their budgets, after which the Committee
may ask any questions related to the detailed materials they have received.
CFO Greene mentioned that each department will present their budget, which has been the practice
in previous years. This year, they are focusing more on the details of department budgets with large
impacts. In the past, they reviewed high-level budgets but had more time than the Commission to
examine individual items. The BAC was already handling those tasks, but recommendations via
motion were transmitted by LTC. That is how the process currently works, but now BAC members
are responsible for drafting documents.
Commissioner Bhatt spoke to committee members of the BAC who were well qualified for the work,
but their frustration was that they did not review the information provided. They did not feel utilized in
an advisory role to do anything meaningful. This is an opportunity to get a fresh perspective and look
at things differently, and she wants to ensure there is something for them to do and produce.
CFO Greene added that it is being adjusted by providing them with a lot of detail. Every year, they
have to produce a detailed budget, going account by account individually. The data is available, but
will be given to the BAC to review, then the department can present it, and they can ask any questions
they have. Perhaps, from that process, it will give them more information to make a recommendation.
Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading, seconded by
Commissioner Bhatt.
The Public Hearing was held, and since there was no one in the audience or on Zoom, it was closed.
Roll Call: 7-0

ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into
the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Dominguez made a motion to adopt the
Ordinance on First Reading; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Roll Call: 7-0. The Second

VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Commissioner Dominguez introduced the Item and explained that by adopting the proposed
Ordinance, the City seeks to ensure uniformity and alignment with Miami-Dade County’s Community
Cat Program while strengthening humane cat management practices within the City. Miami Beach
recognizes that interference with authorized TNVR (trap, neuter, vaccination, return) activities,
including feeding interference, trap tampering, and harassment of caretakers and volunteers,
undermines the City and the County’s goals related to humane animal treatment. She moved her
Item. Seconded by Commissioner Fernandez.
In response to Commissioner Suarez’s concern about feeding penalties, Mark Fishman, Deputy City
Attorney, clarified that this applies only to TNVR activities authorized and conducted by the City.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, further clarified to Commissioner Suarez that the Ordinance
prohibits feeding in a manner that interferes with the TNVR activities. If somebody is feeding while a
TNVR activity is taking place, that would be a violation.
Mark Fishman, Deputy City Attorney, replied to Commissioner Bhatt that this legislation has penalties
pursuant to Sec 10-12 and the fines are based on a first, second, and third offense, going from $50
to $200.
Commissioner Bhatt informed of an individual in South Beach who is not only letting the dog go off
leash into the dunes to chase cats, but he also harasses the feeders and does not seem to care that
he is violating various laws. What recourse do they have?
Mark Fishman, Deputy City Attorney, stated that dogs off leash is one violation, interfering with TNVR
activities is another, and going through the dunes are violations as well, so it depends on what is
happening.
Commissioner Dominguez added that she alerted the Police Department, Major Feldman, the area
Captains, and Park Rangers, who are on alert to find that person.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, noted that what they are describing is not covered by this Ordinance.
This legislation addresses interference with TNVR activities. They are talking about someone
interfering with the legitimate cat feeding program, which is addressed by another Ordinance, as Mark
Fishman mentioned, such as dogs being off-leash or going through dunes. Discussion held.
Commissioner Magazine mentioned the cats at City Hall because he receives inquiries from people
who believe this is their City Hall as well. While the cats might be appropriate in parks, some people
find it very off-putting, though not him, nor anyone on his team, who wants to access City Hall.
Currently, there are nine cats lying on the front steps. Personally, he loves it, but some people who
have contacted him question this.
Commissioner Dominguez explained that there is a colony at City Hall. They are all vaccinated,
neutered, and spayed, and they usually keep to themselves. If someone walks to City Hall, the cats
will not attack. Licensed feeders feed them twice a day.
Commissioner Magazine recommended relocating cats to a better spot than the City Hall steps. The
discussion carried on.
John Norris, Public Works Director, understands that historically, cat colonies existed in certain
locations. As the cat program evolved from the SoBe Cat program and the City began working with
them, those colonies were kept, and they were basically fed where they existed. This has been
ongoing over the years. Discussion held.
In response to Commissioner Suarez’s comment, Deputy City Attorney Fishman clarified that he
cannot explain what led to the legislation; he was only tasked with drafting it. However, if they interfere
with the TNVR feeding, such as putting in unauthorized food, moving food, or bothering or harassing
cat feeders, those actions would violate this legislation. Deputy City Attorney Fishman indicated in
answer to Commissioner Suarez’s question that this Ordinance is for authorized TNVR locations, not
just putting food on the sidewalk.
Public Works Director John Norris clarified that if they are trying to trap a particular cat, they will
withhold food and then use that food to lure the cat to the trap. So, if someone feeds the cats in the
meantime, it defeats the purpose. That is where this whole thing started.

Seconded by Commissioner Fernandez.

or in the audience, the public hearing was concluded.

ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into
the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the
Ordinance on First Reading as is with a referral; seconded by Commissioner Dominguez. Roll Call:
7-0. The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for March 18, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to
notice. Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. David Gomez to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for March 18, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. David Gomez to handle.
REFERRAL:
Referral to the March 12, 2026, Neighborhood Resiliency Projects Advisory Committee. Amy
Knowles to place on the Committee Agenda. David Gomez to handle.
DIRECTION:
Office of the Inspector General to attend the March 12, 2026, Neighborhood Resiliency Projects
Advisory Committee Meeting. Office of the Inspector General to handle.
Commissioner Fernandez explained that the Ordinance builds on the work begun last fall, when an
Ordinance was adopted requiring a supermajority vote before pausing capital improvement projects
costing more than one million dollars once they reached 60% design. The earlier version of the
Ordinance included exceptions limited to a few critical infrastructure projects, such as stormwater
upgrades, fire flow improvements, and water and sewer work. The updated proposal simplifies this
approach. Instead of restricting the stop-the-pause to a narrow category of infrastructure, it now
applies the full definition of capital projects, meaning all projects in the five-year Capital Improvement
Program must follow the stop-the-pause. To pause one of these projects, a 5/7 vote is required once
the project exceeds $1,000,000 and reaches 60% design. At 90% design, a 6/7 vote would be
required. A 4/7 vote would be needed for unforeseen site conditions. However, once taxpayers’
money is spent on these large projects and they hit 60% and 90% design, it should require more than
a simple majority to stop or modify them. He is proud to say that they worked closely with the Office
of the Inspector General on drafting this legislation and that it is supported by Miami Beach United
(MBU) and the General Obligation (G.O.) Bond Oversight Committee. He moved the Item.
Commissioner Dominguez complimented Commissioner Fernandez for the great job he has done on
the Item and in expanding it. She offered a friendly amendment because it makes it seem that they
cannot change after 60% unless it is a simple majority change. Some residents feel, based on
examples that happened in the West Avenue project, that they are not at fault for the changes, as
they are all taxpayers, and they believe they were not consistently communicated with. Therefore,
she suggested adding language stating that after each design phase, the City will communicate with
the taxpayers and residents affected in that neighborhood to help them feel more comfortable.
Commissioner Fernandez clarified that they include resident input at 30%, 60%, and 90% phases as
they proceed with the capital project. It is already planned that they will conduct community meetings
starting early at the 30% design phase, then at the 60% design phase, and finally at the 90% design
phase, which occurs before permitting. If they do not have this process codified, they can incorporate
it.
Commissioner Dominguez added that residents are still concerned. She heard from the
Neighborhood Resiliency Projects Advisory Committee that it was not sent to them for discussion,
and at least four members were worried that communications were not in place. Between First and
Second Reading, can they be notified so they hear directly from the source about the language they
want added here? Commissioner Fernandez agreed, and Commissioner Dominguez seconded the
motion.
David Gomez, CIP Director, stated that during the initial phase of the projects, there is a big push
during the design development stage to engage in community outreach and gather input. However,
it is challenging to obtain agreement on everything they do, which is when they typically approach
either the Design Review Board (DRB) or the Historic Preservation Board (HPB). These discussions
then become part of the record in addition to all the public outreach efforts. Once they reach 90%,
the focus shifts to technical items in the drawings they are developing, so outreach decreases at the
90% mark because they are working on actual permit drawings, and it is no longer considered part
of the design process.
Commissioner Dominguez announced that the upcoming Neighborhood Resiliency Projects Advisory
Committee meeting is scheduled for March 12 at 4:00 p.m.
Commissioner Fernandez noted that the Office of the Inspector General regularly attends the General
Obligation (G.O.) Bond Oversight Committee meetings, which have been made possible through a
partnership between the Committee and the Office of the Inspector General. He suggested that the
Inspector General attend the Neighborhood Resiliency Projects Committee meeting to present the
Ordinance and offer feedback. He expressed his desire for his office to be involved in this discussion
and committed to supporting the guidance of the Inspector General. Having played a key role in
developing this policy, he plans to attend the meeting and follow the Inspector General’s guidance on
the direction the policy should take.
Inspector General Joseph Centorino will be happy to have staff present at that meeting and provide
an explanation. They are always supportive of that sort of input.
A Public Hearing was held.
Matthew Gultanoff, via Zoom, believes that amending the “stop the pause” policy is good fiscal policy.
They have projects all over the City that, in some cases, have reached 100% design and permitting,
yet they are still making last-minute efforts to cancel them. One example (Item C7 U), presented at
today’s Commission meeting and co-sponsored by the sponsor of this Ordinance to stop the pause,
was mentioned, and he asked for that same courtesy. This project is at 100% design, permitted, and
ready for construction, although the Inspector General has raised concerns about past interference.
Additionally, another part of that Resolution, which would cancel a different project under construction,
is scheduled to go to the DRB, an important forum for community feedback, on the March DRB
agenda, where it should be heard. He commended the sponsor for this smart policy and supports it.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, announced the conclusion of the Public Hearing.
A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading as is, with
a referral to the Neighborhood Resiliency Projects Advisory Committee on March 12, 2026, seconded
by Commissioner Dominguez. Roll Call: 7-0. The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for
March 18, 2026.
Mayor Meiner thanked Commissioner Fernandez, noting it as a valuable Item. He briefly described
the amount of work involved, but an Item like this does not do justice to the time Commissioner
Fernandez must have spent to reach this conclusion. He expressed appreciation for his efforts.

ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into
the record. The Public Hearing was held. A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez to adopt
the Ordinance on First Reading, seconded by Commissioner Dominguez. Roll Call: 7-0. The Second
Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for March 18, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice. Lilia Cardillo
to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Marla Alpizar to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Commissioner Fernandez is proud to introduce this legislation on First Reading to extend Chief of
Police Wayne Jones’s participation in the Deferred Retirement Option Plan (DROP) program,
ensuring the continuity of his exceptional leadership in the Miami Beach Police Department (MBPD).
Extending Chief Jones provides stability and, above all, maintains measurable, genuine progress in
the Police Department and public safety, especially when public safety remains the City’s top priority.
Everyone can agree that under Chief Jones’s leadership, the City and Police Department have
achieved extraordinary results. Violent crime has declined by 19%, and property crime and homicide
rates have also declined. This reflects the importance of focused leadership and a department aligned
around clear priorities. Equally important, and worth highlighting, is that while law enforcement
agencies nationwide struggle to recruit and retain Officers, our Miami Beach Police Department has
achieved full staffing of fully budgeted sworn Police Officer positions. This is a remarkable
accomplishment because full staffing means better response times, stronger neighborhood presence,
and improved services for residents and taxpayers of Miami Beach. With great gratitude for the
incredible work of the men and women of the MBPD, there could be no more fitting message as they
approach March, when they face some of their most complex, high-profile events. Supporting their
leadership and ensuring continuity is the best way to support the Officers who stand on the frontlines
every day. He also recognized Eric Carpenter, City Manager, who has been working on this Item as
well.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, strongly supports this Item and thanked Commissioner Fernandez for
bringing it forward. Their Police Chief is considered the best in the country. He has excelled in many
areas, including analyzing crime statistics, implementing technology as a force multiplier to achieve
the best results within budget, managing the promotional process, building a Command Staff that
meets the community’s needs, and handling the ranking staff of employees. The Department's morale
is at its highest point in the entire 13 years he has been here, which speaks volumes about how
effectively this Chief manages his responsibilities. He is fully supportive of giving him two more years
and is eager to see what he will accomplish in that time.
Commissioner Fernandez moved the approval of the Item.
Commissioner Dominguez seconded the motion.
Mayor Meiner is very proud of the Police Department. As mentioned, major crimes are down 19%.
Spring Break the last two years was peaceful and calm. They had a great press conference yesterday
and sent out positive messaging. Homeless numbers are at their lowest ever, mainly thanks to the
work of the Police Department and Dr. Alba Tarre and her team. They lead with compassion because
they offer services no other city in South Florida provides, but they also enforce laws without
compromise. This approach is effective, helping both the community and residents. He appreciates
their efforts; full staffing is the first time in the City Manager’s 30-year career that it has been achieved,
and they are proud. They will continue to push forward with their initiatives, which he has executed
outstandingly. He became Mayor around the same time Wayne Jones became Police Chief, and
since then, there has been a significant improvement in Police presence. However, there are always
areas for improvement, and he and the Chief are committed to addressing them. Officers being out
of their cars has shown some improvement, but remains slow, and they will continue working to
increase visibility at certain points. A new program is coming online to help pinpoint areas and assist
the Police. They provide excellent training and the best equipment and technology, which not only
make the Police Department outstanding and benefit residents but also help Officers do their jobs
safely. It is important that Officers feel protected, and they thank him for recognizing that. Many places
in the country lack leadership that openly supports Officers, and he believes they should be treated
with dignity. He saw a viral video from New York City showing snowballs being thrown at Officers;
based on what he observed, the Officers were just doing their job. The disrespect shown is
unacceptable. He could not imagine being the Mayor of a City where that happens; no Officer should
be treated that way for performing such a difficult job. That is why he respects their work and believes
they should always be supported, trained, and valued. He also thanks Chief Jones for his leadership
and looks forward to working closely with him.
Commissioner Fernandez noted that Mayor Meiner discussed the measurable outcomes, and equally
important is the stability and confidence that Chief Jones has fostered within the Police Department.
They can confidently say that the men and women of the MBPD, who wear this uniform every day,
trust Chief Jones’ leadership. They know he supports them and holds the Department to the highest
standards. This trust is based on what they see and hear on the streets about his leadership. As the
City Manager mentioned, perhaps the most important thing is that he has never seen Police Officers'
morale so high. These are the kinds of things they need to maintain because high morale means they
love their jobs, and the more they love their jobs, the safer the City and its residents will be.
Commissioner Bhatt has observed positive, small progressive changes in the Police Department over
the past few years, largely thanks to Chief Jones’s vision. She looks forward to him continuing this
progress during the next two years, as his legacy will be built on that. Whoever takes over after the
Chief will inherit a foundation laid by him and his colleagues. Regarding training and morale, which
she praises the Chief for, the increased adoption of technology to make policing more responsive,
faster, and safer is noteworthy. For example, the ability to send a drone out within seconds to prepare
the area before Officers arrive enhances safety and showcases incredible technology; embracing
evolving technology benefits everyone. Police Officers wear blue uniforms and take risks because
they run toward danger while others seek cover. Their goal is to ensure everyone protecting the City
is as safe as possible. The Chief has also emphasized diversity. The more the Police Department
reflects the community it serves, the more effective it is. Whether that means more people of color or
more women in leadership roles, ongoing progress is essential. Diversity ensures everyone has a fair
chance to excel if they are qualified, and she applauds the strides made so far. She encourages
further progress so the Police Force better reflects the community. She believes it makes a significant
difference when Officers are those people community members feel comfortable speaking with during
their most frightening moments. She advocates for continuing to embrace this progress and urges it
not to be undone when leadership changes in a couple of years. Keep up the excellent work. Ten
years ago, the Miami Beach Police Department was vastly different; incidents from ten or fifteen years
ago were alarming, horrifying, and unacceptable. As a City, we faced the consequences and
addressed individual issues. This must remain a distant memory and a lesson learned. Even the
slightest backslide could damage the community, the organization, the Department’s reputation, and
the morale of those who serve. None of this is acceptable.
Commissioner Suarez invited Police Chief Wayne Jones to the podium and openly shared that they
met to discuss some of his priorities. One of his main issues was the Marine Patrol. Before his
election, the Marine Patrol was not functioning well, and he clearly expressed this to Chief and his
team. Remarkably, it is now operating smoothly, thanks to Chief Jones. Chief Jones acknowledged
his concerns, and now Marine Patrol is better than ever. If you look out on the Bay, there are almost
no boats. Speeding on the waterways has been addressed, and noise complaints are being handled.
Other concerns included speeding tickets and homelessness enforcement; he told him he would
support extending these efforts but wanted to see measurable results, such as a reduction in
speeding on Collins Avenue and fewer complaints. Holding Chief Jones accountable for these
priorities over the next two years is crucial. He wants significant improvements on ongoing issues like
homelessness enforcement, petty theft, and stolen bikes or scooters, which he believes are linked to
a criminal homeless population preying on residents. Over the next two years, they will hold the Police
Department accountable by tracking their metrics and aiming for substantial progress in these areas.
Chief of Police Wayne Jones had a very positive conversation with Commissioner Suarez, and they
agreed on what needs to be done in the City. They are committed to maintaining momentum to make
the area safer for residents and visitors. He is dedicated to making a difference in reducing those
numbers. He mentioned this privately, and now he is sharing it publicly.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas was present when Wayne Jones was sworn in as Chief, and she will
always remember that moment. All the Chaplains placed their hands on him, and everyone gathered
to pray over him and the work he would do in Miami Beach. He has truly done a great job. They thank
him for his leadership. The Vice-Mayor called him and asked if he really wanted the extension, and
without hesitation, he told her, "Absolutely, I love Miami Beach, and I will continue to make a
difference." There was no hesitation in his voice. He is committed to the community; they know it,
they feel it, and residents love the MBPD and the excellent work they do every day. They thank him
for everything, his hard work and diligence, and everyone in the Department. It all comes from
leadership, and that is him. Thank you very much, and she is proud to support the Ordinance and the
Chief today.
Commissioner Magazine stated that compared to where they were five years ago, the City is night
and day different, and the Police Department is the main reason why. He truly believes they have the
best Police Department in the world. The culture of any organization is set from the top, and it is hard
to have the best Police Department in the world without the best Police Chief, so he is confident that
they do. He thanked him for his work and is proud to support him not only as a Police Chief but also
as a tremendous ambassador to the City. He hopes he continues doing the same job that earned him
their trust, which he has already done.
Commissioner Dominguez added that Chief Jones has done an outstanding job in addressing the
City’s High Impact Weekends, starting with Spring Break, Memorial Day, and any other events they
have. March was their critical month, and Chief Jones delivered. He also engages with neighborhood
associations, speaks to residents, is active in the community, and is accessible, available, and
responsive. This is very important and appreciated. She thanked Chief Jones for his service and is
happy to support him.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that there will be a Second Reading for this Ordinance. Chief Jones,
as the Chief of the Miami Beach Police Department, brings great honor to the City that all of us have
the privilege of serving and representing. While he presented this Ordinance as the Chair of the Public
Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee, he welcomes anyone who wants to join him in
co-sponsoring the Ordinance as a show of support for the Chief and the incredible men and women
who will keep this city safe as they head into March.
The Ordinance was co-primed (sponsored) by all.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, opened the Public Hearing.
Mitch Novick said that it is day and night in his neighborhood for him and his hotel guests to
comfortably use the front porch without being bothered by drug dealers who are no longer loitering
outside the building. The incident last week with the drone was fascinating; the drone was the first
responder on the scene, and it is impressive that the Police Officers were able to make an arrest
during that terrible incident.
With no other participants via Zoom or in the audience, the Public Hearing was adjourned.
A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading, seconded
by Commissioner Dominguez. Roll Call: 7-0.

AMENDMENT:
Increase funding for the Rainbow Crosswalk by an additional $15,000 to cover the cost of a plaque
to accompany the crosswalk replica. If the plaque is not approved by the March 18, 2026, City
Commission meeting, the $15,000 will be returned to the Capital Budget.
Tameka Otto Stewart, Budget Director, presented the Item concerning the Third Amendment to the
FY 2026 Operating Budget. The amendment includes five items, all of which were previously
approved by the City Commission at the February 5, 2026, City Commission meeting. She clarified
that the amendment was necessary to officially allocate the funding for those actions. She then listed
the five items.
1. Replica Rainbow Crosswalk at Lummus Park. The recommendation is to allocate $120,000 from
available General Fund reserves to fund the installation of a replica Rainbow Crosswalk at
Lummus Park.
2. Pre-K Scholarship Expansion Program. The recommendation is to allocate $111,000 from the
General Fund reserves to support 37 families currently on the waiting list for this year’s Pre-K
scholarship program.
3. Additional Support for Commissioner Aides. The funds had previously been transferred from the
General Fund to the Sanitation Fund. The Commission approved transferring $80,000 back to the
Mayor and Commissioner’s office to enable the hiring of a second aide.
4. Gallery and exhibit at Lummus Park. $45,000 is recommended for appropriation for a gallery or
exhibit at Lummus Park, as previously approved by the City Commission.
5. Historic Plaque Pedestal. Appropriation of $5,000 from General Fund reserves to fund a pedestal
for a historic plaque at the Miami Beach Bandshell.
Commissioner Fernandez thanked the Mayor and expressed a desire to amend the allocation of
$120,000 for the Rainbow Crosswalk, increasing the funding by an additional $15,000 to include a
plaque that provides context and explains the significance of the replica to the public. However, if the
plaque is not approved by the March 18, 2026, City Commission meeting, the $15,000 will be returned
to the Capital Budget.
