Tameka Otto Stewart, Budget Director, introduced the Item, which is the third amendment to the FY
2026 Capital Budget. The amendment includes nine items and recommends an overall budget
increase of $81.6 million, along with a $4.3 million transfer between existing projects. She listed the
nine items as follows:
1. Water Main Replacement on Dade Boulevard. Bids have exceeded the approved budget. The
original budget was about $6.49 million, but the lowest bid came in at $7.92 million. The
recommendation was to allocate $1.4 million from an existing project that received alternative
funding through a grant.
2. Stormwater Outfalls Water Quality Improvement Project. The original budget was $2.8 million,
and bids required an additional $1.18 million. The recommendation is to transfer about $1.2 million
from an existing project that currently has over $18 million in funding, noting that the funds will be
prioritized for replacement in a future budget.
3. Fifth Street and Alton Road Garage CCTV Upgrades. $24,000 is requested to upgrade the closed-
circuit television system and add 70 new software licenses. The funding will come from available
savings from 15 completed garage projects.
4. Fifth Street and Alton Road Garage Waterproofing Project. $285,000 will be allocated from
available parking funds for exterior waterproofing and restoration.
5. Bayshore Neighborhood Traffic Calming. The project’s bid exceeded the budget by $1.3 million.
The recommendation is to transfer funds from an existing transportation project to proceed.
6. Normandy Island Neighborhood Traffic Calming project needs about $100,000 more in funding
and suggests transferring funds from an existing transportation project.
7. Citywide Raised Crosswalk Intersection Program. The project is over budget by $231,000. Funds
will be moved from two existing projects with available balances.
8. Rainbow Crosswalk Project. This item is formally funded in the Capital Budget. The funds will be
transferred from the General Fund in the Operating Budget and include the additional $15,000
amendment approved earlier for a plaque.
9. General Obligation (G.O.) Bond Tranche Two. At the previous City Commission meeting, a
declaration of intent to issue additional Tranche Two bonds was approved. This amendment will
allocate those proceeds in the FY 2026 budget.
Commissioner Magazine asked about the City’s ownership and responsibility for the Fifth and Alton
Garage, especially regarding elevator maintenance and capital improvements.
Elizabeth Miro, Assistant Director of Property Management, explained that the City holds a 46%
ownership stake and is responsible for 46% of the Capital Improvement costs. The private partner
covers operational and maintenance expenses, including elevator upkeep.
Commissioner Magazine expressed concern about the recurring elevator outages. Several residents
have reported serious issues, including an incident where a veteran was allegedly stuck in an
elevator. He urged staff to find a long-term solution and highlighted that, although operational control
is with the private partner, the City’s joint ownership raises public perception concerns.
Ms. Miro confirmed that staff have been working with the operator and the elevator service contractor
to pursue long-term solutions.
Commissioner Magazine inquired about activating the rooftop amenity space.
Ms. Miro said that the agreement is currently under legal review and revision.
Commissioner Suarez asked about projects with bids that are much higher than estimates, especially
the Dade Boulevard water main replacement.
John Norris, Director of Public Works, clarified that engineers generate probable cost estimates based
on previous comparable bids. However, construction costs have varied greatly since COVID-19. He
mentioned that market conditions, contractor availability, and competitiveness have affected bid
outcomes.
Kristy Bada, Chief Procurement Officer, confirmed that multiple bids were received for the Dade
Boulevard project, and the low bid reflects current market pricing.
Commissioner Suarez inquired if projects should be rebid when bids go over estimates.
David Martinez, Assistant City Manager, explained that when bids are closely clustered above
estimates, it usually indicates current market pricing. However, if bids are limited or vary widely, the
City might cancel and rebid the project. Many nuances and factors influence the bidding process.
Commissioner Magazine urged staff to maintain scrutiny and market awareness when assessing
future bids.
A motion was made by Commissioner Suarez to adopt the Resolution as amended; seconded by
Commissioner Fernandez.
The Public Hearing was held, and since there were no participants in the audience or via Zoom, the
hearing was closed.
Vote: 7-0.

Commissioner Dominguez introduced the Item. Stanley “Skip” Bertman was a well-known baseball
coach and athletic director for LSU. A graduate of Miami Beach High School, Class of 1956, he played
football and baseball and later returned as a teacher and head baseball coach from 1962 to 1974,
leading the team to State championships and two runner-up finishes. He also coached football and
managed youth leagues in Miami Beach Parks & Recreation. Skip was named Florida High School
Coach of the Year three times. He served as Associate Head Coach at the University of Miami from
1976 to 1983, helping the Hurricanes win the 1982 National Championship. The honors for Skip are
numerous. He earned three varsity letters and played at the University of Miami. He was part of the
inaugural College Baseball Hall of Fame Class of 2006. Naming the Flamingo Park Baseball Field
would honor Skip’s exceptional legacy and lifelong contributions to Miami Beach athletics and
community.
The Public Hearing was held.
Stuart Blumberg said he has been part of this community for 80 years and has heard this conversation
many times. He is glad the City Commission is finally honoring Skip. He grew up with Skip and
considers him a hometown legend who has brought fame to the community. He informed the City
Commission that Skip has health issues, so if they plan to schedule an event, it should be sooner
rather than later. People from across the country will want to attend. He thanked the City Commission,
especially Commissioners Dominguez and Fernandez.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34152 was adopted. Commissioner Alex Fernandez moved to adopt the
Resolution reinstating the Oolite Arts grant agreement and lifting the pause required by Resolution
2024‑33265, including the expanded referral to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee
(FERC); seconded by Commissioner Bhatt. Vote: 6-1; Opposed: Commissioner Suarez. Lissette
Garcia Arrogante to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: No
REFERRAL:
The Item was referred to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee to expand the legislation.
Jason Greene to place on the Committee Agenda Pending List. Lissette Garcia Arrogante to
handle.
DIRECTIONS TIED TO THE REFERRAL:
The Administration is directed to work with Commissioner Joseph Magazine on expanding the
legislation regarding:
• Cultural Arts grant application criteria
• Including needs‑based evaluation
• Consideration of executive compensation
• A review of whether ongoing annual funding should continue without limits (Commissioners
referenced grants being “not evergreen,” “not unlimited,” and “not forever”)
• Ensuring consistent standards are applied across all grantees
Commissioner Suarez emphasized the importance of scrutinizing all taxpayer-funded allocations. He
noted that although a $30,000 arts grant may seem small on its own, such decisions add up and
impact the City’s billion-dollar budget. He clarified that the issue is not whether Oolite contributes to
Miami Beach’s cultural scene but whether public funds should support an organization with significant
financial resources. Referencing Oolite’s FY 2024 tax filing, he pointed out the organization has about
$120 million in assets, including $109 million in publicly traded securities, and earned $4.78 million in
investment income, almost equal to its $4.8 million annual operating costs. He added that the
organization’s net assets grew by roughly $16 million that year, indicating that Oolite is a self-
sustaining institution rather than a nonprofit in need of financial support. Commissioner Suarez also
noted that Oolite’s CEO earned $345,000 in 2024, surpassing the salary of the Miami Beach City
Manager, who manages a $1 billion municipal budget. He expressed concern that over 30% of
Oolite’s operating expenses go toward salaries and executive pay, arguing that public funding should
not bolster compensation packages within well-funded organizations that can sustain themselves
through investment income. He stated that limited taxpayer dollars should instead be used for
neighborhoods, public safety, infrastructure, and services that directly benefit residents.
Consequently, he requested that Oolite be permanently disqualified from the City’s Arts and Culture
Grant Program and that the City more rigorously scrutinize organizations with large endowments
before awarding public funds. Commissioner Suarez also presented a slideshow illustrating Oolite’s
financial standing, including its $120 million in assets, pay levels, investment income, and year-over-
year asset growth. Click here to view the presentation. He reiterated that the organization’s
investment income nearly covers its entire operating budget, demonstrating its capacity to operate
without taxpayer support. He stated that the $30,000 arts grant would be better allocated to resident-
focused programs, public safety projects, infrastructure upgrades, community services, or smaller
nonprofits that struggle to secure funding. He clarified that his stance is not anti-arts but rather aims
to prioritize responsible management of public resources and to support organizations that are truly
in need of financial help. Commissioner Suarez also made it clear that he cannot support giving grant
funds to an organization with over $100 million in assets and executive pay exceeding that of key City
officials. He mentioned that similar oversight is being considered for other nonprofits with high
executive salaries and plans to carefully evaluate all taxpayer-funded expenditures in the future.
Despite potential criticism, he emphasized the importance of a transparent community discussion
about the best use of public money. Finally, he invited comments from his colleagues.
Commissioner Dominguez stated that she wanted to raise some questions to both City staff and
Oolite Arts. During her briefing, City staff expressed support for the Item and showed readiness to
proceed with Oolite as a partner. She highlighted that the grant under review is a matching grant with
specific criteria, and partnering with an arts organization like Oolite demonstrates the City’s
commitment to supporting the arts. Commissioner Dominguez explained that such partnerships
indicate that the City has “skin in the game” and is actively involved in promoting arts and cultural
development within the community. She mentioned that she wanted to better understand why the
City was recommending the Item and to obtain more detailed information.
Tourism and Culture Director Lissette Garcia Arrogante showed support for the grant and emphasized
the advantages of partnering with Oolite Arts. She called Oolite an outstanding organization and
mentioned that the City gains visibility and branding opportunities through its logo appearing on the
organization’s marketing materials. She explained that this exposure helps promote Miami Beach as
a top arts and culture destination. Director Garcia Arrogante reaffirmed that the grant is a matching
grant, meaning Oolite must secure matching funds to qualify for the $30,000 award. She also
introduced Oolite Arts’ CEO, John Abodeely, who was present to speak to the Commission.
CEO John Abodeely affirmed that the grant under consideration is a matching‑grant requirement and
explained that Oolite Arts invests significantly more each year in its Lincoln Road activation than the
amount being requested from the City. He noted that Oolite has owned its historic, 100‑year‑old
building on Lincoln Road for nearly 40 years, where it provides free studio space to 13 resident artists
for one year, along with professional career‑development services. Mr. Abodeely shared that the
organization offers about 50 art classes annually, such as figure drawing and digital media, which
attract participants from across the region. He added that Oolite hosts four exhibition openings each
year in its on‑site gallery, including a free public opening that evening featuring studio visits and work
from alumni. According to Mr. Abodeely, Oolite has supported approximately 1,000 Miami‑Dade
alumni through its programs over the 40 years it has been located on Lincoln Road. He emphasized
the organization’s long‑standing commitment to community activations and stated that, although he
is new to Miami Beach, he is proud to represent an organization that was instrumental in Lincoln
Road’s cultural and economic revitalization dating back to the 1980s, 1990s, and 2000s.
Mayor Meiner began by acknowledging his prior interactions with CEO John Abodeely and
commended him for the positive transformation of Oolite Arts in recent years. He noted that, following
issues the organization experienced several years earlier, Mr. Abodeely and a new Board
successfully revamped the institution, strengthening its partnership with the City. Mayor Meiner
shared that he had visited Oolite’s gallery on Lincoln Road and found the exhibition impressive, with
a strong turnout from the community. He then asked Mr. Abodeely to comment on the financial figures
shown in Commissioner Suarez’s presentation, specifically inquiring whether the numbers presented
were accurate.
CEO John Abodeely responded by explaining that Oolite Arts’ endowment originated from the sale
of one of the buildings the organization previously owned on Lincoln Road. He stated that throughout
Oolite’s 40‑year history, the organization has owned multiple buildings in that area, and the proceeds
from selling one of them, now occupied by a restaurant and a Skechers store, created the endowment
that supports its operations today. Mr. Abodeely emphasized that 100% of the organization’s financial
resources are directed toward its mission of supporting contemporary art and artists. He described
how, before the endowment, Oolite operated on a very limited budget and relied heavily on volunteer
labor, which restricted its capacity. The endowment allowed the organization to professionalize, hire
staff, strengthen its systems and financial oversight, enhance transparency, and expand the services
it provides. Mr. Abodeely explained that the endowment enabled Oolite to offer nearly all of its
programs free of charge to artists and participants. While the organization collects small fees for
certain arts‑based classes, it does not charge artists or participants for any other programs. He noted
that this shift improved Oolite’s ability to launch and support the careers of Miami‑Dade County artists.
He also shared that, because many artists have been displaced by rising housing costs, Oolite has
expanded its reach to a four‑county area to continue serving them. Mr. Abodeely stated that, as a
result of the financial stability provided by the endowment, Oolite has become a more generous and
impactful institution. He concluded by stating that he believes a financially stable nonprofit benefits
the community and, when asked by Commissioner Suarez, noted that his salary is approximately the
same amount that was reported when he joined the organization a year earlier.
Commissioner Suarez expressed strong frustration with Oolite Arts’ request for taxpayer funding,
emphasizing that the organization’s CEO earns over $300,000 annually while the organization holds
substantial assets. Commissioner Suarez stated that, although the grant is structured as a matching
grant, the organization previously sold a building at the peak of the real estate market and is now, in
his view, “flush with cash.” He said he found it offensive and inappropriate for a well-resourced
nonprofit to seek public subsidies when residents in Miami Beach are facing significant financial
pressures, including difficulty paying special assessments and coping with rising housing costs.
Commissioner Suarez reiterated his concerns about providing public dollars to organizations with
more than $100 million in assets and highly compensated executives. He stated that if Oolite intends
to do good for the community, it should do so based on its own resources rather than relying on
taxpayers who are themselves experiencing financial strain. He stated that many residents would be
upset to learn that public funding is being directed to such an organization and voiced his continued
opposition to the funding request.
Commissioner Bhatt inquired how much the City funded for the activation with Adidas.
Tourism and Culture Department Director Garcia Arrogante responded that the City funded $600,000
for the activation with Adidas.
Commissioner Bhatt noted that the Adidas CEO earns between $8 million and $8.5 million annually,
and the company generates more than $25 billion in revenue and approximately $13 billion in profit.
Commissioner Bhatt questioned whether colleagues who expressed outrage over Oolite Arts’ funding
request were equally concerned about allocating substantial public funds to a major global corporation
with far greater financial resources.
Commissioner Suarez responded by contrasting the Adidas activation with the City’s past Spring
Break programming, noting that the City once spent $3.2 million on a concert event featuring Alanis
Morissette that he described as unsuccessful and associated with public‑safety issues, including
shootings and stampedes. He stated that the current $600,000 branding‑focused Spring Break
initiative is a fraction of the prior cost and is not expected to recur at the same expense annually.
Commissioner Suarez supports Commissioner Bhatt’s Blue Zones initiative, which he noted will cost
approximately $8 million to achieve certification, and emphasized that the City invests in initiatives
that align with a broader vision to improve safety and reduce violence during March. He contrasted
these efforts with Oolite Arts, reiterating his concern over providing ongoing taxpayer funding to an
arts organization whose CEO earns more than $300,000 a year and which he described as financially
“flush with cash.” Commissioner Suarez questioned whether taxpayer dollars should continue to
support such an organization without greater scrutiny and asked Commissioner Bhatt directly whether
she believes the City should be doing so.
Commissioner Bhatt clarified that the City is not contributing $8 million toward the Blue Zones initiative
and stated that no City taxpayer dollars will be used for that program. She asserted that the contrary
claim was inaccurate. She stated that she was not comparing the merits of different programs, noting
that the Commission broadly supports multiple Spring activations, including the Adidas activation.
Her earlier comparison was intended only to illustrate that Adidas, like Oolite, has the financial
capacity to carry out its activation without City funding, yet the City still chooses to provide financial
support as part of its marketing strategy. Commissioner Bhatt expressed that she found it notable
that one funding decision was being criticized while another, involving much larger sums, was not.
She pointed out that Oolite’s $30,000 grant would increase to $60,000 under the matching‑grant
requirement and asked CEO John Abodeely to specify exactly how those funds would be used and
how the organization’s efforts would be affected if the grant were not given.
CEO John Abodeely explained that the matching‑grant funds are used to support the presentation of
artwork and free public programming at Oolite’s gallery on Lincoln Road. He stated that the
organization hosts artist talks, curator talks, tours, and free evening events to engage the community.
Mr. Abodeely noted that Oolite also activates empty spaces along Lincoln Road with additional
exhibitions and offers free public access to artist studios several times a year, giving residents
opportunities to meet artists and purchase artwork. He added that Oolite partners with other nonprofits
and organizations throughout Miami Beach and Miami-Dade County to co‑present exhibitions and
expand access to free arts programming throughout the community. If the grant were not awarded, it
would mean adjusting the budget in a specific area, which could result in delaying or suspending a
program.
Commissioner Fernandez noted that a previous Resolution he proposed called for suspending Oolite
Arts funding and required that all current and future grant agreements be paused until a new executive
director is appointed. The Resolution also requested a statement to the City outlining the internal
controls established to address offensive artwork. Commissioner Fernandez inquired whether these
conditions have been met, specifically if the pause is still in effect and if the City has received the
requested statement detailing the organization’s internal controls.
Tourism and Culture Department Director Garcia Arrogante confirmed that the conditions had been
satisfied, and Oolite submitted the requested statement in October 2025.
Commissioner Fernandez noted that several figures had been discussed during the meeting,
including the City’s $600,000 support for an Adidas activation and questions about whether the Blue
Zones initiative would cost the City $8 million. He also referenced a discussion with the City Manager
regarding Art Basel, noting that, as a for-profit entity, Art Basel receives between $1.5 million and $2
million in City fees and waivers. Commissioner Fernandez then compared these larger financial
figures with the current matter and asked how much funding was being requested for Oolite Arts at
this time.
Tourism and Culture Department Director Garcia Arrogante stated that the City withholds the final
$15,000 payment of the Oolite Arts’ FY 2025 grant until the concerns previously raised are resolved.
She mentioned that reinstating Oolite would allow the organization to continue participating in the
City’s Cultural Arts Funding Program.
Commissioner Fernandez clarified that the discussion focused on the second $15,000 payment owed
to Oolite Arts from its FY 2025 grant. He mentioned that this allocation is part of the City’s broader
Cultural Arts Funding Program, which amounts to about $1 million in annual cultural‑arts investments.
He inquired whether City staff have information on the economic impact of this $1 million investment
on the City.
Director Lissette Garcia Arrogante stated that the City’s Cultural Arts Funding Program totals $1.25
million annually and supports approximately 57 organizations. She explained that these organizations
collectively generate more than $330 million in annual economic impact specifically for the City of
Miami Beach.
Commissioner Fernandez cautioned the Commission to remain mindful that, although some entities
receiving City support are for‑profit, they nonetheless play a meaningful role in shaping Miami Beach’s

Commissioner Bhatt responded that once a plan was developed, nearby neighborhoods would be
informed, including charter operators at the Marina and the charter operator on Indian Creek with a
current business tax receipt (BTR). She explained that the plan would address noise prohibitions and
coordination with the Police Department to ensure Marine Patrol presence during the initial period to
enforce and educate vessel operators. She stated that a comprehensive plan was being developed,
but that it was premature to hold a community discussion until the requested data from the United
States Coast Guard was received.
Commissioner Suarez requested that a Sunshine Meeting be held before the Item is brought back to
the Commission, which the two of them could host, to gather input from nearby residents about
potential unintended consequences.
Commissioner Bhatt replied that further communication would occur once data confirmed that the
proposed plan was appropriate.
Commissioner Suarez knows that there will be unintended consequences and emphasized the
importance of informing residents along the 63rd Street canal in North Beach.
Commissioner Bhatt expressed willingness to participate in a Community Meeting.
Commissioner Suarez asked if the meeting could be held before the Item returned for consideration.
Commissioner Bhatt responded that the scheduling would be reviewed. She confirmed that she would
endeavor to make the meeting possible.
Commissioner Suarez inquired if the meeting would be before voting on the Resolution.
Commissioner Bhatt reiterated that she would endeavor to make it happen.
Mayor Meiner thanked Commissioner Bhatt for taking on the issue and noted that it had previously
been addressed by past Commissioners Micky Steinberg and himself before being taken up by
Commissioner Bhatt. Mayor Meiner also thanked Commissioner Suarez for his comments.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, AUTHORIZING AND DIRECTING THE CITY ADMINISTRATION TO (1) ASSERT AND MAINTAIN COMPLETE CONTROL OVER ALL ASPECTS OF CITY-SPONSORED SENIOR EVENTS (SENIOR HOLIDAY PARTY, SENIOR PROM, SENIOR SUMMER BASH, AND THE SENIOR POLICE BALL), INCLUDING ENFORCING ADMISSION REQUIREMENTS AND ALL ASPECTS OF THE EVENTS PROGRAMMING; (2) LIMIT ATTENDANCE TO MIAMI BEACH RESIDENTS WHO ARE 55 YEARS OF AGE OR OLDER AND EMPLOYEES, ELECTED OFFICIALS ATTENDING IN THEIR OFFICIAL CAPACITIES TO PERFORM THEIR OFFICIAL DUTIES, AND OUTSIDE CONTRACTORS NECESSARY TO STAFF AND EXECUTE THE EVENTS, INCLUDING PROGRAMMING AND ENTERTAINMENT; AND (3) ENCOURAGE ALL ATTENDEES TO REFRAIN FROM CAMPAIGNING FOR ANY POLITICAL OFFICE OR CAUSE WHILE ATTENDING THE EVENTS.
items.action: Resolution 2026-34153 was adopted as amended. A motion was made by Commissioner Bhatt to adopt the Resolution as amended, seconded by Commissioner Dominguez. Vote: 7-0. John Rebar to handle.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34153 was adopted as amended. A motion was made by Commissioner
Bhatt to adopt the Resolution as amended, seconded by Commissioner Dominguez. Vote: 7-0. John
Rebar to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
AMENDMENT:
Include any elected official, at any level of government, if they are part of the senior event program.
Commissioner Bhatt explained that they discussed this issue thoroughly and never took action on it,
but she wants to move forward. In response to Commissioner Suarez, she clarified that currently, if
an individual is an elected official who does not have an official role in the Convention Center events
but contributes taxpayer dollars for the enjoyment and benefits of senior City residents, then they are
considered a welcome participant. If someone is a candidate, they may bring campaign materials to
the foyer downstairs and set up a table. However, during this campaign cycle, an individual who had
not yet filed papers to become a candidate was present with a videographer and campaign materials,
and in previous campaigns, someone was seen printing photographs bearing the City seal. She finds
this abusive. She has no issue with residents having the opportunity to meet their elected officials,
whether they are running for office or not, but using taxpayer dollars to facilitate what should be a fun
evening out for residents, who may not get such evenings often, should be reserved for that purpose.
There are plenty of other times to campaign, as people run for different positions unrelated to Miami
Beach, and such behavior is egregious. She and Commissioner Magazine believe enough is enough.
Commissioner Suarez clarified that the Tax Collector has a significant role in Miami Beach. He
understands what she is saying, and it seems unfair. The issue he had, which he is glad was
corrected, was that if they are a candidate, they should be welcome to run; he does not want to give
an unfair advantage to an incumbent. He is thankful for that change.
Commissioner Bhatt explained that if an elected official is welcome to attend, a candidate can come
and bring materials to a table outside, but they are not allowed to go into the ballroom to work the
room. That is what was decided, and it is fair. They will still have access to the people coming in and
out, and this rule prevents the work done by the Parks and Recreation team and Monique at the Scott
Rakow Youth Center from being co-opted for electioneering.
Mayor Meiner noted that they passed legislation stating that elected officials can only place materials
in the front and clarified that even the City Commission could not handle materials in the ballroom.
When State Representatives are elected, they come up and speak to the crowd. Would that be
allowed under this Resolution if they are not City officials?
Commissioner Bhatt clarified that the intent is for elected officials involved in the event, presumably
the Mayor and Commissioners as City officials, to welcome residents and share holiday greetings
and perform related activities. She does not know if they ever considered County elected officials.
Commissioner Magazine added that elected officials representing Miami Beach residents should be
allowed to attend, and for the same reason a candidate does not sit at the dais, because elected
officials attending in their official capacity are not campaigning but fulfilling their duties by engaging
with constituents. He stated that he would like to extend the allowance to any elected official
representing the public and believed that had been the consensus previously.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Rob Rosenwald explained that there was some concern raised a long
time ago, but no alternative was settled upon. The way this is drafted aims to create an open forum
where people can attend their senior events, campaign, or discuss issues with seniors, whether they
have a connection to the City or are trying to serve seniors. This Resolution is written to take control
of that potentially open forum and establish it explicitly as a City of Miami Beach-sponsored event,
ensuring that outside groups cannot enter to sell Avon, campaign, or preach for a church. The
Resolution creates a City-sponsored event that is not open to the public except for those specifically
invited. It allows the City Commission, as elected officials, to still participate if they are part of the
program, which is generally the case. When the City hosts a sponsored event, officials are invited to
attend and may be given a speaking role during the Pledge of Allegiance, a Proclamation, or other
designated duties to justify their participation, without turning the event into an open forum where
anyone can infiltrate and overwhelm the seniors with various materials.
Mayor Meiner asked if County or State officials representing Miami Beach residents and others could
come in.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Rosenwald explained that it was not how it is written.
Mayor Meiner suggested tweaking the language to allow any elected official representing Miami
Beach residents. He thinks it will be a tough time telling County officials that they cannot come.
Commissioner Magazine supports the amendment.
Commissioner Bhatt is fine with making amendments. The aim is to prevent it from becoming an
electioneering event, so if an elected official wants to come in and offer his or her season’s greetings,
that is acceptable.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Rosenwald expressed concern that, if it is open to elected officials but not
candidates, it would create an open forum and violate the First Amendment. He clarified that the City
Commission can attend because they are part of the program, which is factually true for any
municipality.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, added that if the other elected officials are also given a role during
the program, wouldn't the same rationale apply?
Commissioner Magazine stated that Miami-Dade County Tax Collector Dariel Fernandez was just
elected and has been fulfilling his duties since the first event, engaging with constituents. Where this
falls short is that this appears to be some sort of campaign event, but they are present in their official
capacity. The tax collector and County Commissioners are there in their official roles.
Commissioner Suarez clarified that Legal is saying that if they exclude candidates, it could lead to a
potential violation of the First Amendment.
Deputy City Attorney Rosenwald explained that the general rule is that if you have elected officials,
they must also permit candidates.
Commissioner Bhatt is an elected official. Her role is not to campaign; it is to attend events to extend
holiday greetings to the Miami Beach residents she serves, simply giving the greeting and then
leaving.
Commissioner Magazine added that a School Board operates under a different jurisdiction. However,
if it were a Miami Beach school, they would agree for Mayor Meiner to speak there, as it is his
community and he is elected to represent it. A candidate running for Miami Beach office also has the
opportunity to speak to the students when the Mayor is present.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Rosenwald explained that historically, this has been conducted like an
open forum. Unfortunately, this Resolution attempts to move away from what has arguably been an
open forum in the past. He can try to add words if they want to include County officials who are part
of the program, but it becomes less clear whether they were challenged.
Commissioner Suarez is not trying to be difficult. They are all candidates at some point, and there
was a Commissioner he did not like at the time, but why does that person have an unfair advantage?
He understands that Commissioner Bhatt is saying that they, as City Commissioners, will be there in
their official capacity, but just being there is technically campaigning. This is an opportunity for
thousands of people to see and hear them, and as an incumbent, he does not think it is fair to say
they will have a built-in advantage for these events and to exclude potential contenders. If a candidate
wants to appeal to those constituents but cannot because of this law, which gives an unfair advantage
to an incumbent, that is not fair.
Commissioner Bhatt added that it is not an unfair advantage for an incumbent when a person is doing
their job as an elected official. The fact that they are having this debate again and that these events
have been co-opted into a frenzied electioneering effort is exactly why she has been trying to get this
passed for nearly two years. It is grotesque; it is not appropriate. She apologized for the fact that they
already won an election, are doing their job, and that this gives them an unfair advantage as
incumbents. However, he did run and win, and part of his job is interacting with constituents. It is not
the taxpayers' or the City’s fault. The role of Miami Beach is NOT to provide an open forum for
electioneering; if they want to do that, then it is a different conversation and a different event. They
offer candidates, whether incumbents or newcomers, a chance to appear in two- or three-minute
televised videos, broadcast for free, which is optional. What has been evolving through the Parks
Department is intended to provide some relaxation and recreation for senior residents and their
guests, but it has turned into something embarrassing, grotesque, and inappropriate.
Commissioner Magazine stated that he and Mayor Meiner spoke at the Parks and Recreation
Summer Camp Graduations in previous years, not because they were campaigning, and it was five
months after being elected. That is their civic duty. Imagine if they go to the Parks and Recreation
Graduation Ceremony and thank parents and children; the candidate gets to be there and do so with
them, because somehow it is an unfair advantage.
Mayor Meiner believes this is a good discussion and thinks this election cycle went better. He gave
an example from years ago when a candidate arrived with 20 dancers, which was a spectacle. The
legislation at that time did not allow campaign materials in the room, and he thought that was a good
move. However, he feels it gives incumbents an advantage because candidates are not allowed in,
though he personally has no problem with them attending. He frequently hears that this is a chance
for seniors to get out of their apartments. The City hosts a great event, kudos to John Rebar and his
team for organizing it. To him, the bigger picture is figuring out how candidates can participate. He
wants to ensure other elected officials can attend, too, because it would look bad for the City not to
allow them in. Additionally, the seniors want to see their County officials, such as the Tax Collector,
who is bringing a license-renewal office to Miami Beach.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Rosenwald stated that it will be a First Amendment issue. He plans to
draft in a way that minimizes liability. They will be invited to participate in the program to explain what
their office does, as that is the least confrontational approach. The problem is that this event has
traditionally been run as an open forum where everyone can attend, speak to anyone they want, and
anyone can come in. This is the exact opposite of a City-sponsored event, where they control entry
and exit, and what the seniors see and receive from the Parks department. They are making a
significant change, and the wording needs to be precise.
Commissioner Bhatt appreciates that, and at the same time, traditionally the South Beach Marina
was run a certain way, which led to chaos, unhappy residents, and bad business actors. As a result,
they drafted legislation to change that behavior and put restrictions in place to achieve the goal of
behavioral change. How is this different from that? They are taking something that was historically
done one way, which was abused, and now they are changing how it is managed to encourage the
behavior they want to see.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, clarified that what Chief Deputy Attorney Rosenwald is suggesting
is to make changes so that events will be different from what was done in the past.
Commissioner Suarez wants to hear from other colleagues. Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas was just
elected, and what Commissioner Fernandez has to say is because they all attend these events and
there is a discussion about having an unfair advantage from incumbency and possible First
Amendment issues.
Commissioner Fernandez believes that if events are organized for seniors’ enjoyment, he
disapproves of how politicized they have become. He mentioned last year that if the goal is for seniors
to have a good time and socialize, politics should be removed from these events. While they do
appreciate seeing seniors in person and talking to them, the events have become highly politicized,
sometimes causing tension between candidates or between an existing candidate and a soon-to-be
candidate. This shift distracts from what should be the main focus: the seniors’ enjoyment, which
should be the top priority. Instead of discussing how to improve the event for seniors, the focus seems
to be on whether an elected official or candidate can speak or appear, which diverts attention from
the purpose. The event is about seniors with limited opportunities to socialize and get out, so if the
only way he can participate is by standing outside and shaking hands, he is okay with it. Ultimately,
these events should center on seniors’ enjoyment, not political speeches or campaign activities. A
good approach might be for officials to greet and engage with seniors outside the venue, reserving
the inside for seniors to socialize with their neighbors. Last year, when he was a candidate, he chose
not to attend many of these events to avoid the appearance of bias. He felt guilty when a colleague,
Mayor Meiner, implied he was avoiding the event because of politics. However, the focus should
remain on the seniors and ensuring the event’s purpose is preserved. If the goal is to have a
meaningful, enjoyable experience for seniors without political distraction, officials should step back
and let them have their space, free from First Amendment issues.
Mayor Meiner noted that Commissioner Fernandez made valid points and explained that a candidate
could remain at the entrance, handing out materials. He added that the Mayor and Commissioners
would still have the opportunity to interact with attendees once inside during their meal, without
politicizing the event.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas stated that during her recent campaign, she visited all senior events
alone, going from table to table. She did not hand out any materials and often stayed late, walking
some attendees to their buses and talking to them one-on-one, without a videographer or anyone to
take pictures. She personally visited every table, speaking with each one, without hiring anyone to
work the buildings. She walked around, introduced herself, and asked people about their concerns.
Although she was not present at the initial discussion of this Resolution, she agrees that campaign
materials should stop at the ground-floor entrance. However, whether it is an incumbent or a
candidate, they should be allowed to go up into the event, visit tables, and speak with people without
materials or electioneering gear, just walk around and chat.
Mayor Meiner stated that they implemented those changes last year, and materials cannot be handed
out at the event.
Commissioner Suarez stated that Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas attended these events as a candidate,
talked to residents, listened to their concerns, and was elected. This is the perfect reason to involve
a candidate. He is completely against distributing paraphernalia and admits he was guilty at the time.
However, Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas's victory, despite the odds, was due to her ability to connect
with seniors, speak with them, and understand their concerns. That is all they need to know about
this. He does not want to give the impression that seniors will police who they can or cannot see,
especially when it comes to someone who wants to hear their concerns about an issue that might not
make current officials happy. Seniors can be met at the entrance, but that is not the same. They do
not have the time to meet with residents regularly. As an incumbent, he believes this legislation should
be crafted fairly to satisfy long-term goals.
Commissioner Magazine stated that, as a father of a nine-year-old, it would be strange if someone
running for the Commission attended a school or Parks and Recreation event for children. The real
issue is that they are even discussing these senior events as potential campaign opportunities.
Commissioner Bhatt recalls an election cycle when at least one candidate was going to school during
Halloween. They talked to parents as they came in and out with their kids because it was a good
opportunity to intercept parents. She remembers there being a lot of fear about that. The fact that
they are now discussing whether or not it is fair for someone’s election goals is exactly why she
brought up this legislation. She cannot believe they are still talking about it after it has come up two
or three times before, and she just wants to end this cycle. As they did with Spring Break, they shut
it down for a couple of years and completely changed the narrative because it was not working. This
is not the right thing for them.
In response to Mayor Meiner, Rob Rosenwald, Chief Deputy City Attorney, clarified that if the plan is
to allow the County elected officials to participate in the program, he can add language as an
amendment to make that happen.

ACTION: Resolution 2026-34154 was adopted. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt
the Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Bhatt. Roll Call: 7-0. David Gomez to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
DIRECTION:
• The Administration to proceed with the full pedestrianization concept for Ocean Drive, subject to
approval of turnaround designs by Miami‑Dade County’s Department of Transportation and Public
Works (DTPW).
• If DTPW does not approve any turnaround design required for full pedestrianization,
Administration is authorized to develop a hybrid configuration with one‑way vehicular traffic
blended with pedestrianization.
• The Administration to coordinate with DTPW to determine the precise location of required
turnarounds, whether along Ocean Drive or between the alley and Ocean Drive, which will
determine related parking impacts.
• The Administration to prepare a comprehensive plan addressing operational, logistical, traffic,
and business‑impact considerations for the long‑term redesign of Ocean Drive.
• During the transition period, and to avoid duplicative work, the Administration will begin identifying
and developing cosmetic improvements that can be incorporated into the final design.
• Economic Development staff to research comparable pedestrianized destinations and provide
guidance to the Commission on best practices for operations, deliveries, visitor access, hospitality
logistics, and business support. Steven Anthony to handle.
• The Administration is to continue stakeholder outreach with businesses and the community during
the design phase.
• The Administration is to close the existing one‑way southbound permit before submitting the full
pedestrianization permit to the County.
David Gomez, CIP Director, described an Item that started before February 2022, when the
Commission adopted a vision plan created by Zyscovich. This plan looked conceptually at high-level
potential reconfigurations for Ocean Drive. They identified three options: two-way traffic, one-way
southbound, and full pedestrianization. After that, in October 2022, the City contracted Calvin,
Giordano and Associates, Inc. (CGA) to further examine each configuration, identify possible actions,
and develop recommendations so that this Body can decide which configuration to pursue. Each
option has benefits and drawbacks, as shown in the memo. Two of the three options involve a portion
of Lummus Park. Both the two-way traffic and southbound one-way options direct traffic into the Park,
which would require a Countywide referendum. During the evaluation, CGA identified ways to reduce
permitting restrictions. The County has made it clear that the City cannot rely on Ocean Court as an
alternative traffic route. CGA proposed a plan that eliminates reliance on Ocean Court while allowing
turnaround traffic at dead ends. Mr. Wallack earlier mentioned that the Countywide referendum for
the turnarounds was part of the study, as those turnarounds would again occupy a large part of the
Park, triggering a Countywide vote. CGA developed a scheme to remove that portion from the Park,
avoiding that requirement. They met with the County preliminarily, which agreed that this solution is
viable. In May 2025, the Body expressed a clear preference for full pedestrianization, so CGA
examined potential obstacles and benefits and is now recommending further development of that
plan. It is important to note that full pedestrianization would require two-way traffic on each side street.
This means that, as part of the master plan, bike lanes could not be used on those streets because
they would not fit. However, since the streets are small, shared lanes could be incorporated. Some
on-street parking on side streets would need to be removed to accommodate loading zones for
deliveries. The team considered delivering to businesses on Ocean Drive and found they could
accommodate most delivery vehicles on the side streets through loading zones, but the largest
vehicles, such as 18-wheelers, could not access the frontages of businesses, even those on Alton
Court. This could be managed by limiting the size of delivery vehicles, scheduling delivery times, and
using Collins Avenue as a loading zone during suitable hours.
Commissioner Fernandez moved to approve the staff’s recommendation.
Commissioner Dominguez noted that residents and businesses depend on on-street parking and
asked how many parking spaces would be lost.
CIP Director Gomez explained that he does not have an exact number.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, mentioned that the location of the turnaround might depend on the
installation site; their proposal suggests placing the turnaround between the alley and Ocean Drive
to ensure a continuous pedestrian promenade along Ocean. This would mean losing parking spaces
east of the alley. However, another option is to put the turnarounds on Ocean Drive, which would
bring back those parking spaces but could disrupt the pedestrian-friendly design of Ocean.
Commissioner Fernandez added that allowing staff to negotiate with the Miami-Dade Department of
Transportation & Public Works (DTPW) will determine where that turnaround will occur, whether in
Ocean Drive or east of the alleyway and Ocean Drive, which will, in turn, determine the loss of parking.
In addressing Commissioner Dominguez's comments on trash collection, CIP Director Gomez noted
that Ocean Court would remain as it is today so that garbage services can be provided there, given
the number of deliveries and users of the area. They simply cannot use it as a thoroughfare. CIP
Director Gomez explained that ADA parking spaces and drop-offs would be identified at each
turnaround, not only for ADA but for all drop-offs. He informed Commissioner Dominguez that each
of the turnarounds would be designed to allow emergency vehicles access to Ocean Drive.
Per Mayor Meiner’s directive, City Manager Carpenter explained that they examined various
permutations of this Item and appreciated CGA’s thorough work. They discussed many challenges
present in each option, but their recommendation is to fully pedestrianize Ocean Drive and include a
turnaround near the eastern alleyway in the 100 block. This would allow passenger vehicles to turn,
while trucks could turn in the alleyways. Ultimately, they would need the County’s approval for this
plan. If the County does not approve, the Resolution suggests a secondary option: implementing one-
way traffic in alternating blocks, with southbound lanes on Ocean Drive and westbound lanes on the
next street. This would create intermittent pedestrianized blocks if full pedestrianization cannot be
achieved due to a lack of County support.
In response to Mayor Meiner’s inquiry, CIP Director David Gomez explained that the challenge lies
in the permitting process because an existing permit remains open on Ocean Drive for the one-way
southbound, and they must close that process before submitting a new permit for the County's review.
This causes a delay, followed by negotiations with the County on how to proceed. After that,
completing the construction documents would take about eight months, covering the permitting and
bidding processes.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, told Mayor Meiner that the reason for switching from the current one-
way traffic to full pedestrianization is that they believe it is the best long-term solution for the City.
This belief is based on analysis and some ideas the Administration has about the future of Ocean
Drive and Lummus Park. They think this will position the City for success over the next 30 years.
CIP Director Gomez explained that transitioning from the current state to the proposed state enables
the City to expand sidewalks and create better pedestrian areas, as well as more café space, making
it a change to the environment rather than just the road.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, replied to Mayor Meiner that they analyzed altering the one-way traffic
option to be northbound instead of southbound, and he understands that they could possibly choose
one or the other. They believe the southbound option is better because it prevents restrictions on
outbound traffic, unlike the northbound flow. Fifth Street is a larger facility capable of handling traffic
from Ocean Drive. If they redirected everyone northbound, onto Fifteenth Street, there would be
challenges.
David Gomez, CIP, stated that during this process, he learned that the northbound one-way
configuration actually increases potential conflict points because vehicles need to turn left, crossing
pedestrians or other areas, whereas the southbound lane has fewer conflict points. Addressing
Commissioner Dominguez, he said that valet spots would be accommodated on the side streets.
Regarding emergency response times, a bollard system is being considered; they are looking at
active vehicle barriers that drop into the ground, which is an impact of fully pedestrianizing Ocean
Drive. As emergency vehicles approach, the bollards would drop. They need to be careful with
pedestrians, but there should not be a significant difference in response times.
Commissioner Fernandez noted that major destinations like Barcelona have Las Ramblas, New York
has Times Square, and in Paris, during certain times of the year, Triomphe des Champs-Élysées is
partially pedestrianized. They have friends and important stakeholders on both sides of the issue, but
the future of prosperous cities is accommodating pedestrians, creating a vibe for their health and
wellness brand, and it is also good for the economy. Prosperous cities offer pedestrian zones so
restaurants can expand, businesses with limited indoor space can thrive, and people can not only
enjoy the environment but also appreciate their architecture more closely. This is the future, and it
will support and boost the economy of the businesses in these areas, as has been proven in other
tourist destinations where such efforts have been successful.
Commissioner Magazine agrees that this is a long-term global vision, but he has a caveat: they need
to develop a comprehensive plan. He appreciates the vision for Ocean Drive, but the critical mistake
would be neglecting comprehensive urban planning in the surrounding areas. They must make this
vision come alive and add vitality, as Mr. Wallack mentioned, by attracting people. If they are
removing cars, which he believes is essential to making a place special, especially a beachfront plaza,
they need to ensure there are people. Currently, that area has low density. Businesses along Collins
Avenue from Fifth to 12th Streets have declined; the bank on Fifth Street closed, the gym is struggling,
and ground-floor retail is underperforming. That is part of the comprehensive plan. When he considers
pedestrianizing Ocean Drive, he wants to visit after work or school to see thousands of people
rollerblading, jogging, and enjoying Miami Beach’s most beautiful natural resource. But they need to
plan for people to do those activities, requiring comprehensive planning. Without it, they could face
issues similar to those on Lincoln Road. From a photo taken early this morning from Alton Road
looking east, there were no pedestrians, highlighting the need to fill neighborhood gaps to make
Ocean Drive pedestrian-friendly in the long run. He wants this done correctly and thoroughly. It should
become a beautiful pedestrian plaza and, moving forward, one of the world's most exceptional places.
Gianno Feoli, Director of Landscape Architecture and Urban Design at CGA, stated that the vision
for Ocean Drive is to make it more like a linear plaza. The original ideas and the ADCD plan aimed
to create a street without curbs, so there would not be a vertical separation between the roadway and
the sidewalk. The goal was to maintain storefront to park-front continuity and ensure a seamless
connection between Ocean Drive and Lummus Park. That is the overall goal.
In response to Commissioner Magazine’s question regarding a previous direction to commence
implementing improvements along the west side of Ocean Drive, CIP Director David Gomez stated
that the Commission discussed an item about potentially upgrading some of the sidewalk and lighting
on Ocean Drive. They consulted the community and presented options, but there was significant
pushback. The community did not respond well, and the discussion stopped at that point.
Commissioner Magazine added that in some of these comprehensive plans and visions, there will be
people who agree or disagree with anything. They have heard over the years that some of these
projects reach the 10-year mark, and suddenly they back off, which is why West Avenue has not been
completed for 20 years, and Lincoln Road remains unfinished for a long time. He does not want 20
years to pass and for them to have made a commitment to pedestrianize Ocean Drive, only to still be
sitting around with it looking like any normal street and sidewalk. They need to take decisive action
and move forward with this.
Commissioner Bhatt added that change is difficult, complex, and it does not happen all at once.
Besides the comments already made, data show that pedestrianized plazas and streets boost retail
and dining businesses because people stroll, have coffee, shop around, go to the beach, return, and
then go to lunch. It is not the same experience if they are just using Ocean Drive as a shortcut between
points A and B. She watched the film The Bird Cage again, but that is no longer today’s Ocean Drive.
In the 1980s, it was packed with cars, people dressed in Jane Fonda workout outfits, and
rollerbladers; that is not what the City is anymore. This upgrade would enhance the already fantastic
public amenities and make Miami Beach a world-class destination. She is not dismissing the concerns
about how hotel and dining guests will experience this, and those details will be worked out to ensure
a welcoming experience from when visitors leave their vehicles to when they arrive at their
destination. The Ocean Drive Association (ODA) and local businesses can collaborate to create this
beautiful experience. She shared her personal experience and assured that they would get it right.
Last year at the meeting, there was a strong pushback against making changes to sidewalks and
lighting in the Park, before this, which was a valid concern, but it occurred before the decision was
made. Many worried about investing money in something that might be torn up again. Could they
develop the cosmetic aspects with a clear goal in mind and start making improvements that will be
part of the larger plan? That would be a great way to move forward, enhancing the experience as
they transition, as suggested.
Chief of Police Wayne Jones, responding to Commissioner Suarez, explained that COVID-19 was
problematic for many reasons, and the issues related to it were not limited to the closure of Ocean
Drive. From a Police perspective, whether Ocean Drive remains open or closes at some point, they
will police it as best as they can. This is a policy decision, but they are committed to policing whether
it is open or closed. He confirmed to Commissioner Suarez that, if that is the Commission's direction,
the Miami Beach Police Department will commit to managing crowd control on Ocean Drive.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas added that this plan allows sidewalk cafés to continue operating, expand,
and gain more restaurant space to increase their revenue.
In response to Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas, Eric Carpenter, City Manager, explained that they would
have the option to continue holding the Pride Parade on Ocean Drive because they need to keep a
20-foot clear path for emergency vehicles, and they could activate that. It would be similar to having
a parade on Lincoln Road.
Commissioner Fernandez displayed an image illustrating the proposed plan. Click here to view. He
explained that the design would provide expanded pedestrian space, support businesses through
additional café seating, and create a unified pedestrian-oriented plaza adjoining Lummus Park. He
added that this is a beautiful vision where people enjoy the Park, local businesses, architecture, and
events hosted in the City. Commissioner Fernandez stated that the proposal would significantly
expand pedestrian areas and improve the corridor’s functionality.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas opened the public hearing.
David Wallack from Mango’s Tropical does not think people realize that Fifth to Fifteenth Streets are
not like Espanola Way, Miracle Mile, or Lincoln Road, or a typical retail center. These are small hotels,
each with multiple tiny rooms and bathrooms, no swimming pools, and no parking. Their only real
amenity is access to Lummus Park, which they want to take away. This makes the area
noncompetitive, leading to a decline year after year and risking its becoming dead. They have not
planned for the future. What will replace these charming small Deco hotels? They have destroyed
them before in the 1970s, though they were not here then and do not understand that history, and
they are at risk of doing the same again. Darkness, emptiness. Instead, they should consider
redesigning Lummus Park, including the restoration of Hurricane damage all the way to the beach
mound, as the architect envisioned. Lighting the trees as they do in Whistler would help. Ocean Drive
is lit poorly, like a dump. Meridian Avenue is actually more beautiful at night, yet they want to destroy
it. They are overlooking life safety; Chief Jones will do his best to respond, even if delayed. They do
not see that trucks need access for these hotels. Smaller trucks would require four times as many
trips to deliver supplies, walking on hand trucks from block to block five days a week. Police and fire
vehicles cannot get through

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, DIRECTING THE INDEFINITE SUSPENSION OF THE CITY’S MOORING FIELD PROJECT AND CAPITAL PROJECT #65422, WHICH REQUIRED THE INSTALLATION OF VARIOUS ANCHORING LIMITATION AREA AND WATERWAY SIGNS PURSUANT TO RESOLUTION NO. 2023-32646 AND/OR RESOLUTION NO. 2024-32963, UNLESS AND UNTIL THERE IS FURTHER ACTION OF THE CITY COMMISSION DIRECTING OTHERWISE.
items.action: Resolution 2026-34155 was adopted. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the Resolution as amended; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 7-0. David Gomez to handle.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34155 was adopted. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the
Resolution as amended; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 7-0. David Gomez to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
AMENDMENTS:
• Pay the outstanding $12,000 permit processing fee.
• Bring the Item back to the City Commission for further direction approximately 90 days before the
permit expires, with no additional tax dollars spent on the project until then.
• No additional tax dollars shall be spent on the project until further direction is provided by the City
Commission.
Commissioner Suarez explained that one of the first major issues he addressed when he joined the
Commission, along with two other Commissioners and the Mayor, was the cleanup of the City’s
waterways. He stated that at that time, there was a significant buildup of what appeared to be
abandoned boats throughout Biscayne Bay near Miami Beach. Initially, it seemed these vessels had
been abandoned or were deteriorating; however, upon closer examination, it became clear that a
business model had emerged where relatively seaworthy boats were anchored in the waterways and
rented out nightly or monthly, often for cash, similar to short-term rentals. Over about ten to fifteen
years, what started with roughly five boats grew to over 200 vessels scattered across the City’s
waterfront. He has led efforts both locally and at the State level to restore the City’s authority to
effectively manage its waterways. For the first time in many years, the State of Florida has removed
its preemption and granted Miami Beach enhanced regulatory authority, allowing the City to enforce
anchoring limits and address derelict vessel issues. Areas like Sunset Harbor and North Beach were
crowded with vessels, many sinking, leaking fuel, or in an unsalvageable condition. He noted that
enforcement options had previously been limited. After the change in State law and the City’s
adoption of new regulations, the waterways have been cleared. He emphasized that Sunset Harbor
and North Beach now have zero anchored vessels. The Item before the City Commission concerns
a previously proposed municipal mooring field. He recalled that former Commissioner Arriola had
originally sponsored the mooring field project to address the problem of derelict vessels locally. The
goal was to establish a managed mooring field to organize anchored vessels in a regulated area.
However, the situation changed significantly. He indicated that moving forward with the project would
cost about $3 million in additional taxpayer funds, despite an existing mooring field at Watson Island,
about half a nautical mile away, that remains roughly 60% vacant. He recommends canceling the
project to prevent further costs, noting that he has met with neighborhood groups along the bay, and
they have supported discontinuing the project. Click here to view the presentation.
Commissioner Dominguez acknowledged that the original purpose of the mooring field was to give
the City structured control over its waterways, in line with former Commissioner Arriola’s vision. She
expressed concern that about $678,000 has already been spent on planning and permitting. She is
unsure whether canceling the project outright is wise and suggested that suspending or putting the
project on hold might be better than abandoning it entirely, especially considering the prior
investment. She noted that while the waterways are currently clear, this may be temporary, and
circumstances could change in the future.
Commissioner Suarez responded that the $3 million estimate likely understates the full cost, as
uncertainties still exist regarding the needed upland support facility for pump-out services and related
infrastructure. He reiterated that the core issue of unregulated anchoring has already been effectively
addressed through State law changes and local enforcement. Ongoing investment might be
considered “throwing good money after bad" given the successful results achieved under the new
regulatory framework. He also mentioned that setting up a mooring field could lead to about 160
mooring balls in Biscayne Bay, potentially affecting views from residential areas such as West
Avenue, Belle Isle, Sunset Harbour, Venetian Islands, Star Island, Palm Island, and Hibiscus Island.
He pointed out that many of these mooring balls could remain unused, citing Watson Island as a
comparable example.
Commissioner Bhatt said she generally agreed with suspending the project but wanted to keep the
permit process intact.
Commissioner Bhatt said she generally agrees with suspending the project but wants to keep the
permit process open because of the work already done. She asked the Administration if it is possible
to get the necessary permits and keep them active without starting construction.
David Gomez, CIP Director, stated that the City has already received approval from the Florida
Department of Environmental Protection and is awaiting final approvals from the U.S. Army Corps of
Engineers and Department of Environmental Resources Management (DERM). He anticipates
receiving those approvals within two to three months. Once issued, the permits would likely have an
expiration period of more than one year.
Commissioner Fernandez inquired about the total cost and the amount the City has spent so far.
CIP Director Gomez confirmed that approximately $678,000 has been spent to date and that the total
estimated project cost exceeds $3 million.
Commissioner Suarez announced that a $12,000 fee for permit processing remains unpaid. He
recommended bringing the matter back to the City Commission about 90 days before the permit
expires for further guidance.
Mayor Meiner thanked Commissioner Suarez for bringing the Item forward. He noted that addressing
derelict vessels and cleaning up the waterways had been a significant issue for the City and
acknowledged the success achieved following changes in State law. He stated that the mooring field
had previously been controversial, but now he sensed a uniformity that placing the project on hold or
in hiatus would be the best course of action.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he wished to amend the Resolution to keep the mooring field permit
active, pay the outstanding $12,000 permit fee, direct that no further tax dollars be spent on the
project, and have the Item return to the City Commission for guidance approximately 90 days before
the permit expires. He also explained that even if State law changes again in the future, a mooring
field would not necessarily resolve anchoring congestion, noting that vessels could simply anchor
outside the mooring field boundary, as has occurred near Watson Island.
Sara de los Reyes thanked Commissioner Suarez and City Staff for their efforts. She described the
previous vessel congestion in the Maurice Gibb Park area, which at one point had more than 39
vessels in a small basin, raising navigation safety concerns.
Commissioner Suarez motioned to adopt the Resolution as amended, seconded by Commissioner
Fernandez. Vote: 7-0.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, RECOGNIZING AND COMMENDING SUNSET PADEL FOR ITS GENEROUS CONTRIBUTIONS AND COMMUNITY LEADERSHIP IN HOSTING A FUNDRAISING EVENT IN HONOR OF MIAMI BEACH POLICE DEPARTMENT SERGEANT DAVID CAJUSO; AND DIRECTING THE CITY CLERK TO TRANSMIT A CERTIFIED COPY OF THIS RESOLUTION TO REPRESENTATIVES OF SUNSET PADEL.
items.action: Resolution 2026-34156 was adopted by acclamation. Chief Wayne Jones to handle.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34156 was adopted by acclamation. Chief Wayne Jones to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine introduced the Item and explained that although the City
Commission often holds dedicated meetings for awards, presentations, and recognitions, he wished
to highlight what he described as a significant act of community support following the death of Miami
Beach Police Department Sergeant David Cajuso in November 2025. Commissioner Magazine
indicated that the City of Miami Beach is supported not only by its natural environment but by its
residents and local businesses, and described the impact of the Officer’s unexpected passing on the
community. Commissioner Magazine stated that a local small business in Sunset Harbour, Sunset
Padel, organized and hosted a fundraising event to assist Sergeant Cajuso’s family. He noted that
the business is owned by residents who live, work, and raise their families in Miami Beach. He added
that he wished for the owners to provide an overview of the event and its results and invited Rafi Gibly
and Chris Paciello, to speak. He also invited Miami Beach Police Chief Wayne Jones to join them
and provide additional comments.
Chief Wayne Jones explained that the event held at Sunset Padel had been a meaningful occasion
for the community and the Police Department. He said that the business owners organized the effort
voluntarily and that many attendees likely had not known Sergeant Cajuso personally but understood
the importance of supporting the family of a fallen Officer. Chief Jones noted that the Officer’s widow
had been present but was unable to speak due to the difficulty of the circumstances, and he
expressed appreciation on behalf of the Police Department and the family.
Rafi Gibly addressed the Commission and explained that the effort had been supported by every
attendee who entered the facility on the evening of the event. He stated that Sunset Padel contributed
the use of its facility and conveyed the circumstances surrounding Sergeant Cajuso’s passing to the
community, which prompted widespread participation. He added that the Miami Beach Police
Department consistently supports the community and that the business was willing to assist whenever
needed.
Commissioner Magazine asked Mr. Gibly to describe the moment when Sergeant Cajuso’s widow
received the fundraising check.
Mr. Gibly explained that the event had been scheduled early in the evening so she could return home
to care for her three children, and that she had initially been uncertain whether she would be able to
attend due to her circumstances. He noted that the total amount raised exceeded expectations and
that Sunset Padel intended to continue assisting whenever possible.
Commissioner Magazine stated that the event raised approximately $165,000 for the family of
Sergeant Cajuso and noted that the Officer’s widow initially believed the total to be $16,000 before
learning the correct amount. He explained that the contribution would provide meaningful support to
the family.
A photo was taken.
Mayor Steven Meiner acknowledged the efforts of Sunset Padel and the community. He described
the significant public participation at the event and said the community consistently provides support
to families who serve the City. He referenced the Officer’s widow’s remarks at the funeral and
recognized the family’s long‑standing service background.
The Resolution recognizing and commending Sunset Padel for its contributions and leadership in
hosting the fundraiser was adopted by acclamation.

ACTION: Discussion held.
The Committee of the Whole met on February 25, 2026, to conduct the City Manager’s annual
performance evaluation, which had been delayed beyond the contractual evaluation window.
Commissioners generally expressed confidence in City Manager Carpenter’s knowledge,
accessibility, and work ethic, while outlining organizational concerns across departments. Much of
the conversation focused on the need for improved customer service, stronger staff accountability,
and a cultural shift toward problem‑solving rather than rigid rule enforcement. Commissioners cited
repeated examples of staff overlooking basic operational issues, such as downed cones, fallen signs,
and unmet maintenance needs, emphasizing that employees should take greater ownership of field
conditions. Several Commissioners also highlighted challenges within the Planning Department,
noting insufficient staffing for plan review, delays in application processing, and a lack of proactive,
Citywide planning initiatives. They stressed that residents, applicants, and businesses often
encounter obstacles within numerous departments when seeking assistance, and pointed to
inconsistent responsiveness at public‑facing service points. The Neighborhood Affairs Division was
also discussed, with suggestions that its staff should be more present in the field and better equipped
to resolve constituent concerns rather than merely relaying information. Additional discussion
highlighted coordination gaps between the Tourism and Culture Department and the City’s Economic
Development Department, resulting in missed opportunities for businesses during special events and
activations. Commissioners expressed the belief that the City would benefit from leadership, such as
an Assistant City Manager, who resides in Miami Beach and therefore has direct, daily familiarity with
the City’s conditions. The conversation then expanded to governance and policymaking structure,
with multiple Commissioners acknowledging that the current system relies too heavily on isolated
legislative Items rather than the Strategic Plan. They expressed interest in returning to a model in
which the Commission sets broad goals while the City Manager and staff develop coordinated
recommendations. The City Manager agreed, emphasizing that the program‑based budget and
regular strategic check‑ins could help realign policy development with long-term priorities. The
Commission also discussed upcoming leadership transitions in Planning, with strong consensus that
internal candidates should be prioritized to preserve institutional knowledge. The meeting concluded
with a brief discussion of the City Manager’s contract, in which Human Resources clarified that the
Commission may award a merit increase and bonus, though time constraints led to postponing
compensation decisions to a future meeting. The discussion closed with an emphasis on the need
for heightened departmental attentiveness, improved Police visibility, and stronger internal systems
to proactively identify and report operational issues.
