ACTION: Discussion held. Resolution 2026-34157 adopted. A motion was made by Commissioner
Bhatt to adopt an After-the-Fact Resolution, seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 7-0. Chief
Wayne Jones to handle.
AFTER-THE-FACT RESOLUTION:
A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH,
FLORIDA, DIRECTING THE CITY ADMINISTRATION TO STATION NOT LESS THAN ONE (1)
POLICE VEHICLE AT SPECIFIED LOCATIONS ON 5TH STREET, 41ST STREET, AND 71ST
STREET, BETWEEN THE HOURS OF 10:00 P.M. AND 5:00 A.M. DAILY, TO PROACTIVELY ISSUE
CITATIONS FOR ILLEGAL AND EXCESSIVE VEHICULAR MUFFLER, EXHAUST, AND OTHER
NOISE; AND FURTHER, DIRECTING THE ADMINISTRATION TO PROVIDE MONTHLY REPORTS
ON THE RESULTS OF THESE EFFORTS BY LETTER TO COMMISSION (LTC), COMMENCING
APRIL 1, 2026.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
DIRECTION:
1. Administration to deploy Police Officers at three locations: one off the MacArthur Causeway,
one at 41st Street by Indian Creek, and one at 71st Street, from 10:00 p.m. to 5:00 a.m.
2. Do public service announcements regarding noise violations.
Mayor Meiner thanked Commissioner Dominguez for Co-sponsoring and introduced the Item.
Modified mufflers have been a problem in the City for some time. Some high-end sports cars with
modified mufflers produce loud sounds like explosions, but they are legal. There was also an Item to
implement a pilot program, and kudos were given to the Miami Beach Police Department because
five years ago, crime was high, Police visibility was low, and homelessness was an issue. While these
problems still exist, there have been improvements, and the Department is doing well. They need to
keep pushing forward. This has been a frequently discussed issue lately, and a related Item passed
on the Consent Agenda (C7 X) mirrors what the County is doing. It supports County Commissioner
Micky Steinberg’s Noise Ordinance to reduce the 100-foot rule. Now, if an Officer hears a violation at
25 feet from noise coming from a vessel, boat, or vehicle, they will bring legislation to the March 18th
Commission Meeting to coordinate efforts with the County. The Administration is directed to station
Officers at three points off the MacArthur Causeway: 41st Street, Indian Creek, and 71st Street, to
cover the City. This initiative is great because it also increases Police visibility during nighttime hours
from 10:00 p.m. to 5:00 a.m. and represents a concentrated effort to crack down on crime. Few cars
are on the road at night. Years ago, Mayor Meiner worked on the Noise Enforcement Abatement
Team (NEAT), which specialized in identifying violations involving modified mufflers. He then turned
the discussion over to Chief Jones and thanked him for his ongoing efforts on this issue.
Wayne Jones, Chief of Police, received emails and text messages from the Mayor and
Commissioners about noise issues, mostly at night, mufflers, and loud music throughout the City.
They recognize it as a Citywide quality of life concern. They mentioned the County Ordinance of 25
feet, reducing it from 100 feet, and are fully praising it; they want to see that applied throughout the
County and in Miami Beach, providing additional tools to enforce the law. He acknowledged Assistant
Police Chief Morgalo to explain further.
Assistant Chief of Police Daniel Morgalo announced that they began Operation Quiet Streets last
month and will continue moving forward. It addresses loud mufflers and noises coming from vehicles
on City roadways and in areas mentioned by Mayor Meiner and throughout the City. They partnered
with FHP to help on the Causeway on weekends. The Miami Police Department is doing something
similar in the Brickell neighborhood because this is a widespread problem across the County. With
new rental vehicles having loud mufflers, people cruise around, creating issues that are reflected in
the emails and text messages they receive. He is pleased to report that in 2025 they issued 675
citations specifically for loud mufflers and vehicle noise, up from 423 in 2024. In 2026, they are already
on track for a 30 to 40% increase over 2025, with 164 tickets already written for noise violations. They
will keep addressing the issue and working with other municipalities and agencies to raise awareness
and tackle the problem.
Mayor Meiner appreciates the increased enforcement efforts. While he lacks specific statistics linking
loud muffler driving to crime, he targeted overnight hours because they affect residents' quality of life.
Although 675 citations are issued annually, less than two per day, he can see from his apartment that
more than two violations happen every night. He aims to focus a concentrated effort on this issue. He
has spoken with FDLE, thanked Assistant Chief of Police Morgalo, and is pleased that the City of
Miami supports this initiative. He is puzzled by how the same car can repeatedly pass through each
city. To him, it is not just a nuisance but also a safety concern, with a clear public safety aspect. He
calls for a unified message and targeted enforcement. Past campaigns, such as those during Spring
Break and efforts to reduce homelessness, have been successful in lowering numbers. He
emphasizes that the Police Department can quickly communicate that anyone driving through these
areas risks being caught and ticketed.
Commissioner Dominguez has been working on noise issues for some time. She met with Miami
Beach Police Department staff and residents south of Fifth, along West Avenue, Alton Road, and
Collins Avenue. It seems as if, over the last year, the number of disruption incidents has increased
unexpectedly. She submitted this as a priority, suggesting the consideration of noise cameras, which
other countries use. She is not expecting it next year but sees it as a potential solution for the future.
Noise is a hot-button, quality-of-life issue, and she is happy to co-prime this initiative with Mayor
Meiner.
Commissioner Magazine requested to include his name as a sponsor. In response to Commissioner
Magazine's questions, Assistant Chief of Police Daniel Morgalo explained that they are currently
unable to use technology for noise enforcement from vehicles. The City and other municipalities are
lobbying the Legislature for changes, but they can only use decimal meters in specific situations,
especially on the Marine Patrol in the maritime environment. He is unsure whether this regulation
applies to drone technology, as it is rapidly evolving, and if not preempted, it could be an innovative
method to enforce noise regulations.
Commissioner Magazine recognizes that Assistant Chief of Police Morgalo and his team are staying
at the forefront of these daily technological advances and encouraged him to continue this effort. He
praised him for his excellent work. They are a product of their own success. These are the quality-of-
life issues they now need to address to create a safer and more resident-friendly city.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, believes that what Commissioner Magazine is referring to is that
they can currently use noise cameras to monitor and collect data, but they cannot use them to issue
citations. That is one of their legislative priorities to get the State to allow the City to issue citations
using noise cameras.
Mayor Meiner mentioned that New York City uses a system that relies extensively on noise cameras,
and that when a vehicle with a modified muffler is found to be in violation, it can undergo an inspection
and be corrected to avoid penalties. He explained that such inspections cannot occur locally because
State law does not permit them. He noted that while Miami Beach’s noise cameras had captured
significant amounts of data, the City was unable to act on it. He described an internal discussion
regarding whether warnings could be issued, but the Police Department ultimately determined that
warnings could not be legally provided. He stated that although he initially took a different view, he
accepted the Police Department’s position and acknowledged that the current law clearly prohibits
the issuance of citations based on noise‑camera data. He added that he worked with organizations
such as Quiet Communities in Naples and OPEGA to develop recommendations supporting the use
of technological tools, including video and photographic evidence, to identify violators. He noted that
enforcement continues to rely on physical methods, but that the forthcoming reduction of the
enforcement distance from 100 feet to 25 feet should improve enforcement efforts.
Daniel Morgalo, Assistant Chief of Police, added that they released a video on social media with their
Officers conducting this type of enforcement recently that the PIO put out, so they are partnering their
messaging to the community along with the enforcement to get the word out that this is going on, and
they will continue to do that.
A motion was made by Commissioner Bhatt to adopt an After-the-Fact Resolution, seconded by
Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 7-0.

ACTION: Discussion held and direction provided. Commissioner Fernandez moved to instruct the
City Manager to sign the FPL easement agreements only after he is satisfied that all parties have
exhausted their efforts in good faith and that all issues related to utility coordination for the Fifth Street
pedestrian bridge project have been resolved to the City Manager’s satisfaction; seconded by
Commissioner Magazine. Vote: 7-0 David Gomez to handle.
Pursuant to Ordinance 2015-3954, Sec. 2-12(3), Addendum Agenda Item R9 AD was approved by
Mayor Meiner for inclusion on the agenda.
DIRECTION:
Administration to sign the easement agreement once the City Manager feels all parties have
exhausted efforts in good faith.
Commissioner Fernandez explained that the Public Safety & Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee
expressed concerns about communication and coordination with FPL and the developer building a
General Obligation (G.O.) Bond project on behalf of the City. To save time, his proposal is simply to
direct the Administration to sign the easement agreement once the Manager believes all parties have
exhausted their efforts, rather than to repeal it. This is a voter-approved G.O. Bond project, and the
developer is concerned about the uncertainty surrounding the accuracy of the critical transmission
line locations serving 13,000 people. He knows FPL has been a good partner, offering to do and fund
digging up to a certain point, but they need to ensure conversations and negotiations continue
smoothly to avoid delays in the Fifth Street pedestrian bridge over the MacArthur Causeway
infrastructure project. City Manager Carpenter is comfortable with that direction, and Commissioner
Fernandez moved to approve his Item.
Per Commissioner Magazine’s request, Eric Carpenter, City Manager, explained that his team has
been designing the pedestrian bridge and has now gone through at least two foundation designs. In
each case, based on the utility location information available at the time, new utility data has emerged
indicating utilities are present at the site. Consequently, they are now considering a potential third
redesign, which is delaying the process and increasing costs, causing significant friction. They simply
need clear information on utility locations to finalize the design once and for all. In response to
Commissioner Magazine, he added that if they cannot determine the precise utility locations, the
design team and contractor might face excessive liability, making it difficult to proceed with these
uncertainties.
Commissioner Magazine pointed out that they have been promising this General Obligation (G.O.)
Bond project to residents and want to know whose fault it is. The developer’s representative is
present, and the FPL representative calls every day to share her side of the story, but he wants to
hear in public who is responsible. There is definitely fault somewhere. Things were in the ground that
should not have been, and they did not know they were there. That just does not happen randomly.
Two or three parties might be responsible, and he asked the City Manager to clarify the matter.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, stated that, as a utility owner, the City often believes it has utilities in a
certain location but later discovers they are not exactly where it thought. He expressed some
sympathy for another utility owner who is in the same situation. Discussion was held.
Commissioner Magazine noted that if they are a publicly traded multimillion-dollar corporation and
that is their primary business model, they should uphold a higher standard of knowing exactly what
is happening.
Commissioner Fernandez thanked both parties. The project's developer has invested a lot of time
and effort in working with FPL. FPL is taking an unconventional approach. In his opinion, and to
answer Commissioner Magazine's question, he would say USIC is responsible for the company that
was sent out three times to identify the utilities, but each time it failed. Due to the inconsistency in not
pinpointing exactly where the utility is, concerns are raised about the liability if the developer starts
drilling, and what if this company is wrong again.
In reply to Commissioner Magazine, City Manager Carpenter stated that, unfortunately, he is not
entirely sure if USIC is at fault. They are a locating company and are only as accurate as the
information they receive. They have received very inconclusive information from the utilities, mainly
FPL, and have had some difficulty on the City side regarding the relocation of water lines. He cannot
say the City was perfect either, but that is not what is driving this issue now. The water has been
relocated and is out of the way. The current challenge involves the location of the FPL directional drill
that goes beneath the MacArthur Bridge at a depth of 30 to 40 feet. They had drilled shaft poles for
the bridge’s foundation, and during testing, they came into contact with one of the HDPE sheets of
transmission lines. This has caused significant concern because if they had not conducted testing
and had simply augured, they might have injured someone or knocked out power to 13,000 people.
Commissioner Magazine explained in plain language that this pedestrian bridge project needs a
designated land area and an initial concept, with a key aspect being the underground utilities and
their placement. FPL stated they were located in spot x, but during drilling, they were actually found
in spot y. This discrepancy could have led to a critical disaster, which thankfully was avoided. Because
the projects were designed based on utilities being in the locations FPL indicated and considering
alternative sites, the designs the City has repeatedly developed are not feasible. Creating these
designs is a yearlong process, so if redesigns are needed, it will take another year, followed by re-
permitting. As a result, what was supposed to be a project that should have started years ago is now
at least two years delayed, and the overall viability of the project may even be in doubt. Discussion
held.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez stated that Florida Power & Light Company had been responsive and
had participated in discussions following the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life
Committee meeting. He noted that FPL had been communicating with representatives of the project
developer, including Alice and Hector, and that progress was being made. Commissioner Fernandez
explained that he did not feel comfortable with the City Manager signing the easement agreements
approved at the previous meeting until there was certainty regarding a clear path forward, as the City
had worked on the project for an extended period and unresolved issues could threaten the project’s
viability. In response to Commissioner Joseph Magazine’s questions about next steps, Commissioner
Fernandez made a motion to direct the City Manager to sign the easements only when the City
Manager determines that all parties have exhausted their efforts in good faith and that all matters
have been sufficiently resolved. He added that the Administration, including Assistant City Manager
David Martinez, Capital Improvement Projects Director David Gomez, and the City Manager,
continued to meet with FPL and the developer to work through the outstanding issues.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, stated that FPL has agreed to perform soft digging of their lines from
Alton Road until it becomes too deep for them to do so. They want to know the approximate location
and details of the infrastructure, whether it is a single conduit with multiple lines inside or multiple
conduits, but they do not have that level of certainty right now. Based on this information, they can
provide it to the design team to see if they have enough to proceed with a revised design. They also
need to verify with FPL the results of the two other line locates to determine if they are clear or if there
is something else out there that has not yet been identified. He hopes they can complete the redesign
and permitting within 12 to 16 months, but it is definitely a delay.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas is working on an Item for the March 18, 2026, City Commission meeting
to examine the feasibility of routing the bridge beneath the MacArthur Causeway so they do not have
to disturb the FPL lines.
Commissioner Magazine wants to move forward, but it aims to be fair to FPL because Chelsey has
reached out to share the full story, and it would like to hear it publicly.
Christopher Ferreira, an FPL External Affairs Area Manager, provided context and background on
the situation. The feeder lines involved are over 25 years old and have been in the ground since 1999,
before digital and more advanced record drawings were available. They are buried at depths over 30
feet, so they aim to provide the best record drawings they have of what is underground. Utility locates
can identify utilities, but it is the responsibility of the utility and the builder or developer to ensure
proper location. An estimate is given, and then soft digs or other non-intrusive trenching methods are
used to locate them accurately. A contract is in place, and they will go out to dig the bank and identify
where the pipe comes up, gaining a better understanding of its direction. They will share this
information with the bridge group, hoping to gain clarity within a couple of weeks. They have locators
and have even purchased equipment to more accurately determine the locations of facilities. In recent
months, they discussed options to move forward with the builder. A discussion was held, and they
have a solid plan of action to proceed.
Commissioner Fernandez added that the motion directs the Administration to sign the easements
once the City Manager feels confident that everything has been settled and arranged to his
satisfaction.
A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez giving direction to the City Manager, seconded by
Commissioner Magazine. Vote: 7-0.

Action: Report was given.
OLD BUSINESS
OB 1. DISCUSS THE POTENTIAL CREATION OF A SPECIAL TAXING DISTRICT TO FUND
THE IMPLEMENTATION OF GUARD GATES AND/OR THE IMPLEMENTATION OF
OTHER SECURITY FEATURES IN THE VENETIAN ISLANDS. Item withdrawn by sponsor.
OB 2. DISCUSS THE POTENTIAL CREATION OF A SPECIAL TAXING DISTRICT TO FUND
THE IMPLEMENTATION OF SECURITY FEATURES IN THE BAYSHORE AND NORTH
BAY ROAD NEIGHBORHOODS. Item withdrawn by sponsor.
OB 3. DISCUSS ESTABLISHING A MUSCLE BEACH IN NORTH BEACH, CONSIDERING THE
WIDELY RECOGNIZED POSITIVE IMPACT ON HEALTH, COMMUNITY, AND QUALITY
OF LIFE OBSERVED AT MUSCLE BEACH IN SOUTH BEACH, WITH SPONSORSHIP
SUPPORT TO OFFSET PROJECT COSTS AND REDUCE FINANCIAL IMPACT ON THE
CITY. Item not heard and deferred to a future FERC meeting.
NEW BUSINESS
NB 1. DISCUSS POTENTIAL INSTALLATION OF SMALL AEROPONIC GARDENS AT A
LOCATION TO BE DETERMINED WITHIN THE CONVENTION CENTER CAMPUS.
Commissioner Dominguez motioned to have this Item return to the Commission with a
favorable recommendation to consider a budget enhancement as a priority for two small
aeroponic gardens located at the Rum Room as part of the FY 2027 budget process from
the Convention Center fund. Commissioner Magazine seconded the motion. All in favor 3-
0.
NB 2. DISCUSS A TEMPORARY HIRING FREEZE FOR NON-ESSENTIAL POSITIONS.
Commissioner Suarez motioned to have this Item return to the Commission with a favorable
recommendation to direct all Charter Offices, including the City Manager, City Attorney, City
Clerk, Inspector General, and Mayor/Commission office, to approve the advertisement of all
open positions. Commissioner Magazine seconded the motion. All in favor 3-0.
NB 3. DISCUSS/TAKE ACTION ON THE POSSIBLE REVISION OF NON-RESIDENT
ENTRANCE FEES AND/OR THE INTRODUCTION OF RESIDENT GUEST PASSES FOR
CITY POOLS. Item not heard and deferred to a future FERC meeting.
NB 4. DEVELOP OR EXPAND TARGETED ECONOMIC INCENTIVES TO ATTRACT
ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) COMPANIES TO MIAMI BEACH. The Item was heard
and closed.
NB 5. DISCUSS REFUNDING SERIES 2015 RESORT TAX REVENUE BONDS. Commissioner
Dominguez motioned to have this Item return to the Commission with a favorable
recommendation to proceed with the refunding as presented. Commissioner Magazine
seconded the motion. All in favor 3-0.
NB 6. A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI
BEACH ACCEPTING THE RECOMMENDATION OF THE FINANCE AND ECONOMIC
RESILIENCY COMMITTEE TO REFER THE MIAMI BEACH COMPREHENSIVE
FINANCIAL POLICIES TO THE BUDGET ADVISORY COMMITTEE FOR REVIEW AND
ANALYSIS. Two separate motions: Commissioner Suarez motioned to have this Item return
to the Commission with a favorable recommendation to approve the Comprehensive
Financial Policies as amended. Motion seconded by Commissioner Dominguez. All in favor
3-0. Commissioner Suarez motioned to have this Item return to the Commission with a
favorable recommendation to direct the Administration to proceed immediately with the
resurfacing of 17th Street and to repair the sidewalks on 17th Street as needed. Motion
seconded by Commissioner Dominguez. All in favor 3-0.
NB 7. DISCUSS EARMARKING FUNDS COLLECTED BY THE CITY FROM SPEED
DETECTION SYSTEMS IN SCHOOL ZONES, PURSUANT TO SECTION 316.1896,
FLORIDA STATUTES, FOR THE USE OF PUBLIC/PEDESTRIAN/BICYCLIST SAFETY
INITIATIVES. Item not heard and deferred to a future FERC meeting.
NB 8. DISCUSS COMMISSIONING OF A SURVEY OF DRIVERS EXITING MIAMI BEACH TO
INFORM TRAFFIC MITIGATION POLICIES. Item not heard and deferred to a future FERC
meeting.
NB 9. DISCUSS RESOLUTION ESTABLISHING AN ELIGIBILITY REQUIREMENT FOR ALL
CULTURAL INSTITUTIONS SEEKING GRANTS OR OTHER FUNDING (EXCLUDING
SPECIAL EVENT OR SIMILAR SPONSORSHIPS) FROM THE CITY, AND PROVIDING
THAT, AS A CONDITION OF QUALIFICATION, EACH APPLICANT MUST CERTIFY
THAT, DURING THE APPLICANT’S MOST RECENTLY COMPLETED FISCAL YEAR, NO
SALARIED EMPLOYEE, INCLUDING THE EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, RECEIVED ANNUAL
COMPENSATION EQUAL TO OR EXCEEDING TWO HUNDRED FIFTY THOUSAND
DOLLARS ($250,000). Item not heard and deferred to a future FERC meeting.
NB 10. DISCUSS THE CREATION OF A MIAMI BEACH HISTORICAL MUSEUM, AND IDENTIFY
POTENTIAL SITES ON CITY-OWNED PROPERTY, INCLUDING, WITHOUT LIMITATION,
AN UNDERUTILIZED OR VACANT STOREFRONT IN A CITY-OWNED BUILDING, IN
ORDER TO COMPLEMENT THE CITY'S ROBUST CULTURAL OFFERINGS WITH A
NEW INSTITUTION FOCUSED ON THE HISTORY OF MIAMI BEACH. Item deferred to the
April 1, 2026, FERC meeting.
NB 11. DISCUSS RESOLUTION DIRECTING THE ADMINISTRATION TO PUT ITS BEST FOOT
FORWARD AND USE BEST EFFORTS TO HAVE MUNICIPAL AND PRIVATE PROJECTS
IN THE PIPELINE, PERMITTED AND COMPLETED, TO THE EXTENT FEASIBLE, AHEAD
OF THE 2026 WORLD CUP, INCLUDING THE ISSUANCE OF PERMITS FOR NEW
BUSINESSES. Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas motioned to have this Item return to the
Commission with a favorable recommendation to direct the Administration to close Ocean
Drive during the month of the FIFA 2026 World Cup matches in Miami. Commissioner
Magazine seconded the motion. All in favor 3-0.
NB 12. DISCUSS THE ALLOCATION OF FUNDS TO IMPLEMENT A COMPREHENSIVE AND
REGULARLY SCHEDULED SEAGRAPE MANAGEMENT PLAN. Vice-Mayor Matteo-
Salinas motioned to have this Item return to the Commission with a favorable
recommendation to prepare a budget amendment for funding a one-time sea-grape pruning
along the entire length of the beach walk. Motion seconded by Commissioner Magazine.
Approved 3-0.
NB 13. DISCUSS AND TAKE ACTION REGARDING THE POTENTIAL CREATION OF A
PROGRAM FOR MIAMI BEACH RESIDENTS TO ADOPT DOGS AND CATS FROM
MIAMI-DADE SHELTERS, WHERE ADOPTEES CAN BE REIMBURSED OR PROVIDED
VOUCHERS FOR CERTAIN VETERINARY BILLS AND FOOD FOR THE FIRST YEAR.
Item not heard and deferred to a future FERC meeting.
NB 14. DISCUSS AND TAKE ACTION ON THE FUNDING AND CONSTRUCTION OF FOUR
LIGHTED PICKLEBALL COURTS AT BAYSHORE PARK. Commissioner Dominguez
motioned to have this Item return to the Commission with a favorable recommendation to
create a new capital project in year one of the City’s five-year CIP for building pickleball
courts at Bayshore Park, and in year five, a new capital project for the related lighting
enhancements. Commissioner Magazine seconded the motion. All in favor 3-0.
NB 15. DISCUSSION ON INSTALLATION OF ENHANCED LIGHTING AT THE DOG PARK
LOCATED AT 201 2ND STREET. The Item was heard and scheduled to return to the
Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee meeting with an updated cost estimate based
on the discussion.
FUTURE ITEMS
F 1. DISCUSS NEXT STEPS AND FUNDING FOR THE PINE TREE DRIVE AND 46 STREET
TRAFFIC CIRCLE PROJECT. To be heard at the March 4, 2026, FERC meeting.
F 2. DISCUSS EARMARKING ALL RENT IN EXCESS OF THE MINIMUM FIXED RENT
RECEIVED PURSUANT TO THE DEVELOPMENT AND GROUND LEASE AGREEMENT
BETWEEN THE CITY AND MB MIXED USE INVESTMENT, LLC, FOR THE
DEVELOPMENT AND OPERATION OF THE CONVENTION CENTER HEADQUARTER
HOTEL FOR THE PURPOSE OF PROMOTING AND SUPPORTING WORKFORCE AND
AFFORDABLE HOUSING DEVELOPMENT. To be heard at the March 4, 2026, FERC
meeting.
F 3. DISCUSS THE POSSIBILITY OF THE CITY ENTERING INTO ONE OR MORE
AGREEMENTS WITH PRIVATE PARKING FACILITY OPERATORS IN NORTH BEACH IN
ORDER TO INCREASE THE NUMBER OF AVAILABLE PARKING SPACES FOR NORTH
BEACH RESIDENTS. To be heard at the March 4, 2026 FERC meeting.
F 4. A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI
BEACH, FLORIDA, ACCEPTING THE RECOMMENDATION OF THE FINANCE AND
ECONOMIC RESILIENCY COMMITTEE, AT ITS APRIL 19, 2024 MEETING, TO ACCEPT
THE CITY ADMINISTRATION'S UPDATE ON THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH PARKING
DEPARTMENT ENFORCEMENT EFFORTS. To be heard at the March 4, 2026 FERC
meeting.
F 5. A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI
BEACH, FLORIDA, DIRECTING THE ADMINISTRATION TO NEGOTIATE
APPROPRIATE TERMS AND CONDITIONS FOR THE POSSIBLE EXTENSION OF THE
TERM OF THE MIAMI BEACH MARINA LEASE, TO INCLUDE OPTIONS FOR BOTH A
SHORT-TERM (LESS THAN 10 YEARS) AND LONG-TERM (10 YEARS OR MORE)
EXTENSION, AND TO PRESENT A DRAFT TERM SHEET THAT INCLUDES BOTH
OPTIONS TO THE FINANCE AND ECONOMIC RESILIENCY COMMITTEE (FERC) AND
TO THE PUBLIC SAFETY NEIGHBORHOODS AND QUALITY OF LIFE COMMITTEE
(PSNQLC) FOR REVIEW BY EACH COMMITTEE AS SOON AS REASONABLY
PRACTICABLE. To be heard at the March 4, 2026 FERC meeting.
F 6. DISCUSS POTENTIAL SHORT-TERM IMPROVEMENTS AT MIAMI BEACH
PROMENADE (FORMERLY KNOWN AS MIAMI BEACH DRIVE), SITUATED BETWEEN
24TH STREET AND 29TH STREET, INCLUDING REHABILITATION OF SIDEWALKS,
LANDSCAPES, LIGHTING IMPROVEMENTS, AND OTHER NECESSARY AESTHETICS.
To be heard at the March 4, 2026 FERC Meeting.
F 7. DEVELOP A COMPREHENSIVE PLAN TO INTEGRATE UNDERGROUND CISTERNS
WITHIN THE WEST LOTS. To be heard at the March 4, 2026 FERC Meeting.
F 8. DISCUSS THE POSSIBLE ACQUISITION OF CERTAIN OUTLOTS ALONG INDIAN
CREEK DRIVE FOR THE CREATION OF BUS PULLOUT BAY/BUS STOPS TO
AMELIORATE TRAFFIC. To be heard at the March 4, 2026 FERC Meeting.
F 9. UTILITY COST RELIEF PROGRAM FOR TENANTS AND PROPERTY OWNERS. To be
heard at the March 4, 2026 FERC meeting.
F 10. DISCUSS POTENTIAL IMPROVEMENT AND MAINTENANCE AGREEMENT WITH MAC
MANAGEMENT 2, LLC FOR THE LINCOLN LANE NORTH RIGHT-OF-WAY. To be heard
at the March 4, 2026 FERC meeting.
F 11. A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI
BEACH, FLORIDA, AUTHORIZING THE CITY MANAGER TO EXECUTE ANY LAND USE
BOARD APPLICATIONS NECESSARY TO FACILITATE THE REVIEW OF PROPOSED
IMPROVEMENTS TO THE LINCOLN LANE NORTH RIGHT-OF-WAY, ADJACENT TO
THE PROPERTIES LOCATED AT 723 LINCOLN LANE NORTH, 721 LINCOLN ROAD,
AND 741 LINCOLN ROAD; SAID IMPROVEMENTS TO BE UNDERTAKEN IN
CONNECTION WITH A POTENTIAL IMPROVEMENT AND MAINTENANCE
AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE CITY AND MAC MANAGEMENT 2, LLC, THE AGENT FOR
THE CONTRACT PURCHASER OF THE SUBJECT PROPERTIES; AND PROVIDING
THAT THE FINAL DECISION TO PROCEED WITH THE PROJECT SHALL BE MADE BY
THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION FOLLOWING RECEIPT OF A
RECOMMENDATION FROM THE FINANCE AND ECONOMIC RESILIENCY COMMITTEE
RELATING TO THE POTENTIAL IMPROVEMENT AND MAINTENANCE AGREEMENT.
To be heard at the March 4, 2026 FERC Meeting.
F 12. DISCUSS EXPANDED ACCESS AND DISCOUNTED RATES FOR NORTH BAY VILLAGE
RESIDENTS AT NORMANDY PARK POOL AND NORTH BEACH RECREATIONAL
PROGRAMMING. To be heard at the March 4, 2026 FERC meeting.
F 13. DISCUSSION REGARDING THE FEASIBILITY OF ESTABLISHING A CONDOMINIUM
SPECIAL ASSESSMENT ASSISTANCE PROGRAM FOR FINANCIALLY VULNERABLE
RESIDENTS. To be heard at the March 4, 2026 FERC meeting.
F 14. DISCUSS THE PLACEMENT OF ADDITIONAL OR IMPROVED WAYFINDING THAT
WOULD DIRECT GUESTS/CUSTOMERS/RESIDENTS FROM THE MIAMI BEACH
CONVENTION CENTER TO THE LINCOLN ROAD MALL. To be heard at the April 1, 2026
FERC.
F 15. A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI
BEACH, FLORIDA, DIRECTING THE CITY ADMINISTRATION TO PREPARE A PLAN
AND A COST ESTIMATE FOR TRAPPING, AND SPAYING OR NEUTERING ALL

PLAN TO BE PRESENTED TO THE FINANCE AND ECONOMIC RESILIENCY
COMMITTEE ("FERC") AT ITS JULY 26, 2024 MEETING. To be heard at the April 1, 2026

F 16. DISCUSS MEASURES THAT CAN BE TAKEN TO STREAMLINE THE USE OF STAFF
RESOURCES. To be heard at the April 2026 FERC meeting.
F 17. EXPLORE WORKFORCE TRANSPORTATION SOLUTIONS AND EMPLOYER
PARTNERSHIP INITIATIVES WITH THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH.
F 18. DISCUSS PLACING/WRAPPING ARTWORK ON THE FACADE OF THE 17TH STREET
PARKING GARAGE (G5) AND A MURAL THAT LEADS TO LINCOLN ROAD.
F 19. DISCUSS AMENDING PARKING FEES TO PROVIDE FREE PARKING FOR
CONSTITUENTS MEETING WITH THE MAYOR AND COMMISSION OFFICE AT CITY
HALL.
F 20. CONSIDER A REDUCED PARKING RATE FOR THE MIAMI BEACH WORKFORCE,
INCLUDING HOSPITALITY EMPLOYEES.
F 21. DISCUSS THE POTENTIAL CREATION OF A SPECIAL TAXING DISTRICT TO FUND
THE INSTALLATION OF GUARD GATES AND/OR THE IMPLEMENTATION OF OTHER
SECURITY SERVICES OR FEATURES ON FLAMINGO DRIVE.
F 22. DISCUSS THE REMEDIATION RESULTING FROM THE PARK VIEW CANAL REPORT.
F 23. DISCUSS THE ACTIVATION OF ALLEYS IN SOUTH BEACH (ART DECO SIGNS) AND
NORTH BEACH (MIMO SIGNS).
F 24. DISCUSS WATER, SEWER, AND STORMWATER RATE ORDINANCE.
F 25. DISCUSS THE INSTALLATION OF A PLUMBED BIRD BATH WATER FEATURE AT

F 26. DISCUSS APPROVING ITN-2024-008-ND MUNICIPAL CIRCULATOR SERVICES.
F 27. DISCUSS INCLUDING A REQUIREMENT TO REPAVE THE ENTIRE PUBLIC RIGHT OF

F 28. DISCUSS ESTABLISHMENT OF A RECURRING GRANT TO THE MIAMI BEACH POLICE
ATHLETIC LEAGUE IN HONOR OF THE LATE SERGEANT DAVID A. CAJUSO.
F 29. DISCUSSION OF FEASIBILITY OF A LONG-TERM LICENSE AGREEMENT WITH
UNTITLED ART FAIR.
F 30. REFERRAL TO THE FINANCE AND ECONOMIC RESILIENCY COMMITTEE TO
RECONSTRUCT THE NORTH BEACH HISTORIC LOG CABIN AT ITS ORIGINAL
LOCATION AT 8128 COLLINS AVENUE; AND FURTHER, DIRECT THE
ADMINISTRATION TO TAKE ALL NECESSARY STEPS TO PROCEED WITH THIS NEW
DIRECTIVE WITH ALL DELIBERATE SPEED.
F 31. A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI
BEACH, FLORIDA, AUTHORIZING THE CITY MANAGER TO EXECUTE ANY LAND USE
BOARD APPLICATIONS NECESSARY TO FACILITATE THE REVIEW OF PROPOSED
IMPROVEMENTS TO THE LINCOLN LANE NORTH RIGHT-OF-WAY, ADJACENT TO
THE PROPERTIES LOCATED AT 723 LINCOLN LANE NORTH, 721 LINCOLN ROAD,
AND 741 LINCOLN ROAD; SAID IMPROVEMENTS TO BE UNDERTAKEN IN
CONNECTION WITH A POTENTIAL IMPROVEMENT AND MAINTENANCE
AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE CITY AND MAC LR HOLDCO, LLC, THE AGENT FOR THE
CONTRACT PURCHASER OF THE SUBJECT PROPERTIES; AND PROVIDING THAT
THE FINAL DECISION TO PROCEED WITH THE PROJECT SHALL BE MADE BY THE
MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION FOLLOWING RECEIPT OF A RECOMMENDATION

POTENTIAL IMPROVEMENT AND MAINTENANCE AGREEMENT.
F 32. DISCUSS MUNICIPAL CIRCULATOR ADVERTISING SERVICES.
F 33. DISCUSS INDEXING THE LIVING WAGE RATES FOR EMPLOYEES OF SERVICE
CONTRACTORS AND CITY EMPLOYEES FOR THE YEAR 2026, IN ACCORDANCE

F 34. DISCUSS NEXT STEPS FOR THE 19TH STREET PARKING FEASIBILITY STUDY.
F 35. DISCUSS ELIMINATING THE CURRENT 30-DAY WAITING PERIOD FOR NEW CITY
EMPLOYEES TO RECEIVE CITY HEALTH BENEFITS, INCLUDING HEALTH

IMPLEMENTING COVERAGE EFFECTIVE UPON HIRE.
F 36. DISCUSS CHANGING THE SURFACE TO ARTIFICIAL GRASS AT THE DOG PARK
LOCATED AT SOUTH POINTE PARK, AS RECOMMENDED BY THE PARKS AND
RECREATIONAL FACILITIES ADVISORY BOARD (LTC 542-2025), AND TO ALSO
DISCUSS CHANGING THE SURFACE TO ARTIFICIAL GRASS AT THE DOG PARK
LOCATED AT MAURICE GIBB PARK FOR THE SAME REASONS, INCLUDING

F 37. DISCUSS POSSIBLE ACQUISITION OF 819 – 5TH STREET TO HOUSE THE SOUTH
SHORE COMMUNITY CENTER.
F 38. DISCUSS A POTENTIAL INCENTIVE PROGRAM FOR HOTEL AND HOSPITALITY
EMPLOYEES REPORTING HUMAN OR SEX TRAFFICKING
F 39. THE FEASIBILITY, FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS, AND EXPECTED OUTCOMES
REGARDING THE POTENTIAL ESTABLISHMENT OF A MOUNTED (HORSE) POLICE
PATROL.
F 40. CALL ON THE OFFICE OF THE INSPECTOR GENERAL TO PRESENT THEIR ANNUAL
REPORT AT THE FINANCE AND ECONOMIC RESILIENCY COMMITTEE AND ADOPT

MIAMI BEACH AND SUNSET ISLANDS 1 AND 2 HOMEOWNERS ASSOCIATION FOR A
SELF-FUNDED INSTALLATION OF A TURF SPACE AT THE PARK ON SUNSET ISLAND
2.
WITHDRAWN ITEMS
W 1. DISCUSS SENIOR MEAL SITE PROGRAMMING AT SOUTH SHORE COMMUNITY
CENTER. Item withdrawn by Sponsor.

Action: Report was given.
OLD BUSINESS
OB 1. DISCUSS NEXT STEPS AND FUNDING FOR THE PINE TREE DRIVE AND 46 STREET
TRAFFIC CIRCLE PROJECT. This Item was heard and scheduled to return to FERC with
an update when appropriate.
OB 2. DISCUSS EARMARKING ALL RENT IN EXCESS OF THE MINIMUM FIXED RENT
RECEIVED PURSUANT TO THE DEVELOPMENT AND GROUND LEASE AGREEMENT
BETWEEN THE CITY AND MB MIXED USE INVESTMENT, LLC, FOR THE
DEVELOPMENT AND OPERATION OF THE CONVENTION CENTER HEADQUARTER
HOTEL FOR THE PURPOSE OF PROMOTING AND SUPPORTING WORKFORCE AND
AFFORDABLE HOUSING DEVELOPMENT. Item not heard.
OB 3. DISCUSS THE POSSIBILITY OF THE CITY ENTERING INTO ONE OR MORE
AGREEMENTS WITH PRIVATE PARKING FACILITY OPERATORS IN NORTH BEACH IN
ORDER TO INCREASE THE NUMBER OF AVAILABLE PARKING SPACES FOR NORTH
BEACH RESIDENTS. This Item was heard and scheduled to return to FERC with an update
by the June 2026 FERC meeting.
OB 4. DISCUSS A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF
MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, ACCEPTING THE RECOMMENDATION OF THE FINANCE
AND ECONOMIC RESILIENCY COMMITTEE, AT ITS APRIL 19, 2024, MEETING, TO
ACCEPT THE CITY ADMINISTRATION’S UPDATE ON THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH
PARKING DEPARTMENT ENFORCEMENT EFFORTS. Commissioner Suarez moved to
have this Item heard at Commission, with a favorable recommendation directing the
Administration to continue the one-year pilot program as presented. This Item is also to
remain at FERC for future updates. Commissioner Dominguez seconded the motion. All in
favor 3-0.
OB 5. DISCUSS POTENTIAL SHORT-TERM IMPROVEMENTS AT MIAMI BEACH
PROMENADE (FORMERLY KNOWN AS MIAMI BEACH DRIVE), SITUATED BETWEEN
24TH STREET AND 29TH STREET, INCLUDING REHABILITATION OF SIDEWALKS,
LANDSCAPES, LIGHTING IMPROVEMENTS, AND OTHER NECESSARY AESTHETICS.
The Item was deferred to the FERC meeting on April 1, 2026.
OB 6. DEVELOP A COMPREHENSIVE PLAN TO INTEGRATE UNDERGROUND CISTERNS
WITHIN THE WEST LOTS. Item not heard and scheduled to be heard at the April 1, 2026,
FERC meeting.
OB 7. DISCUSS THE POSSIBLE ACQUISITION OF CERTAIN OUTLOTS ALONG INDIAN
CREEK DRIVE FOR THE CREATION OF BUS PULLOUT BAY/BUS STOPS TO
AMELIORATE TRAFFIC. The Item was deferred to the FERC meeting on April 1, 2026.
OB 8. DISCUSSION AND TAKING ACTION ON THE FAVORABLE PUBLIC SAFETY
NEIGHBORHOOD QUALITY OF LIFE COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATION TO EXPAND
THE TREE CANOPY IN NORTH BEACH THROUGH A MULTIDISCIPLINARY FIRM FOR
TWO (2) MAIN THOROUGHFARES, SUCH AS ABBOTT AVE OR DICKENS AVE, AND
EXPLORE PARK VIEW ISLAND WITH ASSOCIATED FUNDING. The Item was not heard.
NEW BUSINESS
NB 1. UTILITY COST RELIEF PROGRAM FOR TENANTS AND PROPERTY OWNERS. The Item
was deferred to the FERC meeting on April 1, 2026.
NB 2. DISCUSS POTENTIAL IMPROVEMENTS AND A MAINTENANCE AGREEMENT WITH
MAC MANAGEMENT 2, LLC FOR THE LINCOLN LANE NORTH RIGHT-OF-WAY. The
Item was heard and scheduled to return to FERC with an update on the final terms of an
Improvement, Management, and Maintenance agreement.
NB 3. DISCUSS/TAKE ACTION TO EXPAND ACCESS AND DISCOUNTED RATES FOR
NORTH BAY VILLAGE RESIDENTS AT NORMANDY PARK POOL AND NORTH BEACH
RECREATIONAL PROGRAMMING. Commissioner Suarez motioned to have this Item
heard at Commission to direct the Administration to draft an agreement between the City of
Miami Beach and North Bay Village for access and discounted rates for certain recreational
activities in each respective municipality. Commissioner Magazine seconded the motion. All
in favor 3-0.
NB 4. DISCUSSION REGARDING THE FEASIBILITY OF ESTABLISHING A CONDOMINIUM
SPECIAL ASSESSMENT ASSISTANCE PROGRAM FOR FINANCIALLY VULNERABLE
RESIDENTS. The Item was heard and scheduled to return to FERC with a revised set of
program criteria based on the Committee's discussion.
NB 5. DISCUSS THE INSTALLATION OF A PLUMBED BIRD BATH WATER FEATURE AT
BELLE ISLE PARK. The Item was heard and is to return to FERC after the PSNQLC
Committee’s recommendation, and for staff to proceed with exploring this project.
NB 6. REFERRAL TO THE FINANCE AND ECONOMIC RESILIENCY COMMITTEE TO DIRECT
ADMINISTRATION TO DRAFT AN AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH
AND SUNSET ISLANDS 1 AND 2 HOMEOWNERS ASSOCIATION FOR A SELF-FUNDED
INSTALLATION OF A TURF SPACE AT THE PARK ON SUNSET ISLAND 2.
Commissioner Suarez motioned to have this Item heard at Commission with a favorable
recommendation to direct the Administration to draft an agreement between the City of
Miami Beach and Sunset Island 1 & 2 Homeowners Association for a self-funded installation
of a turf space at the park on Sunset Island 2. Commissioner Magazine seconded the
motion. All in favor 3-0.
NB 7. DISCUSSION REGARDING THE LIVING WAGE RATES BEGINNING APRIL 2026, IN
ACCORDANCE WITH CHAPTER 2, ARTICLE VI, DIVISION 6, SECTION 2 - 408, OF THE
CITY CODE. Commissioner Suarez motioned to have this Item heard at Commission with
a favorable recommendation to continue Fiscal Year 2025 rates. Commissioner Magazine
seconded the motion. All in favor 3-0.
NB 8. DISCUSS A PROPOSED NEW LEASE AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE CITY (LANDLORD)
AND LITTLE HAVANA ACTIVITIES AND NUTRITION CENTERS, INC. (TENANT) FOR
USE OF APPROXIMATELY 3,500 SQUARE FEET OF GROUND FLOOR FACILITY AND
ADJACENT PLAYGROUND AREA HAVING APPROXIMATELY 1,407 SQUARE FEET
LOCATED AT 1245 MICHIGAN AVENUE, FOR AN INITIAL TERM OF FIVE (5) YEARS,
WITH TWO (2) ADDITIONAL RENEWAL TERMS OF TWO (2) YEARS EACH, AT THE

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, ALLOCATING A PORTION OF THE FUNDS RECEIVED FROM THE BARRY S. STERNLICHT FOUNDATION AS MORE SPECIFICALLY SET FORTH IN THIS RESOLUTION TO HELP DEFRAY THE COST OF THE SENIOR BINGO PROGRAMS AT FEDERATION TOWERS, REBECCA TOWERS, COUNCIL NORTH, AND COUNCIL SOUTH; AND DIRECTING THE CITY ADMINISTRATION TO TAKE ALL STEPS NECESSARY TO GIVE EFFECT TO THIS RESOLUTION.
items.action: The Item was opened and continued to the April 22, 2026 Commission Meeting by acclamation. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by Mayor Meiner. Rafael E. Granado and Lilia Cardillo to place on the agenda.
items.voteBasis: No separate vote identified. A vote has not been inferred.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: The Item was opened and continued to the April 22, 2026 Commission Meeting by
acclamation. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by Mayor Meiner. Rafael E.
Granado and Lilia Cardillo to place on the agenda.
Commissioner Dominguez stated that she pulled the Item to propose amendments that the City
Commission might find favorable. The proposed amendment involves $3,000 for Federation, with
$1,500 having come from County Commissioner Vicki Lopez rather than from City funds. The
additional funding has been requested but not obtained. As a result, the proposed $3,000 allocation
would be for Rebecca Towers only, since that building made a specific request. The other buildings
have not made the same specific request, so those have been taken off the table. During the prior
year, Federation Towers and Stella Maris House requested similar assistance, and she had paid it
out of her own ticket budget. The amount currently under discussion is $3,000, though the original
proposal was for $10,000.
Mayor Meiner explained that he separated the Item from the Consent Agenda because of concerns
not with the Item itself, but with the funding source. The funds in question came from the Mayor and
Commissioners' Office budget, and the current $10,000 grant being used already covers several
fitness classes and related programs. There is concern that using those funds for bingo could
potentially reduce access to other services currently provided under the grant. He stated that, for
the benefit of those in the audience, the City is dealing with a specific $10,000 grant, and the use
of those funds is limited by the grant's terms. The grant is effectively capped and fully allocated,
which is why this discussion is necessary. He also noted that even the reduced amount of $3,000
could impact existing programming.
Commissioner Dominguez stated that she checked with several departments, as senior
programming receives support from multiple sources. While there are no dedicated line items for
seniors within the Mayor and Commission budget, staff identified a promotional budget totaling
$22,000. The uncertainty is whether that budget might be an appropriate source, and suggested
leaving the Item on the table temporarily while working with Veronica Coley, Chief of Staff, Office
of the Mayor and Commission, to determine whether the $3,000 could be funded from that source
instead.
Commissioner Fernandez inquired about the Mayor and Commission Office budget, noting that it
covers senior activities and events, and expressed confusion about how those funds are allocated.
He suggested that occasional briefings would be helpful to better understand the programming
offered and how resources are utilized. It is important to stay informed, and he also expressed
appreciation for the staff, describing them as caring individuals dedicated to serving the elderly.
Mayor Meiner stated that there is a list of available programming that can be shared with everyone.
Ms. Coley has the information, and the programs and expenditures have all been detailed.
Commissioner Suarez asked whether the funds originate from the Sternlicht Foundation or from the
Office of the Mayor and Commission.
Commissioner Dominguez stated that Barry Sternlicht donated $10,000. Since Rebecca Towers
had previously requested $3,000 for bingo during the last visit, a request was made for that amount
to be deducted from the Barry Sternlicht donation. Gloria Campos had told Commissioner
Dominguez that the donation is already being used to support yoga and other classes in those
buildings, in addition to the senior yoga, tai chi, and art classes already provided through the Parks
and Recreation Department. Ms. Campos had explained to her that the grant funds cannot be used
for the bingo program, and concerns have since arisen among the seniors who were contacted,
who worry that some of their existing programs might be cut.
Mayor Meiner stated that Veronica Coley has compiled a list of the programming supported by the
donation, and that list will be shared with everyone. The programming includes Zumba, yoga, and
dance classes at a rate of $50 per class paid to instructors. It also includes programming at Freedom
Towers and other sites. He reiterated that the Barry Sternlicht $10,000 donation is specifically
earmarked for seniors, and therefore, the request was originally made to use a portion of that
funding for the bingo program.
City Clerk Granado asked whether the Item is being deferred or approved as amended.
Commissioner Dominguez stated that she would like to open and continue the Item to the April 22,
2026, meeting.
The Item was deferred to the April 22, 2026, Commission Meeting by acclamation.
Mayor Meiner thanked everyone for a very productive meeting.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, REQUESTING THAT THE OFFICE OF THE CONDOMINIUM OMBUDSMAN OF THE FLORIDA DEPARTMENT OF BUSINESS & PROFESSIONAL REGULATION (DBPR) SCHEDULE ADDITIONAL OFFICE HOURS AT MIAMI BEACH CITY HALL, TO PROVIDE RESIDENTS WITH ADDITIONAL OPPORTUNITIES TO MEET WITH THE OMBUDSMAN REGARDING CONDO- RELATED CONCERNS.
items.action: The Sponsor withdrew the Item. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by
items.voteBasis: No separate vote identified. A vote has not been inferred.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: The Sponsor withdrew the Item. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by
Commissioner Suarez.
Clerk Granado noted for the record that Commissioner David Suarez had separated the Item from
the Consent Agenda.
Commissioner Suarez explained that he recently held a large Condominium Town Hall meeting at
which the Condominium Ombudsman participated. Commissioner Suarez stated that he had
negotiated with the Ombudsman for expanded availability, with the Ombudsman agreeing to provide
office hours in Miami Beach either virtually or in person at least once per week. Commissioner
Suarez explained that the negotiation required considerable time and effort, and he wished to avoid
sending mixed messages to the Ombudsman regarding the Commission’s position. Commissioner
Suarez stated that this was the reason he requested discussion of the Item.
Commissioner Dominguez responded that she had been unaware of the expanded availability and
stated that, in light of that development, the Resolution appeared unnecessary. Commissioner
Dominguez stated that she had previously contacted the Ombudsman and secured an appointment,
though only after significant difficulty. Commissioner Dominguez stated that Commissioners
regularly received email and telephone inquiries from residents concerned about condominium
buyouts and assessments, and often felt unable to provide direct assistance, and that one of the
suggestions from the City’s legal team had been to request expanded Ombudsman office hours.
Commissioner Dominguez requested that the newly negotiated schedule be made publicly available
as soon as possible so residents could begin planning and Commissioners could refer people to the
correct dates. Commissioner Dominguez noted that at present, the Ombudsman holds only three
office‑hour sessions per month.
Commissioner Suarez stated that the newly negotiated schedule would include the first Thursday of
each month for in‑person appointments and virtual availability during the second and fourth weeks
of each month. Commissioner Suarez stated that these expanded hours provided a strong starting
point and that adjustments could be made later if needed after determining the Ombudsman’s
workload. Commissioner Suarez invited Commissioner Dominguez to collaborate after several
months to evaluate the need for further expansion.
Commissioner Dominguez stated that she supported revisiting the matter in six months to determine
whether residents required additional access or resources. Commissioner Dominguez referenced
concerns from condominium residents, including elderly individuals managing significant
assessments, and stated that expanded access to the Ombudsman could provide clearer guidance
than the Commission itself could in many cases. Commissioner Dominguez agreed to collaborate
with Commissioner Suarez.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, asked whether Commissioner Dominguez wished to withdraw the
Item or defer it for six months.
Commissioner Dominguez requested that the Item be withdrawn.
City Clerk Granado announced that Item C7 AF was withdrawn.

items.action: Ordinance 2026-4808 was adopted. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Ordinance 2026-4808 was adopted. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record.
The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on
Second Reading; seconded by Commissioner Dominguez. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Marla Alpizar to handle.
Mayor Meiner mentioned there are seven sponsors and congratulated Chief Jones.
Commissioner Fernandez thanked the entire Commission for joining him in sponsoring this
Ordinance and for recognizing the very important role of continuity and leadership within the Police
Department. This legislation is a policy decision amending the pension plan to allow the Police Chief
to extend his participation in the DROP program from eight years to a maximum of ten years. He
also wants to highlight that the City’s actuary has reviewed the Ordinance and confirmed that it
does not increase costs to the City. In other words, this Ordinance allows them to maintain stability
in leadership without placing any additional burden on taxpayers. Ultimately, and more importantly,
this is about the men and women of the Miami Beach Police Department, the Officers who show up
every day, answer the call of service, and put on their uniforms daily without knowing if they will
return home. They put themselves in harm’s way so residents and visitors can feel safe. A
Department like their incredible Miami Beach Police Department is only as strong as the people
who wear that uniform and serve every day with bravery. Those Officers deserve leadership that
supports, prepares, and equips them with the tools they need for success each day. The results of
this Department under Chief of Police Wayne Jones’ leadership reflect the support he provides his
Officers every day. A Major Crime Statistics chart was displayed. Click here to view. Today, we see
a Department operating with a high level of discipline, purpose, and strong morale; that is why crime
is decreasing, and morale among Police Officers is high. These results begin with the Police
Department's leadership. Chief Jones has fostered an environment where Officers feel supported
by their Chief of Police, well-trained, and equipped to perform at the highest levels expected of
them. This leadership is evident in the Department’s activity and presence throughout the
community. In 2025 alone, the Department responded to more than 81,000 calls for service, 58%
of which were initiated by the Officers themselves. Officers do that only if they feel supported and
have strong morale. This proactive policing results from a workforce engaged and actively working
to prevent crime rather than simply reacting to it. Officers, under the Chief’s leadership, conducted
nearly 5,000 parking and walk patrols, increasing engagement with neighborhoods and visibility.
One of the exciting new developments in the Department is its use of technology to keep the
community safe. Recent drone footage was shown. Click here to view. The video demonstrates
Chief Jones's leadership, but technology alone does not create these results; it is the people and
the leadership guiding them. This leadership is evident during one of the most demanding times of
the year for the City and, importantly, for Police Officers. A news clip on Spring Break, showing
where they were and where they are now, was shown. Click here to see the video. Such a
turnaround does not happen by accident; it occurs when there is strong leadership, clear
expectations from the top, and Officers who know their City stands behind them. Extending the
DROP for Chief Jones is not just about his tenure or keeping him for another two years. More
importantly, it is about maintaining stability, continuing the progress they have seen, and supporting
the Officers of the Miami Beach Police Department who rely on Chief Jones’ leadership every day.
When Officers see that their leadership has the full confidence and backing of the Miami Beach City
Commission, it strengthens the entire Department. With that, he thanked his colleagues for
sponsoring this legislation and expressed pride in supporting their incredible Chief and all the men
and women in blue.
Mayor Meiner stated that it was a good presentation and he enjoyed it. It highlights and resonates
with their residents. He is a strong believer that data and numbers are significant because they tell
a good story. In this case, it does just that. He also believes that is how residents and tourists feel
when they walk down the streets. The good news is that he hears from residents and visitors that
the City has changed significantly, and they feel comfortable walking down the streets with their
families and children, especially on Ocean Drive and other areas. Overall, there is a great story,
especially as it relates to breaking the Spring Break cycle. The major crimes he mentioned, as well
as the homeless numbers, which are the lowest they have ever been in the City, down 60% from
three years ago, show progress. Full staffing indicates a well-motivated Police force, and he notes
many people trying to join, but they are already fully staffed. It was not too long ago that they had
40 open positions in the Department. He commends the entire City Commission, as he also hears
from Chief Jones and other Officers on the street who thank them because not every city has an
elected body that supports the Police the way theirs does. The support is clear: they publicly back
the Police, provide the best available technology, and prioritize safety and crime prevention. Chief
Jones, it is great working with you. You both started around the same time and have worked closely
together. His motivation to continue supporting these efforts is driven by the positive changes he
has seen and by the knowledge that there is more to accomplish. The Police visibility has greatly
improved, and there is still more they can do. They never rest on their laurels, and he believes
Officers appreciate being equipped with the right tools, following training, and performing their
duties with confidence. He thanked everyone, reaffirmed his full support, and looks forward to
working with them over the next few years.
Commissioner Dominguez is very supportive and seconded the Item. Under Chief Jones’s
leadership, they have seen a reduction in crime. He and his team have worked very hard to address
the escalating drug problem that developed during COVID-19 and in the Entertainment District. He
filled all the vacancies, which was an incredible feat. The Chief is very responsive and has built a
strong Command Staff of highly experienced men and women from diverse backgrounds. They
have an excellent team under the Chief, and she looks forward to working with him in the coming
years.
Commissioner Bhatt is very supportive of this as well, and one of the things she has discussed with
Chief Jones is the opportunity to continue and build on the successes he achieved with his
Command Staff. She supports initiatives like 30x30 and making this Department safe and inclusive
for people who are not traditionally seen as Police Officers, because she believes it is crucial for
the community to be policed by individuals who look like them. She will expect to see significant
progress in this area over the next two years, and she will ensure that, regardless of who steps into
his shoes after he leaves, this remains a core priority and a fundamental pillar of the Department
for the future. She knows he can do it, is confident in his vision, and fully supports it. She also trusts
his Command Staff to continue this work after he departs, and they are eager to see what can be
accomplished together in the coming years.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas thanked Chief Jones for all he has done and expressed full support for
this extension. She is very impressed by his work, the team he has built, and the staff he oversees.
Every time she speaks with an Officer, no matter their rank, they all genuinely love their jobs. She
believes this is because they appreciate the positive environment he has fostered within the force
and the team; it is immediately noticeable. She attended Roll Call on Sunday and went on a ride-
along with a Sergeant, and could tell he truly loved his job. He was very detailed in his explanations,
which she found fascinating. She is grateful for that experience, as it showed her how impressive
his team truly is; each Officer takes pride in their work. Residents can see and feel this pride; they
love the Department, love the team, and respect every Officer who protects and helps them. It is
truly impressive. She expressed her gratitude again, saying she could not thank the Chief enough.
When she approached him to work on human trafficking this year, he agreed immediately and
mentioned that he had created the Department’s first human trafficking team several years ago. So,
behind the scenes, he accomplishes a great deal, even beyond what is visible. She truly cannot
thank him enough and supports him wholeheartedly.
Commissioner Magazine loves the Chief and adores what he does. He loves the Chief’s family, and
many people in the City do as well. He is a great ambassador, a great Police Officer, and a great
Chief, and he is proud to work with him moving forward.
Mayor Meiner added that there is so much involved in his responsibilities in a Department like this,
and everything they do is high profile, which increases the pressure. He is very proud of the entire
City because they have received unwavering support from the City Commission, residents, and the
business community, and it takes that kind of backing to build. He also mentions that when this
process was starting, there was talk about potential successors; the Chief has built a deep bench,
which will also be part of his legacy. This is a compliment to the Chief and the entire Department,
which has many good people in senior command and management. At the same time, he likes to
tell residents and others that they are grateful to live in South Florida, feeling it is a safe haven.
Recently, some people from outside the country told him they were considering moving their
businesses here and asked whether the situation would remain the same. He explained that there
are no guarantees in life; things can change quickly, such as leadership changes. We have seen
this happen in other cities, countries, and parts of the world. He also appreciates working with many
good colleagues, including the City Manager, Chief Jones, and other departments. Although
residents might not always see this, he emphasizes that the successes they are experiencing do
not happen by chance or in a vacuum. It takes significant effort and tough decisions, often met with
negative pushback, but they do it because it is the right thing. Today’s success reminds us why
they do it, with Chief Jones playing a significant role.
Commissioner Fernandez added that they all hold very stressful, very challenging high-profile
positions that can sometimes be disheartening, as rewarding and demoralizing as they are uplifting.
At the end of the day, they go home to their families, who are the ones that keep them going. He
recognized Mariana Jones in the audience, Chief Jones’ wife, and expressed that this community
owes her so much gratitude. He knows she is the rock of the family, and that the Chief feels so
supported in doing his job every single day because she is there supporting him and their beautiful
children. The fact that she is here for this milestone moment is truly wonderful. In his office,
Commissioner Fernandez has his two aides who assist him in everything he does, and he would
be remiss not to highlight the incredible team around the Chief. Whether it be Assistant Chief Samir
Guerrero, Assistant Chief Daniel Morgalo, Commander Shantell Mitchell, Celia Maria Ruiz-Paz, or
Ernesto Rodriguez, they can all be reached at any time, day or night, on holidays and weekends,
even Sunday mornings, and they always respond, interrupting their own activities and family
celebrations to address the needs and ensure public safety for the City. Their residents can truly
feel the difference with his leadership, and their Officers are making a meaningful impact in the City.
They support the Chief, and today they stand with him.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, informed that he previously discussed with the sponsor of the Item
and the City Manager that because the Ordinance could entail Administration by the Police
Department that it needed to be referred to Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life
Committee pursuant to Resolution 2025-33496; however, as currently drafted it would be
administered purely by Human Resources so he clarified that there is no need for that referral.
The public hearing was held, and since there were no participants in the audience or via Zoom, the
public hearing was concluded.
Bobby Hernandez, FOP President, stated that although the process was initially contentious, a
meeting with City Manager Carpenter and Assistant City Manager Taxis resulted in a Resolution
ensuring that union members would not be affected, which had been their primary concern. He
noted that three years ago, the Officers were trained in what he described as a vocational school
they called the Police Academy, but they are now in a serious Police Academy, a change he
credited to Chief Jones. He added that the Department no longer operates under a “just‑in‑case”
staffing plan where everyone works every day simply because something might happen. Referring
to his Publix analogy shared with City Manager Carpenter, he explained that one would not walk
into Publix at 7:00 a.m. and see every cash register open just in case a complaint is received, and
the Department is no longer in that position. FOP President Hernandez stated that the current
staffing level of 437 Officers is not a coincidence but the result of strong leadership. He concluded
by expressing that they are very happy for Chief Jones and offered congratulations.
A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading,
seconded by Commissioner Dominguez. Roll Call taken: 7-0.
Chief of Police Wayne Jones is unsure what to say. This past weekend marked 30 years for him in
this great City, which he often refers to as the Capital of the World. He loves it, just like all the men
and women from the Miami Beach Police Department love it, and they do what they do because it
is a great City and they want to make it even better. He is thankful to each elected official for their
confidence in him and the organization, as shown collectively today. He is grateful to his boss for
giving him the space and latitude to serve as Police Chief; they speak on the telephone multiple
times a day and meet several times a week. But it is not for that. They are doing great things, not
because he is brilliant or the best Chief in the country, but because of the people behind him and
standing against the wall in the Chamber. He truly believes he has a Command Staff made of
exceptional Police talent, a team of Officers doing heavy lifting every day who believe in this City,
believe in protecting its residents and visitors, and believe they can make this, as the Mayor says,
the safest city in America. It is that belief that has brought them success. He is honored and grateful,
and today he simply wants to thank each of them for their support. He also thanked his wife, who
showed up unexpectedly and has been there all the time, late at night or early Sunday mornings,
taking on much of the responsibility for raising their twins. It has been a collective team effort, and
he is grateful for that.

items.title: AN ORDINANCE OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, AMENDING CHAPTER 46 OF THE CITY CODE, ENTITLED “ENVIRONMENT,” BY AMENDING ARTICLE IV, ENTITLED “NOISE,” BY AMENDING SECTION 46-152, ENTITLED “NOISES; UNNECESSARY AND EXCESSIVE PROHIBITED,” BY AMENDING SUBSECTION (B) TO REDUCE THE DISTANCE TO ESTABLISH PRIMA FACIE EVIDENCE OF THE SPECIFIED NOISE VIOLATION DURING SPECIFIED HOURS; PROVIDING FOR REPEALER, SEVERABILITY, CODIFICATION, AND AN EFFECTIVE DATE.
items.action: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record. The Public Hearing was held. A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading, seconded by Mayor Meiner. Roll Call taken: 7-0.
