items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into
the record. The Public Hearing was held. A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez to adopt
the Ordinance on First Reading, seconded by Mayor Meiner. Roll Call taken: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for April 22, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Chief Wayne Jones to handle.
TO DO:
• Chief Jones to generate a report identifying how many individuals have received more than one
citation for the same noise violation.
Mayor Meiner introduced the Item and recognized Chief of Police Wayne Jones to explain the details
of the proposed legislation.
Chief of Police Wayne Jones expressed his excitement about providing the Department with another
tool to address some of the concerns the Commission has been raising, which seem to have
intensified over the past few months with numerous residents’ complaints, creating, in his opinion, a
quality-of-life issue. They even received a late-night complaint from the Mayor about noise pollution
and speeding along the Collins Avenue corridor. Operation Quiet Streets was recently implemented
solely to tackle these issues. Current enforcement relies on the 100-foot rule, but reducing it to 25
feet would make a significant difference in enforcement for vehicles and boats in the waterways.
They are proud to note that in 2021, enforcement efforts related to vehicle noise resulted in 76
citations; in 2024, that number rose to 430, and last year, 675. This year, thanks to Operation Quiet
Streets, they have already issued 513 citations and expect to surpass 1,500 at this rate. The Miami
Beach Police Department is dedicated to the community and understands how much this impacts
daily and nightly lives. They are committed to addressing the problem. This issue is not unique to
the City; many other cities and counties face similar challenges. He referenced a recent news article
highlighting what the City of Miami is doing for the same reason. He mentioned that Assistant Chief
Danny Morgado, described as the brainchild behind Operation Safe Streets, is here to answer
questions.
Mayor Meiner stated that during his tenure on the Commission, he has observed a shift in focus
toward improving quality of life, and they are reaching a good place because Spring Break was a
major problem. They have tackled many crimes and misdemeanors that were afflicting the City, and
they started prosecuting those cases. While they still need to continue improving, they have made
significant, exponential progress; the homeless population is down 60% over the last three years,
its lowest count ever. This does not mean there is no more work to do, but complaints about
homeless individuals are now rare. It is something they still need to address. This progress shows
they have improved many aspects of public safety, and one of the main complaints he frequently
receives is about vehicle noise. Since they have made significant improvements in other areas, he
is confident they can address this as well.
Commissioner Bhatt added that numerous enforcement and educational programs have been
implemented, including micromobility regulations on the Beachwalk going forward. One of the
successes they have noted is the absence of repeat offenders. She mentioned that there are always
people who need to be educated, such as first-time visitors, and asked whether they are
experiencing the same pattern with this type of violation or if there are repeat offenders.
Chief of Police Wayne Jones explained that they combine enforcement with an educational
campaign, mostly through social media. He noted that approximately 1.17 thousand people have
viewed the social media content, demonstrating that the community is aware of their efforts and
takes them seriously.
Assistant Chief of Police Daniel Morgalo recalls when he started with the Department as a young
Police Officer, they were issuing citations for loud noise. This issue has come back to the forefront
again after 26 years. As the Chief alluded to, this is not solely a Miami Beach problem; they are
seeing similar complaints from Brickell, in Miami, and other neighborhoods in the tri-County area.
This led to partnering with FHP and collaborating with the City of Miami and other departments to
raise awareness about the issue. Reinforcing what the Mayor said, this is a great opportunity for
the Police Department to focus on community issues like this, as it shows that Officers are doing a
good job keeping the community safe. They are not only chasing robbers and shooters but are also
able to concentrate on quality-of-life issues that matter to residents. Based on the numbers and the
Officers' efforts, their focus on this problem has significantly increased. In 2.5 months, they issued
over 513 citations specifically for loud vehicle noise. Last year, they issued 675, so they are on track
to triple that number this year. If the goal is zero violations, they will try very hard, but he is not sure
if they will ever fully achieve it.
In reply to Commissioner Bhatt, Chief of Police Wayne Jones explained that this was considered a
non-moving violation, so there are no points on the license, but there is a fine associated with it. If
they do not pay the fine, the license is suspended after 30 days. A discussion was held on fines.
In response to Commissioner Bhatt, Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, clarified that this Ordinance
builds on current legislation, stating that noise from a vehicle or vessel via radio or other device is
prima facie evidence of a violation if it can be heard from 25 feet (not 100 feet), so this is unrelated
to other concerns. There is an Item to make a legislative priority, asking the State to allow the use
of cameras to enforce noise citywide. He continued to answer questions from Commissioner Bhatt
and explained that, for repeat offenders, the State would need to enact legislation to increase fees
Statewide. The City does not have the authority to add anything separately.
Commissioner Bhatt added that if it is not too burdensome, she suggested running a report to see
how many people are receiving more than one ticket for the same violation. If it involves new people,
it is a new situation, but if the same 30 people are getting tickets every weekend, that is a different
matter. Chief Wayne Jones to handle.
Mayor Meiner noted that the Chief of Miami recently issued a public plea because one individual
posts loud-noise stunts on Instagram for entertainment. He explained that the problem is the limited
enforcement tools available under State law. Mayor Meiner added that he had previously brought
an Item to implement noise-detecting cameras capable of capturing photos and video, but under
current Florida law, the City cannot use that evidence to issue citations. He contrasted this with
New York, which has an effective program that issues tickets when cameras detect violations and
requires vehicle owners to fix noise issues, with fines exceeding $800 for noncompliance. Because
Miami Beach’s fines are much lower and there is no inspection requirement, offenders have little
incentive to correct the problem.
Chief of Police Wayne Jones suggested that the best approach is to continue the night program
when people are most affected, then celebrate it publicly through social media or other means, and
get the message out to visitors to the City not to rattle engines or play loud music.
Mayor Meiner asked for consensus on R5 M, and a motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez,
seconded by Mayor Meiner.
The Public Hearing was opened.
Mitch Novick, via Zoom, enjoys the conversation but believes the 25-foot threshold should include
businesses, especially along Ocean Drive. Some businesses on the 1000 block play loud music,
and screams can be heard all the way to the shoreline. He pointed out a hotspot at Sixth and
Jefferson Avenue, where golf carts have recently been coming down Sixth Street from Publix and
blasting music, which greatly impacts that section of the beach.
The Public Hearing concluded.
Commissioner Bhatt added that Mitch Novick makes a good point because she sees golf carts in
the Entertainment District with loud music. Who do they belong to, and how are they allowed to
operate like that? She has no problem with music, but it should not be blasting.
Assistant Chief of Police Daniel Morgalo stated that enforcement actions have been taken in the
Entertainment District targeting certain operators, and numerous citations have been issued and
handled. Mr. Novick mentioning that it has moved to Sixth Street demonstrates that their
enforcement efforts in the Entertainment District are effective, but they need to expand them. In
response to Commissioner Bhatt, if they are required to have a BTR and are operating a business,
they collaborate with Code.
Hernan Cardeno, Code Compliance Director, explained that during joint operations with the Police
Department, Code issues violations to operators who do not have a required Business Tax Receipt
(BTR). Police typically arrest the operator and impound the golf cart. He noted that it is a Code
violation because these operators are conducting business on a public roadway and soliciting these
rides without authorization.
Commissioner Magazine reported that Mitch Novick shared a concern he had observed in his
neighborhood this weekend. While he does not want to be the “word police” or too heavy-handed
in government, he believes that what people do inside their own businesses and behind closed
doors is none of his business. However, he mentioned one establishment that had blasting music.
They could debate whether it should be considered outdoor live entertainment, but the music
coming out was so egregious that it would offend anyone. Are there restrictions, even for places
grandfathered in with outdoor live entertainment licenses, that set some decency standards for what
can emanate from their establishments? They must have some regulations.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, stated that the City has the Noise Ordinance. If the sound is
unreasonably loud, it could trigger a Code violation. Some businesses have been grandfathered in,
and there is a threshold based on decibel levels that would require measurement with a decibel
meter. He is referring to Code Enforcement. He believes there may be First Amendment issues
when regulating content. The discussion continued. the Office of the City Attorney will research this
further, but his general understanding is that people can shout profanity in public. A business has
First Amendment rights similar to individuals. There are certain things considered pornographic that
cannot be displayed in public.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that many businesses engage in activities for which the City grants
certain rights or permissions, such as live entertainment, even though they are not inherently
entitled to those rights. Because these permissions increase the value of the business and its
property, he believes the City should at least be able to ask whether the business is willing to
voluntarily agree not to engage in profanity, antisemitic entertainment like what occurred at the
nightclub, or homophobic content. He emphasized that, at a minimum, when the City grants
additional privileges, it should be allowed to request a voluntary proffer from the business affirming
that they will not engage in antisemitic, racist, or homophobic activities.
Deputy Chief City Attorney Rob Rosenwald explained that the question of whether the City can
request a voluntary proffer of something it could not otherwise require is still open. The Commission
has asked the Office of the City Attorney to review this matter, and the Office is actively researching
the issue. He noted that the general rule is that the City cannot impose an unconstitutional condition
on a permit or license. He added that they are considering whether such a voluntary proffer is legally
permissible and how it might be properly formulated. Deputy Chief City Attorney Rosenwald stated
that he would prefer not to discuss the matter in detail on the dais at this time but confirmed that
the Office of the City Attorney is looking into it.
Commissioner Fernandez added that, at the right time, if they have the option, they could perhaps
collaborate with Commissioner Magazine on this, since it directly addresses the issue he is raising.
He thanked the Office of the City Attorney for their research, noting they have invested considerable
time and effort to ensure they establish the right controls and safeguards, doing it correctly so they
do not infringe on anyone’s rights while also protecting and maintaining the community’s values of
being inclusive, protective, and safe. It is an important process when granting rights related to
entertainment, music, and noise, rights they currently lack, to ensure proper safeguards are in
place.
Commissioner Magazine added that the situation was so egregious that he and his daughter could
easily hear the music from across the street. He explained that the lyrics contained profanity and
highly inappropriate language, including multiple offensive slurs, which he said were not suitable
for a family-friendly environment or even basic standards of decency.
Deputy Chief City Attorney Rosenwald added that if the noise violation exceeds the limits set by
CUP or the Noise Ordinance, they can charge accordingly. If an organization is allowed to play
music outdoors, the City generally cannot, in almost all cases, including those being discussed,
control the content of what they do. In response to Commissioner Suarez, he clarified that they
have constitutionally protected rights to music.
Commissioner Bhatt asked why there is a different standard for visually offensive things compared
to verbally offensive things protected under the First Amendment.
Deputy Chief City Attorney Rosenwald explained that the things they can prohibit or restrict under
the First Amendment fall into specific categories like fighting words or true threats, or statements
that incite immediate violence against someone. Words tend to be more associated with such
dangers than a picture on a frame, so in that way, spoken words can be more restrictive because
they have more power and are written.
Commissioner Bhatt clarified that, in this case, it is the opposite: if the phrases from the song were
taken from a cartoon caricature and displayed on a wall, they would be visually repellent and likely
not allowed. However, because they are spoken or sung phrases, they are protected.
Deputy Chief City Attorney Rosenwald clarified that, in this context, whether written or spoken, they
would have the same protection.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, believes Commissioner Bhatt is trying to distinguish between
words and pornography, asserting there is protection. Pornography is not protected under the First
Amendment.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that the words 'explicit' and 'offensive' are judged by whether they are
offensive to the general public. If something cannot be visually represented with a photo or picture
on a public right-of-way because it is offensive to community standards, then why is it acceptable
for the same level of offensiveness to be expressed with words instead of images on a public right-
of-way, if it is also offensive to community standards?
Deputy Chief City Attorney Rosenwald added that, in that context, they would be considered the
same. There is a different legal analysis for obscenity and pornography in situations involving
nudity, which has a different nuance and standard. However, regarding words and whether they
say the “b” word or write it on a sign, they have the same constitutional protection.
Commissioner Suarez noted that Hip Hop, as a genre, frequently includes profanity and phrases
that demean women. He questioned how the City could realistically prevent businesses from
playing Hip Hop music and stated that, although he is not a fan of that content, attempting to
regulate it would be a slippery slope. He pointed out that on one extreme, there are clubs playing
highly offensive content, and on the other, businesses simply playing the Top 10 Hip Hop hits. He
expressed uncertainty about whether the City should begin regulating what music businesses are
allowed to play.
Commissioner Magazine noted that there are usually clean versions of most songs, so businesses
can play whatever they choose. However, if people are walking down the street at 1:00 p.m. and
hear profane language, it becomes a concern. He asked where the line falls and whether such
content is simply allowed, and whether there is anything the City can do about it.
Deputy Chief City Attorney Rob Rosenwald explained that these issues are typically considered at
the outset of legislation or when discussing whether to allow outdoor music. When advising the
Commission, the Office of the City Attorney asks the Commission to consider what people will hear
outside. He noted that the City can regulate noise in a content-neutral way, such as by limiting noise
levels or deciding not to allow outdoor music at all, but once outdoor music is permitted, it cannot
be regulated on the basis of content. Addressing Commissioner Fernandez’s question, he clarified
that speech is not protected by the First Amendment only if it incites imminent violence, meaning a
direct call for immediate violent action.
Commissioner Fernandez suggested that displaying or playing racist or inflammatory language
could emotionally offend or provoke people, using the example of playing music praising the

items.motion: A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading, seconded by Mayor Meiner.

items.title: AN ORDINANCE OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, AMENDING THE CODE OF ORDINANCES OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, BY AMENDING CHAPTER 90, ENTITLED “SOLID WASTE,” DIVISION 3, “RATES, CHARGES, BILLING PROCEDURES,” SECTION 90-133 THEREOF, ENTITLED “SINGLE UTILITY BILLING,” TO RELOCATE THE TABLE OF SANITATION COMMERCIAL IMPACT FEES TO APPENDIX A; BY AMENDING APPENDIX A TO THE CITY CODE, ENTITLED “FEE SCHEDULE,” TO ADD SANITATION COMMERCIAL IMPACT FEES IMPOSED PURSUANT TO SECTION 90-133, AND TO INCLUDE AN AUTOMATIC ANNUAL CONSUMER PRICE INDEX (CPI) ADJUSTMENT FOR SANITATION COMMERCIAL IMPACT FEES, WATER IMPACT FEES, AND SEWER IMPACT FEES IMPOSED BY THE CITY PURSUANT TO SECTIONS 90-133, 110-167, AND 110-169; AND PROVIDING FOR CODIFICATION, REPEALER, SEVERABILITY, AND AN EFFECTIVE DATE.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading as amended. The title of the Ordinance
was read into the record. The Public Hearing was held. A motion was made by Commissioner
Magazine to apply an annual CPI adjustment to the water and sewer connection impact fees,
applicable only to new development or changes in existing water service, seconded by
Commissioner Fernandez. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for April 22, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. John Norris to handle.
AMENDMENT:
• Added an annual Consumer Price Index (CPI) adjustment to water and sewer connection impact
fees, applicable only to new development or upgrades to an existing water service.
• The Commission amended the process by bifurcating the Ordinance, removing the sanitation
component from the motion so it can return on April 22, 2026 for a new First Reading at which
time the Commission will consider whether to implement a retroactive catch‑up, whether to
phase it in, how to protect smaller and older buildings, how to apply CPI going forward, or
possibly take no action.
TO DO:
• Assign Time Certain to Sanitation Item returning in the April 22, 2026, Commission Meeting.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that, before anyone panics, this Item is a correction; it is not new water
fees or anything similar. She explained that these fees have not been updated in close to 30 years,
and it is appropriate to do so now. She then turned the Item over to John Norris for further details.
John Norris, Public Works Director, indicated that, as Commissioner Bhatt mentioned, this
Ordinance updates the commercial sanitation impact fees, which have not been changed since
1998, by applying the Consumer Price Index (CPI) to bring them to current-day value. He added
that the Ordinance also applies annual CPI increases to water, sewer, and sanitation impact fees,
so the City does not find itself in the same situation 30 years from now. In reply to Commissioner
Suarez, he noted that, according to the chart provided, a commercial building with 0–25 units would
see its monthly fee increase from $16 to $34.93, and a commercial building with 101 or more units
would see its monthly fee increase from $50 to $109.16. He clarified that this is an impact fee added
to the solid waste collection bill for that building, and it is revenue that comes to the City to
compensate for the impact of adding that structure.
In response to Commissioner Fernandez, Public Works Director Norris explained that the fee
applies to all commercial developments that impact the sanitation system, not only new
construction. In further response to Commissioner Suarez, he stated that the fee structure applies
to all existing commercial properties and is added to every commercial solid waste bill issued by
Waste Connections or Waste Management. At Commissioner Suarez’s request, he reviewed the
thresholds and rates (as shown in the diagram provided).
Commissioner Fernandez stated his concern about passing additional utility costs on to residents.
He noted that the Commission is working on a measure to reduce the cost of waste collection for
residents, and he does not feel comfortable supporting an increase that would affect existing
buildings, particularly fourplexes and other smaller buildings where naturally occurring affordable
housing is most common. He stated that he could support the fee if it were limited to new
construction, and suggested that the sponsor consider such a friendly amendment. However, he
could not support applying the increase to existing buildings because the increased cost would be
passed on to tenants.
Public Works Director Norris explained to Commissioner Magazine that these fees support the
operations of the Sanitation Division, noting that while solid waste collection is performed by
contracted haulers, the City administers the contracts and requires staff for that purpose. The
proposed sanitation impact fee helps fund those administrative costs. He further clarified that the
water and sewer impact fees function differently, as they apply only when a meter is upgraded or
installed for new development. Sanitation fees, by contrast, appear on the monthly bill.
Commissioner Bhatt addressed City Manager Eric Carpenter and explained that last year, the City
discovered that several fees had not been updated in more than three decades. As a result of that
discussion, held roughly two years ago, the City Commission directed the Administration to review
every fee to ensure CPI adjustments were applied and that fees reflected current cost-assignment
standards. She stated she could not think of any service the City provides today, especially one
requiring updated and extensive operations, that is still being charged at a rate set 30 years ago.
She emphasized that she is not a fan of adding costs to residents and understands the financial
challenges they face; however, residents must also pay a reasonable amount for essential City
services, including trash collection. She noted that the City should not have been placed in this
position, and she found it difficult to believe that no one had identified the issue over three decades.
Nonetheless, she stated that the Commission must “be the grown-ups in the room” and make the
responsible decision to ensure the City does not experience waste-management problems in the
future. She added that the proposed adjustment represents a relatively small amount of money,
and she was not being cavalier in saying so. The City routinely receives calls from residents
reporting trash not being picked up or other sanitation issues. If the City does not update its fees to
align with actual costs, she explained, “something is going to have to give.” She then asked City
Manager Carpenter to walk the Commission through the process used to determine the proposed
amounts, noting that if CPI had been applied each year correctly, the cost would have increased by
only pennies annually and would likely have gone unnoticed, just as it will going forward once annual
CPI adjustments are applied.
City Manager Eric Carpenter stated that the Item reflects what would have occurred if CPI had been
applied annually since the last rate increases were implemented. Over a 30-year period, many of
the fees would have slightly more than doubled. He explained that, even so, the resulting rates
remain relatively small when divided by the number of units in each building, leading to a minor per-
unit increase.
Commissioner Suarez suggested phasing in the increases over several years rather than
implementing the full adjustment at once. He stated that it would be unfair to place the entire burden
on current residents as a result of past financial inaction, and proposed a possible phase-in over
three or four years.
Jason Greene, Chief Financial Officer, stated that Commissioner Suarez’s comments reflected the
fact that the City had not implemented incremental CPI adjustments over the past 20 or 30 years.
If it is the will of the City Commission to phase in the increases, staff can return with that approach.
He then clarified several questions about the Sanitation Fund, noting that concerns were first raised
during a Budget Retreat when the Office of Management and Budget flagged structural deficiencies
in the fund. He outlined the many sanitation-related services that have expanded in recent years,
including litter pickup and the residential sidewalk pressure-washing program, all of which are
supported by the Sanitation Fund. He explained that the fund faced a major structural deficit that
would require either significant rate increases or reductions in service levels. He also noted that
Commissioner Bhatt previously sponsored efforts to examine all impact and connection fees
Citywide that had not been updated in decades. Last year, the first part of the Ordinance addressed
water and sewer connection fees, which had not been updated in 20-30 years; those one-time fees
for new development were corrected by the City Commission. While reviewing them, however, staff
discovered that a CPI escalator had not been added, and that omission is corrected in this
Ordinance. Regarding sanitation impact fees, CFO Greene stated that those fees had not been
updated since 1998. He explained that even though the proposed adjustments appear to double
certain rates, when spread over a 50-unit building, the increase equates to only pennies per month.
He emphasized that the fees support core services that ensure a clean City, clean parks, clean
rights-of-way, and clean sidewalks.
Commissioner Suarez added that condominium owners in Miami Beach are experiencing “a death
by a thousand cuts,” noting recent increases such as FPL rate hikes and condominium special
assessments, and stating that this proposal represents yet another cost. He explained that while
he wants to be financially responsible, implementing the full increase at once is too much. He noted
that Commissioner Fernandez would oppose the idea and stated he might be amenable to a 25%
step increase each year over four years to gradually reach the intended level. He also noted that
the Commission would soon consider the remainder of the water impact fees.
Commissioner Magazine suggested that, at a minimum, the City should begin implementing an
annual CPI adjustment. He emphasized that there has not been a CPI adjustment in 30 years and
that applying CPI annually is necessary to avoid falling further behind. He stated that this should be
the baseline component of the discussion. If the Commission wished to phase in increases or
combine CPI with an additional 1% each year for five years, those options could be explored
between First and Second Reading. However, he requested that, at a minimum, CPI adjustments
begin immediately, even if the underlying fees are not raised at this time, so that the City does not
accumulate another multi-decade gap.
Chief Financial Officer Greene explained that it is ultimately a policy decision whether to phase in
the adjustment. The Commission could choose to implement 50% of the increase now and the
remaining 50% in FY 2027, which would modify the table to reflect an immediate 2026 amount and
a 2027 stepped amount. CPI would then escalate the fees beyond that point. He stated that this
approach could be a reasonable compromise.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas requested data on how many buildings in the City fall within each size
range. CFO Greene indicated that he did not have that information available. The Vice-Mayor stated
that buildings in the 0-25 range, including those with only 8 or 12 units, would end up paying more
than those with over 100 units, which she feels is inequitable. She noted that smaller buildings are
often older, naturally more affordable, and in more financially vulnerable conditions. Although she
understands that the increase is proportional across categories, she remains hesitant because
smaller buildings with fewer households would pay more per unit than larger ones. She requested
more time to evaluate the issue.
Public Works Director Norris stated that another Item is already in progress that will address small
buildings. That Item is scheduled for Second Reading on April 22, and once implemented, those
buildings would move to a different contract structure.
Commissioner Suarez suggested waiting until the related Item is completed and proceeding step
by step. He agreed with Commissioner Magazine on the importance of applying CPI.
Commissioner Fernandez then requested that the motion be bifurcated to address the water fees
separately. He reiterated that he would not vote to pass along additional costs to the City’s
fixed-income residents and those struggling to make ends meet. He noted that while the City sent
a $500 homestead relief check to homeowners to help with rising costs, tenants did not receive
similar assistance, yet tenants will be impacted by these fee increases. He explained that because
the City was unable to extend relief to tenants, he has been working closely with Public Works,
attorneys, and waste haulers to explore ways to reduce residents’ costs, particularly waste-
collection costs. Therefore, he stated that he is not comfortable supporting an additional impact-fee
increase at the same time. If the Commission bifurcates the Item, he would feel more comfortable
moving forward with the portion related to water fees.
CFO Greene inquired whether the proposed bifurcation meant that the table, reflecting the
retroactive CPI “catch-up” rates, would be pulled for now, while the water and sewer impact fees
and the sanitation impact fees would still move forward with future CPI escalators. Members of the
Commission noted that there appeared to be consensus on applying CPI going forward to both the
water and sewer impact fees and the sanitation impact fees; however, the retroactive sanitation
catch-up remained the portion they recommended separating for later consideration.
Commissioner Suarez and Commissioner Fernandez reiterated their preference to bifurcate the
Item.
Commissioner Suarez stated he was comfortable applying CPI on a go-forward basis to both water
and sewer impact fees, but he wanted to separate out the retroactive 30-year sanitation catch-up
for further review.
City Attorney Ricardo J. Dopico recommended bringing back the CPI increases for Second
Reading, and treating the sanitation retroactive component as a new Ordinance on First Reading
at a later meeting, allowing Commissioners time to study the issue and feel comfortable with it.
Discussion continued.
Commissioner Magazine made a motion to bifurcate and move forward with the CPI adjustments
on a pro forma (going-forward) basis. The motion was seconded by Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas.
In reply to Commissioner Fernandez, City Attorney Dopico clarified that the CPI increase would not
take effect immediately; the first CPI adjustment would occur in October, consistent with the City’s
standard fee schedule cycle. He reiterated that no fee increase was being applied today.
Addressing Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas, CFO Greene clarified that water and sewer connection
fees apply only to new construction or meter upgrades, whereas the sanitation impact fee is an
ongoing monthly charge for existing commercial properties. He explained that the Commission, on
First Reading, was approving the CPI escalator for both sets of fees on a going-forward basis. He
further noted that the sanitation CPI adjustment would apply beginning October 1.
Commissioner Fernandez expressed concern about proceeding without clarity on what exactly the
Commission would be voting on with regard to costs, noting “a lot of uncertainty.”
Commissioner Magazine suggested simplifying the matter. He explained that the City had two fees,
both untouched for 30 years, and neither had received CPI adjustments during that time. He stated
that while the original Ordinance proposed a one-time catch-up to account for the past 30 years,
the Commission now intended to shelve the retroactive increase. However, as fiduciaries of the
system, they could not allow the City to continue falling behind. Therefore, on a go-forward basis,
the water, sewer, and sanitation impact fees should all receive an annual CPI adjustment, just as
other City fees do.
City Manager Eric Carpenter confirmed, in response to Commissioner Suarez’s question, that the

The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for April 22, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Thomas Mooney to handle.
Commissioner David Suarez requested that the Planning Director brief the Commission on the Item.
Planning Director Mooney explained that the Ordinance provided a simple amendment to Chapter
7 of the Land Development Regulations (LDRs). He stated that when a new single‑family home
exceeds 60 feet in length and is two stories in height, the Code requires additional side‑yard open
space. This requirement exists to prevent long, uninterrupted two‑story walls. Planning Director
Mooney explained that the amendment clarified and updated where the required open space could
be located, allowing for greater design flexibility while maintaining the same substantive open‑space
requirements. He stated that the amendment was intended to simplify design and permitting,
improve usability of the space, and expedite architectural review, and that both the Administration
and the Planning Board supported the proposal.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt asked why the original regulation required the open space to be
located specifically along the side of the house.
Planning Director Mooney responded that the requirement originated in the mid‑2000s and was
intended to break up long, flat two‑story elevations. He stated that the proposed amendment did
not change the substance of that requirement but expanded the ways the open space could be
configured. He explained that the Ordinance retained the requirement of minimum depth and added
a minimum width, and that the open space must equal at least one percent of the lot area. A property
owner could satisfy the requirement through one large open‑space cutout or multiple smaller
cutouts. He stated that reducing the minimum depth from eight feet to four feet made compliance
more feasible while still achieving the goal of avoiding long, blank elevations.
Commissioner Bhatt asked whether the Code required that the open space be pervious or
landscaped.
Planning Director Mooney responded that at least fifty percent of the required open‑space area
must consist of pervious landscaping or a water feature. He added that the requirement would not
alter lot‑coverage calculations or mandatory open‑space requirements in the front or rear yards,
because it applied solely to the side‑yard area.
Commissioner Suarez stated that the amendment provided flexibility to homeowners and moved to
approve the Item.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez seconded the motion.

items.title: AN ORDINANCE OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, AMENDING CHAPTER 66 OF THE CITY CODE, ENTITLED “MARINE STRUCTURES, FACILITIES AND VESSELS,” BY AMENDING ARTICLE II, ENTITLED “RESTRICTED WAKE ZONES,” BY AMENDING SECTION 66-43, ENTITLED “RESTRICTED AREAS,” TO ESTABLISH A DESIGNATED PUBLIC SWIM AREA, AND CORRESPONDING MOTORIZED VESSEL EXCLUSION ZONE, IN THE WATERS SURROUNDING FLAGLER MEMORIAL ISLAND, ALSO KNOWN AS MONUMENT ISLAND, PURSUANT TO SECTION § 327.46 OF THE FLORIDA STATUTES; AND FURTHER, AUTHORIZING THE CITY MANAGER TO UNDERTAKE AND EXECUTE THE NECESSARY APPLICATIONS AND COORDINATION WITH THE VARIOUS AGENCIES OF MIAMI-DADE COUNTY, THE STATE OF FLORIDA, AND THE UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT IN ORDER TO EFFECTUATE THE ESTABLISHMENT OF THE DESIGNATED PUBLIC SWIM AREA, AND CORRESPONDING MOTORIZED VESSEL-EXCLUSION ZONE; AND PROVIDING FOR REPEALER, SEVERABILITY, CODIFICATION, AND AN EFFECTIVE DATE.

The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for April 22, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Amy Knowles to handle.
Mayor Steven Meiner introduced the Item and noted that he was sponsoring it. Mayor Meiner
thanked Commissioner Dominguez and Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas for joining him as a Co-
sponsor. Mayor Meiner invited staff to provide the presentation.
Lindsey Precht, Deputy Resilience Officer and Assistant Director for Environment and
Sustainability, addressed the Commission. Ms. Precht explained that the Ordinance would allow
the City to proceed with the regulatory permitting process required to establish a designated swim
area around Monument Island. Ms. Precht stated that the designation was a required step under
the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission’s (FWC) permitting process. Ms. Precht
indicated that Monument Island had experienced increasing conflicts between vessels and
swimmers, heavy vessel traffic, boats anchoring close to shore, shoreline erosion, and seagrass
decline resulting from beaching activities. Ms. Precht explained that in 2023, the Commission
prioritized funding for shoreline restoration and establishing either a motorized-vessel exclusion
zone or a swim-only zone. Ms. Precht described the steps taken since that direction, including
consultant procurement, surveys, environmental assessments, conceptual design, and submission
of permit applications in August 2025. Ms. Precht explained that agency feedback clarified what
could be permitted within the Biscayne Bay Aquatic Preserve. While the original concept included
both a motorized-vessel exclusion zone and a public swim-only area, the Florida Department of
Environmental Protection advised that a vessel exclusion zone would require a submerged lands
lease and that such leases were not being issued for that purpose. Ms. Precht indicated that a
public swim area was permit-eligible. Ms. Precht explained that the City had also worked with FWC
to review the draft Ordinance in coordination with the Office of the City Attorney, and FWC confirmed
that the proposed language was appropriate. Ms. Precht stated that the swim-only zone would
extend 150 feet from the shoreline. Ms. Precht explained that the distance was determined in
consultation with Marine Patrol to establish a meaningful safety buffer between vessels and
swimmers, avoid impacts to seagrass and benthic resources, maintain clearance from navigation
routes and deeper water used by boaters, and provide room for regulatory adjustments during the
permit process. Ms. Precht stated that the approach was consistent with Commission goals related
to safety and conflict reduction. Ms. Precht added that approval of the Ordinance was required by
State statute to continue through permitting. If adopted, the staff and the consultant would revise
the engineering drawings to reflect only the swim-zone boundary, remove the motorized vessel
exclusion zone concept, and resubmit all application materials. Ms. Precht stated that the Ordinance
would also be transmitted to FWC.
Mayor Meiner thanked Ms. Precht and stated that the Item reflected the Commission’s efforts to
improve residents' quality of life. Mayor Meiner noted that Monument Island had generated
complaints related to motorized vessels, trash accumulation, and noise. Mayor Meiner expressed
appreciation to the Co-sponsor.
Commissioner Laura Dominguez stated that she had received concerns from residents the prior
day. Commissioner Dominguez asked whether the island was currently designated as a swim-only
area.
Ms. Precht explained that the area was used by swimmers but was not designated as a public
swimming area under regulatory guidelines, resulting in ongoing conflicts with vessels.
Commissioner Dominguez asked how the proposal would affect motorized vessels.
Ms. Precht stated that vessels would be prohibited from entering the swim-only zone and would be
required to remain outside the 150-foot boundary.
Commissioner Dominguez asked whether individuals would still be permitted to swim from vessels
or to use kayaks or paddleboards.
Ms. Precht explained that the swim zone restricted other uses within the boundary, but enforcement
would prioritize excluding motorized vessels. Ms. Precht stated that other portions of the shoreline
could still be accessed by kayaks and paddleboards.
Commissioner Dominguez asked whether motorized vessels could approach the island from other
areas.
Ms. Precht stated that the south side contained smaller riprap revetments that prevented vessels
from approaching too closely.
Commissioner Dominguez asked whether the City was subject to ADA requirements, expressing
concern about elderly individuals who might be unable to swim the distance.
Ms. Precht explained that vessels could position themselves near the outer edges of the swim-zone
buoys, allowing passengers to disembark closer to shore without entering the restricted area. Ms.
Precht clarified that the swim-only zone created a linear boundary, not a complete perimeter.

been removed, resulting in improved conditions. Commissioner Dominguez asked whether that
approach had been considered.

collection through a FIND grant. Ms. Knowles explained that the City supplemented this with an
additional collection day and conducted island cleanups and educational efforts. Ms. Knowles
stated that removing trash cans was not recommended at this time, as public behavior was not yet
consistent with a leave-no-trace model, and removal could worsen litter issues.

in a prolonged recovery operation. Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas stated that this history underscored

ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into
the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Bhatt made a motion to adopt the

The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for April 22, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Hernan Cardeno and John
Rebar to handle.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt introduced the Item and explained that the matter had come to
prominence following a recent incident in which a child was seriously injured by a dog.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that she was a rescue‑dog owner and supporter and emphasized that
the proposal was not intended as an anti‑dog measure, but as a means of addressing irresponsible
pet ownership. Commissioner Bhatt referenced the recent serious incident as well as other reported
situations in which individuals allowed their dogs to be off‑leash, failed to restrain them while
walking, or permitted them to defecate on neighbors’ property without cleaning up. Commissioner
Bhatt stated that even well‑trained dogs could behave unpredictably and that off‑leash conditions
created avoidable risks for the public. Commissioner Bhatt stated that in a dense urban
environment, residents shared limited public space, and the measure was intended to enhance
safety. Commissioner Bhatt moved the Item.
Commissioner Suarez explained that he frequently used South Pointe Park with his dogs and that
the Park’s open layout, which lacked gates, sometimes resulted in dogs running beyond the
designated area toward the lighthouse tower. Commissioner Suarez expressed concern that under
the proposed fine structure, a dog momentarily running outside the park boundary could result in a
citation from Code Compliance or a Park Ranger. Commissioner Suarez asked the Commission to
consider a buffer zone of approximately two hundred feet adjacent to dog parks to prevent
unintended penalties for responsible dog owners. Commissioner Suarez stated that he sought a
reasonable accommodation to avoid punitive enforcement when a dog briefly ran outside the park
perimeter.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that another Commissioner was developing a separate Item specifically
related to South Pointe Park. Commissioner Bhatt asked Police Chief Wayne Jones to confirm the
location of the recent dog‑related incident.
Chief Jones stated that his recollection was that the incident did not occur at South Pointe Park, but
rather at the park located near 53rd Street.
Commissioner Bhatt acknowledged that the Item was on First Reading and stated that she was
willing to discuss Commissioner Suarez’s concerns prior to Second Reading. Commissioner Bhatt
expressed reservations about establishing a two‑hundred‑foot buffer, but stated that the matter
could be evaluated further, including consideration of a smaller distance.
City Attorney Ricardo J. Dopico explained that the title of the proposed Ordinance pertained
specifically to fines and that the City Code already prohibited off‑leash dogs outside designated
areas, including specific exceptions for South Pointe Park under the existing Ordinance. The City
Attorney advised Commissioner Suarez that if he wished to create a buffer zone or special provision
for South Pointe Park, he could bring a separate Item for consideration.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez addressed the Commission and expressed concern that
establishing a buffer zone would create subjective enforcement issues, as residents and
enforcement personnel might not accurately measure distances such as 100 or 200 feet.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that if the policy required dogs to remain on leashes when outside
designated dog‑park areas, that requirement should apply until the animal physically entered the
leash‑free zone.
Commissioner Suarez responded that South Pointe Park was unique because it lacked gates and
contained open walkways, making it possible for dogs to run briefly into adjacent areas.
Commissioner Suarez expressed concern that a Park Ranger could target particular residents,
resulting in unfair enforcement. Commissioner Suarez stated that the Park’s open design was
intentional and encouraged its use, and that most other dog parks were gated. Commissioner
Suarez reiterated that he did not wish to create widespread buffer zones around all dog parks, but
remained concerned about unintended consequences at South Pointe Park.
Commissioner Bhatt encouraged Commissioner Suarez to bring a separate Item addressing South
Pointe Park, so the current Ordinance would remain limited in scope. Commissioner Bhatt
referenced another recent incident in the dunes involving an aggressive person and an aggressive
dog targeting cat feeders, and stated that she remained open to reviewing additional proposals.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that she wished to proceed with this Item as written.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, noted that the Item was a public hearing and confirmed that no
speakers were present on Zoom and no members of the audience requested to speak. City Clerk
Granado announced that a motion had been made by Commissioner Bhatt and seconded by
Commissioner Fernandez. Roll Call: 7-0.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, DIRECTING THE CITY ADMINISTRATION TO ENTER INTO AND/OR OBTAIN, FROM THE FLORIDA DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORTATION (“FDOT”), ANY PERMITS, AGREEMENTS, OR OTHER PREREQUISITES NECESSARY FOR THE PROMPT INSTALLATION OF TRAFFIC DELINEATORS, WITH FUNDING FROM THE CITY ADMINISTRATION’S EXISTING BUDGET, AROUND THE DESIGNATED “NO PARKING” AREAS SITUATED ALONG THE WEST SIDE OF THE SOUTHBOUND LANES OF ALTON ROAD BETWEEN FIFTH STREET AND SIXTH STREET, IN ORDER TO PROVIDE VISUAL AND PHYSICAL DETERRENTS THAT WILL SERVE TO PREVENT THE CONTINUED ILLEGAL STOPPING, PARKING AND LOADING/UNLOADING ALONG ALTON ROAD, ENHANCE PUBLIC SAFETY BY MAINTAINING THE FIRE DEPARTMENT’S UNOBSTRUCTED ACCESS TO FIRE HYDRANTS, AND IMPROVE OVERALL TRAFFIC FLOW ALONG ALTON ROAD AND THE SURROUNDING SIDE STREETS.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34189 was adopted. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt
the Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
William MacDonald and Jose Gonzalez to handle.
DIRECTION:
Directed to the City Manager / Administration:
• Bring back a comprehensive Citywide plan to the April 22, 2026 Commission Meeting
addressing loading, deliveries, enforcement, truck size, departmental coordination, and options
for Code amendments.
• Work with all relevant departments (Planning, Building, Transportation, Parking) to prepare
coordinated solutions for loading/unloading issues.
• Initiate the process for an FDOT Maintenance Memorandum of Agreement (MOA/MOU) to allow
installation of delineators on Alton Road.
• Develop and present options for immediate operational actions, including staffing deployment
and towing resources.
• Investigate obtaining or positioning a medium-duty or heavy-duty tow truck nearby to handle
recurring heavy-truck violations.
• Review CUP/DRB conditions applicable to the building.
• Issue a Notice to Cure for violations of the CUP and place the matter on the next feasible
Planning Board agenda (April 7 or May 5, depending on notice requirements).
• Look into the traffic cones situation at West Avenue/MacArthur Causeway and report back.
John Norris to handle.
Directed to the Office of the City Attorney
• Explore drafting a Code amendment allowing violations to be tied back to adjacent buildings.
• Explore an Enforcement Ordinance requiring non-compliant buildings to hire off-duty Police or
Parking Enforcement to manage loading activity.
Commissioner Suarez stated that the Commission had received numerous emails and photographs
showing delivery trucks parking in the designated no-parking area along Alton Road, which is
causing significant traffic congestion as vehicles approach the MacArthur Causeway/395 overpass.
He noted that Parking Enforcement has visited the area multiple times, yet the issue persists, and
he personally observes delivery trucks parked there frequently. Given the high number of deliveries
associated with the nearby residential building, he expressed concern that drivers continue to treat
the area as an acceptable loading location. Commissioner Suarez requested that the City install
delineators to clearly indicate that parking is prohibited, as current enforcement efforts do not
appear sufficient to address the ongoing problem.
William McDonald, Parking Director, stated that Commissioner Suarez was correct. He explained
that the property creates a “game of whack‑a‑mole,” as enforcement staff clears the area only for
new trucks to appear shortly thereafter. Some delivery drivers who do not service the building daily
simply choose to take the citation rather than comply, and it is almost impossible to tow these
vehicles because, by the time a large enough tow truck arrives, the vehicle is typically gone. He
stated that delineator posts would absolutely serve as a deterrent. Because Alton Road is an FDOT
roadway, the City would need permission to install them. He added that they have been working
with the building’s dockmaster with mixed results: initially, coordination was strong, with the
dockmaster even calling Parking Enforcement when trucks refused to leave, but due to the
property's density and the volume of untimed deliveries, the issue remains a challenge.
In response to Commissioner Suarez, Jose Gonzalez, Transportation and Mobility Director, stated
that Alton Road is a State Road, and installing delineators would require a maintenance and
installation agreement with FDOT. He noted that the City routinely enters into such agreements,
negotiates with FDOT, and then returns the agreement to the Commission for execution. He stated
that this is all that would be required for the City to install and maintain the delineators.
Commissioner Fernandez thanked Commissioner Suarez for bringing the Item and stated that he
would like to co‑sponsor. He noted that in December and January, they received emails from David
Martinez, a resident of Fifth and Alton. He welcomed the Administration’s change in position,
explaining that when he previously inquired about installing delineators, he was advised that the
Administration believed they could worsen conditions by causing vehicles to park on Alton Road
rather than in the striped area, creating additional traffic issues. Since Administration now appears
to have a different view regarding what can be done administratively, he would join Commissioner
Suarez as a co‑sponsor.
Vice‑Mayor Matteo‑Salinas stated that she did not oppose the use of delineators but expressed
concerns, noting, as Commissioner Fernandez had mentioned, that the installation could result in
the lane leading to the Causeway being blocked. She indicated she would support the Item today;
however, if the delineators ultimately cause vehicles to block the lane and no better solution for
loading and unloading is identified, she would bring back an Item to remove the delineators, as
obstructing the Causeway entrance would create significant problems.
Commissioner Bhatt added that the Administration had previously been unsupportive of this
approach due to traffic impact concerns and asked for an explanation of what had changed.
City Manager Eric Carpenter stated that, from the Administration’s perspective, the position had not
necessarily changed. He reiterated concerns that if parking spaces adjacent to the loading dock
area are removed, it is unclear where those vehicles would shift.
Commissioner Suarez asked that an image illustrating current conditions be shown.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that, delineators or not, the broader issue involves trucks choosing to
make deliveries on main thoroughfares during peak hours rather than using designated loading
areas, sometimes because buildings do not want their driveways blocked, and sometimes because
drivers prefer to avoid entering a complicated driveway. She cited examples, such as the Ritz and
the Decoplage, where longstanding conflicts have existed. She expressed concern that the building
in question is extremely dense, located in an already dense area, and appears not to be managing
loading adequately through its dockmaster. She asked how the City could hold accountable those
responsible for complying with zoning laws, land‑use approvals, traffic studies, and parking studies,
which are intended to prevent such issues. She noted that the Parking Department has been
working with delivery companies to sign pledges acknowledging the rules of operation and
suggested exploring whether more dockmasters or additional accountability for building
management may be needed. She emphasized that the issue affects more than just the building's
residents; it could compromise life safety if traffic backs up. Commissioner Bhatt reiterated that she
still did not understand whether the Administration’s position had changed and stressed that, as the
issue becomes Citywide, they must determine how to ensure compliance with the rules of living and
doing business in the City; whether that concerns buildings that exceed infrastructure capacity,
delivery trucks that are too large for City streets, or requiring scheduled delivery permits. She called
for a holistic review involving the Planning, Building, Transportation, and Parking Departments to
develop a coordinated plan. She requested that the City Manager place an Item on next month’s
agenda and have the departments work together to present a comprehensive set of options and
potential solutions.
Commissioner Suarez displayed the images he previously referenced in the discussion. Click here
to view. He stated that a simple fix, such as installing delineators, could help alleviate traffic
congestion at this critical section of the City near Fifth Street and Alton Road. He added that
whenever the City has an opportunity to intervene and make a meaningful difference, it should do
so. While he supports developing a comprehensive plan, he emphasized that the problem is
occurring daily and requires immediate action.
In response to Commissioner Fernandez’s question, Parking Director William McDonald explained
that the City does not have specialized towing equipment capable of removing large heavy trucks;
towing such vehicles would require an off‑island solution. Additionally, most trucks have a driver or
employee nearby. In one of the photos, a truck was unloading, and personnel were walking back
and forth, meaning that even if the City secured a heavy‑duty tow truck, the driver could return to
the cab and move the vehicle before towing occurred. Commissioner Fernandez then recognized
Manny Diaz, from Tremont Towing, and requested that he approach the podium.
Manny Diaz stated that Tremont Towing works closely with the Parking Director. He noted that if
the City needs a medium‑duty tow truck, they can provide one; however, by the time such
equipment arrives on scene, the truck drivers often leave.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that since this is a recurring problem at a predictable location, the
towing resource could potentially be positioned nearby. He noted that the City owns property near
where such a vehicle could be stationed. He emphasized that recurring nuisances require proactive
measures and that nothing will change unless enforcement efforts are strengthened. He expressed
frustration that the Administration previously advised him one way, but now, without notice, its
position appears to have changed. Now that a different solution is being pursued, he stated his
support for Commissioner Suarez and joined the Item as a co‑sponsor. He further stated that as
similar challenges arise throughout the barrier island, the City must ensure towing resources are
readily available. He noted that issuing citations alone does not resolve violations; achieving
compliance is necessary to mitigate impacts. Citations are issued for noncompliance, creating a
domino effect that impacts others. While fines may be issued, the real goal is not punishment but
compliance, and he emphasized the need for Tremont Towing’s collaboration to address this
recurrent issue.
Manny Diaz agreed, stating that they could work together to station a medium‑duty tow truck at all
times. He noted that this is how they handled freight loading zones in the past: tow trucks were
staged nearby, vehicles were removed, and the problem subsided. He stated that the same
approach could be used for heavy‑duty towing.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that she still had two questions, the first being why the Administration’s
position had changed.
City Manager Eric Carpenter responded that he did not believe the position of the Parking Director
or Transportation Director had changed and that his own position had not changed. He reiterated
that installing delineators would shift the problem from the striped area, which is not a travel lane,
into an active traffic lane. Therefore, if delineators are installed, he hopes that Tow Operator Diaz
will have sufficient resources, as the City would likely need to tow vehicles from the travel lane
regularly.
Parking Director William MacDonald clarified that the situation is essentially “six of one, half a dozen
of the other.” He explained that the trucks are currently in violation, and when enforcement officers
respond, they issue a $124 obstruction‑of‑traffic citation in addition to a $1,000 to $5,000
right‑of‑way violation. He noted that compliance is typically achieved about 90% of the time.
However, there is an absolute risk that, if delineators are installed, drivers could simply activate
their flashers and stop directly in the travel lane, acting as if they are invisible. He emphasized that
delineators could push violators from the striped area into an active lane of traffic, and there is no
way to predict how drivers will behave. He further stated that the Parking Department has a freight-
loading zone adjacent to the building, but it is on the opposite side. He described the building's
design as the root of the problem, explaining that if the loading area were oriented differently, it
would work much more effectively.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that this is not a small building, noting that it went to a public referendum,
was extensively designed, and is being marketed at a premium. She expressed concern that the
loading zone is located on the wrong side to accommodate traffic impacts, calling the situation
offensive. While she was unsure whether retrofitting is possible, she stated that the loading location
must be addressed as part of any comprehensive solution. She added that if enforcement is the
primary challenge, then enforcement staff should not wait for complaints; instead, staff should be
stationed at the loading dock during loading hours so violations can be cited immediately. Many
buildings, she noted, have boards, CUPs, and operational plans detailing how loading is to be
handled, and she believes buildings should be held responsible. She asked whether penalties for
repeat offenders could be increased and expressed frustration that the situation is becoming
Citywide. If a solution is not found, she said, it will become unmanageable. She asked that every
option be explored and requested that a comprehensive plan be brought back by the April meeting.
While appreciative of the intent behind the Item, she stated she could not support it at this time
because she believes it will only displace the problem. She emphasized that the City must act
immediately on issues such as staffing and towing resources and should not wait for an FDOT MOU
to move forward with operational solutions.
Commissioner Dominguez stated that she also heard from the Administration that delineators could
shift trucks into the travel lane because the City does not own Alton Road. She noted repeated
references to heavy‑duty tow trucks and asked whether booting could be used instead, questioning
whether boots are limited to passenger vehicles.
Parking Director MacDonald responded that boots can be used on trucks; however, booting does
not solve the core problem. He explained that the City already has enhanced penalties for repeat
offenders, with right‑of‑way violations increasing up to $15,000 for a third offense, levels that often
capture the attention of major delivery companies. The challenge at this particular building, he said,
is that many deliveries are made by one‑time vendors used for moves or specialty furniture
deliveries. While the City regularly sees FedEx, UPS, and Amazon, and has had several meetings
with them, these larger individual delivery companies typically receive a violation once and do not
return.
In response to Commissioner Dominguez’s question about holding the building accountable,
Parking Director MacDonald stated that the Parking Department does not have enforcement
authority over private property and would defer to Code Compliance or the Building Department to
determine whether any enforcement mechanism exists. He noted that Parking cannot issue
violations to the building itself.
City Manager Eric Carpenter added that there is currently no mechanism in the Code to assess
violations against the adjacent building. In response to Commissioner Dominguez, he stated that a
Code amendment would be required to tie such violations to the property. The Office of the City
Attorney will need to explore the possibility of such an Ordinance.
Commissioner Dominguez reiterated that the City Manager had indicated the City does not currently
have a mechanism to hold the building responsible for failing to direct delivery trucks to move, and
that new legislation would be needed to do so. Discussion continued.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that she wants a comprehensive plan outlining what the City can do
immediately, what amendments to the Code may be required, and what long-term solutions are
needed. She noted that the issue cannot be solved on the fly today, though staffing adjustments
and towing resources can be implemented quickly. She requested that by April, staff bring back a
full review of all options, including potential Code amendments, to proactively address the issue
Citywide.
Commissioner Fernandez added that if the City brings back an Enforcement Ordinance, then,
instead of imposing a large fine that simply goes into a City account, the remedy should require the
building to hire off-duty Police Officers or off-duty parking enforcement personnel to perform the
work its dockmaster is failing to do. He explained that this places the burden on the building, rather
than on taxpayers, and ensures active compliance. Once an Ordinance is adopted, if a building is
found not to be in compliance, it should not only be fined but also required to hire off-duty personnel
to manage loading activity.
Commissioner Bhatt further noted that when a building wants to bring in a contractor to trim palms,
a right-of-way permit is required because large equipment must be brought in, and sidewalks may
need to be closed. She suggested that a similar procedure could apply when an 18-wheeler is
needed for a cross-country move. The building could schedule a delivery window with the City, and
if that requires an alternate traffic plan to avoid emergencies, then that should be part of the process.
She noted that the City can tailor such requirements to extremely dense neighborhoods with narrow
streets, including upcoming developments in North Beach. She asked that all relevant departments
work together to bring back an Ordinance next month addressing these considerations.
Commissioner Suarez stated that delineators would be an effective way to reduce the need for a

ACTION: Resolution 2026-34190 was adopted as amended. Commissioner Fernandez made a

VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes

AMENDMENT:
Include authorization for the installation of Israeli-themed banners, including the Israeli flag or the
Star of David, around The Wolfsonian, specifically along Washington Avenue from 10 Street to 11
Street and along 10 Street from Washington Avenue to Lummus Park. Office of the City Attorney
to handle.
TO DO:
The Office of the City Attorney will review existing Land Development Regulations (LDRs) regarding
flags and banners to determine whether the installation of Israeli-themed banners (Israeli flag)
around The Wolfsonian requires an amendment to the LDRs. If an amendment is required, the City
Attorney’s Office will prepare the necessary legislation. Office of the City Attorney to handle.
Commissioner David Suarez explained that Item R7 K involved a proposal to expand the Forever
Proud Light Pole Banner Program as a means of affirming inclusion, supporting communities that
have faced discrimination, and enhancing the character of the Art Deco Cultural District.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he supported the concept and believed the same framework
should be applied to an initiative he was proposing. He requested consideration of a similar banner
program displaying Israeli flags around The Wolfsonian, specifically on Washington Avenue from
10 Street to 11 Street and along 10 Street from Washington Avenue to Lummus Park. He stated
that his intent centered on visibility, safety, and consistency, and that the proposal was unrelated to
foreign policy. Commissioner Suarez noted recent antisemitic incidents in Miami Beach and stated
that the banners would signal support for the City’s Jewish community. He explained that the
proposed location was significant because The Wolfsonian was founded by a Jewish family, and its
founder’s father served as Miami Beach’s first Jewish mayor. He further noted that The Wolfsonian’s
mission includes examining fascism, propaganda, and historical forces connected to the Holocaust,
making the location symbolically meaningful. Commissioner Suarez stated that if the City uses
public space to visibly support one community facing hostility, it should do the same for another,
emphasizing equal treatment and the importance of demonstrating that hate has no place in Miami
Beach.
Mayor Steven Meiner stated that he fully supported the proposal.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez expressed his support, stating that he previously sponsored an Item
seeking to display the Israeli flag in honor of Israel’s 75th anniversary, but that the Item had not
advanced at that time. He stated that communities that have historically faced discrimination should
be supported consistently, and emphasized solidarity with the Jewish community, the LGBTQ
community, Hispanic residents, immigrants, and other communities that have been historically
marginalized. Commissioner Fernandez stated that intolerance directed at one group threatens all
communities and expressed pride in supporting the current proposal.
Commissioner Laura Dominguez asked the City Attorney whether an Ordinance existed that
restricted the display of foreign flags.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, stated that some restrictions regarding flags were contained in the
Land Development Regulations (LDRs). He advised that his Office would determine whether the
proposal would require an amendment to the LDRs and would prepare such an amendment if
needed.
Mayor Meiner confirmed that the Item would be voted on as amended.
Commissioner Fernandez reiterated that the same groups targeted by antisemitism are often
targeted by other forms of intolerance and stated that historically the Jewish and LGBTQ
communities have stood together in parallel efforts to combat hate. He stated that the City must
continue to visibly support communities facing hostility.
Commissioner Suarez clarified that the proposal involved banners, not free‑flying flags, and that
banners may include the Star of David or the Israeli flag.
City Attorney Dopico confirmed that the Star of David alone would not require an LDR amendment
and that his Office would determine whether banner imagery incorporating the Israeli flag would
require a Code change. He stated that if an amendment was not legally required, no amendment
would be drafted.
City Clerk Rafael E. Granado announced that a motion had been made by Commissioner
Fernandez and seconded by Commissioner Suarez, as amended.
Vote: 7-0.
Following the vote, Commissioner Alex Fernandez thanked the Mayor and his colleagues and
stated that he felt a great sense of nachas, using the Yiddish term to express pride and appreciation.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt responded with a light clarification regarding the pronunciation of the
word.

items.action: Resolution 2026-34191 was adopted. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Resolution; seconded by Mayor Meiner. Vote: 7-0.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34191 was adopted. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to
adopt the Resolution; seconded by Mayor Meiner. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Chief Wayne Jones to handle.
DIRECTION:
The Police Department will provide a timeline for completing full Beachwalk camera coverage,
continue conducting regular monitoring and maintenance to prevent visibility obstructions, and
return at the next Commission meeting with an update on the Department’s evaluation of AI‑based
detection tools and whether any Commission action is needed to expedite installation. Chief Wayne
Jones to handle.
Mayor Meiner introduced the Item and thanked Commissioner Alex Fernandez for co-sponsoring
it. He asked who would be addressing the Item from the Administration.
City Manager Eric Carpenter indicated that the Police Department would present.
Mayor Meiner acknowledged recent work by the Police Department during Spring Break and
referenced the increased Police presence in response to global geopolitical developments.
Police Chief Wayne Jones addressed the Commission and stated that the City maintains a robust
camera system across Miami Beach, particularly along the Beachwalk and Boardwalk, consisting
of nearly 1,000 cameras and almost 2,000 camera views. He explained that many of these cameras
are monitored in real time by the Real Time Intelligence Center (RTIC), while others are reviewed
retroactively to assist with solving and mitigating crimes occurring in the coverage areas. He stated
that the Department conducts regular monitoring and will continue doing so.
Mayor Meiner asked how the Police Department ensures that cameras are not obstructed. Chief
Jones explained that the City maintains a camera maintenance program, and staff regularly survey
installation areas, particularly along the Beachwalk, where tree growth can obstruct views and
require trimming. Mayor Meiner asked whether the Police Department has sufficient resources to
maintain operational visibility. Chief Jones stated that camera maintenance is funded through a
dedicated budget line, which supports the trimming and maintenance work.
Mayor Meiner asked about the status of full operational coverage along the Beachwalk.
Chief Jones stated that some coverage gaps remain, not due to lack of desire or funding but
because the installation is occurring in stages. He indicated he would provide a timeline for
completion.
Mayor Meiner referenced the interest expressed by the Mid Beach Neighborhood Association
(MBNA) regarding Beachwalk camera completion.
Chief Jones confirmed the Department’s intention to complete the project.
Commissioner David Suarez asked whether the Department is exploring AI-based tools to detect
potential criminal activity automatically, since constant manual monitoring of the entire Beachwalk
would require numerous Officers.
Chief Jones stated that the Department continually evaluates emerging technologies to enhance
predictive and preventive efforts and is currently pursuing AI solutions. He agreed to provide an
update at the next Commission meeting.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that camera expansion efforts extend into parks such as Bayshore
Park and noted that the Police Department has integrated security infrastructure into park design.
Chief Jones confirmed that Bayshore Park is a high-priority location due to its size and the need for
ongoing situational visibility.
Commissioner Fernandez acknowledged the Department’s practice of participating early in
planning for new public facilities so that security infrastructure is incorporated in advance.
Chief Jones stated that the Department collaborates closely with Public Works, Capital
Improvement Projects, and Parks staff to incorporate crime prevention infrastructure early in project
development.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt noted the City’s upcoming budget planning cycle and asked whether
delays in completing the Beachwalk camera system result from insufficient funding or from
implementation timelines and resource capacity.
Chief Jones stated that funding has been in place for some time and that the primary challenges
relate to time and resource capacity rather than appropriations.
Commissioner Bhatt asked if additional contracting or outside assistance could expedite
installation.
Chief Jones explained that much of the camera installation and maintenance is already
subcontracted.
Commissioner Bhatt then asked Chief Jones to report at the following month’s meeting whether any
Commission action is needed to expedite the system's completion.
Chief Jones agreed.
Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Resolution; seconded by Mayor Meiner.
Vote: 7-0.
