items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, APPROVING THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH STRATEGIC PLAN 2026.
items.action: Resolution 2026-34194 was adopted as amended. Commissioner Bhatt made a motion to adopt the Resolution as amended; seconded by Commissioner Magazine. Vote: 7-0.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34194 was adopted as amended. Commissioner Bhatt made a motion
to adopt the Resolution as amended; seconded by Commissioner Magazine. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Office of the City Manager to handle.
AMENDMENT:
Add a new field to the agenda memo cover sheets to identify alignment with strategic initiatives.
Implementing this change will require programming modifications to the City’s OneMeeting Agenda
Management system. Stephanie Rey Brooks to handle.
Commissioner Magazine introduced the Item and noted that it reflects a good governance
approach. He mentioned that while he appreciates how the City Commission often discusses
details, as it did earlier, this level of attention is vital to effective local government. He pointed out
that when residents go outside their homes, their experiences, such as road safety and the
appearance of trees, are the core concerns of the City. Governance often focuses only on daily
issues, without stepping back to consider broader macro-level challenges. The City can sometimes
lack a larger vision and long-term strategy. This Item, before the City Commission, aims to help set
those parameters. He clarified that this does not mean the City cannot deviate from the plan, but if
it does, it should be able to explain why. He asked the City Manager to continue explaining the Item.
City Manager Carpenter emphasized that this is a very important discussion. He explained that
each year, through the budget process, the City prioritizes its operational goals, but Items like this
look further ahead over multiple years. He likened the process to being in an old-fashioned boat
with 40 rowers. While each stroke of the oar matters, if no one knows the destination, moving the
boat forward becomes difficult. The Item before the City Commission reflects input from the Mayor
and City Commission over the past year. It builds on the City’s history, noting that Miami Beach’s
first strategic plan was established by Resolution No. 2006-26341 and updated in 2015, 2019, and
2023. The current plan remains committed to the City’s mission of providing excellent public service
and safety to all residents, workers, and visitors in the vibrant historic community. It also highlights
the City’s organizational values, including maintaining Miami Beach as a world-class City and
operating as a top team of empowered professionals working toward exceptional results; serving
the public efficiently and respectfully; and conducting business with honesty, integrity, and
dedication. City employees serve as goodwill ambassadors within the business community and
treat residents, staff, and one another with professionalism, kindness, and collegiality. The plan
features several strategic areas and objectives. One goal is to enhance the City’s internationally
recognized reputation by balancing tourism and development efforts to improve the quality of life
and strengthen neighborhoods, schools, and commercial districts. Another goal aims to make Miami
Beach safer by boosting resident satisfaction through safety, cleanliness, and modernized codes.
The plan envisions a resilient coastal City by initiating measures to protect the natural environment
and support long-term community sustainability. It also promotes a connected and engaged City
through multimodal transportation to reduce congestion and improve connectivity among
businesses, schools, and attractions. Lastly, the goal for a smart City is to deliver high-quality,
efficient government services and support for employees.
Commissioner Magazine inquired whether this is the outcome of a retreat held last year.
City Manager Carpenter responded that it is. He explained that it resulted from a two-day retreat
involving six City Commissioners, noting that Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas had participated, although
not in her current role. This reflects the consolidation of many discussions and a significant amount
of thoughtful and thought-provoking exchanges.
Commissioner Magazine asked where this would be publicly visible. He also inquired whether it is
fixed and set in stone, or intended to be a dynamic document that can be adjusted and refined over
time.
City Manager Carpenter replied that the document can be amended by Resolution at any time. It
will inform the City’s budgeting process and also guide the day-to-day direction he provides to City
teams in delivering the best results for the community.
Commissioner Magazine inquired whether there is anything that can serve as a safeguard. For
example, consider a situation where the City adopts a strategic priority to become more walkable
and pedestrian-friendly, but then someone proposes legislation that directly contradicts that goal.
He questioned whether some sort of flag or discussion would occur to identify that the proposal
conflicts with the City’s stated strategic priority.
City Manager Carpenter replied that, in prior iterations, City memos had attempted to incorporate
references to strategic goals and initiatives into the information being presented to the City
Commission. He said the City had moved somewhat away from that practice, in part because it has
not completed a full refresh of the strategic plan since 2019, but he would like to return to that
approach and better dovetail initiatives with the strategic plan.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that over the years, often due to input from residents or previous City
Commissions, additional items have been added to the blue sheet cover memos, such as fiscal
impact and Residents’ Right to Know considerations. She asked whether a checkbox or similar
reference could be included on those cover memos to indicate if a proposed item aligns with one of
the strategic initiatives and, if so, which one. This could serve as a quick reference and help hold
the City Commission accountable.
City Manager Carpenter replied that staff could do that if the City Commission desired.
Commissioner Bhatt asked whether the City Commission would need to vote on that change.
City Attorney Dopico replied that the City Commission could propose an amendment to the Item.
Commissioner Bhatt proposed adding a field to the agenda memo cover sheets to indicate whether
a proposed item aligns with any of the strategic initiatives and, if so, which one. She clarified that
not being aligned would not necessarily mean the Item is inappropriate, but such a notation could
help provide context for the City Commission.
City Manager Carpenter mentioned that this would also include the integration of key performance
indicators.
Commissioner Bhatt agreed with the City Manager.
Commissioner Bhatt made a motion to adopt the Resolution as amended; seconded by
Commissioner Magazine. Vote: 7-0.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, AMENDING THE MODEL VOLLEYBALL 2026 ACTIVATION TO INCLUDE TWO ELECTRONIC MUSIC CONCERTS TO BE HELD ON APRIL 18-19, 2026, BETWEEN 8TH AND 9TH STREETS ON THE LUMMUS PARK BEACHFRONT.
items.action: Resolution 2026-34201 was adopted as is. Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas made a motion to adopt the Resolution as is; seconded by Commissioner Magazine. Vote: 7-0.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34201 was adopted as is. Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas made a motion
to adopt the Resolution as is; seconded by Commissioner Magazine. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Lissette Garcia Arrogante to handle.
Commissioner Fernandez moved the Item; Commissioner Dominguez seconded it.
Commissioner Suarez asked staff to present.
Lissette Garcia Arrogante, the Director of Tourism and Culture, presented the amendment for the
Model Volleyball event. They are requesting additional programming for this year. Model Volleyball
is a longstanding, grandfathered event with the City that has been held for 15 years. This year, they
are proposing to add nighttime activations with DJs on Saturday and Sunday until 11 p.m. Staff met
with the event organizers to reduce their activations on Sunday night to 10 p.m., as it will not be a
tented event, but rather it will be held in the open. As part of their Special Event process, they must
receive approval from the State, and then it is reviewed internally by all departments, including
Environment and Sustainability. They are currently going through that process.
Commissioner Magazine stated that during the College Football Concert, there were complaints
about loud music. He guesses the event drew about 70,000 people, professionally produced by top
event producers worldwide, and it is not even close to the decibel level expected on Sunday
evening.
Director of Tourism and Culture Arrogante explained that any event must follow the County and
City’s Noise Ordinance, which begins at 11 p.m. However, if any noise is heard within 100 feet,
organizers will need to make adjustments or face shutdown. This rule applies to any event at any
time of the day.
Commissioner Magazine stated that he would place his trust in the staff, but he assumed that Model
Volleyball does not intend this to be a one-time event; there would be no return next year if problems
arise. He cautioned that if the organizers fail to meet expectations, the Commission will not revisit
the matter again. Addressing the representatives of Model Volleyball directly, he urged them to be
respectful and manage the event perfectly, emphasizing that there will be no second chance. He
encouraged them to get it right from the start.
Addressing Commissioner Suarez, Director of Tourism Arrogante explained that the event will take
place on Saturday, April 18, and Sunday, April 19, 2026, and it has been an annual event for the
past 15 years.
Commissioner Suarez is concerned about the turtle nesting season and the lights; he had a brief
discussion with Environment and Sustainability Director Amy Knowles to explore ways to reduce
the lights on the beach.
Lissette Garcia Arrogante, Director of Tourism and Culture, mentioned that event organizers will
need to adjust lighting in accordance with the Turtle Ordinance and submit a lighting plan. Most
events conclude by 9 p.m. and are currently in the process of doing so, pending the requirements
set by the State for compliance with the Turtle Ordinance.
In response to Commissioner Suarez, Amy Knowles, Environment and Sustainability Director,
confirmed that the departments will collaborate. The Ordinance updated in October 2024 specifies
requirements for evening events. These events must have a permit or an exemption from the State,
and any lighting used cannot be visible from the beach after 9 p.m. Authorized lighting must be low-
voltage, long-wave, shielded, and directed away from the beach, ensuring that lights do not cause
impact. The discussion was held. The goal is to minimize the impact, but the State may permit
certain conditions, and the City’s Ordinance aims to reduce it as much as possible.
Commissioner Suarez is a big turtle fan and wants to ensure they minimize light pollution.
Lissette Garcia Arrogante, Director of Tourism and Culture, explained that if the State recommends
ending at 9 p.m., they must comply with that time. In response to Commissioner Suarez, she stated
that the City could recommend ending at 9 p.m.
Environment and Sustainability Director Amy Knowles added that the Ordinance recommends
minimizing the light after 9 p.m. Any lights must be turtle-friendly and not visible.
Commissioner Fernandez moved the approval of the Item as amended. Commissioner Suarez
proposed an amendment to ensure the event ends at 9 p.m.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, summarized that the motion is to approve the event, but it is up to
the Special Events permit to reduce the hours.
Commissioner Fernandez moved to adopt the Resolution as amended.
Ricardo J. Dopico, the City Attorney, clarified that the amendment is meant to qualify the Special
Event permit so the music ends at 9 p.m.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, believes the Ordinance, as currently drafted, states that the event
and loadout must happen that evening. Loadout would need to start before 9 p.m., or they would
have to load out the next day.
SECOND SECTION
Commissioner Fernandez believes the event should end at 9 p.m. because if they load out by then,
they might not receive any approval, since it would effectively destroy the event.
Commissioner Fernandez indicated that requiring both the event and the load-out to be completed
by 9 p.m. would effectively prevent the event from taking place.
Commissioner Suarez feels a bit uneasy about holding an event on the beach until 11 p.m.,
especially since it is sea turtle nesting season and, according to the Code, it must end by 9 p.m.
The reason for the load-in and load-out is that trucks arrive on the beach with headlights on, which
could potentially harm sea turtles, and they want to prevent that. The discussion continued about
loading out the next morning.
Olivia Ormos, representing Model Volleyball, explained that the event typically runs from 12 p.m. to
8 p.m. and that the organizers were requesting additional hours into the evening. She stated that
this was the first week they had heard about the sea turtle lighting requirements and that they were
not seeking to do anything inconsistent with City requirements. She noted that they had been asked
to move the Sunday end time to 10:00 p.m., which was not a problem for them. She explained that
they do not load out until Monday and do not conduct any interchangeable load-outs between
Saturday and Sunday. She confirmed to Commissioner Suarez that if the City required the event to
conclude at 9 p.m., they would end at that time and load out the next day.
Michael Malone, on behalf of Model Volleyball, explained that they were told by their production
company, which has produced hundreds of events on Miami Beach, that it had used amber lighting
at an event last year. That is something they can do.
Ms. Ormos added that it is the protocol they were told has been successful in the past, and they
could implement.
Commissioner Fernandez clarified that his concern was not with the event ending later, but with the
possibility that both the event and the loadout would be required to conclude by 9 p.m., which he
stated would “effectively just destroy the event.” After the organizers confirmed on the record that
loadout would occur the following morning rather than at night, he stated that he was comfortable
with the schedule as discussed and with allowing the event to proceed under the hours proposed
in the agenda Item.
Commissioner Suarez reiterated that, according to the Code, there should be no lights on the beach
after 9 p.m. They will conclude the show and then load out the next day to avoid trucks with lights
on the beach, which could cause disruptions.
Addressing Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas, Ms. Ormos noted that they had raised the issue of holding
the concert back in August with City staff, but they were not informed about sea turtles until March
1st.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas expressed empathy because they have a concert less than a month
away, and now they are being told to cut the event by two hours, which she feels is unfair. She
suggested allowing the concert to go until 10:00 p.m. at the very least. While she respects the sea
turtles, she believes they should have been informed about this earlier. The event is already being
promoted, ads are printed, and tickets have been sold. She does not want to pull the rug out from
under them, less than a month before the event. She requested that the concert be allowed until 11
p.m., and if she cannot get her colleagues' support, perhaps 10:00 p.m.; but 9 p.m. is unfair.
Commissioner Fernandez withdrew his motion and endorsed Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas’s
proposal.
Commissioner Magazine asked if there is an appetite for ending at 9 p.m. on Sunday, then they
can go until the originally proposed time on Saturday.
Ms. Ormos mentioned that the hours on Saturday are from 12 to 11 p.m. They were asked to reduce
the hours on Sunday from 11 p.m. to 10 p.m. last week. The event has traditionally ended at 8 p.m.
With this request and in an effort to do something different, the VCA is giving them a significant
grant for this specific moment, so they want to succeed on all fronts.
Amy Knowles, Chief Resilience Officer and Environment and Sustainability Director, reiterated to
Commissioner Magazine that the goal of the Turtle Ordinance is to minimize the light so it is not
visible from the beach; it must be shielded and projected downward. It is a tall order for a concert.
This has been in place since October 2024, and Code will enforce it. She will be out there often as
well, but it is a tall order. She anticipates that if the Model Volleyball event is on the beach after 9
p.m., they would need to comply.
In explaining to Commissioner Suarez, Tourism and Culture Director Arrogante stated that the
representatives of Model Volleyball had just mentioned working with a producer who has been
organizing the event for 15 years and was not aware of the turtle season. This is something all
experienced Miami Beach event producers know. Their producers should be informed. Tourism and
Culture staff had a conversation with Model Volleyball on February 6. An email was received
detailing their plans. Staff reviewed it internally before scheduling a meeting to discuss with the
event organizers. Model Volleyball talked about having a tent for the concert until 11 p.m. and
reducing Sunday hours to 10 p.m. because people work the next day. In addition to this review,
Tourism and Culture staff issue over 600 special event permits each year, so they needed to take
their time to review everything thoroughly.
Commissioner Suarez understands she has a lot on her plate, but at the very least, they passed a
law in 2024 specifically for sea turtle lighting. So, why was it not explained to Model Volleyball that
9 p.m. is the last hour?
Director of Tourism and Culture Arrogante added that the process is presented to the State and
reviewed internally. The review details were submitted last month. Once the State completes its
review, which she mentioned at the beginning of the discussion, it will provide feedback on what
needs to be done for the amber lighting. The Code states that lighting must be minimized; it does
not prohibit all lighting. She deferred to her colleague Amy Knowles, who is more experienced in
this matter, but the Ordinance, as written, does allow them to hold an event with lighting, as long as
it is minimized and follows what Ms. Knowles mentioned. The person who pulled the permit, the
producer who is not present today, understands this.
Commissioner Suarez recognized Olivia Ormos, who attended elementary school with him. This is
a sensitive issue for him; it was also for late Commissioner Mark Samuelian, and he wants to ensure
there are no disruptions. The last thing they want is to see a sea turtle get run over or crushed. It is
not something they desire or want to deal with. He asked if it was possible to put curtains on the
sides? He finds it hard to imagine a concert on the sand without lights spilling over.
Ms. Ormos added that their plan is to do everything they are instructed to do and comply with the
guidelines set by the State. Model Volleyball is not here to undermine the rules, which is why they
have maintained a perfect record for 15 years, and this event has never resulted in an arrest or
shutdown. The Police and the VCA support them; the Police even participate in the tournament.
Everyone loves this event, and it has remained the same for 15 years. They are trying something
different this year and have been transparent about it from the start. They do not want to give
anyone a reason not to allow their return; they want to do everything correctly and openly. They are
grateful to still be hosting on the beach after 15 years, and they are not here to jeopardize future
events.
Commissioner Suarez will be there to participate and ensure that Amy Knowles is present to assess
the lighting situation.
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas acknowledged that Director of Tourism and Culture Arrogante
has many events to manage, especially during this period, and expressed that she wished
communication had occurred earlier to prevent the situation from reaching this point. She
encouraged smoother communication going forward so that event organizers and staff are not
caught off guard.
Director of Tourism and Culture Arrogante said that it all depends on how quickly they get confirmed
written information to proceed.
Ms. Ormos added that it is difficult for them to cancel everything just to get a response when they
are planning a rapidly approaching event, so they try to keep every update as clear as possible.
Ms. Arrogante can vouch that they have been transparent.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas is glad they are in a good place now because this is a successful event,
and she wishes them the best of luck with the concert. She moved the Item.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, clarified that a motion was withdrawn by Commissioner Fernandez.
Lissette Garcia Arrogante, Director of Tourism and Culture, suggested clarifying the hours due to
ongoing back-and-forth.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas made a motion to approve the Item as is. [Clerk’s Note: Although
various, the final motion on the floor was to adopt the Resolution as presented in the agenda.]
Commissioner Suarez believes they can grant what is being asked for; this will be a first. He will be
there along with many others. If there is concern about lighting, Model Volleyball will put its best
foot forward. However, he is willing to remain open-minded and see how things go, and then they
will evaluate after a year.
Commissioner Fernandez emphasizes the importance of being present at the events they vote on.
He apologized for not attending Wodapalooza because he was out of town. The Commission is
often asked to vote on events they cannot physically attend to understand what they are approving
or not approving, including the events’ impact on noise, lighting, sanitation, traffic flow, and other
considerations. The Administration needs to improve in this area because it is difficult to make
informed decisions when the Commission has not experienced the events firsthand, especially
when it's told it cannot visit afterwards. It is important for the Commission to understand these
events when voting. In the past, he attended Model Volleyball and knows the event’s quality, its
benefits for the City, the athletes, and the partnerships it fosters, which really boost the City's
reputation. That experience gives him confidence to support the event again, as he has seen it
firsthand and trusts them as good partners of the City who aim to protect the environment,
businesses, and residents. For the City Manager, it is important to remember that these items
sometimes arise suddenly, and it is difficult for the Commission to support or oppose them without
understanding the event's challenges and merits.
Commissioner Magazine stated that outreach for events such as Future Proof should be
coordinated through the City so that Commissioners can understand what they are voting on and
supporting. He noted that Commissioner Magazine was very kind in reaching out to Future Proof
and making his City Commission colleagues feel welcome, but that such coordination should come
from the Administration. He explained that Commissioners need to experience these events
firsthand because they are often required to vote on them without having the opportunity to observe
their operations or impacts. He added that it can be challenging when elected officials from other
jurisdictions attend and later comment on these events while Commissioners themselves have not
been able to see them, making it difficult to explain the impacts to residents.
Ms. Ormos and Mr. Malone invited the City Commission to attend the event.
Addressing Commissioner Fernandez’s comment, City Manager Carpenter said that sometimes
they face challenges with events the City does not sponsor because such events are not obligated
to provide tickets. However, they have been asking the event promoters to offer opportunities for
elected officials to participate. He believed that Future Proof was reaching out, but he had heard
they did not, which is frustrating.
Commissioner Fernandez is grateful to his colleague for reaching out to [Future Proof] in a collegial
manner, but next year the Commission will have to vote on that again. How can Commissioner
Fernandez make a decision when he is not able to see the impacts and experience them? It just
puts them in a difficult position.
Commissioner Suarez suggested moving forward by putting in writing that during sea turtle nesting
season, no additional activities should impact disorientation, so vendors must be out and finished
after 9 p.m. to avoid putting them in difficult positions.

ACTION: Discussion held.
8:42:22 a.m.
Morning Session
• Kirza J. Raffo, identifying as a member of the Seniors Committee representing Four Freedoms
Tower, appeared with neighbors from the building and explained concerns regarding information
they received about reductions in donations affecting senior programs and classes. Ms. Raffo
indicated an understanding that there might be funding allocated for bingo in several buildings,
and noted that residents at Four Freedoms Tower play bingo every Friday and Saturday without
City funds, relying instead on contributions of small items such as chips, soda, cups, and paper.
Ms. Raffo emphasized that the classes offered through the senior programs were the primary
concern, identifying yoga for balance and muscle strength, dance classes that include hip and
bone exercises, and seated Zumba, which even a 94-year-old resident participates in. Ms. Raffo
described painting as the one non-physical class, noting that it supports mental engagement.
Ms. Raffo explained that the classes have grown over time and help residents physically and
mentally, particularly those who are often alone in their apartments or who have distant families.
Ms. Raffo described various benefits, including instruction on safer ways to fall, and stated that
the classes, transportation, and activities are all important. Ms. Raffo expressed that, rather than
fewer services, there is a need for more services, noting that events such as the Egg
Extravaganza at the Scott Rakow Youth Center have low participation due to a lack of
transportation. Ms. Raffo suggested that transportation options, including rideshare services,
could support attendance. Ms. Raffo concluded by noting that seniors have contributed to the
community, paid taxes, and raised families, and asked that Miami Beach continue its
longstanding support for senior programs
Commissioner Laura Dominguez thanked Ms. Raffo and clarified that the information provided
to the residents was inaccurate. Commissioner Dominguez explained that several seniors had
contacted her, stating that they had been instructed to call her and attend the meeting, which
she believed may have originated from the Mayor’s Office. She explained that she had an
agenda Item intended to add services, not remove them, and stated that she had been working
to secure additional offerings for seniors. Commissioner Dominguez advised that a request for
bingo funding from Federation Towers would be met privately by Miami-Dade County
Commissioner Vicki Lopez, and that Four Freedoms Tower had not requested bingo services,
though Rebecca Towers had. She explained that she intended to amend her agenda Item
accordingly. Commissioner Dominguez stated that the City dedicates significant funding to
senior programs, including senior meals through various programs and activities through the
Parks and Recreation Department. She identified approximately $193,000 in parks funding
allocated to senior services, including contractor costs for classes such as yoga and tai chi, and
noted the City’s annual expenditure of approximately $37,000 on bus transportation for senior
events, which she stated she hoped to increase. Commissioner Dominguez clarified that the
Housing Authority had requested additional funding, that the County would assist with some
expenses, and that her amended agenda Item would reflect a $3,000 allocation. She emphasized
that there were no cuts to services and apologized for the misinformation senior residents had
received.
Mayor Meiner responded to Commissioner Dominguez’s comments, noting that she had
referenced his office and clarifying that he had not instructed anyone to make calls regarding the
issue. Mayor Meiner stated that he had asked his Chief of Staff, who confirmed no calls were
made, and he also noted that Gloria Campos was on vacation.
Commissioner Dominguez responded that she had referred to the Mayor’s Office, not the Mayor
specifically, and reiterated that her intent was to correct the narrative.
Mayor Meiner asked Ms. Raffo if any calls had been received from his Office, and Ms. Raffo
stated that an email had been received from Gloria Campos. Ms. Raffo explained that the email
was sent to Ms. Raffo, Estrella, and other individuals, and that it indicated a donor was reducing
funding by half, which was the cause of concern. Ms. Raffo confirmed that the email did not
instruct them to contact Commissioner Dominguez and that the email did not mention
Commissioner Dominguez by name. Ms. Raffo added that others at Rebecca Towers had
reported receiving calls and that some residents were unaware of the agenda details. Ms. Raffo
reiterated that the email did not direct anyone to call.
• Alina Valdes stated that she appeared at the invitation of Kirza Raffo and noted that Ms. Raffo
had already covered most of the topics she intended to address. Ms. Valdes briefly reminded the
Mayor and Commissioners that, during the election period, seniors were assured they would be
cared for. She expressed appreciation for the services provided, stated that seniors were grateful
to live in Miami Beach, and asked that they not be forgotten.
Mayor Meiner thanked Ms. Valdes for attending and stated that he and the Commission had
made significant efforts to expand services for seniors, expressing confidence that such services
would continue to increase.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez thanked the seniors in attendance and acknowledged that the
Mayor and all Commissioners have consistently supported the senior community. Commissioner
Fernandez described the senior community as an essential part of Miami Beach and emphasized
the Commission's collective respect, appreciation, and commitment to senior residents. He
reflected on a prior discussion in which he had questioned whether a certain event should be
held, and noted that the entire Commission had unanimously supported continuing the event.
He described this unity as an example of how strongly the City values its senior residents and
noted that despite occasional tension in government, the commitment to seniors remains strong
and shared across the Commission.
• Meg Lousteau, Executive Director of the Miami Design Preservation League, addressed the
Mayor and City Commission in support of Commissioner Alex Fernandez’s Resolution R7 H,
scheduled for later on the agenda. She explained that the Resolution would authorize the City
Attorney to explore legal action regarding House Bill 399, which had been passed by the
Legislature the prior week. She stated that the Bill removes the authority of Miami Beach
residents and elected officials to make decisions regarding development within the City.
• Mitch Novick addressed the Commission and referenced the remarks made by Meg Lousteau.
He noted that the House and Senate had approved Live Local 4.0 during the prior week and
expressed hope that the Commission would consider discussing it. He reported that his business
performance in March had significantly improved, stating that there were no longer any disorder
or Police lockdowns outside his home and business. He noted that he had not been familiar with
large fitness events such as Wodapalooza or Hydrox until the previous year, and that many of
his guests over the past weekend had traveled from Switzerland, Germany, Brazil, and Uruguay
to attend them. He thanked the Commission and stated that the City was on a positive path.
• Brenda Jordan addressed the Mayor and Commission and stated that she had lived in Miami
Beach for more than 35 years. She recalled experiences early in her residency, describing the
City as lacking diversity at the time and recounting an instance in which she was appointed to
the Housing Commission but was denied participation because she did not speak Spanish. She
explained that, as an artist, she has contributed to the City's cultural and artistic diversity, but
she has experienced discrimination in a recently revised artist vendor program that she believes
was created without artist input. She stated that individuals with no artistic background had been
involved in designing the program and that artists had been excluded from decision-making. She
explained that her nonprofit organization had been cut out of grants and that she had extensive
experience with arts organizations, including the Art Center of South Florida and Countywide
arts programming. She described widespread misperceptions about Miami Beach’s diversity,
noting that during her work with inner-city children, one student expressed the belief that only
white people lived in Miami Beach. She explained that despite personal experiences with
discrimination, she refused to accept discrimination within the arts community. She stated that
the revised vendor program increased costs, offered no website or updates, and limited
opportunities for artists, including restrictions on the sale of certain types of art, such as jewelry.
She noted that she had sent numerous emails and reminded Mayor Meiner that during the
previous meeting, he had committed to meeting with her. She stated that she attempted to
schedule the meeting but received no response, though she acknowledged assistance from
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas, Commissioner Alex Fernandez, and Commissioner David
Suarez, who she said listened to her concerns even if they did not agree entirely. She stated that
some elderly artists had already been forced to move out of Miami Beach due to affordability
issues and expressed that they should not be disregarded.
Mayor Meiner responded to Ms. Jordan, explaining that he receives many meeting requests and
attempts to accommodate them all. He apologized if she had reached out, and no meeting was
arranged, noting that it was not intentional.
Ms. Jordan replied that he had previously promised the meeting and that the situation had been
ongoing since before the election.
Mayor Meiner reiterated that if she wished to have a conversation, he would make himself
available and again apologized that it had not occurred.
Ms. Jordan stated that she had sent emails, but that they had not spoken individually.
Mayor Meiner committed to speaking with her before the next Commission meeting.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas addressed Ms. Jordan and other artists, stating that she had a
Referral Item scheduled with the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee to
discuss the artist vendor program. She explained that the Committee would review opportunities
to improve the program and engage in further discussions.
Ms. Jordan stated that she had emailed repeatedly, including a detailed outline of how to
structure an artist program.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas confirmed that the referral was the first step toward addressing those
concerns. Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas reiterated her willingness to assist.
Ms. Jordan noted that Commissioner Suarez had good intentions and stated that art
encompasses many media, not solely painting.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas expressed optimism that the Commission would reach a positive
outcome.
Ms. Jordan acknowledged that Commissioner Suarez had good intentions behind the program,
but emphasized her desire for artists to be included in the development process and for subject-
matter expertise to be incorporated. She explained that she was not seeking compensation and
described herself as a cultural ambassador who brings diversity to the community. She reiterated
that she wished to build the program rather than diminish it and thanked the Commission for its
assistance.
• Alberto Galvan addressed the Commission and provided remarks in Spanish. He identified
himself and explained that he was speaking as a friend of Miami Beach residents in need and
stated that he did not have sufficient financial resources. He expressed his hope that
improvements would be made to the artist program.
Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas responded in Spanish and stated that the City had a Committee
where the program would be discussed with the goal of improving it.
• Janet Figueroa addressed the Mayor and Commission, identifying herself as one of the artist
vendors. She noted that she had previously participated in meetings with Vice-Mayor
Matteo-Salinas and Commissioner Fernandez and had spoken with Mayor Meiner and
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt outside of meetings. She expressed appreciation for the time each
had taken to listen. She explained that many vendors in the program are elderly, noting that she
herself would soon be 61 and that participants generally are over age 55. She stated that many
are struggling financially and that personal circumstances often limit their ability to work traditional
jobs. She described being injured in a car accident on the MacArthur Causeway, which resulted
in long-term medical issues that prevent her from returning to full physical labor unless she
undergoes surgery, which she stated could impair her ability to work entirely. She explained that
the artist vendor program is her only source of income. She stated that she lives outside Miami
Beach because she cannot afford housing in the City and compared her mortgage, insurance,
and taxes to the significantly higher housing costs in Miami Beach. She emphasized that she
carefully manages her budget to avoid burdening her children in the future and expressed that
the program is essential for her independence and financial stability. She thanked the Mayor and
Commissioners for listening.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, Meiner noted that no additional speakers were present in the
Commission Chamber and proceeded to hear speakers participating via Zoom.
• Alicia Casanova stated that she was speaking in her capacity as Vice President of the Mid‑Beach
Neighborhood Association (MBNA), as President of the Blue and Green Diamond Condominiums,
representing more than 2,000 residents, and as a lifelong Miami Beach resident. She expressed
support for Commissioner Alex Fernandez’s Resolution, R7 AH, and requested that it be heard
and favorably voted on. She stated that residents understood concerns raised during the Mayor’s
virtual town hall regarding the potential loss of State grant funding if the City used legal resources
to challenge House Bill 399. She emphasized that the issue involved protecting the rights of Miami
Beach residents and their ability to participate in decisions affecting the community. She stated
that the Bill was adopted in a last‑minute action by the Senate and that the City should not be
intimidated by threats of financial consequences. She stated that the Resolution did not authorize
immediate litigation but preserved the City’s ability to pursue legal action if needed based on legal
advice. She emphasized the impact the Bill would have on residents and urged the Commission
to support the Resolution.
• Oscar Vasquez, participating via Zoom, stated that he was a member of the Mid-Beach
Neighborhood Association (MBNA) and Chair of its Beach and Water Quality Working Group. He
reported that members recently attended a meeting concerning the Beachfront Management Plan
and appreciated the opportunity for community input. He thanked Commissioner Fernandez for
his participation and support. Mr. Vasquez stated that the Association had submitted public
comments on approximately 10 areas of concern and expressed an overarching concern that the
draft plan lacked a long‑term vision. He stated that while the draft adequately described existing
conditions, it did not establish a forward‑looking strategy to address environmental challenges
that could render the beach unusable. He emphasized that the beach is one of the City’s most
valuable public assets and stated that the plan should more firmly bind the County to preservation
and accountability. He identified sargassum as the Association’s top concern, citing the need for
enhanced surge response, operational scaling during peak conditions, and long‑term adaptation
strategies. He identified water quality as a second major concern, noting recurring bacteria issues

He stated that the Association also submitted comments related to concession enforcement,

• Johann Moore of Jefferson Avenue, via Zoom, stated that he opposed Item R7 A, which would
authorize the demolition of the South Shore Community Center, and reminded the Commission

He stated that the infrastructure (Fire Station 1) should not be introduced into the residential area,

of Commissioner Fernandez’s proposal to suspend exterior color review requirements for
buildings. He stated that many residents in the Historic District strongly support maintaining

• Judith Smigel, appearing via Zoom, addressed the Commission and expressed appreciation for

Board’s decision based on a finding that procedural due process had been provided, the essential
requirements of law had been observed, and the decision was supported by competent, substantial

adopted. Office of the City Attorney to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Commissioner Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
AFTER-THE-FACT RESOLUTION:
A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH,
FLORIDA, AFFIRMING THE DECISION OF THE DESIGN REVIEW BOARD ("DRB") APPROVING
THE DESIGN REVIEW APPLICATION FILED BY KC PROPERTY HOLDINGS LAND TRUST FOR
THE CONSTRUCTION OF A NEW TWO-STORY, SINGLE-FAMILY RESIDENCE AT 50 WEST DI
LIDO DRIVE, INCLUDING A WAIVER FROM THE MAXIMUM HEIGHT AND A WAIVER FROM
THE SITE WALL PICKETING REQUIREMENT (DRB FILE NO. 25-1112), UPON A FINDING THAT
THE DRB AFFORDED PROCEDURAL DUE PROCESS, OBSERVED THE ESSENTIAL
REQUIREMENTS OF LAW, AND BASED ITS DECISION UPON SUBSTANTIAL COMPETENT
EVIDENCE.
Mayor Steven Meiner welcomed Deputy City Attorney Kallergis to the dais.
Deputy City Attorney Nick Kallergis thanked Mayor Meiner and greeted the members of the City
Commission. He explained that the matter before the City Commission was an appeal of the Design
Review Board's approval of a new two-story, single-family residence at 50 West Di Lido Drive. He
stated that the application included a waiver from the maximum height limitation for single-family
homes and a waiver from the site wall picketing requirement. He indicated that the appeal had been
filed by Michael Krieger, the owner of the property located to the south at 34 West Di Lido Drive. He
explained that because the appeal concerned an order of the Design Review Board relating to a
specific property, the City Commission was sitting in a quasi-judicial capacity. He stated that the
Commission’s decision must be based exclusively on the record before the Design Review Board
and that no new testimony or evidence could be taken. He noted that members of the City
Commission had disclosed any ex parte communications on the record and that copies had been
provided to the parties. He advised that under the City Code, the City Commission could reverse or
th
remand a Design Review Board decision only upon a 5/7 vote and only if the Commission
determined that the Design Review Board failed to provide procedural due process, failed to observe
the essential requirements of law by not applying the correct law, or failed to base its decision on
competent substantial evidence. He emphasized that the City Commission could not re-weigh the
evidence presented to the Design Review Board and could only determine whether competent
evidence supported the decision. He described the order of presentation, beginning with the
petitioner, followed by the respondents, which included the property owner, the applicant, and the
City, and ending with any rebuttal by the petitioner before Commission deliberations.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez asked whether, based on the review of the hearing record and
materials, the Office of the City Attorney's position was that the Design Review Board had followed
all applicable objective criteria.
Deputy City Attorney Kallergis explained that he was serving as counsel to the City Commission for
the appeal and that the City itself was represented by Assistant City Attorney Justin Alexander. He
noted that the parties would have the opportunity to present oral argument under the Code. He
confirmed that the briefs, exhibits, and transcript formed part of the official record, and he
acknowledged the petitioner’s right to present their argument.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine thanked the City Attorney and explained that he had reviewed the
video of the Design Review Board proceedings. He summarized the procedural posture by clarifying
that the applicant had received a favorable ruling from the Design Review Board, and that the
neighbor was appealing that ruling. He indicated that the Commission’s task was not to evaluate
personal agreement or disagreement with the appellant’s position but to determine whether the
Design Review Board acted appropriately in granting the approval.
Commissioner Fernandez asked how much time the parties would have to present their arguments.
Deputy City Attorney Kallergis stated that, consistent with prior appeals, the petitioner would have
10 minutes, the respondents had agreed to divide their 10 minutes, and the petitioner would have a
2-minute rebuttal.
William W. Riley, Jr., attorney for the Petitioner, stated that he represented the appellant, Mr. Krieger,
who he described as the sole neighbor affected by the development approved by the Design Review
Board. He explained that, for efficiency, his client wished to make a statement first, after which he
would present the legal argument. He then invited Mr. Krieger to speak.
Mr. Krieger addressed the Commission and explained that he had been a resident of Di Lido for forty
years, residing at 34 West Di Lido Drive. He indicated that he had lived peacefully for decades and
routinely walked the islands. He described observing a trend of waivers being issued that exceeded
Code requirements. He stated that the purpose of the Code was being undermined by frequent
waivers related to setbacks and height. He explained that his concern regarding 50 West Di Lido
Drive was the approval of a three-foot height waiver above what was permitted by Code without a
present hardship or compelling basis. He stated that exceeding established limits without a
demonstrated hardship conflicted with the written Code and raised questions about the purpose of
adopting regulations if they could be continually exceeded. He indicated that this was not an isolated
occurrence and that repeated exceptions were altering the scale and character of the Venetian
Islands, which he described as historic. He stated that the subject property was a large double lot
with approximately 200 feet of west-facing frontage and an approximately 11,000-square-foot home.
He noted that the applicant had originally requested a two-foot height increase, which he rejected,
and that the request was increased to three feet at the hearing. He stated that the height increase
was not necessary and did not meet the hardship requirement, and that it contributed to what he
considered incremental overbuilding. He asked the City Commission to ensure that deviations were
supported by a legitimate hardship and consistent with regulatory intent. He requested that his
statement be entered into the record.
Commissioner David Suarez asked Mr. Krieger to remain at the podium. He asked whether Mr.
Krieger had requested half a million dollars from the applicant in exchange for his approval of the
project.
Mr. Krieger responded that attorneys for the parties had engaged in negotiations before the hearing
and denied that this was the basis for his appeal.
Commissioner Suarez asked again whether he had requested half a million dollars from the
applicant.
Mr. Krieger denied making such a request.
Commissioner Suarez referenced information indicating that Mr. Krieger had sent a demand letter
to a Miami Beach resident, Melissa Beattie, regarding statements she made about alleged quid pro
quo concerns related to the project.
Mr. Krieger stated that Ms. Beattie had publicly accused him of extortion, which is a criminal
allegation, and that he asked her to withdraw the statement, which she subsequently did.
Commissioner Suarez asked whether Mr. Krieger or any representative had attempted to negotiate
a half-million-dollar settlement in exchange for Mr. Krieger’s support for the project.
Mr. Krieger denied that he or his representatives had engaged in such negotiations and stated that
discussions were limited to matters concerning height.
Commissioner Fernandez asked whether the statements being provided were under oath, noting
that such testimony in quasi-judicial matters was typically sworn.
Deputy City Attorney Kallergis confirmed that the proceeding was quasi-judicial and explained that
oral argument was ordinarily conducted by counsel, although the petitioner had requested to address
the Commission. He acknowledged that witnesses in such proceedings were usually sworn before
providing testimony.
Commissioner Fernandez reiterated that individuals testifying in such matters were ordinarily placed
under oath.
Deputy City Attorney Kallergis stated that he would administer an oath and asked Mr. Krieger
whether the testimony he had provided, as well as any additional testimony he might give, was the
truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.
Commissioner Suarez repeated that discussions had taken place and insisted that Mr. Krieger
provide a simple affirmative or negative response. He reminded Mr. Krieger that he was under oath
and asked that the question be repeated once more.
Deputy City Attorney Kallergis again asked Mr. Krieger to affirm whether the testimony he had given
and would give was the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.
Mr. Krieger responded that before answering the oath question, he wished to clarify that his attorneys
had been negotiating a settlement and that he had not been directly involved in those discussions.
He stated that his testimony regarding that point was truthful.
Deputy City Attorney Kallergis recommended that the remaining argument be limited to counsel for
the parties.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he wished for Mr. Krieger to be under oath because he believed
that significant allegations were being made and sought clarity on that point.
Mr. Krieger questioned what allegations he was being accused of making and indicated that his
concern related only to height.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he wanted Mr. Krieger to respond with a simple affirmative or
negative answer.
Mr. Krieger asked what specific question he was being asked to answer.
Deputy City Attorney Kallergis restated the oath and informed Mr. Krieger that because he had
provided testimony, he would again be asked to affirm whether his current and future testimony
would be truthful.
Mr. Krieger declined to answer the oath question.
Deputy City Attorney Kallergis reiterated his recommendation that the argument proceed through
counsel.
Mayor Steven Meiner accepted the recommendation.
Deputy City Attorney Kallergis explained that under the City Code and general practice, attorneys
presenting oral argument in quasi‑judicial proceedings were not required to be placed under oath,
as they were not testifying. He clarified that the Item was an oral argument and not a public hearing.
Commissioner Fernandez asked whether individuals who wished to testify in such proceedings,
other than attorneys, could be sworn in at the outset in the same manner as typical quasi‑judicial
proceedings.
Deputy City Attorney Kallergis stated that such a procedure had not occurred during his thirteen
years with the City.
Mr. Riley addressed the Commission and noted that the record needed to be clear for any reviewing
court. He explained his understanding that the appellant would present first, the respondents would
follow, and the appellant would then have an opportunity to respond. He requested clarification
because, although his time had been paused, he had a pending procedural question. He
emphasized that clarity was necessary to avoid confusion in the record.
Commissioner Suarez asked whether an offer of half a million dollars had been made to obtain Mr.
Krieger’s approval for the project involving the property owner, Mr. Sanjay (representative of the
applicant).
Mr. Riley responded that the answer was no and asked to provide an explanation. He explained that
before his involvement, the property owner and Mr. Krieger met to attempt to reach an agreement,
but were unable to do so. He stated that Mr. Krieger then retained counsel, and he, as counsel,
began discussing a settlement with the law firm representing the applicant. He stated that the
proposed settlement primarily focused on relocating the outdoor entertainment area from the south
side of the lot adjacent to Mr. Krieger’s property to the north side, where there were no residential
neighbors. He explained that the applicant indicated that relocation was not possible, and Mr. Krieger
expressed concern that the proposal would substantially diminish the value of his home. Mr. Riley
stated that he advised his client that any claim regarding loss of value required empirical support.
He explained that Mr. Krieger obtained a written evaluation from Berkshire Hathaway, which
concluded that the proposed height and resulting canyon effect would reduce property value by
millions of dollars. He stated that this written opinion was submitted to the record. Mr. Riley explained
that the settlement proposal sought mitigation of damages consistent with the professional valuation
and that the requested mitigation amount was $500,000. He emphasized that the proposal was not
intended to secure approval but to offset potential valuation loss if the entertainment area was not
relocated. He explained that the City Code required disclosure of settlement discussions and that he
complied with that requirement. He clarified that the applicant did not provide its own valuation
analysis.
Commissioner Suarez asked what the proposed mitigation amount would accomplish.
Mr. Riley explained that mitigation would offset the anticipated devaluation of the home. He provided
a hypothetical analogy involving adjacent disruptive uses to illustrate how property value impacts
could constitute damages.
Commissioner Suarez stated that the only deviation from the Code was the three‑foot height waiver
and noted that this was not comparable to a disruptive use next door. He questioned how three feet
could result in $500,000 in damages and stated that the location of the entertainment area would
remain the same regardless of the additional height.
Deputy City Attorney Kallergis clarified that no variances had been approved, only a waiver.
Commissioner Suarez restated that the matter involved a three‑foot height waiver.
Mr. Riley responded that height could create shadowing effects and that this was one of their
objections. He explained that the City Code required a view corridor analysis that had not been
submitted. He further stated that the absence of a lighting plan created additional uncertainty
regarding potential overcast conditions. He reiterated that the primary concern was the location of
the outdoor entertainment area and the resulting noise impacts.
Commissioner Suarez stated that the entertainment area could be built without the additional three
feet of height.
Mr. Riley responded that the City had invested extensive resources in developing the Zoning Code
and that waivers were intended only for exceptional circumstances. He stated that an applicant must
demonstrate irregularities or extraordinary conditions to justify height relief. He stated that no such
circumstances existed in this case. He described the expert opinion as concluding that the three‑foot
increase would create a canyon effect, resulting in significant property devaluation. He stated that
the disclosure of settlement discussions had been made as required by the Code and that the Design
Review Board hearing became overshadowed by assertions that the appellant was attempting to
sell approval. He described that multiple speakers were asked during the hearing whether they had
requested monetary compensation. He stated that this narrative overshadowed the substantive
issues. He explained that their settlement proposal offered multiple potential options and that the
applicant had declined all of them.
Commissioner Suarez stated that if the three-foot height waiver had not been requested and the
applicant had kept the outdoor entertainment area in its original location, the circumstances would
have remained the same except for the reduced height. He noted that the Planning Director had
described the increase as de minimis and stated that the situation appeared different in light of a
proposed settlement amount of half a million dollars intended to resolve opposition.
Mr. Riley responded that the proposal was not intended to make the opposition disappear and stated
that neither he nor his client had engaged in such conduct. He stated that his firm had consistently
made disclosures regarding settlement discussions, as required by the Code. He emphasized that
such disclosures were not unusual.
Commissioner Magazine offered a hypothetical involving two neighbors: one sought support for a
minor deviation from the Code, and the other provided assistance in exchange for anything from
minimal compensation to a substantial amount. He stated that such private negotiations were not
typically a governmental concern, provided they were disclosed. He stated that he did not observe
any indication from the Design Review Board proceedings suggesting that the requested waiver had
been granted on the basis of those disclosures. He added that the appellant would have the
opportunity to present further argument regarding whether the waiver had been properly granted.
Commissioner Fernandez referenced materials provided to the City Commission, including a letter
from Jason Zarco. He asked Mr. Riley to confirm the author of the letter.

Berkshire Hathaway.
Commissioner Fernandez asked about Mr. Zarco’s professional qualifications and whether he was
an appraiser.
Mr. Riley responded that Mr. Zarco was a licensed real estate agent and not, to his knowledge, an

items.title: DISCUSS/TAKE ACTION: EXPLORE POSSIBLE NAMING RIGHTS OPPORTUNITIES TO FUND CAPITAL PROJECTS.
items.action: Discussion held. Vice‑Mayor Monica Matteo‑Salinas made a motion directing the Administration to explore naming‑rights opportunities and report back to the City Commission; seconded by Commissioner Alex Fernandez. Vote: 7-0. Melissa Berthier and Steven Anthony to handle. DIRECTION: 1. The Administration is directed to explore possible naming-rights opportunities for City facilities, identify appropriate locations, evaluate existing advertising practices for consistency with the exclusion categories discussed, and return to the City Commission with recommendations. Melissa Berthier and Steven Anthony to handle. 2. The Office of the City Attorney will prepare an Item for the April 22, 2026 Commission Meeting to address Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt’s fundraising concept, and will determine whether to structure it as an Item for Vice‑Mayor Monica Matteo‑Salinas, an Item for Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt, or a combined Item if they prefer to collaborate. Office of the City Attorney to handle.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Discussion held. Vice‑Mayor Monica Matteo‑Salinas made a motion directing the
Administration to explore naming‑rights opportunities and report back to the City Commission;
seconded by Commissioner Alex Fernandez. Vote: 7-0. Melissa Berthier and Steven Anthony to
handle.
DIRECTION:
1. The Administration is directed to explore possible naming-rights opportunities for City facilities,
identify appropriate locations, evaluate existing advertising practices for consistency with the
exclusion categories discussed, and return to the City Commission with recommendations.
Melissa Berthier and Steven Anthony to handle.
2. The Office of the City Attorney will prepare an Item for the April 22, 2026 Commission Meeting
to address Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt’s fundraising concept, and will determine whether to
structure it as an Item for Vice‑Mayor Monica Matteo‑Salinas, an Item for Commissioner Tanya
K. Bhatt, or a combined Item if they prefer to collaborate. Office of the City Attorney to handle.
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo‑Salinas opened the discussion by indicating an interest in exploring
opportunities for naming rights and advertising across City facilities. She referenced a prior
corporate offer related to co‑naming the Convention Center, recalling that Norwegian Cruise Lines
had proposed funding of approximately $11 million for a five‑year term, and asked for confirmation
of the details. She described the context of current cost‑reduction efforts and stated that identifying
additional revenue sources may be advisable. She cited a Miami‑Dade County example of a park
sponsored by Chewy and suggested outreach to corporate partners, including Chewy, for possible
advertising at City facilities. She noted that one of her upcoming budget allocations concerns the
Flamingo Park football/soccer field and that re‑turfing is estimated at approximately $1.3 million.
She proposed engaging Adidas, considering multiple events occurring in the City and increased
interest surrounding FIFA, to pursue a co‑naming arrangement in exchange for funding (e.g.,
branding the track as “Adidas Flamingo Park track”). She stated that she brought the matter for
Commission discussion rather than committee referral to obtain feedback from the full body and to
direct staff to return with ideas and appropriate locations without burdening committee agendas.
City Manager Eric Carpenter asked Marketing and Communications staff to join the discussion and
requested participation from Melissa Berthier.
Office of Marketing and Communications Director Melissa Berthier confirmed that the prior
Convention Center naming proposal was a ten‑year deal and stated that the Commission turned
down the proposal at that time. She indicated that the City does not currently have a sales team
and explained that specialized firms manage naming‑rights sales, typically receiving a percentage
of proceeds; she added that Communications could coordinate with the Economic Development
Department to do its best within existing capabilities. (
Commissioner Alex Fernandez explained that he has traditionally been cautious about naming
rights due to the possibility that a sponsor’s values could later conflict with City policies or
community expectations. He observed that current fiscal conditions differ from those four years ago
when the Convention Center naming proposal was considered, and he noted potential shifts in
revenues and possible Statewide property‑tax changes affecting funding for operations and
maintenance. He stated that it is prudent to explore opportunities with outside entities that have
relevant relationships and negotiation expertise, while acknowledging that not all proposals will be
viable. He reiterated that the Communications Department manages communications and
marketing but does not conduct media sales and added that the City should not engage directly in
the sales functions for naming rights. He described an approach utilizing an experienced outside
entity to manage negotiations and indicated support for the Vice‑Mayor’s motion in light of the
changing financial landscape.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine indicated caution but openness to evaluating acceptable
proposals and emphasized the importance of retaining Commission oversight while avoiding
micromanagement. He provided an example of potential branding of a City facility by Adidas and
jokingly offered a personal contribution of $500 toward a Citywide “Magazine Orange Cone
Removal” capital project.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt stated that she has historically opposed corporate naming rights but
is open to considering opportunities. She expressed reservations about engaging an outside sales
organization to “sell the City,” preferring a curated approach aligned to specific properties and
suitable sponsors. She proposed exploring a municipal fundraising model similar to philanthropic
development used by not‑for‑profit institutions, targeting engagement with high‑net‑worth residents
to underwrite projects or assume maintenance costs, and requested legal guidance on the feasibility
and structure of such fundraising, such as establishing a dedicated City office or engaging a firm.
She clarified that her concept would not involve a political organization or PAC and characterized
the approach as high‑end and long‑term relationship development.
City Attorney Ricardo J. Dopico responded that a similar concept had been considered several
months prior and recalled that, during the Mayor Levine Administration, a fundraising entity
structured as a 501(c)(3) was created but later discontinued due to concerns. He stated that his
Office could revisit the concept and propose guardrails to address previously identified issues,
considering the current economic climate. He advised that the municipal fundraising concept should
proceed as a separate Item and noted that, because the Vice‑Mayor was presiding as acting Mayor
at that moment, she could not make a motion from the Chair; however, he understood her direction
to be a request for Administration to develop potential naming opportunities and return to the
Commission. He explained that the City’s naming process includes multiple steps, such as Public
Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee review, and that some proposals may require
a referendum, ensuring substantial Commission input.
Commissioner Fernandez described the former One Miami Beach foundation created under Mayor
Levine, noting that it had a board of directors, including the late Commissioner Joy Malakoff, and
focused on community contributions for reinvestment in City projects. He suggested that, if
re‑establishing a nonprofit is not feasible, the City could consider hiring a development professional
to cultivate stakeholder relationships and facilitate private contributions for specific initiatives. He
noted that the City can accept private contributions by Resolution and stated that compensation
structures in the nonprofit sector sometimes include percentages tied to funds raised.
Vice‑Mayor Monica Matteo‑Salinas stated that her intent includes exploring partnerships both with
corporate entities and with families interested in supporting neighborhood pocket parks. She
described a recent example involving an upcoming corporate event whose host sought to wrap a
lifeguard stand with a logo, noted that the proposed arrangement would allow this at no charge, and
suggested the City should consider applying fees for such branding. She stated that Muscle Beach
frequently hosts brand activations and suggested evaluating interior banner placements along the
coral wall as a revenue opportunity. She asked staff to identify categories of sponsors to exclude.
Office of Marketing and Communications Director Melissa Berthier asked whether categories such
as alcohol should be excluded from consideration.
Vice‑Mayor Matteo‑Salinas indicated that alcohol and vape products should be excluded.
Commissioner Fernandez added cigarettes, CBD, and THC to the list of excluded categories and
suggested reviewing existing advertising agreements to ensure consistency across platforms.
Office of Marketing and Communications Director Berthier noted that alcohol advertising is not
permitted on trolleys under current practice, but it is permitted on bus shelters.
City Manager Carpenter clarified that the trolley advertising restriction was an administrative, not
legislative, decision and stated that he has directed the Marketing and Communications Department
not to advertise alcohol on trolleys.
Commissioner Fernandez recommended adopting a consistent Citywide standard for excluded
categories.
Commissioner Suarez added that adult‑toy advertising should not be considered.
Commissioner Fernandez observed that revisiting naming rights had previously been controversial
and expressed support for reconsidering the topic to help close funding gaps and maintain
operations and maintenance.
Mayor Steven Meiner indicated that the City has received private‑sector interest related to the water
taxi, including potential partnerships to help fund routes and naming options, and stated that this
aligns with the discussion of naming‑rights opportunities.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez stated that revisiting the topic required initiative, referenced the prior
controversial discussion from four years earlier, commended the Vice-Mayor for bringing the matter
forward again, and supported evaluating opportunities to maintain operations and the level of
service expected by residents.
Vice‑Mayor Matteo‑Salinas asked if there were additional comments.
City Clerk Rafael E. Granado recorded the vote on the motion made by Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas
and seconded by Commissioner Alex Fernandez, directing the Administration to explore
naming-rights opportunities and report back to the City Commission. He announced that the motion
was approved 7-0.
City Clerk Granado noted that Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt had a separate Item she would be
bringing forward.
City Attorney Dopico clarified that his Office would prepare an Item for the April meeting to address
Commissioner Bhatt’s fundraising concept and stated that the matter could be structured as an Item
for Vice-Mayor Matteo-Salinas, an Item for Commissioner Bhatt, or a combined Item if they
preferred to work together.
items.motion: Salinas made a motion directing the Administration to explore naming‑rights opportunities and report back to the City Commission; seconded by Commissioner Alex Fernandez.

items.title: DISCUSS/TAKE ACTION – UPDATE AND DISCUSSION ON POLICE ENFORCEMENT EFFORTS AND DATA RELATED TO EXCESSIVE VEHICULAR MUFFLER AND EXHAUST NOISE THROUGHOUT OUR CITY.
items.action: Discussion held. Item to come back for update at the next Commission Meeting. Chief Wayne Jones to handle. DIRECTION: Prepare an updated report on nighttime muffler and exhaust noise enforcement for presentation at the April 22, 2026 Commission Meeting. Chief Wayne Jones to handle. See also the discussion with Item R5 M.
items.voteBasis: No separate vote identified. A vote has not been inferred.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Discussion held. Item to come back for update at the next Commission Meeting. Chief
Wayne Jones to handle.
DIRECTION:
Prepare an updated report on nighttime muffler and exhaust noise enforcement for presentation at
the April 22, 2026 Commission Meeting. Chief Wayne Jones to handle.
See also the discussion with Item R5 M.
Mayor Meiner previously brought legislation, co-prime-sponsored by Commissioner Dominguez,
addressing residents’ concerns. He asked for an update, specifically on mufflers and loud exhaust.
Some car noises are legal if the vehicle is built that way, but loud exhaust noises are usually illegal.
The recent legislation he introduced with Commissioner Dominguez, supported by the Commission,
focused on nighttime enforcement from 10:00 p.m. to 5:00 a.m., especially when people are trying
to relax and sleep. These cars often drive down the streets intentionally to disturb the peace. Such
vehicles are easier for the Police to locate because there are few of them on the road. He asked
Police Assistant Chief Morgalo to provide information on enforcement efforts and detailed citation
statistics.
Assistant Police Chief Daniel Morgalo reported that in 2025, 675 citations were issued specifically
for loud mufflers and noise from vehicles. So far in 2026, based on recommendations from the City
Commission, guidance, and resident feedback, Chief Jones has prioritized addressing this issue,
focusing on areas outlined in the Resolution: the Fifth Street Corridor, 41st Corridor, both
Causeways, and 71st Street from 44th to 63rd along the Collins corridor. In the first 2.5 months of
2026, they have issued 513 citations, compared to 675 for the entire previous year. Over 80%, or
397 citations, have been written during the midnight shift, which is after 10:00 p.m. and before 6:00
a.m., as directed by the City Commission. They are very proud of their team and the efforts they are
making to prioritize this issue among many others, and they have been successful so far and will
continue to do an excellent job addressing it. If necessary, they will increase efforts. They started
Operation Quiet Streets in January, partnered with the Florida Highway Patrol (FHP), and are also
issuing citations. City of Miami Police are also involved, and social media shows that Fort Lauderdale
and other jurisdictions are facing similar issues.
Mayor Meiner added that it is always good to have Police presence, so there are a few major spots,
whether it be Fifth Street off the MacArthur, 41st, 71st Street, Belle Isle, or the Collins corridor. There
are other areas, but in the legislation that Commissioner Dominguez and he brought, and that the
City Commission approved, they focused on key spots where one car with illegal exhaust can impact
thousands of people. People jump out of their beds; it is unsafe and dangerous from personal
experience, and these cars definitely need to be pulled over. There is a Police-visibility aspect, and
these locations are easy to catch, which is why they have that high level of detail. Most drivers know
they are likely to get caught.
In response to Mayor Meiner, Assistant Chief of Police Morgalo mentioned that from 10:00 p.m. to
5:00 a.m., it is not an issue because the traffic is lighter, which makes it easier to pinpoint specific
vehicles, something that is more difficult in dense traffic. Another benefit is that calls are usually
fewer between 10:00 p.m. and 6:00 a.m., so they have resources available not only for noise
enforcement but also for addressing speeding and reckless driving. This approach maximizes
visibility, improves productivity, and helps direct the main force to the areas most important to the
community and the City Commission. They are happy to return next month and continue reporting
on the great work they are doing.

D/B/A FOUNDATION RISK PARTNERS PUBLIC ENTITY SERVICES, UNTIL A REPLACEMENT AGREEMENT IS EXECUTED AND SERVICES ARE TRANSITIONED. (HUMAN RESOURCES)
items.action: The request was approved. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: The request was approved. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by
Commissioner Fernanez. Commissioner made a Fernandez motion to adopt the Resolution;
seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Marla Alpizar and Kristy Bada to handle.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez, who separated the Item from the consent agenda, addressed the
Commission. He stated that although he fully supported issuing the Request for Proposals, he wished
to briefly discuss the matter to ensure that expectations were properly set for the forthcoming contract.
He explained that the selected consultant would influence the manner in which the City supported its
employee healthcare system and the expectations associated with that work. He asked the staff to
confirm that understanding.
Human Resources Director Marla Alpiza confirmed it.
Commissioner Fernandez noted that healthcare costs traditionally grew rapidly within municipal
budgets and stated that although recent fiscal years reflected better cost containment, it was
important to establish expectations for continued moderation of cost growth. He emphasized the need
for the consultant to focus on employee satisfaction and referenced the prior presence of an on-site
employee-facing representative, which he described as particularly helpful and no longer available.
He stated that he wanted to ensure the consultant understood the City’s expectations regarding both
cost management and service to employees.
Kristy Bada, Chief Procurement Officer, acknowledged the direction and stated that the expectations
would be incorporated.
Commissioner Fernandez moved the Item. Commissioner David Suarez seconded the motion. Mayor
Steven Meiner called for the vote. The Commission voted unanimously. The Item was approved by a
7-0 vote.

Action: Report was given.
PRIORITY ITEMS
1. DISCUSS THE LDR AND COMPREHENSIVE PLAN AMENDMENTS PERTAINING TO THE
