with no discussion.
2. DISCUSS THE CREATION OF A TRANSFER OF DEVELOPMENT RIGHTS (TDR)
PROGRAM FOR WASHINGTON AVENUE. Deferred to a future date with no discussion.
3. DISCUSS AND REVIEW PLANNING/ZONING RESTRICTIONS THAT DELAY THE PERMIT
PROCESS AND CONSIDER POSSIBLE AMENDMENTS. Item Not Reached - Deferred to
April 1, 2026, with no discussion.
REGULAR ITEMS
4. AN AMENDMENT TO THE LAND DEVELOPMENT REGULATIONS OF THE CITY CODE
(LDRS) TO MODIFY THE APPLICATION AND REVIEW PROCEDURES FOR ALL LAND
USE BOARDS AND TO EXPAND THE TYPES OF DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS AND
IMPROVEMENTS LOCATED OUTSIDE OF HISTORIC DISTRICTS AND SITES THAT CAN
BE APPROVED AT STAFF LEVEL (Dual Referral to the Planning Board). Motion – By
Acclamation: Conclude the Item in accordance with the recommendations set forth in the
LUSC memo and an additional recommendation that the Planning Board discuss and provide
feedback regarding the proposal to allow rooftop additions up to 35 feet in height.
5. DISCUSS DEVELOPING ALL OF THE WEST LOTS LYING ALONG COLLINS AVENUE
BETWEEN 79TH STREET AND 87TH STREET INTO A PLANNED CITY PARK IN NORTH
BEACH. Motion – By Acclamation: Continue the Item to the April 1, 2026, LUSC meeting with
the following direction: a. Combine this discussion with the Item 14 as a single the Item under
the sponsorship of Commissioners Tanya K. Bhatt and David Suarez. b. The administration
shall proceed with a park master plan for the west lots. c. The administration shall explore
procurement options for a consultant, including engaging in initial discussions with Savino and
Miller. d. The administration shall convene a town hall/community meeting for additional input
from all affected stakeholders.
6. CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO THE COMPREHENSIVE PLAN AND LAND
DEVELOPMENT REGULATIONS TO INCENTIVIZE THE ABANDONMENT OF RETAIL OR
PACKAGE SALES OF ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES BY BUSINESSES LOCATED ALONG
LINCOLN ROAD. Item Not Reached - Deferred to April 1, 2026, with no discussion.
7. DISCUSS AMENDMENTS TO THE RESILIENCY CODE REGARDING VETERINARY AND
ANIMAL CLINICS IN CERTAIN RESIDENTIAL PERFORMANCE STANDARD ZONING
DISTRICTS. Motion – By Acclamation: Conclude the Item with a recommendation that the
City Commission refer an ordinance to the Planning Board in accordance with the draft text
provided in the LUSC memo.
8. DISCUSS AN LDR AMENDMENT PERTAINING TO A PROPOSED DISTANCE
SEPARATION EXEMPTION FOR TOBACCO AND VAPE USES IN NORTH BEACH. Motion
– By Acclamation: Move the ordinance back to the City Commission with no recommendation.
Additionally, at First Reading, the City Commission should consider including a three (3) year
sunset provision for the exception, with a requirement that all tobacco and vape sales cease
within 3 years.
9. DISCUSS POSSIBLE INCLUSION OF A CHARTER OR PRIVATE SCHOOL WITHIN THE
72ND STREET COMMUNITY CENTER PROJECT. Item Not Reached - Deferred to April 1,
2026, with no discussion.
10. DISCUSS POSSIBLE PROCUREMENT OF A NEW MONUMENT SIGN FOR MAURICE
GIBB MEMORIAL PARK. Motion – By Acclamation: Continue the Item to the July 15, 2026,
LUSC meeting for additional updates. Additionally, the CIP Department is directed to work
with affected stakeholders in the Sunset Harbor neighborhood to develop a sign concept and
bring a separate referral to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee (FERC)
regarding funding for the sign.
11. DISCUSS THE NORTH BEACH WATER QUALITY AND PARK VIEW CANAL REPORT.
Deferred to April 1, 2026, with no discussion.
12. DISCUSS A COMPREHENSIVE BRANDING CAMPAIGN FOR THE ART DECO HISTORIC
DISTRICT OF SOUTH BEACH. Motion – By Acclamation: Conclude the Item with a
recommendation that the City Commission consider a similar branding campaign for historic
districts in North Beach.
13. MONTHLY UPDATES ON HISTORIC HOTEL REDEVELOPMENT ON COLLINS AVENUE
BETWEEN 14TH AND 20TH STREETS, INCLUDING AN OVERVIEW OF PENDING
PERMITS AND PROGRESS UPDATES FROM DEVELOPMENT TEAMS. Motion – By
Acclamation: Continue the Item to the April 1, 2026, LUSC meeting with the following direction:
e. The administration shall reach out to representatives of the Raleigh Hotel and request that
they attend the April 1, 2026, LUSC meeting to discuss the status of the project. f. The
Communications Department shall coordinate marketing efforts with the Delano Hotel to
promote the reopening of the building.
14. DISCUSS FUTURE PROGRAMMING FOR WEST LOTS. Motion – By Acclamation: Continue
the Item to the April 1, 2026, LUSC meeting with the following direction: a. Combine this
discussion with the Item 5 as a single the Item under the sponsorship of Commissioners Tanya
K. Bhatt and David Suarez. b. The administration shall proceed with a park master plan for
the west lots. c. The administration shall explore procurement options for a consultant,
including engaging in initial discussions with Savino and Miller. d. The administration shall
convene a town hall/community meeting for additional input from all affected stakeholders.
15. DISCUSS AND CONSIDER ADOPTING A "LIVE BETTER" PROGRAM, INCLUDING
ZONING AND OTHER INCENTIVES, TO PROMOTE ATTAINABLE HOUSING SOLUTIONS
IN MIAMI BEACH FOR MIDDLE-INCOME INDIVIDUALS AND FAMILIES. Deferred to a
future date with no discussion.
16. DISCUSS DEDICATED BUS LANES ON WASHINGTON AVENUE. Item Not Reached -
Deferred to April 1, 2026, with no discussion.
17. PROVIDE A PRESENTATION OF THE 41ST STREET CORRIDOR PROJECT STATUS
AND FUTURE DIRECTION. Motion – By Acclamation: Conclude the Item with the following
additional recommendations: a. Schedule bi-weekly status updates for all affected
stakeholders. b. Conduct a survey of existing (available) off-street parking spaces within the
41st Street area and plan for a potential future increase in parking demand.
FUTURE ITEMS:
18. DISCUSS THE CREATION OF A TRUST FUND TO SUPPORT CAPITAL
INFRASTRUCTURE IMPROVEMENTS WHEN DENSITY AND/OR FLOOR AREA RATIO
AMENDMENTS ARE BEING CONSIDERED IN THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH.
19. REVIEW EXISTING FENCING REQUIREMENTS IN THE LAND DEVELOPMENT
REGULATIONS FOR VACANT AND ABANDONED PROPERTIES, AS WELL AS
CONSTRUCTION SITES; AND CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO STREAMLINE THE
EXISTING REQUIREMENTS FOR APPLICANTS AND PROPERTY OWNERS (Dual Referral
to the Planning Board).
20. DISCUSS THE CREATION OF A FINANCIAL INCENTIVE PROGRAM FOR LANDLORDS
FOR THE CONVERSION OF SHORT-TERM RENTAL PROPERTY TO LONG-TERM
LEASES.
21. CONSIDER POTENTIAL INCENTIVES, INCLUDING AMENDMENTS TO THE LAND
DEVELOPMENT REGULATIONS AND/OR CODE OF ORDINANCES, FOR THE
PRESERVATION AND RETENTION OF MATURE AND HERITAGE TREES ON PRIVATE
PROPERTY; AND TO REQUIRE MATURE AND HERITAGE TREE PRESERVATION AND
RETENTION AS PART OF PUBLIC CAPITAL IMPROVEMENT PROJECTS IN THE CITY OF
MIAMI BEACH.

PERMIT A TEMPORARY SALES BUILDING WITHIN THE ALTON BEACH BAYFRONT
OVERLAY IN A LIMITED CAPACITY WHEN CERTAIN REQUIREMENTS ARE SATISFIED.
(Dual Referral to the Planning Board).
23. CONSIDER POTENTIAL INCENTIVES FOR THE CONSTRUCTION OF LIVING SEAWALLS
ON PRIVATE PROPERTY AND AS PART OF PUBLIC CAPITAL IMPROVEMENT
PROJECTS IN THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, WHICH MAY INCLUDE AMENDMENTS TO
THE CITY CODE.
24. REVIEW AND CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO CITY POLICIES TO PRIORITIZE
EXPANDING PUBLIC AND PRIVATE GREEN SPACE, ENCOURAGE SUSTAINABLE
LANDSCAPING, AND REDUCE POLLUTION.
25. DISCUSS POTENTIAL INCENTIVES FOR THE INSTALLATION OF GREEN ROOFS ON
NEW AND EXISTING BUILDINGS, INCLUDING POSSIBLE AMENDMENTS TO THE CITY
CODE AND LAND DEVELOPMENT REGULATIONS.
26. DISCUSS INCORPORATION OF RESILIENCY MEASURES IN CITY PARKS AND
GREENSPACE PROJECTS.
27. DISCUSS UNIFORM OVERSIGHT AND REGULATION OF BEACHFRONT CONCESSIONS
AND CHAIR USAGE.
28. DISCUSS ALLOWING THE INSTALLATION OF SECURITY GATES AT REBECCA
TOWERS, A SENIOR HOUSING FACILITY IN MIAMI BEACH.
29. DISCUSS THE POTENTIAL DEVELOPMENT AND IMPLEMENTATION OF CITYWIDE
REGULATIONS PERTAINING TO COMMERCIAL VEHICLE DELIVERIES ON PRIVATE
PROPERTY.
30. DISCUSS AND CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS OF THE
CONSTRUCTION, PARKING, AND TRAFFIC MANAGEMENT PLAN (CPTMP)
REQUIREMENT IN CHAPTER 106 OF THE CITY CODE, INCLUDING WITHOUT
LIMITATION THE SUSPENSION OF A BUILDING PERMIT OR ISSUANCE OF A STOP
WORK ORDER; AND DISCUSS PROACTIVE ENFORCEMENT EFFORTS BY THE POLICE,
CODE COMPLIANCE, AND PARKING DEPARTMENTS WITH REGARD TO PARKING OR
TRAFFIC VIOLATIONS RELATING TO CONSTRUCTION PROJECTS.
31. DISCUSS AND CONSIDER RECOMMENDATIONS RELATING TO THE CITY OF MIAMI
BEACH SIDEWALK MATERIAL/COLOR POLICY, INCLUDING THE REVIEW OF DESIGN
OPTIONS AND MAINTENANCE STRATEGIES FOR MIAMI BEACH RED SIDEWALKS.
32. DISCUSS THE CREATION OF A MIAMI BEACH HISTORICAL MUSEUM, AND IDENTIFY
POTENTIAL SITES ON CITY-OWNED PROPERTY, INCLUDING, WITHOUT LIMITATION,
AN UNDERUTILIZED OR VACANT STOREFRONT IN A CITY-OWNED BUILDING, IN
ORDER TO COMPLEMENT THE CITY’S ROBUST CULTURAL OFFERINGS WITH A NEW
INSTITUTION FOCUSED ON THE HISTORY OF MIAMI BEACH (Dual Referral to Finance
and Economic Resiliency Committee).
33. DISCUSS HOLDING COMPANIES DOING BUSINESS WITHIN CITY LIMITS
RESPONSIBLE FOR EDUCATING THEIR DRIVERS ABOUT THE PROHIBITION OF
BLOCKING/DOUBLE PARKING IN THE RIGHT-OF-WAYS.
34. DISCUSS BEAUTIFYING THE FLYOVER BRIDGE LOCATED AT THE INTERSECTION OF
MACARTHUR CAUSEWAY TO FIFTH STREET IN SOUTH BEACH.
35. BI-MONTHLY UPDATE ON CODE ENFORCEMENT ACTIVITIES, AND THE STATUS OF
SPECIAL MAGISTRATE CASES, INVOLVING PROPERTIES AND/OR BUSINESSES
LOCATED IN NORTH BEACH, AND TO ADDRESS ANY ONGOING CONCERNS AND NEW
DEVELOPMENTS IN NORTH BEACH.
36. DISCUSS STRENGTHENING THE CITY’S GREEN PROCUREMENT POLICIES WITH
REGARD TO SINGLE-USE PLASTIC FOOD SERVICE ARTICLES AND ENCOURAGE THE
USE OF ALTERNATIVES, AND CONSIDER GUIDELINES FOR THE CITY MANAGER TO
NEGOTIATE, AS PART OF FUTURE CITY CONTRACTS, ADDITIONAL RESTRICTIONS
ON THE USE OF SINGLE-USE PLASTICS AND COMMITMENTS TO USE ALTERNATIVE
PRODUCTS.
37. DISCUSS THE STATUS OF THE NORTH BEACH MASTER PLAN.
38. DISCUSS CHANGES IN STATE LAW PERTAINING TO TELECOMMUNICATIONS
FACILITIES IN THE RIGHT-OF-WAY AND CONSIDER CORRESPONDING AMENDMENTS
TO CHAPTER 104 OF THE CITY CODE, ENTITLED “TELECOMMUNICATIONS,” AND
RELATED PROVISIONS IN THE LAND DEVELOPMENT REGULATIONS.
39. DISCUSS ADDING TO THE LAND USE AND SUSTAINABILITY COMMITTEE AGENDA
MONTHLY UPDATES ON THE G.O. BOND BEACHWALK REFORESTATION PROJECT.
40. REQUEST FOR THE ADMINISTRATION TO EXPLORE AND RECOMMEND NEW, MORE
FORWARD-LEANING RESILIENCY CODE UPDATES FOR OUR BUILT ENVIRONMENT.
41. BARCLAY PROPOSAL – LDR AND COMPREHENSIVE PLAN AMENDMENTS (Dual
Referral to FERC and Planning Board).
42. DISCUSS SETTING PARAMETERS FOR PROPERTY OWNERS TO PRESENT CREATIVE
DEVELOPMENT PROPOSALS TO THE CITY ADMINISTRATION AND CITY COMMISSION,
AS AN ALTERNATIVE TO INVOKING THE PREEMPTIONS IN THE LIVE LOCAL ACT, TO
ENCOURAGE LONG-TERM NON-TRANSIENT RESIDENTIAL DEVELOPMENT
(INCLUDING WORKFORCE HOUSING) THAT IS MORE COMPATIBLE WITH THE
SURROUNDING NEIGHBORHOOD.
43 DISCUSS POSSIBLE LEGISLATION INCREASING DISTANCE REQUIREMENTS FOR
ADULT MATERIAL SHOPS.
44. REVIEW CURRENT REQUIREMENTS FOR PROPERTY WALLS AND FENCES IN
SINGLE-FAMILY DISTRICTS, INCLUDING HEIGHT AND SETBACK REGULATIONS,
PARTICULARLY AS THEY RELATE TO RESIDENTIAL PROPERTIES WITH NO
SIDEWALK OR SWALE, AND DISCUSS POSSIBLE AMENDMENTS TO THE LAND
DEVELOPMENT REGULATIONS.
45. DISCUSS AMENDING SECTION 2.1.1.1 OF THE MIAMI BEACH RESILIENCY CODE,
WHICH REQUIRES THE DISCLOSURE OF CERTAIN SETTLEMENT AGREEMENTS
BETWEEN APPLICANTS AND THIRD PARTIES IN CONNECTION WITH LAND
DEVELOPMENT APPLICATIONS BEFORE THE LAND USE BOARDS, TO (1) EXPAND
APPLICABILITY TO ALSO INCLUDE PRIVATE APPLICATIONS BEFORE THE CITY
COMMISSION, AND (2) REQUIRE, AT A MINIMUM, THE DISCLOSURE OF THE MATERIAL
TERMS OF ANY SUCH SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT.
46. DISCUSS POSSIBLE LEGISLATION REGULATING TEMPORARY AND/OR
TRANSITIONAL HOUSING.
47. DISCUSS POTENTIAL ENHANCEMENTS TO THE DEVELOPMENT REGULATIONS IN
RESIDENTIAL SINGLE-FAMILY (RS) DISTRICTS, TO PROTECT AND PROMOTE THE
CHARACTER OF THE CITY’S SINGLE-FAMILY NEIGHBORHOODS.
48. CONSIDER AMENDMENTS TO LAND DEVELOPMENT REGULATIONS TO
DISINCENTIVIZE THE CONSTRUCTION OF SINGLE-FAMILY HOMES BUILT ON
ELEVATED BERMS, INCLUDING REQUIRING DESIGN REVIEW BOARD REVIEW FOR
ALL SINGLE-FAMILY HOMES.
WITHDRAWN ITEMS

49. CONSIDER AMENDING THE CITY’S LAND DEVELOPMENT REGULATIONS TO REQUIRE
A 6/7TH VOTE OF THE CITY COMMISSION PRIOR TO THE ADOPTION OF ANY
INCREASE IN A PROPERTY’S ZONED HEIGHT. Previously Referred by Former
Commissioner Kristen Rosen Gonzalez.
50. DISCUSSION REGARDING FEDERAL AND STATE GRANT PROGRAMS TO FUND HOME
ELEVATION. Previously Referred by Former Commissioner Kristen Rosen Gonzalez.

51. DISCUSS A PROPOSAL TO CONVERT THE CLEVELANDER TO A RESIDENTIAL
PROJECT WITH NO OUTDOOR BAR/ENTERTAINMENT.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, ACCEPTING THE RECOMMENDATION OF THE FINANCE AND ECONOMIC RESILIENCY COMMITTEE AT ITS APRIL 1, 2026, MEETING TO BRING BACK AN ORDINANCE FOR FIRST READING, PUBLIC HEARING, AND DISCUSSION RELATED TO THE WATER, SEWER, AND STORMWATER RATES.
items.action: Resolution 2026-34223 was adopted. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by Commissioners Bhatt, Matteo-Salinas, and Suarez, and Vice-Mayor Dominguez. Commissioner Bhatt moved to adopt the Resolution, seconded by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas. Vote: 7-0. John Norris to handle.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34223 was adopted. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda
by Commissioners Bhatt, Matteo-Salinas, and Suarez, and Vice-Mayor Dominguez. Commissioner
Bhatt moved to adopt the Resolution, seconded by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas. Vote: 7-0. John
Norris to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
DIRECTION:
 Prepare a First Reading Ordinance reflecting the recommendations of the Finance and Economic
Resiliency Committee regarding water, sewer, and stormwater rates.
 Commissioner Matteo-Salinas will sponsor the Ordinance. Commissioner Bhatt will co-sponsor
the Ordinance.
 Place the Ordinance on the May 20, 2026, City Commission Agenda for discussion.
Commissioner Bhatt emphasized the importance of this discussion in an open forum. When residents
call the City because there is a sinkhole or their living rooms are flooded because the neighborhood
impact project was not funded because they did not do this, or they have 18 buildings in North Beach
and nobody can flush the toilets because they do not have money in the enterprise fund to pay for
this, they can take it down the road for another ten years, and the cost then will be inflated, and given
the trajectory, it will be more expensive in 10 years. This is not voting on the issue today, but voting
on giving them the opportunity to have a robust discussion with materials prepared by staff to discuss
what needs to happen and what is the best way to move forward, or if they want to kick the can down
the road for another decade, which is where they are because prior Commissions did exactly that.
They will be doing the community, residents, hospitals, and businesses a huge disservice. An investor
brings millions of dollars to build Class-A office space; they proffer development agreement benefits
to the community, and they are charging top dollar for people to come in and run their businesses in
this movie-like, super-glamorous building, and they are hosting a client meeting to close the deal;
somebody excuses themselves to go to the bathroom, and the toilet backs up. How are they going to
say that they are a world-class City, that they are the leaders in sustainability? Amy Knowles just
toured people from the Netherlands coming here last week to learn how Miami Beach is doing things
to prevent cataclysmic outcomes in the next few years, so this is not even about whether or not they
are going to vote on this; this is just moving it from this nebulous purgatory onto a future Commission
Agenda so they can have this conversation. She made a motion to approve the Resolution.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, explained that this Item is coming out of the Finance and Economic
Resiliency Committee, where the Committee supported bringing forward an Ordinance to the City
Commission to discuss the rate increases. However, as they heard from the City Attorney on the last
Item (R9 AF), the City Attorney cannot bring forward an Ordinance unless there is a sponsor.
Currently, there is no sponsor for the Ordinance, and they are discussing the concept of a utility rate
change, but there is no Item before the Commission that would effectuate that because there is no
Ordinance.
Motion by Commissioner Bhatt to add the Item to next month's Agenda for discussion, seconded by
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, stated that without a sponsor, the Item cannot be reintroduced as
an Ordinance unless an Ordinance amends the existing Code to allow the City Manager to place it
himself. The City Commission needs to sponsor an Ordinance.
Commissioner Bhatt added that they could unanimously move this from purgatory to next month’s
agenda for discussion. It does not mean they are voting; it is just a conversation. That is her motion.
As a reminder, the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee voted unanimously to bring this
back to the Commission.
In reply to Mayor Meiner, Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, clarified that it was referred when the
previously heard Ordinance was bifurcated. The Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee
approved the water connection CPI increases, but the other component was bifurcated and referred
to the Committee.
Chief Financial Officer Jason Greene added that this stems from last year, when there was a
discussion. It has come up twice at the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee, and there was
a discussion about a year ago with sponsors. It also came out of Committee with the unanimous
support of the prior Public Works Director for that utility rate structure. It was tabled at the
Commission, and then they brought it back. It was sent from the Commission to go back to the
Committee for further discussion.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, clarified that it originated at the Strategic Planning Session, when they
discussed the City's infrastructure needs and its long-term viability and success.
Chief Financial Officer Greene added that they also first discussed when the City Commission
approved the $85 million declaration of intent to issue on a water and sewer bond approved two years
ago when they said that it was the last of the financial capacity within the financing model for City’s
capital projects and they would have to come back with a different utility rate structure to effectuate
the millions of dollars in Neighborhood Improvement Projects (NIPs) and critical need projects, so
this has been an ongoing process for years and the Commissions have approved all of the NIPs and
critical need programs for water and sewer, critical needs for stormwater, as they are over a billion
dollars in capital projects, it is a resiliency water quality and infrastructure.
Commissioner Bhatt added that they just stopped the pause and started doing these projects again,
which people are so grateful for, but if they do not even have the conversation, everything they have
approved comes to a grinding halt. She is not suggesting how to vote, and they do not have the matter
before them yet, but they have to have the conversation. It is a complete dereliction of duty not to
have the conversation.
Commissioner Magazine asked if they could move this forward because they are sitting down to
discuss whether they are going to have a discussion.
Mayor Meiner suggested that the City Commission sponsor an Ordinance and bring it to the next
meeting.
Commissioner Fernandez explained that this is not an easy task. It is probably the most responsible
thing to do as a team, and out of collegiality, he agrees.
Mayor Meiner clarified that it will be a discussion about an Ordinance, not a Discussion/Take Action.
Commissioner Suarez is reviewing the numbers on how increases are going, and he is not
comfortable with them now, so he does not necessarily want to be a sponsor, but is happy to discuss
right now. He does not want to sponsor an Ordinance for a rate increase.
Commissioner Bhatt suggested that the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee sponsor it, as
the committee voted unanimously to move it back to the City Commission.
Commissioner Magazine asked how long it would take for that legislation to pass so that City staff or
Administration can sponsor an Ordinance.
Commissioner Bhatt added that this is insane. They are sweating bullets about the fact that they want
to have a conversation about doing something that is fiscally responsible, and they cannot even have
that conversation.
Mayor Meiner suggested doing it as a legitimate Discussion/Take Action, and after reviews, they will
see where they are and draft the Ordinance accordingly. Right now, they are having a conversation
about having a conversation, and he is happy to do it now or at the end of the day.
Commissioner Suarez stated that they are going to have a conversation regardless, and if there are
enough votes to proceed, they will draft the Ordinance and bring it to the next meeting.
In addressing Commissioner Bhatt, Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, clarified that as long as there is
a sponsor, they can vote on the Ordinance. If they have the discussion, someone from the
Commission would need to sponsor, or the Manager, if they allow that to happen.
Commissioner Magazine added that perhaps people will feel more comfortable putting a name to it if
they quantify what it is.
Jason Greene, Chief Financial Officer, noted that a short presentation is available if desired.
Commissioner Bhatt thinks this is a serious topic, that everyone is exhausted, and that it has been a
meaty conversation. They all want to make this happen sooner rather than later, but to ensure the
fairest hearing at 6:25 p.m. after a day of heavy lifting, they will kick the can down the road until the
next meeting.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas stated that she will sponsor the Ordinance to have the discussion.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that she would sponsor it if doing so would allow the Commission to move
forward. She emphasized that the ordinance should ideally be sponsored by the entire City
Commission, noting that all Commissioners share responsibility for protecting residents from flooding
and infrastructure failures.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that one of his challenges with this is that whenever they get to
discussing it, which he is entering into that territory, is shifting the burden. Now, a small property
owner is paying the same for stormwater as a larger property owner, and to him, that is inequity.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that it is not accurate and suggested moving to Discussion/Take Action.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, explained that he placed C7 P on the Agenda to accept the
recommendation of the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee. They are bringing back an
Ordinance next month, either way.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, recapped that Commissioner Bhatt had moved to approve the
Resolution accepting the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee's recommendation to bring
an Ordinance for First Reading and discussion of the water, sewer, and stormwater rates at the May
20, 2026, Commission Meeting. Commissioner Matteo-Salinas has agreed to sponsor the Ordinance,
and Commissioner Bhatt has agreed to co-sponsor it.
Commissioner Bhatt explained that four Commissioners are facing elections next year and may be
concerned about political backlash; however, she stated that she will not refrain from doing what she
believes is right for the City’s financial well-being. She affirmed that she would co-sponsor the
Ordinance and thanked Commissioner Matteo Salinas. Commissioner Bhatt added that others may
criticize her for supporting the effort, but she believes that acting responsibly is necessary and that
residents will ultimately appreciate it.
Mayor Meiner stated that there is more to it than that, but not for today, but he would love to see the
presentation.
Vote: 7-0. The Item is approved as is.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, DIRECTING THE CITY MANAGER TO EXTEND THE OPERATING HOURS OF ALL THREE OF THE CITY-DESIGNATED BARK BEACHES UP TO AND INCLUDING BEACH CLOSING TIME, WHILE MAINTAINING THE CURRENT MORNING START TIME THROUGHOUT THE YEAR.
items.action: Item referred. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by Commissioner Bhatt.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Item referred. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by Commissioner Bhatt.
Commissioner Bhatt motioned to refer the Item to the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life
Committee; seconded by Mayor Meiner. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Mark Taxis to place on the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee Agenda
Pending List. John Rebar to handle.
REFERRAL:
 The Item was referred to the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee.
Commissioner Suarez stated that there are already three dog beaches in Miami Beach, although the
hours are very confusing. The intent of this Item is to make the hours very easy to understand and a
whole lot easier than they currently are. He goes to the beach frequently and sees dogs there at all
times of the day, and no one really enforces the rules. It would be best to contain dogs to particular
areas of the beach rather than having everyone bring their dogs everywhere else. If people see there
is an area where they can bring their dogs in the middle of the day, it will encourage respectful
enforcement of the law.
John Rebar, Parks, Facilities, Fleet, and Beaches, stated that the only addition is that from 51st Street
to 81st Street, we should have staff review this. Our current hours work around the turtle nest
inspections. Regardless of what the City Commission wants to do, he would like to be sensitive to the
turtle hours in the morning.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that she separated this Item because she believes it needs to go to the
Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee before becoming an Ordinance. Residents
have reached out and expressed concern about this Item. She supports making the hours more
consistent, but the details need to be “fleshed out” further.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he has no objection to Commissioner Bhatt’s request.
City Attorney Ricardo J. Dopico stated that this Item is not an Ordinance but a Resolution because it
authorizes the City Manager to set hours based on direction. There will be no Second Reading of the
Item.
Commissioner Bhatt replied that this is an even stronger reason to refer the Item to the Committee.
Commissioner Suarez asked Commissioner Fernandez whether he would be attending the Public
Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee meeting.
Commissioner Fernandez replied that he will be attending.
Commissioner Bhatt motioned to refer the Item to the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life
Committee; seconded by Mayor Meiner. Vote: 7-0.
Handouts or Reference Materials:
1. Email from Rachel Friedman: Request that the Item be pulled from the Consent Agenda and
referred to the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee.

ACTION: Ordinance 2026-4809 was adopted. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record.
The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on
Second Reading; seconded by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Thomas Mooney to handle.
Commissioner Magazine asked whether, when approval is given, there is a fixed time frame or
whether it is handled on a case-by-case basis. Some of the City’s more vibrant areas have surface
parking lots, which are the least-used option. He understands that there could be a temporary
necessity or even a benefit, but he does not want to encourage a 5-, 10-, 15-, or 20-year covered
land play in some of our critical areas. This takes away from walkability and housing incentives. He
does not have an issue with Administrative Review, but is this a permanent approval, or is there a
Sunshine provision?
Commissioner Fernandez replied that the Code already sets a five-year period, with up to another
five years for remedial talk.
Thomas Mooney, the Planning Department Director, agreed with Commissioner Fernandez’s
statement.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that the only thing the Ordinance is touching is that it only changes
the approval process.
Commissioner Magazine stated that this is perhaps not the right forum to discuss this because it is
not the “meat and potatoes” of the issue. He does not agree with approving surface parking lots,
which essentially give a covered land play for ten years. In a sense, this takes away from the next ten
years instead of pursuing the highest and best use of the land.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that he would be happy to work with Commissioner Magazine on
this and to determine how long these approvals can be for.
Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading; seconded by
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, announced that no one in the audience or on Zoom requested to
participate in the Public Hearing.

Amy Knowles, Chief Resiliency Officer, wished everyone a happy Earth Day. She clarified that this
Item on Second Reading ensures that the City does not use consumables and plastic items that can
cause a great amount of litter, and permits us to use reusables.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that the reason they are doing this is that the City Commission
approved the original Ordinance banning plastic and metalized decorations on public property, but
we did not realize that it unintentionally banned decorations that were never meant to be targeted,
including those used by local organizations and cultural events. This Item fixes that unintentional
effect. The policy was already established. This is cleanup language.
Mayor Meiner asked the City Clerk to look up the vote from the First Reading. He, too, has concerns
about unintended consequences.
City Clerk Granado stated that the Item was approved on First Reading 7-0.
Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading; seconded by
Commissioner Bhatt.
The Public Hearing was opened, but no speakers came forward either via Zoom or in person.

ACTION: Ordinance 2026-4815 was adopted. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record.
The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Matteo-Salinas made a motion to adopt the Ordinance
on Second Reading; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Amy Knowles to handle.
Mayor Meiner introduced the Item and provided a brief overview. He explained that residents have
raised concerns about Monument Island, specifically noise, cleanliness, and overall safety. He is
pleased with the Item and, in the broader picture, especially proud of what the City Commission
accomplished to improve and clean up the City’s waterways. He explained that these efforts include
environmental cleanups supported by volunteer organizations, as well as enforcement actions
involving charter boats, Marina activity, and derelict vessels. He thanked Commissioner Suarez for
taking the lead on the derelict vessel issue. The difference is “night and day.” He further noted that
during a Marine Patrol tour a few weeks earlier, he observed that many of the vessels that had been
present were no longer there. He recalled that there had once been approximately 180 boats in the
area, but that they are now gone. These efforts have been a significant win for the City’s residents.
He also noted that the City has increased Marine Patrol service hours, which further strengthened
enforcement and public safety on the waterways. He emphasized that these accomplishments do not
always receive attention, but that they are integral to the City’s quality of life and environmental
protection efforts. He asked Ms. Precht to provide a brief reminder of the Item.
Lindsey Precht, Deputy Resiliency Officer, greeted the Mayor and City Commission and wished them
a happy Earth Day. She stated that she provided a thorough background on the Item during the First
Reading. She explained that the Item allows the City to move forward with the permitting process to
establish a swim-only zone approximately 150 feet from Monument Island's shoreline. The purpose
of the swim-only zone is to create a safer environment for residents and visitors who wish to use the
island and visit the historic monument without the risk of being struck by a boat.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading; seconded
by Commissioner Fernandez.
The Public Hearing was opened, but no speakers came forward either via Zoom or in person.
Roll Call: 7-0.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Ordinance adopted on First Reading. A motion was made by Commissioner Magazine
to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading as amended; seconded by Vice-Mayor Dominguez. Roll Call
taken: 6-1; Opposed: Mayor Meiner. Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for May 20, 2026.
AMENDMENTS:
 One-year sunset provision: The exemption shall automatically expire one year after adoption.
 Code compliance condition: The business must remain free of all Code violations during the
one-year period; any violation will result in the exemption becoming null and void.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: No
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Thomas Mooney to handle.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez explained that Mr. Mohammed Islam purchased a property, unaware of the
Overlay. He and his family own many properties Citywide, and the Overlay would prevent him from
selling certain uses. They had a robust discussion at the Committee, and everyone agreed that if they
sunset the use, they could look at granting this.
Thomas Mooney, Planning Director, clarified that this was discussed at the Land Use and
Sustainability Committee in March. The Land Use and Sustainability Committee sent it to the City
Commission with no recommendation, but suggested that, if it were to move forward, the narrow
exception that was drafted be applicable only for three years. Accordingly, the draft Ordinance for
consideration on First Reading was revised to include that three-year sunset provision.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez moved the Item with that provision; seconded by Commissioner Suarez.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, announced the Public Hearing.
Mohammed Islam thanked the City Commission and explained that the business's main product is
tobacco and alcohol, but tobacco is restricted by City law, making it very harmful to the business.
Small businesses are surviving with this main product. He requested that the City Commission and
the Planning Division help them at least sell tobacco so they can survive. In these circumstances, he
requested that the City Commission officials help them. He was at the Land Use and Sustainability
Committee, and it was approved for three years, so they can proceed.
Mayor Meiner receives complaints about vape shops, and they even had legislation a couple of years
ago prohibiting them.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez explained that it is not a vape shop. Because people from the north and south
of him already sell it, it is allowing a new use that other businesses already have.
Commissioner Bhatt emphasized that the City has a distance-separation requirement for vape shops
and that there is an ongoing effort to reduce the proliferation of vape and tobacco retailers. She
stressed that the proposed exception is not a permanent solution and wanted to be clear for Mr. Islam,
his business partners, and the surrounding neighbors. She explained that, in this unusually opaque
situation, a basic review of neighboring businesses could have reasonably led a buyer to believe the
use was permitted, making it understandable how the misunderstanding occurred. However, she
reiterated that the proposal is intended only as an “exit ramp,” providing time for Mr. Islam to either
reconfigure his business model or sell the business. She noted that three years was longer than some
would have preferred and urged him to use the time wisely. She then asked Planning Director Mooney
to further explain the details of the exception.
Thomas Mooney, Planning Director, explained that this exception is specific to convenience stores
and would not apply to a standalone vape shop. More importantly, the exemption would allow no
more than five percent of the convenience store's floor area to contain these products, so it is a very
limited component of the exemption. With regard to the previous use on this site, if the previous owner
did not disclose any existing Overlays, that is something the property owner may not have been aware
of.
Commissioner Fernandez added that this is such a challenge because they want to help small, locally
owned businesses succeed, and at the same time, what precedent are they setting? A couple of
weeks ago, a business owner came to his office. The owner has a similar type of establishment on
Collins Avenue. An elderly person who could barely speak English bought the building. The
establishment next door can sell cigarette products. His business cannot, so then what do they do?
He is saying yes to one and no to the other. Are they going to be fair? Are they going to allow these
types of exemptions for everyone who comes forward in the City? That is the challenge he has. What
he sees is a civil issue where the property disclosures were not made to someone who bought a
business under a set of understandings that something was not disclosed to them. He sponsored this
legislation, and he feels bad because now they have a business owner who did not get the proper
disclosures from a seller. Is that a civil issue, and what remedies are there?
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, stated that there are certain disclosures, specifically for residential
sales. He does not know whether the same level of disclosure is required in a commercial sale. It
would have been incumbent on the buyer to do the research, but, as Planning Director Mooney
mentioned, this may have been something that is opaque and not easily discernible by the buyer.
Commissioner Suarez noted that at the Committee, he was torn because he understands they are
setting a precedent, which is why he had the original idea to help this Item move forward. They
understand that it was either the seller’s or the buyer’s fault, but at the end of the day, they are not
setting a precedent that will allow vape shops to move forward. What they are signaling is that they
understand there is an issue; they do not know who is at fault, but they are giving a grace period for
this business to adapt and move on. For standalone vape shops, he would be completely against it,
but this store sells a minuscule amount of product. They are telling them that they have three years
to move away from this business model and adapt or sell. He thinks it carefully gives everyone what
they want. They are going to have enforcement in three years, so that property will not be able to sell
that product, and they are essentially calling balls and strikes on who could have been at fault for not
relaying this information. He is ready to vote.
Commissioner Fernandez noted that they have the same issue with other businesses in the
community. This is not the only business in the community with the issue. There are storeowners on
Collins Avenue who came to his office with the same distance-separation issue. The neighbors were
allowed to engage in the activity; they are not. Now, how does he vote for this and tell the other person
on Collins Avenue that he is not going to support them? When they do that, it is going to open the
door in the Entertainment District, Alton Road, and all other areas where they have a distance
separation. It almost happened on Alton Road with “I Love Liquor”, and in fact, they ended up not
doing it because they did not want to set the precedent. It is heartbreaking because he loves Mr.
Mohammed Islam. He is a friend, and he wants to help him and his business, but he needs to support
the vision and the direction that they are taking the City in. How does he say yes to Mr. Islam and no
to the other people coming to his office, who can barely speak English and come crying, asking for
help? What does he tell them?
Commissioner Suarez stated that Mr. Islam moved in as soon as the legislation passed, and that may
have been different in that situation. What Commissioner Fernandez is describing is people who want
permanent use or have been there for a longer period of time.
Thomas Mooney, Planning Director, explained that the legislation regulating tobacco and vape was
adopted in 2017. It was initially an effort by a former Commissioner to regulate tobacco and vape
stores along 41st Street because of their proximity to schools. The legislation was later expanded to
include distance separation for all retail sales of tobacco and vape products citywide, and it went into
effect in 2018. The current regulations have been in place since then. Apparently, when Mr. Islam
acquired the rights to this property, he assumed he could sell tobacco and vape, but he was not able
to because it did not meet the current distance separation requirements. That is why Mr. Islam
requested the relief that was drafted. It is very limited and specific to convenience stores only. It can
be no more than five percent of the floor area, and there is now a sunset provision within the
exemption area, under which anyone who may take advantage of it would have to cease the sale no
later than three years from adoption. In response to Commissioner Magazine, Planning Director
Mooney indicated that he did not know the specifics of when Mr. Islam acquired the rights to it, but
the distance separation legislation has been in place since 2018. The North Beach expansion was
intended to prohibit these uses, but because of SB180, they cannot enforce that provision within the
North Beach Overlay to prohibit them. They amended that section of the Code, but that section would
not be applicable because of SB180. Either way, Mr. Islam would not meet the current distance
separation requirements that are in place.
Commissioner Bhatt added that the problem with this business was that nobody knew that this
Overlay existed, prohibiting this use. Is that the same circumstance for the other businesses? Can
more context be provided?
Thomas Mooney, Planning Director, met with Rene Primo, who has an existing convenience store
within 4332 Collins Avenue that does not meet the 1200 feet separation distance, similar to Mr. Islam.
Those regulations have been in place since 2018, and he had to explain to him that, because there
was no variance provision, there was no other option. He does not know when he acquired the tenant
space.
Commissioner Bhatt added that if all these people are getting caught up because, somehow, an
Overlay prohibits them from doing something that seems like a normal use, and there is no way they
can find out about it, that is a bigger issue. It is not necessarily the City’s job to reach out to prospective
buyers or tenants, but there has to be a mechanism for people to get the information they need when
renting or buying property to understand what uses there are. They have seen other issues similar to
this, where people lease space that used to be a bakery and now want to open a yoga studio, and it
creates this onerous situation because of the way the City’s Land Use and Sustainability Committee
laws are. So how do they address that? She understands the concern because there will be a number
of nonconforming uses. She remembers sitting on the Planning Board, and a property owner came
for a few months straight asking how the City Commission runs the City, when in the same block they
have six businesses doing a version of the same thing, but none of them can do it the same way, and
now this is born out.
Thomas Mooney, Planning Director, added that this is the nature of creating nonconforming uses. It
is difficult to do this now under SB180, but previously, when the City Commission created the Art
Deco MiMo Overlay and expanded it to North Beach, the purpose was to allow existing businesses
to remain, with no new businesses down the line. That is just the nature of establishing nonconforming
businesses. To the extent that they want to take a look at nonconforming businesses and provide
more limited relief, they can certainly do that through amendments to the LDRs.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that the issue is that when someone comes to buy or lease a space, or
to buy a property, there needs to be a clear way for them to know what they can do there. She gave
examples of egregious incidents, but this is such a nuanced issue. On whose shoulders does the
incumbent have to make this knowledge known to the people who are going to be investing their
dollars to create the business? Is it the City's responsibility, the listing agent, or the real estate broker?
Should it be posted in a directory with permitted uses for the space? She does not know, and that is
why she is asking, because these are not going to be two of the issues. This will continue to be
something they have to wrestle with.
Thomas Mooney, Planning Director, receives many requests for Zoning Verification Letters. Whether
a prospective buyer or tenant has very specific questions about what they can and cannot do with
their property prior to entering into a lease or contract for purchase, they will sometimes email the
City to ask whether the use is permitted. The City will reply whether it is or not and, if so, issue a
Verification Letter that he signs on City stationery. The letter states what they can and cannot do.
People sometimes do this for their protection because they do not trust what others are saying, or
because their financial institution is demanding verification that what they are proposing to do is
currently allowed. Most people will reach out and do their due diligence. Ultimately, it falls under the
responsibility of the prospective tenant or future property buyer to understand what they can or cannot
do within the property.
Commissioner Magazine added that they are all sympathetic because Mr. Islam is a pillar of the
community, a good and honest man, an honest broker, and a family man. But there was no City action
that caused this not to be known. It would be keen for somebody buying a bar on West Avenue or in
Sunset Harbour to say he thought he was allowed to operate until 5:00 a.m., even though the City
changed the alcohol hours several years ago. Because he is a good guy, they will let him go until
5:00 a.m. But they have laws, and absent Mr. Islam telling him it was a City fault or that there was
something with the timing, he is really hard-pressed to see that allowance.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez added that Mr. Islam is not a new business owner; he has worked in the City
for decades. The fact that he did not have this information is what is giving her a hard time. There is
a motion and a second, and it does need 5/7 votes. This is really important for Mr. Islam and his
family, and she would like to see support here.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas likes and respects Mr. Islam. She is going to support this Item today
because it sunsets after three years, but she is not a fan of vapes. Per the Planning Director, it is
limited to convenience stores and no more than five percent of the floor area, as confirmed by
Planning Director Mooney. She will support this today because of the sunset provision and the five
percent floor space. She is also interested in hearing what other businesses are doing and whether
they keep to the same restrictions, because it is such a small piece, it helps them, and it is also a
happy medium.
Mohammed Islam explained that distance variance is not harmful, agreed to three years, and said
they can then sell and shut down. He thanked the City Commission.
Commissioner Fernandez wants to ask whether zoning establishes a level playing field, yet they are
making an exemption for one establishment over another. In a situation like that, he asked the City
Attorney because he wants there to be parity. Mr. Islam is here because they know him; he knows
them; he is a good neighbor and a good business owner; and he cares about North Beach. They
know he is not going to abuse the City in every way, but not everyone has that benefit or access to
them, so they are not going to feel comfortable advancing legislation if they were to find themselves
in the same scenario. Could they establish a framework where, if someone is interested in doing
something like this, they could seek a variance from the Board of Adjustment (BOA) and amend the
Code that way, so it goes to the BOA, has a Public Hearing, is publicly noticed, the community can
participate and has an opportunity to weigh in, and everyone in the same situation can apply for a
variance and is considered on a case-by-case basis, as opposed to saying they are going to sponsor
legislation for Mr. Islam because they like him? They had this issue a few years ago. “I Love Liquor”
on Alton Road was not able to apply for a variance, but now they come to this establishment, and
because they know him, they are going to do the exemption. But Rene and Flor came to his office
with a similar situation, and he is going to be a stickler because he is trying to protect the Code and
will not do it. He wants to create a fair and even playing field where everyone who finds themselves
in this situation can be considered, but based on objective criteria, based on public hearings, and
giving an opportunity for the surrounding neighbors, if they have concerns, to find out, be notified,
and participate. Is there a way to do that?
Chief Deputy City Attorney Nick Kallergis noted that the existing Ordinance prohibits variances from
the minimum distance separation requirement. Striking line four at the bottom of Agenda page 1119,
which says "Variances from the requirements of this section shall be prohibited," would essentially
allow an applicant to seek a variance from the Board of Adjustment. The Board would have to find
that the applicant meets the hardship standard for granting the variance, but the applicant would be
eligible to apply.
Commissioner Fernandez indicated that this speaks specifically to Section 7.3.10, the North Beach
Commercial Character Overlay District, but this is not an issue occurring, for example, in the Art Deco

ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading as amended. The title of the Ordinance

The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for May 20, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. William MacDonald to handle.
AMENDMENT:
 Beginning July 1, freight loading zones shall operate Monday through Saturday from 7:00 a.m. to
3:00 p.m., with a maximum allowable parking time of 30 minutes in freight and commercial loading
zones.
Commissioner Fernandez noted that people parking illegally creates a safety risk. It is a daily
frustration for residents and businesses alike. This proposal updates the freight commercial and
passenger loading zone rules to strengthen enforcement and improve overall traffic flow. Penalties
are significantly increased. Freight loading violators on a first offense will now face a $1,000 fine.
Second offenses would increase from $150 to $5,000, and in cases where an illegal stop actually
obstructs a travel lane and disrupts traffic, the Special Magistrate can issue a $15,000 penalty. These
violations bring traffic to a standstill, affect public safety and the quality of life of residents, force drivers
into sudden, dangerous lane changes, and create dangerous conditions for pedestrians and cyclists.
This Ordinance treats these violations with the seriousness they deserve. This was discussed this
morning ad nauseam, which is why they are imposing these very strict penalties that did not exist
before. He moved his the Item.
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez offered an amendment providing that, beginning July 1, all freight
loading zones would operate Monday through Saturday from 7:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m., with a maximum
allowable parking time of 30 minutes in freight and commercial loading zones. She described that the
amendment establishes uniform hours citywide and incorporates the remaining enforcement
language contained in the written amendment she distributed. Vice-Mayor Dominguez explained that
access to parking in the City is limited, and she wants to ensure that residents have access to parking
on Sundays, when loading zones are not traditionally used as much. She added that the 7:00 a.m. to
3:00 p.m. timeframe is reasonable; although she would have preferred hours ending at 11:00 a.m.,
after further discussions, she was advised that 1:00 p.m. or 3:00 p.m. would be more appropriate so
that residents can use those spaces after 3:00 p.m.
Commissioner Fernandez added that one of the challenges residents and visitors face is the
inconsistency of freight loading zone hours, which creates confusion not only for visitors to the City
but also for the delivery industry, which cannot rely on knowing for certain what the loading zone
hours are. Other cities have consistent schedules, so he does not see why it would be a problem for
them to establish this. He likes this amendment and accepted it as a friendly amendment. Vice-Mayor
Dominguez seconded the motion with the amendment.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, announced the Public Hearing. No one in the audience requested to
speak, either in person or via Zoom, and the Public Hearing concluded.
Commissioner Fernandez moved to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading as amended; seconded
by Vice-Mayor Dominguez. Roll Call taken: 7-0.
Commissioner Fernandez inquired if this, as amended, would create throughout the City of freight
loading zones with designated hours unless otherwise changed by Resolution of the City
Commission.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Nick Kallergis stated that it would require a subsequent Ordinance, but
they can work with Vice-Mayor Dominguez on that for Second Reading.
Commissioner Fernandez read the proposed language: the creation of a new freight loading or
commercial loading zone, or the elimination of an existing freight loading zone, shall be accompanied
by a Resolution of the City Commission. They are setting the hours by legislation, and the hours can
only be changed by legislation, so that they give the public consistency and predictability.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Nick Kallergis clarified that adding or removing a zone requires the
Resolution, but the hours are at the City Commission's discretion. Addressing Commissioner Matteo-
Salinas, he confirmed that the amendment includes commercial and freight-loading zones.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, clarified that the hours would be changed by Ordinance; however,
the designated zones could be adjusted by Resolution to provide greater flexibility.
Commissioner Fernandez thanked Vice-Mayor Dominguez for the amendment, which improves the
Ordinance.

Thomas Mooney, Planning Department Director, introduced the Item and explained that, under the
City’s Land Development Regulations (LDRs), any artistic super-graphic on a building that exceeds
100 square feet requires approval from the City Commission, in addition to approval from the
applicable Land Use Board. In this case, the Historic Preservation Board (HPB) has approved two
separate murals totaling approximately 450 square feet. The proposed graphics will be located on
the rooftop, will not be electronic, and will be visible only to rooftop patrons. The Administration
recommends approving the Item.
Paul Savage stated that he represents the Gymage gym and the 2050 rooftop restaurant. The project
has received full approval. The only issue before the City Commission is approval of the rooftop
artistic projection/graphic, which would be visible only to rooftop patrons. There will be full vegetative
buffering on the rooftop, and the applicant will need to comply with applicable regulations to ensure
the graphic cannot be viewed from the City streets. He acknowledged it is late at night, but would like
to show a PowerPoint presentation and promised to be brief. Click here to view the presentation. He
identified the area at the end of Lincoln Road and Washington Avenue. The client operates Gymage
on the second floor, and the application relates to a new rooftop restaurant at the property. The
applicant has received unanimous approval from the HPB, as well as favorable staff
recommendations.

Dominguez.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, ACCEPTING THE RECOMMENDATION OF THE FINANCE AND ECONOMIC RESILIENCY COMMITTEE AT ITS APRIL 1, 2026 MEETING AND APPROVING THE PROPOSED TERMS OF A FIRST AMENDMENT TO THE AGREEMENT OF LEASE DATED SEPTEMBER 1, 1999 BETWEEN THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH (OWNER), AND RK RIVANI, LLC, (TENANT) RELATING TO THE REAL PROPERTY LOCATED AT 1691 MICHIGAN AVENUE (PROPERTY), SAID TERMS PROVIDING, IN PRINCIPAL PART, FOR (I) LEASE TERM EXTENSION FOR TWO (2) TWENTY (20) YEARS OPTIONS; (II) AN INCREASE TO THE BASE RENT; (III) MARKET RENT ADJUSTMENTS CAPPED AT THIRTY-THREE PERCENT (33%) AT EACH OF THE FOUR (4) RENEWAL PERIODS; (IV) CONSTRUCTING APPROXIMATELY 47,000 SQUARE FEET OF OFFICE SPACE AND OTHER IMPROVEMENTS ABOVE THE PARKING GARAGE HAVING AN APPROXIMATE VALUE OF $50 MILLION (EXPANSION IMPROVEMENTS); (V) APPROVING A MAXIMUM BUILDING HEIGHT OF ONE HUNDRED (100) FEET; (VI) ADJUSTING THE TOTAL REQUIRED PARKING FOR THIS GARAGE TO FOUR HUNDRED TWENTY-FIVE (425) PARKING SPACES; AND (VII) ADDITIONAL PUBLIC BENEFITS OF ONE MILLION THREE HUNDRED THOUSAND ($1,300,000) ALL AS SET FORTH IN THE TERM SHEET ATTACHED AS AN EXHIBIT TO THE COMMISSION MEMORANDUM ACCOMPANYING THIS RESOLUTION; SUCH FIRST AMENDMENT TO BE SUBJECT TO A WAIVER OF THE FORMAL COMPETITIVE BIDDING REQUIREMENTS BY A FIVE-SEVENTHS (5/7TH) VOTE AS PERMITTED UNDER SECTION 82- 39(A) OF THE CITY CODE AND TO BECOME EFFECTIVE ONLY UPON (A) THE APPROVAL BY A MAJORITY VOTE OF THE VOTERS IN A CITY-WIDE REFERENDUM AND (B) TENANT’S COMPLETION OF THE EXPANSION IMPROVEMENTS WITHIN A PERIOD TO BE SPECIFIED IN THE FIRST AMENDMENT; FURTHER, DIRECTING THE ADMINISTRATION TO NEGOTIATE A FIRST AMENDMENT WITH TENANT CONSISTENT WITH THE TERM SHEET, WITH THE FINAL FIRST AMENDMENT SUBJECT TO THE PRIOR APPROVAL OF THE MAYOR AND CITY

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34242 was adopted as amended. Commissioner Magazine made a
motion to adopt the Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez, Vote: 7-0.
AMENDMENT:
Replace “senior meal programs” with “senior programs.”
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Ozzy Dominguez to handle.
Commissioner Magazine presented an opportunity that the City has, and he is very excited about it,
as he imagines his colleagues are. They have made tremendous strides in Economic Development.
In fact, for the first time ever, they have four publicly traded companies headquartered in Miami
Beach. They are creating a real economy for real people with high-paying jobs. Part of that is their
incredibly slim office inventory. They are well-positioned, with City-owned land available for lease.
The current office building owner bought the property several years ago and invested roughly $50 to
$60 million in capital improvements. The applicant inherited the property, and occupancy was about
35% to 40%. That tenancy is now up to 80% to 90%, with indications it might move even higher.
Rents have either tripled or quadrupled, and that is direct money coming into the City. Part of this
lease is that the City not only receives a base rent payment from the owner of the office building but
also shares in the upside, as the City gets a percentage of the gross revenues that come into the
project. Because of this project and their continued efforts to diversify the City’s economy, the office
owner came to them and offered to make an additional $50 million investment in the City asset;
however, he is going to need an extension on his lease terms to be able to finance it. That is what
they have here. It was a great opportunity to reevaluate not just what happens 60 years from now
when that lease expires, but Ozzy Dominguez was able to run a very hard yet fair negotiation that
really is going to benefit the taxpayers, not 60 years from now, but actually as soon as this project
starts getting completed. What are they looking at, where is it going, and what is the process? This
still needs to go to the Committee to iron out the final details, and then it will come back to the
Commission for final approval before being sent to the Voter Referendum in November.
Ozzy Dominguez, Division Director of Asset Management, said that, as Commissioner Magazine
noted, they have been in discussions and negotiations with the Rivani group for a couple of months.
This is an exciting project; they have made a lot of strides. There are just two material terms they are
polishing up, and they are confident they will wrap it up by next week. They will bring it back to the
Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee in May, back to the City Commission at the end of
June, and to a Referendum in November. They have agreed to all the other terms but requested two
additional extensions of 20 years each. There are public benefits, and they are excited about the
package. They are at the two-yard line now.
Commissioner Magazine stated that he would leave it to his colleagues whether to discuss the details
at this time or simply refer the Item to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee, since the
Committee will review the remaining points before the Item returns to the Commission.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez agreed that this is an exciting project. She had the opportunity to get a hard
hat tour, and it is beautiful, with more to come. She cannot wait for it to be finished. She loved the
terms and has only one tweak. It says $10,000 a year for the senior meal programs. The word "meal"
should be taken out. It will be an asset on Lincoln Road, and she is very excited.
Commissioner Magazine asked for visuals of the contemplated capital improvements to showcase
their impressiveness.
In response to Commissioner Bhatt, Asset Management Division Director Dominguez explained that
he is currently in discussions with the tenant regarding rent. He stated that the current base rent is
2.5% of sales, and the discussion involves increasing the base rent schedule. The lease operates on
a five-year cycle in which the minimum rent is increased by the lesser of CPI or 12%, and that
calculation will continue. The City is requesting that once Phase 2 of the project receives a Certificate
of Occupancy and after the tenant’s 12-month buildout period, the minimum rent increase by
$500,000. He noted that the tenant is currently paying approximately $300,000, so this increase would
provide a significant revenue gain for the City while maintaining the 2.5% of gross sales requirement.
He further explained that the lease currently includes market rent resets in years 50 and 70, and two
additional resets have been added. The tenant has requested that these resets be capped to ensure
rents remain affordable as the property value increases.
Commissioner Bhatt echoed her colleagues' comments; she has always been impressed by how fully
committed Mr. Rivani is to Miami Beach. He has been doubling down, and she admires people who
walk the walk, not just talk the talk. It appears that his gamble is paying off, and it is good for him,
obviously, but even better for the City.
Commissioner Magazine requested visuals. This is a City-owned asset that they will inherit once the
lease terms end.
Ozzy Dominguez presented the slideshow. Click here to view.
Commissioner Bhatt noted that the renderings and design are thoughtful and beautiful, evocative of
the Miami Beach brand they want to support and promote. She has no comment on the design, but
asked whether it would be possible to create one of these renderings that does not look like this is a
field of grass in Iowa and to place it in context, because that is really telling, if it can be done and is
not costly. This would show the beauty of the architecture, and she suggested changing the
background.
Robert Rivani stated that it is a conceptual model, but they will be building on it.
Ozzy Dominguez, Division Director of Asset Management, summarized in closing that they are
bringing this back to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee on May 6, then moving forward
to Commission for First Reading and Second Reading, and then continuing to Referendum. To clarify
for Commissioner Bhatt, he explained that their deadline is this Friday to make the May 6 Finance
and Economic Resiliency Committee meeting with final terms, after which they can start drafting the
agreement.
Commissioner Fernandez thinks this is so great and is very excited, not just about the work being
done to the building, the quality, the caliber of the tenants, the economic activity this brings to Lincoln
Road, and the potential for the corridor. Kudos to Commissioner Magazine for leading on this.
Robert Rivani explained that they would first satisfy the building's uses for office tenants. There would
be 100 spaces left for the public, which is currently required by the lease, so it is still public parking
set aside for public use.
Commissioner Fernandez added that everyone should consider a conversation held at the Public
Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee about the parking needs of the Convention
Center Hotel, which is a critical economic engine for the Convention Center and for the Convention
Center employees' ability to reach their full potential. A parking deficiency is anticipated for
employees, and they hope employees will either take rideshare or buses to the Convention Center.
They recognize that expecting employees at any given time to use rideshare or buses is unrealistic,
and so, to the extent that it could be considered, perhaps the balance of these parking spaces could
be used to help ameliorate the concerns and the parking needs of the Convention Center Hotel. He
would like to put that out there if the sponsor is amenable to that, and Commissioner Magazine
agreed.
Robert Rivani indicated that it is one of the public benefits.
William MacDonald, Parking Director, commented that they reached out within the last 48 hours and
are working on a long-term lease with them to provide more parking spaces, so it is a win-win for both
of them, and that way, they will provide 110 parking spaces.
Robert Rivani added that they ran a study because he heard from many of the Commissioners about
parking concerns. The transient parking on a monthly basis is five percent of the parking garage, so
they have abundant parking, to say the least, and they are definitely close to having maximum
occupancy in the parking garage.
Commissioner Fernandez thanked him for working with the Convention Center Hotel, noting the
economic impact his project will have on Lincoln Road. Equally important is the hotel, and making
sure that they are able to keep their employees is going to be an important endeavor. He also wants
to thank him for working with Turnberry on finding a solution for that.
Commissioner Bhatt is glad the Parking Director is here to address what they are doing with the
Deauville parking lot. The garage is going to be open in July, and construction will not start for a
couple of years, so they have this empty parking lot. In the negotiations for the Development
Agreement, they discussed parking for construction workers being in the garage, so they need to use
that space so they do not congest North Beach more than it needs to be. No matter what, they will
have spots available for residents. During hurricane or flood events, there will be no construction
workers there due to the weather, and when the hotel is open, there will be no guests because of the
hurricane. The reason she is giving this background is that there are a lot of net spots that can be
managed in a very fluid way, which is a very different business model than what it used to be, which
is third floor for this, fourth floor for that, and fifth floor for that, and it does not matter if one is empty
or not. She would like him to consider whether he would mind talking to Will MacDonald. Her
understanding is that David Martin agreed that the City will manage the parking garage for the
Deauville. They will make the market-rate parking money. No one is getting shortchanged, but it gives
them the ability to make it more flexible and nimble, so they do not have to engage with a third-party
vendor, and it becomes a flexible ecosystem where they are still making money, and they can manage
it with resident rates, but it goes through one central, agreed-upon vendor with agreed-to parameters.
Robert Rivani stated that they are housing 100 to 150 construction cars for the construction
happening at the hotel. In their agreement, they gave their parking spaces for free, so if she wants to
charge a market rate, he is happy to, but they threw in 110 for free for workforce housing.
Commissioner Bhatt added that it is amazing, but if he has 250 spots, he still has another 150 that
are fluid because during the day they are used by employees, but at night they are empty.
Mr. Rivani agreed to consider.
Mayor Meiner thanked Mr. Rivani, noting that he has been an excellent partner with the City. The City
is appreciative and happy that he is investing in the City and working with people who are so
amenable. He also thanked Commissioner Magazine for bringing the Item.
Commissioner Magazine moved to adopt the Resolution, seconded by Commissioner Fernandez, as
amended to include senior programs instead of senior meal programs. Vote: 7-0.

City Clerk Rafael E. Granado stated that there are two At-Large seats and one nominee to the
Affordable Housing Advisory Committee: Charlotte Tomic. She is also being appointed to the Housing
Authority by Mayor Meiner.
Mayor Meiner stated that he appointed Charlotte Tomic to the Housing Authority, subject to
Commission approval. Subsequently, Commissioner Bhatt nominated Charlotte Tomic to the
Affordable Housing Advisory Committee. He invited Ms. Tomic to indicate which board she would like
to serve on and asked City Clerk Granado to confirm whether Ms. Tomic is ineligible to serve on both
boards.
City Clerk Granado stated that she can serve on both because the Housing Authority is a State Board
that is not subject to the City's restrictions.
Charlotte Tomic stated she would be happy to serve on both, if possible.
Commissioner Fernandez asked about the status of the Housing Authority seat.
City Clerk Granado responded that the seat is currently held by former Mayor Matti Bower, whose
term ended on January 20, 2026. Because it is a State Board, there are no term limits.
Commissioner Bhatt asked why Mayor Bower was being removed from the Authority, given that there
are no term limits.
Mayor Meiner stated that board memberships are often changed. He introduced Ms. Tomic’s
background in real estate and marketing, stating that he believes this is a great opportunity to move
forward with new ideas and projects.
Ms. Tomic introduced her background in real estate, public relations, and non-profits, and explained
how she can use it to promote affordable housing.

HOUSING AUTHORITY
• Mojdeh Khaghan, Housing Authority Commissioner Category
TE: 12/31/30 TL: N/A
Reappointed by acclamation by the City Commission.
Commissioner Fernandez motioned to reappoint Mojdeh Khaghan, seconded by Mayor Meiner.
The reappointment was done by acclamation.
• Charlotte Tomic, Housing Authority Commissioner Category
Discussion held regarding Mayor Meiner's appointment of Charlotte Tomic to the Housing
Authority.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that he has great respect for Charlotte Tomic and the work she
does; he wishes to defer to the fact that it is the Mayor's appointment. However, he also has great
respect for Mayor Bower, with whom he has worked closely. Mayor Bower currently holds the seat
and is the only Hispanic member of the Housing Authority. Without her, the board may lose
representation and perspective that support community trust. He described some of Mojdeh
Khaghan and Mayor Bower's hard work and achievements during their time of service, including
securing 306 new Section 8 vouchers and doubling the Section 8 housing funding awarded by the
Federal government. He stressed the importance of having at least one Hispanic member on the
Housing Authority, recognizing that a significant portion of those served by the Housing Authority
are Hispanic. Due to this, he is unable to support or vote to ratify Charlotte Tomic's appointment.
Mayor Meiner explained his decision to appoint Charlotte Tomic. He emphasized that he does not
wish to diminish Mayor Bower's service, who has served with great distinction. He noted that, as
Commissioner Fernandez mentioned, he was unaware that Mayor Bower was the only Hispanic
committee member. He stated that the Committee needed realignment and a new direction. He
also heard from some members that the Authority needed a new focus. He emphasized that this
was not directed at Mayor Bower but at the Committee and that it is his responsibility to ensure
these committees move forward. He added that the Barclay Apartments have long plagued the
City, and when the City put them out to bid, the Housing Authority set them back.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez stated that Charlotte Tomic is terrific and has served on other committees.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez emphasized that former Mayor Maddie Bower has been an important force
in the City’s history and is deeply committed to the Housing Authority. Out of respect for Mayor
Bower’s long service and her dedication to this particular committee, the Vice-Mayor felt that Mayor
Bower deserved to remain on the board and should have been notified or consulted. The
Vice-Mayor added that, if a new direction were needed, there were other committee vacancies
where Ms. Tomic could have been appointed instead.
Mayor Meiner stated that Mayor Bower never reached out to him and that it is incumbent upon the
person seeking the position to express interest. He never received that, and he wanted to mention
that there is more than one way.
Further discussion and clarification were held regarding the appointment of Charlotte Tomic to
Mayor Bower's current seat on the Housing Authority.
City Clerk Granado explained that Mayor Bower will continue to hold the seat until someone else
is appointed to replace her or she is reappointed.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that she holds Ms. Tomic in high regard and nominated her to the
Affordable Housing Advisory Committee.
Vote: 3-4; Opposed: Commissioners Fernandez, Matteo-Salinas, and Bhatt, and Vice-Mayor
Dominguez.
The Mayor’s appointment did not receive the required Commission confirmation.
Mayor Meiner thanked Ms. Tomic and expressed that he believes this is a disservice to our City.
