ACTION: Padel Court Setbacks – Referral to the Land Use and Sustainability Committee. •
The City Commission, by acclamation, referred a broader discussion of Padel court setbacks and
related issues to the Land Use and Sustainability Committee (LUSC). This referral followed a
suggestion by Commissioner Fernandez, with Mayor Meiner concurring. and noting that a
separate Design Review Board appeal related to Padel courts was scheduled later in the day.
Thomas Mooney to handle. See Item C4 AC.
 Mr. Manny Orozco identified himself as a lifelong Miami Beach resident speaking in support of
the towing reform Item. He stated that towing practices in Miami Beach were widely viewed as
predatory and described personal experiences, including being towed from a residential zone for
a marginal violation and receiving both a tow and a citation. He stated that towing practices
disproportionately affected residents and described tactics used by towing operators, such as
claiming that credit card machines were inoperable. He advocated for stronger oversight and
asked the Commission to consider a retrospective appeals window for residents to seek refunds
or fee waivers for marginal violations. He thanked Commissioner Fernandez and Commissioner
Bhatt for sponsoring the towing Item and urged the Commission to include accountability
measures in any reform proposal.
Mayor Meiner acknowledged receiving recent increases in towing complaints and described the
Item as timely.
 Mr. Matthew Gultanoff, identifying himself as a resident of Jefferson Avenue, addressed the
Commission regarding traffic safety. He referenced a recent fatality at a crosswalk on 41st Street
and stated that the victim had followed all pedestrian signals. He also described other recent
incidents involving bicyclists and construction workers. He referenced County data indicating an
increase in fatalities and stated that pedestrian and cyclist safety represented a significant threat
to residents. Mr. Gultanoff mentioned the City’s Vision Zero Action Plan and questioned its 2040
target date, citing Hoboken, New Jersey, as an example of a city that has had zero traffic fatalities
for several years. He asked the Commission what actions would be taken to improve immediate
safety for pedestrians and cyclists.
Mayor Meiner responded, describing upcoming transportation planning discussions at the
Miami-Dade Transportation Planning Organization (TPO), and referenced proposals for
dedicated left-turn lanes on 41st Street that would require coordination with the Florida
Department of Transportation.
 Mr. Mitch Novick stated that he managed two multifamily apartment buildings in Miami Beach. He
expressed concern about a recent 17% increase in his waste-hauling invoices and stated that
only two haulers remained available to residents, compared with several options decades earlier.
He urged the Commission to add a third hauler to increase competition. He also referenced water
rate discussions and expressed concern over cumulative utility rate increases, noting the number
of City employees added over recent years and stating that infrastructure improvements should
be a priority.
 Mr. David Sexton, appearing via Zoom, a resident of Miami Beach, thanked the Commission for
advancing the Byron Carlyle project. He referenced positive RFQ results and stated that one firm,
Brooks Scarpa Architects, had strong community connections due to its local residents and should
be given weight if the finalists were otherwise equal.

ACTION: Discussion held.
Miami-Dade County Commissioner Raquel Regalado, District 7, addressed the Commission to
present the Neuroinclusion Toolkit. She noted her previous service on the School Board and
explained that she attended in her capacity as the parent of two neurodivergent adults. She thanked
the Commission for raising the flag in recognition of autism acceptance and emphasized the
importance of moving from awareness toward acceptance. She discussed the availability of
resources for young children and highlighted the increased challenges that emerge during the
transition to adolescence and adulthood. She explained that she had been working for over a decade
on programming for adults as her own children transitioned into adult services. Commissioner
Regalado described her family’s past participation in programs at Nova Southeastern University and
noted the City’s longstanding partnership with NSU CARD. She explained that the Neuroinclusion
Toolkit had been emailed to the Commission and included QR codes that provided access to the
material. She stated that the Toolkit compiled legislation, data, training practices, and examples of
social stories used in libraries, as well as methods for providing autism-friendly and sensory-friendly
events. She explained that the term neuroinclusion was used because many individuals diagnosed
with autism also have other neurodivergent conditions such as ADHD, dyslexia, Tourette’s syndrome,
epilepsy, or obsessive-compulsive disorder. She noted that neurological conditions span a broad
spectrum that includes developmental delays, brain injuries, dementia, and Alzheimer’s disease. She
stated that one in five residents in Florida is neurodivergent and that sensory-friendly strategies
support both neurodivergent and neurotypical individuals. Commissioner Regalado described
ongoing efforts with the Youth Fair to expand sensory-friendly spaces and hours and emphasized
that the work progresses gradually. She stated that Miami-Dade County and NSU CARD had trained
more than four thousand first responders, reducing unnecessary Baker Act placements and arrests.
She described an example involving a 911 response in which a caregiver relied on the County’s
autism training to assist officers in appropriately interacting with a neurodivergent adult.
Commissioner Regalado discussed barriers to employment faced by neurodivergent adults, including
difficulty obtaining a state identification card. She explained that the County had partnered with the
Tax Collector’s Office to create neuroinclusive days for families to obtain IDs and noted that recent
State law allowed individuals to voluntarily list disabilities on a Florida ID beginning at age five. She
emphasized the importance of accessible IDs for participation in public spaces. Commissioner
Regalado provided an overview of Countywide programs, including training for transit workers and
airport staff. She described the Sunflower Lanyard program for individuals with invisible disabilities
and explained that airport staff distributed the lanyards to travelers. She detailed the MIA AIR
program, which provides practice sessions for boarding procedures, TSA screening, and aircraft
visits, along with social stories in English and Spanish. She explained that caregivers were connected
with TSA Cares for support during air travel. Commissioner Regalado emphasized that all programs
were built within existing County systems and were not intended to create new positions or economic
opportunities but to embed inclusion into current practices. She described the importance of
sensory-friendly events and noted that families often avoided public spaces but were now increasingly
attending events designed for inclusion. She described her upcoming fair in Pinecrest, which would
include opportunities for caregivers to register neurodivergent individuals with the Sheriff’s Office to
ensure first responders had access to essential information during emergencies. She explained that
this voluntary registration could include communication needs, de-escalation information, and vehicle
registration indicators to alert officers when a neurodivergent person might be present. Commissioner
Regalado stated that she would like to see expanded adult programming in Miami Beach. She noted
that the healthcare system was designed primarily for elderly individuals and that without structured
adult programs, neurodivergent young adults could spend decades at home without support. She
emphasized that neurodivergent adults improve with continued intervention and that programming
could be co-located with vocational training and employment opportunities. She explained that the
County modified its hiring practices to remove unnecessary communication requirements and instead
allowed applicants to demonstrate tasks directly. Commissioner Regalado reiterated her willingness
to assist the City and thanked the Commission for its support. She encouraged the development of
more adult programs and stated that she was available for questions.
Mayor Steven Meiner thanked Commissioner Regalado for her presentation and acknowledged the
importance of her work. He noted the challenges faced by families caring for neurodivergent
individuals and emphasized the value of education and concrete actions.
Commissioner Regalado responded by reflecting on her personal experience raising neurodivergent
children and noted that while early years were difficult, progress became evident with time and
community support.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez thanked Commissioner Regalado for her leadership and described
the Toolkit as a meaningful resource developed through public service. He emphasized the relevance
of sensory-friendly training for a destination city such as Miami Beach and noted the importance of
preparing staff in hotels, restaurants, parks, and public safety departments. He thanked
Commissioner Regalado for making the Toolkit available statewide and stated that Miami Beach had
opportunities to expand programming and engage the business community in inclusive initiatives.
Commissioner Regalado responded that the Greater Miami Convention and Visitors Bureau had been
a partner in this work and hinted at an upcoming announcement involving a Miami Beach hotel
becoming fully trained. She encouraged the City to lead in developing autism-friendly spaces and
highlighted NSU CARD as a strong partner. She described the County’s training initiatives for Police
Officers, Firefighters, parks staff, transit employees, and library personnel. She noted that trained
staff become informal ambassadors who promote inclusion throughout the community. Commissioner
Regalado spoke about Miami-Dade County’s reputation for cultural and ethnic diversity and
suggested that the community could also lead in intellectual diversity by recognizing the abilities and
creativity of neurodivergent individuals. She emphasized the importance of reducing stereotypes
through training and engagement. She described ongoing partnerships with organizations such as
Easterseals and detailed programs that place neurodivergent individuals in community-facing roles
at events and in police and parks trainings.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt thanked Commissioner Regalado and asked whether data existed
regarding neurodivergence resulting from traumatic brain injuries, particularly in relation to increases
in micromobility-related accidents. She stated that such data would be helpful for City and County
initiatives.
Commissioner Regalado responded that she could provide data and agreed to work on the request.
Commissioner Bhatt then discussed the City’s efforts to become a health and well-being destination
through the Blue Zones initiative and expressed interest in integrating neuroinclusion into those
efforts. She stated that she would contact Commissioner Regalado to discuss additional
collaboration.
Commissioner Regalado explained that the Toolkit also included training developed with the Jackson
Health System for emergency departments and urgent care centers. She described simple strategies
to make events more accessible, including the use of social stories and sensory-friendly practices.
She emphasized that many of the measures were low-cost and easily scalable.
Mayor Meiner thanked Commissioner Regalado again for her partnership and leadership.
Commissioner Regalado expressed her appreciation for the City’s support and concluded her
presentation.

items.title: CITY COMMISSION FILE NO. 2025-00001 APPEAL, FILED BY ONUR S. GUNDAY, OF AN ORDER OF THE MIAMI BEACH DESIGN REVIEW BOARD (“DRB”) DATED OCTOBER 22, 2025, FOR DRB FILE NO. 25-1104, APPROVING THE CONSTRUCTION OF A NEW GOLF COURSE CLUBHOUSE, THE RELOCATION OF TENNIS COURTS, FOUR NEW PADEL COURTS, THE ADDITION OF THREE COMFORT STATIONS, A NEW DRIVEWAY, A VARIANCE FROM THE REQUIRED ANCILLARY STRUCTURE SETBACK, AND ONE OR MORE WAIVERS, TO REPLACE THE EXISTING CLUBHOUSE.
items.action: The appeal was deferred to the May 20, 2026, City Commission Meeting.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: The appeal was deferred to the May 20, 2026, City Commission Meeting.
Commissioner Suarez moved to defer the appeal to the May 20, 2026 City Commission Meeting;
seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 4-3. Commissioners Monica Matteo-Salinas, Joseph
Magazine, and Tanya K. Bhatt voted against the motion.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: No
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: No
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: No
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
The Office of the City Attorney to handle.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Nick Kallergis, representing the City of Miami Beach in the proceeding,
explained that the matter before the Commission concerned an appeal of a Design Review Board
approval relating to the construction of a new clubhouse and campus improvements at La Gorce
Country Club, located at 5685 Alton Road. He indicated that the appeal had been filed by Mr. Onur
(“Honor”) S. Gunday, the owner of a single-family residence situated west of the Club on Alton Road.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis emphasized that because this was an appeal of a Design Review
Board decision on a specific property, the Commission’s determination must be based solely on the
record that had been before the Board, and no new evidence or testimony could be received. He
noted that only the argument from counsel would be heard. He stated that under the City Code, the
Commission could reverse, remand, or modify a Design Review Board decision upon a five-sevenths
vote if the Commission found that the Board failed to provide procedural due process, failed to base
its decision on competent substantial evidence, or failed to observe the essential requirements of law.
He further explained that, consistent with prior appeals, the petitioner would have 10 minutes for oral
argument, the City and La Gorce Country Club would share their allotted 10 minutes for response,
and the petitioner would then have an opportunity for rebuttal. He concluded by noting that following
the argument, the Commission could deliberate and vote, requiring a five-sevenths vote to affirm and
a simple majority to reverse, modify, or remand.
Attorney Graham Penn, representing La Gorce Country Club, the Respondent, apologized for
interrupting and asked for clarification regarding whether the petitioner’s rebuttal time was included
within the ten-minute presentation period or provided in addition to it. He recalled that the Commission
typically allowed two minutes for rebuttal and requested clarification of the procedure.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis stated that because the appeal was a quasi-judicial proceeding,
he would place counsel under oath and asked whether their testimony would be truthful. After counsel
affirmed, he explained that the oath applied only to the attorneys, as no other witnesses would be
offering testimony due to the quasi-judicial requirement that the record be limited to the evidence
previously presented before the Design Review Board.
Attorney Ralf Brookes, representing the Petitioner/Appellant, Mr. Onur S. Gunday, acknowledged that
while his client had been sworn, only counsel would be speaking.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis indicated that if Mr. Brookes was ready to proceed, the timer
would be set for ten minutes.
Mr. Brookes explained that he had distributed paper copies of the appeal materials so each
Commissioner could easily reference them, given the overall volume of the agenda. He introduced
himself as Attorney Ralf Brookes, board-certified in city, county, and local government law, and
described his municipal and land-use litigation background. He indicated that he would outline three
primary arguments and offer alternative options for the Commission’s consideration. Referring to the
appeal document, he described the four proposed Padel courts included within the La Gorce Country
Club redevelopment plan, explaining that the area currently consisted only of grass and a portable
golf performance structure. He stated that the appeal was based on the position that Padel was not
listed as an allowable use in the GC (Golf Course District) zoning classification and that adding a new
use required a text amendment rather than treating Padel as equivalent to tennis. He described Padel
courts as enclosed facilities with concrete foundations, turf, and surrounding walls of glass or
plexiglass supported by metal poles, emphasizing that the sport is played off the walls and is
functionally different from tennis. Mr. Brookes explained that the proposed courts would be located
approximately twenty feet from his client’s historic residence, designed by architect Robert E. Collins
in 1936. He asserted that the proximity would result in impacts related to noise, lighting, and extended
hours of activity, noting that the courts were proposed for use until 10:00 p.m. He then introduced a
second concern regarding setback requirements for structures on golf courses adjacent to
single-family homes, stating that the setback should be at least seventy-five feet from the property
line, and that Padel courts should be considered structures due to their enclosed configuration. He
further explained that the proposed restroom and golf performance center measured only 151 feet
from the property line, below the required 170-foot setback in other yard areas.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine asked the City Attorney’s Office to clarify the Commission’s scope
of review, specifically whether the Commission was permitted to determine whether Padel was a
permitted use associated with a golf course or what matters the Commission was authorized to
evaluate in the appeal.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis clarified that the Commission’s role was to determine whether
the Design Review Board’s decision was supported by competent substantial evidence, whether the
Board had applied the correct law and followed applicable review criteria, and whether procedural
due process had been provided.
Mr. Brookes continued by referencing the section of the Land Development Regulations listing
permitted uses in the GC District, reiterating that Padel was not listed and was not customarily
associated with a golf course. He discussed the setback deficiencies and explained that the
placement would obstruct views and negatively affect his client’s property. He referenced design
review criteria related to compatibility with surrounding properties, lighting impacts, orientation, and
preservation of view corridors, arguing that the proposed courts did not satisfy those criteria. He
added that the lighting plan had been deferred to the building permit stage, preventing public review
and providing no assurance that lighting would not spill onto adjacent properties. He described the
potential effects on the enjoyment and value of his client’s historic home. Mr. Brookes concluded by
asking the Commission to modify the approval to remove the four proposed Padel courts, clarifying
that he was not seeking denial of the overall redevelopment. He referenced a 2004 settlement
between the City and La Gorce Country Club regarding fencing and view preservation and asked the
Commission to uphold the principles established in that agreement.
Mr. Penn began his portion of the presentation and indicated that he was appearing on behalf of La
Gorce Country Club. He noted that he would share time with Assistant City Attorney Alexander but
intended to focus primarily on responding directly to the arguments presented by Mr. Brookes. He
referenced materials distributed earlier in the morning by Mr. Gunday and reiterated, consistent with
prior explanation by Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis, that the Commission’s decision must be
based solely on the record that had been before the Design Review Board, without the introduction
of new evidence or reconsideration of the underlying merits. He stated that the record demonstrated
that the Board had provided procedural due process, adhered to the essential requirements of law,
and had competent substantial evidence before it when rendering its decision, which he emphasized
was the sole inquiry before the Commission. Mr. Penn stated that Mr. Gunday had not appeared
before the Design Review Board and explained that under Florida law, a party who does not attend
the quasijudicial hearing may be considered to have waived certain arguments by failing to present
them at the appropriate time. He indicated that a party may not challenge a quasijudicial decision
after the fact without having participated in the original proceedings.
Commissioner Magazine asked whether appearing before the Design Review Board was one of the
criteria relevant to the appeal and whether a party could raise objections after the hearing had
concluded if they had not appeared or participated initially.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis recommended that the Commission allow both respondent
attorneys to complete their presentation before he addressed legal questions from the Commission.
He noted that Assistant City Attorney Alexander would present the City’s portion of the response
immediately after Mr. Penn, and that he would then be available to answer any questions from the
Commission following the respondents’ arguments.
Mr. Penn stated that even though arguments may have been waived, he was addressing all of the
petitioner’s points in full. He reiterated that the Commission was not re-deciding the application or
substituting its judgment for that of the Design Review Board. He stated that the Commission’s role
was limited to determining whether the Board provided procedural due process, followed the essential
requirements of law, and based its decision on competent substantial evidence. He asserted that the
record supported the Board’s decision under all three criteria and noted that the approval had been
unanimous. Mr. Penn addressed the arguments raised by Mr. Brookes regarding the use
classification and the setback determination. He explained that the Design Review Board did not have
authority to interpret or apply the Resiliency Code with respect to whether a Padel court was
consistent with the GC Zoning District or whether it should have the same setback as a tennis court.
He stated that these determinations were made administratively by the Planning Director pursuant to
the Resiliency Code. According to Mr. Penn, because the Design Review Board had no authority to
make those determinations, such issues were not properly before the Commission in this appeal. Mr.
Penn also responded to statements regarding potential loss of views from the petitioner’s property,
explaining that Florida law has long held that there is no legal right to maintain a view across another
person’s property. He asserted that such a claim could not serve as a basis to challenge the Board’s
approval. Turning to the issue of compatibility, Mr. Penn stated that the record demonstrated that the
Design Review Board had engaged in extensive discussion regarding the location of the Padel courts,
buffering, hours of operation, lighting, and related considerations. He noted that three specific
conditions addressing the Padel courts were included in the order: a requirement for a solid barrier,
a requirement that the barrier be landscaped, and an existing buffer of twelve trees between the Club
and adjacent properties. He also mentioned conditions prohibiting light projection beyond the courts
and establishing hours of operation. He stated that these matters were thoroughly discussed and that
the record refuted the suggestion that compatibility issues had not been considered. Mr. Penn
concluded by noting that his allotted portion of time was ending and turned the presentation over to
Assistant City Attorney Alexander.
Assistant City Attorney Justin Alexander addressed the Commission on behalf of the Design Review
Board. He stated that the Board respectfully requested that the Commission affirm its order approving
the design application for La Gorce Country Club. He explained that the Board afforded procedural
due process to the petitioner for two principal reasons: first, because the heightened notice standard
suggested by the petitioner would be administratively unworkable and was not required by due
process law; and second, because the City complied fully with the notice requirements in Section
2.2.4.1 of the Resiliency Code. Assistant City Attorney Alexander explained that adopting the
petitioner’s requested notice standard would require Planning Department and City Clerk staff to
verify that each property owner within the 375-foot notice radius affirmatively received mailed notice
of the hearing. He stated that such verification would be impractical and burdensome in both time
and cost. He explained that for this project, 480 property owners fell within the notice radius due to
the large geographic boundary encompassing the golf course. He noted that in denser
neighborhoods, a project could involve thousands of owners, making such a requirement
unreasonable and inconsistent with established due process standards. Assistant City Attorney
Alexander described the three forms of notice required by the Resiliency Code: mailed notice to all
property owners within the radius at least thirty days prior to the hearing; conspicuous posted notice
on the property; and published notice on the Miami-Dade County hosted notice website. He stated
that all three forms of notice were provided in this case, as reflected in the respondents’ appendix.
He noted that the posted notice consisted of a large red sign with bold text and that Mr. Gunday, who
lived adjacent to the project site, likely would have seen the posted notice even if he claimed he had
not received the mailed notice. He added that the record included the correctly printed mailing label
for the petitioner, which constituted sufficient evidence that mailed notice was properly issued.
Assistant City Attorney Alexander concluded by stating that because the petitioner’s proposed notice
standard was administratively infeasible and inconsistent with the law, and because the City fully
complied with the notice requirements of the Resiliency Code, the Design Review Board respectfully
requested that the Commission affirm its decision.
Mr. Penn briefly returned to use the remainder of the respondents’ allotted time. He stated that the
record clearly demonstrated a careful decision by the Board, consistent with codified criteria and
supported by competent, substantial evidence. He reiterated that the Commission’s role was not to
reconsider the merits of the application but to determine whether the Board complied with due
process, applied the correct Code, and had sufficient evidence before it. He stated that all three
criteria were satisfied and requested that the Commission uphold the Board’s unanimous approval.
He indicated that he remained available to answer any questions.
Commissioner Suarez began to ask a question.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis stated that Mr. Brookes would be provided a couple of minutes
for rebuttal.
Mr. Brookes began his rebuttal by referencing pages 13 and 14 of the respondents’ appendix, which
pertained to the posted notice.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis asked that the document be submitted into the record.
Mr. Brookes described the posted notice as a red eight-and-a-half-by-eleven-inch sheet of paper
taped to a telephone pole and expressed concern that such a notice would be difficult to read for
drivers traveling on Alton Road. He stated that the Club should have reached out directly to adjacent
property owners, given the location of the four proposed Padel courts near his client’s residence. He
argued that the design criteria relating to location and compatibility were not satisfied and reiterated
concerns regarding hours of operation, lighting impacts, installation of a twelve-foot wall, and loss of
long-standing views across the golf course dating back to 1936.
Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to uphold the ruling of the Design Review Board.
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez indicated she had questions and asked whether the Design Review
Board considered noise impacts when reviewing proposals, noting that noise was a frequent concern
from residents. She stated that locating a recreational use 20 feet from a backyard seemed unusually
close and asked which body would approve such a configuration.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis explained that the Design Review Board’s role was to review the
design of proposed development. He noted that in this case, the Board included conditions intended
to mitigate impacts such as operating hours, fencing, and the design of the setback wall surrounding
the Padel courts. He clarified that the application required only Design Review Board approval and
did not require Planning Board review. He added that the Club would remain subject to the City’s
Noise Ordinance regardless of whether noise-related conditions were included in the Board’s order.
Commissioner Suarez then asked whether the allegation that Padel courts were not permitted on a
golf course had been addressed, noting that he had been intermittently out of the room.
Mr. Penn responded that the issue had been addressed from the respondents’ perspective, reiterating
that the Design Review Board did not have authority to interpret Zoning Code provisions related to
use or setbacks. He stated that those determinations were made by the Planning Director pursuant
to the Resiliency Code. He explained that because the Planning Director determined that Padel use
was appropriate and that the setback standards aligned with those for tennis courts, those
determinations were not within the Design Review Board’s purview and could not form the basis of
an appeal to the Commission.
Mayor Steven Meiner began to seek clarification from Assistant City Attorney Alexander, at which
point Mr. Brookes requested to respond

items.title: DISCUSS VIABILITY OF INSTALLING SECURITY BOLLARDS IN DESIGNATED AREAS OF THE CITY, INCLUDING BUT NOT LIMITED TO THE NORTH END OF OCEAN DRIVE, THE BEACHWALK ALONG MID-BEACH, AND LINCOLN ROAD.
items.action: Discussion held. David Gomez to handle. DIRECTION: 1. CIP to provide depictions of proposed solutions to Commissioners. 2. CIP to return with short-term recommendations after review. 3. CIP to prepare and present long-term system options.
items.voteBasis: No separate vote identified. A vote has not been inferred.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Discussion held. David Gomez to handle.
DIRECTION:
1. CIP to provide depictions of proposed solutions to Commissioners.
2. CIP to return with short-term recommendations after review.
3. CIP to prepare and present long-term system options.
Commissioner Magazine introduced the Item and stated that it aligns with the broader theme he has
been addressing, the importance of taking pride in the City’s appearance and aesthetics. This Item is
especially important in areas such as Ocean Drive, which he described as the City’s postcard and
one of its most recognizable public spaces. The City takes great pride in the architecture along Ocean
Drive and in Lummus Park. He went there over the weekend, as he often does, and when this area
functions well, it is truly unparalleled and among the best in the world. The City needs to treat its
public rights-of-way with the same level of care and high standards expected of property owners in
the area. Public and private spaces operate as one ecosystem, and both need to reflect the same
level of quality. With security also in mind, the north end of Ocean Drive has been in an ongoing
condition for several years that does not meet the City’s standards for beauty, aesthetics, or public
safety. The area should be maintained as one of the most pristine not only in the City but in the
country and the world. Whenever the City undertakes improvements, it should strive for excellence
and a world-class result. He explained that the current condition, including a partially broken gate that
operates manually, gives the appearance that the City is stuck in a temporary and unattractive
situation. The City should move toward a more permanent, attractive, and functional solution, similar
to what could be seen in world-class areas such as the New York Stock Exchange in downtown
Manhattan. He asked David Gomez to provide more information on potential next steps.
David Gomez, CIP Director, stated that Commissioner Magazine had provided a clear summary of
the issue. However, there are continuing concerns regarding security on the Beachwalk, particularly
the need to restrict unauthorized vehicular access while protecting the safety of Beachwalk users.
The City completed a comprehensive study not only of the areas around Lummus Park but also
Citywide. Staff met with community representatives and with Commissioner Magazine’s Office. City
staff received feedback from the community regarding both the aesthetics and functionality of
whatever system the City ultimately installed. Any proposed system needs to allow appropriate
access for City vehicles, City maintenance vehicles, and, in certain circumstances, private
maintenance vehicles. City staff identified short-term fixes that could be implemented while the City
develops a broader and more permanent solution. Potential long-term solutions have also been
identified. He recently provided a report to the Office of the City Manager and understood that the
Administration likely has not yet had time to review it. Staff is prepared to return with
recommendations for a short-term solution.
Commissioner Magazine asked whether CIP Director Gomez had depictions of the proposed
solutions.
CIP Director Gomez replied that staff has depictions of a few potential solutions, but he did not bring
them to the meeting. He could provide them later that day. One of the options staff reviewed is similar
to the concrete barriers at the end of Fifth Street near Lummus Park. The City is considering a similar
aesthetic for a temporary solution to help control access while remaining mindful of the area's
appearance, particularly in Mid Beach.
Commissioner Magazine stated that vehicles have mistakenly entered and traveled along the
Beachwalk. Thankfully, those incidents have not appeared to be intentional or malicious, but they still
demonstrate the need for action. The City needs to move forward swiftly and thoughtfully. He
emphasized that the City should take pride in these areas because Ocean Drive, the Beachwalk, and
Mid Beach are truly world-class locations. The City needs to implement improvements that reflect the
highest regard for aesthetics while also serving an important public safety function. He would like the
City to be more proactive on these issues rather than reactive.
Mitch Novick stated that he lives in the Entertainment District. He referenced the railroad-style gate
near the Betsy Hotel, which the County had previously ordered removed. The City had spent nearly
$1 million per year on private traffic management, which he believes led to chaos. He recalled a
serious incident in which an individual had both legs amputated after being run over by a tractor-
trailer along Ocean Court. The City cannot close that street because it would greatly disrupt business.
At the southern end, traffic cones are being used, and although those can be improved aesthetically,
public safety must remain paramount. He recalled an incident during the pandemic in which a person
was shot and Fire Rescue could not immediately access the area. The injured individual had to be
transported by golf cart to 15th Street so First Responders could provide assistance. He urged the
City Commission to ensure that any improvements do not interfere with emergency access.
Commissioner Bhatt responded to Mr. Novick’s comments and clarified that the proposed
improvements are not intended to impede access for life-safety personnel. Depending on the system
ultimately selected, Fire engines, Police vehicles, and other emergency vehicles would continue to
be able to access the area. Various systems could alert drivers that they are not permitted to enter
certain areas while still allowing authorized vehicles to pass. In North Beach, she has seen
motorcycles enter on Ocean Terrace and speed down the Beachwalk. People have driven onto the
grass in Lummus Park without realizing they were in the wrong location. The purpose of the
improvements is to prevent unauthorized vehicles from entering pedestrian-oriented public spaces.
Cities in Europe, including medieval cities with very narrow cobblestone streets, use retractable
bollards that can be automatically operated by authorized vehicles or residents. These systems could
keep unwanted traffic out without preventing necessary access. This has been a topic of discussion
for a long time, and she is somewhat frustrated by the delay. However, the matter is moving forward,
and the improvements are necessary for the City. She emphasized that there are ways to implement
the system without impeding the desired flow of traffic.
Commissioner Suarez asked CIP Director Gomez whether the City is receiving State funding for the
bollards.
CIP Director Gomez replied that no State funding is currently available. The current budget includes
only partial funding, and additional funding requests are being submitted as part of the budget cycle.
Commissioner Magazine stated that the City Commission is waiting on the CIP report, which has
been sent to the City Manager. Because the discussion is focused on moving forward, he believes
the Item can be tabled at this moment.
City Clerk Granado asked Commissioner Magazine whether he wanted the Item placed back on the
agenda for the following month or until further direction is needed.
Commissioner Magazine replied that he trusts the Administration to move forward. If necessary, he
would place the Item back on the agenda at a later date.

items.title: DISCUSS/TAKE ACTION ON THE MIAMI BEACH POLICE DEPARTMENT PROMOTIONAL PROCESS AND POTENTIAL MODIFICATIONS.
items.action: Discussion held. Chief Wayne Jones and Marla Alpizar to handle. DIRECTION: 1. The City Manager and the City’s negotiating team should prioritize reforming the Police Department’s promotional process during the next FOP contract negotiations. 2. Explore alternative promotional models. (Examples: hybrid promotional models (merit + testing) or other national models.)
items.voteBasis: No separate vote identified. A vote has not been inferred.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Discussion held. Chief Wayne Jones and Marla Alpizar to handle.
DIRECTION:
1. The City Manager and the City’s negotiating team should prioritize reforming the Police
Department’s promotional process during the next FOP contract negotiations.
2. Explore alternative promotional models. (Examples: hybrid promotional models (merit + testing)
or other national models.)
Commissioner Suarez stated that one of the complaints he receives from many rank-and-file Police
Officers is that the promotional process appears broken in how candidates are selected for promotion
within the Police Department. He finds it surprising that the current process is largely geared toward
written examinations. In his view, the process does not sufficiently account for merit in determining
how leaders within the Police Department are promoted. He does not believe that is fair. He brought
before the City Commission the case of Officer Emmanuel Ofei, whom he believes has gone above
and beyond in performing his duties. This Officer located the criminal suspect, Christopher Pitre, who
had held a City Commission colleague at gunpoint in his parking garage. (A video of the arrest was
shown in the Commission Chambers. Click here to view.) The video showed Officer Ofei, now a
Sergeant, cleverly apprehending Mr. Pitre. The Officer knew the person was the suspect from the
beginning. He made up a story about a person in a white Tesla complaining about him and detained
him in handcuffs. The Officer was able to safely retrieve Mr. Pitre’s fully loaded firearm. Through what
he calls “street smarts,” Sergeant Ofei apprehended the perpetrator with little to no force. However,
when Sergeant Ofei tried to get promoted, he was all the way down the list. Something is wrong with
the system, and the process needs to be changed. He has worked with the Police Chief on the issue
and understands that there is no perfect promotional system. However, during the next round of
negotiations with the Fraternal Order of Police, the City Manager should be directed that reforming
the promotional process is a priority. The process should be based more on merit rather than strictly
on a written examination. The City has recently extended the Police Chief’s contract by two years.
The City Commission has shown confidence in the Chief’s judgment and has deferred to him
regarding how the Police Department should operate. In his view, it would not make sense to extend
that confidence to the Chief while denying him and others in his position the ability to have meaningful
input into who should be promoted. There are other Police agencies that use different promotional
models, including the “Rule of Three” system, under which the Chief could select from among the top
three candidates rather than being required to promote strictly from the top-ranked candidate on a
list. He asked Police Chief Jones to discuss the challenges of the current promotional process.
Police Chief Wayne Jones thanked Commissioner Suarez for bringing the discussion forward. He
stated that the current promotional process is contractual and has been negotiated with the Union.
He explained that the only way to change the system would be through contract negotiations. The
existing system has been in place for approximately fifteen to twenty years. Much of the process was
weighted toward a written examination, with additional components based on assessment testing,
seniority points, and educational points. These elements are combined to produce a ranked
promotional list. Under the current system, the Department is required to promote candidates in the
order in which they appear on the list. For example, if candidates are ranked from 1 to 5, promotions
must be made in that order. There is an opportunity to have a substantive conversation with the Union
about improving the promotional process. A number of promotional models are used nationally, and
some appear to be more modern than the current model used by the Miami Beach Police Department.
A different model can help ensure that the best candidates rise to the top of the list while also giving
the Department appropriate discretion in the final selection.
Commissioner Suarez asked Chief Jones to describe some of the challenges he had observed in the
current system.
Chief Jones stated that he had seen very experienced Police Officers with significant credibility and
equity among Department staff and rank-and-file Officers who had not performed well on prior
examinations. One particular Neighborhood Resource Officer came to mind, although he did not want
to identify the person by name. The Officer knew what he was doing and would have made an
excellent supervisor, but the current process did not adequately reflect that experience and leadership
potential. There has to be a better system than the one currently in place.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he is bringing the matter to his colleagues’ attention after discussing
it with the Chief multiple times over the prior year. He wants the City Commission to direct the City
Manager and the City’s negotiating team to seek a reset of the Police Department’s promotional
process during labor negotiations. He asked Chief Jones whether the issue had been raised in the
last round of negotiations and how strongly the Fraternal Order of Police had opposed it.
City Manager Carpenter stated that the issue would need to be addressed at the next negotiation
session. The Union has pushed back in the past when the City discussed the Rule of Three. He
explained that he is familiar with the Rule of Three because he had worked for more than two decades
in a system that used it, and that system had worked well in that context.
Commissioner Suarez stated that the Police Chief had indicated that he wanted reform and believed
a revised process would make his job easier. He asked his colleagues where they stand on the issue.
Commissioner Fernandez agreed with Commissioner Suarez’s point. The City Commission has
extended the Police Chief’s contract because we trust his judgment, and the Commission should also
trust the Chief’s judgment when it comes to promotions. An examination can measure certain things,
but many important qualities cannot be measured through a test. Leadership presence, judgment
under pressure, and emotional intelligence are examples of skills that an examination cannot
adequately capture. Those qualities can only be evaluated through the discretion and experience of
the Police Chief. He is fully in favor of reforming the promotional process and is glad the discussion
is taking place early so that the City’s negotiating team can incorporate the issue into its strategy.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that she wants to add context and share her thoughts. She has also
spoken with the Police Chief about the issue for some time. She explained that, when she and others
were elected, they entered office during an ongoing Police contract negotiation and were essentially
presented with a negotiated agreement. She stated that there had been significant discussions at that
time about what the City Commission wanted to see handled differently in the next negotiation cycle.
She believes the current system is insufficient and that the Rule of Three alone is not sufficient. The
current system does not adequately account for skills beyond the ability to study for and take a test.
A person could be an excellent Police Officer and not perform well on a test, while another person
could be a poor Officer but a strong test taker. She understands the concept behind the Rule of Three
but has concerns about the possibility of favoritism under a future Administration. Long after the
current City Commission and leadership are gone, a Police Department could theoretically be led by
individuals who promote friends or favor candidates instead of the most qualified Officers. This
possibility concerns her. Based on her discussions with Chief Jones, there are systems used by
Police departments around the country that include elements of both objective testing and merit-
based evaluation. Officers should demonstrate knowledge of the law and best practices, because the
City does not want people wearing the badge without that knowledge. However, the process should
also evaluate Officers’ street smarts, interpersonal skills, and management abilities, because those
were also essential parts of policing. She would like any future contract proposal or update to include
hybrid promotional models.
Chief Jones confirmed that there are more than 18,000 Police Departments in the United States and
that many promotional models are used. He is confident the City could identify a model better suited
to the Miami Beach Police Department.
Commissioner Suarez clarified that he had mentioned the Rule of Three only as an example and was
not insisting on that specific model. Other options exist, including panels with outside chiefs or other
independent evaluators who could assess candidates. The broader point is that the City should not
rely on a single method to judge candidates. He does not believe that the right way to evaluate a
candidate is solely through a written examination or an oral examination conducted before a camera
when the candidate does not know who is evaluating them. He agrees with the concern that the City
should avoid creating a system in which a future Chief could simply promote friends. As in
government, the promotional process could include multiple components that candidates would need
to satisfy before being promoted. He believes there appears to be an appetite for change among the
Commissioners who have spoken. The current system has been in place for approximately twenty
years, and the City should not continue a practice simply because it has existed for a long time. Many
members of the Commission have been elected to challenge the status quo, and the City and its
departments should continue to evolve and strive for improvement. He would like to give clearer
direction to the City’s negotiating team because the issue will likely be contentious. The Union
president is not present, and he believes the Union will likely advocate strongly for its position, as it
is expected to do. However, he stated that the City needs to see a fundamental change in how rank-
and-file Officers are promoted.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that Union representative Reginald “Reggie” Lester is present and may
offer a general perspective. She emphasized that he is not required to speak.
Sergeant Reginal Lester, Vice-President of the Miami Beach Fraternal Order of Police – Lodge 8,
stated that the Union is always willing to work with the City and the Administration to do what is right
for its members and for the City. If an issue arises during contract negotiations, the Union will review
it and do the best it can. During contract negotiations, the City has issues that are important to it, and
the Union has issues that are important to its members. At times, the issues that could most
significantly shape positive change are lost on both sides. Union leadership will come to the table
with open minds and consider change. He agrees with Commissioner Bhatt’s concerns about the
Rule of Three. There is significant concern among the rank-and-file about that type of system. In
Police work, Officers do not always trust individuals, even within their own ranks, and the Rule of
Three system could create a situation where a future Chief could skip over an Officer for reasons
unrelated to merit. These concerns, however, do not have to do with the current Police Chief, the
current Command Staff, or the current City Commission, all of whom are supportive of the Union.
Rather, the concern is related to the fairness of the system itself. While he understands the City
Manager’s familiarity with the Rule of Three and has also worked in a department that used it, his
experience is that the system was good for some but not for most.
Commissioner Bhatt thanked Sergeant Lester for his remarks.
Commissioner Suarez asked Chief Jones whether a Rule of Three system, if included as part of a
broader promotional model, would assist him in his role as Chief.
Chief Jones replied that any Chief would likely say that additional latitude to objectively select the
right candidate for a position would be helpful. However, based on prior conversations, the Union
does not appear likely to support a Rule of Three system. Therefore, the City needs to explore other
ways to improve and modernize the current testing and promotional process.
Commissioner Suarez acknowledged the response and thanked the participants for their discussion.

ACTION: Discussion held. Commissioner Bhatt moved to direct the Administration to return at the
May 20, 2026, Commission Meeting with a First Reading Ordinance implementing a Consumer Price
Index (CPI) adjustment beginning immediately and moving forward, together with the per-unit cost
calculations; seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Vote: 7-0.
DIRECTION:
 Apply the Consumer Price Index (CPI) adjustment beginning immediately and going forward.
 Bring back the charts and per-unit cost calculations for review at First Reading at the May 20,
2026, Commission Meeting.
Rafael E. Granado to notice. Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received.
John Norris to handle.
John Norris, Public Works Director, indicated that they are bringing back the Item with changes
discussed at the last meeting, when they bifurcated this from the water and sewer impacts. They
passed it on Second Reading earlier with just a CPI increase. He presented a PowerPoint
Presentation. Click here to view. In response to Commissioner Suarez’s question, he noted that the
35-year catch-up period was originally for one year, second in two years, and third in two years, with
no catch-up for zero to 25 units. This would come from the hauler's solid waste bill. If a single-family
residential customer, it goes on the water bill for trash, but these are billed directly from the hauler. In
response to Commissioner Magazine, he explained that they have a residential contract that covers
single-family homes up to eight-unit buildings, as of recently. They are working on negotiations to
include 9 to 16 units in that contract, and they are ready to issue an RFQ to multiple haulers for the
commercial multi-family contract. These are rates that come back to the City. There is the hauler’s
rate to haul and dispose of the trash, but franchise fees come back to the City. To Commissioner
Bhatt’s point, he explained that these fees were established to increase the street sweeping program,
but they generally fund sanitation activities within the City. They are unique in their Sanitation Division,
which handles more litter pickup and cleaning throughout the City. Most cities just pick up trash, but
they have activities expanding with the pressure washer and street sweeping throughout the City.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that the fees, whether at their current level or at the most modest step-
up, cover High Impact Weekend sanitation activities, including Memorial Day, Art Basel, and the entire
month of March, as well as any football or FIFA activities, which are not normally budgeted events
because they occur only occasionally. They also cover the Gum Removal program that Commissioner
Suarez brought, residential street cleaning, increased cleaning in the 200-300 block of Lincoln Road,
cleaning after who knows what other events, in addition to regular sanitation maintenance, and
restocking the dog poop stations. Someone in the neighborhood said it covers the things their
residents expect them to do because that is what they told them they do for them. The problem is
that they have been significantly increasing their level of service and have not increased their revenue
to cover the cost of those services in 35 years.
John Norris, Public Works Director, added that there are other revenue sources for the Sanitation
Division, but this is part of that revenue stream that funds Sanitation activities. Fees go up, and
franchise fees are a percentage of the commercial waste bill the customers are getting, so as they
increase, they see an increase in franchise revenue. Discussion continued. Public Works Director
Norris added that there is potential when they go to a multiple hauler system. If they went with five
haulers, that would create more competition, and they could actually see prices go down, which is
what they are hoping for the property owners in the City.
Commissioner Bhatt asked if they could hold off on this until they negotiate with the waste haulers. If
there is going to be savings from increased competition, but they can increase their fees, resulting in
a net-zero change for the residents, that might be the best possible outcome.
John Norris, Public Works Director, recommends at this point that they look at how the commercial
contract will affect revenues and, at a bare minimum, put a CPI increase on this right now so they do
not find themselves in the same situation in 30 years. They can then reassess as they look at what
the potential revenue change is in the commercial contract. Commissioner Bhatt agreed.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, added that it may seem like large numbers, but these figures are
aggregated across buildings with 26 to 50 units, 51 to 75 units, and 76 to 100 units, so the increase
they are discussing is approximately 50 cents per unit per month for most of these buildings. He is
letting them know that the Sanitation Fund has a structural imbalance and that CFO Jason Greene
likes to identify funds with such imbalances, meaning they provide more services than they collect
revenue for on an annual basis, and so they are eating into the fund balance to the point that the next
couple of years will bring some difficult conversations. Discussion continued. As a footnote, this is
one of the best ways to address the structural imbalance in the fund.
Commissioner Bhatt supports moving forward with the CPI. While it is irresponsible for them to
pretend that it should not have been done 35 years ago and that they would not be in this mess, and
to kick the can down the road, she is not having it. Second, it would be very useful to see these
numbers broken down per unit, because 0.50 cents per unit per month is a different conversation
than $24. The way she read it, it was $24 to her bill, but it is not, so they need to make sure that is
communicated. If it is truly the case that, across the board, there will be an increase, no matter what
size the building, with exemptions for smaller ones covered separately, they need to ensure that it is
fifty cents per unit in every situation. It might make more sense to do the CPI today, make that the
going-forward approach, and bring back the charts at First Reading in May to confirm that per-unit
math is correct so residents can remain calm.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, clarified that this is a Discussion Item, not an Ordinance, and that it will
ultimately have to be done by legislation and will need to come back for two readings no matter what.
They are having a conversation today to discuss how they want to position themselves moving
forward. There is probably some value in doing some additional breakdown, but they did not want to
go through the additional step of putting the Ordinance back on if there was not an appetite to take
that up at this time.
Commissioner Bhatt added, jokingly, that the presentation resembled a dress rehearsal for the
upcoming water and sewer impact fee discussion, and she noted that the joke did not land.
Commissioner Bhatt directed the Administration to return with a CPI increase and a math showing
the per-unit cost of usage, then bring it for First Reading. Public safety and utilities are fundamental
functions of government, and if they cannot pay for what they deliver, that is a big problem. They can
have all the bells and whistles in the world and fight all the fights about how they can get it done, but
if they do not make sure that trash is picked up, that toilets flush when needed, and that they can
drink clean water, that is a problem. She was in New York when they had the trash strike, and it is
something they do not want to do.
John Norris, Public Works Director, corrected the record and clarified that the impact fees are
collected on the water bill, not on the waste hauler bill. Discussion held.
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez asked the City Attorney whether the City Manager could be listed as
the sponsor for the Ordinance when it returns for First Reading.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, explained that, under Section 2-14 of the City Code, the City
Manager is not permitted to place an Ordinance on the agenda, and allowing the City Manager to
serve as a sponsor would require an amendment to the Code. He added that one of the
Commissioners may be working on an the Item to address this issue and that such an Item may
appear on a future agenda.
Commissioner Magazine asked for an update on the gum removal and power cleaning process, an
initiative that predates John Norris. As explained to him at the time, the machines are so intense and
powerful that they cannot be used without thorough training. He is often around the City and has
never seen one of these machines in use. In many areas and on many sidewalks he travels, he
notices that the results do not seem satisfactory. Where are they in this cleaning program?
John Norris, Public Works Director, would like to come back to deliver an update because he does
not have the data.
Commissioner Magazine noted that the condition of South Pointe Drive is disgusting and that he is
going to continue harping on the need for better care of the City's appearance and aesthetics. They
brought the tools forward to be able to do so, and he expects to see these machines in motion,
working 24/7. They could even consider renting them out to other municipalities, the Miami DDA, or
other places. Discussion held.
John Norris, Public Works Director, assured the City Commission that the machines are being used.
He rides around town early in the morning, mostly in the Entertainment District, to check, and they
can see everybody in action. Everything is happening as far as keeping the City clean, with a lot of
pressure washing, sweeping, blowing, and trash pickup.
In response to Mayor Meiner’s comment, Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, summarized that the
direction was to apply the CPI adjustment and bring back the math at First Reading.”
Commissioner Bhatt moved to direct the Administration to return at the May 20, 2026, Commission
Meeting with a First Reading Ordinance implementing a Consumer Price Index (CPI) adjustment
beginning immediately and moving forward, together with the per-unit cost calculations; seconded by
Commissioner Suarez. Vote: 7-0.

items.title: DISCUSS/TAKE ACTION: PARKING ENFORCEMENT IN NORTH BEACH.
items.action: Discussion held. COMMISSION DIRECTION:  Administration is directed to issue an LTC within one week outlining a clear and detailed enforcement plan for Zone 26 in North Beach. William MacDonald to handle.  Dedicated Parking Enforcement resources are to be assigned between 6:00 p.m. and 2:00 a.m. to ensure consistent enforcement during Zone 26 active hours. William MacDonald to handle.  Communications Department is directed to publicize the City’s online vehicle-status lookup tool so residents can report abandoned or non-resident vehicles more easily. Melissa Berthier and William MacDonald to handle.  Communications Department is directed to remind E-Gov app users that parking issues can already be reported through the existing app. Melissa Berthier and William MacDonald to handle.  Parking and Mobility Department is directed to enforce parking regulations as instructed by the Commission, including the use of towing when legally applicable. William MacDonald to handle.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Discussion held.
COMMISSION DIRECTION:
 Administration is directed to issue an LTC within one week outlining a clear and detailed
enforcement plan for Zone 26 in North Beach. William MacDonald to handle.
 Dedicated Parking Enforcement resources are to be assigned between 6:00 p.m. and 2:00 a.m.
to ensure consistent enforcement during Zone 26 active hours. William MacDonald to handle.
 Communications Department is directed to publicize the City’s online vehicle-status lookup tool
so residents can report abandoned or non-resident vehicles more easily. Melissa Berthier and
William MacDonald to handle.
 Communications Department is directed to remind E-Gov app users that parking issues can
already be reported through the existing app. Melissa Berthier and William MacDonald to
handle.
 Parking and Mobility Department is directed to enforce parking regulations as instructed by the
Commission, including the use of towing when legally applicable. William MacDonald to handle.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he recently held a North Beach Parking Town Hall meeting, and
one of the largest requests from residents was to see towing used to enforce Zone 26 parking. He
noted that residents report seeing stacks of tickets on cars with no action taken, and that some drivers
do not appear to care about the parking needs of the neighborhood. He explained that the
Commission created Zone 26 approximately two years ago, including an education-based grace
period with no towing written into the pilot Ordinance. The program brought structure and clarity for
residents and visitors, and initially worked well; however, once enforcement lacked consequences,
abuse increased. Last year, the Commission adopted a “Three Strikes You’re Out” towing policy for
Zone 26. He asked the City Manager how many tows had occurred under this rule. The City Manager
deferred to the Parking Director.
Parking Director MacDonald stated that there have been 450 non-commercial tows within the Zone
26 area. He explained that a vehicle becomes eligible for towing after receiving three Zone 26
violations within the same month. However, he noted that towing does not occur exclusively under
that rule, as vehicles may also be towed for other reasons. He described a recent case involving a
vehicle that accumulated two citations per month for several months; although it did not meet the
three-citations threshold, it was designated a scofflaw by Miami-Dade County due to unpaid citations
and was towed on that basis. He stated that determining the number of tows tied specifically to
residential Zone 26 violations would require a review of addresses. He reiterated that the 450
non-commercial tows do not include commercial or freight-loading zone tows and that the Parking
Department will review and provide additional detail.
Commissioner Suarez noted that many North Beach residents feel there is no enforcement. He
reported that Parking Lot 92 will be demolished and replaced by a larger structure, and during this
transition, residents will face added pressure. He stated that violators perceive residential zones as
“low-hanging fruit,” believing that they face little risk of being towed and only a $36 ticket. This places
residents without on-site parking at a disadvantage. He asked how many Parking Enforcement
Specialists were specifically assigned to North Beach.
Parking Director MacDonald explained that the Department does not have a dedicated team solely
for North Beach. Staffing is assigned by shift. Overnight, when Zone 26 requirements apply, the
Department typically assigns one Officer to North Beach. With four shifts, including a 6:00 p.m. to
2:30 a.m. shift, coverage can be adjusted to meet needs.
Commissioner Suarez expressed concern that enforcement is handled in an ad hoc manner and is
not part of a coordinated schedule. He asked how the City Manager recommends ensuring consistent
enforcement.
City Manager Carpenter responded that Zone 26 becomes active at 6:00 p.m., making it primarily an
overnight issue. He stated that the City likely needs to assign dedicated enforcement resources
between 6:00 p.m. and 2:00 a.m.
Director MacDonald added that although the Department has staffing plans, employees may take
vacation or sick leave, and supervisors will reassign coverage accordingly.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that she understood the concerns and noted that similar conditions likely
exist in Flamingo Park. She stated she was initially skeptical of the Zone 26 pilot, but after a full year,
she believes the program works well overall. She acknowledged that while some individuals remain
dissatisfied, the majority have adjusted. She identified Parkview Tower as a more complicated issue
and stated that the alley behind the West Lots, originally included in the program but removed early
on, now needs to be reinstated. She stated that there are reports of overnight camping in that alley
and in parking lots. She explained that Parking is an Enterprise Fund with 24-hour staffing and that
CRA funds may also be used. She emphasized the need for a clear plan to prevent backsliding, and
because North Beach is highly transient, communication efforts must be repeated for new residents.
She suggested that first-time violators receive an educational warning. She then asked the Parking
Director to explain the proposed parking program involving the Deauville site, and noted that she had
spoken with David Martin, who supports the concept.
Commissioner Suarez stated that residents at the Town Hall wanted clearer ways to report
abandoned vehicles. He discovered that residents may check a vehicle’s status through the City’s
online portal and asked Communications to publicize this link and encourage residents to help identify
non-resident vehicles.
Communications Director Berthier agreed to work with IT on the link and distribution.
Commissioner Bhatt added that the City now issues special permits for churches, volunteer
organizations, and for students and teachers, and that the parking database must correctly identify
those tags. If the system does not display a clear red or green result, Enforcement Officers must
reconfirm with the internal database.
Parking Director MacDonald stated that Officers scan all plates before issuing citations and are more
lenient with tickets because they can be reversed.
Commissioner Bhatt noted that residents are not always aware of that.
Commissioner Suarez requested that the Administration issue an LTC within one week outlining a
clear enforcement plan for Zone 26 in North Beach.
Parking Director MacDonald stated that Parking receives calls on a recorded line and must assign
each call a resolution. If an Officer arrives and sees multiple prior citations on a vehicle, the Officer
contacts a supervisor. Some County codes allow towing for violations other than lacking a Zone 26
permit.
Commissioner Bhatt asked Communications to remind E-Gov app users that they may already report
parking issues using the existing app.
Public comment was heard from Luis Salom, who disclosed an interest in Beach Towing and stated
he has lived on Normandy Isle for 40 years. He described recent confrontations with contractors and
stated that enforcement has not occurred consistently since 2023. He expressed concern for his
family’s safety and asked that any tows on his island not be directed to Beach Towing to avoid
negative optics, suggesting Tremont handle them instead.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that similar issues are occurring throughout Bayshore and North
Bay Road, mirroring problems in commercial corridors.
Parking Director MacDonald explained that all islands share a similar condition: technically, there is
no legal parking on the roadway. When Parking receives calls for service, Officers respond and
enforce. When no calls are received, they typically do not patrol proactively because many residents
rely on contractors or domestic workers parking in the roadway. He stated that many of these vehicles
should be cited for obstruction and towed immediately, but residents often object when enforcement
occurs. He stated that the Parking and Mobility Department will enforce in the manner directed by the
Commission.
Mayor Meiner asked if there was consensus. Hearing no objection, the Item was concluded.
