items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: The Item was deferred to the June 24, 2026, Commission Meeting. Commissioners
Bhatt and Matteo-Salinas separated the Item from the Consent Agenda. Commissioner Matteo-
Salinas moved to defer the Item to the June 24, 2026, Commission Meeting, seconded by
Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 7-0. Lilia Cardillo to be placed on the Commission Agenda, if
received. Kristy Bada and John Rebard to handle.
DIRECTION:
The top two-ranked proposers will present at the June 24 Commission Meeting. Kristy Bada to
handle.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas separated the Item from the Consent Agenda to better understand
how it was ranked when it returned to the Evaluation Committee. She could not find in the Commission
Memorandum the scoring details or how it was calculated, but she knows there had been some issues
with this award, and she would like to revisit it here.
Kristy Bada, Chief Procurement Officer, explained that the RFQ contemplated that, if a short list was
approved by the City Commission, which occurred in April, the Evaluation Committee would
reconvene to reevaluate the proposals using the same criteria set forth in the RFQ. The subsequent
Evaluation Committee, held recently, used the same evaluation criteria; however, it was limited to the
three shortlisted firms that were top-ranked by the first Evaluation Committee. In response to
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas, she explained that some of the criteria used were the experience and
qualifications of the proposing firm and team, including the firm that was the bidder and any other key
team members. The next criterion was the financial analysis firm that was part of the team, so it
evaluated their experience and qualifications, as well as their best practices, the approach and
methodology used on prior engagements to accomplish a similar scope of work and projects similar
to what the City was looking for. She clarified that the ranking in the final Evaluation Committee takes
into account the low aggregate scores, as well as each individual committee member's ranking, and
gave some examples of the ranking process. The total ranking of the committee members' final was
13 low aggregate points for Brooks Scarpa Huber Architects, Inc., who landed in second place; Kaller
Architecture had a low aggregate of 17 points, ranking in third place; and Stantec Architecture, Inc.
had a low aggregate of 12 points and was ranked first. The lower the aggregate, the better the rank.
Responding to Commissioner Matteo-Salinas, Ms. Bada stated that Stantec, teamed with MVRDV,
has a local Miami address, but its headquarters are in Denver, Colorado. The second-place firm,
Brooks Scarpa Huber Architects, is located in Fort Lauderdale, Miami, and Los Angeles, and they
have a local presence.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas stated that some residents expressed disappointment that the first
place is not based locally, while the second place is. She just wanted to revisit this further to see what
they could do.
Commissioner Suarez supports bringing the Byron Carlyle back to life. It is a shame it is in its current
state. North Beach deserves and needs a first-run movie-screen theater and a cultural arts center.
He and Commissioner Bhatt have had Sunshine meetings, and he hopes they do both. He has
concerns about the sequencing of this. He understands that if this firm is approved, they will come
back with a design contract in June or July for approximately $2.6 million.
Chief Procurement Officer Bada confirmed Commissioner Suarez’s statement.
Commissioner Suarez thinks they are putting the cart before the horse. They had discussed how this
is going to be funded on an operating basis, and the idea is to have housing units where rent
payments will offset the operational cost of the cultural arts center. He requested to know what the
model looks like before they have its design, including how many units there are and how to
communicate that to the design firm, when they do not even know that themselves and are asking
them to come up with a design for potentially a certain size and height scale. Without that basic
information, how are they going to tell a design firm to design something they do not know the
economics of? Those unanswered questions need to be answered before they move forward with a
$2.6 million project. He is not trying to slow it down; he is not against it; he just wants to make sure
they are set up for success.
Commissioner Bhatt added that they wanted to have that conversation about a year ago, but they
were precluded from doing so for many reasons, which she is not going to judge now. They will have
that conversation with the award winner for this RFQ as part of the next step. It will be part of the
preliminary discussion; there is no design for this project yet. This is the awarding of qualifications to
the team that will design, develop, and construct this project. They are a solid year later than they
had planned. They need those answers, but that is not what this is about. Today is about who gets
the award, and she also pulled the Item from the Consent Agenda because she has significant
concerns about the recipient. With their permission, those are excellent questions that will be figured
out with whoever gets the award. Addressing Commissioner Suarez, she explained that they are
hiring these firms to help the City get to the final product, including a template for how many units and
at what market-rate price. That will be the next conversation after the contract is awarded. Today is
about awarding the contract. The three shortlisted firms were in a dead tie, so that is what they are
trying to award today. They cannot ask them to do the work they are going to embark upon over the
next few years if they do not award and finalize the contract, and then start the work. One of the
preliminary steps they will take is to design what they want and put all the pieces together.
Kristy Bada, Chief Procurement Officer, replied to Commissioner Suarez that the housing component
is a major part of the project and of interest to the City. During the qualification process, the firms'
teams were advised that this was why one of the top firms was asking for a financial firm to conduct
the analysis related to workforce housing.
In addressing comments made by Commissioner Suarez, City Manager Eric Carpenter clarified that
during a discussion about whether to use the consultant to do that work, the consultant suggested
that staff do it. The compromise was to hire a design firm to work with the City on that concept.
Commissioner Bhatt respectfully added that this is why they are here now and that they cannot get
those questions addressed without awarding the contract. They should have awarded it last month,
but they did not because there were three top contenders, three very qualified firms. She requested
a discussion of the recommendation put forth by the three top firms.
Per Commissioner Suarez’s question, Kristy Bada, Chief Procurement Officer, indicated that they
provided all the experiences and qualifications. This was a Request for Qualifications, and they
provided qualifications related to either workforce housing or the cultural component. In their
proposals, they again listed any projects the proposer's design firm had worked on that were relevant
to what the City is requesting. All of that was reviewed by the Evaluation Committee.
Commissioner Bhatt noted that these firms are effectively the same, with minor discrepancies, and
that some people thought one was better than the other. She respectfully suggested that, given that
this has been a project she has been involved in since 2018, that has an enormous amount of
neighborhood concern, and that people who have been involved with it for a long time are part of one
of the bidding teams, the team that gets the award, because the top three were essentially the same,
should go to Brooks Scarpa, as some of the team members have been involved and have spent time.
She thinks they would be the best stewards going forward, given the sensitivity of the neighborhoods,
the community's needs, and the history of how they got here. She moved not to accept the City
Administration’s recommendation and to award the contract to Brooks Scarpa.
Seconded by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas.
Kristy Bada, Chief Procurement Officer, asked whether, if negotiations with Brooks and Scarpa fail,
they would move on to Stantec and then to Kaller.
The City Attorney indicated that negotiating first with Brooks Scarpa, then Stantec, and then Kaller, if
negotiations fail, would be acceptable.
Commissioner Suarez respectfully opposed because this went through a process and City staff
agreed, and it is inappropriate for the Commission, just because they may have a relationship with
Brooks Scarpa, to suspend that process and go with a firm they know. They have done excellent
work, but they went through a process telling people to bid on City projects, and just because they
are politically connected to a person or know someone who does a good job in one neighborhood,
they will favor them.
Commissioner Bhatt wants to clear her name because that suggestion is inappropriate. It is not what
she is doing. She is reflecting the will she has heard from multiple residents and people involved with
the Byron Carlyle since 2018. She feels that if three people are so good that they had to go to a
second round of vetting, the difference in millimeters, why not go with the organization that has desire,
history, and a feel for what the community wants? She resents the implication that he is making that
she is doing a political favor for someone.
Commissioner Suarez added that there is a conflict of interest. They are sending the wrong message,
and it is not good government. They have a process in place, and people have applied. It took a long
time to do. He suggested that, to be fair, the top two present at the Commission level. There is no
basis for the City Commission to select one firm over the other. If they are going to be fair, then have
the top two-ranked present to the City Commission. This sets a bad precedent. He was not provided
with these conversations for this review process. None of them were, so how are they in a position to
make that decision then?
Commissioner Bhatt added that they disagree with the Administration all the time. They spend hours
talking about sewer and rates, and the Administration has a very strong opinion about what they need
to do and has chosen to take a different path. If she has a conflict of interest because this is something
she worked on for a long time before she ever contemplated being a Commissioner, then they all had
conflicts of interest. This is different from water rates, which are more of a legislative priority. This is
a simple design, and who they hire.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas was trying to understand the process and why one firm scored one
point higher than the other. She requested clarification on the process and the requirements. She
suggested deferring for one month to determine exactly which point system was used and to review
other requirements. One of the companies states it is Florida-based, and the other did not specify in
the memo, so she suggested deferring for one month to better understand the grading scale and who
graded what. She has been approached by residents about this, and there is no connection; it is
residents who live in North Beach who reach out to her. That is why she is trying to understand how
it was graded and ranked, as well as resident versus staff input, and how all that played into it.
Commissioner Fernandez seconded the motion.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez announced that a motion to defer the Item had been made by Commissioner
Matteo-Salinas and seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. The Vice-Mayor directed City Clerk
Rafael E. Granado to call the vote.
Commissioner Fernandez noted that, for procurement items, they usually follow staff
recommendations and that he is not sufficiently familiar with the discussion. He asked the City
Attorney whether he could be briefed by the Procurement Director and City Manager without violating
the Cone of Silence.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, explained that if the contract is not awarded, the Cone of Silence
will remain in place until the contract is awarded or the procurement is awarded. He may speak to the
City Manager and the City Attorney, and to residents not affiliated with any of the vendors involved,
but not to the Procurement Director.
Commissioner Fernandez received concerns about this late last night. He then read the memo, the
staff’s analysis, and the rationale for selecting a vendor. It all made sense. They usually do not meddle
with procurement because it is a very defined process they would like to follow, and they usually
accept the staff’s recommendation. To the extent that they do things differently, they defer to the City
Attorney and the City Manager to better inform themselves and get briefed before they make any
conclusive decisions.
Commissioner Magazine does not typically deviate much from what is presented to him. He has not
talked to any of the firms. He knows Commissioner Bhatt has been involved for years with the Byron
Carlyle, and he trusts her judgment. In many regards, official and unofficial, decisions are deferred to
her, so if they are going to vote today, he will trust her judgment and vote in support of Commissioner
Bhatt. If they are going to defer the Item and give the limitations that they have, while he was going
to vote in favor with Commissioner Bhatt partly to keep the process moving, but if the will of the Body
is to defer it for another month, it does not make sense to have the two firms come here and speak
in front of them, because next month he will make the same calculated decision. Does he take the
Administration’s recommendation, or does he trust his colleague who has been intimately involved in
this process for years? But it would have more merit if both of them presented in front of the City
Commission.
Commissioner Suarez suggested having the top two-ranked teams present their qualifications directly
to the City Commission, explaining that if the Commission is expected to act, members should have
a clear basis on which to make a decision. He noted that it would not be fair for a proposer to feel
that their effort was disregarded and stated that allowing presentations would give all Commissioners
the necessary information.
Kristy Bada, Chief Procurement Officer, confirmed she would notify the firms to appear at the June
Commission Meeting.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, announced the motion to defer. Commissioner Matteo-Salinas moved
to defer to the June 24, 2026, Commission Meeting, seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Vote:
7-0.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, CONSENTING TO THE APPOINTMENT OF DEBORAH TACKETT, AS THE PLANNING DIRECTOR OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH.
items.action: Resolution 2026-34252 was adopted. Marla Alpizar to handle.
items.voteBasis: No separate vote identified. A vote has not been inferred.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34252 was adopted. Marla Alpizar to handle.
Mayor Steven Meiner announced that an Item had been approved on the Consent Agenda regarding
the appointment of Debbie Tackett as the new Planning Director. Mayor Meiner acknowledged that
Planning Director Thomas Mooney was stepping down and noted that Mr. Mooney had served the
City of Miami Beach for thirty-three years. Mayor Meiner referenced the length of Mr. Mooney’s
service by comparing the number thirty-three to a sports practice in which a player’s number is retired
in recognition of a long and significant career. Mayor Meiner indicated full confidence in Ms. Tackett’s
ability to assume the responsibilities of the position.
Debbie Tackett thanked Mayor Meiner, City Manager Eric Carpenter, and Thomas Mooney for their
confidence in her. Ms. Tackett indicated that she looked forward to continuing the working relationship
with the Mayor and the Commission.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt addressed Ms. Tackett and explained that they first met when
Commissioner Bhatt was beginning work in the preservation field. Commissioner Bhatt described Ms.
Tackett’s knowledge as consistently relevant to the City’s efforts to maintain valued community
characteristics while also addressing development issues. Commissioner Bhatt referred to the
Planning Department staff, including Rogelio Madan, and noted the department's strong capabilities.
Commissioner Bhatt expressed anticipation for the department’s work and indicated support for Ms.
Tackett.
Ms. Tackett acknowledged the comments and expressed appreciation.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, REINTRODUCING A MORATORIUM ON THE ADOPTION OF ANY ORDINANCE TO INCREASE WATER, SEWER, AND STORMWATER RATES; SAID MORATORIUM TO REMAIN IN EFFECT UNTIL THE EARLIEST TO OCCUR OF THE FOLLOWING: (A) RESCISSION OF THIS RESOLUTION BY A FIVE-SEVENTHS (5/7TH) VOTE OF THE CITY COMMISSION, (B) THE OCCURRENCE OF A PUBLIC SAFETY EMERGENCY DUE TO THE FAILURE OF WATER, SEWER, OR STORMWATER INFRASTRUCTURE, OR (C) THE ISSUANCE OF AN ORDER BY AN AUTHORITY HAVING JURISDICTION REQUIRING THE CITY TO MAKE UNBUDGETED REPAIRS TO ITS WATER, SEWER, OR STORMWATER INFRASTRUCTURE.
items.action: Resolution 2026-34276 was adopted. The Item was heard with related Item C4 T. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by Commissioners Bhatt and Matteo-Salinas.
items.voteBasis: No separate vote identified. A vote has not been inferred.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34276 was adopted. The Item was heard with related Item C4 T. The
Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by Commissioners Bhatt and Matteo-Salinas.
Commissioner David Suarez moved both Items C7 AI and C4 T, and Commissioner Alex Fernandez
seconded the motion. See votes:
C7 AI VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: No
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: No
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: No
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
C4 T VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
John Norris to handle
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt separated the Item from the Consent Agenda and explained that
adopting a moratorium before the Commission’s full discussion of the underlying funding issues would
set a dangerous precedent. She noted the complexity of funding critical infrastructure and indicated
her concern about precluding deliberation before the discussion occurs.
Commissioner Fernandez clarified that the Item does not prohibit discussions. The title refers to the
adoption of Ordinances, and this Body is very much able to engage in discussions, whether at
Committee, at the Budget Retreat, or in the robust discussions at the dais, as recently as the last
meeting. This recognizes the fact that it is very expensive to live in Miami Beach right now. Today’s
economy is working against many of the very residents who will also be affected by water, sewer,
and stormwater rate increases. Residents who live on fixed incomes and Social Security checks,
condominium owners who bought in the City under a completely different framework of State
regulations and are now facing increasing insurance costs and assessments they have to meet, and
single-family homeowners who are facing the increased cost of insurance and have seen their tax
bills go up over time, even though the City is not raising the millage rate, but end up paying more in
taxes. There is a lot working against residents, but that does not prevent this Body from having
discussions. They are very capable of having those discussions and also identifying other means to
deliver critical infrastructure, including how to move millage within the tax bill, as Commissioner
Suarez has proposed, so that when they tax residents, they use and prioritize those dollars on
infrastructure and do not go back and bill them again for something that could end up costing residents
over a thousand dollars a year in increases by 2037. This is concerning because, year after year, it
becomes more difficult for our long-term residents to live in the City. They love to speak about the
wealth, the moves to the City, the billionaires, celebrities, high-end restaurants, and the financial firms
coming to Miami Beach, but they also serve elderly individuals, as reported this morning in the Miami
Today article about the cost of living. Nationally, gas prices jumped 28.4% over the past year, with
South Florida hit harder, exceeding the national increase at 34.2% on the CPI for gas prices,
significantly higher than the national average. Housing costs continued to outpace those in the rest
of the nation. Food costs increased significantly locally and nationally. The cost of medical care went
up significantly. The cost of transportation went up significantly. This was reported this morning in
Miami Today about the impact CPI is having on the cost of living for people in South Florida. There
are things that local government cannot control. They cannot control private insurance companies,
assessments, the price of gasoline, or the price of milk, bread, and eggs at the grocery store, but they
can most certainly control how they currently use the revenues they get now to meet their critical
infrastructure needs, and they can certainly control whether they pass along the burdens of an aging
infrastructure system through utility rate increases to the residents and taxpayers, whom he feels a
great deal of responsibility to protect from further financial burden. That does not prevent them from
engaging in discussions, as they always need to think innovatively over time. He has been speaking
with the Office of the City Attorney about the possibilities. Is there a way that special taxing districts
and neighborhoods want to move forward with it? Is there a way, as Commissioner Suarez proposed,
where they move the millage they are already taxing residents a certain amount, and how about if
they move the same millage less from the General Fund and shift it over to Capital so that they can
meet the critical needs of the community without going back and dipping further into the pockets of
their financially strained families who are going through a tough moment in this economy.
Commissioner Suarez agrees 100% that raising water rates is a regressive tax. If someone is on a
fixed income, they pay more than they normally would at any other time. What he is proposing is
based on millage and property taxes and is progressive (C4 T). It will speak to how much a property
is worth and how much more they can pay. But if they are on a fixed income and live in Rebecca
Towers, for example, and now they have to pay double what they used to pay for water bills and do
not really see it, that is not fair. They have West Avenue Phase III, First Street, and North Shore and
Normandy Isle. These are projects that are not just pipes on the ground; they also include landscaping
and are going to make the area substantially better and uphold value, which is great, but it should
come from a property tax, not a tax across the whole City where they double the rates in four or five
years. He fully understands that it is very easy to say no, which is why he proposed an alternative to
funding these projects. He thinks this is the most equitable way to fund the projects as opposed to
taxing everyone with a regressive tax, as in a shotgun approach. He appreciates Commissioner
Fernandez cosponsoring with him. To Commissioner Bhatt’s point, this will be fleshed out at
committee, but he is offering a path.
5:21:38 p.m.
The Mayor called related Item C4 T, a referral to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee
sponsored by Commissioner David Suarez and co-sponsored by Commissioner Alex Fernandez.
Commissioner Suarez explained that the City has a millage for Capital infrastructure and a separate
amount for general operating funds. He is proposing reducing the millage from one to another, and
they need about $11 million annually for eight years to fund these projects. He is proposing $15 million
so they can still lower their taxes. They may not be able to do the rollback rate, but there will still be
cuts from one department to fund another. That will be fleshed out in discussion, but he proposes a
path for them to fund these projects in a fairer and more equitable way, and they can do that over the
next couple of months.
Commissioner Fernandez is cosponsoring Item C4 T because they already tax residents on a one-
billion-dollar budget, and what Commissioner Suarez is proposing makes sense. Within those dollars,
adjusting the millage and shifting priorities is about allocating them. The bare essentials are public
safety, cleanliness, and critical infrastructure. Those are among the essential functions of municipal
government, and they have to ensure that the taxes they collect are dedicated to those priorities.
Once they meet that, they can continue to build on the other services they provide, but they first need
to prioritize the core functions of the City government without double-dipping residents through rate
increases.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas separated the Item from the Consent Agenda to ask the City Attorney
whether it is feasible to issue a General Obligation (G.O.) Bond to increase water and sewer rates
and fund future projects.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, explained that it is feasible but requires a referendum.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine clarified that utility rate-funded projects are typically financed
through revenue bonds tied to enterprise funds, rather than through General Obligation (G.O.) Bonds.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas suggested a bond that goes to the electorate, so people will have the
opportunity to voice whether they want to tax themselves, rather than leaving it to the City
Commission to pass a tax. If they vote it down, then they vote it down, and if there is support, get it
on the ballot in the fall.
Commissioner Bhatt is interested in the proposal Commissioner Suarez is bringing, cosponsored by
Commissioner Fernandez. Her frustration is that they are making draconian moves with this
moratorium without first having the conversation about how to secure the needed funds for the critical
work, without double-dipping on residents. The City Commission is unified on not wanting to hit
residents who can at least afford it. Her concern is that they have not had those conversations yet.
The last paragraph states that the moratorium cannot be repealed unless they have rescinded the
Resolution by a 5/7 vote or there is a public safety emergency, which is a catastrophe. Having a
consent decree imposed on them by the County, State, and the Federal Government seems
draconian to her. She understands where Commissioner Fernandez is coming from, but as a body,
they had the full presentation from John Norris, Public Works Director; Eric Carpenter, City Manager;
and Jason Greene, Chief Financial Officer, about how to do this effectively in an open conversation,
taking it off the table. She loves that something is going to the Finance and Economic Resiliency
Committee, but she thinks putting it out there and voting on it first is putting the cart before the horse,
and scares her. The City Commission is concerned because the cost of living in Miami Beach is high
under the best circumstances. Friends and neighbors on fixed income or unemployed individuals are
really stressed. No one is trying to punish anyone, but they cannot afford not to move forward with
these projects. She asked John Norris, Public Works Director, to come up and talk about it. She
respectfully made a motion to defer the Item until they have more information from the Finance and
Economic Resiliency Committee, and if in a few months they talk about having a General Obligation
(G.O.) Bond that goes to referendum and they have not come to a better place, then maybe they talk
about a moratorium.
Commissioner Fernandez appreciates that. They have been having these discussions for a long time.
The City Commission has been discussing water and sewer rate increases for several years now, but
has not done so because of the impact on residents' lives. He likes the idea of a referendum on a
bond for residents. That is a tax that will get passed down to the very same people they are trying to
protect. What he likes about the idea, as it relates to finance, is prioritizing City dollars that residents
are already being taxed for. It is not going to ask residents for another tax or millage rate, and it is not
increasing the water rate for them. It is about saying they are already collecting money from them,
but how do they reprioritize it to the critical functions of their municipal government? A City like Miami
Beach with a billion-dollar budget should be able to function within that, and it may mean that, for a
certain period of time, in order to prioritize the essential basic services of municipal government, they
might not be able to fund some extra luxuries for some time, but every budget, even household
budgets, does that. They reprioritize their budgets to accommodate that. It is their very basic
responsibility, and they should not be charging residents more, whether it be through a new tax or
through a water and sewer rate increase, when they are already collecting a significant amount of
taxes from them.
Commissioner Bhatt believes they are in this situation because previous Commissions did not do this
for 30 years, and that is why rates are antiquated. If they had kept up with inflation, they would be in
a much better position. The work has not been done for decades, and it is at the point of critical failure.
They are going to lose millions of dollars in grants if they do not figure out how to do this. Again, she
comes back to the fact that they need to have the conversation, figure out the ways to do it, and look
at the Item being referred to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee to see what it all costs.
But to do this with those three choke points (5/7, critical emergency, or consent decree) seems
draconian and a terrible precedent to set. She asked the Administration and staff to explain. This is
dangerous.
Commissioner Suarez added that Commissioner Bhatt raised a good point: prior Commissions have
not done this, and they have never prioritized their spending, which is the more responsible way to
fund these projects. Commissioner Fernandez's moratorium is an attempt to force the Administration
and the Commission to prioritize where to spend the money. He does not like borrowing money to
spend today; he would not be in favor of a bond because it is just another tax. He would rather focus
on the billion dollars they have each year and prioritize how it is spent. Some luxuries will be cut
down, but the core basic government, public safety, sanitation, and infrastructure will remain. They
are the only City in Florida that has lost residents, yet the budget keeps going up to a billion dollars
for 80,000 residents. This is a good position to be in, where they are not only forcing the Administration
but also the Commission to take a deep look and say where they want to prioritize their billion dollars
every year.
Commissioner Bhatt believes they can do that without this draconian measure.
Commissioner Suarez added that there is another Item on the Agenda to allow City staff to add Items
to the Agenda. If that passes, the Administration can place an Item regarding water and sewer
increases, and this moratorium will prevent that, even if that Item passes. This is a failsafe for anything
that gets passed today or in the future until they prioritize their spending.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that, absent adoption of the moratorium, they would end up with an
Ordinance before the Commission to increase water and sewer rates, and that if the other Ordinance
on the Agenda were to pass, it would give Charter Officers the ability to place an Ordinance on the
Agenda. He noted that all Commissioners represent elderly residents, individuals working multiple
jobs, and residents feeling the stress of the economy, and that these individuals cannot absorb
another increase. He indicated that they have been receiving emails from residents and emphasized
that this issue directly affects quality of life. He explained that the Commission takes pride in focusing
on residents’ quality of life and in advancing that quality of life, but for residents who are not wealthy,
who are not in multi-income households earning hundreds of thousands of dollars, a rate increase
would directly affect their ability to continue living in Miami Beach or to afford rent in the City. He
added that using the water and sewer system is not a luxury, that residents cannot choose not to use
it, and that while people may choose not to go to dinner, buy a new car, or take a vacation, they
cannot choose not to use the City’s water and sewer system.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine acknowledged the discussion and indicated that he supports it;
however, he emphasized that the Commission must be clear about the consequences of adopting
the moratorium. He explained that the projects are large, multiyear infrastructure projects that require
predictable revenue streams and cannot be funded by identifying small savings each year. He stated
that if this is what residents want and it is the Commission's will, he will vote in favor of the moratorium,
but cautioned that the City will not be able to proceed with certain projects without dedicated funding.
He asked Public Works Director John Norris to list the projects, their costs, and the ones for which
funding is not yet available. He explained that the City cannot rely on the hope of year-over-year
efficiencies to deliver such projects and that certainty is required before initiating them. He noted that
a project such as West Avenue, which is a multiyear effort costing approximately $100 million, cannot
begin without secured funding. He stated that residents have expressed a desire for a pause on utility
rates, but he stressed that this decision carries consequences. He added that the cost of living
continues to rise, particularly for renters, and described increases in rental prices over the past
decade as having displaced families and young professionals. He observed that constraints on
housing supply have contributed to these pressures. He noted that while utility costs matter, the
primary financial burden driving residents to leave the City is housing costs. He indicated that he
would vote for the moratorium and requested collegial discussion regarding whether rescission of the
moratorium should require a 4/7 or 5/7 vote. He added that he is prepared to take responsibility for
the decision and reiterated the need for transparency regarding what the City will and will not be able
to accomplish without secured funding for the infrastructure projects.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas echoed Commissioner Magazine’s comments and said she wants to
hear from Public Works Director John Norris. Every time she gets emails about the Commission not
supporting the sewer rates, she does not know which neighborhood is going to be taken out of. People
do not get that side of it, and she wishes they could better educate them. She also requested a list

items.title: AN ORDINANCE OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, AMENDING CHAPTER 78 OF THE MIAMI BEACH CITY CODE, ENTITLED "PERSONNEL," BY AMENDING ARTICLE V, ENTITLED “CLASSIFIED EMPLOYEES’ LEAVE,” BY AMENDING SECTION 78-282 ENTITLED “DEFINITIONS” CLARIFYING THE DEFINITION OF “IMMEDIATE FAMILY” BY ELIMINATING DUPLICATIVE LANGUAGE; BY AMENDING SECTION 78-285 TO ALLOW SERVICE MEMBERS TO CASH OUT ON HOURS ACCRUED IN EXCESS OF THE CARRY-FORWARD CAP OTHERWISE FORFEITED AS A RESULT OF ACTIVE MILITARY DUTY; BY AMENDING SECTION 78-286 TO INCREASE THE CAP ON THE MAXIMUM AMOUNT OF ANNUAL LEAVE HOURS THAT MAY BE ACCRUED FROM 500 HOURS TO 600 HOURS RETROACTIVE TO DECEMBER 31, 2025; BY AMENDING SECTION 78-290 SUBJECTING PAID HOLIDAYS TO COLLECTIVE BARGAINING PROVISIONS GOVERNING HOLIDAY PAY, IF APPLICABLE; BY AMENDING SECTION 78-292 TO AUTHORIZE TRANSFER OF PART OR ALL ACCRUED LEAVE TO AN EMPLOYEE’S 457(B) ACCOUNT UPON RETIREMENT, RESIGNATION, TERMINATION OR DEATH AND AUTHORIZE THE USE OF ACCRUED LEAVE TO BE USED TO EXTINGUISH A DEBT OWED TO THE CITY SUCH AS REIMBURSEMENT OF OVERPAYMENTS THROUGH PAYROLL OR UNPAID INSURANCE PREMIUMS; REPEALING ALL ORDINANCES IN CONFLICT WITH THIS ORDINANCE; AND FURTHER, PROVIDING FOR SEVERABILITY, CODIFICATION, AND AN EFFECTIVE DATE.

ACTION: Ordinance 2026-4816 was adopted. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record.
The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on
Second Reading; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Marla Alpizar to handle.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas introduced the Item, explaining that it is a benefit for City employees
and helps them feel better and appreciate working for the City.
Marla Alpizar, Human Resources Director, explained that this Ordinance and its companion Item for
Unclassified Leave R5 B would allow them to align their Ordinances with their Collective Bargaining
Agreement and would increase the leave accrual maximum to remain constant between years, from
500 to 600. In reply to Commissioner Magazine, she explained that under the current Ordinance,
when vacation is accrued, an employee may receive up to 500 hours. This legislation will change the
year-to-year carryover maximum to 600 hours.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas described a hard-working employee who never takes days off, loves
their job and the City, and does not take their time off now; they can roll over the excess to the next
year.
Human Resources Director Alpizar confirmed Commissioner Matteo-Salinas’ statement.
Commissioner Magazine always hears infamous stories about the Long Island Railroad, where guys
stack vacation days and, when they go to retire, they have all their vacation days and have been
working extra overtime. That is essentially what they base their retirement on in the last years, so
how does that impact pensions, and what are the financial implications for the City?
Marla Alpizar, Human Resources Director, stated that there are no financial implications to speak of
because the cap on vacation payout when an employee leaves the City remains the same, so there
is no change to the final payout cap. This is the amount of leave that can be rolled over from year to
year. Some individuals do not use all their vacation time and, unfortunately, lose it every year. In reply
to Commissioner Magazine, she explained that, when leaving the City, the payout is capped at 620
hours and remains constant. While working in the City, employees can carry over only 500 hours of
unused vacation from year to year. When leaving the City, employees can be paid up to 620 hours.
The cap is set at 600 hours to keep it constant year to year, but when an employee leaves the City,
they may be paid out to 620 hours.
Commissioner Magazine believes there could be significant financial implications of this.
Human Resources Director Alpizar added that the City maintains their liabilities based on the payout
cap of 620.
CFO Jason Greene directly answered Commissioner Magazine’s question and explained that this
would not have a financial impact because a payout is not pensionable, and the pension is based on
annual salary regardless of the payment of unused vacation hours. They only get the payout amount
of the cap at 620 hours. That does not change. It is only what they roll from one year to the next, and
that has no financial impact on the City at all. There is no financial impact. It would just allow the
employee to take a little bit more vacation time next year, and often long-term employees accrue a
certain number of hours that they may lose at the end of the year.
Commissioner Magazine is confused about the number of hours per year. Are they raising the cap
on how many hours they can roll over per year?
CFO Greene clarified that it is not cumulative. It is a maximum of 500 hours, and any unused amount
can be rolled over at the end of each calendar year.
In reply to Commissioner Magazine, Mark Taxis, Assistant City Manager, clarified that when an
employee starts working for the City, they receive up to 2 weeks of vacation, or the equivalent of 80
hours. After the tenth year, the amount increases to three weeks, or about 120 hours, that they can
accrue at that point. In December of every year, 500 hours can be rolled over to the next year without
being lost. If they have 520 hours, when they roll over, 20 hours are dropped, and they only take 500
hours forward. This simply allows a maximum carryover of 600 hours without affecting the final
maximum payout of 620 hours. It does not force employees to take that vacation at the end of the
year just to burn those hours, which is one of the issues they have. They get to the end of the year
and think they can take a vacation, but for whatever work reasons, they cannot. Now they have the
time, so they are not forcing people to take the time off in December. It allows them to carry over
hours to use in January or February, but once they reach 600 hours, that is the maximum. He
reiterated that there is no cost impact; it is only what they can carry over and use at the beginning of
next year.
Commissioner Magazine is having a hard time making sense of that, but he will take his word for it
and hopes it is not like the fox guarding the henhouse. If there is no financial impact, he is in support.
Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading; seconded by
Commissioner Fernandez.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, announced the Public Hearing. With no one on Zoom or in the
audience requesting to speak, the Hearing concluded.
Roll Call: 7-0.

items.title: AN ORDINANCE OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, AMENDING THE MIAMI BEACH EMPLOYEES’ RETIREMENT PLAN CREATED BY ORDINANCE NO. 2006-3504, AS SUBSEQUENTLY AMENDED, BY AMENDING SECTIONS 2, 3, 4 AND 5 TO CORRECT ERRORS IN INTERNAL CROSS-REFERENCING; TO INCREASE THE DROP PARTICIPATION PERIOD FOR MEMBERS IN THE AFSCME BARGAINING UNIT FROM FIVE TO EIGHT YEARS; TO ALLOW FOR THE REEMPLOYMENT OF RETIREES AFTER A PERIOD OF SEPARATION OF AT LEAST SIX MONTHS, CONTINUED RECEIPT OF A RETIREMENT ALLOWANCE DURING EMPLOYMENT, AND FOREGOING ELIGIBILITY TO REJOIN THE PLAN; AND BY CREATING A NEW SECTION 16 OF THE PLAN TO ALLOW EMPLOYEES PARTICIPATING IN THE DEFINED CONTRIBUTION SYSTEM TO JOIN THE PLAN AND VEST IN THE CURRENT SCHEDULE OF BENEFITS AFTER FIVE YEARS OF CREDITABLE SERVICE; REPEALING ALL ORDINANCES IN CONFLICT THEREWITH; AND PROVIDING AN EFFECTIVE DATE.

ACTION: Ordinance 2026-4818 was adopted. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record.
The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on
Second Reading; seconded by Mayor Meiner. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Marla Alpizar to handle.
Per Mayor Meiner’s direction, Marla Alpizar, Human Resources Director, explained that this
Ordinance does three things. First, it extends the DROP from five to eight years for AFSCME
employees, with no fiscal impact. An actuarial statement is attached to the Item. Second, this
Ordinance allows the City to rehire former employees who have been gone for more than six months,
whether or not they have a pension, and to rehire them without a pension but with a 401(k). There
are about twelve long-term employees who, years ago, did not opt for the pension, and this allows
them to opt into the plan on a go-forward basis, which is a normal cost to the system, just like hiring
a new employee.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas received communication from employees who want to opt into the
system but do not want to start at zero and requested that this be addressed. Prior to 2016, they were
allowed to buy time, but that is no longer offered. Is there a way to allow employees to buy some time,
or would that have a financial impact?
Marla Alpizar, Human Resources Director, is not an actuary but understands that if an employee buys
back time, and it is funded by their own contributions, that does not have an immediate fiscal impact
on the City. However, allowing people to buy time using their leave does have a cash impact on the
City. If they buy time into the system, it creates an additional unexpected liability for the pension
system, which will be factored into the cost. Each individual is buying service hours, which means
their pension benefit would be higher.
Assistant City Manager Mark Taxis clarified that in 2006, the City had two systems, a 401(k) and a
Pension System, and employees were given the option to continue with the 401(k) or join the City’s
pension system. A group of individuals chose to stay with the pension system for various reasons.
About 10 employees chose to remain in the 401(k), and years later, they stayed longer than expected
and are now eligible to join the pension system. What is being offered to them is the ability to at least
get in on a go-forward basis. They discussed with the City Manager that there may be an opportunity
in the future to get credit at a cost to them, but right now, it is just to get them into the system. Those
employees in the 401(k) for a number of years have, at best, a sum of money, and they also will have
no Social Security, so in their retirement years they will have no money coming in, no pension or
Social Security, as they have been working in the City for years. This at least gets them in, where
they are starting to get on a go-forward basis, and they do not rule out opportunities for them in the
future.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas thanked Assistant City Manager Mark Taxis and wants to make sure
that those who want to buy in with their own money have that opportunity, so they are not closing the
door on them. How do they make sure that happens? There are a number of folks who have reached
out to her in panic, and they worry.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, added that multiple conversations are underway simultaneously. One
is that if they move from the 401(k) to the Pension System, they are not losing their 401(k). They get
to keep the entire next egg they built up during their time with the City. They are entering a pension
system as if they were new-hire employees and have to go through 5 years in the City to vest in that
program. That gives them the opportunity to start an additional nest egg on top of the one they already
have. If they were to conduct a buyback, many bargaining units across the City are very interested in
having these conversations. There are instances where people can buy back from military service or
former municipal government service that does not have an associated pension. These are not
uncommon, but it is something they would want to do holistically and have a conversation amongst
all the groups rather than just these individuals. In reply to Commissioner Matteo-Salinas, he
explained that they have these conversations every bargaining session. Typically, they try to give
Unclassified employees similar opportunities to folks in bargaining units so they do not create a
situation where people feel they have unequal benefits.
A Public Hearing was held, and with no participants requesting to speak via Zoom or in the audience,
the Public Hearing concluded.
Commissioner Fernandez moved to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading, seconded by Mayor
Meiner. Roll Call: 7-0.

items.title: FREIGHT AND COMMERCIAL LOADING ORDINANCE AN ORDINANCE OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, AMENDING CHAPTER 106 OF THE CODE OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, ENTITLED “TRAFFIC AND VEHICLES,” ARTICLE II, ENTITLED “METERED PARKING,” DIVISION 1, ENTITLED “GENERALLY,” SECTION 106-47 THEREOF, ENTITLED “FREIGHT, COMMERCIAL, AND PASSENGER CURB LOADING ZONES; HOURS; DELIVERIES,” TO MODIFY AND CLARIFY REQUIREMENTS APPLICABLE TO THE USE OF FREIGHT, COMMERCIAL, AND PASSENGER LOADING ZONES; AND PROVIDING FOR REPEALER, CODIFICATION, SEVERABILITY, AND AN EFFECTIVE DATE.

ACTION: Ordinance 2026-4819 was adopted. The Item was heard with companion Item C7 AS.
The title of the Ordinance was read into the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner
Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading; seconded by Commissioner
Matteo-Salinas. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
William MacDonald to handle.
DIRECTION:
 Provide weekly LTCs summarizing towing activity, citations, and enforcement metrics.
 Include updates on Zone 26 in the weekly LTCs if it becomes a concern.
William MacDonald to handle.
Commissioner Fernandez thanked the City Commission for unanimously sponsoring the End
Resident Tows Reform. Today, they are considering two items that work together to achieve strong
enforcement where public safety requires it, but smarter, more proportional enforcement toward
compliance where it can be reasonably achieved without unnecessarily punishing residents who have
placed their trust in them to serve them and improve their quality of life. First is to end resident tows,
one of the most common frustrations they hear from residents. People come home from work late at
night, circle the block to find parking, finally find a space, and wake up the next morning to discover
the car has been towed for a non-safety violation. Maybe they parked a few feet into the yellow curb,
or in the wrong residential zone, or misunderstood the confusing signage, or did not realize that a
spot was painted yellow but that is now faded, and they end up getting towed. These violations should
still be enforced with a traffic ticket or citation, but towing is often excessive when compliance can be
achieved another way. That is why this proposal creates a smarter, data-driven enforcement
framework based on current City data that could eliminate the majority of immediate resident tows on
public property. Under the framework they have before the Commission today, residents would still
receive citations and accountability measures, but would also receive up to three courtesy text
messages per calendar quarter before being eligible to have their cars towed on the fourth violation.
Vehicles remaining in continuous violation for more than 24 hours would also remain tow-eligible, and
that was the recommendation from Miami Beach United (MBU), which has also endorsed this reform.
This year alone, over 1,181 resident vehicles have already been towed in Miami Beach. Under the
reform framework, roughly 62% of those resident tows would not have resulted in an immediate tow
and could instead have been addressed through a parking citation, a first enforcement warning, and
graduated compliance measures. The remaining violations involving genuine safety hazards,
obstruction of dumpsters, blocking a driveway, blocking emergency access, or repeat violations are
still eligible to be towed. In those cases, they are still eligible to be towed, and if they are blocking a
fire hydrant or parked in a handicapped parking space, shame on them; they will get towed. The
reform here, even for those, is to try to achieve the quickest compliance possible. Now, even those
violations will also get a text before a tow notice. Oftentimes, people are close by, and they can quickly
correct a violation before the tow truck arrives, but residents would receive one final text before tow
notification to give them an opportunity to move their cars before the tow is complete. The companion
Item C7 AS is important because it addresses the abuse of freight loading zones, an issue in the City
that creates traffic congestion on roadways, impacts businesses, and affects public safety. C7 AS
enhances penalties for freight zone violations and also creates much-needed consistency and clarity
on freight loading zones Citywide. Currently, freight loading zones operate under a hodgepodge of
schedules and rules that can be confusing for residents. Some freight loading zones end at 11:00
a.m., others at 1:00 p.m., and still others at 3:00 p.m. Some end at different times, making it a
guessing game for residents to know where they can park and at what time. This companion
Ordinance creates a uniform Citywide operating schedule for freight loading zones. When residents
see a freight loading zone, there is no parking between 7:00 a.m. and 3:00 p.m. That is the schedule
for those freight loading zones. No more guessing. These two Items create a more balanced
enforcement mechanism with greater fairness for residents navigating everyday challenges in the
City, stronger enforcement to protect public safety and mobility, and clear, more predictable rules for
everyone using their streets. He moved both Items C7 AS and R5 D.
Commissioner Suarez thanked Commissioner Fernandez for bringing this forward, noting that it is
almost a rite of passage to have one's car towed. He is supportive but wants to caution that North
Beach is going to face a series of parking constraints, with parking lot 92 under construction for maybe
two to three years. They are also going to have many shows at the Bandshell and events in North
Beach. He is supportive of the idea. He wants to avoid residents from South Beach or Mid-Beach
going to North Beach, parking in residential areas, and not mind the $30 ticket, which is easy to do.
Is there a way to prevent that? Some people are going to take advantage of this, and it is not a big
deal for him, but how can they prevent the bad behavior from happening?
William MacDonald, Parking Director, noted that they can establish different enforcement rules for
different zones if directed to do so.
Commissioner Fernandez explained that much of the proposal focused on giving residents the benefit
of the doubt. He indicated that individuals coming into the City and abusing the system would still be
towed on the first violation because they remained eligible for towing. He described the approach as
one that supported residents who had placed their trust in the City by returning that trust to them. He
noted that if the system were abused and the City Commission identified a problem, the policy could
be amended through a simple Resolution. He emphasized that residents should be given the benefit
of the doubt and that an enforcement mechanism would remain in place. He added that violators
would continue to be towed when appropriate and that, upon a first violation, residents would receive
a text message informing them that they were illegally parked and directing them to move the vehicle
immediately.
Commissioner Suarez added that, since North Beach parking is so limited and will be even more
limited once they move to the parking garage, he suggested, specifically for Zone 26, sending a one-
time courtesy non-tow text message. After that, there should be protections for North Beach residents
and their parking.
Commissioner Fernandez agreed.
Commissioner Bhatt indicated that she liked the idea because North Beach will experience significant
parking challenges in the coming years. She asked whether the proposal was viable and whether any
issues existed with its implementation. She noted that she supported the protections already included
in the text and referenced the current wording instructing drivers to move their vehicles immediately.
She suggested modifying the language to direct drivers to move their vehicles within 30 minutes of
receiving the message. She then asked whether the proposal was doable, practicable, enforceable,
or all of the above.
William MacDonald, Parking Director, clarified that they will execute the program; they employ human
beings like anyone else in the City, and there may be some mistakes because the technology is not
yet in place to immediately build an algorithm that tells them what to do in each zone, which makes it
challenging. They have stop gaps in place before the team performs any tows. He listed examples,
such as a team member calling dispatch to repeat the license plate phonetically so dispatch can
check the plate, and they do these things to try to stop mistakes. They can build policies and SOPs
(Standard Operating Procedures) stating that, in this zone, these are the guardrails to follow, and
they will execute them to the best of their ability.
Commissioner Suarez is not trying to single out North Beach. South of Fifth also has very limited on-
site residential parking and many restaurants. People from everywhere else on the beach come and
take over the parking. He is supportive of this Item. It is a great idea, but they need protection because
it is ripe for abuse.
Commissioner Fernandez added that those were the same concerns they had when they initiated the
Text Before Tow Program, namely that residents would abuse it. To the contrary, residents have not
abused it. It has raised awareness by informing someone that they are in violation. He heard from
people who received those text messages that they were able to correct the violation before the
towing truck arrived, and now they are aware of something they are not supposed to do. Another tool
in their toolkit is the ongoing reporting they receive as a City Commission, and they will be monitored
with weekly LTCs summarizing towing activity, citations, and the enforcement matrix. Perhaps they
could get specific as part of that LTC: a weekly update on what is happening in Zone 26, if that is a
concern, so that if they need to correct course, they can do so. He suggested considering adopting it
uniformly throughout the City, and then, if they see abuse somewhere, they can go back and fix it,
but they should give their residents the benefit of the doubt. For the most part, people make innocent
mistakes when it comes to parking, and that has been his experience. People generally are not
looking to intentionally violate parking regulations.
Commissioner Bhatt addressed Rafael Andrade, Esq., in the audience and explained that part of the
towing issue involved residents forgetting or making mistakes, part of it involved City policies and
staff managing challenging circumstances, and part of it involved the City’s towing partners. She
indicated that it was important for towing partners to understand the procedures and to avoid initiating
tows prematurely, noting that once a vehicle was placed on a tow truck, the situation changed
significantly. She described being towed years earlier when she should not have been and stated
that the towing company did not want to hear her explanation, which she characterized as an
operational matter for the business owners. She observed that a clear set of policies and procedures
would need to be understood by towing company ownership and staff once the City issued directives,
as the Commission regularly received emails from individuals who had been towed when they should
not have been. She added that, because the system was becoming more complex, it was essential
to ensure that tow operators understood the requirements and when to apply them.
Rafael Andrade, Esq., representing Tremont and Beach Towing, thanked Commissioner Bhatt,
acknowledged the owners in the audience, and committed to doing their best to meet the City’s
expectations. From his and the owners’ perspective, if they never tow another resident again, they
are thrilled. They are here to cooperate with the City and help however they can with whatever
challenges they face. He thanked the City Commission for inviting them.
Commissioner Suarez asked whether there is an appetite for Zone 26 with more protections. When
that parking lot is demolished, it will spill over to the residents' parking.
Commissioner Fernandez suggested reviewing the matrix, and that is going to be a long project. If
there is abuse, they will know immediately via LTCs about what is happening in Zone 26.
Commissioner Suarez respectfully added that it sounds great, but from his experience, parking
enforcement in Zone 26 is abysmal. When they had an issue with one block on Zone 26, there were
26 citations given. He and his Aide raised the issue, and they issued 26 citations on one block
because he asked them to start enforcing Zone 26. They can wait, but that assumes they have a
robust parking enforcement system, and they do not have that right now.
Commissioner Fernandez added that one of the Items adopted as part of the Consent Agenda
specifically addresses enforcement, including allocating resources for enforcement in North Beach
and in South Beach, where they know there are challenges. What Commissioner Suarez is telling
him is that even if the problem is not even towing, no citations are being issued. One of the policies
they put forward, which was adopted with Item C7 AN, established a dedicated parking enforcement
pilot program that specifically addresses what Commissioner Suarez is asking, including violations of
resident parking in North Beach and South Beach, and ensures that sufficient personnel are available
to conduct that enforcement. Commissioner Suarez is right. Oftentimes, people get home from work
and are unable to find parking because people from outside the City are going in and parking in
residential parking spaces, and those who are trying to protect are being affected. They have taken
that concern into consideration and created this detail, which was approved as part of the Consent
Agenda. He committed to Commissioner Suarez that, as part of this detail being created and the
LTCs they will be receiving, they will know if they see any abuse. At the end of the day, it affects the
residents in North Beach, who will not be able to find parking when they get home from work, and
they will work together to address that if it happens.
Mayor Meiner congratulated the City Commission on a great Item; he thanked his colleagues for
being an example of what Commissioners do to improve residents' quality of life.
Commissioner Fernandez moved to adopt the Items R5 D and C7 AS, seconded by Commissioner
Matteo-Salinas.
The Public Hearing was opened, and, with no one requesting to speak via Zoom or in person, the
Hearing concluded. Roll Call taken: 7-0.
R5 D and C7 AS
Motion made by Commissioner Fernandez to adopt the Ordinance and the Resolution, seconded by
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas. Roll Call: 7-0. Items R5 D and C7 AS were approved.

ACTION: Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into the
record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance
on First Reading; seconded by Commissioner Bhatt, Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Second Reading Public Reading is scheduled for June 24, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice. Lilia
Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received.
Amy Knowles and Francys Vallecillo to handle.
Per Commissioner Suarez’s directive, Amy Knowles, Chief Resiliency Officer, introduced the Item,
which is an approval of an amendment to the Sea Turtle Ordinance. Turtle Season runs from April 1
through October 31 and includes many protections. However, there are many events on the beach,
and this Item allows events on the beach after 9:00 p.m. in April. They still have to comply with the
City Turtle Ordinance, which means minimizing lighting and following all rules. It would not allow
events from May 1 through October 31 after 9:00 p.m. due to lighting issues and the impact on turtles
during the nesting season, which begins in May. From a scientific perspective, this is important as
well and should help reduce the turtle’s rate of disorientation.
Commissioner Suarez noticed that there were many events in April that were very disruptive, with
many lights and machinery on the beach, and that there should be a definite cutoff time in the evening
to prevent any disruptions to their wildlife. Since the Turtle Protection Ordinance, the disorientation
rates have improved, and he asked Ms. Knowles to go into further detail.
Amy Knowles, Chief Resiliency Officer, confirmed that they saw a 9% improvement in 2025, meaning
9% of their nests had hatchlings that did not disorient, which is great. They recently received news
from Miami-Dade County, and it showed about 50% in 2024, rising to 51% in 2025.
Commissioner Suarez thinks they may have issues with some of the events, but he believes they
could find a middle ground to work on this.”
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas is generally supportive of the Item but asked whether the Second
Reading would affect the FIFA concert.
Amy Knowles, Chief Resiliency Officer, clarified that the Ordinance would take effect in May 2027. If
allowed, they would have to stop visible lighting after 9:00 p.m.
Commissioner Bhatt loves the idea of the improvement and asked whether this gives the City the
ability to use the unsightly flood lights in case of a public safety issue, for example, if a crime scene
needs to be established. Does this give the City the ability to do what it needs to in case there is a
public safety issue?
Amy Knowles, Chief Resiliency Officer, explained that public safety is important and a consideration.
If there is a situation where floodlights are warranted, and something horrible is happening, of course,
but they should not be left on at all times during turtle season at night.
Commissioner Bhatt asked whether noise and noise vibration affect the nests as well.
Ms. Knowles has wondered the same, but it is not within the regulatory standards. It is not built into
the standards, and that is coming down from the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission
(FWC). Ms. Knowles added that anecdotally, they have not observed it and are not quite sure about
that. It is not something they have studied here.
Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading; seconded by
Commissioner Bhatt.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, opened the Public Hearing. With no participants requesting to speak
in the audience or via Zoom, the Hearing concluded.

items.title: AN ORDINANCE OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, AMENDING CHAPTER 10 OF THE CODE OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, ENTITLED "ANIMALS," BY AMENDING SECTION 10-11 THEREOF, ENTITLED “RUNNING AT LARGE PROHIBITED; EXCEPTIONS,” BY PROVIDING A GRACE ZONE EXTENDING FROM THE PERIMETER OF THE AREA DESIGNATED BY THE CITY MANAGER FOR THE BENEFIT OF AN OWNER OF AN UNLEASHED ANIMAL WHO INADVERTENTLY ALLOWS HIS OR HER ANIMAL TO STRAY OUTSIDE THE APPROVED PERIMETER; AND PROVIDING FOR REPEALER, SEVERABILITY, CODIFICATION, AND AN EFFECTIVE DATE.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into
the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the
Ordinance on First Reading; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Roll Call: 5-2.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: No
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: No
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for June 24, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. John Rebar to handle.
TO DO:
Reach out to the South of Fifth Neighborhood Association for their input. John Rebard to handle.
Commissioner David Suarez introduced the Item and explained that South Pointe Park’s dog area is
unique because it is not fenced, unlike other dog parks in the City. He noted that the City Commission
had earlier adopted an Ordinance increasing fines for off-leash violations and stated that he wanted
to be mindful of South Pointe Park residents whose dogs may briefly run outside the designated area.
He indicated that his intent was to avoid residents being fined in situations where dogs momentarily
stray from the off-leash area. He moved the Item, and the motion was seconded by Commissioner
Alex Fernandez.
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez noted that there have been past incidents in the City where individuals
have been mauled or attacked by dogs. She observed that the Commission Memorandum attached
to the Item did not contain a City recommendation.
Parks, Facilities, Fleet, and Beaches Director John Rebar explained that staff did not have a strong
recommendation on the Item and emphasized that dog owners are required to maintain control of
their animals at all times. He acknowledged the sponsor’s intent, noting that South Pointe Park
contains the only unfenced dog park in the City and that dogs may occasionally wander outside the
designated area. He reiterated the importance of owners keeping their animals under control. He
added that, to his knowledge, there have been no specific incidents at that location. In response to
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas, Mr. Rebar explained that when the area was created,
residents requested that it not be fenced and that an off-leash area be designated during certain
hours. He stated that this request originated directly from residents of the South of Fifth neighborhood.
City Manager Eric Carpenter clarified that the City would not typically create an unfenced dog park,
but this was done pursuant to a specific request and a corresponding Commission Resolution at the
time, based on circumstances raised by neighborhood residents. He confirmed that staff did not have
feedback from the South of Fifth Neighborhood Association (SOFNA) regarding the current Item.
Commissioner David Suarez stated that the matter had been discussed by the City Commission when
considering increasing fines for off-leash violations. He explained that South Pointe Park contains an
unfenced dog park, and he did not want residents to be cited when a dog briefly wanders outside the
designated area. He noted that fines for off-leash violations were being increased Citywide, but at
South Pointe Park, dogs may inadvertently run out of the area because it is not enclosed. He stated
that he believed a grace period would be a reasonable compromise.
In response to Vice-Mayor Dominguez, City Clerk Rafael E. Granado stated that a Letter to
Commission from the Animal Welfare Committee opposing the Item had been published earlier in the
morning. Click here to view LTC 216-2026.
Commissioner Suarez reiterated that dogs may run out of the designated area and that he did not
believe owners should be fined for brief, inadvertent incidents. In response to Vice-Mayor Dominguez,
he added that if a Park Ranger observed a dog leaving the area, the recent direction regarding
enforcement of off-leash violations could result in a citation.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez stated that he was comfortable with the Item because the dog park in
South Pointe Park is unique. He explained that it is not fenced or enclosed, unlike most dog parks in
the City, which have perimeter enclosures.
Parks, Facilities, Fleet, and Beeches Director John Rebar added that recently approved legislation
would create another off-leash area near Smith & Wollensky for smaller dogs, also located in South
Pointe Park, and also unfenced. He stated that South Pointe Park is the only location in the City
where unfenced off-leash areas are designated.
Commissioner Fernandez added that, in other areas of the City, dog parks are designed to keep
animals within a controlled environment, whereas South Pointe Park was created as an open
environment, which is a characteristic feature of that park. He noted that it is easy for a dog to move
beyond the boundaries of the off-leash area, and once a dog leaves the boundary, the owner is in
violation of the leash Ordinance. He explained that a dog may chase a squirrel, a ball, or another
object beyond the perimeter, and he asked Commissioners to be mindful of this. He added that if the
City determines that dogs should be leashed, it may need to consider enclosing the area. He
observed that more than ten years earlier, the subject of whether to fence the area had been the
subject of significant debate on the dais.
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez stated that the dog park at South Pointe Park has operated without a
fence since 2014 and asked whether there have been incidents or fines that prompted the Ordinance.
She expressed concern that adopting the Item could open complications regarding enforcement and
stated that it was unclear how such a provision would be measured or determined. She noted that
the South of Fifth Neighborhood Association (SOFNA) had not provided input and that the Animal
Welfare Committee opposed the Item. She questioned the need for the Ordinance, given that the
area has operated as an unfenced dog park since 2014.
Commissioner David Suarez explained that the Item was brought forward because the City
Commission earlier in the meeting adopted an Ordinance increasing fines for off-leash violations
citywide. He stated that he supported the increased fines but believed it was inappropriate to fine
residents when dogs briefly stray outside the off-leash area at South Pointe Park, which was
intentionally designed as an open, unfenced space. He stated that he had not been aware of the
Animal Welfare Committee’s Letter to Commission, but would have been willing to discuss it. He said
the proposal reflected common-sense application for a specific dog park in a unique setting. He
expressed concern that residents who regularly use the dog park might receive citations from Park
Rangers or Code Officers if their dogs momentarily ran out while playing.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt stated that she did not know the resident who sent an email, but
summarized the resident’s points. She stated that the area had expanded from an unfenced open
space to the current off-leash area and that dog owners were permitted to have dogs unleashed
within the designated zone, while others could avoid the area if they wished to stay distant from dogs.
She stated that Park Rangers already use discretion, typically issuing warnings to first-time offenders
rather than citations, and that a citation is issued only if there has been a prior issue. She said she
was unsure how enforcement of a grace zone could be measured, given that the perimeter is not
visibly marked, and that enforcement would rely on subjective judgment. She stated that if the current
system has worked effectively, it should continue. She encouraged her colleagues to read the email
and stated that she would not support the Item.
Commissioner Suarez reiterated that, under the Ordinance adopted earlier in the meeting, a dog
leaving the off-leash area could immediately result in a higher fine. He stated that this would not be
fair for this particular location and that he did not want enforcement left to the discretion of individual
Code Officers or Park Rangers. He stated that the dog park has had no issues and that dogs do not
understand boundaries; therefore, a grace period is appropriate for this specific park.
Addressing Commissioner Bhatt’s comments, Police Chief Wayne Jones stated that off-leash
enforcement in this area is not a high-priority issue for patrol officers within the broader scope of daily
police responsibilities.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt added that the existing practice is not for Park Rangers to issue
citations immediately, but for them to encourage dog owners to keep their dogs within the designated
area unless there is a repeated problem, which is how enforcement has operated for years.
Parks, Facilities, Fleet, and Beaches Director John Rebar clarified that the primary role of Park
Rangers is to serve as ambassadors. He explained that they are not mandated to issue citations but
that they are familiar with park users and recognize repeat offenders. He stated that enforcement
begins with educating owners about the boundaries of the area, followed by a warning if necessary,
and that citations are issued only after repeated problems. He stated that it is not the practice of Park
Rangers to cite first-time offenders.
Commissioner David Suarez stated that he did not want enforcement left to the discretion of Park
Rangers or Code Officers and believed the provision should be addressed directly in the Code.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez seconded the Item.
City Clerk Rafael E. Granado announced the public hearing. There were no participants via Zoom or
in the audience wishing to speak, and the public hearing was closed.
A motion was made by Commissioner Suarez to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading, seconded by
Commissioner Fernandez. The motion passed by a vote of 5-2, with Commissioners Bhatt and
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez opposed. The Second Reading public hearing was scheduled for June
24, 2026.
Mayor Steven Meiner directed staff to reach out to the South of Fifth Neighborhood Association for
input.

 Veronica Hennig – Extensive opposition citing public safety, animal behavior, and research

the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Bhatt made a motion to adopt the Ordinance
