The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for June 24, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Chief Wayne Jones, Hernan
Cardeno, and John Rebar to handle.
Commissioner David Suarez highlighted key provisions of the proposed Ordinance, explaining that it
modernizes an outdated section of the City Code. He stated that the amendments would allow
Officers to rescue animals from hot vehicles under exigent circumstances and permit Officers to take
temporary emergency protective custody of animals. He noted that the Ordinance creates a reporting
section to encourage early reporting of suspected animal abuse and enhances animal neglect and
cruelty standards by providing specific, enforceable examples. He explained that the amendments
clarify that failure to seek necessary veterinary care constitutes neglect and that Code Compliance
Officers and Park Rangers, in addition to Police Officers, would be authorized to enforce animal
neglect and cruelty provisions. He stated that both civil fines and criminal charges may run
concurrently and that civil cases may support criminal cases. He explained that amendments to
Section 10-1 revise the definition of “Officer” to include Code Compliance Officers and Park Rangers,
expanding the City’s enforcement reach. Addressing Section 10-3, he noted that the language
changes from “shall issue” to “may issue,” allowing Officers discretion to use warnings, education, or
citations depending on the circumstances, enabling early intervention before matters escalate. He
explained that Section 10-5 clarifies that a person who refuses to sign or accept a notice of violation
in the presence of law enforcement may be arrested and that penalties are amended to align with
other sections of the City Code. He stated that Section 10-20 details standards for proper care,
including adequate food, continuous access to potable water, appropriate ventilation, sanitation,
space, and protection from extreme weather, and prohibits leaving animals unattended in dangerous
vehicle conditions. He added that each day a violation occurs may be counted as a separate offense.
He stated that the section provides clear, enforceable standards and empowers Officers to offer early
education and take proactive action when an animal is in imminent danger, reiterating immunity from
liability for Officers acting in good faith. He explained that Section 10-22 encourages residents and
animal-related businesses to report suspected cruelty or neglect, permits anonymous reporting,
clarifies that it does not create a legal duty to report, and may allow earlier intervention by identifying
cases before animals reach a critical state. He stated that the Ordinance serves as a modernization
of the City’s animal cruelty laws.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt expressed support for the Item and moved its approval, seconded by
Commissioner David Suarez.
City Clerk Rafael E. Granado announced the public hearing. There being no participants in the
audience or via Zoom wishing to speak, the public hearing was closed.
A motion was made by Commissioner Bhatt to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading, seconded by
Commissioner Suarez. The motion passed by a vote of 7-0. The Second Reading public hearing was
scheduled for June 24, 2026.

items.action: Ordinance adopted on First Reading as is. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Matteo-Salinas made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading; seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Roll Call: 7-0.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Ordinance adopted on First Reading as is. The title of the Ordinance was read into the
record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Matteo-Salinas made a motion to adopt the
Ordinance on First Reading; seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
The Second Hearing Public Hearing is scheduled for June 24, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received.
Rafael E. Granado to handle.
TO DO:
 At Second Reading, evaluate whether to retain or remove the 5/7 majority waiver provision for
exceeding the agenda-item limits and prepare alternative language reflecting both options.
 Provide draft clarifying language distinguishing “new” Items from Items returning from Committee
or prior agendas, for Commission review at Second Reading.
 If the Commission chooses to pilot the proposed agenda-limit structure prior to adoption, prepare
a defined test period and accompanying evaluation process for review before formal
implementation.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas introduced the Item. She believes less is more and is trying to limit the
number of Items they put on the Agendas because the more they have here, the less they get done.
They see this month after month, year after year. She emphasized quality over quantity. There are
many much-needed items, many of them from their residents, but they have been legislating this way
since the 1970s. She wants to review internal practices and policies to see how they can operate
more efficiently and get more done. They all want results, so she suggested looking at how they
legislate and what they bring to the Agenda. They can reject this Item, and if it fails, she will not be
mad at anyone. Respectfully, she is trying to figure out how they can get more done. They might
achieve that if they stopped overwhelming themselves and their staff with all the Items.
Commissioner Suarez addressed Commissioner Matteo-Salinas. He thinks this Item is a great idea,
that less is more, and that it puts the onus on the members of this Body to prioritize what is best. They
will get more done this way. It is not going to be as overwhelming as today’s three-book agenda. If
they can cut it down to one book, they will get everything done at every meeting. He is fully in support.
This is good, effective governance.
Commissioner Bhatt loves the Item. She had a similar Item that she withdrew two months ago.
Commissioner Magazine was her co-sponsor for doing the same thing, and she gave up on it because
the Item never got called; she thinks it got lost in the shuffle. She is fully supportive of this. They all
work in different ways and bring their strengths to bear. Her work is to try to get people in a room
together administratively, and once they reach the point where they need Commission legislation
approval, that is when she brings it, which is probably better for everyone for all the reasons stated.
She is supportive of this.
Commissioner Fernandez will always support policies that set standards and adapt the City
Commission’s practices to the needs of the time; this is prudent at the moment. The policy could be
waived by a 5/7 vote, and the City Attorney has confirmed this. If they are going to pass the policy
and this is what they want, then commit to it and not find ways around it, so they can work to make
the Agendas more efficient; otherwise, it is easy to get that 5/7 vote because they are going to be
courteous of each other professionally, and at times someone may have four referrals but might need
to put six referrals to Committee, and they are not going to get in each other’s way. In essence, they
are making the policy ineffective by including the 5/7 vote and suggesting removing the 5/7 vote and
implementing a policy of no more than four referrals to the Commission Committee on the Regular
Agenda.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas agreed with the suggestion.
Commissioner Magazine thanked Commissioner Matteo-Salinas. He wholeheartedly agrees with her
and very much supports her on this Item. It is not about them that less is more; it is also about the
fact that, if not all, much of the legislation they do is for staff, so they have the ideas and they are the
ones carrying out the execution. They have gotten to a point where less is more, not only for them
but also to concentrate on better things and to improve the staff's ability to execute. He quoted a
paraphrase of Jeff Bezos: "Jeff, you have enough great ideas to destroy Amazon; you have to release
your greater ideas at the right rate." He thinks that is something they have to come up with because
they have this monthly deadline for Items and are not given adequate time for ideas to turn into
execution, and that is how they get that operational efficiency. They have enough great ideas, maybe
not to destroy Miami Beach, but to ensure these ideas actually get executed to improve the City to
the degree it can. Limiting some of that helps them, and the staff operates and executes more
efficiently.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez likes the Item as well, but is hesitant to remove the ability to vote to override
the limit via a 5/7 vote, because this Item trims it in half, which is significant. They are a City with
many moving parts and operate at a fast pace, so important things can come up, and they have to
wait until next month. She suggested keeping the 5/7 or increasing it.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that this will force them to be more selective about the Items they
place on the Agenda. If they stick to the rules already in place, including the Resolutions already
adopted on the amount of time they get to speak, they would be able to get through all of their Items.
They have already passed safeguards on that. If they are putting out there that they will limit
themselves to no more than four Resolutions per Agenda, no more than two Ordinances per Agenda,
and no more than four Referrals per Agenda, then they have to commit to that. If something goes on
to the Planning Board, they introduce a referral to legislation that goes to the Board, and now that
comes back. Is that new business that counts against the two Ordinances? This is a new policy
coming forward. There is a distinction in the legislation that says there is a limit on the number of new
Ordinances per meeting, but under Discussion Items and Resolutions, they have a limit of four, and
it does not distinguish between new Items or Items that were not reached, or Resolutions that are
coming out from Committee as per recommendation, so, written right now, how do they interpret that?
He requested that New Discussion Items and New Resolutions be added to the language for clarity.
He previously mentioned that the Resolution under Section D-6 mentioned the waiver by a 5/7 vote.
He would extend it to removing it from the Discussion, Resolutions, and Ordinances so they really
abide by the intent of what they are trying to reform to their Agenda Practices if the sponsor accepts
the amendment.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, added that the language is no more than four may be placed on an
Agenda. If an Item is coming back from a Committee, it is not being placed on the Agenda; it is coming
back with a recommendation from the Committee. They can work to clarify that.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas wants to hear from everyone else, as Commissioner Fernandez
agrees with removing the 5/7 vote requirement, but Vice-Mayor Dominguez does not. She is OK
either way and explained that if there is an emergency Item they need to hear, that could be waived.
She sees both perspectives and is curious to hear what other colleagues have to say.
Commissioner Bhatt agrees with keeping the 5/7 for emergency Items, but it should not apply to
regular business items. Only if it is timely and everyone agrees it is important to discuss, should they
have the option to hear it.
Mayor Meiner believes they have the support to keep the 5/7 vote.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas clarified that she would like to keep it on First Reading. When it comes
back for Second Reading, they can consider this, see how they feel about the 5/7, and discuss it
again. She suggested trying a test run to see if they feel comfortable with this. It is two slash in terms
of the Item, and they want to adjust it some. If they decide to practice this already, they can do a test
run to see how it feels. Right now, it should be kept at a 5/7 of a vote until Second Reading.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading; seconded by
Commissioner Suarez.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, opened the Public Hearing. With no participants in the audience or on
Zoom requesting to speak, the Public Hearing concluded.
Roll Call: 7-0.

ACTION: Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into the
record. The Public Hearing was held. Vice-Mayor Dominguez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance
on First Reading; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
The Second Hearing Public Hearing is scheduled for June 24, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received.
Hernan Cardeno to handle.
TO DO:
 Vice-Mayor Dominguez to meet with Keith Marks and refine language related to administrative
violations and quality-of-life definitions.
 Vice-Mayor Dominguez will ensure that the South of Fifth Neighborhood Association (SOFNA)
board has the opportunity to review and provide input prior to Second Reading.
 Code Compliance Director Hernan Cardeno to clarify administrative vs. non-administrative
violation criteria for potential inclusion in Second Reading amendments.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez noted that current yacht operators have a BTR and a number of boats under
the same BTR. If a violation is not related to public safety or quality of life, the City Manager has the
authority to allow it to continue operating. Under the current wording of the Ordinance, any violation
of any of the boats would prevent them from operating, so this makes it fair because, with 20 boats
under a BTR, everyone is trying to ensure compliance, provided that violations that are not related to
public safety or quality of life still allow them to operate. She moved the approval of the Item, seconded
by Commissioner Fernandez.
Deputy City Attorney Mark Fishman explained to Commissioner Suarez that the operator in question
holds one Business Tax Receipt and that, although it is not common to have fifteen boats, multiple
vessels may operate under a single Business Tax Receipt. He described the legal background, noting
that the City Commission previously amended the cessation time for commercial vessel activity at
public marinas and public marine facilities from 9:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m. He added that the Commission
also created an application and exemption process allowing a commercial operator with no violations
within the prior two years, and who has conducted business in the City of Miami Beach for at least
two years, to apply for an exemption permitting activity until 9:00 p.m., subject to the City Manager or
designee’s discretionary approval. He stated that the proposed Ordinance maintains this framework
but expands eligibility by allowing an operator with one violation in the past two years to apply for the
exemption, again subject to the City Manager’s discretion. If the exemption is denied, the operator
must cease activity at 7:00 p.m. He indicated that, in reviewing an application, the City Manager may
consider the nature of the violation and whether it affected public safety or residents’ quality of life.
He noted that an administrative violation may be treated differently from a violation involving public
safety or resident impact. He further explained that if an operator receives a new violation after
receiving the exemption, the exemption would be automatically revoked unless the issuing authority
dismisses the violation or the operator prevails on final appeal.
Commissioner David Suarez confirmed that an operator with a violation would still be able to apply
under the Ordinance.
Deputy City Attorney Fishman clarified that an operator with one violation may apply, but approval
would remain at the City Manager's full discretion, who would evaluate the nature of the violation and
whether it involved public safety or quality-of-life impacts. He stated that no operator is permitted to
conduct any activity after 9:00 p.m.; all operators must cease operations at 7:00 p.m. He reiterated
that an operator with no violations in the prior two years may apply for the exemption and, if approved
by the City Manager, may operate until 9:00 p.m. The proposed Ordinance would allow an operator
with one prior violation, presumed to be administrative, to apply for the exemption. He explained that
an administrative violation is one that is not substantive, such as a noise offense or a public
disturbance. He stated that the City Manager would evaluate whether a curfew violation occurred
within the last year and whether the violation was upheld or not appealed. He added that, under the
current Ordinance, an operator with such a violation cannot apply and must cease activity at 7:00
p.m. for two years from the date of the violation. He noted that the proposed amendment would allow
an operator with one violation to apply, regardless of the type of violation, while still requiring the City
Manager to consider the nature of the violation when determining whether to grant the exemption or
retain the 7:00 p.m. cessation time.
Commissioner David Suarez asked whether the Ordinance would allow operators to remain in
operation until 9:00 p.m. at public marinas.”
Deputy City Attorney Mark Fishman clarified that an operator may continue activity until 9:00 p.m.
only if the operator applies for and receives the exemption, rather than ceasing activity at 7:00 p.m.
as otherwise required.
Commissioner Suarez observed that Miami Beach Marina is the only public Marina in the City and
asked whether the South of Fifth Neighborhood Association (SOFNA) had provided input on the
proposal, as he was unsure whether the association would support allowing operations until 9:00 p.m.
Mayor Steven Meiner stated that Keith Marks appeared to be on the phone and expressed concern
regarding the proposal. He explained that he and Commissioner Suarez previously sponsored
legislation that limited charter operations. He provided background, noting that four or five years prior,
commercial vessel activity at the Marina was unrestricted, resulting in continuous operations and
ongoing complaints from residents of the South of Fifth Neighborhood Association. The City
implemented a 9:00 p.m. cessation time, which was effective for several years until problems
reemerged. He stated that he and Commissioner Suarez then sponsored legislation changing the
cessation time to 7:00 p.m. He explained that some operators expressed concern, and after
discussions with the City Commission and the South of Fifth Neighborhood Association, the parties
agreed that operators with no violations for two years would be allowed to continue until 9:00 p.m. He
stated that the current proposal would create an exemption, and although he appreciates the Item
sponsored by Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez, he remains concerned about reopening the issue after
prior operational problems had been addressed. Mayor Meiner described a second concern, based
on prior experience with a separate matter several years earlier involving noise violations subject to
the City Manager's discretion. He explained that, at that time, an operator who received a violation
could contact members of the City Commission, and some Commissioners would contact the City
Manager to request leniency. He noted that this resulted in complications, the need for new
legislation, and related litigation. He stated that his concern was not personal to the City Manager but
that such situations place significant pressure on the City Manager from both operators and
Commissioners, and he preferred legislation that does not require discretionary determinations of this
nature.
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez explained that the Item was brought forward because of a situation
that occurred, prompting a review to determine whether revisions were necessary. She stated that
the operator involved holds a Business Tax Receipt (BTR) for multiple boats operating under that
single BTR. She stated that the vessel returned by 9:00 p.m., and all passengers disembarked except
for the boat owners, who exited at 9:04 p.m. She noted that, under the current Ordinance, the late
departure would affect not only that vessel but every vessel operating under the same Business Tax
Receipt, preventing all of them from operating. She stated that this appeared unfair in a situation
where the boat owners made an innocent mistake in believing they could remain on the vessel longer.
She added that, when developing the legislation, Deputy City Attorney Mark Fishman reviewed the
matter to ensure that any exemption would not apply to violations related to public safety or quality of
life. She stated that the operator involved has been working with the City for approximately twenty
years. She noted that she spoke with John Caprio and other representatives of the South of Fifth
Neighborhood Association, who were supportive of the proposal. She added that she also contacted
Miami Beach United, and Robert Selsam expressed support. She emphasized that she conducted
due diligence before bringing the Item forward and believed it was fair and appropriate.
At Mayor Steven Meiner’s request, Code Compliance Director Hernan Cardeno explained that only a
limited number of operators would qualify to return and submit applications under the proposed
amendment. He stated that of thirty-one applications submitted for the hours-of-operation exemption,
twenty-five were approved and six were denied due to one violation. He described the violations as
three for unpermitted hours of operation, two for charter advertising without required information, and
one for failure to display the required Business Tax Receipt decal. In response to Mayor Meiner, he
confirmed that the operator referenced in the discussion received a violation for hours of operation.
He noted that the Ordinance requires vessels to be dark and all activity to cease by 9:00 p.m., not
merely to arrive at the dock and begin unloading.
Commissioner David Suarez recommended opening the public hearing, and City Clerk Rafael E.
Granado opened it.
Keith Marks, participating via Zoom as a member of the South of Fifth Neighborhood Association,
stated that Vice-Mayor Dominguez had spoken with John Caprio about the Item. He explained that,
in his opinion, the proposal required additional refinement and that the Association’s full board had
not yet discussed it. He expressed concern, similar to Mayor Meiner’s, regarding leaving the
determination to the City Manager’s discretion. He stated that defining an administrative violation
would help distinguish between minor administrative issues affecting one vessel among several,
versus operators who have repeatedly arrived after the required cessation time, which was the reason
the restrictions were adopted. He indicated that he would support the proposal if administrative
violations were clearly defined and reviewed by Code Compliance rather than the City Manager, as
he anticipated that boat owners would lobby the City Manager for exemptions. He added that if Marina
operations continue to function well, the proposed change would not be problematic if limited to
administrative violations, but there must be clarity on what constitutes a quality-of-life impact.
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez stated that the definition of quality of life already exists in the Code and
noted that this Item was on First Reading. She indicated that she would meet with Keith Marks to
reach an approach that he considered acceptable.
Keith Marks, participating via Zoom, stated that he supported the Ordinance on First Reading if the
exemptions were defined in a manner that did not require the City Manager's involvement. He
expressed that it would be preferable for Code Compliance, including Code Enforcement Director
Hernan Cardeno, to determine whether a violation was administrative or non-administrative.
Assistant City Manager Mark Taxis explained that the City Commission had already reduced the
hours of operation from 9:00 p.m. to 7:00 p.m. and created an exemption process allowing operators
with no violations to apply for permission to remain operating until 9:00 p.m. He stated that the
proposed amendment would allow additional operators who have had one violation in the past two
years and have been operating in the City for two consecutive years to apply for and potentially
receive the exemption, regardless of how many boats they operate under a single Business Tax
Receipt.
Commissioner David Suarez stated that the Ordinance was brought forward because of the situation
involving the operator whose vessel returned four minutes past 9:00 p.m., one of several vessels
operated under a single Business Tax Receipt.
Deputy City Attorney Mark Fishman stated that 31 applications had been submitted and 6 had been
denied, including the referenced operator. He added that some of the denied operators operated only
a single vessel. He noted that, regardless of the number of vessels under a Business Tax Receipt,
the amendment would allow eligible operators to apply for the exemption.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he understood the challenges faced by some operators, noting that
he frequents the Marina and keeps his vessel there. He acknowledged that certain operators were
adversely affected by prior Ordinances. He added that residents sought relief from problematic
operators and said he was open to considering exemptions for operators with good records, but
emphasized the need to clearly define limits. He noted that an operator may be four minutes late on
one occasion but an hour late on another, possibly creating noise upon return, which would constitute
a quality-of-life concern. He stated that determining these situations would be within the City
Manager's discretion. Deputy City Attorney Fishman confirmed that this is how the Ordinance is
currently structured.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine asked whether the matter was a broad operational issue or related
primarily to one operator.
Deputy City Attorney Fishman explained that six operators were involved, each cited for a different
violation, and that some violations were administrative.
Code Enforcement Director Hernan Cardeno detailed that the six violations consisted of three for
unpermitted hours of operation, two for charter advertising without required information, and one for
failure to display the Business Tax Receipt decal. He noted that the enforcement occurred after the
Ordinances were adopted and that zero-tolerance procedures were in place at Miami Beach Marina,
such that being late by four minutes or forty minutes constituted a violation if the vessel was not dark
by 9:00 p.m.
Commissioner Magazine observed that five of the six violations were minor in nature and not
indicative of significantly problematic operators.
Assistant City Manager Mark Taxis explained that enforcement at the Marina occurred under a
zero-tolerance approach intended to ensure full compliance and make clear that violations would
result in consequences. He stated that, in response to Commissioner Joseph Magazine, one operator
involved in the recent incident had returned to the Marina fifteen minutes before 9:00 p.m., but two
individuals remained on the vessel past the required time. He noted that the City could maintain a
firm enforcement posture and continue to send a message that operators who violate the rules will
not be permitted to move forward. He added that the situation involved a review of past conduct and
that, because a violation had occurred, the operator was not in compliance.
Commissioner Magazine asked whether there was a way to address the single situation without
passing broader legislation.
Deputy City Attorney Mark Fishman explained that the City Commission previously adopted
legislation requiring no violations within the prior two years. He stated that, as noted by Assistant City
Manager Taxis, the operator has a violation. He added that the City Manager would have discretion
only if the City Commission adopted the proposed amendment on First and Second Reading; under
the current Ordinance, the City Manager has no discretion to grant an exemption.
City Clerk confirmed that no additional speakers requested to speak, either in the audience or via
Zoom. The public hearing was closed.
A motion to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading was made by Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez and
seconded by Commissioner Alex Fernandez.
Commissioner Magazine stated that he supported the Ordinance on First Reading, but requested that
neighborhood associations and other stakeholders be in alignment before Second Reading so that
all parties were generally supportive.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez indicated that she would meet with Keith Marks between First Reading and
Second Reading.
The motion passed by a vote of 7-0.

ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into
the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the
Ordinance on First Reading with direction; seconded by Mayor Meiner. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for June 24, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Hernan Cardeno to handle.
DIRECTION:
The Commission directed Deputy City Attorney Mark Fishman to work with Marketing and
Communications Director Melissa Berthier to prepare clear public messaging informing residents and
visitors that fishing is prohibited at the three designated City-owned street-end properties along the
Baywalk, 10th Street, 14th Street, and Lincoln Road, and that fishing is permitted at the jetty and in
restricted swimming areas where allowed, so the public understands exactly where fishing is and is
not allowed. Mark Fishman and Melissa Berthier to handle.
Commissioner Bhatt asked to better understand the Item. She does not want fishhooks and lines
lying around where they can cause trouble for pets and children, and that is not the goal. Her concern
is that they live on a barrier island, and for people who do not live on a waterfront property, this may
be their only opportunity to go fishing with family. They have many public parks along the water with
benches and seawalls, so people can enjoy the beauty of living on an island without having to be self-
limiting or self-selecting for people who are able to afford to live on the water. She is not a fisherperson
but is concerned about making it illegal for other people who enjoy it and have no other access to it.
She does not want this to be a City of haves and have-nots.
Commissioner Fernandez explained that this is about the Baywalk at 10th and 14 Streets and Lincoln
Road, not any other parks or areas. These are some of their most cherished spots along Biscayne
Bay, where residents walk their dogs, and they want to keep them safe. This applies specifically to
those areas.
Deputy City Attorney Mark Fishman confirmed that the restriction applies to the three designated City-
owned street ends along the Baywalk, which are heavily used and crowded. Motorized and non-
motorized forms of transportation have already been eliminated there, except for wheelchairs. This
legislation would provide more opportunities for individuals who want to fish by removing the
prohibition on fishing from the jetty area between 29 and 33 Streets and from restricted swim areas,
in addition to the City-owned designated street ends at 10th and 14th Streets and Lincoln Road.
Addressing Commissioner Bhatt’s comments, Commissioner Fernandez noted that they are doing
this because they do not have jurisdiction in those areas; they can only do it in the City’s right-of-
ways.
Deputy City Attorney Mark Fishman indicated that the properties are City-owned and that, in fact,
Commissioner Bhatt’s concerns are possible, but they rarely occur. Oftentimes, these fishermen are
there early in the morning, when there is better fishing and hardly any swimmers.
Commissioner Bhatt respectfully asked that this be communicated to residents because she has
heard concerns that the way it is being read is that they will not be permitted to fish in certain places,
and she is concerned about that. Is there a way, through social media or other means, or in the places
where people apply for fishing licenses, to let them know that they can fish here but not in other
places? This is an island, and people move here because they are surrounded by water, but they
should still be able to enjoy it, and she wants to make sure people understand.
Deputy City Attorney Mark Fishman will work with Melissa Berthier, Marketing and Communications
Director, to develop a clear, marketing-friendly message that will notify people that fishing is prohibited
at these three properties and that the jetty is reopening with restricted swimming areas, so they can
communicate that.
Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading with direction;
seconded by Mayor Meiner.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, opened the Public Hearing. With no participants in the audience or on
Zoom requesting to speak, the Public Hearing concluded.
Roll Call: 7-0.

items.title: AN ORDINANCE OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, AMENDING CHAPTER 70 OF THE CITY CODE, ENTITLED “MISCELLANEOUS OFFENSES,” BY AMENDING ARTICLE II, ENTITLED “PUBLIC PLACES,” BY AMENDING DIVISION 2, ENTITLED “BICYCLING, SKATEBOARDING, ROLLER SKATING, IN-LINE SKATING, MOTORIZED MEANS OF TRANSPORTATION, ELECTRIC BICYCLES, MOPEDS, MOTORCYCLES, MOTORIZED BICYCLES, AND MOTORIZED SCOOTERS,” BY AMENDING SECTION 70-66 THEREOF, ENTITLED “DEFINITIONS,” BY CREATING AND AMENDING CERTAIN TERMS THEREIN; AND BY AMENDING SECTION 70-71 THEREOF, ENTITLED “ENFORCEMENT, PENALTIES,” BY AMENDING AND PROVIDING FOR ADDITIONAL PENALTIES THEREIN; AND BY CREATING SECTION 70-73 THEREOF, ENTITLED “RESPONSIBILITIES OF MICROMOBILITY DEVICE OPERATORS,” TO ESTABLISH CERTAIN REQUIREMENTS APPLICABLE TO MICROMOBILITY DEVICE OPERATORS; AND PROVIDING FOR REPEALER, SEVERABILITY, CODIFICATION, AND AN EFFECTIVE DATE.
items.action: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record. The Public Hearing was held. A motion was made by Commissioner Bhatt to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading with direction; seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Roll Call: 7-0.

ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into
the record. The Public Hearing was held. A motion was made by Commissioner Bhatt to adopt the
Ordinance on First Reading with direction; seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for June 24, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Chief Wayne Jones to handle.
DIRECTION:
 Staff to return between First and Second Reading with recommendations on incorporating a
mandatory first warning prior to fines and to evaluate whether such a requirement can be codified.
 Maintain an education-first approach, with enforcement beginning after the education period.
 Continue community education and outreach efforts, including school-level, parent-level, and
HOA-level engagement and informational mailings.
 Police Department to continue discretion-based enforcement and education, with warnings as
appropriate and focused enforcement on unsafe behavior.
 Transportation Department to continue implementing safety measures, including signage,
counters, sensors, and pathway improvements.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt introduced the Item and explained that colleagues at the City staff
level, including the Director of Transportation, the Director of Police, various members of the Police
Department, Code, and many others, have been working on micromobility issues to move the City to
a better place. She indicated that change is coming, that they are in the midst of it, and that it has not
been easy. She noted that change is never easy and described micromobility issues as messy. She
described micromobility as a benefit for the community, noting that the City is flat, the weather is
favorable most of the time, and residents do not need to travel long distances. She explained that
many people can benefit from using bikes, e-bikes, and e-scooters. She noted that the challenge is
that the City is built out, has parking constraints, and has unsafe driving conditions involving trucks,
cars, and motorcycles, which are a reality in South Florida. She explained that the goal is to prevent
chaos and unsafe conditions on the roads while the rest of the State and the country catch up on how
to operate these devices safely. She described concerns that many incidents involving micromobility
devices are not captured in formal statistics, even though people are injured, and added that
individuals involved in small crashes may walk away, while the drivers involved may experience
lasting trauma when a rider appears suddenly without a helmet, lighting, or adherence to traffic rules.
She stated that the intent is to put together comprehensive legislation to address as many issues as
possible, to allow all users to coexist safely, reduce vehicular traffic, and provide inexpensive and
accessible mobility options. She referred to a presentation and acknowledged the assistance of her
Aide, Sara Murillo. Click here to view the presentation. In response to Commissioner David Suarez,
she explained that as people previously used bicycles and cars in greater numbers, a conflict point
developed, and because there was no order in the interaction between cars and bicycles, people
riding bicycles were being killed.
Mark Fishman, Deputy City Attorney, added that this legislation includes safety equipment and
regulations for micromobility device operators when operating these devices on the public rights-of-
way. Many of these are State laws that took some doing to get here, but many are already in State
law. He explained that when micromobility devices are operated between sunset and sunrise, they
must have a white front lamp visible at least 500 feet, a red rear light, and a rear reflector visible at
least 600 feet. Fifteen-year-olds or younger operators and passengers of micromobility devices must
wear a properly fitted, fastened, and secured bicycle helmet with a strap that meets federal standards
for bicycle helmets. Brakes must be capable of stopping the device within 25 feet at 10 mph on flat,
level, dry pavement. The micromobility device cannot be used to carry more persons at one time than
the device was designed or equipped to carry. The restriction does not prohibit attaching a trailer or
semi-trailer to a micromobility device if the trailer or semi-trailer is commercially available and
designed for such attachment. They went further into this Ordinance, received a lot of feedback, and
ultimately have done more than the State. They defined a sign-equipped approach to provide
guidance and design or equip requirements to establish that a micromobility device can carry two or
more people. It can include factors such as the manufacturer's designations and specifications on the
product sheet, extra seats installed, an extra set of handlebars, foot pegs, the device's total weight
capacity, the deck's length and width, and similar details. This does that as a starting point, and they
are looking at other things. This is primarily from State law.
Commissioner Bhatt pointed out that this is not coming out of the blue. It is delayed because of other
work, and it has taken a long time to reach this point, but they are to be very careful about this. A
small section of this would take effect immediately, but the bigger things would take effect a year after
passage, giving them time to reach out to the community and provide assistance to get them helmets,
so they can go to school and receive education. There would be traffic enforcement between now
and the effective date of the Ordinance. She clarified that the goal is not to be punitive but to change
behavior so they do not have to pick up people’s body parts off the road. Anyone driving in the City
now, whether driving a micromobility device or in a vehicle, has seen a near miss every time they get
into their cars. They have seen flagrant traffic violations, people driving into oncoming traffic, people
not stopping at stop signs, people driving through red lights, and people crossing four or five lanes of
traffic into oncoming traffic because they do not think the rules apply to them. They are going to
effectuate change and have a year to educate people at the school level, at the parent level, and at
the HOA level, where she plans to mail a postcard to every single household with a website link so
people can understand what is correct, proper, and safe. People can buy these devices off of Amazon
and are not supposed to go more than 20 mph, but they can download an App or take a screwdriver,
make small modifications, and now they are going 59 mph on these devices with no lights, no
requirements, no licensing requirements, and chaos ensues. That is why this is before them, and to
give context to what they have done so far, she invited Jose Gonzalez, Transportation and Mobility
Director, to explain.
Jose Gonzalez, Transportation and Mobility Director, highlighted key initiatives underway as a result
of the micromobility working group that Commissioner Bhatt has chaired for the past two years. These
initiatives are intended to enhance the safety of micromobility users, bicyclists, pedestrians, and
anyone using shared-use paths or sidewalks throughout the City. They completed the installation of
signage, including many signs along the Beachwalk, the Baywalk, and the Cutwalk. The signage is
very clear and tells all users to stay to their right and follow the rules of the road. They drew a white
skip center line down the Beachwalk to the Baywalk and up to Fifth Street, where micromobility
devices are not permitted. Many signs have been installed stating that motorized transportation is not
permitted on those shared-use paths, telling people to stay to the right and slow down as they
approach the curve. They walked the entire Beachwalk, with part of it by bike and the rest on foot. In
areas with dangerous curves or sidewalk issues, they addressed them through signage or legislation
requiring abutting property owners to trim shrubs along the Beachwalk, particularly. There has been
significant improvement in that regard over the past several months.
Commissioner Bhatt added that Police Officer Julio Blanco is the City’s Poster Boy for the Beachwalk.
He is not here today, but the number of infractions has gone down significantly just by putting these
clear guidelines in place, so everyone knows the rules of engagement. There are still offenders.
Officer Blanco was run over on his e-bike by someone who took him out, and he broke his elbow and
was out for a few weeks. It is not perfect, but the number of tickets and violations, or even stops to
educate people, has gone down significantly, so they know this is effective.
Jose Gonzalez, Transportation and Mobility Director, added that early on, they did not have much
data on usage, including how many micromobility devices, bicycles, and pedestrians were using these
critical shared-use paths in the City, including the Beachwalk. To address this, they installed eleven
counters along bicycle lanes throughout the City. Those counters distinguish between bicycles and
micromobility devices. Specifically, along the Beachwalk, they are in the process of installing six
sensors that can also detect whether it is a scooter, a bicycle, or a pedestrian, and can measure
speed as well. Digital speed feedback signs are being installed along the Beachwalk. In reply to
Commissioner Suarez’s question, Jose Gonzalez, Transportation and Mobility Director, stated that
based on the device specifications and wheelbase, sensors are placed on the pavement and,
depending on the distance, can tell whether it is a scooter or a bicycle. He is not sure about how or if
these sensors differ between an e-bike and a regular bike, but he will find out.
Commissioner Bhatt thinks it depends on the size of the e-bike because some are built heavier, but
regardless, those are already installed.
Commissioner Suarez wants to be mindful of the data they receive and whether there is an
assumption that there are this many micromobility devices. He knows road bikes that can go 30 mph
to 40 mph.
Commissioner Bhatt clarified that this applies to all devices, not just electrified bikes. People need to
operate vehicles safely, so they are distinguishing between what they can and cannot do. He hears
Commissioner Suarez’s concerns.
Jose Gonzalez, Transportation and Mobility Director, added that they developed a flyer outlining
where micromobility devices are allowed or not, the different regulations that exist across the City
depending on the type of path, and that they conducted a Micromobility Town Hall sponsored by
Commissioner Bhatt in September 2025, along with other similar educational, enforcement, and
engineering efforts to try to raise awareness and improve the safety of all users.
Commissioner Suarez thinks it makes sense to require all scooters to have white lights and proper
brakes, but they have to consider enforcement after year one. If there are kids going to school five
blocks away on a scooter without a helmet, are they really going to have Police Officers pull them
over and give them a ticket?
Commissioner Bhatt clarified that the goal is not punitive and that Officers have discretion to stop,
engage, and educate rather than stop and write a ticket. If the individual is a totally irresponsible
operator violating rules, that might result in an actual violation. If a twelve-year-old on a scooter does
not have a helmet, an Officer in the school zone may remind him to wear one next time. That is part
of the education process. In the Netherlands and other countries, that is part of the school curriculum.
There are two different points, but at one point, they cannot advance to a certain grade level without
completing Safe Rider Classes on a bike or scooter. That is because it is so important to their well-
being not to fall off and hit their head or get creamed by oncoming traffic. That is what they are going
to be doing. They have a fleet of six new e-bikes that will be used Citywide. They identified with the
Police Department hot spots where adults ride in an unsafe manner, and they are going to add Police
presence to educate people, as they did on the Beachwalk. It is not punitive; it is about education.
Commissioner Suarez gets it, and respectfully, he is just having a dialogue. He will probably be the
one trying to work through this, and he wants to work with her. He understands that it is not punitive,
but at the end of the day, if the Officer’s discretion is to write a fine to a fourteen- or fifteen-year-old
going to school because the kid does not want to obey the law, he does not want to see a Police
Officer pull them over, and the kid may run away. There are all sorts of reasons why a fifteen-year-
old may not want to get pulled over, and the Police Officer's discretion is to say he has seen the kid
not wear a helmet five times while riding the scooter to MBSH, and he is going to write him a ticket.
He does not know if he feels comfortable with that. Assuming that after the first year of the educational
period, they have the information they worked with the School Board on, he thinks three or four years
down the line, he is not sure if he feels comfortable with a Police Officer dealing with a fifteen-year-
old for not wearing a helmet and giving them a citation.
Deputy City Attorney Mark Fishman clarified that riders under the age of sixteen must wear helmets
when operating a micromobility device. In response to Commissioner Suarez’s question, he explained
that codifying this makes it easier for enforcement to have their definitions in the City Code and for
the Office of the City Attorney not to have to do mental gymnastics with the State laws for bicycles
and to extrapolate e-bikes.
Commissioner Suarez fully understands the intent and believes his colleague is coming from a very
good, very maternal place. They are both parents, and they both care. The unintended consequence
is that Police Officers will pull over teenagers for not wearing a helmet. He is not sure he feels
comfortable with that. Commissioner Bhatt suggested that he not support it. Commissioner Suarez
explained that the best use of Police resources currently is not to target teenagers not wearing a
helmet, because there are greater dangers to teenagers in Miami Beach than to those riding mobility
devices without a helmet.
Commissioner Bhatt does not think that the Police Officers are going to pull over a kid for not wearing
a helmet unless the kid is doing other things that are egregiously dangerous. They have to trust their
Officers, who have better things to do, to look out for the well-being of their residents when unsafe
behavior occurs. It is not great for teenagers not to wear a helmet, but if that kid is popping wheelies
and zooming in and out of traffic, that is a different conversation, and that is the behavior they are
trying to address. Three or four years from now, if this goes properly, they will not even have this
conversation. She has seen kids, and the helmet is the least of the problems. These are all things
that they are going to work on.
Commissioner Suarez does not believe a helmet mandate will prevent bad behavior on the road.
Commissioner Suarez asked Commissioner Bhatt whether she would be open to a possible
mandatory warning for individuals beyond the educational period.
Commissioner Bhatt encouraged Police Officers to issue a warning first. If there is a way to have a
conversation, they can do that. If the individual being pulled over has an attitude, they get the ticket.
She deferred to the Officers. There will be training involved, and they can give an appropriate verbal
warning. If people are obstinate in their attitude and do not try to understand what the deal is, then a
ticket is given.
Commissioner Suarez respectfully suggested adding language that a warning must be given to
individuals. They are dealing with individuals whose brains have not fully formed, and for one reason
or another, they may enter into an egregious agreement with a Police Officer who pulls them over
and issues a ticket. This solves the problem. They receive a one-time warning with no further
warnings after that, but he suggested codifying the fact that residents receive a first warning.
Commissioner Bhatt suggested going back to the team and speaking with them to see how they can
return for Second Reading.
Commissioner Suarez agreed.
For context, Commissioner Bhatt explained that other States are holding parents accountable for their
children’s actions and sending parents to jail because their kids are causing mayhem. They are not
there yet, but they could be. All she is suggesting is doing everything they can to make it easier for
residents to get educated, and it is not a terrible idea to keep it in place for the next few years until
this becomes common practice. A small postcard serves as a reminder of how to use these devices
and whom to contact to learn how to ride them safely. They give everyone the benefit of the doubt,
but at the end of the day, they do not want to be picking up pieces from children, parents, or anyone
from the road, nor do they want the trauma of someone who did not see the kid or the 25-year-old
coming out of nowhere with no lights or helmet, and now the driver has PTSD or has ruined his or
her life because he or she inadvertently hit somebody.
Commissioner Suarez believes the intent is educational, and part of the process is a warning during
the educational period, with enforcement coming after that. He would like to mandate a warning
before any fines are issued to teenagers.
Commissioner Bhatt will work with the team between Firs

ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into
the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Matteo-Salinas made a motion to adopt the
Ordinance on First Reading; seconded by Commissioner Bhatt. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for June 24, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Office of the City Attorney to
handle.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas thanked the Mayor for his co-prime sponsorship and expressed
appreciation for the support. She explained that the Item tightens the City’s municipal habitual
offender Ordinance. In the past, an individual could be considered a habitual offender after being
convicted four times within a specified period. The proposed Ordinance would tighten those
requirements for certain municipal offenses. Many individuals who commit crimes are repeatedly
convicted, sent to jail, and then released, only to return to Miami Beach and prey on residents, visitors,
and businesses. The Item was intended to strengthen the City’s ability to address those repeat
offenders.
City Attorney Dopico provided clarification. He explained that the proposed tightening would apply
only to certain municipal offenses, which generally involve quality-of-life issues, such as cannabis
violations, urinating or defecating in plain view, public camping, and being in a park after hours. Other
Ordinances in the City Code that relate to State law offenses would remain subject to the existing
four-strike requirement. He explained that the City could not change those requirements unless and
until the State amends its habitual offender statute.
Mayor Meiner asked for clarification on whether the City could change the requirement even if the
offense is contained in a Municipal Ordinance.
City Attorney Dopico explained that if the Municipal Ordinance were similar to State law or had been
adopted pursuant to State law, the four-strike requirement within one year would have to remain in
place unless and until the State changed the law.
Mayor Meiner asked whether there is a separate Item that addresses this issue as a legislative
priority.
City Attorney Dopico replied that there is.
Commissioner Fernandez thanked Commissioner Matteo-Salinas for bringing the Item forward. He
also thanked the Mayor for serving as a co-prime sponsor and asked to be added as a co-sponsor.
Mayor Meiner thanked Commissioner Fernandez and noted that Commissioner Magazine also
requested to be added as a co-sponsor.

ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into
the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the

VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes

Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes

Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes

The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for June 24, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Mark Taxis, Hernan Cardeno,
Chief Wayne Jones, and William Macdonald to handle.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez addressed the Commission and explained that residents had raised
concerns for years regarding large unpermitted house parties and the strain these events placed on
surrounding neighborhoods. Commissioner Fernandez indicated that enforcing such events was not
easy and required significant resources from the City Administration, including Code Compliance, the
Police Department, the Fire Department, Parking, and Sanitation. Commissioner Fernandez noted
that these departments often had to deploy a substantial number of personnel to maintain safety and
order. Commissioner Fernandez described the current situation in which, during designated
high-impact periods, a homeowner who hosted a large-scale party without obtaining a special event
permit caused the City to absorb the associated enforcement costs. Commissioner Fernandez stated
that law-abiding homeowners, residents, and taxpayers were ultimately responsible for covering the
cost of personnel, equipment, and emergency responses triggered by these unpermitted events.
Commissioner Fernandez explained that the proposed Ordinance established a straightforward
cost-recovery process so that, when a violation occurred, the property owner, rather than the public,
would be responsible for reimbursing the City’s expenses. Commissioner Fernandez described that
the Ordinance created a new subsection in the City Code authorizing the City to bill for enforcement
costs and, if unpaid, to place a lien on the property. Commissioner Fernandez indicated that the
purpose was to ensure fairness and to prevent violations of the City Code from financially burdening
law-abiding residents of the City of Miami Beach. Commissioner Fernandez moved the Item.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt seconded the motion and indicated support for the Item.
City Clerk Rafael E. Granado announced that the Item was a public hearing. City Clerk Granado
observed that no speakers were present in the Commission Chambers and no participants were
present via Zoom.
Roll Call: 7-0.

Commissioner Dominguez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading; seconded by
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez explained that this Item amends the Special Magistrate compensation
ordinance. He noted that the City Manager currently has the authority to amend the compensation
for the Chief Special Magistrate, while compensation for the other Special Magistrates must be
amended by Ordinance of the City Commission. Commissioner Fernandez suggested that the City
Commission consider including a provision allowing future compensation adjustments to be made by
Resolution rather than by Ordinance to streamline the process and avoid the requirement of two
readings.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas indicated support for the suggestion and asked whether such a
provision could be added.
City Attorney Ricardo J. Dopico indicated that the proposal would be reviewed.
Commissioner Ferandez said that, depending on the outcome of the City Attorney’s review, the
change might be incorporated between First and Second reading, or alternatively, may require a
separate Item.
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas, identified as the sponsor of the Item, confirmed willingness to
include the suggested change as part of the legislation.
City Attorney Dopico then explained that the title of the Ordinance would need to be reviewed to
determine whether the proposed revision could legally be added at this stage. If not, a separate Item
would be prepared.
A motion to approve the Item was made by Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez and seconded by
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas.

ACTION: Resolution 2026-34288 was adopted. Commissioner Bhatt made a motion to adopt the
Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Voice vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Jose Gonzalez to handle.
Jose Gonzalez, Transportation and Mobility Director, introduced the Item, which formalizes the City’s
relationship with North Bay Village. North Bay Village has been using the City’s operator to provide
trolley service during Cultural Crawl events at North Bay Village’s cost. As part of that service, the
trolley extends into North Bay Village with a few stops and pickup and drop-off locations, bringing
people to North Beach along 71st Street and other areas, including the Fountain District and the
Bandshell area. It has been popular in North Bay Village, and they have really enjoyed this
partnership. He reiterated that it has been at North Bay Village’s expense and will continue to be. So
far, they have a commitment through the end of this Cultural Crawl season in July of this year. This
agreement formalizes the relationship and establishes a mechanism for North Bay Village to
reimburse the City, because up until now, Miami Beach has been fronting the funds for this service
once a month.
Commissioner Bhatt recently spoke with Mayor Rachel Streitfeld, who loves the program. Everybody
in North Beach loves it, and it would be awesome to expand it down the road when ready. However,
her recollection was that there had been a concern about the pricing, and that North Bay Village and
Miami Beach were working to figure out the right pricing, as it was expensive for them.
Jose Gonzalez, Transportation and Mobility Director, believes Commissioner Bhatt is referring to a
permanent service that may be implemented in the future with the trolleys to North Bay Village.
However, regarding this Item and the service during the Culture Crawl, both parties are 100% on
board.
Commissioner Bhatt made a motion to adopt the Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez.
Voice vote: 7-0.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, APPROVING A TEN PERCENT (10%) DISCOUNT ON THE ANNUAL RESIDENTIAL PARKING PERMIT REGISTRATION FEE, AS AUTHORIZED IN CITY CODE SECTIONS 106-76 THROUGH 106-84, FOR (1) CITY OF MIAMI BEACH RESIDENTS WHO ARE SIXTY-FIVE (65) YEARS OF AGE OR OLDER, AND (2) CURRENT OR FORMER MILITARY RESIDENTS.
items.action: Resolution 2026-34289 was adopted as amended. Commissioner Matteo-Salinas moved to adopt the Resolution as amended to include low-income seniors and military personnel, seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 7-0.
items.voteBasis: Multiple roll calls appear in this item. Open the minutes to match each vote to its motion; no single vote is inferred here.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34289 was adopted as amended. Commissioner Matteo-Salinas moved
to adopt the Resolution as amended to include low-income seniors and military personnel, seconded
by Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
AMENDMENT:
Include a 10 percent discount for low-income seniors age 65 and older and for current and active-duty
military members.
William MacDonald to handle.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas introduced the Item. She noted that she had separated the Item from
the Consent Agenda for clarification. The idea is to offer a military discount on registration fees.
Unfortunately, the senior discount did not specify that it was intended for low-income seniors, not all
seniors, so she offered that amendment and moved her Item. This is only for low-income seniors and
the military to receive a modest 10% discount.
Seconded by Commissioner Fernandez.
Commissioner Fernandez suggested doing something more significant than 10%. It is Commissioner
Matteo-Salinas’s Item, but he wonders whether they can offer more to seniors who are not always in
the best position.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas agrees with whatever works financially and whatever works at the dais.
She would love to offer a larger discount and would love to hear from her colleagues. Commissioner
Matteo-Salinas suggested increasing the discount to amend the Item to provide free parking for low-
income seniors and military professionals.
Mayor Meiner mentioned that he is sitting next to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee
Chair and would like to hear how this will affect the City's fiscal position.
Commissioner Magazine stated that this is not how they legislate. If they are going to do it, be serious
about the policy, not just say start at $10, then go to $20. Do I hear free? Yes. If they are going to do
it, specify who it is, what it is going to cost the City, and make a sound judgment. They are just about
to pass it, and they do not know what fiscal impact it will have.
Commissioner Bhatt noted that they do not have an analysis. There are other Items on the Agenda
that discuss waiving fees, and on principle, there is a case to be made for waived fees. But instead
of generalizing categories, which are not precise, why would someone who might be 67 years old
and living in a $20 million home get discounted parking? She agrees with the goal, and military
veterans are a different category. She suggested looking at best practices, coming back to the City
Commission with a proposal, and assessing the impact in cities around the country. This is how they
treat military veterans, who deserve all the respect and benefits they can approve for having put their
lives in harm’s way for the greater good of the country. No one is arguing that, but figure out the best
way to do it before they make decisions on the fly. At the same time, as they are going through this
budget process, where they are trying to keep taxes steady and billions of dollars of infrastructure
work that is currently unfunded and necessary, all of a, sudden it starts adding up. She supports the
goal. She suggested that they open and continue the Item to next month to come back with a plan
and make it happen in a measured way.
Mayor Meiner added that there are good suggestions here, but this will require staff input on the
financial impact. He added that Commissioner Matteo-Salinas has the votes for a 10% discount and
may consider something more in the future if that is the call.
Commissioner Magazine added that even 20% of this quantifies what it is. When they make a
decision, they should have a rhyme and reason for it. If they are about to vote on that, he suggested
having something tangible. They do not need to refer to the Finance and Economic Resiliency
Committee just to get that quantification.
William MacDonald, Parking Director, explained that they do not have any data identifying whether
residential permit holders are military veterans, active-duty service members, or their ages, as this
information is not collected or requested. In response to Commissioner Magazine, he added that the
annual registration fee in Zone 2 is $56 per year and that Altos del Mar is just over $200 per year.
Discussion followed regarding aggregate fees collected from permit registrations, and the Parking
Director confirmed that the total is less than a million dollars. He stated that implementation would
involve adding another question to the application, requesting documentation such as a CAC card or
DD-214 for military status, and that if income were used as a qualifier, they could discuss respectful
methods to best serve that population.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas clarified that even if they bumped to next month, they do not have that
quantification as they do not collect those details, and Parking Director MacDonald validated the
statement.
Commissioner Bhatt added that they might want to contact the VFW Post for an estimate of the
number of veterans living in the City.
William MacDonald, Parking Director, indicated that they have email addresses for those with
residential permits so they can send out an anonymous poll.
Commissioner Magazine said he did not want to pursue that approach. He explained that if they had
the data, that would be fine, but he did not want to try to solve the issue that way. He noted that the
aggregate amount collected annually from residential parking permit registration fees is less than one
million dollars and that the proposed discount would apply to only a small portion of that total.
Ricardo J. Dopico, City Attorney, clarified that there are restrictions in the City’s parking bond
covenants that he would want to review before implementing a free parking program. He added that
the impact may be de minimis and therefore may not matter, but he was not prepared to provide that
recommendation today.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas said she did not expect such a robust discussion and requested that
the 10% discount be adopted for seniors age 65 and older who are low income (AMI less than 80
percent) and for current and active-duty military members. She explained that she preferred to move
forward rather than defer the Item and have it go through multiple iterations, which could result in it
returning unchanged. She moved her Item, seconded by Commissioner Fernandez.
Commissioner Magazine expressed support for getting something done and apologized to
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas if he had jumped in hastily, noting that the discussion had moved in
five seconds from 10% to 20% to free. He said that wherever they chose to land, as long as there
was thought put behind it, he would support it. He explained that he saw the conversation moving
quickly, but did not believe the Item needed to go through different iterations. He stated that he
supported whatever Commissioner Matteo-Salinas wanted to do and that there was no need to
prolong the discussion. He said it had been a helpful discussion regarding the aggregation and
collection of data, and that she should not constrain herself to what was originally proposed if she
believed a different number worked. He confirmed that she had his support.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas said she was fine with the 10% discount as written to help residents
and explained that the concept originated from a request made by a senior who approached her. She
indicated that she felt 10% was small but fair. She moved the Item, and Commissioner Fernandez
seconded the motion.
A motion was made by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas to adopt the Resolution as amended to include
low-income seniors and military personnel, seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. The motion
passed 7-0.
Mayor Meiner recognized Commissioner Matteo-Salinas for a good job done.
2:12:01 p.m.

Commissioner David Suarez made a motion to adopt an After-the-Fact Resolution directing that when

VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes

Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes

R7 F2 - AFTER-THE-FACT RESOLUTION:
A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH,
FLORIDA, DIRECTING THE CITY ADMINISTRATION TO TEMPORARILY PAUSE THE ISSUANCE
OF FINES FOR EXPIRED ELEVATOR CERTIFICATES OF OPERATION UNTIL SUCH TIME THAT
THE CITY HAS OBTAINED UP-TO-DATE ELEVATOR CERTIFICATES OF OPERATION FOR ALL
CITY-OPERATED ELEVATORS, EXCEPT WHERE IT IS DETERMINED FROM THE RESULTS OF
ANY INSPECTION THAT, IN THE INTEREST OF THE PUBLIC SAFETY, AN ELEVATOR IS IN AN
UNSAFE CONDITION.
John Norris to handle.
DIRECTION:
Ensure that all City-operated elevator inspections and recertifications are completed within 30 days,
and provide an update to the City Commission next month. John Norris to handle.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine said that many older buildings are approaching their 40-Year
Recertification inspections, and one of the biggest challenges is updating elevators and obtaining
certifications. He explained that this issue is especially significant for older buildings with only one
elevator, including senior buildings that City Commission members have visited. He recalled
attending an event approximately a year earlier at a senior building where one elevator was out of
service, causing residents to wait ten minutes. He described this as both a life-safety and quality-of-
life concern and emphasized that restoring dignity to residents is important in the most serious cases.
He added that even in multifamily buildings that are not facing the most extreme circumstances,
residents want these issues addressed expeditiously, and that more buildings are experiencing
challenges with elevator inspections.
Pursuant to Commissioner Magazine’s direction, John Norris, Public Works Director, explained that
the Item came up after a complaint about a building in Mid Beach that had a few senior citizens in it,
but that has since been resolved. In that case, part of the responsibility was the contractor, who was
not ready for the inspection, and there were communication issues that have since been resolved.
They now have a plan to prioritize buildings with only one elevator, move them ahead, and schedule
the elevator inspection so the elevator can be brought back online. Additionally, elevator inspectors
are encouraged to communicate with the contractors to ensure they know what they need to do, so
they do not have to return for multiple inspections. One challenge is that these inspections can take
an entire day, depending on the building's size, so they need to ensure that, when they arrive, the
building is ready to pass the first inspection. They are working to coordinate that.
Commissioner Magazine appreciates the Public Works team's work.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas requested to cosponsor the Item. It is a great Item. Someone reached
out to her about an 11-floor building where the elevator was broken, leaving seniors stuck on the
upper floors, unable to climb up or down. It was a mess. She loves this Item, thanked Commissioner
Magazine, and asked to cosponsor.
Commissioner Suarez thinks it is rich that the City continues to fine residents and buildings, while its
own elevators are expiring and City staff are not being reprimanded for this. Meanwhile, condominium
residents have expired tags and are being penalized, while they are not. They should not penalize
any residents until all the elevators in the “City of Miami Beach” facilities are up to Code, at the very
least. Commissioner Suarez asked whether the elevator in City Hall was currently expired.
Parks, Facilities, Fleet, and Beaches Director John Rebar responded that it was due for a new
inspection.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, clarified that it is a slippery slope they have to be careful about because
there are different levels of safety concerns. Their elevator inspectors are careful to take elevators
out of service when they are not functioning properly, but the legislative purview is theirs.
Commissioner Suarez is not in favor of fining anyone in the City until the City-maintained and -
operated elevators are fixed.
In response to Commissioner Bhatt, Parks, Facilities, Fleet, and Beaches Director John Rebar
explained that City Hall elevators are working properly but currently require a non-life-safety-related
repair modification to obtain a valve certificate. They have a plan in place.
Frank Garcia, Facilities Management Division Director, explained that each unit may have a minor
item that does not warrant shutting the unit down but is still a compliance-related item. One of the
challenges they face when scheduling these inspections is that multiple parties are involved, including
the Public Works Elevator Section, Fire Alarm, the vendor, and the elevator maintenance and repair
contractor used by the City. As a result, getting all parties on the same page for the inspection can
be difficult, which is why they are seeing a lag in those certificates as of late.
Commissioner Bhatt asked whether the same set of inspection requirements applied to private
condominium buildings, and Mr. Garcia confirmed that the same protocol is used for private buildings.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that the City has all the people in one building, and it is still difficult for the
City to get it done. When they conduct elevator inspections, is there a breakdown of what needs to
be fixed, how long the cure window is, and whether it is a life-safety issue? What triggers a fine?
John Norris, Public Works Director, is unsure and is trying to obtain more information from the
inspectors. Mr. Norris noted that elevator inspectors are often in precarious field conditions during
inspections, which may be why he had not yet received a response from them.
Commissioner Suarez moved for an After-the-Fact Resolution because staff do not know what is
going on either. He does not want any residents in Miami Beach to be fined for their elevators until
every single elevator operated by the municipality of Miami Beach is up to Code.
The motion was seconded by Commissioner Fernandez.
Commissioner Fernandez added that they need to lead by example. If the City itself is unable to
comply for whatever reason, how can it burden its own residents, who have access to fewer
resources, with the fines associated with this? There are ways to push for compliance without
attaching a fine.
Commissioner Bhatt agrees with the notion of leading by example. She is also concerned that fines
are used like a stick when the carrot does not work. She fears that property managers or owners of
multifamily buildings with elevators may not know, and she does not want to get into a situation where
the property owner or manager is not complying and it becomes a life-safety issue because they know
they are not going to be fined. To her, that is a slippery slope and a tricky needle to thread. She does
not want to open the floodgates to people who are not doing what is right by the residents in these
buildings.
Commissioner Suarez added that they can still issue a warning; they are just not imposing a fine. If
there is a life-safety issue and the elevator is no longer functional, they are not just issuing a fine or
a warning; they are saying not to use the elevator, which is a different matter. What he is saying is
that if the certification lapses because the board changes over or they were not following through,
there should not be a fine until all City-operated elevators are fixed, because the City should be
leading by example.
Commissioner Fernandez asked whether, when issuing these violations, they differentiate between
a life safety violation and a general maintenance violation.
John Norris, Public Works Director, confirmed Commissioner Fernandez’s statement and requested
more information on what is going on with the City Hall elevator
