items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, CALLING FOR A CITY COMMISSION WORKSHOP TO BE HELD ONCE EVERY TWO MONTHS COMMENCING MARCH 2026, AFTER 5:00 P.M., IN THE CITY COMMISSION CHAMBERS AT MIAMI BEACH CITY HALL, FOR A PILOT PERIOD OF ONE YEAR, TO ALLOW THE CITY COMMISSION TO DISCUSS SPECIFIC ISSUES, STRATEGIC GOALS, AND MAJOR PROJECTS IN A MORE INFORMAL SETTING; AND PROVIDING FOR A DR. STANLEY SUTNICK CITIZENS’ FORUM TO OBTAIN PUBLIC INPUT AT THE COMMENCEMENT OF EACH WORKSHOP.
items.action: Resolution 2026-34293 was adopted as amended. Commissioner Bhatt made a motion to adopt the Resolution with changes; seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Vote: 7-0.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34293 was adopted as amended. Commissioner Bhatt made a motion
to adopt the Resolution with changes; seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Vote: 7-0.
AMENDMENTS:
Beginning in September, the workshops would be held in the Sunshine every other month from 4:30
p.m. to 7:30 p.m. in the City Manager’s Large Conference Room, with limited staff present and no
memos prepared other than a simple list of topics to be included on the Agenda for discussion.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Office of the City Attorney and Rafael E. Granado to handle.
Commissioner Magazine stated that this is about finding ways to make government more efficient
and effective for the people. He has attended every City Commission meeting dating back ten years,
but he has always thought about ways to make their government work better for the people. A lot of
times in the City, he thinks they do things just because it is the way it has always been done, and he
has frustrations about how the process can work. One of the things Commissioner Joseph Magazine
believes is missing in the process, in some regard, is the ability to think comprehensively. What was
very difficult for him to adjust to was being unable to talk freely with his colleagues about many issues.
He thinks a lot of people do not understand that, but because of the Sunshine law, he cannot
brainstorm with his colleagues and say what is good or bad about the City. When they legislate each
month, and they all have legislative items, it is quite robust when people's business gets done, laws
get passed, Ordinances and priorities are set. He does not feel they get the collective to brainstorm
enough and think comprehensively, so they do a lot of micromanaging, but they lose the ability to just
sit there and converse, discuss, and brainstorm, where that is best served at a macro level when they
talk about a comprehensive plan for the City. They go through hundreds of Items per month, and
while they all have merit and consequences, almost every single Item heard today is on a very micro
level, a microcosm of small things happening in the City, but they do not discuss these comprehensive
plans. Residents also have two opportunities to speak to the Commission, first during Sutnick Hour,
where time is limited, and then again during public discussions, which are also conducted in a
formalized manner, where the public is allotted two minutes to speak before the discussion returns to
the Commission. The public gets two minutes to speak, and then the discussion turns to the
Commission, so it is not a formalized process. He is proposing a pilot program: a monthly Sunshine
meeting with no set Agenda. They can put Items on the agenda, but not legislation; nothing will be
passed, and it is just work in progress. They all go to so many different meetings and neighborhoods,
but this would be comprehensive, Citywide, everybody, every neighbor is welcome to attend. He
thinks they should host it, whether in City Hall or in a large community discussion room, where they
go to the community, but it would be adding another tool in their toolkit about how to conduct the
people’s business, how to think comprehensively outside the box, and how to make the government
more efficient to better work for the people. The thought is a pilot program: one evening per month
for a couple of hours to get together in the Sunshine and talk in a more informal manner, without
specific legislative Items, and to talk comprehensively. Commissioner Magazine explained that the
goal of these discussions is to consider how to make the City the best place in the world and how to
make government work better for the people they serve.
Commissioner Fernandez loves this idea. Some of the best discussions they have had as
Commissioners have not been about specific legislative action on Agenda Items; they have taken
place during a Sunshine meeting to discuss, toss around ideas, and share their concerns. He thinks
it is great. To his point, they have many Items on the Commission Agenda that address many of the
issues, but they do not have many opportunities, if any, to discuss the vision or the future, what they
want the City to be. He fully supports this and encourages it. He forgot Commissioner Magazine had
this Item on the Agenda, but recently they had an issue: they wanted to discuss an Item that had not
been referred, but was important at the Public Safety Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee
meeting. They were not able to put the Item on the Agenda because it was not referred. It was
generally the same idea. They wanted an update on something regarding one of their departments,
and just wanted to have the conversation without taking action, just talking as colleagues. When they
put their collective experience and perspective together, they can come up with some great outcomes
beyond the individual, piecemeal legislation that they all work on individually. That is a challenge.
They all work individually, but they rarely have the opportunity to come together and discuss things
as one.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas loves the idea, which is why she cosponsored the Item. She feels they
miss many good topics about the City when they sit up here because they run out of time, and this
only happens once a month. Things come up in between that they need to discuss and move on
quickly, and they do not have that opportunity.
Commissioner Magazine suggested starting meetings once a month and perhaps starting in the
summer. It does not have to be as long as the Commission meeting, so it can be held at 5:00 p.m.
Not all City staff must be present. He does not want staff to feel that everybody needs to be there at
all times. He wants to be efficient in government, so he is thinking once a month for a couple of hours
in the evening. It would be an open Sunshine session and a more effective way for people to come
and talk to them, rather than two minutes to speak during Sutnick. He is thinking of collaborative
conversations back and forth among each other and, most importantly, with staff as well.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas added that this will evolve as they start this and see what comes out
of it, but she would like to see them maybe talk about public transportation or other topics, such as
affordable housing, and just speak on one topic. Cleanliness or FIFA would have been nice to have
these prior to the event, but this is a lovely idea, and she suggested seeing where this goes. She
appreciates Commissioner Magazine bringing this and thinks it is very necessary.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez agreed that it is a good idea, but noted that meeting once a month would be
too frequent. She explained that the Commission already meets monthly, along with the Commission
Committee meetings they participate in, and regardless of whether they ask staff to attend, staff will
inevitably be involved after hours, which can be burdensome. She added that even with close friends,
she appreciates making plans, but meeting every month can become too much. She emphasized that
she loves the idea, believes it is important, and is looking forward to participating.
Commissioner Bhatt said she loves the idea and explained that when she previously served as MBU
President, she and Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas discussed holding open community
meetings to address issues in a holistic manner. Over the last two and a half years, during
Commission panels, the Commissioners have sometimes tried to have holistic discussions, but are
pulled back when the discussion is broader than the specific Item. She worries and would like to limit
staff’s obligation to attend, since they have families to care for. Maybe an idea is to pick a topic every
month and have a couple of people show up to focus on that, rather than everybody. She loves this
and would like to cosponsor with them. It is a great initiative. She clarified that no memos are being
prepared.
Commissioner Magazine thanked Commissioner Bhatt and said that if there are concerns about staff
constraints, perhaps they can hold meetings during the day one month and toward the evening the
next, or just start with bimonthly. He is not dogmatic about it. He just wants an opportunity to discuss
more freely a lot of things happening in the City. Nothing is voted on.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Nick Kallergis clarified that the Code requires that any Item to be
discussed, even at a workshop, be printed in the Agenda. It does not mean that a full memo has to
be prepared, but the Items to be discussed at that meeting would need to be included in the Agenda.
Mayor Steven Meiner explained that the Resolution, as written, provided for the workshops to be held
every other month, and he indicated that he preferred beginning with that schedule to evaluate how
it works. He suggested placing a two-hour cap on the meetings, and the Commission then discussed
possible durations, including two hours, two and a half hours, and up to three hours, with
Commissioner Joseph Magazine indicating he would be agreeable to a three-hour meeting and
offering to provide pizza for the first meeting if the time were extended. Mayor Meiner noted that six
years earlier, the Commission had routinely met until midnight, and that legislation was later adopted
requiring Commission meetings to end at 7:00 p.m. He added that having a defined time limit
encourages efficiency because everyone is aware that a clock is running, and he referenced timing
mechanisms used in sports as an example.
Mayor Meiner recommended that there be limited staff. For example, during budget meetings, the
entire department of directors is present, and he understands, but they do not want to utilize all their
department heads.
There was consensus to have only limited staff present. There was also agreement to hold these
meetings every other month. During this discussion, the Commission agreed that the workshops
would be scheduled from 4:30 p.m. to 7:30 p.m., reflecting the consensus that the meetings could
run for up to three hours.
In response to Mayor Meiner’s question, Commissioner Magazine would like to start with the City’s
urban planning and take it from there to see what works, what does not, and what changes can be
made. These discussions are critical for the City, but they do not fit into these nice boxes for
legislation. Commissioner Magazine noted that the Commission needs this type of discussion for
planning purposes, but he emphasized that he wants the opportunity for open-ended conversations
with his colleagues.
Commissioner Fernandez added that in the setting of a Sunshine meeting in the Conference Room,
where they can sit around the table, look at each other, and have that discussion, that is how
Commission Committees used to be, and that has been some of their most robust discussions. The
meetings are open to the public, minutes are taken, and it is all recorded. But there are a lot of times
they see that the dialogue changes when they are sitting in Chambers, when they are separated from
the public. They sit up here, and the public is down there, and a lot of times, people change their tone
and conversation because they are being recorded on cameras. He would suggest that they consider
that. For the public and long-term residents, they feel that sometimes meetings were more
approachable and welcoming when everyone was at the same level, the way the Commission
Committee meetings used to be. Commissioner Fernandez explained that City Clerk Granado had
been present when the Commissioners sat around the table, and residents sat around the room,
without a separation between officials and the public, which contributed to welcoming and engaging
discussions.
Commissioner Bhatt suggested using the City Manager’s Large Conference Room. She moved to
approve the Item with acceptance of the recommendations. Seconded by Commissioner Suarez.
City Clerk Rafael E. Granado announced that Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt made a motion to adopt
the Resolution as amended, which was seconded by Commissioner David Suarez. Vote: 7-0
AMENDMENTS:
The amendment provided that beginning in September, the workshops would be held in the Sunshine
every other month from 4:30 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. in the City Manager’s Large Conference Room, with
limited staff present and no memos prepared other than a simple list of topics to be discussed.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34295 was adopted. Commissioner Bhatt moved to adopt the
Resolution, seconded by Vice-Mayor Dominguez. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Chief Digna Abello and Marla Alpizar to handle.
6:41:53 p.m.
Mayor Steven Meiner called Fire Chief Digna Abello to address the Commission before proceeding
to the next agenda Item. Mayor Meiner stated that the City had experienced a loss during the past
week and noted that mental health was a central component of the circumstances. Mayor Meiner
indicated that the meeting could not continue without acknowledging what the Fire Department was
experiencing.
Fire Chief Abello explained that she had attended a funeral service a few hours earlier, where she
delivered a eulogy and participated in the burial of a friend and colleague, Hans Estrada. Fire Chief
Abello described the difficulty of fulfilling her duties as Fire Chief while also ensuring that the Fire
Department continued to serve residents and maintain public safety. She indicated that ten individuals
from the Department who had been sent to the funeral to pay their respects to their classmate had
already returned to duty and were back on their assigned apparatus. Fire Chief Abello stated that
losses of this type were becoming more common in some departments and described the situation
as one that some agencies experienced frequently. Fire Chief Abello asked those present to consider
how many colleagues within their own professions had died by suicide. She indicated that she had
experienced two such losses within two years. She stated that in the hundred-year history of the
Department, Miami-Dade County had experienced eight Firefighter suicides under the leadership of
its Fire Chief, and that another member had died approximately six months earlier. Fire Chief Abello
described the difficulty of these circumstances and referenced her roles as a leader, a member of the
Department, a parent, and a colleague. She recounted that the previous day had been her son’s
eleventh birthday and that he believed she would be at the Station for the customary birthday
acknowledgment. She explained that she arranged for her son’s godfather, who is a close friend and
colleague hired with her eighteen years earlier, to take her son to an arcade because she needed to
attend the funeral viewing and services. She described that her son initially believed she was joking
about not being at the Station and that an image she had sent earlier, which depicted members of
the Department’s C-Shift, had reinforced his assumption. Click here to view the image. She clarified
that the confusion occurred because she had briefly returned home to retrieve a jacket she had
forgotten before going to the funeral. Fire Chief Abello stated that she attended both the viewing and
the burial and that she was one of four individuals who had been present at the colleague’s residence.
She described seeing the colleague’s condition firsthand and stated that she had seen him two days
earlier when he had assisted her in removing bags from her vehicle, and that she had no indication
of his condition at that time.
Commissioner David Suarez asked why losses of this nature occurred so frequently in the firefighting
profession and how the City could provide support.
Fire Chief Abello responded that personnel in firefighting and public safety roles often had to
desensitize themselves to the events they experienced while on duty. She explained that employees
could return home after a difficult day and be required to immediately transition into parental
responsibilities without time to process what had occurred. She referenced the recent sailboat
incident and explained that the individual involved had recently been charged. She noted that
Firefighters who responded to that incident, including two who were twenty-three and twenty-four
years old with less than two years of service, might now be required to revisit the incident, review
images, and re-experience the circumstances during the investigative process. Fire Chief Abello
explained that Firefighters, Dispatchers, and other public safety personnel operated continuously,
and that the Fire Department functioned twenty-four hours a day. She noted that Dispatchers
answered emergency calls for Police, Fire, and residents, and referenced the work of public works
staff who responded to incidents such as sinkholes. She described a recent incident in which a new
Fire Engine encountered a sinkhole at three o’clock in the morning while the crew was responding to
a residence that was flooded. She described the sudden and unexpected nature of that event and its
impact on the personnel involved. Fire Chief Abello described a motorcycle accident she had
responded to during her career. She recounted seeing the condition of the injured individual, who had
sustained significant injuries, and described observing that the person had not been wearing
protective gear appropriate for riding a motorcycle. Fire Chief Abello stated that she learned four
years later of the individual’s survival during an interview with a Firefighter applicant who identified
the injured person as a family member and described that the individual had undergone medical
treatment, including amputation, and had continued riding motorcycles following the accident. Fire
Chief Abello described how cumulative traumatic exposure over many years affected the daily lives
of Firefighters. She explained that she engaged in specific habits related to situational awareness,
such as positioning herself in public spaces to face exits and planning for alternative escape routes
in an emergency. She noted that these behaviors were ingrained through years of experience. She
explained that Firefighters, Dispatchers, Ocean Rescue personnel, and Police Officers regularly
encountered traumatic situations and that their responsibilities continued without interruption
regardless of personal impact. She described how operational demands affected her ability to take
leave and stated that she frequently lost unused hours because she was unable to take time off due
to ongoing responsibilities. She referenced the challenges associated with being unable to reduce
staffing when employees call out, noting that Fire apparatus must operate with minimum personnel,
and absences often require mandatory overtime to maintain service levels. She stated that the
colleague who had passed away had given 18 years of service to the City and that she herself had
23 years of service, having been hired at age 21. She also explained that her spouse monitored the
meeting because understanding her work environment helped maintain communication at home. Fire
Chief Abello reiterated that the nature of the profession requires continuous readiness and that the
Department’s responsibilities do not end at five o’clock. She indicated that calls continued regardless
of staffing levels and that these continuous demands contributed to the challenges faced by
personnel.
Mayor Meiner acknowledged Fire Chief Abello’s comments and stated that Commissioner Tanya K.
Bhatt had an agenda Item related to the topic. Mayor Meiner indicated that the Item (R7 AB) should
be called next so that the discussion could continue.
6:51:26 p.m.
Mayor Meiner called Item R7 AB, which was sponsored by Commissioner Bhatt, and noted that the
Item was co-sponsored by Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas.
Commissioner Suarez asked for a direct response from Fire Chief Digna Abello on how the City could
better support the Department. Commissioner Suarez indicated that he wished to hear the Chief’s
response before moving into the broader discussion of proposed Item R7 AB.
Commissioner Bhatt formally called the Item and requested that the related slide be displayed. Click
here to view. Commissioner Bhatt stated that the matter had been discussed the previous year but
was not included in the final budget. She expressed deep admiration for Fire Chief Abello’s presence
at the meeting despite the personal and professional hardship the Chief was experiencing,
referencing long hours spent eulogizing, attending services, and responding to Commission
questions. Commissioner Bhatt referenced conversations with City Manager Eric Carpenter regarding
the events of the night of the loss and stated that she had met a Miami Beach resident who is a
psychiatrist at the University of Miami, with whom she had spoken about the Fire Department’s and
Police Department’s efforts in addressing mental health matters in professions where such openness
is uncommon. She described her pride in the collaborative efforts between departments, noting that
the Police Department had been involved longer but that the Fire Department, under Fire Chief
Abello’s leadership, was rapidly progressing in its mental-health and wellness initiatives.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt described learning additional details about the incident and explained
that she had been informed that Firefighter Hans Estrada was found by a close friend and by
Firefighter Estrada’s son. Commissioner Bhatt indicated that receiving this information was personally
triggering because she and her daughter had previously found her other daughter in similar
circumstances, which made the details of the incident difficult for her to hear. Commissioner Bhatt
noted that such personal impact did not relate to budget decisions but emphasized the emotional
difficulty of the subject. She cautioned against minimizing public-safety needs and expressed
frustration with individuals who questioned the necessity of equipment, facilities, or resources for
Firefighters. She explained that the absence of frequent structure fires in Miami Beach was due to
preventive actions taken by Fire Department personnel, including handling gas leaks, evacuations,
and other emergency conditions. Commissioner Bhatt described the types of traumatic situations
Firefighters encounter, including incidents such as the motorcycle case previously referenced by Fire
Chief Abello. She explained that such trauma would require years of therapy for many individuals.
She emphasized that Firefighters and Police Officers routinely experience repeated traumatic events
within short periods. Commissioner Bhatt urged the Commission to fully fund the proposed Mental
Health and Wellness Coordinator position, explaining that the City should not delay action until a
future fiscal year. She recommended utilizing General Fund reserves to implement the position
immediately and incorporate it permanently into future budgets. She stated that she did not want to
wait until another tragedy occurred and moved the Item for approval.
Mayor Meiner acknowledged the motion and requested to hear from City Manager Eric Carpenter.
City Manager Carpenter expressed appreciation to the Fire Department for its work during a difficult
period. He stated that he had committed to Fire Chief Abello that the City would take any necessary
steps to prevent additional losses. City Manager Carpenter acknowledged significant investments the
Commission had already made, including the replacement of self-contained breathing apparatus and
bunker gear. He explained that during the previous budget cycle, he and Fire Chief Abello had agreed
to fund a temporary mental-health support position with the intention of transitioning to a permanent
position in the following year. He affirmed his commitment to continue supporting that plan and
indicated that the Administration welcomed the Commission’s interest in accelerating the timeline.
City Manager Carpenter indicated that he and Fire Chief Abello would determine the required funding
mechanisms and expressed gratitude to the Commission and community for their support of the
Department.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez expressed condolences for the Department’s loss and described the current
circumstances as heartbreaking. She expressed gratitude for the Department’s service and asked
whether the proposed Mental Health and Wellness Coordinator position would be sufficient or
whether additional measures were needed.
Fire Chief Abello responded that the position would not resolve all issues but would represent
meaningful progress. Fire Chief Abello explained that Miami-Dade County had four similar positions.
She referenced a recently issued LTC concerning school behavioral health services and described
increased demand reflected in data showing significant growth from 1,370 requests to 2,522. She
referenced a personal example involving her son’s classmate, whose family had experienced the loss
of the child’s mother to suicide, and described the importance of behavioral-health support beginning
early in life. She explained that the role involved mental resiliency and emotional intelligence and that
its responsibilities extended far beyond post-traumatic stress matters. Fire Chief Abello emphasized
the importance of having an accessible resource available without fear of retribution or employment
concerns and noted that the Employee Assistance Program provided assistance on a broad range of
issues but was not a specialized resource solely for public-safety personnel. Fire Chief Abello further
explained that she had been utilizing a Police Department hostage negotiator to provide briefings and
debriefings at Fire Stations. She stressed that the program required evolution and that Firefighters,
Dispatchers, and Ocean Rescue personnel must understand the range of available resources. Fire
Chief Abello referenced the colleague who had passed away, explaining that the individual had gone
to Court on the day of the incident and had been facing profound personal challenges. She indicated
that the Proposed Mental Health and Wellness Coordinator Position would not address all needs but
would establish continuity and resilience within the program and help the Department move toward
models used by Miami-Dade County, thereby reducing reliance on outside agencies.
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas expressed condolences to Fire Chief Abello and the entire Fire
Department. She urged Fire Chief Abello to take bereavement leave and suggested that the City
request support from Miami-Dade County to temporarily staff fire operations, which would allow
members of the Fire Department to take needed time off.
Fire Chief Abello thanked the Commissioner and acknowledged the presence and support of
Commissioners David Suarez and Monica Matteo-Salinas at the events the previous evening. She
described the emotional impact experienced by Firefighters who believed they had missed signs that
could have prevented the loss.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez next addressed the Commission and Fire Chief Digna Abello. He
expressed condolences to the Fire Department and described the support shown by its members at
the funeral services for Firefighter Hans Estrada. Commissioner Fernandez referenced the qualities
attributed to Firefighter Estrada by those in attendance, including courage, compassion, and
selflessness, and acknowledged the magnitude of the loss to the Department. Commissioner
Fernandez emphasized that the incident underscored the need for continued attention to mental
health matters and encouraged employees and community members to speak up, seek assistance,
and reduce stigma. He explained that seeking help required strength and reiterated the Commission’s
commitment to supporting public safety personnel.
Mayor Meiner requested that Human Resources Director Marla Alpizar address the Commission.
Director Alpizar explained that the City maintained a comprehensive Employee Assistance Program
(EAP), available free of charge to all employees and members of their households. She described
the program as a confidential starting point for employees seeking resources to address various
personal challenges. She described the importance of interpersonal support within the workplace and
encouraged employees to check on one another. Director Alpizar also explained that health plans
available through the City and through the Police and Fire Health Trust included behavioral-health
benefits and that the City maintained a wellness program addressing overall health and resiliency.
She expressed support for expanding mental-health resources for public-safety personnel and
acknowledged the unique demands placed upon Fire and Police Department employees.
Commissioner David Suarez then addressed Fire Chief Abello and asked what actions the City could
take to support the Department.
Fire Chief Abello responded that creating a behavioral-health specialist position knowledgeable about
public-safety work would be a critical first step. She explained that such a professional would
understand the specific environment in which Firefighters operated, including the lifestyle,
expectations, and terminology. Fire Chief Abello indicated that she wished for the Police Department
to be involved collaboratively so that both departments could work together rather than in isolation.
She described her efforts to develop peer-support programs since 2014 and referenced the
Department’s emotional-support dog, Deco, who was still completing training. She stated that there
was supporting data for such programs, but explained that a dedicated full-time specialist would help
build ongoing relationships with personnel. Fire Chief Abello explained that some employees
contacted her directly for personal matters, such as relationship issues, and she emphasized the
importance of having a professional who could assume that role to avoid concerns about blurred lines
or misinterpretation of the Fire Chief’s involvement.

VOTES:

AMENDMENT:
 Waive the Convention Center 501(c)(3) requirement.
Mayor Meiner introduced the Item and stated that it concerns a request for a fee waiver of
approximately $33,000 for the Miami Business Club. He noted that representatives from the Miami
Business Club are present and available to answer questions. The Miami Business Club has become
part of the growing business ecosystem in Miami Beach and South Florida. Significant capital,
business activity, family offices, and companies in finance and technology have been moving into the
region. He noted that the Miami Business Club contributes to that environment by hosting monthly
events, generally at local Miami Beach restaurants or bars, drawing between 75 and more than 200
young professionals from throughout South Florida. He further stated that the Miami Business Club
has begun hosting Friday events and that he has attended many of the gatherings. He believes it is
important for residents and professionals moving into the area to see City leadership actively involved
in the community. He invited Stefan Lingmerth, Founder of the Miami Business Club, to provide more
information.
Stefan Lingmerth, Founder of the Miami Business Club, explained that the organization hosts monthly
events to bring together the local business community. The Miami Business Club is now seeking to
hold its inaugural annual gala at the Miami Beach Convention Center, specifically in the Sunset Vista
Room. The organization has worked with the City and determined that the Convention Center is a
beautiful venue, but very costly. The Miami Business Club is run by volunteers, does not charge
membership fees, and has a limited budget. He further stated that the organization intends to partner
with charitable organizations, including Miami Waterkeeper, and possibly a second charity. The lower
the event costs, the more funds can be directed toward charitable donations.
Mayor Meiner thanked Mr. Lingmerth and asked City Attorney Dopico to address a concern that has
arisen.
City Attorney Dopico replied that the City has learned the Convention Center’s fee-waiver policy
requires the organization to be a 501(c)(3). The Miami Business Club is a not-for-profit organization,
but does not have 501(c)(3) status with the Internal Revenue Service. If the City Commission wishes
to proceed, it could waive the 501(c)(3) requirement for this request. He further noted that staff could
later review whether an existing Resolution or policy would need to be amended for similar
circumstances in the future.
Commissioner Magazine stated that the Miami Business Club is a nonprofit entity registered in
Florida, but has not obtained Federal 501(c)(3) status. He clarified that the request is not for the City

ACTION: Resolution 2026-34298 was adopted. Commissioner Fernandez moved to adopt the
Resolution; seconded by Mayor Meiner. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes

John Rebar to handle.
Mayor Meiner thanked John Rebar and acknowledged the Lincoln Road BID. He recognized
Annabelle Llopis, who was in the audience. He noted that Lincoln Road has seen many recent
activations and that a FIFA store has recently opened, which he described as a positive addition. He
stated that walking down Lincoln Road feels robust and alive. He then asked Mr. Rebar to proceed
with the Item.
John Rebar, Parks and Recreation Director, introduced the Item and stated that it concerns extending
the City’s funding for maintenance and hospitality services provided on Lincoln Road by the Block-
by-Block company.
Commissioner Magazine asked whether the Item could be explained first for the benefit of the public.
Members of the public present here today may not know what the Item involves.
Mayor Meiner stated that this Item concerns the Second Amendment to the Lincoln Road BID
Memorandum of Understanding (MOU). He asked the Administration and the Lincoln Road BID
representative to explain the services provided under the agreement.
Annabelle Llopis, Executive Director of the Lincoln Road BID, stated that the BID and the City have
maintained an MOU since approximately 2017 as part of a partnership to support cleanliness and
hospitality services on Lincoln Road. The current service provider is Block-by-Block, which has
worked in urban districts locally and across the country. Block-by-Block serves as the eyes and ears
of Lincoln Road. Its responsibilities include identifying quality-of-life issues, assisting during incidents,
performing light cleaning, working with tenants, helping visitors, and serving as a liaison with the City.
Commissioner Magazine asked why the City does not provide those services directly.
Mr. Rebar replied that the services are provided through a partnership.
Commissioner Magazine stated that he walks along Lincoln Road every day and regularly observes
what is working, what is not, and what needs to be fixed. He expressed concern that, even during
peak season, the City is not getting the expected return on its investment despite spending significant
funds on pressure cleaning and related services. He asked who is responsible for cleaning Lincoln
Road.
Mr. Rebar replied that various City departments perform maintenance on Lincoln Road. Facilities
handles painting and repairs; Sanitation handles trash and cleaning; Greenspace assists with
landscaping and related needs; and other departments maintain fountains and public spaces. Block-
by-Block provides an additional service, similar to ambassadors, and its members can be seen on
Lincoln Road wearing their shirts and carrying pails.
Commissioner Magazine asked whether individual shop owners or businesses have any
responsibility for cleaning the public areas in front of their properties, or whether those responsibilities
fall entirely to the City and its partners.
Mr. Rebar replied that private businesses are responsible only for their own areas, while the public
right-of-way is maintained by the City and its partners.
Commissioner Magazine asked about the deep cleaning and pressure washing of Lincoln Road.
Mr. Rebar explained that the City handles heavy-duty pressure washing and that Sanitation crews
work in the area throughout the day, emptying trash and assisting with cleanup. The BID provides
litter pickup. In preparation for the World Cup, City teams recently conducted a walkthrough and are
performing deep pressure cleaning along Lincoln Road.
Commissioner Magazine stated that he wants the City Commission and staff to conduct a
walkthrough of Lincoln Road on the morning of May 21 or May 22. He stated that he walks the area
every day and does not believe the World Cup should be the catalyst for cleaning Lincoln Road to a
world-class standard. The area should be maintained at that level regardless of a major event. He
asked that a walkthrough be scheduled so staff and the City Commission can evaluate the conditions
together.
Mayor Meiner stated that this Friday morning coincides with a Jewish holiday, and stated he would
not be able to attend then, but that he could participate if the walkthrough occurs on the following
morning.
Commissioner Magazine asked whether the amendment increases funding.
City Manager Carpenter replied that the amendment incorporated a CPI increase based on the
amount agreed the previous year. The agreement remains a partnership, with both the City and the
BID funding portions of the Block-by-Block services. One of the fundamental purposes of creating a
BID is to allow the district to tax itself and contribute to enhanced services.
Commissioner Magazine stated that he understands the purpose of the BID but would like clarification
on what is being amended in the original agreement.
City Manager Carpenter replied that the amendment includes the CPI increase and extends the
agreement by an additional year.
Mayor Meiner thanked staff and the BID. The recent activations on Lincoln Road have been excellent,
including the Pink Ping Pong activation, which has drawn thousands of people. His daughter told him
about the event, and he took her to see it. The activation has been incredible.
Ms. Llopis stated that approximately 9,000 people have attended that activation. She also referenced
the Swatch event, describing it as an interesting global product drop.
Commissioner Magazine thanked Ms. Llopis for the work she has done.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas stated that she wishes to co-sponsor the Item. She explained that she
has seen the Block-by-Block employees walking along Lincoln Road, wearing their shirts, smiling,
and helping people. She described the program as great and appreciated the BID’s investment in it.
Ms. Llopis stated that the Lincoln Road BID has invested more than $221,000 per year in the program
and has covered the cost of the office space used by the Block-by-Block team. There is significant
support and contributions from the private sector, which makes the partnership successful. The
program allows the BID and City to respond more quickly to issues because Block-by-Block staff can
immediately report conditions or incidents to the BID and, when necessary, to the City. She added
that she is available on Thursday or Friday for the walkthrough.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that she believes the Block-by-Block staff have been memorialized in a
public art or storytelling project. She recalled that two of the individuals have been depicted discussing
their jobs and the work they do. In addition to providing helpful services, they have become part of
Miami Beach in a meaningful way.
Mayor Meiner thanked Ms. Llopis for working with him on this Item and the BID for its support and
hard work.
Commissioner Fernandez moved to adopt the Resolution; seconded by Mayor Meiner. Vote: 7-0.

ACTION: The hearing was held. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to remand the matter to the

the City Attorney, Thomas Mooney, and Rogelio Madan to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: No
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: No

AFTER-THE-FACT RESOLUTION 2026-34299:
A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH,
FLORIDA, REMANDING TO THE DESIGN REVIEW BOARD ("DRB"), ON A FIVE-SEVENTHS
(5/7TH) VOTE PURSUANT TO SECTION 2.2.4.8 OF THE MIAMI BEACH RESILIENCY CODE,
THE ORB'S DECISION APPROVING THE DESIGN REVIEW APPLICATION FILED BY LA GORCE
COUNTRY CLUB, INC. FOR THE CONSTRUCTION OF CERTAIN IMPROVEMENTS ON THE LA
GORCE COUNTRY CLUB CAMPUS, LOCATED AT 5685 AL TON ROAD (DRB FILE NO. 25-1104)
FOR THE LIMITED PURPOSE OF CONSIDERING THE SITING AND DESIGN OF THE
PROPOSED PADEL COURTS, UPON A FINDING THAT THE DRB DID NOT BASE ITS DECISION
REGARDING THE SITING AND DESIGN OF THE PROPOSED PADEL COURTS UPON
SUBSTANTIAL COMPETENT EVIDENCE; AND FURTHER, AFFIRMING THE DECISION OF THE
DRB IN ALL OTHER RESPECTS UPON A FINDING THAT THE DRB BASED ITS DECISION UPON
SUBSTANTIAL COMPETENT EVIDENCE, AFFORDED PROCEDURAL DUE PROCESS, AND
OBSERVED THE ESSENTIAL REQUIREMENTS OF THE LAW.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Nick Kallergis introduced Item R9 E, the Design Review Board Appeal
Number 25-11045685, filed by Mr. Gunday. Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis explained that the
appeal was first heard by the City Commission at its April 22 meeting. He indicated that the City
Commission heard oral argument from all parties during that meeting. He described that, following
a lengthy discussion, the City Commission deferred the Item to the present meeting to provide the
petitioner an opportunity to resolve the dispute with the respondent, the La Gorce Country Club.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis stated that all oral arguments had already been heard and that
the Item was properly before the City Commission for a vote. He advised the City Commission that
reversing, modifying, or remanding the Design Review Board decision required an affirmative vote
of five members; otherwise, the Design Review Board decision would stand. He further indicated
that any party aggrieved by the City Commission’s decision could file a subsequent appeal in Circuit
Court.
Commissioner David Suarez asked what would occur if no motion to affirm was made.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis explained that his recommendation was for the City Commission
to take a vote in order to allow the dispute to continue through the appropriate legal process. He
clarified that if there were no motion to affirm but a motion to reverse was made and failed, the
Design Review Board decision would remain in effect because five affirmative votes were required
for reversal.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez asked a follow-up question confirming the procedural consequences
of a failed motion to reverse.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis restated that a failed motion to reverse would result in the
Design Review Board decision being upheld.
Commissioner Suarez asked whether there was a procedural motion available requiring only four
votes, noting his recollection that five votes did not appear available to reverse, but that there might
be four votes that disagreed with the Design Review Board’s decision. He asked what course of
action the City Commission should take under those circumstances.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis stated that the parties had already presented oral argument and
had been given an opportunity to meet, and that his understanding was that no agreement had been
reached.
Commissioner Suarez asked whether the parties were allowed to speak.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis explained that appeals before the City Commission are not
evidentiary hearings. He indicated that, if the City Commission wished, he would not object to hearing
an update from the parties; however, any decision should be based solely on the record before the
Design Review Board. He advised that comments today should be limited to an update on the
parties’ discussions.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis then addressed the process used at the prior hearing and asked
whether any individuals who would provide an update needed to be sworn. He instructed individuals
to raise their right hand and administered the oath for truthful testimony.
Onur S. Gunday, Justin Alexander, and Graham Penn took the oath.
Commissioner Suarez asked whether the City Commission could hear testimony that was not new
evidence but related to what had previously occurred and whether such testimony could be
considered in the decision.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis clarified that any substantive testimony would constitute new
evidence. He stated that the only permissible comments should be limited to updates on the parties’
discussions and reiterated that the City Commission should base its decision on the Design Review
Board record.
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez asked whether the parties had communicated as previously directed
and whether any agreement had been reached. She indicated that the pending matter before the
City Commission was limited to determining whether the Design Review Board had fulfilled its
responsibilities.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis confirmed that reversing, modifying, or remanding the decision
required a five-sevenths vote and explained that such a vote must be supported by one of three
findings: that the Design Review Board failed to provide procedural due process, failed to observe
the essential requirements of the law, or issued a decision not supported by competent, substantial
evidence. He indicated that, in the absence of one of these findings, the Design Review Board’s
decision must be upheld.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez asked whether Commissioners could receive a refresher on the matter if
needed.
Commissioner David Suarez noted that the parties were willing to provide an update.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez indicated that such an update would likely be appropriate.
Graham Penn asked whether there would be a time limit for updates. He identified himself for the
record and stated that he appeared on behalf of La Gorce Country Club. He introduced the club’s
president, Peter Hochfelder, Scott Robbins from the club, and his law partner, Michael Larkin. He
described that, as previously discussed at the Office of the City Attorney with Mr. Justin Alexander,
he believed the appeal lacked merit. He explained that the club followed the City Commission’s
directive after the prior hearing and reached out to Mr. Onur S. Gunday and his counsel to discuss
potential ways to address the concerns. He indicated that the club emailed Mr. Brookes, counsel for
Mr. Gunday, to schedule a meeting and that a meeting ultimately occurred. He described the meeting
as not highly successful but stated that the club subsequently provided Mr. Gunday with a letter and,
later, a set of proposed conditions to accompany a proffer if the appeal proceeded. He indicated that
these conditions included significant revisions to the plans relating to the paddle courts and
operational changes. He stated that the response received from Mr. Gunday earlier that day
reiterated objections concerning the legality of the use, which he asserted was not an issue within
the Design Review Board’s jurisdiction or the City Commission’s scope of review. He explained that
the Planning Director had determined prior to the application’s consideration by the Design Review
Board that the use was consistent with the City Code. He stated that the club worked extensively to
develop proposed conditions intended to reduce impacts on Mr. Gunday and that these were
rejected. He concluded by asking whether the City Commission wished to receive additional
information.
Commissioner Suarez asked Mr. Penn to allow Mr. Gunday to speak.
Mr. Onur S. Gunday described that, over the prior six months, he had attempted to schedule a
meeting with representatives of La Gorce Country Club and that his attempts were unsuccessful. He
explained that he had submitted proposals to relocate the paddle courts toward the parking area and
suggested the possibility of constructing a parking structure and placing the courts adjacent to it. He
expressed concern that the proposed location next to his home would obstruct his view, noting that
the area currently consisted of open green space, and he described the planned structure as
approximately ten feet in height. He also discussed the lighting associated with the courts and the
potential impacts on adjacent residences. He asked the City Commission not to approve the Design
Review Board’s decision and to reverse it. He expressed concern that allowing the courts could lead
to additional development on the golf course. He referenced a photograph intended to depict the
current view from his residence and described the open landscape. He stated that the proposed
paddle courts constituted structures and referred to information he had presented at the previous
hearing. He also referenced historical documents containing a covenant noting “undeveloped land”
and described language appearing on surveys dating to the 1920s.
Mr. Penn objected to the introduction of new evidence, stating that the proceeding was not an
evidentiary hearing and that the record was limited to materials previously submitted to the Design
Review Board.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis stated that the City Commission’s decision must be based on
the Design Review Board record.
Commissioner Suarez asked whether a motion could be made to remand the matter to the Design
Review Board for re-review.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis explained that such a motion would require five affirmative votes
and could be made on a specific finding.
Commissioner Suarez asked whether another Design Review Board decision would return to the
City Commission or could be appealed independently.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis stated that any subsequent Design Review Board decision
could itself be appealed.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he believed a second review by the Design Review Board was
appropriate and announced his intention to make a motion.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis clarified that this would constitute a motion to remand and that
the City Commission would need to determine that one of the required findings had been met.
Commissioner Suarez asked whether the finding needed to be specified.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis stated that the Resolution would need to specify the applicable
finding.
Commissioner Suarez asked for clarification regarding the three prongs.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis restated that the City Commission could find that the Design
Review Board decision was not supported by competent, substantial evidence, that procedural due
process was not provided, or that the Board failed to follow the essential requirements of the law.
He indicated, based on the prior meeting discussion and the commissioners’ current comments, that
Commissioner Suarez’s motion related to whether the Design Review Board’s decision regarding
the location of the paddle courts was not supported by competent, substantial evidence.
Commissioner David Suarez indicated that the appropriate standard was whether the Design Review
Board met the required criteria.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Nick Kallergis responded that the motion would require a second and a
vote.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine stated that he would not support the motion. He explained that his
position was not based on agreement with the Design Review Board’s reasoning or on sympathy
toward the petitioner, but on the strict criteria governing quasi-judicial review. He observed that the
City Commission’s responsibility was not to decide whether the Board’s decision aligned with
personal preferences but whether one of the required legal findings had not been met. He stated
that, after reviewing the matter during the prior month and again at the present meeting, he did not
see any procedural deficiencies in the Design Review Board’s action and believed the Board met
the required standards.
Commissioner Suarez stated that one of the prongs for reversal involved notice requirements and
recalled discussion indicating that Mr. Gunday had not received notice. Commissioner Suarez
referenced electronic information suggesting that notice had not been provided to Mr. Gunday and
explained that the only notice presented at the hearing was a red sign on the property, which
Commissioner Suarez believed would not have been visible unless someone happened to pass by.
Commissioner Suarez suggested that this issue could potentially constitute an additional basis for
consideration under the applicable criteria.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis explained that the City Code required three forms of notice for
Land Use matters: posting on the property, mailing to owners within the required radius, and
publication. He stated that the record contained evidence that the notice was posted on the La Gorce
Country Club property, that the mailing requirement applied to properties within the designated
distance of the site, and that publication was completed. He explained that case law does not require
proof that each property owner confirmed receipt, but that proof of mailing is sufficient. He noted that
the petitioner’s property appeared on the mailing list for the Design Review Board hearing.
Commissioner Suarez stated that, based on his understanding of the applicable criteria, the first
prong involved whether the Design Review Board lacked sufficient evidence to support its decision.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis responded that this determination was for the City Commission
to make.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt stated that, based on her recollection, the prior discussion included
references to potential sound impacts on adjacent properties. She recalled that the topic was
mentioned but not extensively developed and that no sound studies were included. She expressed
uncertainty about where the reference to the absence of sound studies originated, but believed the
matter had been raised.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis explained that sound studies were not required for the Design
Review Board review.
Commissioner Bhatt noted that although sound studies were not required, the topic was discussed
and raised questions about how the Design Review Board could evaluate the location of the
proposed structures without considering impacts beyond visual effects. She stated that she believed
the issue had not been fully explored and that the Design Review Board might need to revisit the
topic. She explained that the record reflected some discussion, but she felt additional consideration
was needed.
Commissioner Suarez agreed, stating that the Design Review Board could be given another
opportunity to consider the matter, including the concerns raised about the location and the
associated impacts. He stated that sending the application back for further review would allow the
petitioner an additional opportunity to address issues and would give the Design Review Board
another chance to evaluate the matter. He described the potential impacts on the affected residence
and stated that he believed another review would be appropriate. He noted that if the Design Review
Board reached the same conclusion after revisiting the matter, the City Commission would proceed
based on that outcome.
Commissioner Fernandez requested clarification from counsel regarding any procedural or notice
defects associated with the Design Review Board’s consideration of the application. He asked
Assistant City Attorney Justin Alexander whether any procedural issues or notice defects were
present.
Assistant City Attorney Alexander explained that the petitioner asserted that notice had not been
received, but the City and applicant maintained that notice was provided based on the mailing labels
required under the Resiliency Code. He explained that the staff member responsible for preparing
the mailing labels reviewed the materials before the Item was placed on the Design Review Board
agenda, and that Mr. Onur S. Gunday’s name appeared on the mailing list.
Commissioner Fernandez requested clarification regarding the total number of required notices and
asked how many property owners should have received notice.
Assistant City Attorney Alexander responded that 480 property owners fell within the required notice
radius and that no other notice-related concerns were raised.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that he could not support remanding the matter to the Design
Review Board. He explained that the City Commission’s scope of review was limited and that,
although he understood the petitioner’s concerns, the City Commission could only act upon the
criteria established under law. He stated that remand required one of the applicable findings
involving procedural error, legal deficiency, or lack of competent, substantial evidence, and he did
not believe those findings were present. He expressed agreement with Commissioner Magazine’s
position and indicated that he could not support sending the matter back to the Board.
Commissioner David Suarez asked who serves as the decision-maker on the appeal and who
weighs factual matters, inquiring whether that role belonged to the City Commission.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Kallergis explained that the Design Review Board served as the trier of
fact, and the City Commission is the decision-maker on the appeal.

items.title: DISCUSS/TAKE ACTION: ADMINISTRATION'S CONTEMPLATED INCLUSION OF MOTORCYCLES AND MOTOR SCOOTERS IN THE RESIDENTIAL PARKING PERMIT PROGRAM (RPPP).
items.action: After-the-Fact Resolution 2026-34300 was adopted. Discussion held. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to prohibit the City Administration from imposing any scooter or motorcycle parking fees beginning in June, and Commissioner Fernandez seconded the motion. Vote: 7-0. William MacDonald to handle. DIRECTION:  Hold off on implementing the scooter-motorcycle registration program until the Commission has a full discussion and determines next steps  Do not impose any scooter or motorcycle parking fees on residents.  Administration to bring back a proposal for the Commission to consider at the next meeting. AFTER-THE-FACT RESOLUTION:
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: After-the-Fact Resolution 2026-34300 was adopted. Discussion held. Commissioner
Suarez made a motion to prohibit the City Administration from imposing any scooter or motorcycle
parking fees beginning in June, and Commissioner Fernandez seconded the motion. Vote: 7-0.
William MacDonald to handle.
DIRECTION:
 Hold off on implementing the scooter-motorcycle registration program until the Commission has
a full discussion and determines next steps
 Do not impose any scooter or motorcycle parking fees on residents.
 Administration to bring back a proposal for the Commission to consider at the next meeting.
AFTER-THE-FACT RESOLUTION:
Commissioner Suarez was briefed that the City Administration was unilaterally considering scooter-
motorcycle permit fees without placing the proposed fees on the Agenda for the seven members of
the Commission to vote on. He does not consider this an operational issue; it is a new fee, and he
does not think the City Administration should unilaterally apply fees to residents. He understands the
need to gather data on where there are more scooters throughout the City; however, that should not
require a fee or a permit. The City Administration can do that without imposing new fees. He asked
the City Manager whether this program is still contemplated by City staff.
City Manager Carpenter indicated that he would welcome the Parking Director to add any additional
information. The City Manager added that the program is scheduled to roll out on June 1st. His
understanding is that the existing Parking Ordinances allow this to be implemented, and, based on
the Parking Department's recommendations, they felt this would help address some of the challenges
they have been facing with motorcycle and scooter parking. He welcomed the Parking Director to add
any comments.
Commissioner Suarez has a big problem with the Administration imposing fees on residents without
their input. At a minimum, that should never happen unless it is placed on the Agenda by the City
Commission for elected officials to decide. City Administration should not impose fees.
Commissioner Fernandez thanked the Mayor and told Commissioner Suarez that he agreed with him
100 percent.”
Commissioner Suarez added that, respectfully, the City Administration is completely out of line on
this. Second, scooters and motorcycles are more efficient when it comes to parking. Seven or ten
scooters and motorcycles can fit in a single spot for a car. He understands that there are a lot of
challenges when a scooter or bike is left in the middle and does prevent anyone else from parking,
but they can address that easily with dedicated scooter parking spaces and an Ordinance for
motorcycle parking designated spots that do not take up a whole lane. At the very minimum, he is
wholeheartedly opposed to the City Administration imposing fees on residents and unilaterally ending
a tradition that encourages smaller transportation devices in the City by providing parking
infrastructure. They do not want to make it harder, but easier. He wants to see how his colleagues
feel about this and whether they can accomplish its intent without raising fees or creating a
bureaucratic process to obtain a permit for some of these transportation devices.
Commissioner Fernandez agreed with Commissioner Suarez 100%. He has a Citywide motorcycle
decal on his motorcycle, and it costs approximately $134 per year. For those who purchase that, if
they live in a residential zone, they are probably already purchasing it to park in one of these metered
spaces. When a person goes in and buys the Citywide motorcycle pass, it should also include, as
part of that, the residential zone that they live in. Maybe that is something that can be done, and they
can park in those designated motorcycle or scooter areas so that people are not parking a scooter or
motorcycle in a full parking space that could be used by a vehicle. They would still direct people to
scooter or motorcycle, but not add the fee. People are already registering their motorcycles with the
City through this annual pass, and maybe when they buy the pass, they also include, as part of that,
the residential zone that they live in. Is that possible?
William MacDonald, Parking Director, stated that it is 100% possible and that they fully support it.
Commissioner Suarez does not want the City Administration to impose the fee.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, added that they are open to a free, straightforward way of registering
vehicles so they know who has what.
Commissioner Fernandez added that his point is that even when something is not fee-free, any fee
to be imposed on the residents and taxpayers of the City of Miami Beach should be considered,
debated, voted on, and approved by those elected by the residents, not by the City Administration.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, welcomed the City Attorney to explain what the Ordinance allows and
what it does not.
Commissioner Suarez does not think they should impose any fees before a discussion occurs, so
where does that leave them right now? He would make a motion to prohibit the City Administration
from imposing a scooter parking fee for residents starting in June.
In response to Commissioner Bhatt, William MacDonald, Parking Director, noted that, by best
practice, registration, especially in residential zones, is the preferred approach. Under the Ordinance,
the term covers automobiles, motor vehicles, and motorcycles, and under Florida Statute,
motorcycles are already included within the definition of automobiles and motor vehicles. He
explained that previous directors focused on sustainability efforts by choosing not to require
registration for motor scooters inside residential zones. The challenge he has faced over the last year
is that, without registration, control is impossible. If registration is not required, and places like
Flamingo Park can see 25 scooters lined up in a row, it is impossible to tell whether they are workers
going to the Entertainment District or residents, because registration is not required.
Commissioner Suarez asked to consider a dedicated parking spot for scooters and motorcycles and
to pass an Ordinance stating that motorcycles or scooters cannot park in regular motor vehicle
parking spots.
William MacDonald, Parking Director, continued that when he first got here, the team had started
painting those spaces in certain areas of the City. The challenge was that, because there was no
control, if somebody was parked outside, they had no way of knowing whether the people were
residents or supposed to be there. They hope that registering two-wheel vehicles will provide the data
needed to know that 15 two-wheel vehicles exist on the block, so they can create a space that aligns
with residents’ needs and avoid taking up unnecessary space by blindly going out and painting a
motorcycle or scooter parking stall, which takes away from vehicle parking.
Commissioner Suarez added that it would be part of the Parking Department’s job to know where the
hot spots are. He cannot imagine that there are no more than a few hot spots with insufficient scooter
parking in the designated areas. It seems too much of a shock and too much of an approach to require
a fee and make everyone registered because of a few problems here and there.
Mayor Meiner added that there is consensus against charging a fee.
Commissioner Suarez clarified that in South of Fifth, there are plenty of spots where motorcycles park
in regular parking spaces when they should be parking in the scooter zone, and there is plenty of
parking in the scooter zone. They just choose to do that. Does that require a City Commission
Ordinance for that to happen?
William MacDonald, Parking Director, stated that it does not, but his only request is that if these
scooter zones become unregistered areas, so any scooter can park in any residential zone within the
scooter areas, and if that displaces a resident and then a resident is cited for not parking in a scooter
zone, it becomes an enforcement challenge.
Eric Carpenter, City Manager, committed not to charge any fees.
Mayor Meiner suggested that staff come up with a proposal to consider at the next meeting.
The City Manager explained that they would hold off on implementing the program until the
Commission has had a robust conversation and determines the appropriate next step.
Commissioner Suarez made a motion to prohibit the City Administration from imposing any scooter
or motorcycle parking fees beginning in June, and Commissioner Fernandez seconded the motion.
Vote: 7-0.
items.motion: Suarez made a motion to prohibit the City Administration from imposing any scooter or motorcycle parking fees beginning in June, and Commissioner Fernandez seconded the motion.
