items.title: DISCUSS/TAKE ACTION – ADVANCING A COMPREHENSIVE CITYWIDE WATER TAXI PROGRAM TO IMPROVE MOBILITY AND CONNECTIVITY.
items.action: Discussion held and direction given. Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Jose Gonzalez to handle. DIRECTION:  Review different options for advancing the water taxi program and return to the City Commission with those options, including associated costs.  Evaluate the feasibility of hiring a lobbyist who specializes in Miami-Dade County government, specifically to support funding efforts for the water taxi program.  Continue drilling down into the KPFF and TPO feasibility studies, including detailed evaluation of each proposed dock location, required improvements, and estimated construction costs.  Prepare the detailed feasibility and cost information in time for consideration during the Fiscal Year 2027 budget process.  Prepare for future expansion by ensuring that potential landing sites are identified, permitting requirements are understood, and documentation is ready so that the City can move quickly if funding becomes available.
items.voteBasis: No separate vote identified. A vote has not been inferred.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Discussion held and direction given. Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if
received. Jose Gonzalez to handle.
DIRECTION:
 Review different options for advancing the water taxi program and return to the City Commission
with those options, including associated costs.
 Evaluate the feasibility of hiring a lobbyist who specializes in Miami-Dade County government,
specifically to support funding efforts for the water taxi program.
 Continue drilling down into the KPFF and TPO feasibility studies, including detailed evaluation
of each proposed dock location, required improvements, and estimated construction costs.
 Prepare the detailed feasibility and cost information in time for consideration during the Fiscal
Year 2027 budget process.
 Prepare for future expansion by ensuring that potential landing sites are identified, permitting
requirements are understood, and documentation is ready so that the City can move quickly if
funding becomes available.
Mayor Steven Meiner thanked Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez and Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt and
noted that the Item had universal support among the City Commission. He thanked Jose Gonzalez
for his work on the water taxi program over the past several years and stated that the service has
been an incredible success. He noted that the water taxi currently operates free of charge on
weekdays, running between Maurice Gibb Memorial Park and the Venetian Marina, and that the
program has received widespread attention from the State, Miami-Dade County, the Downtown
Development Authority, and the Transportation Planning Organization (TPO). He explained that he
brought the Item forward because Mr. Gonzalez has been actively working to secure funding to
expand service, including adding weekend operations and increasing service frequency. He stated
that the service currently runs once per hour for 12 hours each day, increasing to every 30 minutes
beginning at 4:30 p.m., and that the goal is to achieve 30-minute service throughout the day. He also
described ongoing efforts to expand the number of pick-up and drop-off points, including potential
locations in the South of Fifth (SoFi) neighborhood, North Beach, Mount Sinai Medical Center, the
Kaseya Center, and locations along the City’s north–south corridor. He stated that the ability for
residents to board at locations such as 81st Street or 87th Street and travel through Mid-Beach or
South Beach would significantly improve connectivity. He requested an update from Mr. Gonzalez
and noted that obtaining funding can be challenging, but opportunities exist through outside agencies
and potential private partnerships.
Transportation and Mobility Director Jose Gonzalez thanked Mayor Meiner and stated that staff was
excited about the water taxi as the newest addition to the City’s transportation portfolio. He reported
that average daily ridership is approximately 1,000 passengers per day and that ridership began at
approximately 800 passengers before increasing to current levels. He explained that staff is working
on multiple fronts, including maintaining the current service and exploring expansion opportunities.
He noted that the service operates between Maurice Gibb Memorial Park and the Venetian Marina.
He stated that at Maurice Gibb Memorial Park, construction challenges are expected as the Marine
Patrol building is scheduled for reconstruction, and construction impacts will continue for several
months, possibly up to one year. He explained that staff is working with the contractor to identify the
best location for passenger amenities, including an upgraded restroom facility with ADA accessibility,
to replace the existing portable units. He noted that the identified location is within the parking lot.
In response to Mayor Meiner, Mr. Gonzalez stated that the primary constraint on expanding service
is funding. He explained that a second vessel could operate throughout the day if additional funding
were available; however, due to existing budget limitations, the service operates with a single vessel
for most of the day and adds a second vessel at 4:30 p.m. to accommodate peak-hour demand until
approximately 7:30 p.m. He stated that, to maintain the current funding structure of 50 percent from
the Florida Department of Transportation and 50 percent from City funds, staff has reapplied for
assistance through the FDOT Public Transit Service Development Program, which funds up to 50
percent of annual operations and maintenance for up to three years. He stated that the program is
approaching its third year in the upcoming fiscal cycle and that the City has applied for Fiscal Year
2028 funding for half of the total cost of operating the service. He reported that the total cost of the
service is approximately $1.5 million. He noted interest from Miami-Dade County and the
Transportation Planning Organization (TPO), but explained that some stakeholders believe the City
should charge a fare to help subsidize the operating cost.
Mayor Steven Meiner stated that he and Commissioner David Suarez recently presented the water
taxi program at the Transportation Planning Organization (TPO) meeting, where there was some
disagreement from several Miami-Dade County Commissioners. He noted that County
Commissioner Lopez supported the City’s position that the service should remain free. Mayor Meiner
asked whether there was anything the City Commission could do collectively, such as adopting
additional Resolutions directed to specific agencies, to further enhance funding opportunities.
Transportation and Mobility Director Jose Gonzalez explained that several City Commission
resolutions had already been adopted and transmitted to the Florida Department of Transportation,
Miami-Dade County, the Transportation Planning Organization (TPO), and the Citizens’ Independent
Transportation Trust. He stated that the City had asked those agencies primarily for financial support.
Mayor Meiner noted that the service has been extremely successful, with approximately 8% of
passengers turned away due to capacity limits. He stated that he had recently visited the water taxi
with his family, and they were unable to board, demonstrating the level of demand. He explained
that the vessel has a maximum capacity of fifty-five passengers. He added that the program provides
an efficient way to cross Biscayne Bay in approximately 18 minutes and that it is impressive to
residents when they learn that the City has offered weekday service for nearly a year at a cost of
approximately $1.2 million. He described the program as an efficient, scenic, and enjoyable
transportation option.
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas stated that it was an excellent Item and requested to be added
as a co-sponsor. She stated that the City could explore private sponsorship opportunities, such as
advertising inside the water taxi or promotional partnerships with local businesses. She noted that
brands might seek exposure due to the volume of ridership, which is approximately 1,000
passengers per day. She asked which department would manage potential sponsorship activities.
City Manager Eric Carpenter replied that both the Transportation and Mobility Department and the
Marketing and Communications Department would be involved. He stated that the Transportation
team has significant experience working with advertisers through bus shelter contracts and static
signage, and that both departments work collaboratively to identify strategies to increase revenue.
Director of Marketing and Communications Melissa Berthier added that staff had spoken with
Outfront Media about potential advertising opportunities, but Outfront expressed limited interest
because current ridership volume was not yet sufficient for their business model.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt stated that this illustrated the challenge and that the City should seek
partners who understand the long-term value of joining the program early, as ridership continues to
grow. She stated that Outfront may not be the appropriate partner at this stage.
Commissioner Suarez stated that Mayor Meiner had witnessed the concerns raised by County
Commissioners at the TPO meeting and that there appears to be support from Miami-Dade County
for the program. He explained that one concern raised by the County was that, if they were to request
funding from the State, there must be evidence that the City is attempting to make the program
financially sustainable. He stated that this could involve considering a small fare, possibly one dollar,
which might help in expanding routes. He added that while he understands that free transportation
increases ridership, introducing a minimal fare could potentially open new funding opportunities and
allow for expansion of service.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt stated that the concept of charging different rates for tourists and
commuters was an interesting approach and that a monthly pass could also be considered. She
noted that many members of the Commission were working to identify private funding sources and
stated that she was working with one of the City’s major employers on this effort. She added that the
upcoming Blue Zones initiative could help secure funding because it addresses major quality-of-life
issues and could expand the City’s access to grants, private philanthropy, and underwriting. She
stated that she would be interested in determining whether private funding could be secured first in
an effort to keep the service free, or in exploring multiple strategies concurrently before making a
decision. She expressed enthusiasm about extending the service north and south and noted that
discussions had occurred regarding potential landing sites from 71st Street down to the Miami Beach
Marina. She explained that the City should not wait for funding to be finalized before beginning the
preparatory work needed for expansion. She stated that sites should be identified, costs understood,
and permit applications prepared so the City can move forward quickly once funding is obtained.
She emphasized the need to avoid delays that could add years to the permitting process. She
acknowledged staffing limitations but stressed the importance of planning in advance to avoid being
unprepared if funding becomes available. She asked about bicycle and e-scooter access, and Jose
Gonzalez confirmed they are allowed, with a limit of four devices per trip due to capacity constraints.
Commissioner Bhatt added that as the service becomes more commuter-oriented, and with
Commissioner Lopez working to identify parking options on the Miami side, the City should consider
strategies to support last-mile connectivity. She suggested that during peak hours, the City could
evaluate whether fewer passengers or additional vessels could be deployed so that more bicycles
and e-devices could be accommodated, allowing commuters to use the water taxi as a reliable
transportation option. She described the initiative as excellent.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine thanked Mayor Steven Meiner for his leadership and asked City
Clerk Rafael E. Granado to add him as a co-sponsor. He stated that with respect to charging fares,
and without full knowledge of the funding discussions at the Transportation Planning Organization
(TPO), he believed that to qualify for Federal or State funding, the City may need to demonstrate
progress toward making the program self-sustaining. He referenced an interview he heard earlier in
the day in which the value of free services was discussed and noted that charging a small, symbolic
fee may not generate meaningful revenue but could reduce ridership. He explained that the decision
would be whether to implement a substantial fare intended to move toward sustainability or keep the
service free.
Mayor Meiner stated that in the past, the City had attempted water transit services operated by
private companies, which he opposed because they charged high fares and failed to attract riders.
He stated that although there may be an opportunity in the future to introduce a minimal charge, the
current program is still in its early stages, ridership continues to increase, and there is strong
community enthusiasm. He emphasized the importance of removing cars from City roads and
described the water taxi as an efficient transportation alternative. He stated that South Florida is in
a “Code Red” condition for congestion, and while major infrastructure projects such as Baylink would
cost over $1 billion and take years to complete, the water taxi provides weekday service for
approximately $1 million per year. He added that for $10 to $20 million, a full network could be
developed. He stated that the cost is nominal compared to other transportation proposals and noted
that significant funding discussions are underway. He stated that he has engaged with members of
Congress regarding Federal funding, but that Federal agencies have wanted to see demonstrated
success before providing grants. He stated that the program now has the ridership performance
necessary to support future applications. He added that he brought the Item forward because the
entire Commission supports the program, and the City must continue moving it forward together.
Transportation and Mobility Director Jose Gonzalez explained that staff had discussions with a
representative from the Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) and that one of the key points
learned, as previously referenced by Mayor Steven Meiner, is that in order to apply for Federal
funding, the City must demonstrate program success and must also show due diligence regarding
dock locations and associated costs. He stated that staff is currently working on this effort by taking
the initial feasibility study prepared by KPFF, a national water taxi consultant, and conducting a more
detailed analysis. He noted that the Mayor’s Item lists several potential landing sites, all of which
appear in either the KPFF feasibility study or the Transportation Planning Organization (TPO)
feasibility study. He stated that those studies are high-level assessments and that staff must now
evaluate each location to determine feasibility and the cost of constructing a dock at each site. He
explained that completing this work will better position the City to apply for capital funds through
FIND and the Federal Transit Administration. In response to Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt, he stated
that staff is currently in the scoping phase and does not yet have detailed cost estimates, and that
additional funding may be required to proceed to the next phase of evaluation.
Commissioner Bhatt requested that the information be available for consideration during the Fiscal
Year 2027 budget process. Jose Gonzalez to handle.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez stated that free transportation services tend to be successful. He
noted that Metrorail has seen strong success because it is fare-free and that municipal trolley
systems throughout the region are successful in large part because they do not charge riders. He
added that the current water taxi service's success is attributable to its fare-free nature and
expressed concern that imposing a user fee could reduce ridership and undermine the program's
viability. He recommended that the City consider hiring a lobbyist who specializes in Miami-Dade
County government to focus on advancing funding opportunities for the water taxi program, which
he described as a transformative and cost-efficient mode of transportation compared to other
proposed options.
Mayor Meiner agreed with the suggestion and directed the City Manager to return with a proposal.
Christina Baguer to handle.
City Manager Eric Carpenter stated that staff would review the concept, evaluate what approach
makes sense, and ensure that any effort produces more financial benefit than cost.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine stated that he supported Commissioner Alex Fernandez’s
suggestion regarding the potential hiring of a lobbyist who specializes in Miami-Dade County
government to assist with advancing funding efforts for the water taxi program. He remarked that,
despite the number of lobbyists who regularly appear before the City, none undertake efforts
specifically for the benefit of the community or the City in which they live and work. He noted that
this was an important point to consider as they evaluate strategies to secure funding and support for
the program. Additional discussion followed regarding the potential cost of hiring a lobbyist, the need
to evaluate available options, and the importance of ensuring that any such effort would provide
meaningful value to the City.
Mayor Meiner agreed and stated that various approaches could be explored. He added that he
appreciated Commissioner Fernandez raising the issue because it highlights the need to evaluate
potential strategies. He stated that the primary concern is the amount the City would be required to
spend on such efforts.
City Manager Carpenter stated that staff would review different options and return with
recommendations.

items.title: REFERRAL TO THE FINANCE AND ECONOMIC RESILIENCY COMMITTEE A DISCUSSION OF A PROPOSED NEW AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE CITY AND SODEXO LIVE! FOR FOOD AND BEVERAGE MANAGEMENT SERVICES FOR THE MIAMI BEACH CONVENTION CENTER AND CAMPUS.
items.action: No action was taken. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by Mayor Meiner. The Item will be placed on the July 22, 2026 Commission Meeting. Lilia Cardillo to place the Item on the agenda.
items.voteBasis: No separate vote identified. A vote has not been inferred.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: No action was taken. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by Mayor
Meiner. The Item will be placed on the July 22, 2026 Commission Meeting. Lilia Cardillo to place
the Item on the agenda.
Mayor Meiner remarked that he separated the Item from the Consent Agenda and noted that he
intended to do something he did not believe he had ever done. He asked the Commission not to
approve the referral. He acknowledged there were three sponsors and co-sponsors, yet felt certain
information was important to place on the record. He stated that Sodexo does an outstanding job
serving convention customers. The problem, he explained, is that the Convention Center remains
empty at night and on weekends, and many nonprofits would like to utilize the space for annual
charity dinners and other events during those unused periods. He emphasized that any scheduled
convention would, of course, take priority. Mayor Meiner explained that residents could also use
the space for weddings, which occurs only to a limited extent. He stated that each time such events
are proposed, the City encounters substantial obstacles because of Sodexo’s extremely high costs.
He expressed frustration, noting that he had brought an Item forward several years ago, but the
issue extended beyond any particular Item. He stated that he had repeatedly urged Sodexo to
establish a rate that could reasonably serve residents and nonprofits. He referenced the Miami
Business Club, recalling that the City had recently authorized a gala at the Convention Center. He
noted that the organization was experiencing major challenges with Sodexo and explained that the
Commission would hear directly from the Miami Business Club. Mayor Meiner stated that he had
met with Sodexo on multiple occasions, with City Manager Carpenter present at those meetings.
He said that a significant nonprofit, Bikur Cholim of Miami Beach, conducts exceptional work
assisting families of patients at Mount Sinai Hospital and had long wished to host its 600-to-700-
person dinner at the Convention Center. Yet, despite being a Miami Beach-based organization
overwhelmingly attended by Miami Beach residents, they could not do so because the fees were
prohibitive. He stated that a few weddings and events had been held at the Convention Center, but
only after persistent advocacy. He described the recurring struggles he and City Manager Carpenter
experienced when trying to assist residents and nonprofits. He added that if Sodexo felt such events
were not profitable, they should allow other caterers. However, the contract gives Sodexo full
authority over Convention Center food services. He expressed surprise that Sodexo was seeking
approval of the Item given his longstanding concerns. He stated that Sodexo had asked him to
sponsor the Item, and he had declined due to his frustration, despite recognizing that Sodexo is a
good provider. He called the situation a disservice to residents.
Commissioner Magazine noted that the Mayor’s comments aligned with concerns he had heard for
years. He stated that nonprofits hosting events for low-income children had struggled with Sodexo’s
pricing, even when seeking low-cost options such as chicken fingers. He added that high-profile
events faced the opposite challenge when trying to create luxury or VIP experiences that Sodexo
could not accommodate, while the contract prevented bringing in outside operators capable of
meeting those expectations. Commissioner Magazine said he was comfortable slowing the referral
to allow discussion, acknowledging that he did not believe the Mayor intended to pivot away from
Sodexo entirely. Instead, he hoped Sodexo would address these long-standing concerns. He stated
that he welcomed efforts to thread the needle in a way that preserved Sodexo’s strengths while
resolving recurring issues reported by various organizations.
Mayor Meiner responded that Sodexo generally does a good job. He emphasized that his objections
were focused on contract structure rather than performance. He reiterated that the City was doing
a disservice to nonprofits, charities, and residents who wished to utilize the taxpayer-funded
Convention Center but could not afford Sodexo’s prices. He explained that residents seeking to
host weddings at the venue often ended up in Sunny Isles or elsewhere because of cost barriers.
He stated that this hindered community access to a public facility the City invested heavily in
improving.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Fernandez stated that Sodexo performs exceptionally well for major conventions at
the Miami Beach Convention Center. He praised the food quality, service, and staff engagement,
noting that many employees are local residents. He said that he is always confident in the quality
of meals served at the venue, which had not always been the case in the past. He added that large
events benefit from Sodexo’s strengths and that the quality aligns with the significant investment
the City made in renovating the Convention Center. Commissioner Fernandez expressed sensitivity
to the Mayor’s concerns. He said that the Convention Center, built with taxpayer dollars, should be
accessible not only for usage but also affordability. He suggested exploring whether Sodexo might
allow an opt-out provision for smaller, community-focused events or whether such events could be
segregated from the contract, especially since they are not Sodexo’s primary revenue generators.
He stated that large conventions are Sodexo’s focus, but during slower periods, flexibility could
benefit local nonprofits or residents wishing to host weddings. He said that pricing flexibility for local
organizations or carving out smaller events from the contract could preserve Sodexo’s core
strengths. He added that Style Saves, a nonprofit providing school supplies to underprivileged
children, previously attempted to bring in donated food but could not due to strict contract
requirements. He emphasized that while Sodexo produces excellent food, its high-quality pricing
makes smaller charitable events financially unrealistic under the current structure. He expressed
willingness to explore improvements that would allow community groups to afford food services
during slow seasons.
Mayor Meiner thanked Commissioner Fernandez and then invited Miami Business Club
representative Nataliia Onyskiv to speak.
Ms. Onyskiv expressed appreciation for the City’s approval of a thirty-three-thousand-dollar fee
waiver at the previous meeting. She stated that the Miami Business Club was working to host a
charity gala on October 10, 2026, in the Sunset Vista Room at the Convention Center, benefiting
Miami Waterkeeper. She explained that the organization partnered with the City of Miami Beach to
support a local environmental cause focused on maintaining clean waterways. Ms. Onyskiv stated
that when the organization agreed to hold the event, it did not realize that, on top of a thirty-
thousand-dollar minimum spend required by the exclusive catering vendor, it would be unable to
meet that threshold due to pricing. She explained that menu costs were significantly higher than
expected once mandatory service charges and sales tax were added. She noted that the service
charge was twenty-four percent, followed by a nine percent sales tax. She provided calculations to
illustrate the issue. A fifty-dollar chicken entrée, including salad and dessert, cost approximately
seventy dollars after the service charge and tax. A ninety-dollar filet mignon entrée increased to
roughly one hundred twenty-two dollars per guest once those fees were applied. She stated that a
bottle of La Marca Prosecco retailing for under twenty dollars cost nearly sixty-eight dollars under
Sodexo’s pricing, and a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc approached eighty-eight dollars. She added that
comparable high-end Miami restaurants, despite operating full-service establishments with higher
overhead, charged similar or lower prices. She emphasized that Sodexo charged premium rates,
then added substantial service charges and tax on top. Ms. Onyskiv stated that the surcharge
structure added further complications. Sodexo imposed a fifteen percent surcharge if orders were
finalized within thirty days of the event and twenty percent if finalized within seven days. At the
same time, it required one hundred percent prepayment thirty days before the event. She explained
that most galas finalize attendance during the final month, meaning organizers were required to
pay in full before knowing the final guest count, while also facing surcharges for adjustments. She
said this created substantial risk and made planning difficult. She noted that these costs undermined
the benefit of the City’s venue waiver, because food and beverage costs quickly exceeded fifty-four
thousand dollars for five hundred attendees. Adding wine service brought costs above sixty-three
thousand dollars, nearly double the City’s waiver. She stated that Sodexo’s structure made the
Convention Center financially inaccessible for charity galas and other nonprofit events. With no
.June 24, 2026
alternative catering options and no competitive bidding, organizers had no choice but to accept the
pricing. She explained that this challenged not only her organization’s event but also the ability of
nonprofits, community groups, and local organizations to host events at the Convention Center.
Mayor Meiner thanked Ms. Onyskiv for her remarks.
Doug Connor, Senior Vice President of Sodexo Live, addressed the Commission and stated that
he and his team had held multiple conversations regarding the concerns raised. He said that
Sodexo had agreed to provide food and beverage at cost for 501(c)(3) charity events at the
Convention Center once the agreement moved forward. He affirmed that this would be Sodexo’s
position.
Mayor Meiner asked whether Sodexo had notified the Miami Business Club of this commitment.
Mr. Connor replied that they had not, explaining that he was unaware the organization had been
meeting with Maria.
Ms. Onyskiv responded that she had spoken with two members of the Sodexo team and believed
there had been a misunderstanding about communication. She attempted to clarify the sequence
of conversations and the information her organization had received. As she began to clarify the
sequence of conversations, Mayor Meiner redirected the discussion, back to the Item.
Mr. Connor stated that he, Andy, Wendy, and Ms. Onyskiv could meet after the Commission
meeting to resolve the issue.
Mayor Meiner responded that the matter could not be solved simply through a post-meeting
discussion, adding that the issue had repeatedly surfaced over the years. He stated that although
he did not wish to raise the matter in this forum, he felt it was the only way to compel Sodexo’s
attention.
Mr. Connor said he understood. He noted that Sodexo had also agreed to provide local residents
with a twenty percent discount off menu pricing and would provide that commitment in writing to the
Commission later that day. He said Sodexo wanted to support the community fully, agreed that
residents should have access to the Convention Center during dark periods, and supported its
involvement in community and charitable activities. He stated that Sodexo was one hundred percent
aligned with that position.
Mayor Meiner stated that he would not negotiate the matter during the meeting. He explained that
discussions would continue through the City Manager and that the Item would return next month
once Sodexo presented its proposal.
Mr. Connor thanked the Commission for the opportunity to continue working toward a solution.
Commissioner Fernandez added that the Sodexo’s team was excellent and consistently delivered
quality service. He reiterated that small nonprofits faced different financial realities than major
conventions such as Art Basel. He stated that Style Saves, for example, had previously attempted
to bring in donated food but could not because of the contract. He said that while the quality of
Sodexo’s food is high, smaller community organizations cannot afford it. He suggested exploring
flexibility that would allow donated food for events such as school supply distributions, noting that
children’s events with donated pizza should not face obstacles.
.June 24, 2026
Mr. Connor responded that Sodexo had already accommodated Style Saves in past years by
donating water and labor, and that Sodexo was happy to continue doing so. He said this was not
an issue.
Steven Anthony stated that the matter before the Commission was simply a referral to the Finance
and Economic Resiliency Committee, and that all issues raised during the discussion would still
need to be negotiated and voted on at a later time.
Mayor Meiner responded, asking Mr. Anthony to allow him to run the meeting. He noted that he
understood the procedural point but was not calling the Item for a referral vote.

1. DISCUSS LDR AMENDMENTS PERTAINING TO THE WASHINGTON AVENUE

Commission for First Reading with the following recommendations: a. The maximum unit

number of residential units eligible for the proposed incentives shall be provided. The LUSC
discussed a cap of 250 units and directed the Administration to provide a recommendation
for First Reading. c. The minimum lot size for eligible developments within the incentive area
will be reduced from 13,000 square feet to 6,500 square feet. d. New developments eligible
for the proposed incentives will not be permitted to obtain zone-2 on-street parking permits.

ACTION: The Resolution was not adopted; instead, the Commission approved a dual referral
to the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee and the Finance and
Economic Resiliency Committee. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas. Motion made by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas to dually
refer the Item to the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee and the Finance
and Economic Resiliency Committee, seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 7-0. Mark
Taxis to place on the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee pending
list. Jason Greene to place on the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee pending list.
David Gomez to handle.
Clerk’s Note: The Item shall first be heard by the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life
Committee, and thereafter by the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee, before returning to
the City Commission.”
.June 24, 2026
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas explained to her colleagues that she separated the Item from
the Consent Agenda to refer it to the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee.
She believes the Commission can do better with this. The Holocaust Museum, which just opened,
needs more parking, as does the Botanical Garden. She stated that she has a couple of ideas for
a solution and would like to discuss them further at the Committee. Commissioner Matteo-Salinas
motioned to refer the Item to the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee,
seconded by Commissioner Alex Fernandez.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine stated that although he is not always able to attend Committee
meetings, he is firmly opposed to removing green space or trees to make way for additional
concrete.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas asked David Gomez about cost reduction.
David Gomez, CIP Director, explained that there is an option they are exploring that would change
the layout in a way that the County had previously indicated it would not approve; however, staff
recently received indications that the County may be willing to reconsider.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas responded that, given those circumstances, she would like to
discuss it further in Committee.
Commissioner David Suarez emphasized that the Item carries financial implications and raised the
question of whether it should also be referred to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that he believes the issue also has quality-of-life and
neighborhood implications. There is a general parking issue, especially around the Botanical
Garden, the Chamber of Commerce, and neighboring residential buildings, with residents
complaining about the lack of parking in the area. He explained to Commissioner Suarez that he
understands there are financial implications.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas explained to her colleagues that she knows of a private funder,
Norman Braman, who is willing to help fund the project.
Commissioner Suarez reemphasized the idea that there are financial implications.
Mayor Steven Meiner asked Commissioner Suarez whether he meant that, in addition to the Public
Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee, the Commission should refer the matter to the
Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee.
Commissioner Suarez affirmed and asked whether there would be any financial costs to the City.
Mayor Meiner suggested waiting to see what the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life
Committee recommends.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Suarez asked whether, when it is sent back to the Commission, it will then have to
be sent back to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee.
Commissioner Bhatt suggested that the Commission could make a dual referral to both
Committees.
Commissioner Fernandez asked whether they could make a motion to refer the Item to the Public
Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee and then have that outcome referred to the
Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee. He explained that this would be similar to the
Commission’s process for LDR Amendments, which are first referred to the Land Use and
Sustainability Committee before proceeding to the Planning Board.
City Attorney Ricardo J. Dopico advised that the Commission may issue a dual referral and allow
the Chair of the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee to determine whether the Item
requires a hearing.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that he would like the Item to first go to the Public Safety and
Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee and then to the Finance and Economic Resiliency
Committee before it is heard again by the Commission.
Mayor Meiner asked Commissioner Magazine whether he agreed with that.
Commissioner Magazine agreed.
Motion made by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas to refer the Item to the Public Safety and
Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee and the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee,
seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 7-0.
items.motion: motion to refer the Item to the Public Safety and Neighborhood Quality of Life Committee and then have that outcome referred to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, ACCEPTING THE RECOMMENDATION OF THE FINANCE AND ECONOMIC RESILIENCY COMMITTEE, AT ITS MAY 6, 2026, MEETING, TO AMEND THE CITY’S TROLLEY ADVERTISING AGREEMENT WITH OUTFRONT MEDIA TO ALLOW FULL VEHICLE WRAP ADVERTISING ON CITY TROLLEYS.
items.action: The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by Vice-Mayor Dominguez. The Item was deferred to the July 22, 2026, Commission Meeting. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to defer the Item, seconded by Mayor Meiner. Vote: 7-0. Lilia Cardillo to place on the agenda. Jose Gonzalez to handle. .June 24, 2026
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by Vice-Mayor Dominguez. The Item
was deferred to the July 22, 2026, Commission Meeting. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion
to defer the Item, seconded by Mayor Meiner. Vote: 7-0. Lilia Cardillo to place on the agenda.
Jose Gonzalez to handle.
.June 24, 2026
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: No
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Clerk’s Note: Item C7 Q was reconsidered earlier in the meeting as part of the procedural
clarification occurring during discussion of Item C7 A. Vice-Mayor Dominguez stated that Items C7
A and C7 C had been separated from the Consent Agenda by mistake, and that the intended items
for separation were Items C7 O and C7 Q. After approving Items C7 A and C7 C, the Commission
voted 7-0 to reconsider Items C7 O and C7 Q.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez explained that she separated this Item from the Consent Agenda to speak
on behalf of the Transportation Committee (Transportation, Parking and Bicycle-Pedestrian
Facilities Committee) and Miami Beach United (MBU), both of which have expressed their
preference that the trolleys' windows not be wrapped due to safety concerns.
Commissioner Suarez expressed support for the Item, noting that the City’s transportation fund is
projected to face a deficit. He explained that while the City expects to close the funding gap with
additional resources, fiscal responsibility remains necessary. Because the City fully funds the
trolleys through taxes, he emphasized the importance of maximizing their value, as other cities do
with fully wrapped buses, including those operated by Miami-Dade County. He added that wrapped
buses typically use perforated window coverings that still allow passengers to see out, even if
visibility from the outside is limited. Therefore, he does not see an issue with implementing this
approach.
Transportation Director Jose Gonzalez explained that advertising wraps use different perforation
ratios, and the City’s advertising vendor, Outfront Media, uses a 50/50 perforation. He noted that
this ratio is designed to maximize passenger visibility while still providing effective advertising
space. According to the vendor, a 50% perforation is the market standard, and there is no commonly
used option with less visibility.
Commissioner Suarez asked how much value the City will receive by having a full wrap on the
trolleys and if the City is bound to Outfront Media as the sole provider for advertising.
Transportation Director Jose Gonzalez stated that while the City is preparing to issue a competitive
solicitation for future advertising services, the current contract remains with Outfront Media. He
explained that at the most recent Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee (FERC) meeting,
the Committee recommended amending the existing agreement to allow full exterior wraps on the
trolleys. Historically, the City has not wrapped the entire vehicle; the current contract limits
advertising wraps to the area between the front and rear wheels and the rear panel. Transportation
Gonzalez noted that, according to Outfront, expanding wrap coverage to the full exterior would
increase advertising revenue, though the vendor did not provide a specific projected amount. He
will try to have a number for the next FERC discussion.
Mayor Meiner added that he would like to know the exact amount of the revenue increase before
moving forward with the Item.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas expressed support for moving forward with allowing full trolley wraps,
acknowledging concerns but noting that many creative approaches still allow visibility in and out of
the vehicles. She suggested that lighter or modified window treatments could address those issues.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas recommended approving the Item and trying it out, with the
understanding that if any problems arise, the City can revert to the previous approach. She
emphasized that full wraps are widely used on trolleys around the country and internationally, and
they generally work well. Her position was to proceed with the change in an effort to increase
advertising revenue.
Commissioner Fernandez inquired whether the vehicles procured for the trolleys have the traditional
design and whether that came at a premium to the City.
Transportation Director Gonzalez responded that the vehicles have a classic American trolley
design and that they cost more.
Commissioner Fernandez indicated that he would like to defer the Item. While he understands the
value of advertising, given the revenue changes the City will experience, the City has already made
a fiscal investment in the traditional design. He would like to know the specifics of the revenue
increase and the price of the classic American trolley design before moving forward.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine noted that he had been inclined to suggest a deferral as well to
obtain quantitative revenue projections and to consult with both MBU and the Transportation
Committee. He explained that their opposition prompted him to reassess the Item more carefully.
Commissioner Magazine added that, independently, he might have initially opposed the Item;
however, when considering the broader context, specifically that advertising revenue has helped
maintain or expand trolley service levels despite funding deficits, he recognized the need for a fuller
evaluation. He expressed willingness to reach out to both groups to provide the complete context
and stated that once the quantitative information is available, the Commission can revisit the Item
and provide a fully informed opinion next month.
Commissioner Fernandez moved to defer the Item; seconded by Mayor Meiner. Vote: 7-0.
items.motion: Fernandez made a motion to defer the Item, seconded by Mayor Meiner.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, DIRECTING THE CITY ADMINISTRATION TO CREATE A PUBLIC CITY OF MIAMI BEACH EMPLOYEE SALARY PORTAL TO INCLUDE A FIVE-YEAR SALARY HISTORY FOR EACH EMPLOYEE FOR TRANSPARENCY AND GOOD GOVERNANCE.
items.action: Resolution 2026-34328 was adopted. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas. Commissioner Suarez moved the Item, seconded by
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34328 was adopted. The Item was separated from the Consent
Agenda by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas. Commissioner Suarez moved the Item, seconded by
Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 6-1. Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas voted No.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: No
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Frank Quintana and Marla Alpizar to handle.
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas stated that she understood that employee salaries are public
records, but she believed the salary portal could be harmful. She explained that residents may look
up individual employees online and publicly criticize or bully staff members based on their
compensation. She described a scenario in which a resident calls Code Compliance, looks up the
responding Officer, and comments online that the Officer is overpaid. She said the Item did not sit
well with her and expressed concern that the portal would expose staff to further bullying. She
stated that she could not support the Item.
Commissioner Suarez thanked Commissioner Matteo-Salinas and said that he understood her
concerns. He noted that all City employees are public servants and that a certain level of
transparency is expected. He stated that the City of Miami and Miami-Dade County already publish
salary information and that he did not see anything wrong with providing more transparency in
government. He added that even if someone dislikes a particular employee, they still have the right
to access public information, including salaries. He said he would support the Item. He added that
although people may dislike certain employees, that does not prevent them from being privy to
public information
Mayor Steven Meiner stated that, although he shared some concerns about employee morale,
transparency would ultimately prevail. He said he supported the Item and noted that the
Commission had previously adopted several transparency initiatives, including audits and contract
oversight measures. Although he acknowledged the concerns raised by Commissioner Monica
Matteo-Salinas, he explained that transparency would ultimately prevail and that he would therefore
.June 24, 2026
support the Resolution.
Commissioner Magazine stated that he had a similar Item intended to create a broader fiscal
transparency portal to track every dollar spent by the City, including Commission expenditures. He
asked whether both portals could be developed simultaneously and whether the salary portal would
take longer. He said the salary portal seemed simple, as it merely linked readily available data.
Frank Quintana, Chief Information Officer, stated that both the salary and fiscal portals were
technically feasible. He explained that both would pull information from the City’s HR and financial
systems. He said the fiscal portal would be more labor-intensive because of the complexity of the
financial system, whereas the salary portal involved a direct pull of employee data. He said the two
portals would likely be tiered by effort, with the salary portal completed first. He stated that
developing the fiscal portal would require additional discovery.
Commissioner Magazine asked whether it would be possible to forgo the salary portal if the broader
fiscal portal could be built within a month. Commissioner Magazine suggested that if the fiscal portal
takes longer, the salary portal should proceed independently to avoid delaying Commissioner
Suarez’s Item.
Commissioner Suarez said his conversations with CIO Quintana indicated the salary portal could
be completed relatively soon. He believed the two portals should remain separate. He said the
salary portal should remain a stand-alone tool, so the public could easily look up employee salaries
without navigating a broader fiscal portal.
CIO Quintana stated that, while the two portals shared some elements, they required separate
development. He reiterated that the salary portal was far simpler than the fiscal portal and that he
could not responsibly provide a completion date for the fiscal portal because it required deeper
analysis. He said initial review of the Item suggested the salary portal was straightforward.
City Manager Eric Carpenter asked, through the Mayor, whether CIO Quintana had reviewed the
addendum requiring a five-year salary look-back.
CIO Quintana confirmed that he had.
Mayor Meiner stated that he saw benefits to creating the portal. He said he had recently observed
misinformation about salaries circulating online and that a City-hosted portal could dispel such
misinformation.
Commissioner Magazine agreed, stating that although salary information already existed on
external websites, it was not the City’s data. He noted that external sites such as GovSalaries.com
could generate misleading impressions.
Commissioner Bhatt asked whether the portal would display salaries by position or by individual
employee name. She expressed concern that listing employees by name approached doxxing and
could create public safety risks. She said she supported salary transparency but was wary of
attaching salaries to individual employee names, adding that in the private sector, transparency by
job classification can empower negotiation.
CIO Quintana stated that external salary aggregation sites did not receive data directly from the
City and were often outdated by one to two years. He said the intent of the Resolution was to provide
more timely and trustworthy information through the City’s official website.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Suarez responded that salary information is already public record. He believed the
City should provide a more transparent and reliable source than external websites. He said he
preferred a City-maintained site to ensure accuracy.
Commissioner Fernandez said that similar salary portals existed in other jurisdictions. He expressed
concern about employee morale and unintended consequences. He noted that neighboring
jurisdictions frequently attempt to recruit City employees and that salary transparency could make
it easier for them to do so. He said he did not want to facilitate talent loss, particularly when existing
public records already provided salary information upon request.
City Manager Eric Carpenter added that the City had the most talented workforce in the County and
that other agencies regularly attempted to recruit City employees. City Manager Carpenter said
agencies often compete by offering better salaries, benefits, or flexible work schedules.
Commissioner Fernandez continued that external websites may not have up-to-date salary data
and that making the most current information readily available could incentivize outside agencies
to target City employees, contributing to turnover.
Commissioner Suarez responded that agencies attempting to recruit City employees could already
access salary data on existing websites. He said the salary portal simply increased transparency
and provided accuracy. He stated that he did not understand the pushback, as the data was already
accessible, and he favored a City-hosted site to ensure trustworthy information.
City Attorney Ricardo J. Dopico, speaking through the Chair, stated that he wanted to offer
clarification that might provide some calm. He explained that the State had adopted a Statute earlier
in the year requiring municipalities to publish employee salary information on a quarterly basis
beginning January 1 of the following year, and that the Resolution would allow the City to comply
ahead of the mandate.
Mayor Meiner reiterated his support. He noted that transparency is necessary in government and
that, although he had concerns similar to those of Commissioner Matteo-Salinas, he supported the
Item.
Commissioner Magazine stated that, unlike private companies governed by SEC reporting
requirements, municipalities operate with taxpayer dollars. He said that transparency requirements
understandably differ between the public and private sectors.
The Mayor asked for the vote.
Commissioner Suarez moved to adopt the Resolution, seconded by Commissioner Fernandez.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas reiterated her belief that the State’s preemption made the Resolution
inevitable, but she emphasized that the portal could place a target on employees and reduce the
City’s competitiveness as an employer.
Mayor Steven Meiner noted that other jurisdictions, such as Miami-Dade County and the City of
Miami, already have access to salary information or can readily obtain it, given the public nature of
the data.
The vote was taken. The Item was adopted 6-1, with Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas voting
No.
.June 24, 2026

ACTION: Resolution 2026-34334 was adopted as amended. Commissioner Fernandez made a
motion to adopt the Resolution selecting Brooks Scarpa Huber Architects Inc. as the top-ranked
proposer, seconded by Commissioner Bhatt. The motion passed 6-1, with Mayor Meiner opposed.
FIRM SELECTION VOTE:
Commissioner Bhatt: Brooks Scarpa Huber Architects Inc.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez: Brooks Scarpa Huber Architects Inc.
Commissioner Fernandez: Brooks Scarpa Huber Architects Inc.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas: Brooks Scarpa Huber Architects Inc.
Commissioner Magazine: Brooks Scarpa Huber Architects Inc.
Commissioner Suarez: Brooks Scarpa Huber Architects Inc.
Mayor Meiner: Stantec Architecture Inc.
Brooks Scarpa Huber Architects Inc. was designated the top-ranked proposer.
SECOND-RANKED FIRM VOTE:
Commissioner Suarez: Kaller Architecture
Commissioner Fernandez: Kaller Architecture
Commissioner Magazine: Stantec Architecture Inc.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas: Stantec Architecture Inc.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez: Stantec Architecture Inc.
Commissioner Bhatt: Stantec Architecture Inc.
Mayor Meiner: Stantec Architecture Inc.
Stantec Architecture Inc. was designated the second-ranked proposer.
.June 24, 2026
AMENDMENTS:
 Brooks Scarpa Huber Architects Inc. was designated the top-ranked proposer.
 Stantec Architecture Inc. was designated the second-ranked proposer.
 The contract must be brought back to the City Commission for review prior to execution.
David Gomez, Kristy Bada, and Thais Vieira to handle.
Meeting, the Commission requested that the proposers return and provide presentations on their
experience and qualifications. She noted that each proposer was prepared to deliver a five-minute
presentation addressing those points and, upon concluding their remarks, would answer any
questions the Commission might have.
Arturo Vasquez del Mercado, Principal and Senior Architect at Stantec Architecture Inc., the
first-ranked proposer, stated that he has been a Miami Beach resident for 15 years and appreciates
the work the City Commission has done to improve the neighborhood. He explained that when he
moved to the City in 2010, he lived at 74 Street and Byron Avenue and has witnessed the
transformation of the neighborhood, which he believes presents an opportunity to create an anchor
that can unify the community and expand the resources that residents wish to see in such a facility.
He noted that Stantec has been in the area for nearly 25 years. He clarified that paperwork
referenced by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas indicated a Denver license only because Stantec
acquired the firm he and his partners founded, and that the acquisition enables them to bring experts
from across the country. Their office, however, has always been local, and he moved to Miami
Beach because he wanted to reside in and celebrate the City's diversity. Mr. Vasquez del Mercado
stated that the project represents a unique opportunity for adaptive reuse of a building that is
meaningful to many residents. Based on his experience with the neighborhood's evolution, they
assembled both an internal and external team of experts to provide local knowledge and technical
capability. He referenced his design work on the Gale Hotel and stated that he is pleased that
Santorini is moving into that space, as he considers it an important institution. He added that he
frequently uses Flamingo Park and appreciates the City's efforts to preserve it. He remarked that
he is familiar with the City Commission because he often sees its members at community locations.
He explained that the boards displayed illustrate their understanding of the neighborhood and the
potential for the building to become a cultural anchor. He recognized Commissioner Suarez's
interest in the housing component and how it could offset operational costs. Their specialists, he
said, understand those issues. He noted that factors such as parking and area median income
levels will influence the final number of units but emphasized the importance of providing attainable,
high-quality housing that does not price out residents. He recalled having to move from Byron
Avenue to Euclid Avenue due to rising costs, underscoring the need for affordability. He reviewed
his background in adaptive reuse and new construction, citing his work on the Jackie Gleason
Theater, the Gale, and the Berkeley Shore. He introduced Gustavo, a team member with 30 years
of experience in resiliency and adaptive reuse, who understands what can be preserved and what
requires new construction to deliver a significant building the City can be proud of. He also
introduced MDRDV, an international firm with local experience and expertise in creating iconic
imagery. He stated that the building should celebrate the past while looking to the future, and that
residents expressed a desire for a facility of which they can be proud. Mr. Vasquez del Mercado
acknowledged Commissioner Bhatt's long involvement with the project and asked for her
confidence in their team. He quoted Winston Churchill, saying that people shape their buildings and
then their buildings shape them, a guiding principle in his 30-year architectural career. He
expressed appreciation for the Commission's consideration. He referenced additional residential
and performing arts projects completed by their team, including a Wynwood development created
before the neighborhood's transformation. He noted that their work consistently incorporates an arts
component. He explained that their performing arts specialists from New York would contribute to
this project, while he and Gustavo would oversee the residential portion and the building's
.June 24, 2026
expression within the broader neighborhood context. He described projects shown on the boards
that performed well during the interview phase and appealed to the selection committee because
they combine housing with performing arts facilities. He stated that there are multiple ways to
incorporate both components into the Byron Carlyle project, and that these can be analyzed to
provide a beautiful community building accommodating all intended uses. He further described a
collage depicting their concept of bringing residents together and creating a functional and
emotionally connected building that integrates with the Bandshell, nearby parks, and the
neighborhood. He emphasized that the building is more than a structure and should serve as a
community asset. He noted that their project manager was unable to attend because she was
traveling with her family, but that she has a long history of working with the City as a principal at
CP3S. He stated that their team already holds a contract with the City and is continuing that
relationship and opportunity.
Commissioner Magazine asked Mr. Vasquez to describe his idea for the project, what the City
should expect, and what his vision would be for bringing it to life.
Arturo Vasquez, Principal and Senior Architect at Stantec Architecture Inc., the first-ranked
proposer, explained that the building must function as a modern facility capable of supporting a
unique mixture of uses. He stated that it should open to the community and the neighborhood and
connect people not only to the activities inside the building but also to the Bandshell and the park
across the street. He emphasized that the facility should not be surrounded by overwhelming
development. Mr. Vasquez remarked that the City Commission has an opportunity to create a
center that anchors the arts for the City, not only for Miami Beach but for Miami as well. He noted
that there is no comparable building in either city. His vision, he said, is a building that extends
beyond itself and becomes part of the broader arts and cultural landscape of North Beach.
Commissioner Magazine thanked him for his passion for Miami Beach.
Angie Brooks, Managing Principal of Brooks Scarpa Huber Architects Inc., the second-ranked
proposer, stated that she was born and raised in Florida and that her partners grew up in Miami.
She explained that their firm is a globally recognized, woman-owned practice founded 35 years
ago, with offices in Fort Lauderdale, Miami, and Los Angeles. Their team has completed cultural
arts projects around the country, including Hollywood, Florida, as well as thousands of units of
housing, including two apartment projects located nearby. Ms. Brooks noted that they are currently
working on two cultural arts projects, one of which has virtually the same program as the Byron
Carlyle, combining performance space, cultural space, and workforce housing over retail in Culver
City. She stated that their team knows North Beach well and introduced her partner, Jeffrey Huber,
for a short presentation.
Jeffrey Huber, Project Architect, provided a presentation and explained why he believes their team
