ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading with direction. The Item was heard
with R5 D. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record. The Public Hearing was held.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas moved to adopt the Planning Board’s version of the Ordinance on
First Reading, seconded by Commissioner Bhatt. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for September 10, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to
notice. Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Deborah Tackett to
handle.
DIRECTION:
Between First and Second Reading, the City Commission requested the following:
 The applicant and City staff shall explore a potential public benefit contribution toward returfing
the Flamingo Park football field.
 The applicant and City staff shall evaluate additional community benefit opportunities.
 The applicant shall conduct further outreach to WAVNA prior to Second Reading.
.June 24, 2026
 The applicant and the Parking Department shall coordinate to ensure that underutilized parking
associated with the project is made available to the surrounding area zone at Miami Beach
public parking rates.
 The applicant and City staff shall evaluate increasing the residential percentage above the
current 50 percent request, consistent with staff recommendations and Commission comments.
 The Office of the City Attorney and the Planning Department shall refine Ordinance language
relating to year-round housing requirements and the potential elimination of short-term rentals
for any property included in a unified site.
Mayor Meiner informed his colleagues that Item R7 D has a time certain of 3:00 p.m., as noticed
and not before that time. He stated that they may need to pause their discussion of Items R5 C and
R5 D at 3:00 p.m. in order to take up R7 D, and that they would return to R5 C and R5 D afterward.
Deborah Tackett, Planning Director, introduced a private application similar to the one discussed
earlier for the property at 1600 Washington Avenue. This is a request by a private property owner
of the old Epicure site to provide long-term residential housing in exchange for certain zoning
incentives. The site is located within the CD-2 Zoning district, which has an allowable FAR of 2.0;
the request is to increase it up to 3.5 FAR. There is also a request to increase the height from the
maximum allowable 65 feet to 150 feet, and all of this would be predicated upon a voluntary proffer
that there shall be no short-term rentals as part of the project in perpetuity. The application also
requests an increase in density. The current allowable density is 100 units per acre, and they are
asking for 150 units per acre. Staff is generally supportive of the proposal. Their recommendations
are consistent with another initiative sponsored by Commissioner Suarez for the Greater Lincoln
Road/17th Street area and this property. Staff recommends moving this forward with a requirement
that the project contain more focus on residential units. As drafted, the property owner is requesting
only 50 percent of the new FAR and new construction to be used for residential. Staff believes that
it should be 80 percent so that all of the uses above the ground floor would be residential, with the
exception of approximately 20 percent. Staff is also concerned about the vehicular traffic impacts
of this site, which is a very challenging intersection. The applicant has agreed to increase
micromobility facilities as part of the project and in the area, but they would like to include all required
parking per Parking District I. Staff recommends that a maximum of 50 percent of the required
parking per Parking District I be allowed due to the vehicular intensity of the site. They are also
recommending that any existing short-term rentals on the property be discontinued as part of this
residential use incentive. The Epicure site currently does not contain short-term rentals; however,
the adjacent property where Trader Joe’s is located is a residential project with a legal short-term
rental. Staff recommends that if that property is included in this application, those short-term rental
uses be discontinued.
Neisen Kasdin, Esq., and Cecilia Torres-Toledo of Akerman LLP, representing the applicant, along
with David Berg, principal of Infinity Collective and developer of the Alton City Center Overlay site,
gave a brief presentation. Mr. Kasdin also wished to discuss with the City Commission the Planning
Board version of the Ordinance, which was distributed the night before and is important for the
Commission to understand. Click here to view. He explained that in order to have a vital and viable
community, there must be places where people can live, work, shop, and play, and that is what is
lacking and what this Overlay will help bring to this part of Miami Beach. He noted they already
have a model in the revitalization of Sunset Harbour, which has become that kind of
three-legged-stool mixed community with residential, retail, and office uses; that is how they reduce
commuting and make it more convenient for Miami Beach residents. He stated there are many
benefits to the Overlay and broad support from the community, organizations, and particularly
employers. A manager from a large restaurant and beverage operation shared that their employees
do not have places where they can live, particularly managers and senior staff, because units are
unavailable. Mount Sinai Hospital experiences similar difficulties because almost all of its
.June 24, 2026
employees must commute. This application fills a need and has broad community support. Mr.
Kasdin explained that the Ordinance went to the Planning Board, which held a public meeting with
input from neighbors and interested parties, and then it went back to the Planning Board. The
Planning Board drafted and approved a specific Ordinance, which was not in the original package
and was distributed the night before. The Planning Board version reflects their response to the
needs and demands of the community. They have the ability to include parking, although the
amount will ultimately be determined by conditional use. They have a ratio requiring at least 50
percent residential, which is important because the project will be mixed-use with retail, office, and
residential. He encouraged the City Commission to adopt the Planning Board version, noting the
Planning Board spent significant time on this and provided guidance accordingly. Mr. Berg stated
he was available for any questions and thanked the City Commission, Planning Director Tackett for
their conversations, and Nick Kallergis in the City Attorney’s Office.
In addressing Vice-Mayor Dominguez’s concerns, David Berg noted that all concerns received were
reviewed and that he emailed Vice-Mayor Dominguez correspondence addressing each concern
point-by-point. A response was also distributed to WAVNA, though some of their concerns were
inaccurate. As shown in Mr. Kasdin’s presentation, they are offering a robust set of public benefits.
Mr. Berg stated he was happy to address any concerns. In continued comments from Vice-Mayor
Dominguez, he explained that a Letter of Intent went out to Mount Sinai Hospital for a certain
number of units to determine interest; the idea is bulk unit allocation at a discounted fair market
value with shuttle services, and the same offer is being extended to the hospitality industry and
large employers. Discussion held. He explained there will be a residential loading zone and an
office loading zone in the alley away from the main street. They have a breezeway that addresses
queuing so nothing occurs in the traffic area of West Avenue or Alton Road. Parking was one of the
biggest components of their private application and differs from the Lincoln Road legislation
because they need parking. Responding to Vice-Mayor Dominguez, Mr. Berg noted they do not
have an agreement in place with the City, although the City Commission approved a Resolution
weeks ago. As a show of good faith, they allowed staging without an agreement. They are currently
staging there now, and as long as they are not breaking ground, they will be able to continue using
the space.
Mayor Meiner announced that they would take a timeout for Item R7 D, as it was noticed as “not
before 3 p.m.” Clerk’s Note: Items R5 C and R5 D were called again at 3:08:37 p.m.
In responding to Commissioner Matteo-Salinas, David Berg noted that one of the most important
benefits offered is that they are delivering the City’s Comprehensive Plan “to a T,” an initiative that
the City put forth, and that this is a good-faith effort and a prototype to combat Live Local by following
the City’s Comprehensive Plan. Public benefits include working with SOBE West to beautify the
alley at Alton Court and enhancing landscaping; burying the FPL lines; offering a community paddle
court; providing parking to residents for overnight parking at Miami Beach parking rates; retail
parking will not be a charge parking; providing EV charging; increasing micromobility; creating a
breezeway and a walkable pedestrian alley from West Avenue to Alton Road to provide easier
access to the Alton Road corridor and Lincoln Road west. They are reducing traffic. The prior
project, which was all office with large 20,000-square-foot floor plates, would have increased traffic
substantially more than their project. They are creating over 700 construction jobs during the project
and expect over 350 permanent jobs through their uses. Over a ten-year period, they will deliver
over $30 million in tax revenue to the City. They have a 4,500-square-foot Blue Zone hub that will
focus on longevity, wellness, community, and the nine foundations of Blue Zones, which will benefit
residents, office workers, and the community as a whole. They are revitalizing the retail corridor
with live, work, and play uses and bringing residents to the area, including Art in Public Places,
among other components.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Bhatt stated that the short-term rental covenant is six months and a day and that her
desire is to get closer to year-long residences. Between First and Second Reading, she requested
an analysis of extending the minimum rental term beyond six months and a day.
David Berg, Principal of Infinity Collective, explained that the reason for nine months is to provide
flexibility for hospitality workers who may be staffing up or down based on seasonality, and it also
provides flexibility for rent-roll management. They do not want all leases to roll over at the same
time, so they sometimes need to stagger lease rollover. If they have a heavy rollover in June, for
example, they may offer a 15- or 16-month lease or a lease of less than twelve months, perhaps
nine months, so that rollover can be managed across the year. It is not intentional to have short-term
rentals; there is no intention to do so, and it is not their business plan. However, not being tied
strictly to twelve months allows some flexibility in managing rollover. Nine months is a happy
medium but is more art than science as they are trying to manage rollover risk. Responding to
Commissioner Bhatt, he stated that they are not attached to 17 West. The concept is a covenant in
lieu for zoning purposes, but the ownership structures are different. There are some investors in
that deal who are in their deal, but many investors in that transaction are not part of theirs. He noted
that the intent should not be lost: their project will not have any short-term rental allowance at all;
they intend full-year rentals. They will deliver 150-plus apartment units to the community. The other
property is a 20-unit project, and he cannot control what they do, their existing license, or how they
operate their business, but a 20-unit short-term rental should not be a challenge to delivering 150
long-term units.
Commissioner Bhatt added that they are trying to be creative in funding other projects throughout
the City. She knows he is not building high-end luxury condominiums, but a few blocks away is
Flamingo Park, the heart and soul of the South Beach community, and the football field is in need
of re-turfing. Between First and Second Reading, she requested continuing conversations about
the possibility of directing a community benefit to that.
Mr. Berg agreed.
Commissioner Magazine noted that his entire life is in this corridor. He is raising his daughter on
Sixth and West; his parents live there; his private office is on 17th; Alton Road is right across the
street; and City Hall is here, so his entire life is there. He believes they are on the verge of something
special: a corridor between Washington Avenue, Lincoln Road, Alton Road, and 17th Street going
down into Sunset Harbour, where they can create something vibrant and something to be proud of.
They are at a fork in the road because, although there is excitement, when he looks out his office
window, he sees an abandoned dialysis center and derelict buildings, ten times more derelict than
any new development. He appreciates the outreach, shared some reservations, and noted he is 90
percent happy and is not going to let the other 10 percent get in the way. He appreciates the time
spent speaking with the surrounding neighbors and neighborhoods. He personally values WAVNA,
having begun his involvement in the City with some of those members, understands their
challenges, and cannot ignore them, so he asked Mr. Berg not to either. He knows a letter was sent
in response and suggested having another meeting and working with them to identify areas of
compromise. He also appreciates the hours spent with other neighborhood groups. He noted that
Tom Hawkins approached him at the gym and expressed support for the project, and that only
happens because the developer is community-minded and does outreach. His comments about
16th Street and Washington Avenue focused on creating a vibrant mixed-use environment that
fosters affordability and strengthens the local economy. He stated that the western end of Lincoln
Road is a dead zone. Segafredo is leaving. He walks Lincoln Road every morning, and until noon,
they do not see a soul. The people who go there in the morning are those who live nearby, not
destination shoppers. That is the type of consumer they need to bring back to help local retail. Every
person in the City will say one of their top priorities is revitalizing Lincoln Road and the retail
.June 24, 2026
corridors. It is his adamant belief that the problem is the lack of walkability and the lack of residents
living in those areas. Many businesses have closed due to the loss of customers. They have lost
the full-time residential population, and by having full-time residents in this corridor, he hopes to
restore it. He wished the developer luck.
David Berg, Principal of Infinity Collective, commented that there is not a single person in the
community who has reached out to them that they have not engaged in conversations, not one.
They had one or two meetings with WAVNA and five to seven hours of conversations with their
Board Members. They are always open to conversation; anyone who calls them has their cell phone
numbers and can reach out at any time. Per Commissioner Magazine’s direction, Mr. Berg will
reach out to WAVNA one more time. He stated that they take development and housing very
seriously. This is where someone lives, which is very sacred; it is where family, children, and pets
are. It is a sacred responsibility to provide housing for safety reasons, community needs, and
neighborhood creation. It is critical for them to engage with the community because that is the
definition of socially responsible development. It is not a talking point; it is a sacred, critical business
point for them.
Commissioner Fernandez added that there is a critical need for non-luxury rental housing in the
City. They see the displacement of long-time residents to other areas of Miami on the mainland
where they can find inventory like this at prices they can afford. When discussing affordability in
Miami Beach, this is important. He asked how affordability is achieved here because staff raised
concerns with the amount of space dedicated to office as opposed to residential. His inclination is
to consider what impact increasing residential space would have, as it is not every day that they
have the opportunity to have new rental inventory in the City, and whether adjustments could be
accommodated.
David Berg, Principal of Infinity Collective, responded that the commercial component of the project
is what allows them to deliver attainable housing because the cost of building rental housing now
is generally cost-prohibitive, which is why most buildings go condo across the country, particularly
in South Florida. Using quick math, the retail and commercial corridors of Alton Road and Sunset
Harbour can deliver perhaps $100 per square foot in triple-net rents, whereas housing is closer to
$60 per square foot gross, which nets to approximately $40 per square foot. There is a $40 to $60
per-foot swing for commercial space compared to residential. By having commercial space, they
are able to deliver residential at an attainable price point. He stated that there is some room to go
above 50 percent residential; they can move a little bit, but they cannot go to the 75 percent being
requested.
Commissioner Fernandez directed Mr. Berg to work on that and prioritize as much housing
inventory as possible in this corridor. He noted that the project started with a higher height request
of 200 feet and asked Mr. Berg to explain.

ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The Item was heard with R5 F. The title
of the Ordinance was read into the record. The Public Hearing was held. A motion was made by
Commissioner Fernandez to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading with direction, seconded by
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas, for Items R5 E and R5 F. Vote: 7-0.
Clerk’s Note: Commissioner Suarez was absent during the vote. Upon his return to the dais,
Commissioner Suarez voted in the affirmative on Items R5 E and R5 F; therefore, his vote is duly
recorded as yes for both Items.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
DIRECTION:
Between First and Second Reading, the City Commission directed the Administration as follows:
 Consider codifying strict requirements in the Land Development Regulations that the developer
must comply with in order to build the project.
 Require that applications be filed by a specified date; otherwise, the incentives will sunset and
be automatically repealed.
 The Planning Department shall work with the applicant to develop proposed minimum and
average unit sizes for inclusion in the Ordinance.
.June 24, 2026
 The applicant shall consider unit size adjustments and explore outside dates for permit
approvals to help ensure timely project completion.
 The applicant shall consider foregoing the ability to utilize Live Local as part of the discussions
prior to Second Reading.
 Conduct outreach to the Flamingo Park Neighborhood Association to address concerns raised
by its members.
 Engage in a discussion on how to mitigate the risk of newly constructed retail spaces remaining
vacant.
 Evaluate whether the restriction on short-term rentals should be extended to require year-round
leases rather than six months and one day.
 Consider the issue of setbacks to ensure a safe and robust pedestrian environment consistent
with Washington Avenue’s future role as a transit corridor.
The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for September 10, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to
notice. Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Deborah Tackett to
handle.
Deborah Tackett, Planning Director, stated that the proposal seeks to incentivize non-transient
residential use at the 1600 Washington Avenue property. She explained that the applicant is
proposing an increase in FAR from the currently allowable 2.75 to 3.25, resulting in an additional
0.5 FAR, which equates to approximately 50,000 square feet of additional buildable area on the
site. She noted that the applicant is also requesting a height increase. Although the allowable height
is 100 feet, the applicant is proposing a new development that would exceed that limit by 50 feet,
for a requested maximum height of 150 feet. She clarified that the applicant is not requesting an
increase in density, as 150 units per acre are already permitted, and the proposed project complies
with that standard. She added that the Historic Preservation Board approved the project at its May
meeting, contingent upon the required land development regulation modifications being adopted.
She stated that the Administration is supportive of the proposal and recommends approval at First
Reading and scheduling the Second Reading for September. Because this Item includes an FAR
increase, she noted that the Planning Department will schedule an additional public meeting
between First and Second Reading. She explained that the first public meeting occurred after the
First Reading at the Planning Board and that members of the public will again have an opportunity
to participate and provide comment. Responding to Mayor Meiner, she clarified that the meeting is
not a Commission Meeting but is open to the public. She stated that it is typically held on Zoom,
and although it will take place during the summer when many residents are traveling, the
Department will be able to accommodate remote participation.
Neisen Kasdin, Esq., introduced the team representing the applicant, 420 Lincoln Road
Development, along with Ambassador Paul Cejas and Trudy Cejas, longtime Miami Beach
residents. He referenced a presentation and noted that the project has been endorsed by the
Washington Avenue and Lincoln Road BIDs. He explained that Ambassador Cejas has owned the
property for more than 30 years and has been a strong steward of the site, one of the largest historic
office buildings in the City, investing millions of dollars in its restoration. He stated that the missing
component needed to strengthen Washington Avenue and Lincoln Road is residential use, which
Ambassador Cejas seeks to bring to the area.
Responding to Commissioner Fernandez, Planning Director Tackett explained that the current
density allowed in the CD-3 district is 150 units per acre. She stated that the current intensity, or
FAR, is 2.75 for this property and that the calculations reflect approximately 50,000 square feet of
additional area for the site, including the garage.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Fernandez remarked that the current FAR does not allow access to the full
residential potential under the Zoning Code, and Ms. Tackett agreed.
Deborah Tackett, Planning Director, further explained to Commissioner Fernandez that surrounding
buildings in the City Center had the highest intensity zoning in terms of FAR and height. She noted
that most buildings constructed since the late 1980s to 1990s are maxed out at 100 feet. She added
that the 407 Lincoln Road building exceeds 150 feet, so taller structures exist in the immediate
vicinity, which is one reason the Administration supports the request. In response to continued
questions from Commissioner Fernandez, Planning Director Tackett stated that the Decoplage is a
nonconforming building within its zoning district and is therefore maxed out on FAR and height at
approximately sixteen stories, which is taller than what would be permitted on that site today.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that the City has a need for housing. He explained that he recently
met with a major stakeholder who indicated that they had sought to rent a block of units for their
employees, but the closest available option was in Coral Gables at the Lifetime building. He noted
that the Commission has discussed affordability in several contexts, including water and sewer
rates, parking, and towing, but that affordability in housing is achieved through supply. He
emphasized the importance of working with private partners to identify areas suitable for growth so
the City can preserve the historic fabric of other neighborhoods. He stated that he feels comfortable
with the proposal because, as the applicant’s representative indicated, this area has traditionally
been the downtown of Miami Beach. He added that an office building sits on City-owned land across
the street and that he understands there is a potential buyer for that property, which currently sits
mostly empty. He stated that the City must find a way to ensure that people working in buildings
such as these, as well as those working at City Hall, hotels, Mt. Sinai, and Loews, have the ability
to live in the City. He remarked that rents in areas like Flamingo Park are not competitive with other
neighborhoods, where renters obtain greater value for the same price, creating a growing housing
challenge. Neisen Kasdin replied to Commissioner Fernandez that the project will include a mix of
units, including studios and one- and two-bedroom residences, although the final mix has not yet
been determined.
Ambassador Paul Cejas stated that he has had the honor and privilege of owning the property for
many years. He explained that when the building was constructed, it was the second air-conditioned
building in the United States, second only to one on Park Avenue in New York, and that he and his
wife are proud of that history. He noted that the asset had been dilapidated when they acquired it
and that they spent millions of dollars restoring the building nearly thirty years ago. He stated that
the restoration was successful and that they remain proud of the work. He explained that they do
not turn over properties, but rather hold their assets because they believe in the City and live here.
He added that they have been involved in many civic and cultural endeavors, noting that his wife
serves on the Board of The Bass and that they have contributed to the New World Symphony. He
remarked that he is proud to be from Miami Beach. He also mentioned that his wife was present
because they would be celebrating their forty-fourth wedding anniversary in two weeks and added
with humor that he believes in happy wife, happy life. He thanked the Commission for considering
the Item. He stated that they have received approvals in the past, but in one instance the architects
mistakenly shifted a building into the alley, which is required to service tenants on Lincoln Road
who depend on that access to unload merchandise. Because the existing building was inadvertently
moved into the alley, they were unable to construct the previously approved project. He explained
that the plans have now been corrected and that the Historic Preservation Board approved the
project with the requirement that the existing historic building be represented within the structure of
the new development. He stated that the approval is contingent upon the Commission’s action and
that they are pleased to preserve portions of the historic structure. He emphasized that they are
committed to building the project.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Fernandez remarked that one of the concerns frequently expressed by residents is
that the majority of new development over the past several decades has consisted of luxury
condominiums. He noted that such development has displaced longtime residents and has not been
affordable for the average City resident, with most new buildings consisting primarily of
condominium units. He stated that this project is a fully rental development.
Neisen Kasdin, Esq., representing the applicant, clarified that the project is not only rental but is
also subject to a covenant that runs with the land and requires it to remain rental with no short-term
rentals. He noted that the covenant can only be released by a six-sevenths vote of the Commission,
even for future buyers. After discussion, he reiterated that the restriction is permanent unless
released by that threshold vote.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that his concern is that when buildings include extensive
amenities, the market rate often increases, causing the units to shift from attainable and affordable
rentals to higher-priced units. He noted that more amenities typically translate into higher rents.
Neisen Kasdin, Esq., stated that the building will include the amenities necessary to attract tenants,
but it is not intended to be a luxury building. He explained that the proposed unit breakdown includes
thirty-six studios, one hundred forty-four one-bedroom units, and thirty-two-bedroom units. He
stated that the studios are approximately five hundred square feet, the one-bedroom units are in
the eight-hundred to nine-hundred-square-foot range, and the two-bedroom units are approximately
eleven hundred square feet. He explained that the units are designed for working members of the
community. In addressing Commissioner Fernandez, he noted that an existing nightclub use on the
property would be required to cease once the Ordinance is adopted.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that he is comfortable with the proposal. He explained that the
City needs attainable rental housing and does not need additional luxury condominiums, of which
there is already an excess. He added that the project aligns with the City’s desire to move away
from grandfathered five a.m. establishments. He expressed gratitude to Ambassador Cejas for
bringing the Item forward.
Ambassador Paul Cejas clarified that this is the first time he has engaged in development and that
the project was designed to serve the rental market explicitly. He explained that the building will
include certain features, such as a gym, that contribute to residents’ health and wellbeing, noting
that similar features exist in luxury condominiums and apartments. He explained, however, that
such features will be offered at market rates appropriate for attainable housing. He emphasized that
the project is intended to be affordable for people who live and work in Miami Beach. He stated that
he is not a developer but an investor and that his long-term investment approach has been evident
since he acquired the property at 420 Lincoln Road.
In addressing Mayor Meiner’s specific question, Chief Deputy City Attorney Nick Kallergis explained
that a Development Agreement is a tool available when a public project or public property is
involved. He stated that such agreements are also appropriate when significant public infrastructure
will be affected. He clarified that the proposal before the City Commission was submitted as a
private application to amend the LDRs, that the project itself is entirely private, and that there is no
public component present.
Mayor Meiner remarked that the City has experienced situations in which an approval is granted
and no action follows. He stated that he wished to have assurances carved into the legislation to
establish time limitations that would ensure the project is completed. He added that the City is
providing something of value and should therefore protect itself. He clarified that he did not believe
the applicant intends not to build the project, but that unforeseen circumstances occur and
.June 24, 2026
safeguards are necessary.
Deborah Tackett, Planning Director, stated that the Ordinance as drafted does not contain a sunset
provision. She said that the Administration would support the inclusion of such a provision and could
incorporate it should the City Commission recommend doing so.
In accordance with the Mayor’s direction, Chief Deputy City Attorney Nick Kallergis explained that,
for Second Reading, the Ordinance could require that applications be filed by a specific date. He
stated that if applications are not filed by that date, the incentives would sunset automatically and
be repealed. He added that, with respect to public benefits, the Ordinance follows the structure
used in many recent incentive programs considered by the City Commission. He explained that
developers must satisfy certain benchmarks to qualify for incentives.
Mayor Meiner asked whether any public benefits were being offered to City residents and inquired
about the assessed value of the property if the City Commission approves the Item. He asked what
increase in value would result from the zoning change. Chief Deputy City Attorney Nick Kallergis
stated that he did not have a clear answer. Eric Carpenter, City Manager, stated that he did not
believe the Administration had a dollar figure associated with the proposed FAR increase.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Nick Kallergis added that although the Code amendment may positively
affect the value of the property, the City is not a party to a transaction. He explained that the City
Commission should therefore view the matter as a policy question and determine whether the
planning policy merits adoption. He stated that while the City Commission may amend the
Ordinance, the decision should be based on planning considerations rather than transactional
value.
Mayor Meiner reiterated that he is separating the valuation question from the policy question but
that he would like to understand the value being granted by approving the zoning change.
Commissioner Fernandez directed a question to Neisen Kasdin, asking whether it would be
possible to require that any property owner benefitting from the adopted Ordinance enter into a
Development Agreement so that the City Administration could negotiate public benefits. He asked
whether the Ordinance could be amended to require a Development Agreement before building
permits are issued, thereby allowing the City Manager to negotiate in the City’s best interest.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Nick Kallergis explained that the City Commission cannot condition
legislative approval of a Code amendment on the receipt of consideration from an applicant. He
noted that if the City Commission wished to see certain matters addressed from a planning
standpoint, such requirements should be incorporated directly into the project through legislative
provisions.
In response to Mayor Meiner’s question regarding the Development Agreement for 1250 West,
Chief Deputy City Attorney Nick Kallergis explained that the structure of that project differed
because it included a private component intertwined with public elements. He stated that several
public facilities were involved, including the Baywalk and the site of the Bikini Hostel, which will
become a park. He said these factors necessitated a Development Agreement.
Neisen Kasdin explained that in the case of 1250 West, there was a public safety issue that required
the property across the street to be purchased and closed, along with other public improvements.
He stated that, in exchange, the increase in development rights for that project was many times
greater than what is being requested in the present Item, which concerns property of much higher
value. He stated that it is essential to understand both the public benefit and the restrictions being
.June 24, 2026
placed on the property owner. He explained that the City’s Comprehensive Plan outlines the
framework for how the City should be developed, and zoning exists to implement those policies. He
stated that the current proposal follows that framework. He noted that the covenant placed on the
property restricts the applicant to rental apartments only. He stated that the applicant already faces

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Ordinance 2026-4825 was adopted. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record.
The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on
Second Reading, seconded by Vice-Mayor Dominguez. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
David Gomez to handle.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that he had been working closely with the Office of the Inspector
General (OIG) and several committees on the proposed expansion of the Stop the Pause
Ordinance. He explained that the original 2025 Ordinance required a supermajority vote to impede,
amend, or cancel a Capital Improvement Project costing more than $1 million. The legislation was
adopted to prevent the waste of staff time and resources invested in design work and engineering
when projects were halted after reaching a shovel-ready stage. He remarked that the proposal
before the Commission broadens the Ordinance to include all capital projects valued at more than
$1 million and raises the voting thresholds for canceling or pausing those projects. He thanked the
Neighborhood Resiliency Committee and Vice-Mayor Dominguez for encouraging extensive
outreach. He said the public will now benefit from a project kickoff meeting once a contractor is
brought on board, allowing neighbors to provide input at the outset rather than after significant
taxpayer dollars have already been spent. Commissioner Fernandez moved the Item.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez thanked Commissioner Fernandez for bringing the Item forward and for
attending multiple committee meetings to incorporate resident feedback. She seconded the motion.
City Clerk Granado opened the public hearing. There were no speakers on Zoom or in the audience.
Roll Call: 7-0.

habitual misdemeanor offenses and shortens certain timelines. The Item makes it easier to keep
habitual misdemeanor offenders off the streets.
Mayor Steven Meiner informed his colleagues that it takes four convictions within a twelve-month
period to be labeled a habitual offender, which can increase penalties. He explained that this Item
would make it three offenses within a two-year period to address recidivists. He ended by saying
he is happy to partner with Commissioner Matteo-Salinas on the Item and called it a good piece of
legislation.
The City Attorney, Ricardo J. Dopico, clarified that the four offenses still apply to the existing
offenses, and the shorter period applies to most. Some newly added offenses are quality-of-life
violations, including smoking cannabis, urinating or defecating in public, consuming or possessing
alcohol in public, conducting business on the streets, and staying in parks after hours.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas moved to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading, seconded by
Mayor Meiner.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine asked what procedures the Municipal Prosecution Team must
follow. He explained that the message being sent is that the Commission is done with the same
people repeatedly terrorizing the City. It is not a large swath of problem makers that the City has;
rather, it is a very small number of individuals. He then turned to the Chief of Police and asked
whether it was a fair assumption that the most violent and serious crimes were not committed by
first-time offenders.
Chief of Police Wayne Jones stated that Commissioner Magazine is correct. He explained that,
anecdotally, the Police experience is that people who commit various crimes in the City are multiple
offenders, sometimes even offending across the country in multiple states. This year alone, some
people they arrested already had dozens of arrests in the City, in Florida, and across the country.
Commissioner Magazine states that he would like to spend more time working with or speaking to
the Municipal Prosecution Team. They are receiving a clear message that the City is done with this.
.June 24, 2026
He continues by saying that the Commission wants to protect its residents, visitors, tourists, and
the City. He again highlights that the Municipal Prosecution Team is receiving a clear, unified
message about the direction the Commission wants to take, and he thanks them for all the work
they do. He ends by saying that it is not just about managing caseloads, but about getting the people
who are terrorizing the community off the streets.
Mayor Meiner explained to his colleagues that he has a meeting with the Municipal Prosecution
Team next week to determine whether there is anything the Commission can do to help. He says
that early on, when they did not have the robust team they have now, they were not prosecuting.
He had put in legislation that essentially required the prosecution to do its job, and he explains how
that shows the Commission is collectively willing and able to work and bear the brunt of this issue.
He then highlighted the example of an individual with eighty-seven prior arrests and asked why
someone always in the middle of trouble was on the street in the first place. He ended by saying
that there are too many people terrorizing the City and recidivists who should not be on the streets.
Roll Call: 7-0.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, APPROVING, FOLLOWING FIRST READING, AS AUTHORIZED UNDER SECTION 1.03(B)(1) OF THE CITY CHARTER AND SECTION 82-37 OF THE CITY CODE, A FIRST AMENDMENT (FIRST AMENDMENT) TO THE AGREEMENT OF LEASE DATED SEPTEMBER 1, 1999 BETWEEN THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH (OWNER), AND RK RIVANI, LLC, (TENANT) RELATING TO THE REAL PROPERTY LOCATED AT 1691 MICHIGAN AVENUE (PROPERTY), SAID FIRST AMENDMENT PROVIDING, IN PRINCIPAL PART, FOR (I) A LEASE TERM EXTENSION FOR TWO (2) ADDITIONAL TWENTY (20) YEAR OPTIONS FOR A TOTAL REMAINING TERM OF ONE HUNDRED SIX (106) YEARS; (II) AN INCREASE TO THE BASE RENT AND PERCENTAGE RENT; (III) MARKET RENT ADJUSTMENTS CAPPED AT TWENTY PERCENT AT LEASE YEAR FIFTY AND SEVENTY AND ANY SUBSEQUENT MARKET RENT ADJUSTMENTS TO BE CAPPED AT THIRTY-THREE PERCENT; (IV) THE CONSTRUCTION BY TENANT OF APPROXIMATELY 47,000 SQUARE FEET OF OFFICE SPACE AND OTHER IMPROVEMENTS ABOVE THE PARKING GARAGE AT THE PROPERTY HAVING AN APPROXIMATE VALUE OF $50 MILLION (EXPANSION IMPROVEMENTS); (V) A MAXIMUM BUILDING HEIGHT OF ONE HUNDRED (100) FEET; (VI) THE ADJUSTMENT OF TOTAL REQUIRED PARKING FOR THIS GARAGE TO FOUR HUNDRED TWENTY-FIVE (425) .June 24, 2026 PARKING SPACES; AND (VII) THE PROVISION BY TENANT OF ADDITIONAL PUBLIC BENEFITS HAVING A VALUE OF ONE MILLION THREE HUNDRED THOUSAND DOLLARS ($1,300,000); WAIVING THE FORMAL COMPETITIVE BIDDING REQUIREMENTS BY A FIVE- SEVENTHS (5/7TH) VOTE AS PERMITTED UNDER SECTION 1.03(B)(1)(IV) OF THE CITY CHARTER AND SECTION 82-39(A) OF THE CITY CODE; SUCH FIRST AMENDMENT BEING SUBJECT TO THE APPROVAL BY A MAJORITY VOTE OF THE VOTERS IN A CITY-WIDE REFERENDUM AND CONDITIONED ON TENANT’S OBTAINING A MASTER BUILDING PERMIT FOR THE EXPANSION IMPROVEMENTS BY OR BEFORE JULY 1, 2031 AND

ACTION: Resolution adopted on First Reading. The Title of the Resolution was read into the
record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Magazine made a motion to adopt the
Resolution on First Reading, seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 7-0. The Second
Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for July 22, 2026.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Vice-Mayor Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for July 22, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to notice.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Ozzie Dominguez and Office
of the City Attorney to handle.
DIRECTION:
Between First and Second Reading:
 Keep the current public benefits in place as negotiated.
 Have the sponsor team meet with neighbors in the surrounding area, including the Palm View
Neighborhood Association, to determine what is important to them and what they want.
 Explore whether the variance between current lease revenues and the prospective increased
revenues can be directed toward infrastructure needs in the Palm View neighborhood.
 Avoid allocating public benefit funds toward temporary, short-term Lincoln Road projects so as
not to waste funds when long-term infrastructure needs exist.
 Continue evaluating infrastructure funding needs, particularly in Palm View, during the broader
budget discussions.
Commissioner Magazine introduced the Item and explained that one of the things that has helped
this chart a different path forward, away from the anything-goes nightlife and partying image that so
often was synonymous with Miami Beach, is attracting businesses. They are building a real
economy, and at times, what gets lost in that is not just these high-level office buildings, but also
what was, for so long, missing in Miami as a region and in Miami Beach: opportunity for everyday
people. When he moved to New York City out of college, he believed he could be anything. There
.June 24, 2026
were opportunities, and that is even romanticized in songs, such as "If you can make it in New York
City, you can make it anywhere." That was not always the case with Miami Beach or Miami in
general. For so long, it was a city in a region where people could move here and have a great life,
or people could move here without much opportunity for upward mobility. He is proud of the
Commission for helping further that charge. It was actually the late former Commissioner Samuelian
who was one of the original champions of economic development and office overlay incentives,
which really helped set that path in motion, and he is proud to help carry the torch on. For full
disclosure, the applicant and property owner is a very good friend of his. He was not involved in
negotiating a single Item of any of the terms, as that was all done by City staff. There is nothing that
would prevent him from acting impartially or fairly in this. The terms were negotiated with City staff.
This allows a City-owned asset to receive a $50 million investment from the property owner, which
he can only make if he has a longer lease extension to recoup that money. Ultimately, the City will
inherit the asset, and, most importantly, what they get in the interim. Now they have a lease
agreement in place that gives them a gross percentage of the rent received from the building. When
the property owner bought the property years ago, it was 30% occupied, and rents were struggling
for a Class B-type property. He made a substantial investment, and now he is almost fully occupied
with rents that are much higher. The City receives a percentage of rent, so they have a vested
interest in that building performing well, which becomes even more important in November, when
homestead property taxes are going to be on the ballot. It becomes more critical than in Miami
Beach and other cities and municipalities in Florida to diversify their revenue stream and receive a
substantial increase in revenues from commercial properties, as this project does. He asked Ozzy
Dominguez, Division Director of Asset Management, to focus on the lease revenues they are
receiving now and what they are pro forma. So not only is the property owner making substantial
capital investments in an asset that they will inherently get, but they also get increased value right
now, every single year, for revenues that will be needed more than ever in November. He
appreciates the work the team has done, which has been months of negotiations back and forth,
but he is very excited because, to him, this is not just one asset that they are talking about, but it
marks the new pace that they are turning in Miami Beach.
Ozzy Dominguez, Division Director of Asset Management, added that this would be a great
partnership with an existing tenant who will continue to invest in this asset under a lease with the
City. The ground lease agreement runs through 2052 with two 20-year extensions. This new
amendment will provide for two additional 20-year extensions to the property. It will increase the
gross revenue percentage from 2.5% to 3%, allowing them to generate more revenue, especially
once they complete their expansion. They have a base rent structure that increases every five
years. Through 2027, that base rent is $392,000; in 2028, with a minimum percentage increase of
12%, it will increase to $439,000. With the new structure, they have increased minimum rents for
the second phase of the project. If the tenant receives the TCO by January 1, 2033, the minimum
rent will increase to $500,000 plus a 12% increase. He replied to Commissioner Magazine that
when Phase II gets TCO or CO, and it is an increase, the City will receive it for the life of the lease,
compounded by the five-year total increases, and they will continue to escalate. At the end of the
day, the minimum base rent will increase to $575,000, plus the 12% escalations that correspond to
those years. In addition, if the TCO is not achieved between January 1 and December 31, 2033,
the minimum rents will increase to $515,000. The reason they included this is that they want to keep
the tenant motivated to get the project done, and if there is a delay that causes a potential
percentage of gross revenue, they want to be able to capitalize on that as well, so the City is not
out and the tenant feels motivated. The Administration is extremely confident that the tenant will
meet every benchmark. The Administration has set several benchmarks to ensure the tenant does
not fall behind, stays motivated, and gets the project permitted, TCO, and open and operating. By
the end of 2033, the base minimum rent would have increased to $575,000 plus the 12%
escalations for the corresponding years. Additionally, the tenant has agreed to $1.3 million in public
benefits to include: $600,000 in cash contributions for the Lincoln Road Master Plan, $100,000 for
.June 24, 2026
tipsters for human trafficking programs, $50,000.00 in total cash contributions to support the Miami
Beach Sister Cities Program, $250,000 for general programs, $300,000 for parking programs
valued for 110 parking passes that the Parking Department could convert into passes for workforce
employees or Miami Beach residents at City rates instead of private developer rates. There is also
the contribution to the Art in Public Places, which is 2% of the hard construction costs. He
recognized Mr. Larkin.
Michael Larkin, representing Robert Rivani, is here with Robert and Nicolas Rodriguez. They are
pleased to be here seeking this lease amendment. Mr. Rivani took over an aging City asset that
was hardly leased and increased occupancy to almost 100%, even while undergoing Phase I
renovation of the existing building. That goes to show what a great salesman he is and how much
he has energized the City asset. Now he wants to embark upon Phase II, which consists of new
office square footage, a 6,000-square-foot restaurant, and padel courts, all in an attached addition
on the south side of the existing office building. Mr. Larkin proposed modifying one public benefit:
reduce the $100,000 for maintenance/restoration of a religious institutional use in the Palm View
neighborhood to $50,000, and add a $50,000 category for a 17th Street Master Plan; he will work
with Ozzy and City Attorney Ricardo J. Dopico to formalize the change for Second Reading on July
22. As Ozzy Dominguez mentioned, there is a series of public benefits they are happy to offer the
City. One of the public benefits requires a $100,000 payment for the maintenance and restoration
of a religious institutional use in the Palm View neighborhood. In further discussions with the elected
official, they requested that amount and added a new category, the creation of a 17th Street Master
Plan, at $50,000, with maintenance for the religious use at $50,000. That would be the only change,
and they can work with Division Director of Asset Management Dominguez and City Attorney
Ricardo J. Dopico in formalizing that change as they come back for Second Reading on July 22,
2026.
Ozzy Dominguez, Division Director of Asset Management, continued that the Administration
recommends that the City Commission adopt the Resolution accepting the recommendation of the
Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee at the June 5th meeting and set the Second Reading
for July 22, 2026.
Commissioner Suarez added that, respectfully, the public benefits are great and everybody has a
passion project, but he would like to propose something else if his colleagues agree. They are going
through a budget crisis, whether they like it or not. Last night, he received a text message from a
resident that read, “You're supporting this Rivani lease thing; Palm View is listed as a public
beneficiary but never even heard about it until yesterday.” He is supportive of the project, but the
public benefit portion should be directed toward infrastructure. The City has the West Avenue
project with at least a $7 million gap. Why not have the developer pay toward that, which will greatly
enhance the value of his property while also helping meet infrastructure needs? As Commissioners,
their primary responsibilities are public safety and infrastructure, and they have had productive
discussions at the Budget Hearing about how to pay for some of these projects. He thinks the
benefits they are willing to offer should go to infrastructure.
Commissioner Magazine suggested threading that needle while preserving these public benefits.
Part of that was that if they agree to this, they are going to be getting more money each year, not
50 years from now, but starting almost immediately because of the new leases.
In reply to Commissioner Magazine, Ozzy Dominguez explained that upon TCO, the additional cost
is $50,000 or $60,000, but the rent kicks in once the project opens and operates and revenue starts
coming in, with an extra bump from the 3% on the new project that was not originally generating
any gross revenue for the City at all.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Magazine suggested that the variance between what they will receive prospectively
and what they are receiving currently could be directed toward the Palm View infrastructure project,
which will enable these public benefits to remain in place while also addressing very much-needed
infrastructure challenges in the Palm View neighborhood.
Commissioner Suarez agreed to look into that between First and Second Reading, but in his
opinion, it is good practice to have a developer agreement to fund infrastructure. This Item will go
to Referendum, and although he does not personally think it will pass, if the ballot question states
that public benefit will fund infrastructure, it will be a better sell to all residents. That is his two cents.
It will be a shame if this goes forward and does not pass the referendum, and nothing gets funded.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez explained that they had several discussions about the public benefits and
the project, and that this is going to transform that area. She is very excited about it. She has had
a hard hat tour, and a lot of really good things are going to happen there. With respect to the public
benefit, the total dollar value was $1.3 million, with $200,000 for general, and they broke it down
into other pieces. Discussion held.
Ozzie Dominguez indicated that $300,000 is the real value because it is related to the parking
passes and parking that they are going to be providing. That has no hard monetary value to them,
so in total it is really $1 million plus the Art in Public Places contribution.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez added that those are the things that can help the community without using
taxpayer dollars, and when they look at infrastructure projects, there are hundreds of millions of
dollars over many years, so $1.3 million in public benefit would not even make a dent in any of it.
She asked CFO Jason Greene whether they are in a budget crisis, as she does not feel they are.
Do they need to look at their numbers and tighten their belts for next year, especially if the property
tax Item passes the voters? Are they in a budget crisis today?
CFO Jason Greene explained that, as someone who is always fiscally conservative, it is important
to scrutinize every expenditure and ensure it is being spent in the most prudent way. As they
discussed at the Budget Workshop last week, they are in a situation where the increase in taxable
values is smaller than needed. When they meet in July to start going through the budget, they will
end at a minimum of about $8 million in cuts. The City Commission requested a rollback rate budget,
which the Administration will be delivering and which will be closer to a $15 to $17 million cut. It is
important to distinguish between recurrent and one-time items. On a recurring basis, they look at
recurring revenues coming in, and Commissioner Magazine was alluding to that with leases, which
are recurrent revenues for the next 50 to 100 years. The property is a one-time Item, and there is a
philosophical debate about how to utilize this one-time money.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez added that, given the amount of public benefits discussed at the Committee
and now at the Commission, she is comfortable keeping it as negotiated. She would love to hear
from her colleagues. Discussion held.
Commissioner Suarez is supportive of the Item and thinks it is great for Lincoln Road and the overall
well-being of the City. He had an idea for the public benefit of $1 million, aside from the parking, to
take that benefit and put it toward infrastructure. They have a $7 million West Avenue Phase III that
is underfunded, so whatever cost they can bring down, and time and time again from emails he has
received, why not have the developer pay for it? This is a perfect example of how they can do that.
It may not make a huge dent, but $1 million is $1 million, and it could help. All the benefits are great,
but infrastructure and public safety come first and foremost. They are going to make budgetary cuts
not only to satisfy what he thinks is going to pass this November, but also for the rollback rate, so
he is prioritizing the public benefit dollars for infrastructure and paying down that price tag.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Fernandez noted that there are a number of public benefits associated with this Item,
for example, the 17th Street Master Plan. They all want to see the street improve in the heart of the
neighborhood. There is the Cuban Hebrew congregation, which he has heard about for a long time
from neighbors in the area, and the lack of maintenance because it is an aging congregation and
they do not have the membership or revenue to maintain the property itself. They have a chance to
make direct improvements to the neighborhood. He is going to give deference to the sponsor of the
Item, the Chair of the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee, who has been very focused
on their infrastructure projects and has always guided them responsibly on these matters. Perhaps
a better approach could be reinvesting the dollars from the lease into the infrastructure. That might
be a way in which this renegotiated agreement can help support infrastructure projects, but there
are needs within the business community around Lincoln Road that affect the quality of life of
residents. There is a need for property maintenance on properties fronting 17th Street, and there is
a need for envisioning what the future of 17th Street is going to look like, for which they need these
dollars. He gave deference to Commissioner Magazine, as he has been working hard on this Item.
Commissioner Magazine appreciates Commissioner Suarez’s comment; this is not about what they
want but about what passes in November. He suggested moving this along to Second Reading and,
in the interim, put it on the sponsor team to go out and talk to neighbors in the surrounding area
and to the Palm View Neighborhood Association, to find out what is important to them and what
they want, because they are elected to represent their constituents and he wants the public benefits
to be in line with what they want. They have a tremendous starting point; he does not picture them
deviating materially, but if there is $100,000, they can shift from something they wanted to
something more needed, and they can have those conversations within the next month. The deal
team should be having conversations with the neighborhoods; he agrees with Commissioner
Fernandez and suggested the same. For the increase in the next couple of years in the pro forma
prospective lease payment, they may receive, and they can direct those funds to neighborhood
improvements in that area, such as infrastructure projects and related initiatives.
Commissioner Suarez noted that for the Lincoln Road improvements, they had a discussion a year

ACTION: Resolution adopted on First Reading. The Title of the Resolution was read into the
record. The Public Hearing was held. A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez to adopt
the Resolution on First Reading, seconded by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas. Vote: 7-0. Second
Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for July 22, 2026.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
David Gomez to handle.
David Gomez, CIP Director, introduced the First Amendment and Restated Development
Agreement for 1250 West Avenue. The amendment consists of five components: 1) extending the
deadline to obtain the easement agreements for the three Baywalk links (this does not alter the
completion deadline, only the time the developer has to establish the easement agreements); 2)
clarifying the developer’s ability to construct the Baywalk behind 1250 over water instead of over
land (it aligns with the plans for the adjacent properties, and they will have to transition to the
property north of them to allow them to construct that piece over water); 3) modifying the property
description to allow an increase in ground retail space from 4,000 square feet to 17,000 square feet
to accommodate a fitness center and other amenities as proposed; 4) documenting that the City’s
.June 24, 2026
floodplain management requirements in effect at the time of building permit submittal will govern
the project (as is standard practice); 5) minor technical cleanup language (e.g., removing the name
of a former owner). In reply to Mayor Meiner, he clarified that there is no increase in FAR.
Commissioner Fernandez addressed the applicant and indicated that, most importantly to him, the
residents who have lived at 1250 West and have to move receive the assistance needed to continue
living in the City. He asked where they are today with the rental assistance and how many people
are going to benefit.
Michael Larkin, representing the applicant, explained that 107 tenants qualified. Ten checks have
been sent via FedEx, and seven have been delivered. There are 35 tenants whose checks will be
mailed by June 30, and at least 62 tenants have not yet told them where they are going to live; once
they do, they will send checks. In response to Commissioner Fernandez, he noted that letters can
be sent as a follow-up to remind them that this is their time. If they do not tell them within a year’s
time, the money goes to the City, and the City can allocate it to them. In reply to Commissioner
Fernandez, he added that the total amount of assistance provided to tenants is $548,000. He noted
that checks are being issued as lease terminations occur and that assistance is provided when
tenants confirm their new housing plans. In continued questions from Commissioner Fernandez,
he confirmed that there is no height increase, no new ground-level construction, and no FAR.
Commissioner Fernandez moved to adopt the Resolution on First Reading, seconded by
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, announced the Public Hearing.
Daniel Ciraldo, via Zoom, cautioned the public that multiple lawsuits have been filed this week by
the owner against tenants for eviction, and he is not sure why that was not disclosed. He asked
whether that can be discussed and whether the City can provide assistance to these tenants who
are being evicted due to a Commission-approved FAR increase that did not go to the voters.
Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, noted that with no one else on Zoom or in the audience requesting
to speak, the Public Hearing was closed.
A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez, seconded by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas, to
adopt the Resolution on First Reading. Vote: 7-0.
Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for July 22, 2026.

ACTION: Resolution 2026-34335 was adopted. Commissioner Alex Fernandez made a motion
to adopt the Resolution, seconded by Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
John Rebar to handle.
Corinne Ouelhadj Engel introduced herself and asked to say a few words. She has called Miami
Beach home for nearly 15 years and is the founder of the French American Association of Craft and
Trade, a non-profit organization run entirely by volunteers. She said that as an artisan herself, she
supports craftsmanship and small businesses. It is not just her profession; it is her soul. She
informed the Commission that the French Market was established during the pandemic to support
artisans and small business owners in continuing their work during a challenging time. She
explained that since then, it has become a community. They carefully select their artisans to ensure
quality, authenticity, and professionalism. After their first year in South Pointe Park, they were proud
to see the positive impact the market had, with residents saying they enjoyed the atmosphere and
sense of community. She said that they are committed to being respectful neighbors, paying close
attention to cleanliness, organization, safety, and the overall experience for residents, visitors, and
local businesses. She continued by saying that in a world driven by mass production, preserving
craftsmanship and supporting small businesses are more important now than ever. She thanked
the City of Miami Beach Events and Recreation Department for its support of the French Market.
She also thanked Mayor Steven Meiner and the rest of the Commission for their support and trust
to artisans. She ended by saying that the organization is run mostly by women and families.
Mayor Steven Meiner responded that he remembers some of the culinary events they held, which
featured hundreds of participants and French media coverage.
Ms. Engel responded that the organization supports all of the artisans. One way they do this is
th
through contests to let their work shine. Their next major event is on October 25 for the best
croissant and best baguette in Florida, for which they expect over 600 visitors.
John Rebar added that the Administration fully supports and is excited to continue its relationship.

Matteo-Salinas. Vote: 7-0.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34336 was adopted. Commissioner Matteo-Salinas made a motion to
adopt the Resolution, seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Jose Gonzalez and Tameka Otto Stewart to handle.
Mayor Steven Meiner stated that he had brought an Item to help seniors get to Walmart last year.
He also added that getting around is a challenge for some seniors, citing seniors who live in
Rebecca Towers and Stella Maris as examples. He ended by acknowledging his support for
continuing to provide transportation for seniors before turning it over to Commissioner Monica
Matteo-Salinas.
Commissioner Monica Matteo Salinas informed her colleagues that during a recent visit to the Stella
Maris house in North Beach, she learned that residents appreciated having transportation to
Walmart off of Miami Beach once a month, because they don’t have cars and, as they are elderly,
it is difficult for them to get to and from the grocery store. She added that they don’t live in a walkable
area near a grocery store, so they would have to take public transportation. Most of the seniors she
spoke to want to be able to visit a grocery store at least once a week, which she believes is
reasonable. Some of them asked for twice a week. She stated that she doesn’t believe they have
the budget for that, but that they do have the budget for the proposed Item. The Item states that the
seniors would have access to transportation three times a month to the local Publix, and once a
month to the Walmart off of Miami Beach in case they need to get anything that Publix doesn’t have.
A motion was made by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas to approve the Item, seconded by
Commissioner Alex Fernandez. Vote: 7-0.
Commissioner Tanya Bhatt asked to be a co-sponsor to the Item.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine asked whether the City has any services in some of the elderly
communities that help facilitate online ordering, and suggested that it would be a good idea.
City Manager Carpenter responded that he did not have the answer but would coordinate with the
Housing and Community Services Department to look into the matter.
items.motion: Matteo-Salinas made a motion to adopt the Resolution, seconded by Commissioner Fernandez.

items.action: Resolution 2026-34338 was adopted. Vice-Mayor Dominguez made a motion to adopt the Resolution, seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 6-0. Absent: Commissioner Suarez.

Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes

Chief Digna Abello and Tameka Otto Stewart to handle.
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez stated that during a recent meeting with Fire Chief Digna Abello and
members of her team, they discussed the importance of partnering with OneBlood to strengthen
life-safety capabilities within the Fire Department. She invited Fire Chief Abello to elaborate.
Fire Chief Digna Abello informed the Commission that the Department was requesting support for
a new initiative that would allow frontline rescue units to carry whole blood. She said that Miami
Beach would be the first jurisdiction in Miami-Dade County to implement this measure and that
fewer than 2% of agencies statewide currently do so. Since December, the Department has
responded to 115 trauma calls, and approximately 10 to 15 of those patients could have benefited
from the availability of whole blood. Fire Chief Abello explained that saline does not transport
oxygen to vital organs and does not clot, while whole blood does both. She emphasized that having
whole blood on rescue units would significantly increase survival chances for critically injured
trauma patients. She added that the Department was working with the hospital to ensure that blood
supplies could be rotated before expiration. Fire Chief Abello noted that the Medical Director was
available online if additional information was needed.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez moved to adopt the Resolution, seconded by Commissioner Fernandez.
Vote: 6-0. Absent: Commissioner Suarez.
