items.action: The Committee of the Whole Meeting was held. The Item was continued to July 22, 2026. The Mayor and City Commission held a discussion regarding the annual evaluation of City Manager Eric Carpenter, focusing on overall performance, alignment with Commission priorities, and whether a merit increase or compensation adjustment was appropriate at this time.
items.voteBasis: No separate vote identified. A vote has not been inferred.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: The Committee of the Whole Meeting was held. The Item was continued to July 22,
2026.
The Mayor and City Commission held a discussion regarding the annual evaluation of City Manager
Eric Carpenter, focusing on overall performance, alignment with Commission priorities, and whether
a merit increase or compensation adjustment was appropriate at this time.
Mayor Steven Meiner opened by noting that the purpose of the review was to assess the City
Manager’s progress in key areas and determine next steps.
City Manager Carpenter emphasized that his work centered on delivering the City’s strategic
priorities, public safety, cleanliness, infrastructure, housing, and culture, while improving operational
efficiency, strengthening the municipal workforce, and enhancing service delivery. He expressed
pride in the City’s progress over his two-year tenure and welcomed candid feedback.
Mayor Meiner expressed concern that policing practices, particularly Officer visibility, had not met
commitments made during contract negotiations and noted moments when he felt the City Manager
had not fully supported him or other Commissioners.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez recognized general improvement but raised concerns about
economic development, workforce vacancies, such as the Building Department leadership role, and
staff actions that appeared misaligned with the Commission's direction. He cited examples such as
public safety uniforms and freight-loading zone policies.
Commissioner David Suarez cited inadequate parking enforcement and cleanliness in North Beach,
expressing frustration that these issues often required his personal intervention. He also identified
challenges in public safety and homelessness and questioned whether the City Manager’s
residence outside Miami Beach affected the City Manager's daily situational awareness. While
acknowledging the success of Spring Break operations, he emphasized that the Commission’s
legislation and policy direction played a significant role in that outcome, and he stated that he would
not support a merit increase.
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez praised City Manager Carpenter’s responsiveness, work ethic, and
leadership, while urging a renewed focus on recruiting top-tier talent in tourism and economic
development.
Commissioner Fernandez reaffirmed his trust in City Manager Carpenter, clarifying that his
concerns were not meant to diminish confidence in the City Manager’s integrity.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine commended City Manager Carpenter but noted growing
complacency within the workforce and a need for renewed accountability. He urged the
Administration to focus on day-to-day operational issues, ensure greater employee presence in the
field, and embrace proactive thinking about major opportunities, such as tourism innovation and
upcoming global events.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas also expressed high regard for City Manager Carpenter’s
personal performance while raising concerns about employee management, departmental
leadership consistency, and policy execution. She recommended stronger guidance for directors
and leadership development initiatives.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt shared positive resident feedback on improvements in North Beach
and highlighted the importance of strong leadership in tourism and culture, while also noting gaps
in routine issue detection and the need for greater staff engagement in assessing field conditions.
Mayor Meiner observed that the general consensus was that the City had improved but still had
substantial room for progress, particularly in visible policing, operational consistency, and response
to everyday quality-of-life concerns.
The discussion then shifted to compensation.
Mayor Meiner stated that City Manager Carpenter had not received a merit increase in 2025
because the issue had not been discussed. He noted that if the Commission were to approve 3%
merit increases for both years, the City Manager’s compensation would increase accordingly.
Commissioner Suarez stated that the City was in the middle of the budget process and that he did
not believe increases could be justified at that time. He stated that, based on his view of
performance and the need to reduce the budget, he would not support a merit increase.
Commissioner Magazine asked whether the City Manager’s compensation figure represented
salary only or salary plus benefits.
The City Manager confirmed that he believed it reflected salary.
Commissioner Magazine also asked whether the contract included a potential bonus.
The City Manager stated that while one was contemplated, it was discretionary and he was not
requesting it.
Commissioner Magazine stated that if he voted against a merit increase, it would not be due to
performance concerns but because he viewed the starting salary as already substantial.
Commissioner Bhatt asked whether the City Manager receives an annual cost-of-living (COLA)
adjustment.
The City Manager stated that he receives the same adjustment provided to rank-and-file
employees.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas asked whether he had received the most recent adjustment, and the
City Manager confirmed that he had.
Mayor Meiner stated that he entered the meeting inclined to support a 3% merit increase for one
year only, emphasizing that he believed the City Manager’s performance exceeded the lower rating
referenced earlier, although improvement was still expected. He stated that he would support the
increase if there was Commission consensus.
Commissioner Fernandez noted that a 3% increase represents a significant adjustment at the City
Manager’s compensation level.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Suarez stated that the question was whether current conditions warranted a 3%
increase in addition to the COLA adjustment already provided.
Commissioner Fernandez asked whether the budget process could result in the loss of salaried
positions in Police, Fire, or Ocean Rescue.
The City Manager stated that Police and Fire contracts include no-layoff provisions, though
reductions through attrition might be necessary to meet rollback requirements.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that if the City could potentially lose public safety or resident-facing
positions, he could not justify increasing the compensation of an already highly compensated City
Manager, even though he believed the City Manager was doing a good job.
Mayor Meiner stated that he did not view the issues as equivalent, noting that turnover and savings
could also come from senior positions and that the City Manager role carries unique responsibilities.
Commissioner Suarez responded that City employment is a privilege and that a merit increase
should not be motivated by concern that the City Manager might leave.
Mayor Meiner stated that his support was based on performance.
Commissioner Suarez suggested waiting six months and reconsidering a merit increase if
noticeable improvement occurred, stating that doing so could incentivize progress on issues
discussed.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez stated that she did not believe delaying recognition was fair because the
City Manager had already completed the prior year, had performed strongly, and had helped
manage major events. She stated that reconsideration for the following year might be reasonable,
but the prior year deserved recognition.
Mayor Meiner stated that the City had achieved many positive outcomes, including resort tax
performance and increased visibility tied to major international events. He stated that, while he had
frustrations, the overall picture was positive and recognition was appropriate. He clarified that he
was proposing one 3% merit increase, not two.
Commissioner Magazine stated that, drawing from private-sector experience, there were years
when employees performed well but did not receive raises due to financial constraints. He pointed
to the COLA adjustment the City Manager had already received.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas stated that she believed certain major opportunities had not been
handled as effectively as they could have been, and she referenced FIFA-related activations that
her office and Commissioner Magazine’s office helped facilitate. She stated that while these
activations ultimately generated meaningful benefits, she was concerned that the Administration
had not identified or initiated these opportunities earlier. She then asked for clarification regarding
compensation adjustments.
The City Manager confirmed receiving a 3% COLA adjustment in consecutive years.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas stated that approving an additional 3% merit increase would
effectively amount to a combined 6% increase for that year.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Bhatt clarified that the proposal was a 3% merit increase for 2026 only, separate
from the COLA adjustment, and that the 2025 merit issue had not been addressed previously.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that the decision was challenging because the City Manager is
responsive, hardworking, committed, and acts with integrity. He noted that integrity in public service
cannot be quantified. However, given the City’s fiscal constraints, including discussions about utility
rates and potential impacts on resident-facing positions, he could not justify the increase on financial
grounds, despite supporting it on its merits. He also noted that the City Manager began at a lower
salary and progressed from there.
The City Manager explained that his contract promised Tier B retirement, but he later learned he
would need to fund his own entry into that tier at high personal cost.
Commissioner Magazine stated that he was not frustrated with the City Manager and would
evaluate his performance positively, but believed his current level of compensation was adequate.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez asked to proceed with a vote on the 3% merit increase.
Mayor Meiner clarified that the discussion concerned a 3% merit increase for 2026 only.
Commissioner Magazine stated that he would ask all Charter Officers to show leadership during a
difficult budget year. He noted that Charter Officers are highly compensated and that decisions may
affect other employees’ positions. For that reason, he stated that Charter Officers should accept
the COLA adjustment and forego merit increases this year.
Commissioner Bhatt suggested a compromise of a 1.5% merit increase instead of the full 3%, noting
that the City Manager deserved recognition but that the City faced financial pressures. She stated
that a reduced increase would acknowledge performance while demonstrating shared
responsibility.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez stated that other employees had received merit reviews the prior year when
the City Manager had not, and she believed that was inequitable.
Commissioner Fernandez asked the City Manager to elaborate on the Tier B matter.
The City Manager explained that his contract aligned his benefits with those of prior City Managers,
excluding additional vacation time. He noted that because the position tends to have a shorter
tenure, clarity on retirement was important. He stated that although Tier B was included in his
contract, concerns arose upon review of the implementing Ordinance, leading him to fund his own
entry into Tier B over multiple years at no cost to the City.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that this context altered his perspective on the compensation
discussion, noting that public perception of the City Manager’s compensation did not reflect his
personal costs associated with Tier B. He asked whether there was a way to address that issue so
that the public record more accurately reflected the circumstances.
The City Manager stated that he would be willing to forego discussion of merit increases for the
past two years if the Commission wished to have a broader conversation about Tier B.
Mayor Meiner stated that the Tier B context was significant, as public perception would otherwise
focus solely on compensation levels during a budget reduction period.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Magazine stated that he would support a 1% merit increase across all Charter
Officers and would not support a higher percentage for any one of them, noting that his position
was based on fiscal conditions rather than performance.
Mayor Meiner stated that he was open to discussing all Charter Officer compensation together, but
noted that time was limited and other Charter Officers had not yet spoken.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas stated that she supported a 3% merit increase for the City Manager
because of the Tier B issue.
City Attorney Ricardo J. Dopico stated that if the Commission opted for a reduced merit increase, it
could consider providing additional vacation time.
Commissioner Magazine stated that he would support additional working vacation days that could
not be cashed out. He then moved for a 1% merit increase across all Charter Officers, along with
one additional week of non-cashable working vacation.
Commissioner Fernandez asked the City Manager how he felt about adjusting his salary to account
for the Tier B issue.
The City Manager responded that the matter would require a broader discussion.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that resolving the issue too quickly would not serve anyone well and
that several legitimate concerns had not yet been fully addressed.
Mayor Meiner asked whether the Commission wished to continue the discussion at the July 22,
2026, Commission Meeting.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez stated that she believed the votes existed to proceed on the City Manager’s
Item, but that the discussion appeared to be moving toward continuation.
There was a consensus to continue the Item to July 22, 2026.

items.title: DISCUSS/TAKE ACTION – ISSUANCE OF A REQUEST FOR LETTERS OF INTEREST (RFLI) OR REQUEST FOR PROPOSALS (RFP) FOR THE CITY-OWNED PROPERTY LOCATED AT 7605 COLLINS AVENUE FOR RECREATIONAL AND PUBLIC USE, IN ALIGNMENT WITH COMMUNITY PRIORITIES.
items.action: Discussion held. Motion by Commissioner Fernandez to direct the Administration to draft a Request for Letters of Interest (RFLI) for the City-owned property located at 7605 Collins Avenue for a Marine Science Center, consistent with the community’s expressed preferences. The draft RFLI will return to the City Commission for review in July. The motion was seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Vote: 7-0.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Discussion held. Motion by Commissioner Fernandez to direct the Administration to
draft a Request for Letters of Interest (RFLI) for the City-owned property located at 7605
Collins Avenue for a Marine Science Center, consistent with the community’s expressed
preferences. The draft RFLI will return to the City Commission for review in July. The motion
was seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Kristy Bada and Ozzie Dominguez.
Commissioner Fernandez explained that the Item had remained on the agenda for a long time, and
credited aides for providing notes to keep track of its progress. He stated that the longstanding goal
had been to transform the property into a dynamic community asset. He described extensive
conversations with residents from North Beach and neighbors living directly across from the site,
all of whom voiced strong interest in converting the house into a Marine Life Center or museum. To
achieve this, he said, the City had explored different approaches, ideally aiming toward a
public-private partnership that would relieve the City of shouldering the financial burden. He
expressed interest in hearing the views of his colleagues and noted that the original purpose of the
Item was to discuss the potential issuance of an RFLI to measure community interest from
organizations that could operate the site without requiring additional taxpayer funding. He
emphasized that the City possesses the asset and can make it available to an operator that could
.June 24, 2026
activate it without additional City outlays.
Commissioner Suarez agreed and added that nearby residents, along with entire condominium
associations, supported establishing a Marine Science Learning Center. He noted that the concept
aligned with the mission of the QEC (Committee for Quality Education in Miami Beach), which had
fully endorsed the idea. He said that North Beach lacked adequate educational projects and that
this initiative would be an important step forward. Commissioner Suarez described the proposal as
an opportunity to honor Miami Beach’s marine habitat and referenced existing Commission
initiatives that carried the same theme. He expressed support for moving the process forward and
determining what groups might be interested in using the property without additional taxpayer
expense.
Commissioner Fernandez proposed making a motion directing the City administration to prepare
an RFLI to identify interest in the site’s potential use. He asked whether the draft RFLI should return
to the City Commission for review before being released and requested guidance from City
Manager Eric Carpenter.
The City Manager explained that, in similar situations, the Commission typically directs the
Administration either to draft and circulate the document or to draft and return it for Commission
approval. He asked the Commission to clarify which approach it preferred.
Commissioner Suarez stated that, based on prior discussions, there had been substantial interest
in establishing a Marine Science Center, which aligned with what had been communicated to
residents. He suggested beginning with that focus and measuring interest among potential
operators.
City Manager Carpenter agreed.
Commissioner Fernandez asked why the draft RFLI would not return to the Commission.
Commissioner Suarez said he might be confused and create further detail.
City Manager Carpenter described the RFLI as similar to an RFP or RFQ, where the City requests
proposals from outside entities that may manage the property as a Marine Learning Center. He said
the question remained whether the Administration should circulate the draft without review or return
it for approval before circulating it.
Commissioner Fernandez stated his preference for drafting the RFLI and returning it to the
Commission to allow time for sharing it with neighborhood residents. He emphasized that the idea
originated with residents living near the property, who had approached Commissioners about the
concept. He said that, before issuing the RFLI, he wished to present a draft to neighbors out of
respect for their longstanding advocacy.
Kristy Bada, Chief Procurement Officer, clarified that an RFLI is an informal process intended to
gauge interest from vendors or prospective proposers who might later participate in a formal
solicitation. She explained that the RFLI does not result in a contract and may remain open for
approximately 30 days, although the timeline can be adjusted. Commissioner Suarez referenced
the timeline, and Kristy Bada reiterated that the period is flexible.
City Manager Carpenter confirmed that the administration could draft the RFLI and return it to the
Commission if that was its direction.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Suarez remarked that the building had been left unused for some time after the City
acquired it and expressed support for taking action, adding that he wished to review the draft.
Commissioner Fernandez agreed and requested the draft at the next meeting to ensure
transparency for neighbors. He stated that the RFLI must clearly articulate that the facility must be
fully self-funded, with the City providing the space but not operational dollars, capital investment or
financial support. He described the property as a premium oceanfront site in an exceptional city and
said the RFLI should determine whether any group was willing to self-fund operations.
Commissioner Magazine asked whether the Commission should cast a wider net, noting that the
site could support family-related and child-focused uses beyond marine science. He said that
broadening the scope would not prevent choosing a marine-related operator later, but might give
the City a fuller picture of interest. He indicated that he would support the sponsors’ direction but
believed that gauging broader interest could be valuable.
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas agreed with Commissioner Magazine. She suggested
expanding the RFLI to include nonprofit organizations generally, saying she wished to understand
the needs of North Beach and determine which nonprofits were interested in office space or
collaborative uses. She referenced the Rhythm Foundation, which had a separate Item seeking
temporary use of the space, and said they might be an appropriate fit. Commissioner Matteo-
Salinas said that the City should listen to its nonprofit community and consider sharing the space
among multiple organizations.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that prior property owners had attempted to commercialize the
site, leading to strong neighborhood opposition. He said the residents in the area felt most
comfortable with a Marine Life Science Center and museum, which could become an important
cultural and educational investment for North Beach. He said he preferred to honor the residents’
longstanding advocacy and maintain the marine focus. He added that if responses proved
underwhelming, the City could reassess the scope later.
Commissioner Suarez agreed and said Commissioners had already navigated extensive
discussions with residents. He said that restarting the process would not be advisable and that a
Marine Science Center was the most appropriate use for the property, especially given its location
east of Collins Avenue. He described the site as ideal for educational programming for families and
children. He noted that the intent was for families and children to learn about marine science at the
facility.
Mayor Meiner called for the vote.
City Clerk Granado stated that Commissioner Fernandez moved to direct the Administration to draft
an RFLI and return it to the City Commission in July (July 22, 2026), and that Commissioner Suarez
seconded the motion.
City Clerk Granado asked for all in favor. Commissioners responded aye. He asked if anyone
opposed. Hearing none, City Clerk Granado announced that the Item was approved by a vote of
seven to zero.
.June 24, 2026

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Discussion heard with Item R7 AH. Commissioner Magazine moved to defer Item R9 AH
and bring Items R7 AH and R9 AH back at 11:00 a.m., time certain, at the July 22, 2026 Commission
Meeting, with direction for the City Attorney to prepare two draft General Obligation (G.O.) Bond
ballot questions for Commission review. Mayor Meiner seconded the motion. Vote: 7-0. The Item
is deferred to July 22, 2026.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
DIRECTION:
 The City Attorney to draft two General Obligation (G.O.) Bond ballot questions for Commission
review.
 Place Items R7 AH and R9 AH on the July 22, 2026 Commission Agenda with an 11:00 a.m.
Time Certain.
Lilia Cardillo to place on the July 22, 2026 Commission Agenda, if received. John Norris,
Jason Greene and Office of the City Attorney to handle.
Mayor Meiner called the Stormwater funding Items and explained that his colleagues can be very
direct or they can discuss the issues and continue the Item. He suggested getting through as much
as they can on the Agenda so they have a better understanding when they have the next
Commission Meeting.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he would prefer voting on the options they like and perhaps taking
a straw Ballot vote.
Mayor Meiner then called Items R9 AH and R7 AH.
Commissioner Magazine stated numerous times that he has a fundamental disagreement with
funding Stormwater and wastewater projects through a General Obligation (G.O.) Bond, as doing
so could add potential stress to the overall General Fund, especially with the uncertainty
surrounding possible Property Tax Reform and how the bond markets may view Florida municipal
debt. That being said, if it is the will of his colleagues, he will be supportive. However, he believes
that there are several projects the City has planned for years, including West Avenue Phase III and
First Street, and that both projects are unique because they have tens of millions of dollars in State
grant funding that would be at risk if the City does not move forward. He stated that even if the City
pursued a broader $800 million General Obligation (G.O.) Bond program and voters ultimately
rejected it, they would still need to advance those projects, and therefore he suggested moving
them forward now to eliminate uncertainty. He noted that the moratorium the Commission placed
on rate increases has already been in effect, unofficially, for a year and a half, during which the rate
decision has been deferred. He recalled that the Administration originally proposed approximately
$800 million of borrowing, but that if the City advanced only those two priority projects, the borrowing
would be closer to $125 to $175 million, which would equate to approximately $3 to $4 per month
per household in the near term. He described that cost as manageable and emphasized that the
City must complete these projects because it has already spent tens of millions of dollars on them
and because the State funding at stake is substantial. Despite his philosophical preference on
funding mechanisms, he stated he would go along with the will of the Body if they choose to pursue
a General Obligation (G.O.) Bond, but suggested carving out those two specific projects and issuing
Stormwater Revenue Bonds so work could begin immediately.
Mayor Meiner stated that he was in line with what Commissioner Magazine mentioned.
In response to Commissioner Fernandez’s question, City Manager Eric Carpenter indicated that
the lifespan of water, sewer, and Stormwater infrastructure is between fifty and eighty years. In
addressing Commissioner Fernandez’s comments, the City Manager noted that if the City
Commission wishes to proceed with that direction, staff can prepare an approximately $800 million
General Obligation (G.O.) Bond program that covers all of the projects.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Fernandez requested to know the average and median impact a homeowner would
pay if the City pursued a General Obligation (G.O.) Bond.
Jason Greene, Chief Financial Officer, noted that Option 1 is to fund the entire eight-year Capital
Program through a General Obligation (G.O.) Bond program, which would involve borrowing
approximately $784 million in debt, including $337 million for Stormwater, $447 million for Water
and Sewer, with the comprehensive program totaling about one billion dollars. A presentation was
shown. Click here to view. Option 1 is to fund Water, Sewer, and Stormwater through a General
Obligation (G.O.) Bond. The other option emerging from the Finance and Economic Resiliency
Committee was a bifurcated model: Stormwater through a General Obligation (G.O.) Bond and
Water and Sewer through utility rate adjustments. CFO Greene explained that both options would
fund Stormwater through a General Obligation (G.O.) Bond in the amount of $337 million, with the
primary question being whether Water and Sewer should be funded through utility rates or included
in the General Obligation (G.O.) Bond. The Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee, through
a motion by Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas, recommended the bifurcated approach. In reply
to Commissioner Fernandez, CFO Greene explained that the Annual General Obligation (G.O.)
Bond Debt Service projection uses updated data from the Property Appraiser. Under that model,
the Max Debt Service is projected in 2035, and for a median Homesteaded property valued at
$317,000, the cost would be approximately $210 annually, and about $616 annually for the average
Homesteaded property. In response to questions from Commissioner Fernandez, CFO Greene
explained that the combined Stormwater and Water and Sewer impacts under Option 1 would be
approximately $725 annually for the median Homesteaded single-family home, and for the median
Residential property (including homesteaded and non-homesteaded), the maximum impact would
be reflected in the 2035 year of the projection. CFO Greene also explained two additional options
considered by the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee: a utility rate increase limited to
West Avenue Phase III and First Street, and a third option covering those two projects plus any
critical Public Works projects, referred to as the “Public Works Super Slim Down Option.”
Commissioner Fernandez stated that with the General Obligation (G.O.) Bond, the median
Homesteaded property would pay approximately $210 annually, compared to the other option being
about $500 more, while still funding the completion of all projects. From his perspective, he favors
this approach because he sees it as a generational improvement for the City. He explained that
residents today will benefit but so will future residents and major commercial property owners who
will enjoy the improvements long after they are completed and will contribute to the cost over time.
He stated that this approach avoids placing the entire burden on today’s residents and allows the
cost to be distributed over thirty years. He asked whether commercial properties pay a larger
percentage than residential properties toward General Obligation (G.O.) Bond repayment.
CFO Greene noted that the City’s tax base is primarily residential, with homesteaded properties
accounting for a little over twenty percent and commercial properties for less than fifty percent.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that his preference is to fund all projects at the lowest possible
cost to residents today. He added that if economic conditions were different, insurance, inflation,
and wages, he might favor a different model; however, given current circumstances, City residents
are facing unique financial pressures, and his preference is to proceed through a General Obligation
(G.O.) Bond.
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas stated that there are multiple options on the table, but the
two General Obligation (G.O.) Bond options are: first, a bifurcated approach with Stormwater funded
through a General Obligation (G.O.) Bond and Water and Sewer funded through utility rates; and
second, a full General Obligation (G.O.) Bond that consolidates Stormwater, Water, and Sewer for
.June 24, 2026
the November ballot, which would be a larger amount. Discussion held.
CFO Greene added that the General Obligation (G.O.) Bond debt estimate would be approximately
$785 million for the consolidated program. He explained that the reason the bifurcated version
requires a different amount is the structure of the financial model, which relies more on
pay-as-you-go (PAYGO) using surplus cash generated by the utility fund. Under the hybrid model,
the City would borrow about $646 million, or roughly $140 million less than the full General
Obligation (G.O.) Bond approach.
In response to questions from Commissioner Matteo-Salinas, Public Works Director John Norris
explained that the Water and Sewer rate increase is significantly less than the original proposal of
about $15 per month and would average approximately $7 per month during the rate-increase
period, based on 5,000 gallons of monthly usage. Public Works Director Norris explained that Miami
Beach has very large houses with large meters, many condominiums, and smaller single-family
homes. While the average usage may be higher, the discussion has focused on the median
household; therefore, the analysis relies on 5,000 gallons, which tracks closer to the median than
the average. Discussion held.
Addressing Commissioner Matteo-Salinas, CFO Greene explained that a smaller home might use
around 3,000 gallons a month, but the median analysis is skewed upward by very large homes;
consequently, 5,000 gallons is a reasonable proxy for the median or slightly above. He stated that
the $7 to $8 per month increase represents about a sixty percent decrease from the original $15
estimate. If the General Obligation (G.O.) Bond is used on the Stormwater side; the G.O. debt
service would max out in 2035 at about $90 annually for the median Homesteaded property and
about $265 annually for the average Homesteaded property.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas expressed a preference for bifurcation, stating that consolidating all
needs into a single large General Obligation (G.O.) Bond could be harder to pass because of the
larger number.
CFO Greene explained that funding Water and Sewer through utility rates is a stronger long-term
model because it generates revenue to support PAYGO and future issuances as debt is retired,
improving the financial sustainability of the utility fund. He reiterated that the hybrid model results
in approximately $140 million less in total debt issuance.
Commissioner Magazine offered a hypothetical, stating that if the City borrows $1,000 and there
are 100 payors, each pays $10. If Property Tax Reform passes in November and homesteaded
payors are removed from the ad valorem base, the same $1,000 must still be repaid by a smaller
pool, increasing the burden on remaining payors. He noted that roughly half of the remaining base
would be residential non-homesteaded renters and stated that this could significantly impact them.
CFO Greene stated that, in a worst-case scenario, a little over ten percent of total properties could
be at zero ad valorem under the constitutional amendment, leaving a smaller pool to cover the same
debt service obligation. He emphasized the practical effect: fewer payors means higher millage for
those who remain.
Mayor Meiner stated that, based on calculations circulated, the worst-case impact could be
approximately $25 million in a billion-dollar budget.
CFO Greene explained that the potential impact on the City’s General Fund property tax revenue
had been estimated at approximately $10 million, and he noted that changing the non-homesteaded
cap (from five percent to ten percent previously discussed) would limit growth going forward. He
.June 24, 2026
reiterated that, as Commissioner Magazine stated, the debt service must be met, and fewer payors
would require higher millage to do so.
Commissioner Magazine clarified that if the City borrows through a General Obligation (G.O.) Bond
and Property Tax Reform passes, the ad valorem burden would be borne by a smaller portion of
the tax base. He stated that homesteaded taxpayers could be exempt from paying ad valorem
under the amendment, leaving the remaining payors holding a larger share of the obligation.
CFO Greene explained that if a homeowner’s taxable value is $250,000 and the exemption is
$250,000, the homeowner would pay zero, would not pay toward the General Obligation (G.O.)
Bond or municipal taxes, and would still receive City services and benefits. He added that
approximately 20% of the base is commercial, with residential constituting the remainder; non-
homesteaded residential accounts for the largest share.
Commissioner Magazine noted that those are the people who would be left holding the bag.
Commissioner Suarez stated that the poorest homeowners would not contribute toward the General
Obligation (G.O.) Bond, while homeowners with greater wealth would shoulder the cost.
CFO Greene explained that, theoretically, if the constitutional amendment passes, a homesteaded
property with a $150,000 taxable value and a $150,000 exemption would pay zero. He added that
the calculations being discussed are based on the existing $150,000 exemption and the current
median homesteaded property value of approximately $315,000.
Commissioner Magazine stated that it is not the wealthiest homeowners who would be exempted;
rather, the amendment creates a sliding scale in which homesteaded homeowners do not pay, and
renters ultimately carry the burden. He added that it is a straightforward concept.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that the City does not have any control over what Tallahassee proposes
in future years, nor over how State voters will act on the current proposal. She explained that Option
1 splits the burden: part of the needed work would be funded through utility rate increases based
on usage. She stated that a renter in a small apartment without outdoor water use would consume
less, while a larger home with extensive landscaping, a pool, and numerous fixtures would consume
more and therefore pay more. She described this as proportional and equitable. Commissioner
Bhatt asked how a one-bedroom apartment could reasonably use the same amount of water as a
four-bedroom home. She added that the City is attempting to share the burden among all users of
the system, who rely on water service functioning without failure. She explained that the Finance
and Economic Resiliency Committee had been united in recommending a bifurcated model in which
part of the burden is shared through a General Obligation (G.O.) Bond and part through utility rates
based on usage. Public Works Director Norris confirmed that this is Option 1. She noted that
significant uncertainties make managing the City’s infrastructure challenging and that the City has
deferred utility rate discussions for decades.
City Manager Eric Carpenter informed Commissioner Bhatt that the last utility rate increase was a
five-year rate schedule adopted in 2019, but that it ended up below inflation.
CFO Greene added that, beginning in 2020, the Commission adopted utility rate increases that
were artificially low, resulting in a more than ten percent loss relative to inflation. He explained that
the proposed rate increases, originally in the six-and-a-half percent range before transitioning to
CPI, would require approximately three years of increases simply to recover the ten percent gap.
He noted that CPI is currently approximately 4.2 percent and may decrease to a more standard
range of two to three percent, although that still exceeds past inflation levels. He added that these
.June 24, 2026
increases would help make up for the prior deficit.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that the Commission is working to reach a point where, through
circumstances beyond its control at both the local and statewide levels, it can fix aging infrastructure
and insulate the City from catastrophic failures. She explained that Option 1 shares the risk
equitably among all users: part based on usage and part based on homestead property taxes. She
added that Option 1 allows the City to proceed with the most urgent needs as costs continue to
escalate. She stated that the City can continue the broader policy discussion through November,
when voters decide a portion of the matter, while still beginning work now. She emphasized that all
Commissioners have worked hard toward an equitable solution and that Option 1 reflects that.
Public Works Director Norris confirmed. Commissioner Bhatt made a motion to support Option 1,
seconded by Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas.
Commissioner Suarez asked for the projected numbers for a full General Obligation (G.O.) Bond
funding approach for all projects and requested the cost to the median homesteaded owner in Miami

CFO Greene stated that for a median Homesteaded property, valued at approximately $375,000 in

He added that the average Residential property would pay approximately $616.28 or $800 annually.
He noted that there is a significant difference between the median and average values in Miami

annualized cost to the median Residential property under that model.

A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez to suspend Red Light Camera enforcement for right turn violations Citywide immediately, except at the intersection of 17th Street and Alton Road, where right turns on red are already prohibited. items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Discussion held. Item heard with C4 S. After-the-Fact Resolution 2026-34339 adopted.
A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez to suspend Red Light Camera enforcement for
right turn violations Citywide immediately, except at the intersection of 17th Street and Alton Road,
where right turns on red are already prohibited. The motion was seconded by Vice Mayor
Dominguez. Vote: 5-2, with Commissioners Bhatt and Matteo-Salinas opposed. Chief Wayne
Jones to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: No
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: No
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
AFTER-THE-FACT RESOLUTION:
A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH,
FLORIDA, DIRECTING THE ADMINISTRATION TO SUSPEND THE ISSUANCE OF RED-LIGHT
CAMERA CITATIONS AND NOTICES OF VIOLATION FOR RIGHT TURNS ON RED LIGHTS
CITYWIDE, WITH THE EXCEPTION OF THE INTERSECTION OF 17TH STREET AND ALTON
ROAD.
Clerk’s Note: Pursuant to Ordinance 2015-3954, Sec. 2-12(3), Addendum Agenda Item RDA 1
was approved by Mayor Meiner for inclusion on the agenda.
Commissioner Fernandez thanked Mayor Meiner for including Item R9 AI on the Agenda. He
acknowledged the importance of the Red-Light Camera system for traffic safety, but explained that
he has been receiving an overwhelming number of complaints from residents who are being cited
while making right turns on red. In many of these cases, the citation images show vehicles fully
stopped with brake lights illuminated, yet violations are still being issued. Commissioner Fernandez
noted that he had initially placed an Item on the Agenda seeking a way to cancel the contract
altogether, but after discussions with the Police Chief and the City Attorney, it appeared possible to
address right-turn violations without suspending the entire program. If there is a legal pathway to
suspend enforcement of right-hand turn violations captured by the Red-Light Camera system, he
suggested that the Commission consider that option.
Mayor Meiner thanked Commissioner Fernandez and explained that work had already been
underway with the Office of the City Attorney and Police Chief Wayne Jones before Commissioner
Fernandez placed the Item on the agenda. Mayor Meiner noted that several outstanding legal
questions delayed the appearance of his Item, as additional research was required. Mayor Meiner
invited Chief Jones’s perspective and stated that, while not a supporter of Red-Light Cameras
generally, terminating the program could present complications. Mayor Meiner emphasized the
distinction between drivers who proceed straight through an intersection after the light turns red, for
whom the citation is warranted, and drivers making right turns at very low speeds. Mayor Meiner
acknowledged receiving many complaints and expressed sympathy for residents who come to a
virtual stop yet still face substantial fines, even though no dangerous behavior appears to occur.
Chief of Police Wayne Jones thanked the Commission for bringing the Item for discussion. Red-
Light Cameras were implemented on the premise that they reduce crashes at intersections and
thus save lives. Currently, there is a threshold in place, but people are not stopping. They have
.June 24, 2026
videos to support every infraction, and in most cases, when making right turns, the driver slows
conservatively. The right-turn threshold is seven (7) mph. They can activate the cameras to rate
that if a vehicle goes seven (7) mph or more through that intersection, they can raise that threshold
to 50 mph. In clarifying to Mayor Meiner, he explained that, under the way the system works, there
is a preset threshold: if someone slows down to 7 mph or more, the camera is activated, and a
photo is taken of them. On a Red-Light Camera, if they go four (4) mph, they do not get a ticket,
and the speed is gauged through the camera, but they have to come to a complete stop. The idea
is not to roll through the intersection but to come to a stop, and people are cited for not stopping.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that he has received a significant number of complaints and
believes many residents think they are stopping or are performing what Chief Jones described as
a California Roll. He expressed skepticism that simply raising the speed threshold would resolve
the issue, as he does not fully trust the underlying technology. Living near a Red-Light Camera, he
often observes drivers abruptly braking when the light changes, causing the vehicle behind them to
rear-end them. While the system may reduce dangerous T-bone collisions, he noted that other
types of accidents continue to occur. Commissioner Fernandez acknowledged the public safety
purpose of the program, but stated that he would prefer a complete suspension of right-turn
enforcement. He questioned whether the cameras are properly calibrated and who verifies the
recorded speeds. In his view, the real concern is drivers who run red lights, which can continue to
be enforced without maintaining right-turn violations.
Mayor Meiner clarified that drivers proceeding straight through an intersection would continue to
receive citations, and that the proposed change applied only to right-turn violations. He noted that
there were two intersections he was aware of where complaints had been particularly frequent.
Chief Jones stated that the intersection at Chase Avenue and Alton Road had been especially
problematic. He added that, in recent months, the volume of complaints about Red-Light Cameras
Citywide had exceeded the number received in the past five years, noting that he had received yet
another complaint earlier that day. Chase and Alton remained the location with the highest number
of concerns.
Commissioner Fernandez reported receiving complaints from 41st Street, while Vice-Mayor
Dominguez identified Dade Boulevard and 17th Street. Commissioner Fernandez added that he
had also received complaints from Washington Avenue and 17th Street. He expressed concern that
elderly residents may be disproportionately affected, as they tend to be less aware drivers and are
now facing citations exceeding $180. He stated that the City is working to improve quality of life and
affordability for residents through measures addressing parking, towing, and other issues, and he
believes the current enforcement practices unfairly impact elderly individuals in particular.
Commissioner Fernandez moved to suspend right-turn enforcement on Red-Light Cameras and
noted that, if technology improves, the Commission could revisit the issue in the future.
In response to Mayor Meiner, Chief Jones stated that he had no safety concerns regarding the
proposed suspension of right-turn enforcement and that the Police Department could implement it
if directed. He noted that there is one intersection, 17th Street and Alton Road, where right turns on
red are already prohibited, and recommended maintaining enforcement there for movements from
westbound 17th Street to northbound Alton Road. A brief discussion followed regarding pedestrian
activity at that intersection, general safety concerns, and the City’s past practice of enforcing
right-turn stops prior to the installation of Red-Light Cameras. Chief Jones added that long before
Red-Light Cameras existed, officers enforced failures to stop properly, and they would continue to
do so.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas stated that she respects Commissioner Fernandez but did not
support the Item and intended to vote against it. She acknowledged that he raised valid questions
about the camera's functionality. If the number of citations was increasing, it did not necessarily
mean more drivers were running red lights; it could also indicate a technological malfunction. She
questioned how the cameras are tested and whether equipment issues, for example, damage to
wiring, could affect accuracy. Although she remained opposed to the Item as a whole, she
expressed concern about the reliability of the technology.
Chief Jones explained that, while he could not speak to the technical testing procedures of the
vendor, every alleged violation is reviewed by a Police Officer before issuance. The camera
captures the event, notifies the reviewing Officer, and the Officer verifies the infraction before a
citation is mailed. He reiterated that every citation undergoes this review process.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that she does not support eliminating the system entirely. She
expressed willingness to consider raising the speed threshold if that would address the concerns
raised. She shared that she had been struck by vehicles multiple times and emphasized the
increasingly hazardous behavior of drivers. She noted that when drivers, cars, pedestrians, and
micromobility users intersect, the results can be serious. Before discontinuing right-turn
enforcement altogether, she preferred a six-month pilot program to raise the threshold while
ensuring that the cameras are functioning properly. This would avoid penalizing largely responsible
drivers while still capturing those making aggressive right-turn movements, which she observes
frequently. She stated that the cameras serve as a deterrent and that removing all safeguards would
be unwise. Her preference was for a pilot using an elevated threshold recommended by staff to
achieve an appropriate balance of public safety.
Commissioner Suarez referenced legal articles regarding judicial findings that certain red-light
camera systems were unconstitutional. He summarized a Broward County case in which the Court
found that the system improperly presumed the registered owner to be the driver, shifting the burden
onto the owner to prove otherwise. Commissioner Suarez questioned whether it was the owner’s
responsibility to identify the actual driver to avoid receiving the citation.
Chief Jones confirmed that vehicle owners have the option to contest citations in Court, as with any
traditional traffic citation, and may present evidence that another individual was operating the
vehicle at the time.
Commissioner Suarez stated that the system contains a fundamental flaw because the citation does
not identify the actual driver of the vehicle. When a violation is issued, the burden falls on the
registered owner, who may or may not have been using the car, to prove that someone else was
driving. This often requires an uncomfortable conversation with another individual. He expressed
support for the Item and added that, given recent Court findings, he does not expect the system to
remain in place much longer. In his view, the cameras do not meaningfully improve driver behavior.
Mayor Meiner asked how confident Police Department staff were that the technology accurately
measures vehicle speed. If the system is reliable, he would be inclined to consider raising the
threshold.
Chief Jones responded that he is fairly confident in the system’s accuracy. Raising the threshold
may address the recurring problem at certain intersections, particularly Chase Avenue and Alton
Road, where drivers slow, see no oncoming traffic, and then cruise through the intersection without
realizing they are still being captured by the camera. In reply to Commissioner Suarez, he noted
that he does not know the technical details of how the system measures speed. Discussion
continued between Commissioner Fernandez and Chief Jones regarding calibration practices for
.June 24, 2026
speed-tracking devices, including whether the Red-Light Camera system might misinterpret a
stopped vehicle as running a red light, how often speed-tracking lasers are calibrated compared to
the cameras, and whether wide intersection angles could lead to inaccurate readings.
Commissioner Fernandez suggested that some cited drivers may have fully stopped before turning
right, but the camera could be misinterpreting the movement as running a red light, particularly at
intersections with wide angles. Chief Jones stated that he would need to consult with the vendor,
but reiterated that every violation is reviewed by a Police Officer before issuance.
Commissioner Fernandez maintained that drivers turning right are not traveling at seven miles per
hour, and this is why he hesitates to support raising the threshold. He is not convinced that
increasing the speed limit will resolve the issue. His suspicion remains that the problem stems from
flawed technology or the camera registering red-light running rather than right-turn behavior. He
reaffirmed his preference to keep his motion as drafted, suspending right-turn enforcement if legally
permissible. He added that, in his view, 17th Street and Alton Road should be treated like any other
intersection; at 17th and Washington Avenue, drivers must stop before turning right; at 17th and
Alton Road, right turns are prohibited, but both scenarios require uniform treatment. Commissioner
Fernandez stated that he does not support Red-Light Cameras generally and believes their practical
effect has become revenue generation, contrary to the intent of the State and the City when the
program was created. He also noted that the person driving the car is not always the person being
cited, which he considers inherently unfair. Having stepped back from his original proposal to
suspend the entire program, he stated that he is now comfortable with suspending right-turn
enforcement uniformly citywide, with the exception of 17th Street and Alton Road. Commissioner
Fernandez concluded that an infraction is an infraction, but the broader issue is the long-term use
and constitutional viability of this type of technology. He stated that, while he respects the desire to
maintain enforcement at a specific intersection, the Commission must also consider the matter of
principle, and he will need the necessary votes to proceed.
Mayor Meiner stated that he agreed with the general direction of the discussion but maintained a
safety concern regarding the prohibited right turn at a major intersection.
Chief Jones responded to Commissioner Suarez and explained that the City shares revenue from
the citations with the contracted vendor.
Commissioner Suarez added that at the 17th Street and Alton Road intersection, drivers frequently
begin honking, fail to notice the prohibition sign, and then move without realizing the restriction. He
agreed with Commissioner Fernandez that he does not support generating revenue for a private
company through a system that cannot determine who was actually driving the vehicle. He noted
that enforcement conducted by a Police Officer is fundamentally different, and he argued that if a
restriction is applied at one intersection, consistency would require applying it Citywide, which they
clearly do not want.
Mayor Meiner observed that two colleagues wished to remove the Red-Light Camera enforcement
at 17th Street and Alton Road. He emphasized that the restriction exists for safety reasons and is
required under law.
Commissioner Bhatt reiterated her proposal for a six-month pilot program to raise the speed
threshold.
Commissioner Magazine stated that he would support either increasing the threshold or eliminating
right-turn enforcement, while keeping straight-through enforcement intact. He added that the
Commission should not debate single intersections in isolation.
.June 24, 2026
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas stated that she would not support the Item. She noted that the City
is often dangerous for pedestrians and that drivers need to slow down, calm down, and stop.
Although each Commissioner raised compelling points, she remained opposed.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez expressed support for the motion and seconded it. She agreed with
maintaining enforcement at 17th Street and Alton Road. Further discussion followed.
Mayor Meiner reiterated his concern about that intersection, noting that there is significant activity
and complexity at that location.
Chief Jones informed Commissioner Fernandez that there had not been recent pedestrian or
bicyclist incidents reported at 17th Street and Alton Road.
Commissioner Suarez asked Transportation staff why the prohibition exists.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas noted that fatalities had occurred at the intersection and emphasized
that the restriction prevents dangerous movements.
Transportation and Mobility Director Jose Gonzalez explained that FDOT evaluated the intersection
several years ago. Alton Road is a State Road, and FDOT examined crash data, sight-distance
constraints, and pedestrian volumes before determining that right turns on red should be prohibited
from westbound 17th Street to northbound Alton Road. That restriction has been in place for several
years, and the absence of recent crashes likely reflects drivers complying with that rule, creating
the safest conditions for pedestrians.
Commissioner Suarez added that 17th Street is one of the most challenging intersections in the
City. Unlike most locations where right turns on red are permitted, the prohibition at this intersection
stands out, and there are additional intersections with similar conditions.
Commissioner Bhatt added that some intersections have problematic sight lines. The City is working
with FDOT to install a “No Right on Red” sign at Bay Drive and 71st Street, heading east, because
the roadway curves sharply and drivers often believe the path is clear when it is not. Vehicles
frequently travel at high speeds at that location, and the number of near-miss collisions has been
significant. She noted that right-turn restrictions are sometimes necessary depending on visibility
and stated that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. She reiterated Commissioner
Matteo-Salinas’s earlier point that drivers need to slow down and calm down, as they will not arrive
any faster if they end up in an ambulance or receive a citation. She emphasized that these safety
measures exist for a reason and should be maintained.
Commissioner Ferna
items.motion: A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez to suspend Red Light Camera enforcement for right turn violations Citywide immediately, except at the intersection of 17th Street and Alton Road, where right turns on red are already prohibited.

BEACH RESIDENTS. Item was not heard.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, APPROVING AN INCREASE TO THE CONSULTANT SERVICE ORDER (CSO) ISSUED PURSUANT TO THE PROFESSIONAL SERVICES AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE CITY AND HML PUBLIC OUTREACH LLC, FOR ADDITIONAL PUBLIC INFORMATION OUTREACH (PIO) SERVICES REQUIRED FOR THE WEST AVENUE PHASE II NEIGHBORHOOD IMPROVEMENTS PROJECT, IN A NOT TO EXCEED AMOUNT OF $608,172.00, SUBJECT TO APPROVAL OF THE FIFTH AMENDMENT TO THE FY 2026 CAPITAL BUDGET, FOR A REVISED TOTAL CSO AMOUNT OF $1,003,422.00; AND FURTHER, AUTHORIZING THE CITY MANAGER TO EXECUTE THE CSO CHANGE ORDER.
items.action: Resolution 2026-34345 was adopted. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda by Commissioner Suarez. A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez to adopt the Resolution; seconded by Vice-Mayor Dominguez. Vote: 5-2; Opposed: Commissioners Magazine and Suarez.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34345 was adopted. The Item was separated from the Consent Agenda
by Commissioner Suarez. A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez to adopt the Resolution;
seconded by Vice-Mayor Dominguez. Vote: 5-2; Opposed: Commissioners Magazine and Suarez.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: No
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: No
David Gomez to handle.
TO DO:
 Administration to research and report back on the average amount other cities allocate for
communications in large capital projects, for comparison to Miami Beach’s practices.
At the request of Commissioner David Suarez, Director of Capital Improvements David Gomez
explained that HML Public Outreach LLC serves as the City’s Public Information Officer for the West
Avenue project, which began in 2021. He stated that the Item requests a contract extension through
the projected completion year of 2029, for total funding of approximately one million dollars, or an
average of $125,000 per year. He explained that HML Public Outreach’s role is extensive due to the
size and complexity of the project, including public outreach, interaction with residents, coordination
among property owners and managers, City staff, consultants, and contractors, which exceeds the
workload typical for similar projects. Original estimates anticipated approximately twenty-five hours
per week across the firm’s staff; however, the firm is now approaching the equivalent of two full-time
positions. He stated that they conduct regular biweekly meetings with residents, arrange meetings,
prepare project collateral, respond to thousands of emails, schedule harmonization meetings, and
follow up with properties regarding harmonization agreements. He noted that harmonization
agreements have been completed for Segments 2 and 3, a large percentage are complete for
Segment 6, and additional agreements are scattered across other segments; they are not yet at one
hundred percent.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he separated the Item from the Consent Agenda because he
believes the service is redundant, as the City already has a Neighborhood Affairs Division. He
questioned why the City would spend close to one million dollars on outsourcing when in-house
departments already exist for such functions. He stated that a million dollars in taxpayer funds could
be used more efficiently. He noted that the original approval occurred in 2021, predating at least three
Commissioners, and stated that he would not have supported it initially. He added that the
Commission had just discussed saving money from the operating budget, and in his view, outsourcing
a million dollars for communication and outreach is unnecessary.
Director Gomez stated that the City uses a combination of in-house and contracted efforts depending
on the project. He explained that a project of this scale and intensity would overwhelm City staff if all
outreach responsibilities were performed internally. He noted that Neighborhood Affairs manages
outreach for many projects, such as the Promenade, but larger projects typically require private PIOs
due to staffing flexibility and adaptability. He explained that a recent DERM permitting issue required
three PIO staff members to assist with inspections, coordinate with property managers, answer
questions from affected buildings, and support the inspection team. He stated that when additional
staff resources are required, pulling in-house staff removes them from duties they must perform
elsewhere.
City Manager Eric Carpenter added that the Neighborhood Affairs Division is composed of PIOs
pulled from individual departments. He stated that the Division includes three PIOs: one in South
Beach, one in Mid-Beach, and one in North Beach. He explained that there are not multiple
departments performing this work and noted that the requested contract would provide the equivalent
of two full-time positions for this project. He stated that two of the billed hours per week are at the
$110 rate, while the majority of hours fall within the $79 to $89 range.
Commissioner Suarez stated that the cost appears high and emphasized that outreach depends on
management practices. He noted that Commissioner Alex Fernandez conducts a monthly tour of
West Avenue without compensation. He reiterated that he is not supportive of spending a million
dollars for functions such as emails, websites, and WhatsApp communications when the City has a
department that can perform such work. He added that budget constraints, potential tax cuts, and
financial pressures strengthen his opposition.
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez stated that the City was not forced to adopt its rollback rate and
continues discussing how best to use that choice. She noted that several emails were received
regarding this Item, and one from a business owner emphasized the importance of the PIO team
given the complexity of the project and the remaining duration of approximately 144 weeks. She
stated that the project has been complicated and disruptive with many moving parts, and she believes
the expenditure is justified.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine stated that this Item exemplifies a situation where the City must
work more efficiently. He explained that the City already has several communication functions,
including Public Information Officers and the Neighborhood Affairs Division, and he does not support
adding contracted communication resources. He stated that he lives in the neighborhood and became
involved in the City because of the projects in the area, and believes there are likely five teams
delivering similar messaging. He stated that this is not about needing more resources but about
working smarter. He added that based on what staff described, he is hard-pressed to believe the
workload merits outsourcing unless they are literally receiving thousands of emails.
Director of Capital Improvements Gomez informed the Commission that in the last two years staff
has conducted more than 250 harmonization meetings, over 100 stakeholder meetings, more than
500 one-on-one meetings, and tracked 550 issues. He stated that staff issued more than 100 project
updates, coordinated biweekly meetings, managed WhatsApp contacts, and maintained the project
database containing contact information for over 400 individuals, which is nearly a full-time
responsibility.
Commissioner Magazine reiterated the need to work smarter. He stated that the City cannot have
PIOs and also contract out communications, and that the City must constrain the growth of
government. He stated that although the work is important, if they do not set boundaries and focus
on doing more with less, the City will never achieve the desired efficiency. He added that this Item is
one of those instances where he must say they need to work smarter and harder.
Commissioner Suarez suggested that the million-dollar expenditure could be better allocated to other
projects such as the Teen Club. He stated that outsourcing functions the internal departments can
perform is not a good use of taxpayer funds. He asked how many emails Director Gomez had received
since the program began, and Director Gomez stated he did not have the number. Commissioner
Suarez stated that there should be an exact number and added that scheduling meetings and
managing a WhatsApp group should be responsibilities carried out by Neighborhood Affairs.
In addressing Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt, City Manager Carpenter explained that if the Item is not
approved, some of the tasks currently performed will not occur.
Commissioner Magazine stated that if he told his employer that work would be reduced because a
resource was lost, he would be fired. He said the City has to deliver and must do so with fewer
resources.
City Manager Carpenter informed Commissioner Bhatt that harmonization agreements are on the
critical path of the project.
Director Gomez stated that Section 3 is complete, most of Section 4 is complete, and the next focus
is Section 6. He stated that the City is currently in construction for Sections 2 and 3.
Commissioner Suarez stated that City staff has sufficient time to meet with residents and property
owners for matters that are years away from construction and that this is the role of government. He
stated that if the City moves toward contracting out government functions, that is a separate
discussion. He stated that Commissioner Magazine is correct that the City should work more
efficiently, and he cannot believe the impression the City is giving residents if they suggest delivering
less service because they do not want to pay someone to manage WhatsApp groups, websites, or
meeting schedules. He stated that those functions must occur regardless and should be completed
by staff. He asked what Neighborhood Affairs is doing if those tasks are not being handled internally,
and questioned why the City would pay extra for outside services.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that in her view, staff does not have enough personnel to complete all
required work, so the City must either hire additional employees or find other ways to complete the
work.
City Manager Carpenter stated that the City has a large capital budget and each project within the
Capital Work Plan requires public-information support. He explained that most projects are handled
by the in-house Neighborhood Affairs Division; however, this project represents a one-hundred-
million-dollar capital undertaking that requires additional hands-on communication and real-time
information. He stated that staff is constantly asked to provide updated resources and communication,
and that additional outside support is needed. He added that in management, City staff is intended
to handle the “troughs,” while contracted resources are used for the “crests,” meaning the peaks of
workload associated with large, complex projects. City Manager Carpenter stated that this project
clearly represents one of those peaks and requires augmentation with outside communication
resources. He explained that the request covers two and a half years of service and that the City has
already expended approximately $400,000, totaling roughly six years of service.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that one of the greatest challenges with the project has been delays
caused by misinformation, which significantly increased costs. He explained that reducing
communication, while he trusts the internal team’s dedication, would risk slowing progress on
harmonization agreements. He noted that staff are still working with certain properties on drainage
issues, Baywalk matters, and other outstanding concerns. He stated that complaints began
decreasing once communication increased, including greater onsite presence, direct communication
channels, and WhatsApp coordination. He added that the communication support is needed not only
for current conditions but through the next two years, as the project moves toward projected
completion in 2028. He stated that large government construction projects commonly dedicate 1% to
2% of the total project budget to public communication, and because this project totals approximately
one hundred million dollars, the request falls within industry norms. He added that such
communication prevents misinformation that previously caused delays, resulting in significant
additional costs.
Mayor Steven Meiner called for the vote. City Clerk Rafael E. Granado announced that a motion had
been made by Commissioner Fernandez to accept the Resolution, seconded by Vice-Mayor Laura
Dominguez.
Mayor Meiner stated that he had hesitancy regarding the Item; however, City Manager Carpenter
presented a compelling argument. He stated that although he was not fully comfortable with the
request, he trusted the City Manager’s judgment and agreed it was necessary, noting that the
requested amount represented less than one percent of the total project budget. He acknowledged
that he shared some of the sentiment expressed by Commissioner Suarez and Commissioner
Magazine.
In reply to Commissioner Suarez, City Manager Carpenter stated that the Neighborhood Affairs
Division consists of four employees and that the Communications Department includes the
Neighborhood Affairs Division.
Assistant Director Linda Stevens explained that Communications totals eighteen employees, four of
whom are in Neighborhood Affairs.
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas clarified to Commissioner Suarez that two or three
Communications employees work in the booth managing Commission meetings and therefore cannot
perform Neighborhood Affairs duties. She stated that the question was fair and that the City must
clearly define staff responsibilities, noting that residents sometimes misunderstand departmental
tasks and may incorrectly assume all employees perform the same functions.
Commissioner Suarez stated that roles and responsibilities evolve and that he was basing his
concerns on what was described in the memorandum, which listed tasks such as answering emails,
developing websites, and managing WhatsApp groups. He stated that such tasks could be performed
internally and reiterated that outsourcing those responsibilities is unnecessary.
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez stated that the Communications Department has staff with specialized
roles, including four audiovisual specialists who support Commission meetings and other City events,
and who are not assigned to walk-throughs with residents. She added that the department also has
design and photography staff who produce collateral for all City departments and cover more than
150 events per year. She explained that although there is some overlap in writing and
communications, the work required for this project involves personnel who can conduct meetings,
walk sites, and oversee detailed field coordination. She stated that it is a different skill set from staff
who support audiovisual operations or design functions. Vice-Mayor Dominguez emphasized that the
argument suggesting the department’s eighteen employees are unoccupied is inaccurate. She stated
that there is already a motion and a second on the floor, and that the Commission should proceed to
vote according to each Commissioner’s judgment.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine stated that with the extensive communication needs associated with
this project and communications work conducted through outside vendors, he questions whether a
policy or legislation is needed. He expressed frustration that Commissioners are often left to
communicate staff-level decisions directly to residents on social media, particularly in the primary
Facebook groups that serve as major communication platforms in the community. He noted that staff
is not interacting on those platforms, despite being responsible for communications, and stated that
although the issue may not be specific to this discussion, it is an important concern. He explained
that while resources are being dedicated to communications, the City’s primary public-facing
platforms are not being used by staff, which he finds problematic.
Assistant Director of Marketing and Communications Linda Stevens, responding to Commissioner
Suarez, stated that the Communications Department has three staff members assigned to the design
and photography team, who create all printed and digital collateral for departments and photograph
City events. She stated that the team covers more than 150 events per year. She explained that staff
roles differ, and not all employees perform the same function or have the same skill set required for
this project’s communication needs.
Commissioner Suarez suggested reducing the number of photographers and design staff and instead
hiring personnel whose skills align more closely with the communication and public-outreach needs
described for this project. He stated that this is his position regarding the Item.
Mayor Steven Meiner stated that he appreciates the work of the Neighborhood Affairs staff in
attendance and thanked them for their efforts, noting that this discussion reflects the legislative
process.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez stated that he values being respectful of Commissioners’
neighborhood concerns and that when issues arise in his neighborhood, he appreciates deference.
He stated that for North Beach items he likes to defer to Commissioner Bhatt and likewise respects
Commissioner Magazine’s input on West Avenue, where residents are directly impacted. He stated
that the residents benefit from this service and asked Commissioner Magazine for his preference on
the Item, given his daily experience with the project.
Commissioner Magazine stated that he would likely vote in opposition but acknowledged the points
raised. He stated that he understands arguments supporting staff augmentation and noted that
residents reached out in real time to say the service was valuable and much needed. He explained
that his earlier comments were broader and thematic, not specific to this Item. He stated that
community leaders who have spent significant time on these projects expressed support, and their
feedback is meaningful. He stated that although he may vote against the Item, he recognizes the
residents’ perspective.
Mayor Meiner stated that he initially leaned against the Item, but after receiving messages from
residents that Neighborhood Affairs staff was able to assist with issues in real time, he reconsidered
his position. He stated that the City is about to begin work on 41st Street, another project requiring
significant communication with both residents and businesses. He asked the Commission to consider
communication funding norms used by other municipalities and counties.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that he believes this expenditure aligns with common practices in
major capital projects, noting that large construction efforts affecting daily commutes and quality of
life often all

ACTION: The Item was deferred to the September 10, 2026, City Commission Meeting. Lilia Cardillo

VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
