Pursuant to Ordinance 2015-3954, Sec. 2-12(3), Addendum Agenda Item C7 AS was approved by
Mayor Meiner for inclusion on the agenda.
Commissioner Suarez explained that the Commission had just held a lengthy discussion on how to
save taxpayer dollars in the upcoming budget year and asked whether there was consensus around
consolidating certain departments. He referenced Tourism and Economic Development as an
example of departments that could be merged to reduce costs, similar to previous consolidations of
Fleet, Facilities, and Parks. He added that Parking and Transportation had also been consolidated
and was functioning smoothly at that time. He asked City Manager Carpenter how many directors the
City has.
City Manager Carpenter responded that there are 42 directors.
Commissioner Suarez asked how many departments the City has.
City Manager Carpenter responded that there are 21 departments.
Commissioner Suarez stated that this amounts to “a director for every 4,000 residents,” and noted
that government overhead could be reduced to lessen the tax burden.
Commissioner Fernandez asked whether the Item was a Consent Item.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez clarified that it had been backed out and was supplemental.
Commissioner Bhatt requested deferral, stating that the Item was added after 6 p.m. the night before
and she had not seen it until the morning of the meeting. She said she would not vote for something
she had not had the opportunity to read. She made a motion to defer the discussion.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez noted that the Resolution contemplated a presentation in October.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that the Item was “only an evaluation.”
Commissioner Bhatt reiterated that she had not read the Item and did not want to vote on it.
Commissioner Suarez asked whether the Commission was deferring a presentation on potential
consolidations.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that voting for legislation not read is “bad practice” and does not serve
residents well.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas agreed.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez stated that if deferred to September, the memo would still state October.
Commissioner Bhatt responded that the memo could be adjusted to November or December.
Commissioner Suarez stated that the rollback rate discussion was based on a budget that was
“cooked,” putting “Police Officers, Firemen, and cats on the chopping block,” and emphasized that
the Item offered an opportunity to shrink managerial levels and reduce burden.
A motion was made by Commissioner Bhatt to defer the Item, seconded by Commissioner Matteo-
Salinas. Vote: 6-1. Commissioner Suarez opposed.

Deborah Tackett, Planning Department Director, explained that the proposed amendment would
allow the City to post notices for Planning Board amendments and certain minor applications,
including GU waivers, on the Miami-Dade County website instead of publishing them in The Miami
Herald. She noted that in 2024, City voters approved a Charter amendment permitting public hearing
notices to be posted on the County website in place of the newspaper publication. In 2025, the City

hearings, including Historic Preservation Board, Design Review Board, and Board of Adjustment
applications. She stated that the omission of Planning Board amendments and minor applications
was, in her opinion, an oversight, and this amendment serves to make the noticing process consistent
for all public hearings issued by the Planning Department.

ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into
the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Magazine made a motion to adopt the
Ordinance on First Reading; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for October 14, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to
notice. Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Deborah Tackett to
handle.
Commissioner Magazine explained that the intention behind the proposal is to improve the City’s
overall aesthetic and beautification efforts, especially in areas where vacant lots or future
development sites remain inactive for extended periods before obtaining building permits. He noted
that current requirements mandate chain-link fencing with green mesh for visibility and safety, but
these fences often become torn, unattractive, and inconsistent with the visual standards the City
strives to maintain. He emphasized that his proposal would not impose a mandate but would instead
give property owners the option to install enhanced, more visually appealing fencing, similar to the
artistic, ceramic-style installations seen around the Convention Center hotel, to elevate the look of
neighborhoods such as Lincoln Road and beachfront corridors. Commissioner Magazine
acknowledged the nuances surrounding visibility concerns for vacant lots but encouraged discussion
on possible mitigation strategies, and deferred to Planning Director Tackett to clarify technical details.
Planning Director Tackett explained that the Ordinance would resolve the frequent lag between the
issuance of a demolition permit and the later approval of a building permit for an already-approved
project. To address this gap, the Ordinance would allow property owners to install an artistic graphic
construction fence for up to 12 months instead of following vacant-property standards. She noted that
the Ordinance also permits renderings of the approved or proposed project to be displayed at a much
larger scale, correcting the previous treatment of project renderings as signage. Planning Director
Tackett emphasized that renderings are valued by the community because people like to see what is
planned for a site, and stated that both staff and the Planning Board support the proposal.
Commissioner Fernandez asked for clarification on whether this Ordinance would restore the ability
to see through the fencing.
Planning Director Tackett explained that for vacant properties and active construction sites, mesh
fencing has always been permitted and that requirement is not changing. Instead, the Ordinance
simply expands what is allowed by permitting more artistic graphic treatments on the fencing, without
altering the underlying visibility standards.
Commissioner Bhatt expressed strong support for the proposed fencing changes, noting that seeing
what future development will look like is exciting for residents and improves neighborhood aesthetics.
She shared an example from her own street where a vacant lot’s deteriorating mesh fencing has
generated multiple code violations and negatively impacted the area’s appearance. Commissioner
Bhatt stated she is happy to see a solution that allows more attractive fencing options. She suggested
a friendly amendment requiring that any property choosing to install a solid artistic fence first comply
with or enroll in the Police Department’s no-trespassing program. She explained that this agreement
is important for addressing homeless-related trespassing, vagrancy, and public-safety issues,
because it allows Police to respond immediately at the first call once the fence is up.
Mayor Meiner thanked the sponsor for bringing the Item forward and noted that improved
construction-site fencing can make a noticeable difference in how properties awaiting building or
development appear to the public. He referenced Deauville Beach Resort as an example, explaining
that its enhanced fencing creates a presentable and attractive appearance when driving by. He
emphasized that similar improvements could help other properties look reasonable and
well-maintained during the period before construction begins.
A Public Hearing was held, and with no participants requesting to speak via Zoom or in the audience,
the Public Hearing concluded.

Commissioner Fernandez. Roll Call: 7-0.

items.title: AN ORDINANCE OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, AMENDING CHAPTER 10 OF THE CODE OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, ENTITLED "ANIMALS," BY AMENDING SECTION 10-11 THEREOF, ENTITLED "RUNNING AT LARGE PROHIBITED; EXCEPTIONS," BY PROVIDING A GRACE ZONE EXTENDING FROM THE PERIMETER OF THE AREA DESIGNATED BY THE CITY MANAGER FOR THE BENEFIT OF AN OWNER OF AN UNLEASHED ANIMAL WHO INADVERTENTLY ALLOWS HIS OR HER ANIMAL TO STRAY OUTSIDE THE APPROVED PERIMETER; AND PROVIDING FOR REPEALER, SEVERABILITY, CODIFICATION, AND AN EFFECTIVE DATE.
items.action: Ordinance 2026-4830 was adopted as amended. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading, as amended, to establish a two-minute grace period; seconded by
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Ordinance 2026-4830 was adopted as amended. The title of the Ordinance was read
into the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the
Ordinance on Second Reading, as amended, to establish a two-minute grace period; seconded by
Commissioner Fernandez. Roll Call Vote: 5-2 (Vice-Mayor Dominguez and Commissioner Bhatt
opposed).
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: No
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: No
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
John Rebar and Hernan Cardeno to handle.
AMENDMENT: The five-minute grace period was reduced to a two-minute grace period.
Commissioner Suarez stated that there has been a lot of misconception online. He clarified that
the Item does not extend an off-leash Dog Park beyond South of Fifth, but instead provides a grace
zone because the South of Fifth Dog Park is unique in the sense that it has no fence. Commissioner
Suarez pointed out that if a dog runs out for a second to chase a ball, like his dog does all the time,
there should not be a penalty from any enforcement agency of the City. He believed that it struck
a perfect balance of enforcement and leniency for pet owners, considering the Dog Park is not
fenced.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez said that her concerns are the same as they were before. She agreed that
the Park is unique because it is unfenced but felt concerned about adding leeway for unleashed
pets outside of that particular area because many residents had written her and sent videos of
incidents at the park. She added that something to maybe look at in the future would be a fence,
because dogs have bitten people and gotten into fights with other dogs, and the area is not without
issues.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that she shared those concerns. Just because a dog runs outside of
the existing parameters does not mean that the owner is going to be cited, as Police use judgment
and discretion in non-major enforcement situations. Thus, she did not believe that expanding the
area would make anything better. In fact, she believed it would make it worse. It would become
harder to enforce because it is more complicated. She had residents reach out about issues with
dog owners whose dogs were off-leash, attacking children, cat feeders, and other dogs. She ended
by saying there needs to be less chaos and that she would vote No.
The Public Hearing was opened.
Joanna Barinska, via Zoom, asked to play a video titled “Off-Leash,” but the request was denied
because it had not been pre-approved or vetted by Communications staff.
Brian Teasley, via Zoom, stated that he felt that Commissioner Suarez “did a sales job” on the
Commission during the First Reading. He stated that in cases where a dog momentarily strays
outside the park while chasing something, nobody is currently being given a ticket. He explained
that the proposal actually creates an off-leash zone extending 100 feet around the current off-leash
park, within which dogs may be off-leash for up to five minutes. He stated that he walked the 100-
foot perimeter and that it includes the entrance fountains, the walkway along the water, and the
artistic lighthouse where people picnic. He warned that if the Ordinance passed, owners of
dangerous dogs could exploit the grace zone, staying off-leash longer than five minutes when no
Park Ranger is present, and when enforcement eventually arrives, owners would simply leash their
dogs.
Andres Asion, via Zoom, stated he frequents the park with his dog two to three times a day and is
very familiar with the area. He agreed that the idea of a fence is a great idea. He stated that he
has never seen a Park Ranger issue a ticket to anyone with an off-leash dog. He believed that the
City was trying to prevent something that has never actually occurred. He mentioned that he is
curious to know how many citations have ever been given for off-leash dogs, noting that when
Park Rangers come by and see people running with their dogs off-leash, the Rangers simply tell
owners to leash their dogs, and owners comply. He ended by recommending that the fence idea
be implemented for that area.
With no one else requesting to speak, the Public Hearing portion ended.
Commissioner Bhatt made clear that his comments were made as a longtime dog lover and
rescuer. She mentioned that she has two rescue dogs at home and none of them are ever let off-
leash. She stated that dogs, like people, can react unexpectedly, even if well-trained, and may
have an adverse reaction or be provoked. She emphasized that this is a public safety issue and
stated she would be very supportive of installing a fence to create a large, contained off-leash Dog
Park.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he does not see the big issue with the particular Dog Park. It is
the only Dog Park in Miami Beach that is unfenced by design. He shared that he does not want
enforcement left solely to the discretion of an Officer or Park Ranger to decide whether to issue a
citation. He said the Item provides checks and balances on enforcement. He agreed with a
previous caller that five minutes may be too long, and stated he would amend the grace period to
two minutes, which he believes is plenty of time for an owner to retrieve a dog that accidentally
goes outside the boundary. He reiterated that the Ordinance does not create a 150-foot off-leash
zone, but instead a two-minute grace period for accidental boundary crossing. He asked to make
an amendment changing the grace period from five minutes to two minutes.
City Attorney Ricardo J. Dopico said that he would prepare the amendment.
Commissioner Magazine expressed his support for the Ordinance as amended. He joked he would
have a “short leash” on the off-leash zone, and said that if any issues arise, the Commission should
revisit it. He noted that the issues raised by Mr. Teasley were laid out eloquently, and clarified that
the Commission does not want this Ordinance to signal that Rottweilers, Dobermans, or other large
breeds are allowed to roam free off-leash; the amendment is simply to accommodate a brief grace
period. He stated he was fine supporting it with that understanding.
Commissioner Suarez stated for the record that he has had pitbulls, and they are the most loving
dogs. He did not want to vilify them because they were bred to be family dogs and, at the end of
the day, are domesticated animals. He stated that who raises a dog is what determines behavior,
not the breed.
Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading, as amended,
to establish a two-minute grace period; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Roll Call Vote: 5-
2 (Vice-Mayor Dominguez and Commissioner Bhatt opposed).

items.title: AN ORDINANCE OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, AMENDING CHAPTER 70 OF THE CITY CODE, ENTITLED “MISCELLANEOUS OFFENSES,” BY AMENDING ARTICLE II, ENTITLED “PUBLIC PLACES,” BY AMENDING DIVISION 2, ENTITLED “BICYCLING, SKATEBOARDING, ROLLER SKATING, IN-LINE SKATING, MOTORIZED MEANS OF TRANSPORTATION, ELECTRIC BICYCLES, MOPEDS, MOTORCYCLES, MOTORIZED BICYCLES, AND MOTORIZED SCOOTERS,” BY AMENDING SECTION 70-66 THEREOF, ENTITLED “DEFINITIONS,” BY CREATING AND AMENDING CERTAIN TERMS THEREIN; AND BY AMENDING SECTION 70-71 THEREOF, ENTITLED “ENFORCEMENT, PENALTIES,” BY AMENDING AND PROVIDING FOR ADDITIONAL PENALTIES THEREIN; AND BY CREATING SECTION 70-73 THEREOF, ENTITLED “RESPONSIBILITIES OF MICROMOBILITY DEVICE OPERATORS,” TO ESTABLISH CERTAIN REQUIREMENTS APPLICABLE TO MICROMOBILITY DEVICE OPERATORS; AND PROVIDING FOR REPEALER, SEVERABILITY, CODIFICATION, AND AN EFFECTIVE DATE.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Ordinance 2026-4832 was adopted. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record.
The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Bhatt made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on Second
Reading; seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Chief Wayne Jones, Hernan Cardeno, John Rebar, and Melissa Berthier to handle.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt introduced the Item, explaining that it has been a couple of years in
the making, with extensive input from the Transportation Committee (Transportation, Parking, and
Bicycle-Pedestrian Facilities Committee), electric-bicycle and micromobility-device users, bicyclists,
pedestrians, Miami Beach Police Department (MBPD), Park Rangers, Code Compliance, Marketing,
and numerous other City departments. She stated that the goal is to establish a framework that
encourages micromobility while setting parameters for safe usage. She noted that the City has seen
devastating accidents in which pedestrians suffer severe injuries. She stated that the Ordinance
codifies provisions already in State law and clarifies a definition in State law that is unclear, so that
the definition is clear in the City’s Ordinances.
Deputy City Attorney Mark Fishman stated that after First Reading, the definition of “motorized means
of transportation” was clarified. He explained that the State defines micromobility devices as
motorized transportation devices but then includes bicycles and other human-powered devices, which
is nonsensical. He stated that adding the word “motorized” before “micromobility devices” in the City’s
definition allows regular pedal bicycles to continue to be used on the Beachwalk. Without that change,
regular bicycles would be prohibited on the Beachwalk, which is not the Commission’s intent. He
added that factors for determining whether a micromobility device is designed or equipped to carry
more than one person now also include wheel size and seat size as considerations for MBPD.
Commissioner Bhatt referenced a recent article regarding rising electric-bicycle injuries among youth.
She noted that Miami-Dade County had a lengthy discussion about banning electric micromobility
devices on certain County roads and that other municipalities may adopt portions of the County’s
Ordinance. She stated that the City is not seeking a ban but rather a thoughtful approach that allows
micromobility and ensures safety. She stated that speed-feedback signs will be installed on the
Beachwalk by the end of the summer and that the City is exploring additional communication methods
to educate users. She stated that the State declined to take a leadership role, leaving cities to manage
the issue individually. She stated that the process is long-term and incremental and moved the Item,
requesting support.
Deputy City Attorney Fishman, responding to Commissioner David Suarez, stated that State law
simply requires determining whether a device is designed or equipped to carry more than one person.
He stated that an additional set of handlebars is one factor that may be considered.
Commissioner Suarez seconded the motion.
The Public Hearing was opened.
Matthew Gultanoff stated that he emailed the City Commission the previous day and thanked
Commissioner Bhatt for working with stakeholders throughout the process. He stated that under the
existing Ordinance, riders who remove the battery from an electric bicycle are compliant because the
bicycle is not operating as a motorized means of transportation. He explained that many residents
now only own electric bicycles. He stated that he removes his battery to comply with the law when
riding on the Beachwalk due to safety concerns on City streets. He explained that under the proposed
language, a bicycle with the battery removed would be considered a motorized means of
transportation and therefore prohibited, forcing families to ride on dangerous streets. He stated that
enforcement is feasible because an officer can check whether a battery is present. He stated that
determining the residency status of the vehicle owner parked illegally is far more labor-intensive than
checking whether a bicycle has a battery, and Officers or Park Rangers could simply ask the rider to
stop and verify.
Commissioner Bhatt explained that, in response to Mr. Gultanoff’s concerns, she and the Office of
the City Attorney discussed the matter and agreed that although a rider may be asked to stop if
operating an electric bicycle with the battery removed, that rider would not be penalized. She stated
that codifying battery-removal language would make the Ordinance less clear for bicycles with
integrated batteries, where a Park Ranger or Officer cannot see whether assistance is available and
must rely on a rider’s statement. She stated that the City does not want to give riders a license to use
prohibited devices on the Beachwalk. She explained that, for now, riders who remove the battery and
pedal at low speeds, even though the Beachwalk is not ideal because of high pedestrian volume, will
not receive a violation. She stated that this approach preserves discretion for enforcing agents while
the City continues evaluating long-term solutions.
Deputy City Attorney Fishman stated that the modification to the definition of “motorized means of
transportation” does not affect the issue raised by Mr. Gultanoff. He explained that battery removal is
a relatively new concern that had not been contemplated. He stated that the current Code defines
motorized means of transportation as a device propelled by something other than human power,
which is ambiguous and could be interpreted either based on how the bicycle is propelled at the
moment or how it is manufactured. He stated that legality could be argued either way. He explained
that the City intends to accommodate battery-removed bicycles for now and will prepare guidance for
Officers instructing that if a bicycle cannot provide motorized assistance because the battery is
removed, then no violation should be issued until future clarifying language is adopted by the City
Commission.
Commissioner Bhatt added that the Ordinance will take effect in August of next year and asked for
time to implement changes incrementally. She stated that protected bike lanes or a second
Beachwalk would be ideal but are not currently feasible. She stated that after two years of work, the
City should implement the Ordinance, collect data, and adjust if necessary. She noted that speed-
feedback monitors will be installed on the Beachwalk before the Ordinance takes effect, and new
information may emerge that could guide future amendments. She emphasized the importance of
educating the public and encouraging safe behavior before making broad changes.
Mr. Gultanoff thanked Commissioner Bhatt for the clarification. He stated that he remains concerned
because relying on Officer discretion means the rule is not codified. He said that, in his view, the
matter should be clearly permitted rather than discretionary.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that MBPD and Park Rangers have discretion and that the goal is to
encourage safe behavior rather than punish riders. She stated that egregiously unsafe behavior limits
discretion, but minor issues may be handled with warnings. She stated that trained, emotionally aware
Officers are capable of assessing situations, and Park Rangers apply the same approach. She stated
that guidance from the City Attorney will ensure consistency. She added that after six months of
implementation, the Commission can review whether amendments are needed once speed-feedback
data is gathered. She emphasized that the public should understand why helmets, safe speeds, and
responsible behavior are critical.
Mr. Gultanoff reiterated his concern that without codification, enforcement remains discretionary.
Deputy City Attorney Fishman, responding to Commissioner David Suarez, stated that if an Officer
chooses to issue a citation, the law is ambiguous and he will provide guidance and clarification.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he witnessed a special-needs teenager at South Pointe Park riding
an electric bicycle without a battery who was arrested and taken to TGK. He stated he wants to ensure
similar incidents do not occur again.
Deputy City Attorney Fishman clarified that written guidance will direct Officers not to issue citations
when a bicycle’s battery is removed. He noted that if a rider commits a separate offense, such as
possessing contraband or assaulting an Officer, a citation or arrest may occur based on that behavior
rather than the bicycle.
Commissioner Bhatt added that the Ordinance does not apply to ADA electric-assist devices.
The Public Hearing concluded.
A motion was made by Commissioner Bhatt to approve the Ordinance on Second Reading, seconded
by Commissioner Suarez. Roll Call: 7-0.

ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into
the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the
Ordinance on First Reading; seconded by Vice-Mayor Dominguez. Roll Call: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for October 14, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to
notice. Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Deborah Tackett to
handle.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that he would give his presentation at Second Reading since this
was a First Reading.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez expressed concern about the issue. She stated that during the time the
suspension has been in effect, a business in Sunset Harbour painted a “hideous” color which then
began peeling.
Commissioner Fernandez asked her to state the business name on the record.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez responded that the business was Harbour Club.
Commissioner Fernandez explained that Harbour Club had originally painted the building, the color
later faded, and they were unable to repaint without going through the extensive Land Use Board
process.
Director of Planning Deborah Tackett provided background. The property owner requested to paint
the building a deep pink color, which exceeded the Planning Department’s administrative approval
authority; they were directed to the Design Review Board process. The owner objected to the length
of the 3- to 4-month process. Planning staff advised that if the color were lightened, it could be
approved administratively, but the owner insisted on the deep pink. She explained that Commissioner
Fernandez’s Ordinance would allow use of the paint color without requiring DRB approval.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that the distinction between shades of pink is not obvious to the
average observer and that additional layers of review can create unnecessary burdens in time and
cost for businesses and homeowners.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez stated she was comfortable advancing the Item to Second Reading.
The Public Hearing was opened. The City Clerk recognized two speakers via Zoom:
1. Tim Carr, who did not speak.
2. Sara de los Reyes, via Zoom, stated that when the building was originally painted, she warned
the property owner that the paint would fade quickly. The owner dismissed her concerns, and the
paint did eventually fade.
With no other speakers present, the Public Hearing concluded.
Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading; seconded by
Vice-Mayor Dominguez. Roll Call: 7-0.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: The Item was deferred to the September 10, 2026 Commission Meeting. The title of
the Ordinance was read into the record. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to defer the Item to
September. Approved by acclamation. 7-0. Rafael E. Granado, City Clerk, to notice. Lilia Cardillo
to place on the September Commission Agenda, if received. Amy Knowles to handle.
DIRECTION RESULTING FROM R5 T (TURTLE NESTING PROTECTION ORDINANCE):
 Defer the Item to the September 10, 2026 Commission Meeting.
 Bring back a revised ordinance with a clear definition of “legacy events” (for potential
grandfathering/eligibility during nesting season).
 Add an explicit $50,000 deposit requirement (in addition to any Tourism & Culture deposit) for
events during nesting season, with the deposit usable for enforcement in the event of lighting-plan
violations.
Amy Knowles and Francys Vallecillo to handle.
Per Commissioner Suarez’s direction, City Attorney Ricardo J. Dopico explained that the legislation
requires a $50,000 deposit as part of the process, in addition to any other security deposit required
by Tourism and Culture, and clarified that this deposit would be used to hold event producers
accountable for lighting-plan violations during the turtle-nesting season.
Commissioner Fernandez proposed an amendment to include an exception for the July 4 event, and
Commissioner Suarez indicated he was agreeable. He further suggested applying the $50,000
deposit requirement to all events occurring during the restricted period, with July 4 as the sole
exception due to fireworks.
Commissioner Magazine stated that the City has a flagship event, F1 Carbone Beach, which occurs
the first or second week of May (around May 15), and asked whether Commissioner Suarez would
be amenable to grandfathering that event or extending the permitted start date to May 15.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that the purpose of the Ordinance is to protect sea turtles during nesting
season and questioned whether carving out dates or weeks would leave nests unprotected. She
asked what protections would apply if nests are present during an exempted event.
Amy Knowles, Chief Resilience Officer, explained that event producers would still be required to
obtain State permits and approvals and to use sea-turtle-friendly lighting as much as possible. In
response to Commissioner Bhatt, she noted that the Ordinance prohibits special events on the beach
after 9:00 p.m. between May 1 and October 31, and that Commissioner Suarez was asking to allow
the July 4 event. She also clarified that any nests are roped off and that the City requires an event
lighting plan (low-intensity, correct color spectrum, shielded from the ocean) to demonstrate
compliance with both the City’s Ordinance and FWC rules.
In reply to Commissioner Suarez, Commissioner Magazine described that the F1 Carbone Beach
event typically occurs during the first week of May and fell on May 15 this year. He stated that this
event has been a flagship of the City for the past five or six years, attracting strong attention and high-
caliber press. He noted that the event has operated without any issues, and he asked whether to
grandfather that event or extend the permitted start date to May 15 to accommodate it. He also stated
that grandfathering existing longstanding events would prevent the Commission from picking winners
and losers.
Chief Resilience Officer Knowles answered Commissioner Suarez’s question and explained that
under the amendment proposed, Carbone Beach would not be able to operate an event on the beach
after April 30, because events on the beach after 9:00 p.m. between May 1 and October 31 would be
prohibited. She stated that Carbone Beach would require an exemption, because its operating dates
fall after May 1. Addressing Commissioner Suarez, she further explained that the State defines sea
turtle season as beginning May 1, while the City’s season begins April 1 because Miami Beach’s
nesting season starts earlier than in the rest of Florida. She noted that there were some nests in April
this year, but the bulk of nesting begins in May.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas stated that she believed they had historically held both the July 4
activation and the Carbone Beach event during this period, and asked whether any of those events
had harmed sea turtles.
Chief Resilience Officer Knowles responded that it is hard to say definitively, but that mother sea
turtles can be spooked or disoriented by activity, may return to the ocean without nesting, and
hatchlings are attracted to artificial light and may not make it to the ocean. She explained that loss of
available nesting space due to beachfront use can also restrict nesting. She stated these conditions
are known risks and that impacts are difficult to quantify
Commissioner Fernandez stated that July 4 is a national holiday and “in a category of its own,” but
that the City has legacy events, and that grandfathering existing long-standing events is desirable in
order to remain fair across the board. He stated that new events should not be permitted, but
long-standing, historically permitted events should be allowed to continue.
In reply to Commissioner Suarez, Francys Vallecillo, Tourism and Culture Interim Director, explained
that for legacy events, the biggest event is Carbone Beach during F1 Weekend, which has run for
about four or five years. She stated that they also have the Air & Sea Show, depending on what
components the event includes. She noted that this year the Air & Sea Show included concerts on
the west side, but they still required a lighting plan, and if nothing occurs on the east side, the
restrictions would not affect them. She stated that these are the biggest events during May.
Commissioner Suarez asked what the purpose of the Ordinance is if the City is going to “waive it for
everyone.”
Chief Resilience Officer Knowles clarified that, based on this year, they had ten events after 9:00 p.m.
throughout the season; last year they had twelve events after 9:00 p.m. on the beachfront. She
explained that this information comes from staff identifying nighttime events requiring sea-turtle
lighting accommodations. She also confirmed that these nighttime events occurred during the nesting
season window defined by both the State and the City.
Tourism and Culture Interim Director Vallecillo added that they worked with event organizers to
identify the ten events, but they were not annual or major events. She clarified that Commissioner
Fernandez’s office had requested a list of annual events earlier in the year, and this list differed from
the non-annual nighttime events identified for lighting compliance.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that his Office asked for a list of annual events so he could better
understand the scope, and he was not informed that there had been thirteen events the prior year.
Commissioner Magazine noted that they essentially have one annual recurring event-Carbone
Beach-that has not had any issues, and that it predated all members of the current Commission. He
stated that he does not see his role as eliminating a high-profile flagship event that has brought great
press and attention to the City. He added that the Commission is agreeing not to allow any new
events during the restricted season, which he said is “a huge win,” and stated that this is a good place
to land, but he deferred to the sponsor for a final decision.
In answering Commissioner Suarez’s question, Chief Resilience Officer Knowles added that last
year’s full season had a total of 210 nests (including some relocations from the Bal Harbour beach
range), and that the County has advised the City that this year is trending toward a record number of
nests.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he is not trying to impede events such as F1 Carbone Beach, which
still must comply with lighting requirements. He proposed applying the $50,000 deposit to all events
during the restricted period (with July 4 as the sole exception due to fireworks), and emphasized that
existing events must still submit a lighting plan. He stated that if an event violates the approved lighting
plan, a penalty shall be withheld against the deposit, and asked whether his colleagues were
amenable to this approach.
Chief Resilience Officer Knowles replied to Commissioner Magazine that State law requires all light
to be sea-turtle-friendly and not visible from the beach, which she described as very difficult in
practice. She explained that the City requires a lighting plan to demonstrate compliance; lights must
be the correct color, low-to-the ground, and shielded from the ocean. She stated that it is extremely
difficult for an event to meet all these requirements, and that the City does the absolute best it can to
enforce them.

shielded from the ocean. She stated that it is extremely difficult for an event to meet all these
requirements, and that the City does the absolute best it can to enforce them.
Commissioner Suarez asked whether they could require a deposit that would be withheld if any
lighting-plan violations occur.
City Attorney Dopico explained that the City can treat legacy events the same as any other event,
applying the $50,000 deposit, and stated that these events would be allowed to operate during the
restricted period only if they meet all other requirements.
Commissioner Suarez suggested meeting halfway with his colleagues by allowing events on May 1
and permitting legacy events to continue, while still enforcing the deposit and lighting-plan
requirements.
Tourism and Culture Interim Director Vallecillo informed Commissioner Fernandez that the 2025 list
of events consisted of the Air & Sea Show, the Sports Illustrated event on the Collins Park beachfront,
the World Ocean Celebration, the City’s Fourth of July activation, and the MindTravel
Live-to-Headphones concert. She noted that she included the times of each event and that not all go
beyond 9:00 p.m., so only the Air & Sea Show and the Sports Illustrated event would be impacted if
they extended past 9:00 p.m.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that he prefers not to exempt only one event, because what one
Commissioner values may not be what another values. He stated that if an event has been
longstanding in the community, he would “rather make a way to embrace them,” and then allow the
number of legacy events to reduce naturally over time as they discontinue, noting that no new events
should be added during the protected period.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he would defer the Item to September. He noted that there is ample
time and suggested that the Commission receive clarification on what constitutes a legacy event. He
stated that he was not trying to push anyone to vote on something he himself was not comfortable
with.
The Item was deferred to the September 10, 2026 Commission Meeting by acclamation.

items.title: AN ORDINANCE OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, AMENDING CHAPTER 54 OF THE MIAMI BEACH CITY CODE, ENTITLED "FLOODS," BY AMENDING ARTICLE Ill, ENTITLED "RESILIENCE STANDARDS FOR TIDAL FLOOD PROTECTION," TO MODIFY THE ENFORCEMENT, PENALTY, AND COMPLIANCE PROVISIONS FOR VIOLATIONS OF THIS ARTICLE, AND ADOPT OTHER CLARIFYING AMENDMENTS; AND PROVIDING FOR REPEALER, SEVERABILITY, CODIFICATION, AND AN EFFECTIVE DATE.
items.action: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into the record. The Public Hearing was held. Vice-Mayor Dominguez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading; seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Roll Call: 6-0. Commissioner Fernandez recused himself.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: The Ordinance was adopted on First Reading. The title of the Ordinance was read into
the record. The Public Hearing was held. Vice-Mayor Dominguez made a motion to adopt the
Ordinance on First Reading; seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Roll Call: 6-0. Commissioner
Fernandez recused himself.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Abstained / Recused – See Form 8B
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
The Second Reading Public Hearing is scheduled for September 10, 2026. Rafael E. Granado to
notice. Lilia Cardillo to place on the Commission Agenda, if received. Amy Knowles to handle.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez stated for the record that he would be recusing himself from
discussing and voting on this Item because his spouse and he reside on a property with a seawall
abutting the Biscayne Waterway, and he may directly or indirectly benefit from the adoption of the
amendments in the Ordinance. He then exited the Chambers.
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez stated that she has worked on strengthening seawalls in regard to
construction standards. The Item gives more time for repairs if there is overtopping that impacts an
individual property. This does not include the right-of-way, a neighbor’s property, or public property.
She noted that this additional time applies only when the overtopping affects the owner’s upland
(personal) property solely.
Chief Resilience Officer Amy Knowles explained that the City has 55 miles of seawalls, 91% of which
are privately owned, and that a fair number of these are very low. Thus, during king tides and other
times of the year, overtopping is common. She stated that the Ordinance is a triaged approach to
compliance because seawalls are very expensive. Under the existing Ordinance, if overtopping
impacts the public right-of-way, corrections are required within two years. What is different here is
that, if the overtopping is limited to personal property onto the upland, corrections must be made
within five years, allowing more time to plan.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt asked, if a seawall overtops and water becomes fetid in the yard, how
much time that homeowner would have to fix the seawall.
Chief Resilience Officer Knowles responded that the homeowner would have five years. Vice-Mayor
Dominguez added that the homeowner must first receive a violation notice before the five-year
remediation period begins.
Commissioner Bhatt clarified that she has been approached by residents whose neighbors are
inattentive and let their seawalls overtop; the yards become a disaster, and adjacent properties must
deal with the consequences without recourse because it is technically not their property.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez reiterated that the property owner would first have to get a violation and then
would have five years to address the issue.
Commissioner Bhatt asked what happens if it also affects the neighbor’s property.
Chief Resilience Officer Knowles stated that if overtopping affects a neighbor, the correction period
is two years. The only condition where more time is granted is when overtopping affects the owner’s
property solely. She added that, in a situation as dire as described by Commissioner Bhatt, there
could also be a building (structural) violation requiring a quicker time frame.
Chief Deputy City Attorney Nick Kallergis added that such conditions may also give rise to a property
maintenance violation that Code Compliance can enforce.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez emphasized that receiving additional time requires the owner to demonstrate
annual progress toward remediation. Owners cannot wait until the final year to start; they must show
they are progressing each year.
The Public Hearing was opened. City Clerk Rafael E. Granado stated he saw no one on Zoom and
no one in the audience requesting to speak. The Public Hearing was then closed.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on First Reading; seconded by
Commissioner David Suarez. Roll Call: 6-0. Commissioner Alex Fernandez recused himself and did
not vote.

ACTION: Ordinance 2026-4833 was adopted. The Item was heard with R5 AH and R7 M. The title
of the Ordinance was read into the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner Fernandez
made a motion to adopt the Ordinance on Second Reading; seconded by Vice-Mayor Dominguez.
Roll Call: 7-0. The vote applied to Items R5 AG, R5 AH, and R7 M, which were considered together.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Planning Director Deborah Tackett to handle.
Commissioner Fernandez explained that the legislation modifies the maximum setback requirements
in the GU-zoned area. He stated that current maximum setback requirements limit how the City may
redevelop a GU-zoned property. By adopting this amendment, the City would allow a GU-zoned
property to have greater setbacks. He noted that applicants usually seek variances to reduce
setbacks, but this proposal is unique because it increases setbacks without altering FAR or height.
He stated that the amendment strictly removes the maximum setback requirement.
Planning Director Deborah Tackett added that the Performance Standard Districts south of Fifth
Street are the only districts in the City that require a maximum setback. All other districts use minimum
setback requirements. She stated that enforcing maximum setbacks on public property is challenging
due to facilities such as parking, public restrooms, and park structures that should not necessarily be
placed at a five-foot line. She noted that the Administration supports the amendment, and the
Planning Board also recommended approval.
Commissioner Fernandez moved the Item. Seconded by Vice-Mayor Dominguez.
City Clerk Rafael E. Granado announced the Public Hearing, and seeing no participants via Zoom or
in the audience, the Public Hearing concluded.
Combined Motion for R5 AG, R5 AH, and R7 M:
A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez to adopt the Items, seconded by Vice-Mayor
Dominguez. Roll Call taken: 7-0. Items approved. The vote applied to Items R5 AG, R5 AH, and R7
M, which were considered together.

ACTION: The City Commission considered Items R7 A, R7 B, R7 C, and R9 D together. No action
was taken on the Resolution as noticed under Item R7 A. After debate and multiple motions, the
Commission did not adopt the hybrid General Obligation (G.O.) Bond model (R7 B) nor the General
Obligation (G.O.) Bond-only model (R7 C). Instead, the Commission approved an alternate approach:
a $450 million, rate-funded Capital Improvement Plan financed through water, sewer, and stormwater
rate increases, and directed the Administration to return in September with the revised project list and
corresponding rate adjustments.
Option 1 (R7 B - Hybrid Model) - Failed:
A motion by Commissioner Bhatt, seconded by Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas, to approve
the Resolution on the hybrid model (R7 B) failed, 3-4. Opposed: Mayor Meiner and Commissioners
Fernandez, Magazine, and Suarez.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: No
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: No
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: No
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: No
Option 2 (R7 C - General Obligation (G.O.) Bond-Only) - Failed:
A motion by Commissioner Suarez, seconded by Commissioner Fernandez, to adopt the Resolution
on the General Obligation (G.O.) Bond-Only model (R7 C) failed, 2-5. Opposed: Commissioners
Magazine, Matteo-Salinas, Vice-Mayor Dominguez, Commissioner Bhatt, and Mayor Meiner.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: No
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: No
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: No
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: No
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: No
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Option 3 - Rate-Funded CIP Program ($450 Million) - No General Obligation Bond - Passed:
Commissioner Joseph Magazine made a motion to authorize a total of $450 million in projects to be
financed through water, sewer, and stormwater rate increases, seconded by Commissioner Alex
Fernandez. The motion passed 5-2, with Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez and Commissioner David
Suarez opposed.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: No
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes

AFTER THE FACT RESOLUTION 2026-34383 (R7 A1):
A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH,
FLORIDA, RESCINDING, ON A FIVE-SEVENTHS (5/7THS) VOTE, THE MORATORIUM ON THE
ADOPTION OF ANY ORDINANCE TO INCREASE WATER, SEWER, AND STORMWATER RATES
REINTRODUCED VIA RESOLUTION NO. 2026-34276; AUTHORIZING A $450 MILLION CAPITAL
IMPROVEMENT PLAN FOR WATER, SEWER, AND STORMWATER PROJECTS (PLAN), THE
PROJECT LIST FOR SAID PLAN BEING SUBJECT TO FINAL REVIEW AND APPROVAL BY THE
MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION, TO BE FINANCED BY WATER, SEWER, AND STORMWATER
RATE INCREASES; AND FURTHER, DIRECTING THE CITY ADMINISTRATION TO PREPARE
THE FOLLOWING FOR CONSIDERATION BY THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION AT THE
SEPTEMBER 10, 2026 MEETING: (I) A REVISED PROJECT LIST REFLECTING THE REVISED
PLAN, AND (II) A DRAFT ORDINANCE FOR FIRST READING/PUBLIC HEARING AMENDING THE
CITY'S WATER, SEWER, AND STORMWATER FEE RATES TO IMPLEMENT THE
CORRESPONDING RATE INCREASES NECESSARY TO FUND THE PLAN.
DIRECTION:
Pursuant to After-the-Fact Resolution 2026-34383, which authorizes $450 million in water, sewer,
and stormwater capital projects to be financed through utility rate increases, the Administration is
directed to return in September 2026 for First Reading Public Hearing of the Ordinance implementing
the rate-funded Capital Improvement Plan. The Administration shall present:
 The revised Capital Improvement Plan reflecting a total program cost of $450 million.
 The water, sewer, and stormwater rate increases required to fund the program.
 The updated project list, with projects removed in reverse chronological order until the authorized
amount is achieved.
John Norris to handle.
Public Works Director John Norris introduced the Items and stated that Option 1 is an all-G.O. Bond
option to fund the ten-year Capital Improvement Plan (Item R7 B), and Option 2 is the hybrid option
(Item R7 C). He explained that a few months ago the Administration presented a rate-increase
proposal for water, sewer, and stormwater. Under the hybrid option, the Administration would request
a water and sewer rate increase representing approximately half of the previously proposed rate
increase, and then pursue a General Obligation (G.O.) Bond for stormwater projects associated with
the ten-year CIP. A presentation was shown. Click here to view the presentation.
Commissioner David Suarez stated that he and Public Works Director Norris had been discussing
the matter over the prior several days and that he wants to achieve the most equitable solution for
residents. He noted that the single-family home calculations assume 5,000 gallons of water usage
per household per month. He stated that condominium analysis is more complex because
condominium buildings use master meters. The City must sample multiple buildings and divide total
consumption by the number of units to generate average usage per unit. He stated that a household
with a median property value of $318,000 using 5,000 gallons per month faces slightly higher costs.
He added that households with full-time residents generally use 5,000 gallons or more, while units
occupied seasonally, such as snowbird units, skew average usage downward. He asked Public
Works Director Norris which option is more expensive for a median-value household using 5,000
gallons per month.
Public Works Director Norris stated that the answer depends on assessed property value. For
median-value and below, the all-General Obligation (G.O.) Bond option would be more
advantageous, saving approximately $97 annually. He clarified that the numbers provided to the
Commission reflect the highest debt-service year, 2035, and that costs would increase progressively
until that point. He acknowledged that his prior statement should be clarified accordingly.
Commissioner Suarez added that median-value households are disproportionately impacted under
the hybrid option, and that Miami Beach’s most financially challenged residents may pay more under
the hybrid approach than those in higher-value homes. He stated that the water and sewer enterprise
fund must remain solvent, and decades of underinvestment have contributed to current challenges.
He stated that he wants to hear from his colleagues on how they weigh affordability for residents who
are financially vulnerable.
Public Works Director Norris stated that the City used average consumption figures based on building
characteristics. He stated that lower-assessed units, typically one- or two-bedroom condominiums,
have fewer fixtures and lower water usage, often averaging about 3,200 gallons per month. He stated
that this would reduce cost impacts relative to larger units. He stated that the City sampled 18
condominium buildings of varying sizes, locations, and ages. He noted that lower-value buildings
benefited more under the all-General Obligation (G.O.) Bond option. He stated that if each unit had
an individual meter, the analysis would be simpler, but currently usage must be averaged across
buildings. He stated that this exercise helps determine the best overall approach to funding the Capital
Improvement Plan.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine thanked the Administration for its efforts and the Commission for
being cost-conscious while prioritizing critical infrastructure and resiliency projects. He said the
discussions have become highly detailed and complex. He stated that the Commission should step
back and simplify the question: the City must advance critical infrastructure and resiliency projects
that have been delayed for years, and residents face affordability challenges due to high living costs.
He stated that the Administration’s project list totals approximately $775 million in present value and
includes items with no feasible path to completion within ten or twelve years, such as First Street
Phases III and IV. He stated that the scope is too large to complete with existing staffing and that
borrowing for projects unlikely to begin for fifteen years is inefficient. He proposed scaling down the
borrowing amount to approximately $430 million, consistent with the utility-rate portion of the hybrid
option, and focusing solely on mission-critical stormwater and water projects supported by significant
State and federal funding. He stated that this approach would save money for all residents across
income levels, reduce costs by approximately $300 million, avoid construction paralysis, and deliver
essential infrastructure while preserving affordability. He stated that, in September, the Administration
could return for First Reading with a revised borrowing authorization of approximately $450 million,
reflecting a scaled-down and realistic approach.
Public Works Director Norris responded to Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt and clarified that the City
borrows as needed, so debt service for later-phase projects does not hit immediately. He stated that
if the first five years of projects are spread over ten years, the City would realize savings; however, if
the City executes all first-five-year projects within five years and then repeats that same approach for
the second half of the CIP, the financial impact would be similar to the original schedule. He added
that the Administration has already spread the program significantly, determining early on that the
original timeline was not deliverable and pushing work out to a manageable (though aggressive) CIP.
He asked Chief Financial Officer Jason Greene to comment on the financial impacts.
Commissioner Magazine stated that the Commission could use the utility-rate portion that exists in
the hybrid method while not moving forward with the General Obligation (G.O.) Bond portion, thereby
borrowing less. He said the City would need to reconfigure the utility-rate portion of the revenue bond,
but since they are only authorizing now, and because the proposed rates already reflect the borrowing
assumptions, the Commission could cap the program and direct that $450 million in projects be
financed under the utility-rate mechanism until the Commission revisits the discussion. He stated that,
by definition, this produces a smaller increase than either the full General Obligation (G.O.) Bond or
the hybrid option.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that under a hybrid approach, the ballot action must occur today in order
to meet the November ballot deadline; otherwise, the City would be another year out. She asked for
background on why the Commission is at a critical juncture and how long the City has been working
toward this. She noted that CPI increases on water rates were not implemented for decades, leading
to a backlog of projects. She said she is not claiming that all projects will be completed in ten years,
but she is concerned about deferring decisions on half the projects to a future Commission that may
not have the resolve to act, unless it can be shown that those deferred projects truly do not materially
affect residents Citywide.
Public Works Director Norris stated that CPI increases have been implemented by Ordinance for
water and sewer (not for impact fees, which the Commission corrected a few months ago). He stated
that he has been working on this since he arrived and that two prior Public Works Directors also
worked on the rate increase, for approximately two to three years.
Chief Financial Officer Jason Greene stated that the effort dates back to 2017, when the City
developed the Critical Needs and NIP programs. He said a rate Ordinance set rates at CPI, but the
first four to five years were artificially low, and inflation outpaced CPI, leaving the City about 10%
behind. He stated that when Public Works projected 2035 rates, the proposed water and sewer rate
Ordinance produced roughly a 10% increase compared to the existing Ordinance, indicating that if
CPI had been set correctly since 2017, the City might not be here, at least on the water and sewer
component. He stated that since April 2025, utility rates were brought to the Finance and Economic
Resiliency Committee and received unanimous endorsements multiple times, but were postponed; in
parallel, the Commission directed the Administration to explore General Obligation (G.O.) Bonds,
leading to the hybrid model the Administration recommends.
Commissioner Alex Fernandez stated that the City maintains a prioritization list ranking projects by
criticality, and funding has been structured accordingly. He said the presentation compared total
monthly resident costs, including utility charges and the annual General Obligation (G.O.) Bond share
converted to a monthly amount. He noted that single-family scenarios assumed 5,000 gallons/month,
and that condominiums averaged 3,200 gallons/unit, per Public Works Director Norris. He stated his
goal is to deliver mission-critical projects at the lowest possible cost, which is why the Commission
enacted the moratorium on water and sewer rate increases. He asked how Commissioner Magazine’s
proposal could be more beneficial to the City, homeowners, and condominium owners.
Public Works Director Norris stated that, for median assessed value and below, the approach
suggested would be less beneficial to those households. He explained that water and sewer are user
fees, while stormwater is a per-unit assessment. He stated that households can control water usage
(and thus sewer), but every household pays a stormwater assessment. He added that, similar to
FPL/gas bills, utility costs are a larger portion of income for lower-income households; therefore, a
utility-rate increase tends to affect lower-income residents relatively more than higher-income
residents. He said adding a General Obligation (G.O.) Bond component introduces progressivity on
the stormwater side.
Commissioner Magazine replied that this is only true if borrowing amounts are the same. He stated
Public Works Director Norris was answering under the assumption of equal borrowing, which he is
not proposing. He stated that saying “lower-income households are more impacted” would be
incorrect under his proposal because the City would be borrowing hundreds of millions less.
Public Works Director Norris clarified that any utility-rate increase, like any utility bill, affects lower-
income households more than higher-income households on a relative basis.
CFO Greene stated that the total capital program for the period is $1.1 billion, funded through a mix
of pay-go cash and debt financing. He explained that Commissioner Magazine’s proposal would
eliminate the General Obligation (G.O.) Bond component, revisit the entire program, and identify
which projects from the $1.1 billion will move forward now versus be postponed further into the future.
Commissioner Fernandez added that placing more of the program on utility rates shifts a greater
relative burden, regardless of the ultimate borrowed amount, onto lower-assessed homes and
moderate-income residents, while placing more of it on General Obligation (G.O.) Bonds, causing
higher-assessed property owners to carry a larger share.
Public Works Director Norris agreed.
Commissioner Magazine suggested borrowing the same amount under utility-rate financing as in the
hybrid proposal, using the same mechanism so there is no shifting. He asked what happens to lower-
income households if, in November, the homestead exemption is increased and then substantially
expanded over time, meaning households with assessed values of $5-$25 million that currently pay
toward General Obligation (G.O.) Bond debt service could be removed from that tax base. He asked
what that would do to lower-income households and renters, who would be left carrying the burden
as homesteaded taxpayers are removed. He reiterated that General Obligation (G.O.) Bonds are
funded via property taxes, and if a large portion of property taxpayers are removed from paying, the
remaining tax base would necessarily shoulder the debt service.
Commissioner Fernandez requested clarity on the property-tax reform going to voters. He stated that,
if it passes, the homestead exemption would increase to $150,000 in the first year and to $250,000
in the second year. He noted there is no proposal to eliminate property taxes from TRIM notices and
asked the City Attorney to confirm that legislation contemplates allowing municipalities to optionally
further increase the homestead exemption by local action. He stated that, if the reform passes, by
year two many homeowners at or below the median assessed value could be insulated from the
General Obligation (G.O.) Bond impact because their exemption would rise. He added that a
significant share of owners around the $318,000 median could be protected, and said that is helpful
clarity.
Chief Financial Officer Jason Greene stated that, for a homesteaded property at the very low end
(approximately $250,000 assessed value), if the constitutional amendment passes, such owners
could pay no property taxes, creating a tax-burden shift to the remaining tax base. He clarified to
Commissioner Fernandez that the illustrative change is $200,000 (since $50,000 is already included
in the current $318,000 median scenario), and the median would theoretically shift downward.
Commissioner Joseph Magazine stated that lower-income homeowners may gain exemptions;
however, 66% of City residents are renters who receive no exemptions and would bear shifted costs.
He reiterated that he supports moving forward with water, infrastructure, and resiliency, but opposes
authorizing borrowing for projects 15 years out. He stated the City should fund mission-critical work
now, reprioritize by authorizing a lower borrowing amount, and revisit more ambitious phases in five
to seven years. He said he cannot support borrowing
