ACTION: Resolution 2026-34387 was adopted as amended.
R7 G (Operating Millage) - As Amended
A motion was made by Commissioner Suarez to adopt the Resolution setting the proposed operating
millage at 5.8060 mills, seconded by Commissioner Magazine. Vote: 5-2; Opposed: Commissioner
Bhatt and Vice-Mayor Dominguez.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: No
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: No
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
R7 G (Debt Service Millage)
Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Resolution establishing the debt service
millage rate of 0.2693 mills; seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
DIRECTION:
A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez directing Administration to identify noncritical
efficiencies that could achieve a 5.7040 millage rate, seconded by Commissioners Magazine and
Suarez. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Jason Greene and Tameka Otto Stewart to handle.
Management and Budget Director Tameka Otto Stewart stated that the second Item, R7 G, concerns
the City’s maximum millage rate. She explained that, as discussed at the prior Friday meeting, the
Administration recommends leaving the operating millage flat, the same as FY 26, and reducing the
debt service millage rate. In reply to Commissioner Suarez, she stated that the recommended
operating millage is 5.8560 mills and the voted debt service millage rate is 0.2693 mills.
Commissioner Suarez noted that the Commission had just voted to raise water and sewer rates and
suggested offsetting that impact through the millage so that residents would remain neutral with
respect to water and sewer increases. He acknowledged that the Commission was required today to
set the floor for the millage rate and asked what the cost of the rate increases would be and whether
they could be offset through a lower millage.
Chief Financial Officer Jason Greene stated that he could not provide that information and, in
response to questions from Commissioner Suarez, explained that the Public Works Department had
just been given direction and must now work with its rate consultant to recalculate rates. He stated
that he had no estimate regarding what the rates would be or what the average impact would be, and
that there was no way to guesstimate theoretical utility rate adjustments. He emphasized that today’s
vote merely sets the maximum millage rate for September, at which time the Commission retains
flexibility to decrease it. He added that providing the maximum flexibility is important, consistent with
Friday’s recommendations, when the Commission made a series of reductions that gave them room
to maneuver. In reply to Commissioner Suarez, he stated that if the Commission voted today to adopt
a rollback millage rate, then every item for which funding was restored on Friday would need to be
reversed and canceled on the floor.
Management & Budget Director Otto Stewart stated that the rollback millage rate is 5.5762, and the
ceiling (maximum) operating millage rate is 5.8560 mills.
Commissioner Suarez stated that they could further lower the millage rate in September but asked
whether there was consensus to meet halfway now by reducing the millage rate so that residents
would be guaranteed a lower rate next year. For example, instead of 5.8560 mills, reducing to 5.65
mills.
Commissioner Magazine stated that he wholeheartedly supports lowering the millage rate and that
this is how he approaches each budget cycle. He felt it was premature to set a specific rate today but
was comfortable setting a ceiling with the confidence that the millage rate will not increase. He stated
that if they set the budget at a rollback rate now, he would still seek additional cost savings in
September, but he did not yet know what the rate would be.
Commissioner Suarez stated that they intend to move toward a rollback and not maintain a millage
that simply covers the operating budget. He said the Commission should commit to offsetting recent
increases in water, sewer, and stormwater rates and take additional steps to provide cost savings to
taxpayers.
In reply to Commissioner Magazine, Chief Financial Officer Green reiterated that the Administration
recommends keeping the millage flat due to a “yellow flashing caution” entering FY 28 with the
upcoming Constitutional Amendment, which he said is very likely to pass. He explained that this will
result in millions of dollars in additional deficit, and that based on property value trends, there is no
reason to expect that next year will not have a deficit similar to or greater than this year. He stated
that the City had a $7 million deficit this year and may need to cut $10 to $15 million next year. Even
if the millage rate is decreased to save half a million dollars, that reduction simply adds to next year’s
deficit. Any cuts made now would require additional cuts next year, which, while not guaranteed,
would be his professional prediction.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that the Commission has a very robust budget process and that this year
it has been even more detailed through the collective desire of the Body to examine a line-by-line
document, hold lengthy conversations, and search for efficiencies and cuts that may be difficult. She
stated that it is premature to impose a “false cap” before the budget process is complete. She added
that Commissioners are trying to find the best path forward and do not yet have all the answers, which
is why the Commission will meet again in September and once more in October. She stated that she
would not support imposing a false ceiling because it is easy to reduce the rate now and continue
reducing it, but dropping it too low could put constituents in harm’s way, potentially requiring difficult
decisions about cuts to public safety, which she is unwilling to do before the process is complete. She
stated that everyone on the dais is concerned about affordability and they spent multiple hours
discussing it in connection with infrastructure needs. She reiterated that it is premature to roll back
the millage any further at this point.
Management & Budget Director Otto Stewart clarified that reducing the operating millage by 0.05
mills from the Administration’s recommendation would save approximately $46 for the average
homeowner and reduce City revenues by $2.6 million.
Commissioner Magazine stated that the Commission had already identified cost reductions beyond
what was requested, including several million dollars in additional savings. He stated that reducing
the millage would require addressing a $6.9 million deficit, plus another $3 million to accommodate
further reductions.
Management & Budget Director Otto Stewart added that, based on Friday’s discussion, the City
currently has a $4.2 million surplus set aside for September for further consideration.
Chief Financial Officer Green stated that this surplus represents a budget stabilization reserve. He
reiterated that the City may face a $10 million deficit next year, and there are hundreds of thousands
of dollars in items Commissioners may consider restoring in September. He stated that any millage
reduction now limits offsetting options.
Commissioner Magazine stated that, given the $4 million in additional savings identified, if they
reduce the millage rate by 0.05 mills, the incremental effect is approximately $2.65 million. He stated
that he could support Commissioner Suarez in lowering the millage rate now or alternatively maintain
the maximum millage rate and revisit it in September to determine whether to reduce it further or keep
it the same while funding additional infrastructure needs. He stated that he was comfortable
proceeding in whichever direction Commissioner Suarez preferred.
Commissioner Suarez stated that he wants to provide tax savings immediately and would support
lowering the millage by 0.05 mills, which would leave approximately $1.5 million available for
allocation. He stated that this is beneficial because the Commission would then have a defined
amount to determine how best to allocate funding.
Commissioner Magazine added that the Commission has a line-item budget, meaning commissioners
can individually review and identify additional cuts. He stated that $4 million is not the maximum
amount of cost efficiencies he intends to pursue. He stated that backing into the lower millage rate is
consistent with the floor of his goals, and his intention over the next month is to continue reviewing
the budget line by line to find additional savings.
Commissioner Suarez made a motion for a maximum operating millage of 5.8060; seconded by
Commissioner Magazine.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas stated that she did not feel comfortable making this decision “on the
fly.” She appreciated what her colleagues were trying to do and was not necessarily opposed, but
she wanted more time to process the proposal and speak with staff. She stated that, as Commissioner
Bhatt mentioned earlier, the budget process is not complete, Commissioners are not aligned on where
they want to cut or save, and they are still hearing from residents about reductions that have already
occurred. She stated that she wanted to be fair to residents by allowing them to participate in the
existing process before adjusting the current millage ceiling.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez stated that she was “in the same boat.” She said that the Commission held a
robust budget discussion on Friday and went through many different items, and reducing the millage
too much would cut services that make the City unique. She stated that residents would not
appreciate losing essential services. During her budget review, she noted that the City recommended
a slightly reduced millage of 0.006 mills less than required to service the General Obligation (G.O.)
Bonds, and recommended keeping the operating millage flat. She stated that this is what she would
support today.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that he needed to air a frustration he had last Friday. He recalled
that in December, several Commissioners had voted to request a rollback budget and options for a
rollback budget. He stated that what they received, in his view, was a “poison-pill” rollback budget,
intentionally designed to include only critical services that no responsible official would cut. He stated
that everyone who appeared on that list deserved a public apology because the list demoralized
employees working in essential positions. He stated that he did not believe the Commission ever
received a true rollback budget. He added that the budget is the most important public policy
document the Commission passes, and the situation placed Commissioners in a difficult position. He
said he believed the rollback budget provided was politicized and designed to prevent adoption of a
real rollback rate. He offered a public apology to Sanitation workers, Firefighters, Parks employees,
and Police Officers because they were placed on that list. He stated that he had felt this way since
last Friday and needed to place the frustration on the record.
Commissioner Suarez agreed. He stated that the proposed rollback budget cuts were “a cooked
document,” noting that it included frontline Police Officers working on ATVs whom he fully supports
funding, because those Officers patrol the streets directly. He stated that this was why he introduced
an Item the previous day to consolidate some departments to save money, which Commissioner
Fernandez agreed to co-sponsor. (See Item C7 AS.) He added that the Commission had an
opportunity to set the standard in Miami-Dade County by adopting a rollback rate, but the
Administration’s proposal made that difficult. He emphasized that Commissioners do have a process
and that today’s millage vote is part of it. He stated that the Commission has the ability now to lower
the millage rate. He noted that a motion and a second were already on the floor for a 0.05 mill
reduction to 5.8060, and he wanted to “get the win now” for taxpayers and continue the process the
Commission is already in.
Management & Budget Director Otto Stewart clarified that the Administration is recommending
5.8560 mills for the Operating General Millage and that the proposal before the Commission would
reduce it to 5.8060 mills.
Commissioner Magazine stated that, in order to balance the budget at the recommended millage rate,
the City faced a $6.9 million deficit. He explained that reducing the operating millage by 0.05 mills
would require identifying an additional $2.6 million in cost savings. He noted that the Commission had
already found $4.2 million in excess cost savings during Friday’s budget process, well beyond the
targeted amount. He added that this would allow the Commission to add items back into the budget
and still have room. He stated that his goal was to identify further efficiencies because he agreed with
what he described as the “poison-pill” nature of the rollback budget exercise. He explained for the
public that the meaning of the “poison-pill” analogy was this: if someone asked him to cut off one of
his limbs, he would sarcastically reply “take my head,” because no reasonable person would choose
to lose an arm. He stated that the rollback budget exercise operated in a similar fashion, because
many departments proposed cuts that no reasonable person would accept, prompting predictable
rejection. He stated that the resulting list of proposed cuts signaled that the rollback budget was set
up in a way that ensured failure, and that while significant cuts were ultimately found, some of the
proposed reductions were not the most efficient or reasonable areas to trim. Commissioner Magazine
stated that, to bring the discussion full circle, he seconded Commissioner Suarez’s motion, explaining
that adopting the 5.8060 operating millage rate would lock the Commission into a rate that still
provided considerable leeway beyond what had already been agreed to.
Commissioner Fernandez added that his focus is on what residents ultimately have to pay. He stated
that while they must move forward with necessary infrastructure projects, which will impose costs on
residents, the goal should be to keep residents’ tax bills flat. He asked what millage rate would
accomplish that outcome.
Management & Budget Director Otto Stewart stated that a millage rate of 5.7040 mills would keep
the average resident’s tax bill flat but would reduce the budget by $8 million, creating an additional
deficit.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that the Commission should consider adopting a 5.7040 millage rate
because it protects residents in the absence of adopting a rollback rate. He proposed directing
Administration to identify potential savings in nonessential services.
Mayor Meiner reminded his colleagues to speak through the Chair.
Commissioner Magazine stated that 5.7040 is the aspirational goal for September once the rate
analysis is refined. He stated that he supports Commissioner Suarez’s motion because it sets them
on the path toward that direction and allows Administration more time to analyze what millage rate
would offset recent infrastructure costs. He stated that they do not have that analysis at present.
City Manager Eric Carpenter responded to the “poison-pill” comment by stating that the budget
exercise included a 5% reduction across all departments, and that Administration provided both a
program budget and a line-item budget. He stated that he is comfortable discussing the matter further.
R7 G (Operating Millage) - As Amended
A motion was made by Commissioner Suarez to adopt the Resolution setting the proposed operating
millage at 5.8060 mills, seconded by Commissioner Magazine. Vote: 5-2; Opposed: Commissioner
Bhatt and Vice-Mayor Dominguez.
Management & Budget Director Otto Stewart introduced R7 F and explained that the voted debt
service millage rate is 0.2693 mills.
R7 G (Debt Service Millage)
Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Resolution establishing the debt service
millage rate of 0.2693 mills; seconded by Commissioner Suarez. Vote: 7-0.
DIRECTION:
Commissioner Fernandez asked Administration to find real efficiencies in the budget that are not
critical services but could help achieve a 5.7040 millage rate, which would keep the average resident’s
tax bill flat. He stated that the Commission must not repeat what happened with the rollback budget,
which he described as unfair both to Commissioners and to frontline employees whose critical
positions were placed on the rollback list. He stated that in a one-billion-dollar organization, there are
areas where noncritical efficiencies can be found without reducing levels of service in Sanitation or
Public Safety.
He made a motion directing Administration to return to the City Commission with proposed savings,
stating again that they must not repeat what occurred with the rollback exercise. Commissioners
Magazine and Suarez seconded the motion. Vote: 7-0.

items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34388 was adopted as amended. The Item was heard with R7 I. The
Title of the Resolution was read into the record. The Public Hearing was held. Commissioner
Magazine made a motion to adopt the Resolution as amended, seconded by Mayor Meiner.
Amendments: Increasing public benefits by $200,000, directed to flooding and resiliency
infrastructure, allocating $500,000 per year for five years from Phase II revenues for flooding and
resiliency infrastructure, and dedicating $100,000 from Lincoln Road public benefits to trolley and
transportation services. Vote: 6-1. The vote applied to both R7 H and R7 I, which were considered
together.
AMENDMENTS:
 Accept the developer’s additional $200,000 one-time contribution, with the $200,000 directed to
flooding and resiliency infrastructure.
 Dedicate $500,000 per year for five years, beginning upon opening of Phase II, toward flooding
and resiliency infrastructure, funded from all Phase II revenue.
 Allocate $100,000 from Lincoln Road public-benefits funding to trolley and transportation services.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: No
Ozzie Dominguez to handle.
Commissioner Magazine introduced the Item, explaining that the City-owned office property, operated
under a land lease with this private individual, has already invested $50 million in capital
improvements that have significantly benefited the City through further economic development, and
importantly, the City receives a gross percentage of revenue from the project. He emphasized that
the more the project earns, the more the City earns, noting that this revenue participation is
increasingly important as the Commission remains budget-conscious and seeks to restore funding to
residents, especially in light of developments in Tallahassee. He stated that the proposal before them,
discussed extensively, would allow a Phase II expansion in which the property owner would invest
an additional $50 million in capital improvements that would not only increase future revenue from
the new phase but also enhance revenues received from Phase I. He turned the Item over to Ozzy
Dominguez and asked him to highlight the incremental amounts of money the City would begin
receiving almost immediately from the project, not just from the new construction but also from the
increased revenue share. Commissioner Magazine thanked Ozzy and his team, noting the months
of negotiation with the property owner and describing the relationship as a partnership, given that
both parties share the same piece of land.
Ozzy Dominguez, Asset Management Division Director, stated that, as Commissioner Magazine
mentioned, they have been back-and-forth with the developer negotiating terms. The amendment
would grant the developer two additional 20-year extension options. He explained that the developer
will add 47,000 square feet of rentable area on the roof of the current garage, which they are already
permitted to do, but in order to make the $35-$50 million investment, they are requesting the
additional lease term so they have the opportunity to recover that investment. When Phase II begins,
the City’s percentage contribution will increase from 2.5% to 3% of total revenue collected, including
rents for both retail and office space. He added that the two 20-year options will generate revenues
not currently contemplated under the agreement that expires in 2092, bringing approximately $234
million to the City over the long term. The immediate benefit of Phase II, he noted, is roughly $18
million in additional revenue during the first term. He reminded Commissioners that, during the
previous Commission Meeting, Commissioner Suarez asked whether the additional funds generated
through this project could help offset the City’s capital infrastructure deficit. Asset Management
Division Director Dominguez stated that his recommendation, outlined in the memo, is to allocate
$500,000 per year from Phase II revenues toward infrastructure needs. In response to Commissioner
Suarez, he explained that five years was simply a starting recommendation and that the allocation
could be extended to reach the full $6-6.5 million infrastructure deficit if the Commission wished.
Commissioner Suarez stated that while the public benefits are appreciated, he believes all public
benefits should be directed to infrastructure. He listed the proposed benefits: $100,000 for Blue Zones
restaurant certification, $100,000 for a human-trafficking tip line, $50,000 for Sister Cities, and
$600,000 for Lincoln Road improvements and/or Lincoln Road art. He suggested that all of these be
redirected exclusively to infrastructure, noting that residents often ask why developers are not
contributing more toward infrastructure. He stated that this project presents a clear opportunity for a
developer to contribute directly to infrastructure instead of directing $600,000 to Lincoln Road art, and
he asked his colleagues for their views on this approach.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez added that the public benefits amount mentioned is a drop in the bucket
compared to the almost one million dollars being given as part of this project. She explained that the
funds are intended for use in and around Lincoln Road; for example, Sister Cities events have taken
place at Lincoln Road restaurants, and the $50,000 allocated to Sister Cities is meant to be spread
over five years to help revitalize those restaurants when Sister Cities diplomats and dignitaries visit
from around the world. She noted that each Commissioner brings different perspectives about what
makes the City special. While infrastructure is important, she stated that so are the cultural and
community elements that make Miami Beach iconic.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas stated that she had suggested that $100,000 be dedicated to a tip line
for suspected human trafficking, provided the tips lead to an arrest or conviction. She emphasized
that this is not a personal pet project but is critical to her and to the public safety of the City, especially
in light of a recent high-profile arrest in Miami involving Andrew Tate and his brother. She noted that
human trafficking prevention is a serious priority and appreciates Commissioner Suarez’s suggestion,
but she would still prefer to keep the $100,000 for human trafficking tips if possible.
Mayor Meiner thanked Commissioner Matteo-Salinas for her work with the State Attorney’s Office on
human trafficking. He stated that a recent training event involved nearly one hundred law enforcement
personnel, and highlighted that the Miami Beach Police Department has its own dedicated human
trafficking unit, the only city in Miami-Dade County to have one. He applauded the collaboration
between multiple law enforcement agencies and commended her efforts.
Commissioner Magazine stated that he agrees with Commissioner Suarez about the importance of
infrastructure and believes the City can achieve multiple goals. He explained that the public benefits,
totaling $1 million, were discussed at length over several months by his colleagues. He said the
Administration’s recommendation to dedicate five years of $500,000 per year from the incremental
Phase II funding would result in $2,500,000 going directly to infrastructure. He added that during the
County’s budget process, transportation funding had been cut, and many workers and residents rely
on transit to reach Lincoln Road. He proposed allocating $100,000 of the $600,000 Lincoln Road
funding toward trolley and transportation services. He reiterated support for Commissioner Suarez’s
recommendation to direct $500,000 per year toward flooding, resiliency, and infrastructure, noting
this represents a significant win for the City: about $1,300,000 in initial public benefits across art,
Lincoln Road revitalization, and transportation, plus $2,500,000 in new Phase II infrastructure
funding, with millions more in future revenue that can be allocated each year as priorities evolve.
Commissioner Suarez stated that the core functions of government are public safety, infrastructure,
and sanitation, and, with all due respect, allocating $600,000 for art improvements on Lincoln Road
while the City faces nearly $1 billion in infrastructure needs is offensive to voters. He emphasized that
every dollar directed to infrastructure is one fewer dollar in taxes residents must pay, and stated that
this is his priority and where he stands.
In responding to Commissioner Suarez’s question, Asset Management Division Director Dominguez
explained that five years was only a starting point. Once Phase II begins, the City could begin
allocating $500,000 per year toward infrastructure. He emphasized that the Commission may extend
the allocation period beyond five years if it wishes, including up to the full $6 million discussed by
Commissioner Suarez.
Commissioner Fernandez explained that, as it relates to public benefits, he would leave the final
determination to what the applicant proffers and to the sponsor of the Item, because these are proffers
being made and the sponsor should finalize them. He stated that he appreciates the significant
investment being proposed, supports revitalizing Lincoln Road, and noted that there are numerous
developments underway from the east end of Lincoln Road to the NoLi (North Lincoln Road) project.
He added that private investment on City-owned property will help revitalize Lincoln Road and
acknowledged that public benefits do arise from such projects.
In reply to Commissioner Fernandez’s questions, Asset Management Division Director Dominguez
stated that the two independent appraisals obtained concluded $3.9 million per year and $3.2 million
per year as fair market ground rent. He clarified that fair market appraisals are only tools to understand
how appraisers value a property; they do not indicate what the City can enforce under the existing
agreement, which is not in a market-reset period. The City is currently locked into the terms of the
present lease. He explained that staff presented and discussed the appraisals with the developer, but
given the substantial investments being made in Phases I and II, the developer returned with different
financial offers, and negotiations went back and forth accordingly.
Commissioner Fernandez noted that the City is a landlord in an agreement with a tenant and cannot
reset rents outside a market-reset period. He asked how the City quantifies the tenant’s $50 million
investment in new construction when negotiating financial terms.
Asset Management Division Director Dominguez explained that staff considered the investments
already made in the building, the caliber of tenants brought in, the planned 47,000 square-foot
expansion, and the additional revenue the City will receive both immediately and over the extended
40-year term.
Commissioner Fernandez explained that, in essence, the developer’s investment is treated as the
principal consideration for extending the lease term and adjusting the rent structure.
Asset Management Division Director Dominguez added that with the potential continued growth of
the project, based on revenue projections, the developer’s revenues could be substantially higher
than currently forecast, and higher revenues would directly generate more revenue for the City.
Commissioner Fernandez added that the amendment grants an additional two twenty-year terms,
and asked whether the City had obtained an analysis of how the additional forty-year extension would
impact the market value of the tenant’s leasehold interest. He noted that no such analysis was
performed and asked how staff determined that the City is receiving adequate compensation for
granting forty additional years.
Asset Management Division Director Dominguez responded that staff relied on projected revenues,
expected rent growth, and increases in base rent as the basis for determining compensation. He
explained that the total projected revenue for the two twenty-year terms is approximately $248 million
based on a 3% annual growth rate and a 12% periodic adjustment, though revenues could be higher
depending on future rental performance. He emphasized that projections are conservative and
grounded in standard growth assumptions.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that the forty-year extension increases the value of the leasehold.
He noted that Mr. Rivani is a businessman, and that after investing in the property and participating
in Lincoln Road’s renaissance, he may eventually choose to sell his leasehold interest. He asked
whether the City receives participation rent or a transfer fee if the tenant later sells the leasehold and
recoups his investment, emphasizing the need to ensure taxpayers obtain maximum benefit. He
added that if the City wanted to receive the full appraised rent value for the property now, it is not well
positioned because this is not a rent-reset period. However, he asked whether, at the next rent reset,
the City can seek its fair market value under the agreement, and Asset Management Division Director
Dominguez confirmed that the agreement allows the City to obtain fair market value during the next
reset period.
Commissioner Fernandez then asked how the City could obtain fair market value if a cap is imposed
on future rent resets.
Asset Management Division Director Dominguez stated that if the amendment is approved, the rent-
reset caps would apply during future resets. He added that the cap request is tied solely to this
amendment.
Commissioner Fernandez noted that under the existing agreement with Mr. Rivani, there is no cap
on rent resets. Under the proposed terms, there would be a cap, which concerns him because
although he sees the long-term value of $248 million, he will not be present sixty years from now to
experience it. He stated that while the long-term revenue projections are strong, imposing a cap could
create a less favorable long-term position for future taxpayers and future Commissions. He asked
how the City could avoid limiting the ability of future residents to obtain fair market rent.
Asset Management Division Director Dominguez explained that staff was not in favor of including a
cap, but the developer insisted, on two or three occasions, that the only way he could secure a return
on his $50 million Phase I investment and proposed $35-$50 million Phase II investment was by
having a controlled cap on the market resets. The developer requested 20% caps for the first two
resets and 33% caps for the final two resets.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that he appreciates that the proposed amendment puts the City in
a better position generally, except when future taxpayers attempt to obtain true fair market rent. He
reiterated that imposing caps could limit future Commissions and taxpayers. He said he needs
guidance from the City Manager, as Asset Management Division Director Dominguez indicated the
Administration did not want caps, but ultimately negotiated them because they were a priority for the
developer.
City Manager Eric Carpenter stated that in negotiations there are priorities for both sides. He
explained that the rent-reset cap was a priority for the developer, while the City’s priority was
increasing the base rent and percentage rent above current levels so that the City could begin seeing
returns immediately. He stated that although the Administration would prefer not to have caps, at the
end of the day the amendment reflects give-and-take between the parties, and staff was ultimately
able to negotiate higher rent levels and higher percentage rent in exchange for accepting the caps.
Commissioner Fernandez thanked Mr. Rivani for the investment he is making in the City, noting that
he has a tremendous vision and that the Commission wants to see the project come to fruition. He
stated, however, that he must remain mindful of the voters and must be able to look residents in the
eye and say the terms being sent to them are better now than under the existing agreement. He
reiterated that the rent-reset cap concerns him because it is a change that may be perceived as less
favorable to the City in the long run.
Mr. Rivani stated that it is important to understand what he called “the tale of two buildings.” He
explained that 1601 Washington Avenue, the sister building to this property, was developed more
than twenty years ago but has become a blight on the City as a failed development. He said they are
here trying to discuss what fair market value will be sixty years from now, but pointed out that they
have already doubled the revenue of the current building over the past two years by approximately
$300,000 per year. He stated that over the next twenty years, the City will be able to put close to $20
million into its budget from the expansion, an amount the City would not receive if the Phase II building
is not constructed. He argued that there is no crystal ball showing where commercial real estate or
office demand will be sixty years from now, nor whether the first floor of the building might be
underwater due to rising sea levels. He added that the City should view the extension as “a better
gamble,” producing an immediate return, strengthening the redevelopment and resurgence of Lincoln
Road, and creating a win-win for all parties. He explained that commercial rent-reset caps nationwide
often range between 10% and 15%, whereas the proposed caps of 20% for the first two resets and
33% for the last two resets are significantly higher. He added that for the first $50 million already
invested in the building, no concession had been requested from the City. He described the
amendment as a partnership in which the developer makes a significant investment and seeks a
longer lease term to support that investment, benefiting Lincoln Road, the City’s constituents, and

ACTION: Resolution 2026-34392 was adopted. The Title of the Resolution was read into the record.
The Public Hearing was held. A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez to adopt the
Resolution; seconded by Mayor Meiner. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
David Gomez to handle.
Director of Capital Improvements David Gomez reminded the Commission that at the last meeting
there was a First Reading of an amendment and restatement of the development agreement for 1250
West Avenue. He stated that the amended agreement includes five changes. The first extends the
deadlines to obtain easements and upland agreements from areas responsible for building Baywalks;
it does not change the final deadline but gives the developer more time to secure agreements. The
second clarifies that the Baywalk segment directly behind 1250 West Avenue may be constructed
over water, allowing it to connect to the segment directly south at 1228 West Avenue. The third alters
the allowable square footage for non-residential areas by reducing the ground-level square footage
from 4,000 to 2,000 square feet while allowing certain uses, such as spa facilities, in the sub-
basement level. The fourth clarifies the applicability of the City’s floodplain regulations, stating that
floodplain requirements will apply at the time the building permit is submitted. The final change makes
technical updates by removing the name of the former owner, adding the name of David Martin, and
updating defined terms.
Commissioner Fernandez stated that the most important issue for him is ensuring displaced tenants
have a “soft landing.” He asked the applicant for an update on rental-relocation checks.
Mr. Larkin, representing the applicant, stated that 106 tenants were classified as bona fide lessees.
In June, 51 checks totaling $750,000 were mailed. On July 31, an additional 35 checks totaling
$450,000 will be mailed. He stated that they hope to send the remaining checks in August and aim
to have all remaining checks mailed by Labor Day.
Commissioner Fernandez noted that the total amount is approximately $1.2 million and asked why
35 tenants had not yet received their checks.
Mr. Larkin explained that those tenants had not provided forwarding addresses. Under the agreement,
the preference is to provide payment directly to tenants, but after one year the funds revert to the
City.
Commissioner Fernandez confirmed that the 51 tenants who provided addresses received their
checks and that the 35 remaining tenants had not yet received payment.
The Public Hearing was opened. City Clerk Rafael E. Granado recognized Mr. Ciraldo, a resident
appearing via Zoom.
Mr. Ciraldo thanked Commissioner Fernandez for raising questions regarding displaced tenants. He
stated that he had previously commented on eviction lawsuits filed against certain tenants and read
the names of individuals involved in the litigation. He urged the Commission to reconsider
“grandfathering” underground parking garages, stating that sea-level rise may inundate such
structures.
City Clerk Granado stated he saw no additional participants in Zoom or in the audience. The Public
Hearing was then closed.
A motion was made by Commissioner Fernandez to adopt the Resolution, seconded by Mayor
Meiner. Vote: 7-0.

ACTION: Resolution 2026-34394 was adopted. Commissioner Bhatt made a motion to adopt the
Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Fernandez. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes

Jose Gonzalez to handle.
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt informed her colleagues that the Item had been discussed several
months ago and that changes were made based on data analysis. She stated that the Item was
self-explanatory, noting five co-sponsors, and initially asked to call the vote.
Commissioner David Suarez asked whether someone could outline the changes before taking action.
Transportation Director Jose Gonzalez stated that over the past several months, the Department of
Transportation had worked with the United States Coast Guard and had held a community meeting
to obtain feedback on the proposed schedule that the Coast Guard had put forward. He explained
that the City’s traffic study recommended hourly bridge openings; however, the Coast Guard did not
support hourly openings. As a result, bridge openings must continue every 30 minutes during non-
restricted times. He noted that the 63rd Street Bridge already has significant restrictions, with three
hours during the morning peak and three hours during the afternoon peak during which the bridge
does not open. He added that while vehicles have alternatives, vessels do not, making hourly
openings a non-starter for the Coast Guard. Director Gonzalez stated that another proposed change
involved the on-demand schedule and determining the most appropriate time to begin such a
schedule. Pursuant to the City Commission’s direction, staff held a community meeting, and residents
expressed support for an on-demand schedule during very late evening and early morning hours
rather than a fixed schedule. Residents raised concerns that vessels missing an opening might linger
and create noise.
Commissioner Suarez asked when the on-demand schedule would begin. Director Gonzalez replied
that on-demand operations would start at 11 p.m., the time at which both traffic and vessel volumes
significantly decrease. He stated that the schedule would run until 7 a.m. and would balance vehicular
needs, marine access, and neighborhood quality-of-life concerns. Commissioner Suarez asked when
the on-demand schedule would end.
Director Gonzalez replied that the end time is 7 a.m. and clarified that weekday morning restrictions
would resume at that time, lasting until 10 a.m. He noted that those restrictions are unchanged.
Commissioner Suarez asked how the schedule operates on weekends.
Director Gonzalez explained that on weekends the bridge would open on demand at the hour and
half-hour from 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. He added that from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m., the bridge would also operate
on demand, consistent with weekday operations, noting that the on-demand period applies seven
days a week.
Commissioner Suarez thanked Commissioner Bhatt for addressing his concerns when the Item was
first heard and stated that the revised approach strikes an ideal balance between vessel traffic and
neighborhood quality-of-life needs in the surrounding area.
Commissioner Bhatt made a motion to adopt the Resolution, seconded by Commissioner Alex
Fernandez. Vote: 7-0.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, DIRECTING THE CITY ADMINISTRATION TO PREPARE A REQUEST FOR QUALIFICATIONS (RFQ) FOR AN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE CONSULTANT TO EVALUATE OPPORTUNITIES FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE-BASED EFFICIENCIES, WORKLOAD REDUCTIONS, CONTRACTING OPPORTUNITIES, EXPENDITURE REDUCTIONS, AND LONG- TERM COST SAVINGS ACROSS ALL CITY DEPARTMENTS, INCLUDING, WITHOUT LIMITATION, RESIDENT SERVICES, PERMITTING, PROCUREMENT, CONTRACTS, FINANCE, HUMAN RESOURCES, WORKFORCE MANAGEMENT, PUBLIC RECORDS, ADMINISTRATIVE FUNCTIONS, AND OTHER CITY OPERATIONS, WITH SUCH RFQ TO REQUIRE THAT THE SELECTED CONSULTANT BE COMPENSATED ON A CONTINGENCY-FEE BASIS, WITH PAYMENT TIED SOLELY TO VERIFIABLE SAVINGS IDENTIFIED AND REALIZED BY THE CITY AS A RESULT OF THE CONSULTANT'S RECOMMENDATIONS; AND FURTHER DIRECTING THE CITY ADMINISTRATION TO EVALUATE WHICH CITY FUNCTIONS OR POSITIONS MAY BE APPROPRIATELY CONTRACTED OUT, CONSOLIDATED, AUTOMATED, REDUCED THROUGH ATTRITION, OR OTHERWISE RESTRUCTURED IN ORDER TO REDUCE GOVERNMENT EXPENSES, IMPROVE ACCOUNTABILITY, BETTER CONTROL STAFFING COSTS AND WORK HOURS, AND PREPARE THE CITY FOR ANTICIPATED FISCAL PRESSURES.
items.action: Resolution 2026-34395 was adopted. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas. Vote: 7-0.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34395 was adopted. Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the
Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Frank Quintana and Kristy Bada to handle.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas separated the Item from the Consent Agenda (on June 24, 2026) to
ask whether it should be referred to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee (FERC). She
stated that she needed clarification on what the Commission intended to accomplish with the
proposal.
Commissioner Suarez explained that the purpose of the Item was to identify efficiencies where
artificial intelligence (AI) could assist government operations. He noted that the proposed consultant
arrangement would be entirely contingent-based, meaning the City would incur no cost unless
measurable savings were achieved. He stated that AI is now widely used and saw no reason to delay
the Item, especially as the City is seeking ways to reduce operating costs. He called the Item a “no-
brainer.”
Mayor Meiner reminded the Commission that he previously sponsored a successful initiative to
incorporate AI into various levels of City government, as well as a pilot program in the Building
Department to apply AI to permitting.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas asked whether the consultant itself would be an AI system or whether
the City would hire a consultant to recommend which AI tools to use.
Commissioner Suarez clarified that the City would not be using AI directly; instead, the consultant
would use AI tools to identify efficiencies on the City’s behalf, again on a contingent-fee basis.
Chief Information Officer Frank Quitana provided additional context, noting that the proposal
stemmed from staff discussions about structuring professional services agreements more creatively.
The goal, he explained, was to avoid traditional flat-rate consultant expenses by tying payment to
actual deliverables and results. He noted that there are multiple ways to structure such agreements,
and the intent was to align compensation with measurable outcomes.
Commissioner Suarez emphasized that the Commission is focused on reducing expenses and
lowering the millage rate, and that the Item directly supports that effort. He questioned the need to
send the Item to committee.
Mayor Meiner informed the Commission that high-level technology professionals, including a former
senior Google executive, recently offered their assistance to the City at no cost. He questioned
whether the City should explore those opportunities before formally hiring a consultant.
Commissioner Bhatt cautioned that high-level technology firms have faced public criticism nationally
and stated that she would not support relying on external offers without proper vetting.
Mayor Meiner reiterated that any proposal would return to the Commission, but noted that the City
might have opportunities to obtain similar services without entering into a paid consulting agreement.
Chief Information Officer Quintana stated that receiving professional services for free or at no cost is
outside of their professional scope.
City Manager Carpenter commented that they would gladly accept free services rather than paid
services whenever possible.
Commissioner Suarez returned the discussion to the Item and explained that the proposal was
structured so that a consultant’s compensation would be tied solely to demonstrated savings. Suarez
gave an example: if the consultant identified $10 million in savings, the consultant might earn 10% of
that amount. Commissioner Suarez emphasized that the consultant would not request payment
upfront for projected savings; instead, they would present options, and any negotiated fee would be
contingent on actual results.
Commissioner Fernandez reported that they recently spoke with representatives from Tyler
Technologies, whose systems the City already uses. Commissioner Fernandez explained that Tyler
described examples from other jurisdictions, including Collier County, where AI tools reportedly
identified approximately 22% in potential budget reallocations and about $40 million in efficiencies
while improving service delivery. Commissioner Fernandez stated that issuing a solicitation at this
stage would not disadvantage the City, noting that any future contract award would require
Commission approval and implementation decisions would remain with the Commission and the City
Manager. Commissioner Fernandez concluded that, given the preliminary nature of the Item, there
were no concerns with moving forward.
Commissioner Bhatt asked Chief Information Officer Quintana how sensitive information such as
employees’ home addresses, dates of birth, and Social Security numbers would be safeguarded.
Commissioner Bhatt expressed concern that AI systems can behave unpredictably and referenced
an article describing an AI system that exceeded its programmed constraints. Commissioner Bhatt
reiterated support for exploring efficiencies but emphasized the importance of protecting sensitive
data for the City’s 2,200 employees and 82,000 residents.
Chief Information Officer Quintana acknowledged the concern and explained that AI used in City
operations is governed by strict privacy requirements, applicable laws, and internal policies. Chief
Information Officer Quintana stated that they would never recommend allowing any external AI
system unrestricted access to City data because AI systems must be trained to search for specific
items and do not independently access all information. Chief Information Officer Quintana noted that
consultants would work only with defined systems, such as financials, personnel management, or
permitting, and would train their tools on controlled datasets tailored to those functions. Chief
Information Officer Quintana added that the AI tools developed in-house are segmented and do not
communicate with other systems, ensuring protection of City information. Chief Information Officer
Quintana clarified that these evaluations do not require sensitive personal data such as Social
Security numbers or home addresses. Chief Information Officer Quintana also expressed skepticism
toward vendors that make broad claims without demonstrating capabilities. Chief Information Officer
Quintana explained that the proposed model allows a consultant to demonstrate technology on a
small scale using test data, enabling the Commission to make informed decisions before considering
any expansion.
Commissioner Matteo-Salinas stated that she would still prefer the Item to be heard at the FERC,
noting that all Items exceeding $75,000 are required to be referred. She agreed with preparing the
RFP but wanted its structure to be informed by feedback received at FERC.
Commissioner Suarez responded that the proposal involved no fee or flat fee. He stated that the cost
to the City would remain zero unless a consultant generated savings for residents, and that any fee
would be determined only when the solicitation came back with demonstrated results. Commissioner
Suarez reiterated that the City is working to save as much money as possible and emphasized that
frontline workers would not be cut. He added that the Item presents a clear opportunity to identify
efficiencies and questioned why it needed referral to FERC if it would return without cost.
Mayor Meiner stated that he was supportive and agreed with Commissioner Suarez. He added that
he would also like to explore whether other companies could provide similar services at the same or
higher level of quality.
City Manager Carpenter requested flexibility to craft something more comprehensive than a
contingency-based agreement, noting that contingency-based firms he has worked with in
government are not necessarily the people that he would want to be making these decisions with.
Mayor Meiner acknowledged this point.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez agreed that it was worthwhile to explore the proposal but cautioned that AI
requires close oversight. She referenced Federal government experiences where contracts involving
AI technologies resulted in large errors and inflated costs. She stated that it is hard to keep AI
accountable. Vice-Mayor Dominguez reiterated that the Commission must ensure AI is not solely
responsible for determining savings, as accountability can be difficult. She supported referral to FERC
but understood why some believed referral was unnecessary without a fixed price. She noted that
past consultant engagements were typically around $250,000 and believed such cost considerations
should be evaluated in the future.
Mayor Meiner noted that Chief Information Officer Quintana and City Manager Carpenter recently
briefed him on ongoing efforts to incorporate AI throughout the City and indicated that those initiatives
would continue. City Manager Carpenter affirmed.
Commissioner Suarez made a motion to adopt the Resolution, which was seconded by Commissioner
Matteo-Salinas. The motion passed 7-0.

Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes

John Rebar to handle.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that the Resolution authorizes one of the City’s existing vendors, Savino
& Miller Design Studio, an excellent landscape architecture firm that recently completed a
long-planned and desired project in Mid-Beach at Bayshore Park. She explained that the firm
examined the underutilized West Lots and envisioned how they might be used differently without
eliminating parking or removing the services that must remain in that area. They considered how to
use the land mass more effectively to create another world-class park with a variety of potential
amenities. She noted that the Resolution marks the beginning of a planning process that will be open
to the public, but that the effort needs a clear starting point. She added that Savino & Miller Design
Studio is well suited to initiate that process.
Commissioner Bhatt made a motion to adopt the Resolution, seconded by Commissioner Fernandez.
Vote: 7-0.

David Suarez.

items.title: A RESOLUTION OF THE MAYOR AND CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF MIAMI BEACH, FLORIDA, DIRECTING THE CITY ADMINISTRATION TO SIGNIFICANTLY INCREASE THE NUMBER OF RETIRED POLICE VEHICLES THAT ARE CONVERTED INTO POLICE DECOY VEHICLES; AND FURTHER, DIRECTING THE CITY ADMINISTRATION TO DEPLOY SUCH POLICE DECOY VEHICLES, WHICH SHOULD BE OUTFITTED WITH SOLAR-POWERED ELECTRIC SYSTEMS, OR OTHER APPROPRIATE TECHNOLOGY SUFFICIENT TO OPERATE THEIR EMERGENCY OVERHEAD LIGHTS, THROUGHOUT THE CITY IN ORDER TO ENHANCE PUBLIC SAFETY AND DETER CRIMINAL ACTIVITY.
items.action: Resolution 2026-34399 was adopted. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas. Vote: 7-0.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Resolution 2026-34399 was adopted. Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt
the Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas. Vote: 7-0.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
DIRECTION:
 Police Department and Fleet Management to evaluate the feasibility and cost of adding monitoring
or video-recording capability to decoy vehicles.
 Police Department to confirm which retired vehicles remain eligible (i.e., not yet de-striped) and
provide an updated list of vehicles that can be outfitted and deployed as decoys.
Chief Wayne Jones and Carlos Berriz to handle.
Mayor Meiner stated that the City has used decoy Police vehicles over the past year equipped with
solar-powered battery packs that illuminate the emergency lights. He explained that these newer
vehicles resemble active patrol vehicles, making them more effective than older decommissioned
cars, which are more recognizable as decoys. He noted that twenty-seven retired vehicles are
pending auction and could instead be repurposed. He added that outfitting each vehicle with solar-
powered systems costs approximately $890, or about $24,000 in total.
Operations Division Major Marlen Rivero stated that, in coordination with Fleet Management, the
Police Department identified twenty-seven vehicles nearing retirement that could be equipped with
solar panels. She explained that installation costs are approximately $870 per vehicle. She stated
that twelve decoy vehicles are currently deployed and have been effective. She added that the key
to their continued utility is strategic placement and periodic relocation. She reported that auction
revenue would be approximately $3,600 per vehicle.
Mayor Meiner observed that Commissioner Fernandez had previously sponsored an Item to place
Police vehicles at strategic entrance points and noted that expanding the decoy program would
complement that effort.
Commissioner Fernandez asked the City Manager whether funding for the earlier proposal had been
included in budget enhancements.
Mayor Meiner stated that his intent was to emphasize the value of decoy visibility. He described an
example from a retail store where shoplifting and loitering declined significantly after a decoy vehicle
was deployed nearby.
Major Rivero stated that the decoy vehicles are in high demand and widely requested by the
community. She explained that the solar panels allow the red and blue lights to remain illuminated,
which increases deterrence because a darkened, unlit vehicle is more likely to be identified as a
decoy.
Mayor Meiner proposed that the City retain, rather than auction, the twenty-seven vehicles.
Commissioner Suarez asked whether any decoy vehicles have monitoring or recording capability.
Major Rivero stated that they do not.
Mayor Meiner asked whether Fleet could evaluate the cost of adding such capabilities.
Major Rivero responded that she did not have cost information and could confer with Fleet.
Chief of Police Wayne Jones stated that decoy vehicles are an excellent deterrence tool and are
highly requested by residents and businesses. He stated that he could obtain cost information
regarding video streaming and provide it to the Commission.
City Manager Carpenter stated that some of the twenty-seven vehicles may already have been
stripped of decals and would need to be assessed individually. He recommended outfitting the next
group of available vehicles.
Chief Jones clarified that some vehicles had been prepared for auction and others referenced by
Major Rivero were in the decommissioning process.
Major Rivero stated that the twenty-seven vehicles are expected to reach their retirement timeline in
the coming months.
Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Resolution, seconded by Commissioner
Matteo-Salinas. The motion passed by a vote of 7-0.
items.motion: Fernandez made a motion to adopt the Resolution; seconded by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas.

REFERRAL:
Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee
AFTER-THE-FACT RESOLUTION: 2026-34400 - Authorizing, retroactively, the month-to-month
extension of the agreement with Sodexo Live! through December 2026.
Mayor Meiner recommended referring the Item to the Finance and Economic Resiliency Committee
and noted that the Item included a slight extension of the existing agreement. He asked City Manager
Eric Carpenter to elaborate.
City Manager Carpenter stated that the referral would allow the Committee to review the proposed
new contract and to discuss extending the current agreement with Sodexo Live! on a month-to-month
basis through December.
Mayor Meiner added that while Sodexo performs exceptionally well during large-scale convention
events, smaller resident or charitable events of five hundred people or fewer pose challenges, and
the Commission would continue working on appropriate contract language.
Commissioner Fernandez expressed appreciation for Sodexo and stated that they have agreed to
offer a 25% discount for residents, to provide certain donations to 501(c)(3) organizations to ensure
events remain at cost, and to add additional Kosher caterers to increase competition.
Doug Connor, Senior Vice President of Sodexo Live, addressed the Commission and stated that they
plan to add five Kosher caterers who have worked with them in the past and that they remain open
to contract options.
Commissioner Fernandez made a motion to refer the Item to the Finance and Economic Resiliency
Committee (the motion encompassed the month-to-month extension described during the
discussion), seconded by Vice-Mayor Dominguez. Vote: 7-0.

items.title: DISCUSS/TAKE ACTION – UPDATE ON POLICE ENFORCEMENT EFFORTS AND DATA RELATED TO EXCESSIVE VEHICULAR MUFFLER AND EXHAUST NOISE THROUGHOUT OUR CITY.
items.action: Discussion held. Chief Wayne Jones to handle. DIRECTION: Provide a breakdown of citations issued during nighttime hours via LTC. Chief Wayne Jones to handle.
items.voteBasis: No separate vote identified. A vote has not been inferred.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION: Discussion held. Chief Wayne Jones to handle.
DIRECTION: Provide a breakdown of citations issued during nighttime hours via LTC. Chief Wayne
Jones to handle.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez stated that the Item has been on the agenda for some time and that the
Commission receives monthly enforcement reports through Letters to Commission (LTC). She noted
that the increase in citations has been significant. She also reported meeting with SOFNA (South of
Fifth Neighborhood Association) and other stakeholders regarding quiet zone signage and explained
that a pilot program South of Fifth began a few weeks ago. She asked the Miami Beach Police
Department for an update on noise-related enforcement.
Operations Division Major Marlen Rivero stated that she is proud of the Department’s enforcement
efforts. She reported that year-to-date, 1,401 citations have been issued for vehicular noise violations,
more than twice the 675 issued the prior year. She noted that the Department has made the issue a
priority and that enforcement has been going very well.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez asked whether Officers have been able to issue citations based on the new
quiet zone signs.
Major Rivero responded that the signage effort is still very new. In Area 1 Zone, approximately 213
citations have been issued for loud exhaust and 252 citations for loud music, making it the area with
the highest enforcement activity. She stated that she visited the quiet zone sign at Fourth Street and
found it clear, although she could not confirm whether citations were being issued directly as a result
of the signage. She added that the Department is pleased with early results.
Vice-Mayor Dominguez thanked Major Rivero, stating that the Commission appreciates the
Department’s efforts and wants to keep the matter a priority in response to neighborhood concerns.
Mayor Meiner asked whether the citation data included a breakdown of nighttime hours.
Major Rivero stated that the current report is organized by areas and violation types and does not
reflect nighttime breakdowns. She explained that enforcement has focused on loud exhaust, loud
music, loud noise, and horn violations.
Mayor Meiner asked whether nighttime-specific data could be provided.
Major Rivero affirmed and added that there is substantial enforcement activity between the afternoon
and midnight overlap, and that the Department can provide the requested breakdown.
Mayor Meiner thanked Major Rivero, noting that excessive vehicular noise, especially modified
mufflers during late-night hours, is one of the most frequent complaints received by the Commission.

items.title: DISCUSS POTENTIAL AMENDMENTS TO THE SINGLE-FAMILY DEVELOPMENT REGULATIONS TO EXPEDITE PLANNING REVIEW.
items.action: A motion was made by Commissioner Bhatt to refer the Item to the Planning Board using Option 2; seconded by Commissioner Suarez. The referral included direction to transmit a draft Ordinance based on Option 2 with a broad title to allow flexibility during Planning Board review. Vote: 7-0. REFERRAL TO PLANNING BOARD: Refer Option 2 to the Planning Board, along with a draft Ordinance containing a broad title that can accommodate adjustments recommended during Planning Board discussion. James Seiberling to place on the Planning Board Agenda. Deborah Tackett to handle.
items.voteBasis: Item-specific vote extracted from the minutes.
items.recordExcerpt:
ACTION:
A motion was made by Commissioner Bhatt to refer the Item to the Planning Board using Option 2;
seconded by Commissioner Suarez. The referral included direction to transmit a draft Ordinance
based on Option 2 with a broad title to allow flexibility during Planning Board review. Vote: 7-0.
REFERRAL TO PLANNING BOARD:
Refer Option 2 to the Planning Board, along with a draft Ordinance containing a broad title that can
accommodate adjustments recommended during Planning Board discussion.
James Seiberling to place on the Planning Board Agenda. Deborah Tackett to handle.
VOTES:
Mayor Steven Meiner: Yes
Commissioner Tanya K. Bhatt: Yes
Vice-Mayor Laura Dominguez: Yes
Commissioner Alex Fernandez: Yes
Commissioner Joseph Magazine: Yes
Commissioner Monica Matteo-Salinas: Yes
Commissioner David Suarez: Yes
Per Commissioner Suarez’s direction, Deborah Tackett, Planning Director, explained that two options
were provided, and they asked for direction. Option 1 would be the extreme scenario with
simplification where they would be given a height and setbacks, and anything could be built within
that envelope provided; Option 2 is more nuanced but would go a long way to simplifying the
regulations and speeding up the permit review process. Single-family homes take an excessive
amount of plan review over time because of the complexities of the regulations. They are confident
that they can move forward with either of the proposals but would recommend that they give them
direction today to refine Option 2, which provides better protections for property owners and
neighborhoods. She further clarified that staff is recommending a referral to the Planning Board. In
response to Commissioner Suarez, she explained that a brand-new single-family home, a first run, is
going to be a four-hour review for a permit staff because the requirements are so complex, writing
out the comments, and typically they would be in communication with the architect, because
sometimes the architects do not understand certain sections that they have in the single-family. If
they have an outdoor area, it may or may not count as lot coverage; it depends on how deep the
overhang is, and so it not only takes a considerable amount of time to review but then to explain some
of their comments to the design professionals is also very time-consuming. That is what she has
found in reviewing homes herself, and it is a lot of back and forth with the property owner and/or the
architect-contractor for everyone to get on the same page. She thinks they can do better and keep
the intent of the single-family regulations, which is to provide protections for adjacent neighbors, but
simplify it so they can keep these things moving along.
Commissioner Suarez prefers Option 2, which gives them a better approach.
Planning Director Tackett then clarified the legal process: after the Planning Board discusses the draft
Ordinance, the matter must return to the City Commission for referral, and then it must go back again
to the Planning Board for formal consideration. She stated that this multi-step loop is required unless
the Commission chooses a different legislative pathway.
Commissioner Bhatt asked whether staff should prepare an Ordinance before sending it to the
Planning Board or whether the Board should review the concept first.
Planning Director Tackett stated that staff is asking for direction to prepare an Ordinance that is
consistent with Option 2 and a referral to the Planning Board. She stated that if the Planning Board's
discussion results in significantly different guidance, the Ordinance would need to be revised anyway.
Commissioner Bhatt made a motion to refer Option 2 to the Planning Board to discuss before they
prepare the Ordinance.
Deborah Tackett, Planning Director, added that they can bring a discussion to the Planning Board
and a referral back to the City Commission. She explained that whether an Ordinance title must be
revised depends on whether the Planning Board changes the scope of sections being amended. The
title can be written broadly to anticipate flexibility, but if the Board directs amendments to additional
or different sections of the Code, a re-notice and re-advertisement may be required. She stated that
crafting a broad title would avoid most re-noticing issues except where the Planning Board gives
completely different direction.
Commissioner Suarez stated that the process is ridiculous and it is exactly why they need this
because they have this long process that gets drawn out and government just gets in the way with
red tape. He stated that if it must go to the Planning Board, then back to the City Commission, then
back to the Planning Board again, the process can take six months. He stated this is one of the
biggest pain points that residents raised when the Commission knocked on doors, getting a permit,
and they have the ability to fix it now. He stated he prefers the more nuanced approach of Option 2
and supports sending it to the Planning Board and having it come back again.
Commissioner Bhatt stated that if it goes to the Planning Board for discussion and there is an
Ordinance prepared and the discussion ends up giving different guidance, they would have to revise
the Ordinance anyhow. She is not trying to add layers of time to this but just get the most effective
way to get feedback that they can see before it becomes the law of the land. She asked if it is viable
to go to the Planning Board with a prepared Ordinance and then, if changes are needed, revise it.
Commissioner Bhatt asked whether staff could create the Ordinance title broad enough to cover every
possible scenario so that re-noticing would not be required if only some portions of the Code were
amended.
Planning Director Tackett reiterated that whether they would have to re-notice depends on whether
the Ordinance title changes. She stated that a broad title can cover most eventualities, but a
fundamental shift in direction from the Planning Board would require a re-notice. Commissioner Bhatt
stated that such a fundamental shift would be a larger policy issue and retracted her amendment,
agreeing to send Option 2 with a broad title and draft Ordinance to the Planning Board.
Commissioner Suarez seconded the motion.
A motion was made by Commissioner Bhatt, seconded by Commissioner Suarez, to refer Option 2
with a draft Ordinance and broad title to the Planning Board. Vote: 7-0. Referral approved.

had been separated from the Consent Agenda by Commissioner Matteo-Salinas. A motion was made
by Board Member Tanya K. Bhatt to defer RDA-2 and C7 O Resolutions to the October 14, 2026
Commission Meeting, seconded by Board Member Alex Fernandez. The vote on the motion to
defer applied to both Items together and carried by acclamation: 8-0.
