DIRECTION:
 The Item was deferred to the October 14, 2026 Commission Meeting.
 The Office of the City Attorney to review RDA and HOME loan documents and determine whether
options such as modifying SRO placements or pursuing a deed-in-lieu scenario exist for future
consideration.
 Coordinate a Sunshine Meeting (City and County) with Board Member Vicki L. Lopez to clarify
MBCDC’s role in the portfolio transfer and address outstanding questions related to the SRO
program.
 Clarify what authority the City may have, as mortgage holder, regarding the number and type of
SRO placements at Meridian Place and other portfolio buildings.
Rafael E. Granado to notice. Lilia Cardillo to place on the October 14, 2026 Commission
Agenda, if received. Dr. Alba Tarre and the Office of the City Attorney to handle.
Director of Housing and Community Services Alba Tarre stated that the Item requests approval for
the assignment and assumption by Miami-Dade County of the RDA and City loan documents for
Meridian Place Apartments, a 34-unit affordable senior housing property located at 530 Meridian
Avenue. She explained that the property carries a $1.5 million RDA loan from 2007 and a $2.8 million
City HOME loan from 2011, both with affordability covenants through September 25, 2043. Director
Tarre stated that City approval is required because the City is a party to both loan documents. She
explained that the transfer is part of the County’s ongoing acquisition of the remaining Miami Beach
Community Development Corporation (MBCDC) portfolio, a process previously approved for the
Jefferson Apartments in 2024. She stated that, in exchange for assuming the loans, the County will
fund needed repairs, assign Royal American Management to operate the property, satisfy several
outstanding mortgages, and maintain all existing affordability restrictions through 2043. She noted
that Executive Director Cristian Arango of MBCDC and County staff were present to answer
questions.
Executive Director Cristian Arango introduced himself and stated that, in conjunction with Director
Tarre and her team, they were present to address questions regarding Meridian Place or other
properties within the MBCDC portfolio that will ultimately transfer to Miami-Dade County.
In response to Board Member David Suarez, Director Tarre explained that MBCDC is transferring its
entire portfolio to the County due to long-standing challenges with maintenance, repairs, and
sustaining the financial viability of the properties. She stated that MBCDC served as the City’s CHDO
(Community Housing Development Organization) when RDA and HOME funds were originally
invested. She explained that because the City holds two mortgages on the property, the transfer must
be approved by the Board. She added that the County is better positioned to maintain the buildings
moving forward.
City Attorney Ricardo J. Dopico clarified that the Item authorizes the assignment of the mortgage and
loan documents from MBCDC to Miami-Dade County.
In reply to Mayor Steven Meiner, Director Tarre stated that the City’s investment through RDA and
HOME dollars was already made and that approval of the Item preserves long-term affordability for
the property.
Board Member Monica Matteo-Salinas welcomed Board Member Vicki L. Lopez from Miami-Dade
County and stated that she separated Item C7 O from the Consent Agenda because she has
concerns related to the building. She stated that she previously discussed the matter with Board
Member Lopez because Royal American Management and the County are currently operating the
property. She noted that the Affordable Housing Advisory Committee discussed concerns at its
meeting the previous evening. She emphasized that she is not attempting to delay the transfer and
expressed appreciation to the County for assuming the portfolio and ensuring the continuation of
affordability. She stated that the City does not have the funding or workforce capacity to take on the
properties and that the portfolio is complex. She added that the Advisory Committee questioned
whether the County could financially make the City whole for RDA and HOME investments, because
the City will not receive repayment. She stated that the building at 530 Meridian Avenue has had
safety issues, referencing a recent shooting involving a tenant. She explained that she lives across
the street and frequently hears from neighboring residents. She stated that the building can be
problematic and asked that the County remain vigilant and proactively address issues that may arise.
She added that most buildings in the portfolio operate well and will be in capable hands under County
ownership.
Board Member Lopez thanked Board Member Monica Matteo-Salinas for her comments and stated
that she had not been aware of the public-safety concerns at the building. She directed County staff
to identify measures to ensure resident security and to prevent similar problems across portfolio
properties the County is accepting and managing.
Housing and Community Development Asset Manager Alexandro Bolaños (on behalf of Miami-Dade
County) stated that Meridian Place presents operational challenges because 20 units are reserved
for formerly homeless households. He explained that the County coordinates with the Homeless Trust
and the City of Miami Beach Housing Authority and noted that the asset had been over-leveraged.
He stated the County has paid over $1 million in institutional debt to date and is absorbing additional
debt, and that approximately $1 million was expended on exterior work addressing water intrusion
and repainting; he said the building has been cleaned up and occupancy has stabilized. He added
that the County is engaging a consultant to implement Crime Prevention Through Environmental
Design (CPTED), assessing hidden or exposed areas, and developing a plan to increase visibility
and remote monitoring to discourage bad behavior. He stated that problems are addressed quickly
and that turnover is high because the population is hard to serve; residents are referred into the
program, and due to resident-selection criteria for an elderly building, the property may accept only
about 1 in 10 applications. He said the referenced incident appears to be isolated, and emphasized
that the County has invested significant capital and intends to maintain compliance. Addressing Board
Member Lopez, Asset Manager Bolaños stated the building contains 34 units, 20 single-room-
occupancy studios and 14 one-bedroom units, with the one-bedrooms restricted at ≤60% AMI.
Board Member Lopez stated that she is seeing similar issues in buildings on the mainland and locally
where elderly residents live in properties that also reserve units for formerly homeless individuals.
She said elderly residents report feeling unsafe and emphasized the need for wraparound services
rather than housing alone, citing mental-health and support needs (therapeutic, medical, and job-
training services) that help ensure a safe transition without negatively impacting other residents. She
asked Asset Manager Bolaños to comment on steps being taken and reiterated the goal of successful,
healthy placement alongside the elderly population.
Asset Manager Bolaños stated the program at Meridian Place is Housing First, meaning no
wraparound services are embedded, and that assistance is tied to 30% AMI, so contract rents at 30%
AMI leave the program operating at a deficit. He explained the property cannot underwrite on-site
supportive services under current revenue and that, absent additional funding, property management
is left to perform case-management functions for which it lacks capacity. He said he supports
supportive housing models and cited Villa Matti as an example that works due to HUD support and
adequate fiscal resources, whereas Meridian Place relies on a local Housing Authority contract
without that avenue. He stated the County will continue working on the issue and hopes to improve
over time, but acknowledged it is a difficult blend to mix formerly homeless residents with elderly
housing without on-site wraparound.
Board Member Matteo-Salinas stated that she appreciates Board Member Lopez’s responsiveness
and reiterated that multiple concerns exist at the building. She said open communication is essential
to ensure resident safety for those in the building and the surrounding block, and that County and
City teams should proactively mitigate concerns as they arise.
In response to Board Member Joseph Magazine, Legal Counsel Shahrzad Emami (for MBCDC)
stated she has served the CDC pro bono for over ten years and is assisting in the assets’ transfer to
Miami-Dade County. She said all projects in the portfolio carry affordability covenants, including this
property, and that funding sources vary (HUD and State programs). She stated this building includes
HOME funding, a Federal subsidy that flows from HUD to the State and then to participating
jurisdictions such as the City of Miami Beach, which receives annual allocations that are invested in
affordable-housing projects.
Board Member Magazine stated that the area faces a Citywide affordability crisis across income
levels, especially for working families, noting reports that Miami has become more expensive than
New York. He said this is a working neighborhood where families, two-parent households, and single
mothers try to make ends meet. He stated that if the development were not government-owned, it
would revert to market-rate housing serving working-class families; instead, he said, the City is paying
to house formerly homeless individuals there, removing units from working residents. He asked
whether the program places individuals directly from the street into housing without intermediate steps
and asserted that doing so in the middle of a working-class neighborhood is incompatible and has
led to safety incidents. He stated this approach is unacceptable, and criticized taking housing “offline”
from working families, many of whom did not originate from Miami Beach, while paying to place
formerly homeless individuals in those units.
Legal Counsel Emami, representing MBCDC, stated that she has worked as an affordable-housing
attorney and advocate for twenty-five years and teaches Affordable Housing Law at the University of
Miami. She stated that she knows the subject area thoroughly and understands Board Member
Magazine’s concerns about the building’s location and the possibility of serving a different population.
She explained that if the building were converted to market-rate housing, single working mothers
would not be able to afford to live there because rents in that area of Miami Beach are too high for
most families.
Board Member Joseph Magazine stated that Flamingo Park contains similar market-rate housing
where single mothers raise their children. He said the overwhelming majority of Flamingo Park
housing is not luxury housing but organically serves the working class, and noted that a colleague
seated beside him lives there as a single parent raising her children. He stated it is inaccurate to claim
that single working mothers could not afford market-rate housing in the neighborhood, and asserted
that this type of housing is what is being taken offline. He explained that every unit removed from the
market increases the cost of housing for working families, citing basic supply-and-demand
economics. He stated that if formerly homeless residents are placed directly from the street into units
within a working-class neighborhood, without intermediate steps, surrounding units become more
expensive and the neighborhood dynamic becomes incompatible.
Board Member Alex Fernandez stated that the City has a population in need of housing funded by
public dollars, with restrictive covenants governing affordability levels and eligible populations,
including those at 30% AMI and formerly homeless individuals. He said the challenge is not who is
being housed but the lack of wraparound services. He explained that both elderly and formerly
homeless residents need case-management support to ensure stability, and without it, problems
eventually reach City offices or result in incidents such as those described. He asked whether, on a
temporary basis, case-management support could be explored until the City, County, and Board
Member Vicki L. Lopez determine how to provide wraparound services more permanently. He added
that, especially at 30% AMI, the residents are often elderly, and the lack of services presents
significant challenges.
Director of Housing and Community Services Alba Tarre explained that placements into these units
are made by the Miami-Dade County Homeless Trust. She stated that when the City contributed
HOME and RDA funds years ago, the City did not impose restrictions requiring homeless placements.
Those restrictions arose later because of additional funding sources added to the project by the
County, not the City.
Housing and Community Development Asset Manager Alexandro Bolaños stated that the Homeless
Trust component was added in 2014 as a ten-year agreement, which has matured and now operates
on an annual renewal cycle. He explained that the agreement expired in 2024 and is renewed
annually because they are not in a position to remove tenants. He stated that the funding is federal
HUD funding administered through the Miami Beach Housing Authority, and because rents are low,
the Housing Authority continues to support those placements.
Addressing Board Member Fernandez’s concerns, Director Tarre stated that the City invested HOME
dollars in 2011, setting a thirty-year affordability covenant for households up to 80% AMI. She
emphasized that the City’s intention was affordable housing, not homeless housing, and that the
homeless component was introduced later through County funding sources. She stated that the units
were originally managed by MBCDC and now managed by the County, but the vouchers driving these
placements come from the Homeless Trust and the Miami Beach Housing Authority.
